Bindings and the edges from derived entries to their observations form the dependency graph over which invalidation propagates.

observation capture

The resource boundary on a tool’s return path that limits the bytes, memory, storage, and time spent receiving output. It is distinct from context staging, which limits what the next model call receives.

observation crossing

The error of inserting a late result into an obsolete turn as though it had been available when the model made its next decision. It confuses the history of an operation with the evidence admitted to a particular continuation.

observation eligibility

The permission for a tool response to enter the current continuation’s next model context. A call can lose eligibility, through timeout, pause, cancellation, or plan revision, while its external outcome remains unresolved and its operation stays in the operation table.

observation loss masking

Excluding supplied observations from direct token-prediction loss while retaining the permitted context needed to train selected policy responses. Policy authorship alone does not make a token a desired target, and masked context can still affect gradients through later predictions.

on-policy data

Training examples drawn from the state distribution of the policy being trained.

opaque handle

A runtime-issued, typed reference to stored bytes that a tool argument can name without the bytes entering model context. The data’s restrictions travel with the handle, and resolving it must apply the same release policy as the bytes themselves.

operation ID

An identifier for one intended effect, preserved across the transport attempts that carry it, while each request and reply pair has its own attempt ID. A deliberately repeated request needs a new operation ID even when its arguments are identical.

operation table

The part of the trajectory record that retains each logical operation’s identity, its transport attempts, the evidence received for it, and the component responsible for settling it. Withdrawing a call’s observation eligibility does not remove its entry.

optimistic concurrency control (OCC)

A concurrency scheme that lets work proceed privately and validates the conditions required for publication afterward. It exposes parallelism at the price of revalidation and discarded work.

orphaned resource

A resource that is allocated and billed with no owner, typically because a delayed creation arrived after its operation was closed on an empty lookup.

outbox

A durable collection of requests awaiting delivery. Recording an outcome and inserting its notification into the outbox in one local transaction keeps a crash from preserving the outcome while losing the notification obligation.

outcome check

A check that assesses a completed candidate against a criterion, such as whether a repaired service passes a regression test.

outcome reward model

A learned model that predicts a score for a completed candidate, as trained verifiers do when ranking sampled solutions. It assigns feedback to the outcome, though it may inspect the full reasoning trajectory as well as the final answer.

output headroom

The generation allowance reserved within the context window for a call’s output. A request is admissible only if its represented input plus this reserve fits in the window.

outstanding liability

The reserved amount still backing unsettled operations at a reporting cutoff. Reports separate it from settled spending, which is only a floor on the task’s price.

title: Glossary
text:
paged KV block table

A per-sequence software mapping from logical token blocks to the physical KV blocks that store their key and value entries, so a sequence can grow by acquiring another block without relocating its existing blocks.

parameter-efficient fine-tuning

Fine-tuning that freezes the base model and trains a small added parameter set, an adapter, released alongside it.

parametric recall error

The fraction of proposed tool calls that use an argument name from the training schemas that the current schema does not contain, a sign the model recalled an interface instead of following the delivered one.

Pareto improvement

A change in which at least one component of an oriented metric vector improves and none worsens. It is a stronger progress condition than counting any single improved metric.

pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\)

The probability that at least one of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) runs of the same task passes a specified criterion, averaged over the stated task distribution. It measures candidate availability; the deployed selector may fail to return the passing candidate. The usual formula assumes independent, identically distributed runs conditional on the task.

pass\(^\IndependentAttemptCount\)

The probability that all \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) runs of the same task pass a specified criterion, averaged over the stated task distribution. Under conditionally independent runs it measures same-task consistency, which differs from all-success probability across independently drawn new tasks.

paused-state policy

The serving system’s choice of what to do with a request’s attention state while its trajectory waits, for example on a tool: keep it on the accelerator, move it elsewhere, or drop it and reconstruct it when needed. It trades accelerator capacity against storage, transfer, and recomputation at resumption.

pessimistic lease

Ownership of a resource acquired before a worker acts, so a conflicting worker waits instead of discarding work, at the price of serializing every holder. It suits resources whose effects cannot be branched and discarded.

phantom effect

An external effect with no recoverable intent under the runtime’s declared failure model. Preventing it requires recording intent before dispatch and storage that survives the failures the design claims to tolerate.

pipe deadlock

A circular wait between two bounded pipes, as when a host and child process each block writing to a full pipe while waiting for the other to read. The fix is structural: service reads and writes from one readiness loop, or dedicate a reader to each output channel.

pivot action

The designated commitment in a bounded region of a plan after which restoring the region’s precommitment conditions is no longer an available recovery strategy. Required approval and current admission checks precede its dispatch, and follow-up duties can remain afterward.

policy

A distribution over the model’s next response given the interaction history delivered through that decision, with trainable parameters. It acts only through the constructed model input, not through direct access to the full environment state.

policy distillation

Training that transfers behavior from a teacher configuration into a student, usually to make that behavior cheaper at deployment. The teacher can differ in model, prompt, or search budget, and its outputs pass the same target admission as any other candidate.

policy staleness

The gap between the policy version that sampled a record and the version that learns from it, which arises when collection and training overlap.

preference comparison

Compatible alternatives placed under a common context with a justified preference attached. Two runs form a valid pair only when their starting information, available actions, and criterion coverage match, and a failure takes the rejected slot only when its assessment says what was wrong.

prefill

The phase of a model call that processes the prompt. All prompt tokens share one read of the weights, so prefill is limited by arithmetic and costs far less time per token than decode.

prefill-decode disaggregation

Assigning the prefill and decode phases of requests to different workers so that each phase’s resources and parallelism can be chosen separately. It requires handing attention state from the prefill worker to the decode worker, and it composes with chunked prefill.

prefix cache

The serving system’s index of retained KV state, keyed by exact token prefix and computation configuration, from which a later request with the same beginning attaches state instead of prefilling it. The saving recurs at every turn whose prefix survives, and a hit confirms matching tokens and configuration, not that the information they encode is current.

prefix-cache timing channel

A side channel opened when a service permits prefix-cache reuse across security domains: an attacker who submits candidate prefixes and observes response timing learns which matching state is resident, without the model following any instruction.

prefix hit rate

The token-weighted fraction of prompt tokens, over a specified set of requests, whose compatible KV state is actually reused rather than recomputed, after availability, permission, and block-boundary restrictions. Potential token matches overstate it.

premature fine-tuning

Fine-tuning a model to compensate for a defect, such as a missing fact or an ambiguous schema, that a cheaper intervention would remove. It spends the most expensive remedy on the intervention ladder where a lower rung suffices.

probability ratio

The probability the current policy assigns to a recorded token divided by the probability the behavior policy assigned to it at the same delivered prefix, both under the declared sampling convention.

process group

On a POSIX host, the set of processes that one signal to the group reaches. Giving a job its own process group lets cancellation signal the descendants that remain in that group; detached processes need a separate containment mechanism.

process reward model (PRM)

A learned scorer that assigns a value to each intermediate step of a candidate trajectory, conditioned on the task and the preceding steps. Its step scores let search prune a branch before it spends a full candidate’s budget, and a low score is fallible evidence.

process supervision

Assigning feedback to intermediate reasoning steps rather than to final outcomes. See also process reward model (PRM).

product quantization

A vector compression method that splits each vector’s dimensions into subvectors and stores each subvector as the one-byte index of its nearest centroid in a per-subspace codebook. Queries stay in full precision and compute approximate distances from a precomputed lookup table; combined with coarse partitioning into cells it forms IVF-PQ.

prompt injection

Attacker-controlled content that attempts to redirect the model’s behavior away from the authorized task. Its entry point decides how much authority it can reach.

proposal

Model output that names an action or an answer the runtime may adopt. It carries no effect and no authority until the runtime validates, authorizes, and executes it.

protected field

A field that a compaction pass must retain, checked against the source before the working context is replaced, such as tested artifact identities, the failed assertion, check status, and task constraints.

proximal policy optimization (PPO)

A policy-gradient method that learns a value function, shared with the policy or held in a separate critic, as its baseline and uses a clipped surrogate objective to limit the incentive for probability-ratio changes. It can use either an external check or a learned reward model.

title: Glossary
text:
quarantined reader

A model invocation with a separate input context and a restricted result contract that extracts from selected untrusted material without authority to execute its instructions. The planner receives the admitted extraction rather than the raw material, and the runtime still authorizes every proposed action.

quarantining rule

The rule that a payload whose invocation status is anything other than completed may not be released as a completed candidate for action or task acceptance. The runtime may keep the fragment for diagnosis, but inspection cannot authorize it or reclassify it as complete.

title: Glossary
text:
radix prefix cache

A prefix cache that indexes token sequences with a compressed prefix tree whose edges may span several tokens. Following matching edges from the root finds the longest cached prefix and its KV storage, so a new request processes only the remaining tokens.

raw-payload handle

A reference to a retained record, such as a full test log, that an authorized tool can fetch subject to retention, permissions, and tool access. It places a route to the record in the model’s input rather than the record’s contents.

read-your-writes consistency

A session guarantee under which a reader always observes its own earlier writes, for example by having a query carry the minimum log position a replica must have applied before answering.

reasoning budget

A limit, set in the call surface, on how many tokens a reasoning model may spend thinking before it answers.

reasoning model

A model trained with reinforcement learning on tasks whose answers can be checked, so that it produces long intermediate traces that propose, check, and backtrack within one generation. Its reasoning tokens are metered output tokens, and it cannot observe results of checks it never ran.

reciprocal rank fusion (RRF)

A method for combining ranked retrieval lists by summing \(1/(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant+\FusionInputRank)\) over lists containing an item, where \(\FusionInputRank\) is its one-based rank and \(\RankFusionSmoothingConstant>0\) is a smoothing parameter. Absence from a truncated list contributes zero. Fusion avoids directly combining incompatible raw scores; it does not establish the relevance or correctness of the result.

reconciliation

An authorized, bounded query about the effect of an operation whose outcome is uncertain, used to settle it when the endpoint lacks a usable deduplication contract. An operation-specific receipt is stronger evidence than an observation that the desired state currently holds, since another actor may have produced that state.

recovery demonstration

A curated record or selected segment that pairs evidence of a mistake, fault, or incomplete observation with a response assessed as appropriate under the task’s criteria and current authority. The response may diagnose, correct, wait, or hand off; admission does not endorse every recorded action or require completion of the original task.

reference monitor

The enforcement component through which every access to a protected resource passes; it must be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to verify. In an agent runtime, the host’s validation and authorization path is the reference monitor for proposed tool calls.

reference policy

A frozen policy, usually the starting checkpoint, used as a regularizer that penalizes drift away from it. It is distinct from the behavior policy that generated the current rollouts.

reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR)

Policy optimization using rewards computed by automated checks of specified properties of outputs or interactions, such as tests or proof checkers. An automated verdict is evidence about its checked property, not a complete specification of task success or a substitute for runtime enforcement.

rejection-sampling fine-tuning

Fine-tuning on sampled outputs selected because they pass a check. The check selects an output under its criterion; which intermediate steps deserve imitation still requires target review.

repair episode

The unit a runtime bounds when repairing a failure: it has an identity, the task and candidate versions it concerns, an attempt counter, and an explicit allowance. The counter increments at admission rather than on success, so failed or interrupted work cannot escape the limit.

replay

Execution against recorded inputs at a stated boundary with live effects disabled. Folding recorded decisions reconstructs a projection; rerunning harness logic against captured inputs tests its behavior and can reveal differences or capture limits.

request compression ratio

The serialized token count of a reference request built from the available history without compaction, divided by that of the request an evaluated policy builds, with both counted with the same tokenizer. It is a representation ratio, not a quality metric.

required-field retention

An audit metric for compacted context: the number of required items represented correctly, in value and scope, divided by the number of required items assessed. The mere presence of a field with the right name does not count.

reset contract

A statement of the conditions under which an execution environment may serve a new lease and the state a reset must cover. That state extends beyond the workspace directory to background processes, open connections, modified runtime state, and pending work in host services.

residency tax

The factor \(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\) by which a retained tool wait divides the memory-bound rate of turns, since a kept KV slot is paid for over the whole wait as well as generation. The ratio of wait to generation, not the wait alone, decides whether keeping state is affordable.

resident-fit bound

The number of sequences whose KV payload fits in the KV pool at once.

resource footprint

The declared set of state that one tool call reads and writes. If neither of two calls writes anything the other reads or writes, the pair can be dispatched concurrently, but only as far as the declarations are trustworthy; shared state a footprint omits voids the condition.

restart intensity

A bound on the number of child restarts within a declared window, beyond which a repeatedly failing child becomes an escalated failure of its supervisor rather than an unbounded retry loop.

resume

The protocol for continuing a trajectory after interruption: establish current ownership, reconstruct compatible state from available authoritative history and artifacts, account for outstanding operations and charges, and recheck authority and dependencies before admitting new work.

retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

The pattern of supplying retrieved external material with a model request. In pre-staged use the runtime retrieves before the call; contrast agentic retrieval, in which the model issues searches during the loop.

retrieval contract

The specification of a read from durable storage: the information requested, the permitted scope and resource limits of the read, and the provenance, applicability, and completion information returned with its results. It makes a bounded result interpretable before it enters a model call, so an empty or truncated response is not mistaken for absence.

return

The total reward a rollout accumulates; with only a terminal score and no discounting, it equals that score. The learning objective is its expectation under the policy.

revalidation

Obtaining fresh evidence that a stored record still applies. Retrieving or using a record is not reconfirmation, so creation, last access, and last confirmation times are kept as separate fields.

revisable candidate plan

A record of proposed work and the evidence supporting each part, not of operations already performed, so the runtime can regenerate only the parts whose support has changed. Revised parts still face the same checks.

reward

A numerical signal assigned to a rollout under a stated rule. In the simplest case it is a single terminal score with no intermediate rewards.

reward hacking

A policy raising its measured reward through behavior that does not accomplish the task the reward was meant to measure, by exploiting gaps in what the reward checks or by reaching and altering the mechanism that computes it.

role confusion

A failure in which a model trained to predict the text that follows a tool call continues past its own call with an invented result instead of yielding the turn. The runtime rejects such a turn, because generated text is model output rather than an observation.

rollout

One sampled trajectory recorded under identified task, policy, environment, and harness conditions. Each fresh rollout needs its own candidate and assessment records.

rollout fixture

A versioned task, paired with a grading specification, that supplies fresh interactions during reward-based learning. The grading specification states what the reward measures.

rollout reset

Restoring a fixture’s declared initial conditions before a new rollout, which can include processes, cached files, service state, credentials, and pending external operations, not merely an empty directory. A local snapshot restores only local state.

runaway retry loop

A trajectory that keeps proposing well-formed variants and diagnostics after failures, passing every per-call limit and fair-share check while consuming resources without moving the task toward acceptance. Only a bound on the whole trajectory, enforced outside the model, guarantees that it ends.

runtime

The deterministic software around the model, often called the harness, that decides whether each proposed action is permitted and dispatches it through a tool. Permission stays with the runtime; generating the name of an operation grants the model nothing.

title: Glossary
text:
saga

A structure for long-lived transactions that gives up isolation across the whole sequence, commits each step separately, and pairs each step with a compensating step.

satisficing

A stopping objective that seeks the first result meeting stated acceptance criteria and stops searching once a candidate meets the required evidence standard and any approval conditions.

scheduling charge

The declared unit a fair scheduler deducts when it admits a model call. A conservative form charges the call’s full input-token count plus its allowed output-token count, measuring admitted token allowance rather than actual output, cost, or task value.

schema augmentation

Creating related training examples under declared interface changes, updating everything needed to keep each target valid in its new context. Each result is a derived example whose lineage and use are reviewed.

schema-following accuracy

The fraction of proposed tool calls that name a declared tool and whose keys and value types satisfy that tool’s current schema.

scope rule

The rule that an observation or record supports claims only about the artifact versions and conditions it recorded, and no broader one. Every later transformation, such as compaction, summarization, or invalidation, must preserve it.

sealed test

A test whose protected contents and execution are outside the candidate’s permitted access. This protection limits direct inspection or modification but does not establish complete task coverage, grader correctness, or statistical independence.

self-consistency

Selecting among sampled candidates by majority vote over their final answers. It works when answers are short and comparable and fails when candidates share the same error.

semantic compensation

A new operation intended to establish declared application postconditions after an earlier effect. Its success requires scoped outcome evidence; it need not restore prior history, charges, or every observed state, and it can leave residual duties.

semantic memory

Stored generalizations abstracted from specific events. In an agent the semantic record is always derived, and its support is the episodic record beneath it.

semantic watchdog

A runtime policy that uses task-relevant observations, such as repeated captured state, stagnant verification results, or repeated actions and outcomes, to flag possible nonprogress and choose a bounded intervention. Its signals are fallible evidence; what the runtime enforces is the hold on further work.

sequence packing

Placing variable-length training examples in shared buffers while preserving their intended attention boundaries, position conventions, prediction targets, and loss aggregation. Reduced padding does not by itself establish equivalent predictions or a particular speedup.

sequential probability ratio test (SPRT)

A sequential test that accumulates a log-likelihood ratio between two specified hypotheses as outcomes arrive and stops when the ratio crosses one of two declared boundaries. Declaring this use of accumulating evidence in advance avoids the inflated false-positive rate of repeatedly applying a fixed-sample test.

service principal

An identity for the automation service itself, as distinct from a user on whose behalf it may act. Either kind of identity can carry narrow or broad permissions.

settlement

Establishing an uncertain operation’s effect status from evidence or an enforced endpoint contract. If the available checks cannot resolve it, the runtime preserves the unknown outcome and withholds unsafe repetition rather than treating a key or probe as proof.

settlement identity

The durable key under which one final charge is recorded in the budget account, so repeated delivery of the same usage evidence updates the account at most once. A reused identity with a different amount is a reconciliation fault.

shadow execution

A release stage that tests a candidate against authorized copies of current inputs without assigning it the live task. See also canary release.

shared blackboard

A coordination arrangement in which workers claim tasks and publish versioned artifacts through a shared store, so coordination moves into shared task and artifact state. It still requires enforcing claim ownership, publication rules, and dependency validity.

shared-kernel container

An isolation envelope that confines host processes with configured operating-system controls: namespaces restrict views, access controls and system-call filters restrict operations, and resource controllers bound consumption. The host kernel still handles permitted calls, so it is only as strong as that kernel and its configuration.

sharing domain

The set of callers permitted to benefit from one another’s cached prefixes. Restricting reuse to it closes cross-domain prefix-cache timing channels, at the cost of fewer reuse opportunities.

shingle

A local feature used to compare records for near-duplicates, such as a short token sequence or a bounded subtree of parsed code.

source generation

A version identity for a source’s state, assigned under the source’s update contract and stronger than a filesystem modification timestamp. Derived index entries record the generation they came from, so current-state queries can reject entries from superseded generations.

source of record

The designated evidence source against which a particular claim is checked, such as a repository for a file’s contents at a revision or a recorded user statement for that user’s preference. The designation fixes where a claim is checked and confers no authority or permission.

span (tracing)

A record of one observed operation, with an identity, start and end boundaries, attributes, and optional timed events. Parent relationships express nesting, and links connect asynchronous work that does not fit one nested lifetime.

specification boundary

The distinction between proposing a task contract and adopting it as binding. Models can assist requirements, designs, and tests; authorized principals adopt goals, grants, acceptance criteria, and revisions, and own the residual duties after acceptance.

speculative decoding

A serving method that uses draft proposals and a target-model acceptance rule. Distribution-preserving variants retain the target distribution under their algorithmic assumptions; net latency and cost depend on accepted prefixes, verification work, batching, and load.

spending alarm

A retrospective monitor on the charge rate over a trailing window. It can trigger investigation or a hold on new work, but the spending it measures has already happened.

split leakage

Information about an evaluation target reaching training through a related record, such as another solution to the same underlying task placed on the training side of a split.

stale-policy window

The interval, under cached authorization, in which a newly revoked grant may still be accepted. Its bound must cover cache age, renewal, expiry, and clock assumptions and must hold through a partition.

stale-return rate

The fraction of evaluated current-state queries that return any record made inapplicable by a relevant source change, with historical queries reported separately. An empty response scores zero, so the rate is always reported beside evidence coverage.

stale-support rate

The fraction of decisions requiring current evidence that treat superseded support as current. A historical reference to an older state is not an error; using it to assert a property of the current state without support is.

standby reserve

A pool of clean, unassigned execution instances, also called a warm pool. Admission consumes one and binds it to a task; provisioning replenishes it, and an ended lease rejoins only after its reset contract is satisfied.

state-delta verification

Checking specified properties of an observed change between declared initial and resulting environment states, using measurements tied to the relevant versions and task criteria. It distinguishes a claimed repair from an observed change that meets the selected checks.

stateless cursor

A pagination token that carries its own position, such as a query digest, last key returned, and issue time, together with a message authentication code only the tool can produce. Abandoning it costs the server nothing, at the price of reading current rather than snapshot data and a longer token.

static plan

A plan that declares its possible stages and dependencies, including conditional branches and bounded retries, before execution, so its handoffs are inspectable and a worst-case resource bound can follow.

static reservation

A KV allocation policy that reserves a contiguous buffer for the configured token cap when a request is admitted. The request grows without reallocating, but the unused remainder stays unavailable to every other request for as long as the reservation lives.

stochastic computer

The single map, drawn once in the introduction, that relates the parts of an agentic system to the parts of a computer: the model to a processor, context and stores to memory, tools to input and output, the runtime to an operating system. It is a map for orientation, not a mechanism.

stop reason

The service’s report, retained in a model response, of why generation yielded control, such as a finished turn, emitted tool calls, the output limit, or a stop sequence. The runtime keeps it as raw evidence alongside the normalized status it derives.

storage invalidation

The exclusion of a derived record, such as an index entry, vector, summary, or cached result, from current-state retrieval once a relevant change to its source makes it inapplicable, independent of when a replacement is built.

streaming

Delivery of response content before generation finishes. A delivery chunk may carry part of a token, several tokens, or a protocol event, so a runtime follows the service’s framing contract rather than equating chunks with tokens.

streaming cancellation

A harness request that asks the serving service to stop generating a reply in progress, closes the invocation’s eligibility to produce an actionable candidate, and retains partial content only for bounded diagnosis. A canceled or truncated payload cannot become a dispatchable call.

structural retrieval

Retrieval over program structure rather than text, distinguishing an enclosing function, a declaration, and an identifier used in an expression. A parser supplies the syntax tree and source spans, and symbol resolution or further analysis adds relationships between definitions and references.

structured progress record

A continuation record that preserves a trajectory’s state in named fields, such as current task requirements, relevant observations, hypotheses, artifact identities, and unfinished work, so the next call can continue after the detailed history leaves the prompt. It is not an execution checkpoint.

subgraph resynthesis

A revision tier that replaces an artifact and all its descendants, asking the model to bridge from the still-supported frontier to the downstream requirements that remain unchanged.

supersession

Replacing a stored record with a new version for the same subject and scope while marking the old version superseded, which ends its eligibility for current decisions but keeps it as history.

supervised fine-tuning (SFT)

Adjusting trainable model parameters to increase the likelihood of selected target tokens under their supplied prefixes. Training an agent this way inherits both a target-selection contract and a conditioning contract.

supervision tree

The structure that assigns responsibility for child lifetimes and outstanding work among agents.

supervisor-worker topology

A coordination arrangement, also called orchestrator-worker, in which one coordinator decomposes the task, dispatches children, and integrates their receipts.

system-call tax

The per-call cost an isolation envelope adds to a mediated system call, up to three terms: crossing a privilege boundary, checking or emulating the request, and handing control to another thread or process.

title: Glossary
text:
tail sampling

Choosing which detailed traces to retain using evidence accumulated later, such as a failed acceptance check or an unusually costly run. It concentrates diagnostic storage on important cases, so the retained collection is deliberately unrepresentative of ordinary traffic.

tail waste

The uninitialized slots in a sequence’s final KV block. With \(\KvBlockSize\) tokens per block it ranges from zero to \(\KvBlockSize-1\), and a length divisible by \(\KvBlockSize\) wastes nothing.

taint tracking

Runtime tracking of data origins and dependencies through transformations, used to enforce policy at later uses. Integrity provenance and confidentiality answer different questions; through a model, conservative propagation records a policy assumption rather than proven semantic causation.

task account

The account of an initiated task that includes all its attempts and delegated branches once, plus its share of capacity and operations costs. Failed or canceled branches stay in the account after their output is discarded.

task contract

The five-part specification of a delegated task: its goal with negative scope, the environment, the permitted actions, the available observations, and the completion criteria at a stated evidence level.

task fixture

A versioned package of the initial state and dependencies needed to instantiate a task, such as a starting repository, dependency versions, service behavior, and permitted data. It sets the conditions of an attempt; separate acceptance criteria judge the result.

task group

The repeated attempts, paraphrases, derived fixtures, and solution-equivalent variants of one underlying problem, grouped so they are treated as one task. The group records the basis on which its members were judged equivalent.

teacher forcing

Predicting each selected token from the recorded preceding tokens, including earlier selected responses, rather than from a freshly sampled continuation.

temperature

A positive sampling parameter that divides the logits before softmax. Lower temperature concentrates probability on higher-scoring tokens and higher temperature flattens the distribution; it carries no information about whether an answer is correct.

temporal-difference residual

The sampled one-step quantity \(\TemporalDifferenceResidual_k = \TurnReward_k + \PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_{k+1}) - \PolicyRemainingReturn(\InteractionHistory_k)\), whose conditional expectation equals the advantage when the value function is exact. One residual is a single noisy sample, and estimated values add further error.

test-tampering defense

Controls protecting designated acceptance logic and evidence from modification or interference by the agent and its submitted artifacts. Read-only test files are one control, not a complete grader-protection boundary.

test-time compute

Inference computation spent on a single decision beyond one model call, through longer reasoning, additional candidates, or check-and-revise rounds, before the runtime admits a result.

test-time compute budget

The per-decision allowance of processed and generated tokens, model calls, checks, and elapsed time that a runtime may spend, with the model’s weights fixed, before it must select a candidate, abstain, or escalate. An exhausted budget is not evidence that the best remaining candidate is acceptable.

test-time deliberation rollout

One bounded candidate-generation path within a decision, possibly including checks and revisions conditioned on observations, produced with the model’s weights fixed.

threat model

A statement of what the attacker controls, what must remain protected, how the controlled material enters the task, and what outcome counts as a violation. A list of attack names fixes neither the boundary nor the success criterion.

time per output token (TPOT)

The average interval between generated tokens after the first in a streamed model response.

time to first token (TTFT)

The client-observed interval from sending a model request to receiving its first generated token. It includes queueing and transport as well as the prefill pass that produces that token’s distribution.

time-to-live (TTL)

A policy that sets an age after which the runtime requests a refresh of an observation. It is a refresh heuristic chosen for the task’s change rate and cost of error, not a validity test, since a younger observation may already be outdated and an older one may still be current.

time-travel replay

Reconstructing supported recorded state at a retained historical boundary from compatible checkpoints, history, and required artifacts. Its scope depends on capture and retention; it does not recreate arbitrary past external-world state.

token averaging

A loss normalization that assigns equal coefficients to every selected target token’s loss. Context and padding tokens are never counted.

token budget

The per-iteration limit on token positions a chunked-prefill scheduler admits, where each decode request contributes one position and each prefill chunk contributes its length. It bounds work per iteration, not time, so it must be calibrated against measured gaps between output tokens.

token entropy

The entropy of a specified next-token distribution at a delivered prefix, measuring uncertainty over the vocabulary. Reports must state whether it is the model’s distribution or the sampler’s after temperature, filtering, and constraints.

tokenizer

A component that maps text into identifiers from a finite vocabulary. A token may be a word, part of a word, whitespace, punctuation, or a combination, so token boundaries need not match the boundaries of an identifier or a JSON field.

tombstone

A durable exclusion marker that suppresses retrieval of a record, or of every record from a source generation, before physical cleanup finishes. It records ineligibility, not erasure.

tool

An interface to an operation in the environment, such as reading a file, applying a patch, or running a test. The model can only propose a tool call; the runtime decides whether it is dispatched.

tool-choice control

A serving-interface control that constrains whether the model proposes a tool call at all: it may allow an optional call, require a call, require one named tool, or forbid calls. Forcing a call shapes the proposal but authorizes nothing.

tool descriptor

The description of a tool operation that communicates its purpose, arguments, result, and relevant effect semantics. It helps the model choose and parameterize the operation; the runtime and endpoint enforce the contract.

tool-wait problem

Retained serving state held idle while a slow tool runs, forcing a choice between keeping, moving, or dropping that state before the next model call.

top-\(\TopTokenSampleCount\) sampling

A sampling restriction that keeps the \(\TopTokenSampleCount\) highest-scoring tokens, with a defined tie rule, and renormalizes their probabilities.

top-\(\NucleusProbabilityMass\) sampling

A sampling restriction, also called nucleus sampling, that keeps the shortest set of most probable tokens whose cumulative probability reaches a threshold \(\NucleusProbabilityMass\) and renormalizes it. Unlike top-\(\TopTokenSampleCount\), the number of tokens kept varies with the shape of the distribution.

torn dependency read

A hazard in which a worker observes an intermediate mixture of state, such as a changed interface whose callers are not yet updated, that no worker proposed.

trace

A graph of spans recording one trajectory’s model calls, tool calls, approvals, and child agents, with their durations, token counts, and outcomes, used to measure and attribute behavior rather than to recover it.

trajectory

The ordered sequence of recorded states, proposed actions, runtime decisions, and observations through which one delegated task proceeds, from its first context to its acceptance, stop, or escalation. It is the unit of engineering in agentic systems.

trajectory curation

Selecting, labeling, and transforming recorded interactions for a declared learning use while preserving the evidence and constraints that justify that use. Its output is a versioned artifact with specified consumers, not a collection of success labels.

trajectory goodput

Distinct task completions accepted under a declared contract per unit of elapsed observation time. Goodput per dollar instead divides accepted tasks by the full included cost, retaining failed and canceled work; it is the reciprocal of cost per accepted task when the relevant denominators are positive.

trajectory-level sticky routing

Assigning a configuration at the task or trajectory boundary and preserving it through continuation, retries, and resumed work, so one measured task never mixes baseline and candidate behavior. It is a stable configuration assignment, not a promise to keep one physical model instance.

trajectory log

The append-only, ordered sequence of typed events (delivered model inputs, returned replies, admissions, control changes, and observed tool outcomes) from which a deterministic reducer rebuilds a trajectory’s control state. Recorded claims are not automatically external truth.

trajectory record

The per-trajectory control state that the harness owns and the model cannot write directly: identity, lifecycle state and version, per-call limits, actual and reserved consumption, grants and leases, observation eligibility, unresolved effect obligations, and references to context, live plan, log, and workspace.

trajectory saga

A workflow that records its constituent actions and coordinates compensating actions when their established effects must be remediated, while preserving unresolved outcomes and dependencies. Compensation is registered before forward dispatch and follows dependencies and outcome evidence.

transaction isolation

The transaction property that specifies which concurrent observations and interleavings are permitted. Serializable isolation has the effect of some serial order but need not preserve real-time order.

trusted computing base

The set of components whose correct operation a claimed protection depends on. Changing the isolation envelope changes that set and the interfaces exposed to untrusted code.

turn

One step of a trajectory: one model call and the runtime’s handling of the action it proposes. The runtime’s record marks whether each proposed action was rejected, dispatched, or completed.

turn boundary

A local admission boundary before a model invocation or tool dispatch at which the harness checks whether continuation remains permitted. Reaching this boundary does not establish that earlier remote effects have ended.

two-phase commit

A protocol that coordinates one atomic commit decision among participating resource managers: each participant prepares and preserves recovery state, and a participant that votes to commit cannot then abort unilaterally. A prepared participant may block while it cannot learn the decision.

typed task envelope

A versioned child assignment binding task identity, input references, scoped authority, resource limits, completion requirements, and a bounded return format. The runtime enforces those bindings; schema validity alone establishes neither authority nor successful completion.

title: Glossary
text:
uncertain outcome

The recorded status of a dispatched operation whose effect the runtime can neither confirm nor exclude, because its reply was lost, late, or never produced. It stays unsettled until an endpoint deduplication contract, a reconciliation query, or an authorized decision establishes what happened.

universal scalability law (USL)

Gunther’s model of relative capacity for a fixed workload divided among \(\WorkerCount\) workers, \(\WorkerCount/(1+\ContentionCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)+\CoherencyCoefficient \WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1))\), where \(\ContentionCoefficient\) is the contention (serialized share) and \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) the coherency (pairwise reconciliation) cost. Nonzero coherency gives it a peak beyond which adding workers lowers capacity.

untrusted span

Text staged in a request whose origin the runtime can record but whose content it did not author and cannot vouch for. Encoding keeps the span in its field, yet the model may still follow an instruction it contains. See also indirect prompt injection.

usable working context

The context content, organization, and length with which a specified model and invocation configuration meet a chosen quality criterion on a stated workload. It is established only by evaluation and is usually much shorter than the nominal context capacity. See also nominal context capacity.

user-space kernel

An isolation envelope that interposes another implementation of the application’s operating-system interface, such as gVisor’s Sentry, in front of the host kernel. Applications depend on the interfaces it supports, and exposed resources still need their own constraints.

title: Glossary
text:
verification gap

The distance between the probability that at least one of \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) runs passes (pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\)) and the probability that all \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) pass (pass\(^\IndependentAttemptCount\)). A selector with a reliable checker can turn availability into one accepted delivery, but work that must pass every time it recurs gets only consistency.

verifier

A check whose criteria and observations the candidate under assessment cannot modify. Its role in acceptance depends on the task’s evidence contract, and passing one verifier is narrower than task acceptance.

verifier cascade

An ordered sequence of declared predicates that routes a recorded trajectory to a learning artifact, stopping that route at the first predicate that does not pass. Predicate order changes checking cost without changing the accepted set.

verifier-guided selection

A selection policy that returns a candidate only when a verifier, a check whose criteria and observations the candidate cannot modify, passes it, and abstains when no candidate passes.

verifier isolation

Protection of an assessment from both the running agent and the code the agent submits, so the agent cannot touch the verdict. Isolation settles who can alter the verdict, not whether the checks cover the intended task.

visible test

A test whose cases the agent can inspect. Visible tests are useful for diagnosis but also expose the examples a candidate can be fitted to. See also sealed test.

vocabulary mismatch

The problem that people describe the same thing with different words, so a query phrased by symptom may share no terms with the source that answers it. Identifier splitting, synonym expansion, query reformulation, or dense retrieval can recover some matches.

title: Glossary
text:
wait policy

The declared rule stating which tool results end a trajectory’s wait. The return to a ready state passes through a guarded transition that evaluates the policy again.

whole-trajectory cost

The total cost attributed to one execution attempt across its model calls, environment, assessment, and required finalization within a declared accounting boundary. Cost per accepted task aggregates it over a cohort’s attempts and divides by the distinct accepted tasks.

Wilson score interval

A confidence interval for a binomial rate that uses the hypothesized rate rather than the observed one in the variance. Unlike the Wald interval, it neither collapses to zero width when every outcome agrees nor extends below zero near the boundaries.

working-set decision

The runtime’s choice of which source excerpts, observations, constraints, and unresolved questions belong in the next model request, selecting the information that supports the next bounded step.

workspace lease

A binding of a workspace to its task, owner, permitted operations, and lifetime. It lets edits and selected caches persist across turns without making them available to the next tenant.

write-ahead logging

Durably recording an admitted request, with its authorized intent and admission state, before dispatching it. The durable history then identifies an operation that might have executed even if its reply never reaches the worker; inferring that a missing intent was never dispatched additionally requires the completeness rule.

write amplification

Bytes written per byte of new state. For full snapshots it arises from serializing unchanged state again at every checkpoint, so it grows with trajectory length, while delta checkpoints avoid it.

title: Glossary
text:
zero ambient authority

The property that the model itself holds no rights to read, change, or reach anything; every effect it proposes takes place only through a grant and a capability the runtime issues and enforces.

zero-contrast group

A completed group of rollouts whose rewards are all equal, so every group-relative advantage is zero and the reward term supplies no gradient. Equal rewards say nothing about how diverse the attempts were.

title: 1 Typed Tool Interfaces
text:
An agent’s tool interface must describe what a call means, reject invalid inputs, and expose enough outcome information for the runtime to continue safely. This appendix provides a bounded argument-schema example, endpoint-contract questions, and quantitative templates for decoding and catalog costs. It supports interface design and review without prescribing a framework or replacing the main text’s treatment of tool use and execution containment.


Select the section that matches the observed failure at the tool boundary. Each entry pairs the failure signature with the descriptor, schema, or result-envelope change that prevents it:

When calls fail validation or confuse units, section 1.1 supplies schema constraints and distinguishes them from execution obligations.
When malformed calls consume repair turns, section 1.2 compares their expected latency with the overhead of constrained decoding.
When retries risk duplicate effects or delegation changes authority, section 1.3 separates operation identity from capability enforcement.
When a catalog consumes context or causes selection errors, section 1.4 supplies accounting formulas and a comparison worksheet.




Writing “path must stay inside the workspace” in a tool description tells the model what to propose, but leaves an unvalidated ../ traversal free to pass unless the schema and runtime enforce the constraint. A tool schema has two readers, since the model uses its names and descriptions to propose arguments while the runtime validates the proposal before considering a grant (Tool Interface Schemas). Because a description communicates intent without enforcing it, the distinction between assertions and annotations in the JSON Schema validation specification (Wright et al. 2022) supports five checks on this boundary:

Wright, Austin, Henry Andrews, and Ben Hutton. 2022. JSON Schema Validation: A Vocabulary for Structural Validation of JSON. Internet-Draft draft-bhutton-json-schema-validation-01 (JSON Schema 2020-12).

Close each fixed argument object with additionalProperties: false, so the validator rejects undeclared fields rather than silently forwarding them. A constrained decoder can enforce the same restriction only when its supported schema subset includes it.
Put mandatory fields in required. An optional field needs explicit absence semantics; the default annotation does not insert a missing value during validation (JSON Schema, n.d.). Any defaulting step is part of the runtime’s argument-normalization contract.
Bound input size as well as type. Use finite maxLength limits for strings and maxItems limits for arrays, including bounded elements and nesting; constrain numeric values with appropriate minimum and maximum limits. A pattern restricts size only if the pattern itself imposes a finite length bound. Enforce request-byte and parser limits before schema validation, since a validator cannot undo an oversized allocation.
State units and conventions in field names and descriptions. A name such as timeout_ms reduces ambiguity, but a range check cannot detect that a plausible number was intended in seconds. Conversion and interpretation must agree across the caller, adapter, and implementation.
For object variants, prefer a required tag with a distinct const value in each branch when it clarifies the operation. A tag is a design aid, not a prerequisite for validation: anyOf accepts one or more matching branches, while oneOf requires exactly one (JSON Schema, n.d.). The selected decoder and validator must support the chosen construction.

Descriptors may also state side effects and repeat behavior. These are separate from authority: a read can disclose sensitive information, an idempotent update can be unauthorized, and a permitted mutation may still be unsafe to repeat. Runtime policy and the endpoint’s implemented contract determine approval and retry handling, not an annotation alone (Tool Interface Schemas).


An exact-replacement file tool can express a small edit without requiring the model to reproduce the whole file, and the teaching descriptor in listing 1 bounds every variable-length argument with an explicit finite limit. Those limits are illustrative policy choices, not recommended universal values. The outer name, description, and parameters fields form a teaching descriptor, not a standardized tool protocol. The $schema declaration (JSON Schema, n.d.) belongs to the argument schema inside parameters; the runtime validates the proposed argument object against that schema, not against the outer descriptor.

JSON Schema. n.d. Understanding JSON Schema. JSON Schema documentation.



Listing 1: Bounded edit arguments: A teaching descriptor with a closed argument object and finite string limits; authorization and atomic mutation remain implementation obligations.


{
  "name": "file_edit",
  "description": "Replaces an exact block in an existing workspace file. Match counting uses the original file and non-overlapping matches. Zero matches fail; multiple matches fail unless allow_multiple is true. Match-check failure leaves the file unchanged.",
  "parameters": {
    "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "path": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Absolute path to the target file, inside the workspace root.",
        "pattern": "^/([a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+/)*[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+$",
        "maxLength": 1024
      },
      "old_str": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The exact block to replace, including indentation and newlines.",
        "minLength": 1,
        "maxLength": 16384
      },
      "new_str": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The replacement text. May be empty to delete old_str.",
        "maxLength": 16384
      },
      "allow_multiple": {
        "type": "boolean",
        "description": "If true, replace every non-overlapping match in the original file; if false, fail unless exactly one match exists."
      }
    },
    "required": ["path", "old_str", "new_str", "allow_multiple"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  }
}



The required Boolean makes repeat-match intent explicit; a descriptor with an optional Boolean would instead need a documented normalization rule. JSON Schema measures maxLength in characters, not serialized bytes or model tokens. The request transport therefore needs its own byte bound, while context construction needs its own token accounting. Replacement size also differs from result-file size: repeated replacements can expand a file beyond either string bound.
The implementation must enforce the advertised match behavior and workspace boundary: because a path pattern does not establish confinement and checking a unique match before an uncoordinated write does not prevent a concurrent change, the endpoint must resolve and authorize the actual target, enforce the match precondition together with the mutation, and bound both the resulting file and the returned observation. Even then, a missing response still requires the operation-identity contract below, because a schema cannot establish whether an edit committed.
Keep the published schema, normalization rules, and implementation version together. Generating a schema from a typed argument model can reduce transcription drift, but it does not prove that a decoder, validator, and implementation accept the same inputs. Contract tests should include missing required fields, extra fields, oversized strings, wrong types, and valid boundary values. Tests must also exercise advertised behavior outside the schema, including concurrent edits and uncertain outcomes.



Tools adapted from existing service interfaces often carry patterns that suit a programmer calling from code but mislead a model proposing from a description, so table 1 pairs each recurring schema defect with its hardened form and boundary effect.



Table 1: Tool Schema Anti-Patterns: Common schema patterns that mislead a model or defeat the validator, the hardened form of each, and its effect on the boundary.











Anti-pattern
What goes wrong
Hardened form
Effect




Untyped argument bag (args: dict)
Undeclared keys can pass through without field-level checks
Explicit typed fields with additionalProperties: false
The validator rejects undeclared fields; a supporting decoder can exclude them


Unbounded inputs (string with no limit)
One call carries an argument larger than the tool or the context can hold
maxLength, maxItems, and explicit windowing parameters
Argument size is bounded before dispatch


Ambiguous object variants
The model mixes fields that belong to different operations
A required tag with branch-specific constraints
Branch intent is explicit; validation still depends on the complete schema


Implicit units (timeout: 30)
Seconds, milliseconds, and minutes are confused
Units in the name (timeout_ms), range bounds, and agreed conversion
Meaning is documented; plausible wrong-unit values can still pass validation


Whole-file rewrite (content: str)
Output length grows with the file, risking truncation and unrelated changes
Exact replacement of a block (old_str, new_str)
Output length depends on the selected block and replacement






The last row can matter for latency when generated output lies on the critical path (The Cost of a Model Call). A whole-file rewrite pays decode time for every unchanged line, and Comparing Output Interfaces works an example in which the rewrite misses a per-call deadline that an anchored diff meets. Exact replacement has its own cost when the selected anchor is ambiguous or stale; the right representation depends on the edits the workload requires.




A model that samples freely can emit malformed arguments. Under a supported grammar and correct masking, a generation that reaches an accepting completion belongs to that grammar; truncation or interruption does not supply a complete valid call (Grammar-Guided Decoding, Finite-state constrained decoding). Decode-Loop Mechanics develops mask placement and storage. Here the narrower question is whether masking overhead is lower than the expected latency of one repair under a stipulated comparison.
Let a tool call carry \(\OutputLength\) output tokens at \(\PerTokenDecodeTime\) per token, let masking add \(\PerTokenMaskingTime\) per token, let \(\UnconstrainedParseFailureRate\) be the rate at which unconstrained calls fail to parse, and let a repair turn cost \(\RepairTurnLatency\) of latency, including the re-sent context and the regenerated call. The expected latency without constraints, allowing one repair, is
\[\mathbb{E}[\UnconstrainedCallLatency] = \OutputLength \, \PerTokenDecodeTime + \UnconstrainedParseFailureRate \, \RepairTurnLatency\]
and with constraints it is
\[\ConstrainedCallLatency = \OutputLength \, (\PerTokenDecodeTime + \PerTokenMaskingTime)\]
Setting the two equal gives the break-even error rate
\[\BreakEvenParseFailureRate = \frac{\OutputLength \, \PerTokenMaskingTime}{\RepairTurnLatency}\]
Under this model, constraining reduces expected latency when the malformation rate exceeds \(\BreakEvenParseFailureRate\). Measure the inputs for the actual model, schema, and prompt, and express both time terms in the same unit. The ratio is dimensionless. If it exceeds one, eliminating every parse failure would still not repay the stipulated mask overhead; if repair latency is zero, the ratio is undefined and the original latency expressions should be compared directly.
The comparison holds generated length and base decode cost fixed and includes at most one repair. It omits schema-compilation and setup costs; include those when they are not already amortized or shared. A policy that stops quickly after a failed repair may look faster while completing fewer tasks. Use the break-even only among candidates with comparable task quality and completion requirements, and measure residual malformed or interrupted outputs rather than assuming that every constrained call completes.
Even an accepting, syntactically valid call can name a nonexistent file, exceed the task’s authority, or request the wrong operation. Completion checks, validation, grants, and execution limits therefore remain necessary (Grammar-Guided Decoding).



Operation identity and authorization solve different problems. An idempotency key identifies an intended operation across attempts; safe deduplication depends on the endpoint’s effect and result contract (Retrying Uncertain Actions). A capability represents scoped authority whose enforcement is developed in Capabilities and Credentials. Neither artifact, by its presence alone, establishes that a call is safe.


Generating a fresh UUID inside a retry loop makes every network timeout look like a brand-new mutation to the receiving endpoint. Instead, the runtime must assign an identifier to the intended operation and retain it across retries and recovery. A fresh transport attempt can have a new call identifier while referring to the same operation. Conversely, two separately intended operations may have identical arguments and still need distinct identities. Deriving an identifier from recorded inputs or storing a generated identifier are both possible; either method requires enough durable state to recover the same identity after a crash.
The endpoint binds this identity to the authorized scope and request payload and rejects conflicting reuse. If canonical serialization is used to compare payloads, its rules must match at both ends. Identity does not authorize the request, and hashing arguments alone cannot distinguish an intentional second operation from a retry.



When a retried request arrives with the same operation ID, an endpoint that only returns “success” or “error” cannot tell the caller whether the first attempt is still running or failed partway through. A useful status model distinguishes an unseen operation, work in flight, a completed operation with a retained result, and an operation whose effect is in doubt. These states describe the required behavior, not a complete implementation:

Admission. Claim the operation under the endpoint’s concurrency and durability contract, checking scope and payload consistency.
In flight. A repeated request must not start an independent execution of the same effect. It can obtain status or wait under the endpoint’s defined limits.
Completed. A repeat returns the retained outcome under the service’s result-retention contract.
In doubt. Preserve uncertainty and reconcile it; do not release the operation for blind repetition merely because an exception occurred.

The difficult boundary lies between performing the effect and retaining its outcome. A host-side map that calls an external service and then writes COMPLETED leaves a crash gap. Closing it requires support that couples identity to the effect, such as a transaction within the effect-owning service or that service’s own deduplication contract. An expiring claim does not make an older executor unable to commit; any takeover must account for that executor.
The contract must also state how long operation identities and outcomes remain recognizable. After a deduplication record expires, an absent record may mean forgotten work rather than a never-issued operation. A retry beyond the retention window needs reconciliation or another endpoint guarantee; the identifier alone no longer establishes repeat safety.
A reconciliation probe supplies scoped evidence. Finding the pre-dispatch state does not prove that a delayed request cannot still act. If neither the endpoint contract nor terminal evidence establishes that repetition is safe, the operation remains unresolved and the runtime escalates or withholds the repeat (Retrying Uncertain Actions). Durable Execution develops preservation of intent and outcome across crashes; this appendix does not substitute a short cache implementation for that protocol.



An idempotency key prevents duplicate execution of the same request, but does not check whether the caller is allowed to touch the target object in the first place. The capability tuple \(\CapabilityGrant=(\GrantRights,\mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant,\GrantCondition,\GrantExpiryTime)\) in Capabilities and Credentials describes the rights \(\GrantRights\), objects \(\mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant\), condition predicate \(\GrantCondition\), and expiry time \(\GrantExpiryTime\) that govern access. A protected handle or verified token can represent the grant; the tuple alone is not its enforcement. The runtime binds each use to the task and caller, resolves the actual target within the permitted scope, and checks the operation and current conditions. A lexical path prefix does not establish confinement against indirection or concurrent changes.
For delegation, let \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\CapabilityGrant)\) denote the accesses a grant permits. A derived child must satisfy
\[\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant).\]
An issuer must authenticate the parent and validate the proposed narrowing before issuing a child. It must preserve associations between rights, objects, and conditions, not merely compare unrelated sets of names. Holding a narrower child does not revoke a broader parent. Several children must share the parent’s aggregate resource allowance rather than each receiving an independent copy of its budget (Capability Delegation).
Execution needs further controls beyond a predicate checked at dispatch. Trusted accounting and reservations govern concurrent resource consumption; a caller-supplied estimate is not a meter. Expiry or revocation must govern existing handles and ongoing work where the policy requires it. A workspace lease adds ownership, teardown, and reuse obligations rather than obtaining them from the expiry field alone (Workspace leases).
These requirements are an implementation checklist, not a complete authorization library. The envelope and mediated services must prevent bypass of the checks, and an already issued external effect can remain unresolved after a grant expires.




A catalog can expose separate service operations or combine work behind more general interfaces. The interface-to-functionality trade-off also appears in modular software design (Ousterhout 2018), but tool count alone does not determine usability or authority. Designing the Active Toolkit separates granularity from catalog staging and evaluates both under a workload. This section isolates a stipulated token comparison.

Ousterhout, John. 2018. A Philosophy of Software Design. Yaknyam Press.


Suppose every one of \(\CatalogStagingCallCount\) model calls stages the same \(\StagedDefinitionCount\) definitions, contributing an average of \(\DefinitionSerializedSize\) tokens each in the final serialization. Excluding other request content, this fixed-catalog policy sends
\[\CatalogDefinitionTokens = \CatalogStagingCallCount \cdot \StagedDefinitionCount \cdot \DefinitionSerializedSize \tag{1}\]
tokens of tool definitions. For two fixed catalogs under the same call count, their token ratio is \(\FirstCatalogDefinitionCount \FirstCatalogDefinitionSize/(\SecondCatalogDefinitionCount \SecondCatalogDefinitionSize)\). Fewer definitions reduce catalog tokens only when their combined serialized size is smaller. A general interface with a long instruction manual can cost more than several concise specialized interfaces.
On-demand staging changes the per-call count. If call \(\ModelCallIndex\) stages \({\StagedDefinitionCount}_i\) definitions with mean serialized contribution \(\DefinitionSerializedSize_i\), replace the product in equation 1 with \(\sum_{i=1}^{\CatalogStagingCallCount} {\StagedDefinitionCount}_i \DefinitionSerializedSize_i\). Record the tokenizer and serialization convention, including any shared framing, so the estimates can be checked against actual requests. Selection calls and catalog-discovery observations need separate accounting. Neither formula establishes equal functionality, grants, selection quality, or task outcomes.
Compatible available prefix state can reduce recomputation, and qualifying cached-input billing can reduce price, without releasing logical context capacity. A changed descriptor affects reuse from its first divergence, not necessarily the entire earlier prefix (Staging the Next Invocation).
Comparing narrow and general catalogs across definition cost, tool selection, observation shape, and enforcement (table 2) separates the surface property of a catalog from the underlying runtime measurement or authority obligation.



Table 2: Narrow Versus General Tool Catalogs: How catalog shape affects definition tokens, tool selection, observations, and where authority is enforced.











Dimension
Many narrow tools
A few general tools
Consequence




Interface surface
More operation-specific names
Fewer names with more expressive arguments
Count alternatives and argument complexity separately


Definition tokens
Depends on staged count and serialized size
Depends on staged count and serialized size
Measure \({\StagedDefinitionCount}_i \DefinitionSerializedSize_i\) rather than inferring cost from tool count


Selection
More interfaces may offer task-specific choices
Fewer interfaces may require more argument composition
Compare selection and argument errors under the same workload


Observations
Can expose task-specific structured results
Can expose a shared result envelope
Either design must preserve status, scope, and omissions


Enforcement
Per-operation checks can coexist with shared containment
Expressive operations require limits on their possible effects
Both need authorization and execution enforcement






General tools can express effects that are difficult to infer from their arguments alone. Their execution envelope must enforce the permitted reach (Agent Sandboxes). Narrow signatures do not remove that obligation: their implementations can still access resources, invoke other programs, or contain defects.



A catalog comparison needs a fixed workload and acceptance policy. For coding tasks, a command runner, file viewer, exact-replacement editor, and structured search interface form one possible candidate. They need not be four separate tools, and a candidate that requires additional model calls may spend more even if each request carries fewer definitions. Attributing an improvement to catalog shape therefore requires recording the workload, staged tokens, selection errors, authority reach, and end-to-end outcomes across both candidates (table 3).



Table 3: Catalog comparison worksheet: Fields that make a workload-specific comparison interpretable rather than equating fewer tool names with a better interface.










Comparison field
Record for each candidate
Interpretation




Workload and acceptance
Same task set, source versions, checks, and completion deadline
A faster rejection is not an accepted task


Available operations
Required effects, argument expressiveness, and unavailable operations
Compare functional coverage before token savings


Staged definitions
Actual serialized tokens per model call and the staging policy
Count all calls, including discovery and repair


Selection and arguments
Wrong-tool choices, invalid arguments, and ambiguous requests
Separate interface selection from argument construction


Observation contract
Status, provenance, omitted output, and capture limits
A short result may omit the evidence needed to continue


Authority and effects
Reachable resources, approval conditions, and repeat behavior
Fewer tool names do not imply narrower authority


End-to-end outcome
Accepted tasks, unresolved outcomes, total cost, and latency distribution
Retain failures and recovery work in the accounting






Each operation also needs explicit input, execution, and observation bounds that match its mechanics: a file viewer’s line window does not bound its returned bytes because one line can be arbitrarily long, whereas a search tool needs limits on its input expression as well as its work, matches, and captured output; similarly, an editor needs a resulting-file bound in addition to bounded replacement strings, while a command runner needs containment and resource accounting beyond a timeout argument. These remain endpoint obligations even when several operations share one implementation.
A compact catalog is useful when it reduces the total work required to finish the specified tasks without weakening the acceptance or authority contract. Specialized interfaces can instead reduce ambiguity and expose narrower effects. The worksheet supports that decision; it does not prescribe a catalog size.

Listing 1: Bounded edit arguments: A teaching descriptor with a closed argument object and finite string limits; authorization and atomic mutation remain implementation obligations.


{
  "name": "file_edit",
  "description": "Replaces an exact block in an existing workspace file. Match counting uses the original file and non-overlapping matches. Zero matches fail; multiple matches fail unless allow_multiple is true. Match-check failure leaves the file unchanged.",
  "parameters": {
    "$schema": "https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/schema",
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "path": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "Absolute path to the target file, inside the workspace root.",
        "pattern": "^/([a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+/)*[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]+$",
        "maxLength": 1024
      },
      "old_str": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The exact block to replace, including indentation and newlines.",
        "minLength": 1,
        "maxLength": 16384
      },
      "new_str": {
        "type": "string",
        "description": "The replacement text. May be empty to delete old_str.",
        "maxLength": 16384
      },
      "allow_multiple": {
        "type": "boolean",
        "description": "If true, replace every non-overlapping match in the original file; if false, fail unless exactly one match exists."
      }
    },
    "required": ["path", "old_str", "new_str", "allow_multiple"],
    "additionalProperties": false
  }
}



The required Boolean makes repeat-match intent explicit; a descriptor with an optional Boolean would instead need a documented normalization rule. JSON Schema measures maxLength in characters, not serialized bytes or model tokens. The request transport therefore needs its own byte bound, while context construction needs its own token accounting. Replacement size also differs from result-file size: repeated replacements can expand a file beyond either string bound.
The implementation must enforce the advertised match behavior and workspace boundary: because a path pattern does not establish confinement and checking a unique match before an uncoordinated write does not prevent a concurrent change, the endpoint must resolve and authorize the actual target, enforce the match precondition together with the mutation, and bound both the resulting file and the returned observation. Even then, a missing response still requires the operation-identity contract below, because a schema cannot establish whether an edit committed.
Keep the published schema, normalization rules, and implementation version together. Generating a schema from a typed argument model can reduce transcription drift, but it does not prove that a decoder, validator, and implementation accept the same inputs. Contract tests should include missing required fields, extra fields, oversized strings, wrong types, and valid boundary values. Tests must also exercise advertised behavior outside the schema, including concurrent edits and uncertain outcomes.



Tools adapted from existing service interfaces often carry patterns that suit a programmer calling from code but mislead a model proposing from a description, so table 1 pairs each recurring schema defect with its hardened form and boundary effect.



Table 1: Tool Schema Anti-Patterns: Common schema patterns that mislead a model or defeat the validator, the hardened form of each, and its effect on the boundary.











Anti-pattern
What goes wrong
Hardened form
Effect




Untyped argument bag (args: dict)
Undeclared keys can pass through without field-level checks
Explicit typed fields with additionalProperties: false
The validator rejects undeclared fields; a supporting decoder can exclude them


Unbounded inputs (string with no limit)
One call carries an argument larger than the tool or the context can hold
maxLength, maxItems, and explicit windowing parameters
Argument size is bounded before dispatch


Ambiguous object variants
The model mixes fields that belong to different operations
A required tag with branch-specific constraints
Branch intent is explicit; validation still depends on the complete schema


Implicit units (timeout: 30)
Seconds, milliseconds, and minutes are confused
Units in the name (timeout_ms), range bounds, and agreed conversion
Meaning is documented; plausible wrong-unit values can still pass validation
