Output length grows with the file, risking truncation and unrelated changes
Exact replacement of a block (old_str, new_str)
Output length depends on the selected block and replacement






The last row can matter for latency when generated output lies on the critical path (The Cost of a Model Call). A whole-file rewrite pays decode time for every unchanged line, and Comparing Output Interfaces works an example in which the rewrite misses a per-call deadline that an anchored diff meets. Exact replacement has its own cost when the selected anchor is ambiguous or stale; the right representation depends on the edits the workload requires.

title: 1 Typed Tool Interfaces
text:
A model that samples freely can emit malformed arguments. Under a supported grammar and correct masking, a generation that reaches an accepting completion belongs to that grammar; truncation or interruption does not supply a complete valid call (Grammar-Guided Decoding, Finite-state constrained decoding). Decode-Loop Mechanics develops mask placement and storage. Here the narrower question is whether masking overhead is lower than the expected latency of one repair under a stipulated comparison.
Let a tool call carry \(\OutputLength\) output tokens at \(\PerTokenDecodeTime\) per token, let masking add \(\PerTokenMaskingTime\) per token, let \(\UnconstrainedParseFailureRate\) be the rate at which unconstrained calls fail to parse, and let a repair turn cost \(\RepairTurnLatency\) of latency, including the re-sent context and the regenerated call. The expected latency without constraints, allowing one repair, is
\[\mathbb{E}[\UnconstrainedCallLatency] = \OutputLength \, \PerTokenDecodeTime + \UnconstrainedParseFailureRate \, \RepairTurnLatency\]
and with constraints it is
\[\ConstrainedCallLatency = \OutputLength \, (\PerTokenDecodeTime + \PerTokenMaskingTime)\]
Setting the two equal gives the break-even error rate
\[\BreakEvenParseFailureRate = \frac{\OutputLength \, \PerTokenMaskingTime}{\RepairTurnLatency}\]
Under this model, constraining reduces expected latency when the malformation rate exceeds \(\BreakEvenParseFailureRate\). Measure the inputs for the actual model, schema, and prompt, and express both time terms in the same unit. The ratio is dimensionless. If it exceeds one, eliminating every parse failure would still not repay the stipulated mask overhead; if repair latency is zero, the ratio is undefined and the original latency expressions should be compared directly.
The comparison holds generated length and base decode cost fixed and includes at most one repair. It omits schema-compilation and setup costs; include those when they are not already amortized or shared. A policy that stops quickly after a failed repair may look faster while completing fewer tasks. Use the break-even only among candidates with comparable task quality and completion requirements, and measure residual malformed or interrupted outputs rather than assuming that every constrained call completes.
Even an accepting, syntactically valid call can name a nonexistent file, exceed the task’s authority, or request the wrong operation. Completion checks, validation, grants, and execution limits therefore remain necessary (Grammar-Guided Decoding).

title: 1 Typed Tool Interfaces
text:
Operation identity and authorization solve different problems. An idempotency key identifies an intended operation across attempts; safe deduplication depends on the endpoint’s effect and result contract (Retrying Uncertain Actions). A capability represents scoped authority whose enforcement is developed in Capabilities and Credentials. Neither artifact, by its presence alone, establishes that a call is safe.


Generating a fresh UUID inside a retry loop makes every network timeout look like a brand-new mutation to the receiving endpoint. Instead, the runtime must assign an identifier to the intended operation and retain it across retries and recovery. A fresh transport attempt can have a new call identifier while referring to the same operation. Conversely, two separately intended operations may have identical arguments and still need distinct identities. Deriving an identifier from recorded inputs or storing a generated identifier are both possible; either method requires enough durable state to recover the same identity after a crash.
The endpoint binds this identity to the authorized scope and request payload and rejects conflicting reuse. If canonical serialization is used to compare payloads, its rules must match at both ends. Identity does not authorize the request, and hashing arguments alone cannot distinguish an intentional second operation from a retry.



When a retried request arrives with the same operation ID, an endpoint that only returns “success” or “error” cannot tell the caller whether the first attempt is still running or failed partway through. A useful status model distinguishes an unseen operation, work in flight, a completed operation with a retained result, and an operation whose effect is in doubt. These states describe the required behavior, not a complete implementation:

Admission. Claim the operation under the endpoint’s concurrency and durability contract, checking scope and payload consistency.
In flight. A repeated request must not start an independent execution of the same effect. It can obtain status or wait under the endpoint’s defined limits.
Completed. A repeat returns the retained outcome under the service’s result-retention contract.
In doubt. Preserve uncertainty and reconcile it; do not release the operation for blind repetition merely because an exception occurred.

The difficult boundary lies between performing the effect and retaining its outcome. A host-side map that calls an external service and then writes COMPLETED leaves a crash gap. Closing it requires support that couples identity to the effect, such as a transaction within the effect-owning service or that service’s own deduplication contract. An expiring claim does not make an older executor unable to commit; any takeover must account for that executor.
The contract must also state how long operation identities and outcomes remain recognizable. After a deduplication record expires, an absent record may mean forgotten work rather than a never-issued operation. A retry beyond the retention window needs reconciliation or another endpoint guarantee; the identifier alone no longer establishes repeat safety.
A reconciliation probe supplies scoped evidence. Finding the pre-dispatch state does not prove that a delayed request cannot still act. If neither the endpoint contract nor terminal evidence establishes that repetition is safe, the operation remains unresolved and the runtime escalates or withholds the repeat (Retrying Uncertain Actions). Durable Execution develops preservation of intent and outcome across crashes; this appendix does not substitute a short cache implementation for that protocol.



An idempotency key prevents duplicate execution of the same request, but does not check whether the caller is allowed to touch the target object in the first place. The capability tuple \(\CapabilityGrant=(\GrantRights,\mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant,\GrantCondition,\GrantExpiryTime)\) in Capabilities and Credentials describes the rights \(\GrantRights\), objects \(\mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant\), condition predicate \(\GrantCondition\), and expiry time \(\GrantExpiryTime\) that govern access. A protected handle or verified token can represent the grant; the tuple alone is not its enforcement. The runtime binds each use to the task and caller, resolves the actual target within the permitted scope, and checks the operation and current conditions. A lexical path prefix does not establish confinement against indirection or concurrent changes.
For delegation, let \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\CapabilityGrant)\) denote the accesses a grant permits. A derived child must satisfy
\[\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant).\]
An issuer must authenticate the parent and validate the proposed narrowing before issuing a child. It must preserve associations between rights, objects, and conditions, not merely compare unrelated sets of names. Holding a narrower child does not revoke a broader parent. Several children must share the parent’s aggregate resource allowance rather than each receiving an independent copy of its budget (Capability Delegation).
Execution needs further controls beyond a predicate checked at dispatch. Trusted accounting and reservations govern concurrent resource consumption; a caller-supplied estimate is not a meter. Expiry or revocation must govern existing handles and ongoing work where the policy requires it. A workspace lease adds ownership, teardown, and reuse obligations rather than obtaining them from the expiry field alone (Workspace leases).
These requirements are an implementation checklist, not a complete authorization library. The envelope and mediated services must prevent bypass of the checks, and an already issued external effect can remain unresolved after a grant expires.

title: 1 Typed Tool Interfaces
text:
A catalog can expose separate service operations or combine work behind more general interfaces. The interface-to-functionality trade-off also appears in modular software design (Ousterhout 2018), but tool count alone does not determine usability or authority. Designing the Active Toolkit separates granularity from catalog staging and evaluates both under a workload. This section isolates a stipulated token comparison.

Ousterhout, John. 2018. A Philosophy of Software Design. Yaknyam Press.


Suppose every one of \(\CatalogStagingCallCount\) model calls stages the same \(\StagedDefinitionCount\) definitions, contributing an average of \(\DefinitionSerializedSize\) tokens each in the final serialization. Excluding other request content, this fixed-catalog policy sends
\[\CatalogDefinitionTokens = \CatalogStagingCallCount \cdot \StagedDefinitionCount \cdot \DefinitionSerializedSize \tag{1}\]
tokens of tool definitions. For two fixed catalogs under the same call count, their token ratio is \(\FirstCatalogDefinitionCount \FirstCatalogDefinitionSize/(\SecondCatalogDefinitionCount \SecondCatalogDefinitionSize)\). Fewer definitions reduce catalog tokens only when their combined serialized size is smaller. A general interface with a long instruction manual can cost more than several concise specialized interfaces.
On-demand staging changes the per-call count. If call \(\ModelCallIndex\) stages \({\StagedDefinitionCount}_i\) definitions with mean serialized contribution \(\DefinitionSerializedSize_i\), replace the product in equation 1 with \(\sum_{i=1}^{\CatalogStagingCallCount} {\StagedDefinitionCount}_i \DefinitionSerializedSize_i\). Record the tokenizer and serialization convention, including any shared framing, so the estimates can be checked against actual requests. Selection calls and catalog-discovery observations need separate accounting. Neither formula establishes equal functionality, grants, selection quality, or task outcomes.
Compatible available prefix state can reduce recomputation, and qualifying cached-input billing can reduce price, without releasing logical context capacity. A changed descriptor affects reuse from its first divergence, not necessarily the entire earlier prefix (Staging the Next Invocation).
Comparing narrow and general catalogs across definition cost, tool selection, observation shape, and enforcement (table 2) separates the surface property of a catalog from the underlying runtime measurement or authority obligation.



Table 2: Narrow Versus General Tool Catalogs: How catalog shape affects definition tokens, tool selection, observations, and where authority is enforced.











Dimension
Many narrow tools
A few general tools
Consequence




Interface surface
More operation-specific names
Fewer names with more expressive arguments
Count alternatives and argument complexity separately


Definition tokens
Depends on staged count and serialized size
Depends on staged count and serialized size
Measure \({\StagedDefinitionCount}_i \DefinitionSerializedSize_i\) rather than inferring cost from tool count


Selection
More interfaces may offer task-specific choices
Fewer interfaces may require more argument composition
Compare selection and argument errors under the same workload


Observations
Can expose task-specific structured results
Can expose a shared result envelope
Either design must preserve status, scope, and omissions


Enforcement
Per-operation checks can coexist with shared containment
Expressive operations require limits on their possible effects
Both need authorization and execution enforcement






General tools can express effects that are difficult to infer from their arguments alone. Their execution envelope must enforce the permitted reach (Agent Sandboxes). Narrow signatures do not remove that obligation: their implementations can still access resources, invoke other programs, or contain defects.



A catalog comparison needs a fixed workload and acceptance policy. For coding tasks, a command runner, file viewer, exact-replacement editor, and structured search interface form one possible candidate. They need not be four separate tools, and a candidate that requires additional model calls may spend more even if each request carries fewer definitions. Attributing an improvement to catalog shape therefore requires recording the workload, staged tokens, selection errors, authority reach, and end-to-end outcomes across both candidates (table 3).



Table 3: Catalog comparison worksheet: Fields that make a workload-specific comparison interpretable rather than equating fewer tool names with a better interface.










Comparison field
Record for each candidate
Interpretation




Workload and acceptance
Same task set, source versions, checks, and completion deadline
A faster rejection is not an accepted task


Available operations
Required effects, argument expressiveness, and unavailable operations
Compare functional coverage before token savings


Staged definitions
Actual serialized tokens per model call and the staging policy
Count all calls, including discovery and repair


Selection and arguments
Wrong-tool choices, invalid arguments, and ambiguous requests
Separate interface selection from argument construction


Observation contract
Status, provenance, omitted output, and capture limits
A short result may omit the evidence needed to continue


Authority and effects
Reachable resources, approval conditions, and repeat behavior
Fewer tool names do not imply narrower authority


End-to-end outcome
Accepted tasks, unresolved outcomes, total cost, and latency distribution
Retain failures and recovery work in the accounting






Each operation also needs explicit input, execution, and observation bounds that match its mechanics: a file viewer’s line window does not bound its returned bytes because one line can be arbitrarily long, whereas a search tool needs limits on its input expression as well as its work, matches, and captured output; similarly, an editor needs a resulting-file bound in addition to bounded replacement strings, while a command runner needs containment and resource accounting beyond a timeout argument. These remain endpoint obligations even when several operations share one implementation.
A compact catalog is useful when it reduces the total work required to finish the specified tasks without weakening the acceptance or authority contract. Specialized interfaces can instead reduce ambiguity and expose narrower effects. The worksheet supports that decision; it does not prescribe a catalog size.

title: Distributed State Foundations
text:
An agent runtime relies on distributed systems guarantees when it records intent, calls a tool, or hands work to another worker. This appendix provides histories, boundary comparisons, and failure examples for interpreting those guarantees without assuming that a local transaction governs an entire task. The chapters retain the agent-specific admission, persistence, and compensation protocols.


Use the observed ambiguity to select the relevant background. Each entry isolates one distributed-systems guarantee that agent runtimes rely on when recording intent, dispatching tools, or handing work across workers:

When timestamps appear to disagree about which operation happened first, section 1.1 distinguishes causal order from an enforced operation order.
When a design claims that an update is atomic or durable, section 1.2 identifies the state and failures the claim must cover.
When recovery invokes transactions, sagas, or a write-ahead log, section 1.3 separates their guarantees.
When a reply is lost, section 1.4 distinguishes repeated execution, repeated effects, and result recovery.
When a replacement worker takes ownership, section 1.5 explains how the resource excludes a stale holder.

These distinctions help interpret, but do not replace, the endpoint’s actual contract. The main-text chapters referenced in each section specify the additional runtime protocols required for end-to-end safety.



Two workers read the same configuration version and independently prepare replacements. Sorting their log entries by wall-clock timestamp does not decide which replacement may publish. The clocks may differ, and even perfectly ordered observations would not prevent both workers from acting on the old version.
A causal history records dependencies rather than inferring them from timestamps. Lamport’s happened-before relation includes a process’s local event order, message transmission before its receipt, and the transitive consequences of those relationships. Events unrelated by this relation are concurrent. A logical clock preserves the implication from causal precedence to increasing clock values, but the converse does not hold; unequal logical timestamps need not establish a causal relationship (Lamport 1978).

Lamport, Leslie. 1978. “Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System.” Communications of the ACM 21 (7): 558–65. https://doi.org/10.1145/359545.359563.

Herlihy, Maurice P., and Jeannette M. Wing. 1990. “Linearizability: A Correctness Condition for Concurrent Objects.” ACM Transactions on Programming Languages and Systems 12 (3): 463–92. https://doi.org/10.1145/78969.78972.
An endpoint can impose a stronger contract on its operations. Under linearizability, each completed operation appears to take effect at one point between invocation and response, consistently with the object’s sequential specification. If one operation returns before another starts, that order must be respected. Overlapping operations can take either order if their results fit that specification. The original correctness condition (Herlihy and Wing 1990) concerns observable histories, not synchronized clocks.
For the configuration example, suppose the endpoint provides a linearizable conditional update that compares an expected version and replaces the value and version together. When both workers supply the same old version, one update succeeds and advances the version, so the other cannot also succeed against that stale precondition. That guarantee holds only if versions never cycle back to an old identifier and every conflicting writer goes through the enforcing boundary, since a separate read followed by an unconditional write does not implement this operation.
The comparison protects only what it covers. If publication also depends on a changing permission record elsewhere, checking the configuration version alone leaves that permission unchecked at publication. Operation order therefore needs an explicit state boundary, not merely an ordering label.



A service can commit a database update while a notification sent to another service remains undelivered. Calling the update a transaction does not place the notification inside it. The guarantee comparison in table 1 separates claims that often appear together but answer different failure questions.



Table 1: Distinct Transaction Guarantees: Each property requires a declared boundary; none supplies the other properties by its name alone.










Property
What the contract specifies
What does not follow




Atomicity
Which changes commit or abort together
Unrelated remote effects participate


Isolation
Which concurrent observations and interleavings are permitted
Every isolation level gives serial execution semantics


Durability
Which acknowledged changes survive which failures
Every copy or failure domain survives


Application consistency
Which state constraints each committed transition preserves
The store understands whether a task result is correct






Atomicity concerns the commit unit, whereas durability concerns persistence after commitment (Gray 1981). A process can recover from a crash using an intact local disk, yet lose that same history if the disk disappears permanently. Replication changes the survivable failure set only when the acknowledgment policy requires the relevant replicas to preserve the update. The word “durable” must therefore identify both the acknowledgment and the assumed failures.
Isolation concerns interference during concurrent execution. Serializable execution has the effect of some serial ordering of the participating transactions; it does not necessarily preserve their real-time order. A transaction operating at weaker isolation may observe a different class of histories. Even serializability cannot repair an incorrect transaction that violates the intended application rule when run alone. The engineer must establish both a correct state transition and the concurrency contract under which it runs.
For a workflow spanning independent endpoints, the boundary test is to identify which operations participate in one commit decision. Anything outside that set needs its own completion and recovery contract. Classical coordination mechanisms preserve this distinction.



A database crash can leave modified pages on disk while other modifications remain only in memory. A distributed workflow adds another difficulty: one participant may have committed while another has not received a decision. Transaction recovery addresses these cases only where the storage and participants implement the required protocol.


When a workflow updates two independent stores, a crash after the first store commits can leave the second store aborted unless both stores first agree to hold their changes in a prepared state. Two-phase commit coordinates that atomic commit decision among participating resource managers. During preparation, each participant establishes that it can commit and preserves the required recovery state. A participant that votes to commit cannot then abort unilaterally merely because it stops hearing from the coordinator. The final decision determines whether the participants commit or abort (Gray 1981). Preparation is consequently a recovery obligation, not a readiness hint.

Gray, Jim. 1981. “The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations.” Proceedings of the Seventh International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB) 7: 144–54.
The protocol requires cooperating participants. Writing “prepare” into a runtime log does not enlist an unrelated service or make its effect reversible. Moreover, a prepared participant can have to wait when it cannot learn the decision. A design must account for this blocking and for the resources retained while waiting; an atomic decision is not a promise of bounded completion time.



Holding database locks across a multi-minute tool call or human approval wait blocks every concurrent writer on the service. To avoid long-lived locks, a saga divides a long operation into separately committed transactions with compensating transactions for partial execution (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). Intermediate effects can become visible because the whole sequence does not retain one transaction’s isolation. A reservation followed by cancellation illustrates the distinction: cancellation is a new state transition, not deletion of the earlier history.

Garcia-Molina, Hector, and Kenneth Salem. 1987. “Sagas.” Proceedings of the 1987 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 249–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742.
The application must specify what compensation restores and what remains. Charges already incurred or observations by another client may survive it. The original saga abstraction relies on the system’s ability to execute the required compensations; a remote workflow must separately handle compensators that fail or remain uncertain. The Trajectory Saga Pattern develops the agent-specific obligation records and evidence needed for that case.



If a process crashes after overwriting a data page on disk but before recording what changed, recovery cannot tell whether the page holds the old state, the new state, or a torn mix of both. Write-ahead logging prevents that ambiguity by imposing an ordering between recovery information and persistent changes. Before a database writes a modified page to persistent storage, the log information needed to recover that change must be durable. Before it acknowledges a durable commit, the required transaction log prefix must survive the promised failures. This ordering permits recovery even when the data pages themselves have not all been flushed.
ARIES organizes recovery into analysis, redo, and undo (Mohan et al. 1992). Analysis reconstructs recovery state; redo repeats relevant logged history; undo removes effects of transactions designated for rollback while logging the undo work. Prepared transactions awaiting a commit decision must retain their unresolved status. ARIES’s page-oriented redo and support for logical undo are more general than restoring an old byte image for every operation. Transaction log chains help locate earlier records, but a particular record layout is an algorithm choice, not the definition of write-ahead logging.

Mohan, Chandrasekaran, Don Haderle, Bruce Lindsay, Hamid Pirahesh, and Peter Schwarz. 1992. “ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 17 (1): 94–162. https://doi.org/10.1145/128765.128770.
A runtime’s durable intent borrows the ordering requirement, not the database’s control over remote state. Recovering a request record does not establish that the endpoint executed it. Durable Intent Before Dispatch develops this distinction for trajectory dispatch; interpreting an uncertain reply additionally requires the endpoint’s repeat contract.




A client times out after requesting a state change. The server may never have received the request, may still be executing it, or may have completed it and lost the reply. A timeout alone does not distinguish those histories. Remote procedure call protocols therefore separate retransmission handling from the caller’s knowledge of execution (Birrell and Nelson 1984).

Birrell, Andrew D., and Bruce Jay Nelson. 1984. “Implementing Remote Procedure Calls.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (1): 39–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/2080.357392.
Idempotence means that repeating an operation has the same effect on the specified state as applying it once, under the stated conditions. It does not require identical replies. An expected-version update can reject a repeat after an earlier success, protecting the state while leaving the caller uncertain which attempt succeeded. Conversely, a repeated “set” can overwrite an intervening writer even when setting the same value twice is idempotent in isolation.
Deduplication needs a stable logical operation identity and an enforcing record at the effect boundary. A restricted implementation can atomically commit a local mutation together with the operation’s identity and result. Repeated delivery of that identity then recovers the recorded result instead of repeating the mutation. If the record and effect commit independently, a crash between them recreates the ambiguity. Reusing an identity with different arguments must also be rejected or otherwise resolved by the declared contract.
Result retention bounds the guarantee. Once the endpoint discards the record, an old request must not silently become a new operation unless the contract permits that behavior. “Exactly once” is meaningful only with a stated effect boundary, identity scope, retention rule, and failure model; it does not imply eventual completion through indefinite outages. Retrying Uncertain Actions applies these distinctions to tool outcomes without treating a timeout as permission to repeat an effect.



A worker pauses long enough to lose its lease. A replacement acquires ownership, but the old worker later resumes and sends a buffered write. The ownership service’s new grant does not itself stop that request at the resource.
A lease grants ownership for a bounded interval under a declared timing contract. A fencing token enables enforcement at the resource. One design attaches an authenticated ownership generation to requests and records the current generation at the resource. After the replacement’s generation is installed there, the resource rejects requests from older generations. The Chubby sequencer mechanism (Burrows 2006) exemplifies resource-side validation of a lock generation.

Burrows, Mike. 2006. “The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely-Coupled Distributed Systems.” USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI).
We can test the handoff by delaying the old worker’s write until after installation of the new fence. Rejection demonstrates the intended exclusion for that trace. If the write arrives before installation, comparing generations alone cannot detect expiration of the old lease. That requires a lease-validity contract or a handoff protocol that establishes the fence before relying on exclusion.
The current holder can issue several distinct operations under the same generation; fencing does not deduplicate them. Nor does a larger integer establish authority unless the resource authenticates its grant. These distinctions keep ownership, repeat handling, and effect settlement separate. An implementation must enforce each guarantee where the corresponding state can change.

Durability
Which acknowledged changes survive which failures
Every copy or failure domain survives


Application consistency
Which state constraints each committed transition preserves
The store understands whether a task result is correct






Atomicity concerns the commit unit, whereas durability concerns persistence after commitment (Gray 1981). A process can recover from a crash using an intact local disk, yet lose that same history if the disk disappears permanently. Replication changes the survivable failure set only when the acknowledgment policy requires the relevant replicas to preserve the update. The word “durable” must therefore identify both the acknowledgment and the assumed failures.
Isolation concerns interference during concurrent execution. Serializable execution has the effect of some serial ordering of the participating transactions; it does not necessarily preserve their real-time order. A transaction operating at weaker isolation may observe a different class of histories. Even serializability cannot repair an incorrect transaction that violates the intended application rule when run alone. The engineer must establish both a correct state transition and the concurrency contract under which it runs.
For a workflow spanning independent endpoints, the boundary test is to identify which operations participate in one commit decision. Anything outside that set needs its own completion and recovery contract. Classical coordination mechanisms preserve this distinction.

title: Distributed State Foundations
text:
A database crash can leave modified pages on disk while other modifications remain only in memory. A distributed workflow adds another difficulty: one participant may have committed while another has not received a decision. Transaction recovery addresses these cases only where the storage and participants implement the required protocol.


When a workflow updates two independent stores, a crash after the first store commits can leave the second store aborted unless both stores first agree to hold their changes in a prepared state. Two-phase commit coordinates that atomic commit decision among participating resource managers. During preparation, each participant establishes that it can commit and preserves the required recovery state. A participant that votes to commit cannot then abort unilaterally merely because it stops hearing from the coordinator. The final decision determines whether the participants commit or abort (Gray 1981). Preparation is consequently a recovery obligation, not a readiness hint.

Gray, Jim. 1981. “The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations.” Proceedings of the Seventh International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB) 7: 144–54.
The protocol requires cooperating participants. Writing “prepare” into a runtime log does not enlist an unrelated service or make its effect reversible. Moreover, a prepared participant can have to wait when it cannot learn the decision. A design must account for this blocking and for the resources retained while waiting; an atomic decision is not a promise of bounded completion time.



Holding database locks across a multi-minute tool call or human approval wait blocks every concurrent writer on the service. To avoid long-lived locks, a saga divides a long operation into separately committed transactions with compensating transactions for partial execution (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). Intermediate effects can become visible because the whole sequence does not retain one transaction’s isolation. A reservation followed by cancellation illustrates the distinction: cancellation is a new state transition, not deletion of the earlier history.

Garcia-Molina, Hector, and Kenneth Salem. 1987. “Sagas.” Proceedings of the 1987 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 249–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742.
The application must specify what compensation restores and what remains. Charges already incurred or observations by another client may survive it. The original saga abstraction relies on the system’s ability to execute the required compensations; a remote workflow must separately handle compensators that fail or remain uncertain. The Trajectory Saga Pattern develops the agent-specific obligation records and evidence needed for that case.



If a process crashes after overwriting a data page on disk but before recording what changed, recovery cannot tell whether the page holds the old state, the new state, or a torn mix of both. Write-ahead logging prevents that ambiguity by imposing an ordering between recovery information and persistent changes. Before a database writes a modified page to persistent storage, the log information needed to recover that change must be durable. Before it acknowledges a durable commit, the required transaction log prefix must survive the promised failures. This ordering permits recovery even when the data pages themselves have not all been flushed.
ARIES organizes recovery into analysis, redo, and undo (Mohan et al. 1992). Analysis reconstructs recovery state; redo repeats relevant logged history; undo removes effects of transactions designated for rollback while logging the undo work. Prepared transactions awaiting a commit decision must retain their unresolved status. ARIES’s page-oriented redo and support for logical undo are more general than restoring an old byte image for every operation. Transaction log chains help locate earlier records, but a particular record layout is an algorithm choice, not the definition of write-ahead logging.

Mohan, Chandrasekaran, Don Haderle, Bruce Lindsay, Hamid Pirahesh, and Peter Schwarz. 1992. “ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 17 (1): 94–162. https://doi.org/10.1145/128765.128770.
A runtime’s durable intent borrows the ordering requirement, not the database’s control over remote state. Recovering a request record does not establish that the endpoint executed it. Durable Intent Before Dispatch develops this distinction for trajectory dispatch; interpreting an uncertain reply additionally requires the endpoint’s repeat contract.

title: Distributed State Foundations
text:
A client times out after requesting a state change. The server may never have received the request, may still be executing it, or may have completed it and lost the reply. A timeout alone does not distinguish those histories. Remote procedure call protocols therefore separate retransmission handling from the caller’s knowledge of execution (Birrell and Nelson 1984).

Birrell, Andrew D., and Bruce Jay Nelson. 1984. “Implementing Remote Procedure Calls.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (1): 39–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/2080.357392.
Idempotence means that repeating an operation has the same effect on the specified state as applying it once, under the stated conditions. It does not require identical replies. An expected-version update can reject a repeat after an earlier success, protecting the state while leaving the caller uncertain which attempt succeeded. Conversely, a repeated “set” can overwrite an intervening writer even when setting the same value twice is idempotent in isolation.
Deduplication needs a stable logical operation identity and an enforcing record at the effect boundary. A restricted implementation can atomically commit a local mutation together with the operation’s identity and result. Repeated delivery of that identity then recovers the recorded result instead of repeating the mutation. If the record and effect commit independently, a crash between them recreates the ambiguity. Reusing an identity with different arguments must also be rejected or otherwise resolved by the declared contract.
Result retention bounds the guarantee. Once the endpoint discards the record, an old request must not silently become a new operation unless the contract permits that behavior. “Exactly once” is meaningful only with a stated effect boundary, identity scope, retention rule, and failure model; it does not imply eventual completion through indefinite outages. Retrying Uncertain Actions applies these distinctions to tool outcomes without treating a timeout as permission to repeat an effect.

title: Distributed State Foundations
text:
A worker pauses long enough to lose its lease. A replacement acquires ownership, but the old worker later resumes and sends a buffered write. The ownership service’s new grant does not itself stop that request at the resource.
A lease grants ownership for a bounded interval under a declared timing contract. A fencing token enables enforcement at the resource. One design attaches an authenticated ownership generation to requests and records the current generation at the resource. After the replacement’s generation is installed there, the resource rejects requests from older generations. The Chubby sequencer mechanism (Burrows 2006) exemplifies resource-side validation of a lock generation.

Burrows, Mike. 2006. “The Chubby Lock Service for Loosely-Coupled Distributed Systems.” USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI).
We can test the handoff by delaying the old worker’s write until after installation of the new fence. Rejection demonstrates the intended exclusion for that trace. If the write arrives before installation, comparing generations alone cannot detect expiration of the old lease. That requires a lease-validity contract or a handoff protocol that establishes the fence before relying on exclusion.
The current holder can issue several distinct operations under the same generation; fencing does not deduplicate them. Nor does a larger integer establish authority unless the resource authenticates its grant. These distinctions keep ownership, repeat handling, and effect settlement separate. An implementation must enforce each guarantee where the corresponding state can change.

title: Mathematical Foundations
text:
This appendix supplies mathematical background for reasoning about agent trajectories, resource use, evaluation, and learning. It collects reusable models and derivations whose details would interrupt the chapters’ engineering arguments. Each entry identifies its assumptions and the decisions it can support, so a reader can check a result or adapt a calculation without treating an idealized model as a guarantee about a deployed agent.


Choose the reference problem rather than reading the entries in sequence. Each group isolates one family of formal models and points back to the chapter where the engineering decision is made:

When context, observations, and progress signals are being confused with state or guarantees, section 1.1 separates their formal roles.
When an output constraint or representation approximation needs a precise scope, section 1.2 supplies the language, matrix, and geometric models.
When long jobs or repeated work dominate cost, section 1.3 derives queueing and cadence relationships.
When an evaluation or release claim needs statistical support, section 1.4 identifies the experiment, estimator, and decision assumptions.
When a trajectory-training result needs to be checked, section 1.5 gives the relevant gradients and conditional bounds.
When adding workers or reviewers changes performance, section 1.6 separates parallel speedup from correlated assessment error.

Each group is a lookup collection. Follow the entry’s return reference for the engineering decision in the main text; the derivation is optional depth, not a replacement for that decision.



A runtime can limit actions without knowing the complete environment state. These entries distinguish probabilistic state estimation, bounds on admitted steps, and the propagation of security labels.


A tool result exposes only part of the environment an agent acts on. A partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP) separates that observation from the underlying state (Kaelbling et al. 1998). One discounted formulation is the tuple

Kaelbling, Leslie Pack, Michael L. Littman, and Anthony R. Cassandra. 1998. “Planning and Acting in Partially Observable Stochastic Domains.” Artificial Intelligence 101 (1–2): 99–134. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0004-3702(98)00023-X.
\[\langle \PomdpStateSpace, \PomdpActionSet, \PomdpTransitionFunction, \PomdpRewardFunction, \PomdpObservationSet, \PomdpObservationFunction, \DiscountFactor \rangle\]
with an initial-state distribution specified separately. Its components have distinct roles:

\(\PomdpStateSpace\) contains environment states, including relevant remote state and concurrent activity.
\(\PomdpActionSet\) contains available actions.
\(\PomdpTransitionFunction\) determines the transition distribution \(\EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\NextDecisionProcessState \mid \DecisionProcessState,\TrajectoryAction)\) to the next state.
\(\PomdpRewardFunction(\DecisionProcessState,\TrajectoryAction)\) specifies the modeled reward.
\(\PomdpObservationSet\) contains possible observations.
\(\PomdpObservationFunction(\TrajectoryObservation \mid \NextDecisionProcessState,\TrajectoryAction)\) gives the observation distribution after an action and transition.
\(\DiscountFactor \in [0,1)\) discounts future rewards in this formulation.

The state must contain enough information for the assumed transition law to be Markov. A reward is a chosen objective signal, not a certificate of correctness or permission to act. Finite-horizon tasks can instead use an undiscounted objective with a declared terminal convention.
Let \(\InteractionHistory_t=(\TrajectoryObservation_0,\TrajectoryAction_0,\TrajectoryObservation_1,\ldots,\TrajectoryAction_{t-1},\TrajectoryObservation_{t})\) denote the interaction history before action \(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\). The belief state is a probability distribution over environment states conditional on that history, not the history’s token representation:
\[\BeliefState_t(\DecisionProcessState)=\Pr(\RandomEnvironmentState_t=\DecisionProcessState\mid \InteractionHistory_t).\]
For a finite state space and an observation with positive probability, Bayes’ rule gives
\[\BeliefState_{t+1}(\NextDecisionProcessState)=
\frac{\PomdpObservationFunction(\TrajectoryObservation_{t+1}\mid \NextDecisionProcessState,\TrajectoryAction_{t})
\sum_{\DecisionProcessState} \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\NextDecisionProcessState\mid \DecisionProcessState,\TrajectoryAction_{t})\BeliefState_t(\DecisionProcessState)}
{\sum_{\NormalizingNextState}\PomdpObservationFunction(\TrajectoryObservation_{t+1}\mid \NormalizingNextState,\TrajectoryAction_{t})
\sum_{\DecisionProcessState} \EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\NormalizingNextState\mid \DecisionProcessState,\TrajectoryAction_{t})\BeliefState_t(\DecisionProcessState)}.\]
The numerator predicts the next state and weights it by the received evidence; the denominator normalizes the distribution. A zero denominator signals an observation outside the assumed model’s support, not a valid posterior update.
A language-model agent usually acts from a selected context \(\TurnContext_{t}\), which can summarize or omit parts of \(\InteractionHistory_t\). Generated reasoning tokens can influence its policy, but do not become external observations merely by appearing in context. Neither \(\TurnContext_{t}\) nor a verbal confidence claim establishes that the agent represents a calibrated \(\BeliefState_t\). The formal model therefore clarifies what the implementation approximates; it does not prove that its context is sufficient. Observation freshness checks in Context Invalidation and plan revision in Revising Candidate Plans address the consequences of incomplete or outdated evidence.



An agent loop that retries a failing test without a monotone counter can run indefinitely while appearing active on every turn. A ranking function establishes a finite bound on admitted steps under explicit transition assumptions. Suppose \(\RankingFunction_t\) is a nonnegative integer and every admitted step decreases it by at least one:
\[\RankingFunction_{t+1} \le \RankingFunction_t - 1.\]
Then at most \(\RankingFunction_0\) such steps can be admitted. An enforced remaining-step allowance is one example: decrement it when work is admitted and refuse another admission at zero. This bounds the count, not the duration of a step, task completion, or termination of previously dispatched remote work. Deadlines and outstanding-effect contracts remain separate (Budgets and Ceilings).
A task-progress measure has a different obligation: it must reflect the chosen task and observations. Useful investigation can leave candidate state unchanged, and an exploratory change can temporarily worsen a check result. Hash recurrence and stagnant metrics are therefore fallible signals for intervention, not ranking-function proofs (Semantic Watchdogs).
Expected-drift arguments require an explicit stochastic stopping model and its assumptions. Merely adding a distance-to-goal term to remaining tokens or spending does not establish such a result, because the quantities have different units, their transitions need not share a monotonic direction, and a resource bound alone does not prove useful progress.



When a prompt combines an authenticated operator instruction with an untrusted issue comment, the runtime needs a formal rule to decide which label governs the combined context. An information-flow security lattice expresses an ordering on security labels and operations for combining them:
\[\SecurityLabelLattice = \langle \SecurityLabelSet, \sqsubseteq, \sqcup, \sqcap \rangle\]
where \(\SecurityLabelSet\) is the set of security labels, \(\sqsubseteq\) is the label ordering, \(\sqcup\) is the join operator (least upper bound), and \(\sqcap\) is the meet operator (greatest lower bound). A runtime must separately specify how this ordering governs each protected use or destination.
Integrity provenance and confidentiality answer different questions. Integrity concerns the evidence permitted to influence a decision; confidentiality concerns permitted recipients. As a small illustration of integrity-dependency propagation, let \(\IntegrityTrustLabel \in \{\text{Trusted}, \text{Untrusted}\}\) use this order:
\[\text{Trusted} \sqsubset \text{Untrusted}\]
Here Trusted means qualified under the policy for a specified use rather than universally true. An authenticated task instruction can establish permitted scope without certifying every factual assertion it contains. A protected runner’s observation can support a particular test result under its execution contract, whereas a README’s claim that the test passed cannot substitute for it. Untrusted records any dependency not so qualified, though this two-element example is not a complete policy for both integrity and confidentiality.
For a context \(\TurnContext_{t}\) containing labeled input segments \(\LabeledRecord_i\), a conservative aggregate label joins their dependencies:
\[\IntegrityTrustLabel(\TurnContext_{t}) = \bigsqcup_{i=1}^{|\TurnContext_{t}|} \IntegrityTrustLabel(\LabeledRecord_i)\]
Under this conservative policy, selecting any untrusted input makes the aggregate carry untrusted provenance. The join summarizes tracked dependencies rather than measuring causal influence inside attention. Extraction into typed fields therefore does not clear provenance, and derived summaries or stored records retain the relevant dependencies. A trusted decision may endorse a particular use on stated evidence, while authorized release of confidential data remains a separate declassification decision. Information-Flow Policy applies these distinctions at the operation and destination boundary.




Constrained output, repository ranking, and compressed retrieval representations solve different problems. The results below expose the mathematical assumptions behind each mechanism and the limits of its guarantee.


A structured tool proposal must remain a viable prefix of the permitted output language while it is generated. For a regular language, a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) can track that constraint (Willard and Louf 2023). Unbounded recursive nesting, as in general JSON syntax, is not a regular-language problem; it requires additional parser state. The finite-state model below applies to regular subsets or explicitly bounded structures.

Willard, Brandon T., and Rémi Louf. 2023. “Efficient Guided Generation for Large Language Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2307.09702.
Let the automaton be
\[\ConstrainedDecodingAutomaton=\langle \AutomatonStateSet,\ByteAlphabet,\AutomatonTransitionFunction,\DecodingConstraintState_0,\AcceptingStateSet\rangle,\]
where \(\AutomatonStateSet\) is a finite state set, \(\ByteAlphabet=\{0,\ldots,255\}\) is the byte alphabet, \(\AutomatonTransitionFunction:\AutomatonStateSet\times\ByteAlphabet\to \AutomatonStateSet\) is the transition function, \(\DecodingConstraintState_0\) is the initial state, and \(\AcceptingStateSet\) is the accepting set. Invalid transitions enter a rejecting sink. Its extension to byte strings satisfies
\[\AutomatonTransitionFunction^*(\DecodingConstraintState,\EmptyByteString)=\DecodingConstraintState,\qquad
\AutomatonTransitionFunction^*(\DecodingConstraintState,\AlphabetByte \ByteString)=\AutomatonTransitionFunction^*(\AutomatonTransitionFunction(\DecodingConstraintState,\AlphabetByte),\ByteString).\]
Assume each ordinary vocabulary token \(\VocabularyToken\) decodes to a fixed nonempty byte string \(\TokenByteDecoding(\VocabularyToken)\), and handle special tokens separately. If a tokenizer uses context-dependent decoding, its state must also enter the constraint machine. Define \(\LiveAutomatonStateSet\) as the states from which some finite sequence of ordinary vocabulary tokens reaches \(\AcceptingStateSet\). A transition that merely avoids a syntax error is insufficient if no tokenized completion remains possible.
At state \(\DecodingConstraintState_t\), the permitted ordinary tokens are
\[\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)=
\{\VocabularyToken:\AutomatonTransitionFunction^*(\DecodingConstraintState_t,\TokenByteDecoding(\VocabularyToken))\in \LiveAutomatonStateSet\}.\]
Permit the end-of-sequence token only when \(\DecodingConstraintState_t\in \AcceptingStateSet\). Mask all other disallowed special tokens. If \(\AllowedTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\) includes the permitted ordinary tokens and any permitted end token, the masked logits and probabilities are
\[\MaskedTokenLogit_{t,\VocabularyToken}=
\begin{cases}
\StepTokenLogit&\VocabularyToken\in\AllowedTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t),\\
-\infty&\VocabularyToken\notin\AllowedTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t),
\end{cases}
\qquad
\Pr(\SequenceToken_t=\VocabularyToken\mid \TokenPrefix)=
\frac{\exp(\MaskedTokenLogit_{t,\VocabularyToken})}{\sum_\NormalizerTokenIndex\exp(\MaskedTokenLogit_{t,\NormalizerTokenIndex})}.\]
This normalization requires at least one allowed token with finite logit. If later sampling filters eliminate all such tokens, decoding must report failure rather than normalize an empty support.
Starting from a live initial state, induction establishes that every admitted ordinary token preserves the possibility of a valid completion. A generation that ends with a permitted end token therefore belongs to the specified language. The argument does not guarantee termination within a token budget, nor does it preserve the unconstrained model’s sequence distribution. A cutoff can leave an incomplete prefix that must not be accepted as a complete tool proposal.
For a fixed finite automaton and tokenizer, token masks can be precomputed per state. The table removes repeated vocabulary–automaton traversal, not every cost of applying a mask or sampling; Decode-Loop Mechanics accounts for its placement beside the sampler. Syntactic acceptance still says nothing about whether the named object exists, the action is authorized, or the proposed operation satisfies the task.



To build a compact repository map within a token budget, a runtime can model the codebase as a directed graph \((\RepositoryGraphVertexSet, \RepositoryGraphEdgeSet)\) of symbol definitions and references. Declare the edge direction before ranking: following references and following reverse dependencies answer different questions. Let \(\RepositoryEdgeWeight_{ij}\ge0\) be the weight of an edge from symbol \(\RepositoryEdgeSourceIndex\) to symbol \(\RepositoryEdgeTargetIndex\), and let \(\PersonalizationVector\) be a nonnegative personalization vector whose entries sum to one. Normalize each nonempty row of \(\RepositoryEdgeWeightMatrix\) to a probability distribution; for a dangling symbol with no outgoing edge, use \(\PersonalizationVector^T\) as its row. The resulting matrix \(\RepositoryTransitionMatrix\) is row stochastic.
For a chosen damping factor \(0\le \PageRankDampingFactor<1\), the personalized PageRank vector satisfies
\[\PageRankScoreVector=(1-\PageRankDampingFactor)\PersonalizationVector+\PageRankDampingFactor\RepositoryTransitionMatrix^T\PageRankScoreVector.\]
Initialized with a probability vector, each iteration preserves nonnegativity and unit total mass. Because multiplication by \(\RepositoryTransitionMatrix^T\) is nonexpansive in the vector \(1\)-norm, the damped update contracts differences by at most \(\PageRankDampingFactor\), giving a unique fixed point. Personalization can favor symbols implicated by the task, but this preference is an input to the ranking rather than evidence that a symbol is necessary.
Sorting symbols by score and packing them within a token budget produces one candidate repository map. Multi-Hop Retrieval considers this ranking as an optional graph prioritizer; a runtime can pre-stage such a map under the policy described in Agentic Retrieval. Ranking and packing do not guarantee that the selected symbols preserve a complete dependency path or supply the evidence a task needs.



An existing attention-state matrix can be approximated by a lower-rank matrix, trading storage for reconstruction error. The truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) gives an error bound for this approximation. It is not a derivation of learned latent-attention architectures or a guarantee about task quality; The Footprint of Retained Attention State distinguishes those model-design and storage choices.
Let \(\AttentionKeyMatrix^{(\ell)} \in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength \times \AttentionHeadDimension}\) denote the uncompressed Key activation matrix for layer \(\ell\) across an active sequence of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens. The singular value decomposition factors \(\AttentionKeyMatrix^{(\ell)}\) into orthogonal singular vectors:
\[\AttentionKeyMatrix^{(\ell)} = \KeyLeftSingularMatrix \KeySingularSpectrumMatrix \KeyRightSingularMatrix^T = \sum_{i=1}^{\min(\SequenceLength, \AttentionHeadDimension)} \KeySingularNumber_i \KeyLeftSingularVector_i \KeyRightSingularVector_i^T\]
where \(\KeyLeftSingularMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{\SequenceLength \times \SequenceLength}\) and \(\KeyRightSingularMatrix \in \mathbb{R}^{\AttentionHeadDimension \times \AttentionHeadDimension}\) are orthonormal basis matrices, and \(\KeySingularSpectrumMatrix\) contains ordered singular values \(\KeySingularNumber_1 \ge \KeySingularNumber_2 \ge \dots \ge \SmallestKeySingularNumber \ge 0\).
A rank-\(\TruncationRank\) truncated SVD approximation \(\TruncatedKeyApproximation^{(\ell)}\) retains the first \(\TruncationRank\) singular components, with \(0\le \TruncationRank\le \KeySpectrumLength=\min(\SequenceLength,\AttentionHeadDimension)\):
\[\TruncatedKeyApproximation^{(\ell)} = \TruncatedKeyLeftSingularMatrix \TruncatedKeySpectrumMatrix \TruncatedKeyRightSingularMatrix^T = \sum_{i=1}^{\TruncationRank} \KeySingularNumber_i \KeyLeftSingularVector_i \KeyRightSingularVector_i^T\]
By the classical Eckart-Young-Mirsky Theorem, the truncated matrix \(\TruncatedKeyApproximation^{(\ell)}\) is the mathematically optimal rank-\(\TruncationRank\) approximation to \(\AttentionKeyMatrix^{(\ell)}\) under both the spectral norm (\(\|\cdot\|_2\)) and the Frobenius norm (\(\|\cdot\|_\FrobeniusNorm\)). Specifically, the minimum Frobenius reconstruction error is determined entirely by the discarded tail singular values:
\[\min_{\operatorname{rank}(\RankConstrainedMatrix) \le \TruncationRank} \|\AttentionKeyMatrix^{(\ell)} - \RankConstrainedMatrix\|_\FrobeniusNorm = \|\AttentionKeyMatrix^{(\ell)} - \TruncatedKeyApproximation^{(\ell)}\|_\FrobeniusNorm = \sqrt{\sum_{j=\TruncationRank+1}^{\KeySpectrumLength} \KeySingularNumber_j^2}\]
For a nonzero matrix, the fraction of total squared Frobenius norm, often called activation energy here, preserved by the rank-\(\TruncationRank\) approximation is
\[\RetainedSpectralEnergyFraction = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^\TruncationRank \KeySingularNumber_i^2}{\sum_{i=1}^{\KeySpectrumLength} \KeySingularNumber_i^2}.\]
The zero matrix has zero reconstruction error at every rank, but its energy fraction is undefined because the denominator is zero. For \(\TruncationRank<\KeySpectrumLength\), the spectral error is \(\FirstDiscardedSingularNumber\). Cauchy–Schwarz therefore bounds the error of each unscaled query–key dot product by \(\|\QueryVector\|_2\FirstDiscardedSingularNumber\); at \(\TruncationRank=\KeySpectrumLength\) the error is zero. Scaled attention scores inherit the corresponding scaling factor.
A steeply decaying spectrum permits a small matrix reconstruction error. It does not establish a small error after attention normalization or preserve task acceptance. Measure the spectrum and the resulting behavior under the intended workload rather than selecting rank from energy retention alone.



When an embedding dimension grows into the hundreds or thousands, the Euclidean distance from a query to its nearest candidate can approach the distance to its farthest candidate, weakening spatial-tree pruning in Dense and Hybrid Retrieval. To make the assumptions behind that behavior explicit, this section derives the volume of a \(\AmbientDimension\)-dimensional Euclidean ball and examines conditions under which distance contrast deteriorates. These conditional geometric results are not a guarantee that every learned embedding collection defeats spatial indexes or requires approximate search.


The volume of a \(\AmbientDimension\)-dimensional Euclidean ball of radius \(\BallRadius\) is given by:
\[\BallVolume(\BallRadius) = \int_{\|\IntegrationPoint\|_2 \le \BallRadius} \DerivativeOperator\IntegrationPoint = \BallRadius^\AmbientDimension \cdot \BallVolume(1)\]
To compute the unit ball volume \(\BallVolume(1)\), we integrate the separable Gaussian function \(\exp(-\|\IntegrationPoint\|_2^2)\) over all \(\mathbb{R}^\AmbientDimension\):
\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^\AmbientDimension} e^{-\|\IntegrationPoint\|_2^2} \DerivativeOperator\IntegrationPoint = \prod_{i=1}^\AmbientDimension \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} e^{-\IntegrationPointCoordinate_i^2} d\IntegrationPointCoordinate_i = (\sqrt{\pi})^\AmbientDimension = \pi^{\AmbientDimension/2}\]
Switching to spherical polar coordinates, with differential surface area \(\SphereSurfaceArea(\BallRadius) = \frac{\DerivativeOperator}{d\BallRadius} \BallVolume(\BallRadius) = \AmbientDimension \cdot \BallRadius^{\AmbientDimension-1} \BallVolume(1)\):
\[\int_{\mathbb{R}^\AmbientDimension} e^{-\|\IntegrationPoint\|_2^2} \DerivativeOperator\IntegrationPoint = \int_0^\infty e^{-\BallRadius^2} \SphereSurfaceArea(\BallRadius) d\BallRadius = \AmbientDimension \cdot \BallVolume(1) \int_0^\infty \BallRadius^{\AmbientDimension-1} e^{-\BallRadius^2} d\BallRadius\]
Applying the substitution \(\SquaredRadiusSubstitution = \BallRadius^2\) (\(d\SquaredRadiusSubstitution = 2\BallRadius d\BallRadius\)):
\[\int_0^\infty \BallRadius^{\AmbientDimension-1} e^{-\BallRadius^2} d\BallRadius = \frac{1}{2} \int_0^\infty \SquaredRadiusSubstitution^{\frac{\AmbientDimension}{2} - 1} e^{-\SquaredRadiusSubstitution} d\SquaredRadiusSubstitution = \frac{1}{2} \ContinuousFactorialFunction\left(\frac{\AmbientDimension}{2}\right)\]
Equating the Cartesian and spherical integrals:
\[\pi^{\AmbientDimension/2} = \AmbientDimension \cdot \BallVolume(1) \cdot \frac{1}{2} \ContinuousFactorialFunction\left(\frac{\AmbientDimension}{2}\right) = \BallVolume(1) \cdot \frac{\AmbientDimension}{2} \ContinuousFactorialFunction\left(\frac{\AmbientDimension}{2}\right) = \BallVolume(1) \cdot \ContinuousFactorialFunction\left(\frac{\AmbientDimension}{2} + 1\right)\]
Solving for \(\BallVolume(1)\) and scaling by \(\BallRadius^\AmbientDimension\) yields the closed-form volume:
\[\BallVolume(\BallRadius) = \frac{\pi^{\AmbientDimension/2}}{\ContinuousFactorialFunction\left(\frac{\AmbientDimension}{2} + 1\right)} \BallRadius^\AmbientDimension\]
For an outer shell of relative thickness \(\ShellRelativeThickness\) (\(0 < \ShellRelativeThickness < 1\)), the volume of the inner sphere of radius \(\BallRadius(1 - \ShellRelativeThickness)\) is \(\BallVolume(\BallRadius(1 - \ShellRelativeThickness)) = (1 - \ShellRelativeThickness)^\AmbientDimension \BallVolume(\BallRadius)\). The fraction of total volume contained in the outer shell is:
\[\frac{\BallVolume(\BallRadius) - \BallVolume(\BallRadius(1 - \ShellRelativeThickness))}{\BallVolume(\BallRadius)} = 1 - (1 - \ShellRelativeThickness)^\AmbientDimension\]
As \(\AmbientDimension\to\infty\), \((1-\ShellRelativeThickness)^\AmbientDimension\to0\) exponentially fast for fixed positive \(\ShellRelativeThickness\). This is a statement about uniform volume within a ball. It does not establish the distribution of learned embeddings, which can occupy a structured subset of their ambient space.



Distance concentration can reduce the relative contrast between the closest and farthest candidates (Beyer et al. 1999). The following sufficient-condition argument makes the fixed-dataset-size assumption explicit; it does not say that a nearest neighbor ceases to exist.

Beyer, Kevin, Jonathan Goldstein, Raghu Ramakrishnan, and Uri Shaft. 1999. “When Is ‘Nearest Neighbor’ Meaningful?” International Conference on Database Theory (ICDT), 217–35. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-49257-7_15.
Let \(\StoredIndexVector_1, \dots, \LastCandidateEmbeddingVector\) be independent random vectors in \(\mathbb{R}^\AmbientDimension\) drawn from a distribution with finite moments, and let \(\SearchQueryEmbedding\) be an independent query vector. Define \(\NearestCandidateDistance(\RetrievalCollectionSize, \AmbientDimension) = \min_{1 \le i \le \RetrievalCollectionSize} \|\StoredIndexVector_i - \SearchQueryEmbedding\|_\DistanceNormOrder\) and \(\FarthestCandidateDistance(\RetrievalCollectionSize, \AmbientDimension) = \max_{1 \le i \le \RetrievalCollectionSize} \|\StoredIndexVector_i - \SearchQueryEmbedding\|_\DistanceNormOrder\).
Assume distances are positive almost surely, so the relative contrast has a nonzero denominator. Suppose each query–candidate distance has the same finite positive mean and finite variance at dimension \(\AmbientDimension\), with relative variance satisfying
\[\lim_{\AmbientDimension \to \infty} \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\|\StoredIndexVector - \SearchQueryEmbedding\|_\DistanceNormOrder)}{\mathbb{E}[\|\StoredIndexVector - \SearchQueryEmbedding\|_\DistanceNormOrder]^2} = 0\]
then for any fixed dataset size \(\RetrievalCollectionSize\) and any \(\RelativeContrastTolerance > 0\):
\[\lim_{\AmbientDimension \to \infty} \Pr\left( \frac{\FarthestCandidateDistance(\RetrievalCollectionSize, \AmbientDimension) - \NearestCandidateDistance(\RetrievalCollectionSize, \AmbientDimension)}{\NearestCandidateDistance(\RetrievalCollectionSize, \AmbientDimension)} \le \RelativeContrastTolerance \right) = 1\]
To derive the result, let \(\MeanQueryDistance\) be the common mean distance. Chebyshev’s inequality bounds the probability that one distance differs from \(\MeanQueryDistance\) by more than \(\RelativeDeviationBound\MeanQueryDistance\) by its relative variance divided by \(\RelativeDeviationBound^2\). A union bound over fixed \(\RetrievalCollectionSize\) makes the probability of any such deviation tend to zero. This step needs no independence between distances, which share the query. On the complementary event, with \(0<\RelativeDeviationBound<1\),
\[\frac{\FarthestCandidateDistance-\NearestCandidateDistance}{\NearestCandidateDistance}
\le\frac{2\RelativeDeviationBound}{1-\RelativeDeviationBound}.\]
Choosing \(\RelativeDeviationBound\) small enough for the specified \(\RelativeContrastTolerance\) proves the displayed convergence. If \(\RetrievalCollectionSize\) grows with dimension, the union bound requires additional control over that growth.
Reduced contrast can weaken pruning based on distance bounds, but does not prove that every tree index must visit every leaf. Index geometry, intrinsic dimension, query distribution, and approximation tolerance determine the actual work. The engineering use of this result is to test those assumptions against the intended retrieval workload, not to infer index performance from ambient dimension alone.





Queueing and recovery estimates depend on which resource is held and which work must be repeated. These models make that boundary explicit before deriving a delay or a cadence.


Long service times delay later arrivals when a worker must finish its current task before admitting another. To isolate that effect, consider a stationary \(\Glyph{M}/\Glyph{G}/1\) queue with Poisson arrivals at rate \(\ArrivalRate\), one first-come, first-served server, and independent, identically distributed service times \(\RequestServiceTime\) independent of the arrival process. Assume an unlimited waiting room, no abandonment, \(\ServingUtilization=\ArrivalRate\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]<1\), and a finite second moment. The Pollaczek–Khinchine mean waiting-time formula is
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestQueueTime] = \frac{\ArrivalRate \mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime^2]}{2 (1 - \ServingUtilization)}.\]
The role of the second moment follows from residual service. A service interval of length \(\RealizedServiceTime\) contributes area \(\RealizedServiceTime^2/2\) under its remaining-service curve. Averaging these areas over time gives mean residual work \(\ArrivalRate\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime^2]/2\). A Poisson arrival sees that time average. The queued jobs ahead contribute \(\mathbb{E}[\QueuedJobCount]\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\), and Little’s law gives \(\mathbb{E}[\QueuedJobCount]=\ArrivalRate\mathbb{E}[\RequestQueueTime]\). Thus
\[\mathbb{E}[\RequestQueueTime]
=\frac{\ArrivalRate\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime^2]}{2}
+\ServingUtilization\mathbb{E}[\RequestQueueTime],\]
which yields the displayed formula. The derivation concerns waiting before service, not total response time or a tail percentile.
Heavy-tailed service can make the second moment large; an idealized model with finite mean but infinite second moment has infinite mean waiting time even at stable positive load. Agent systems need not satisfy the queue’s arrival or service assumptions. In particular, tool waits, batching, retries, and call-level admission change the service boundary. Scheduling Concurrent Trajectories uses that boundary to compare interference policies, while Capacity for Trajectories separates worker, workspace, and cache holding times.



A task’s unconstrained demand can vary widely even when every individual model call has an output ceiling. An enforced turn limit bounds admitted trajectory steps; a deadline constrains a different quantity and depends on how outstanding work is handled. Tail modeling describes demand within those controls, not a reason to remove them.
For a continuous Pareto reference model \(\ParetoTaskDemand\) with minimum \(\ParetoMinimumDemand>0\) and index \(\ParetoTailExponent>0\),
\[\Pr(\ParetoTaskDemand>\DemandThreshold)=\left(\frac{\ParetoMinimumDemand}{\DemandThreshold}\right)^{\ParetoTailExponent},
\qquad \DemandThreshold\ge \ParetoMinimumDemand.\]
A measured integer step-count tail can approximate this shape over a stated range, but is not literally this continuous distribution. Integrating the tail gives a finite mean only for \(\ParetoTailExponent>1\) and a finite second moment only for \(\ParetoTailExponent>2\):
\[\mathbb{E}[\ParetoTaskDemand]=\frac{\ParetoTailExponent \ParetoMinimumDemand}{\ParetoTailExponent-1},
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[\ParetoTaskDemand^2]=\frac{\ParetoTailExponent \ParetoMinimumDemand^2}{\ParetoTailExponent-2}.\]
Each expression applies only in its respective finite-moment range. For \(1<\ParetoTailExponent\le2\), the mean exists and the variance is infinite in the unbounded model. For \(\ParetoTailExponent\le1\), even the mean is infinite. A capped variable \(\min(\ParetoTaskDemand,\DemandCap)\) has finite moments for every finite \(\DemandCap\); a finite observed tail cannot establish that an actual deployment has infinite variance.
Step count is also not service time. To use the queueing result in section 1.3.1, the model must describe service at the selected resource boundary. Variable call lengths and external waits can change that distribution even at a fixed number of turns. Capacity planning therefore needs means for average load, measured tails for service targets, and explicit limits for admitted work. No single fitted tail index replaces those three obligations (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}\)).



Frequent verification consumes resources; delayed detection can waste subsequent work. A cadence model is useful only after identifying which failures a check detects and which work can safely be repeated. It does not schedule mandatory authorization or precondition checks, and it cannot reverse an external effect.


Consider \(\UsefulStepCount\) useful generation steps with homogeneous generation cost \(\StepGenerationCost\) per step and verification cost \(\VerificationCheckCost\) per check. Express both costs in the same unit, such as money or serial elapsed time; do not add money to latency. Suppose checks occur every \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) steps, errors occur at constant rate \(\GenerationStepErrorRate\) per useful step, and errors are rare within an interval. Assume each check detects the modeled error, the extra work between error and detection averages \(\CheckIntervalStepCount/2\) steps, and recovery costs \(\ErrorRecoveryCost\) per error independently of \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\).
Ignoring partial final intervals and repeated errors during recovery gives the first-order model
\[\VerificationScheduleCost(\CheckIntervalStepCount)\approx
\UsefulStepCount \StepGenerationCost+\frac{\UsefulStepCount}{\CheckIntervalStepCount}\VerificationCheckCost
+\UsefulStepCount\GenerationStepErrorRate
\left(\frac{\CheckIntervalStepCount}{2}\StepGenerationCost+\ErrorRecoveryCost\right).\]
The two cadence-dependent terms vary in opposite directions. Differentiating their sum for positive continuous \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) gives
\[\frac{d\VerificationScheduleCost}{d\CheckIntervalStepCount}
=-\frac{\UsefulStepCount \VerificationCheckCost}{\CheckIntervalStepCount^2}
+\frac{\UsefulStepCount\GenerationStepErrorRate \StepGenerationCost}{2},
\qquad
\CheckIntervalStepCount^*=\sqrt{\frac{2\VerificationCheckCost}
{\GenerationStepErrorRate \StepGenerationCost}}.\]
Consequently, the relaxed verification count is \(\VerificationCheckCount^*=\UsefulStepCount/\CheckIntervalStepCount^*\). Independence from \(\UsefulStepCount\) follows from the homogeneous, long-run assumptions, not from a universal property of agent tasks. Actual schedules use feasible integer intervals, handle the final partial block, and respect deadlines and mandatory checks. Error bursts, state-dependent check power, and correlated recovery attempts require a different model.



A second model assumes that any erroneous block must be generated again from its start. Partition \(\UsefulStepCount\) useful steps into blocks of \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) steps, with \(\CheckIntervalStepCount\) dividing \(\UsefulStepCount\). Let each step succeed independently with probability \(0<\StepSuccessProbability<1\), each generation take \(\StepGenerationTime>0\), and each block check take \(\BlockCheckTime>0\). A check perfectly distinguishes successful from failed blocks. Every retry starts from the same recoverable state, draws independent outcomes, and has the same duration; reset overhead is negligible. No attempt has an externally visible effect that a retry would duplicate.
The block succeeds with probability \(\StepSuccessProbability^\CheckIntervalStepCount\), so its number of attempts is geometric with mean \(\StepSuccessProbability^{-\CheckIntervalStepCount}\). The expected completion time is
\[\ExpectedRunCompletionTime(\CheckIntervalStepCount)=\frac{\UsefulStepCount}{\CheckIntervalStepCount}\,
\frac{\CheckIntervalStepCount \StepGenerationTime+\BlockCheckTime}{\StepSuccessProbability^\CheckIntervalStepCount}
=\UsefulStepCount \StepSuccessProbability^{-\CheckIntervalStepCount}\left(\StepGenerationTime+\frac{\BlockCheckTime}{\CheckIntervalStepCount}\right).\]
Set \(\StepFailureHazard=-\ln \StepSuccessProbability>0\). Differentiating \(\ln \ExpectedRunCompletionTime(\CheckIntervalStepCount)\) gives the stationary equation and its positive root:
\[\StepFailureHazard \StepGenerationTime \CheckIntervalStepCount^2+\StepFailureHazard \BlockCheckTime \CheckIntervalStepCount-\BlockCheckTime=0,\]
\[\CheckIntervalStepCount^*=
\frac{-\BlockCheckTime+
\sqrt{\BlockCheckTime^2+4\StepGenerationTime \BlockCheckTime/\StepFailureHazard}}
{2\StepGenerationTime}.\]
The derivative changes from negative to positive at this root. Compare feasible integer block sizes rather than rounding blindly. When \(\StepFailureHazard \BlockCheckTime/\StepGenerationTime\ll1\), the leading approximation is
\[\CheckIntervalStepCount^*\approx\sqrt{\frac{\BlockCheckTime}{\StepFailureHazard \StepGenerationTime}}
\approx\sqrt{\frac{\BlockCheckTime}{(1-\StepSuccessProbability)\StepGenerationTime}},\]
where the second approximation additionally requires \(\StepSuccessProbability\) close to one. If \(\StepSuccessProbability=1\), this model favors the largest permitted block because no regeneration is needed.
The absent factor of two distinguishes complete-block regeneration from a model that charges only average lost or wasted work within an interval. These models cannot be interchanged merely because both have square-root optima. Checkpointing in Checkpoints often reconstructs recorded events instead of regenerating model actions; that runtime must use its actual reconstruction cost and unresolved-effect contract.




A checkpoint can reduce work that must be repeated after a failure, but saving it also interrupts useful execution. Young’s first-order model balances these terms (Young 1974). Let \(\CheckpointInterval>0\) be useful execution time between completed checkpoints, \(\CheckpointWriteTime>0\) their fixed duration, and \(\MeanTimeBetweenFailures\) the mean time between failures. Assume rare Poisson failures independent of progress, small checkpoint overhead, reliable saved state, and restart cost \(\JobRestartTime\) independent of \(\CheckpointInterval\).

Young, John W. 1974. “A First Order Approximation to the Optimum Checkpoint Interval.” Communications of the ACM 17 (9): 530–31. https://doi.org/10.1145/361147.361115.
To first order, failures occur approximately uniformly within a useful-work interval, so each loses an average of \(\CheckpointInterval/2\) work. Ignoring failures during saving and recovery gives approximate overhead per unit useful time
\[\CheckpointOverheadRatio(\CheckpointInterval)\approx
\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval}
+\frac{\CheckpointInterval}{2\,\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}
+\frac{\JobRestartTime}{\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}.\]
Differentiation isolates the cadence-dependent terms:
\[\CheckpointOverheadRatio'(\CheckpointInterval)=-\frac{\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^2}
+\frac{1}{2\,\MeanTimeBetweenFailures},
\qquad
\CheckpointOverheadRatio''(\CheckpointInterval)=\frac{2\CheckpointWriteTime}{\CheckpointInterval^3}>0.\]
The minimizing interval of this approximate cost function is therefore
\[\OptimalCheckpointInterval=\sqrt{2\,\CheckpointWriteTime\,\MeanTimeBetweenFailures}.\]
Restart cost raises overhead but does not move this optimum because it is constant with respect to \(\CheckpointInterval\). A more complete model can include failures during saving and recovery; Daly (2006) develops such refinements. They do not follow by adding restart time to \(\CheckpointWriteTime\) in the displayed square root.

Daly, J. T. 2006. “A Higher Order Estimate of the Optimum Checkpoint Interval for Restart Dumps.” Future Generation Computer Systems 22 (3): 303–12. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.future.2004.11.016.
This calculation applies only when failure loses work that must be re-executed. A durable agent may instead reconstruct recorded state without resampling its past decisions. Checkpoints models that different cost. Neither a saved state nor this timing calculation rolls back committed external actions; their recovery protocol remains necessary.




A release decision requires a declared experiment and criterion. These entries separate sample planning, repeated-run estimands, sequential evidence, and cost-sensitive escalation.


Treating repeated runs of the same 20 tasks as 200 independent trials understates confidence-interval width and can make noise look like a release-ready gain.
