By this measure, a model-directed loop can earn its cost in phases such as root-cause diagnosis, where the next diagnostic step cannot be listed in advance, while deterministic control handles the predictable orchestration around it. On a production remediation attempt priced in section 20.4.2, for example, model calls are a small fraction of the attempt’s cost; whether additional diagnostic calls earn that cost depends on the relative acceptance improvement measured against a matched baseline under the same contract and latency constraints.
The second question asked what operational machinery must surround the model. The answer scales with the task’s exposure to state, authority, and horizon. Carrying state across turns requires selectively retrieved context, explicitly budgeted serving state, and durable audit records that preserve source authority, whereas exercising authority over external services adds typed, mediated action interfaces, definitive effect settlement before any retry loop runs, and process containment enforced beneath the model. When those actions span a multi-turn horizon, the runtime must also wrap the trajectory in a supervisory harness, record a write-ahead log of intent before committing each external side effect, and register compensating workflows for actions that cannot be reversed cleanly. A read-only lookup needs little of this protective scaffolding, whereas an autonomous remediation agent operating on live production systems needs all of it.
The third question asked how operators verify that a task has actually succeeded. The answer requires objective evidence collected from an authoritative endpoint that directly monitors the target system, evaluated against an explicit contract adopted by system owners before execution began. This verification must satisfy a pre-declared closure evidence level, with any residual uncertainty explicitly quantified and assigned to an accountable owner. A model’s self-generated report never serves as evidence, however coherent or persuasive, because a component executing within the loop cannot certify its own output. Stated as an operational acceptance rule, this is the discipline of invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).
Each answer is easy to state for a single component. Agent systems fail most often where the answers must hold across the boundaries between components, because services that pass their own tests can still drop an in-flight task when state, authority, and verification move from one to the next. Keeping those boundaries closed across a complete trajectory rests on the fifteen invariants developed across the book.



Across Parts I through VI, each invariant was derived in the subsystem that owns it, and table 1 collects all fifteen in one reference organized by the three H·S·A exposures, pairing each principle with its governing equation or structural contract and the design consequence it predicts. Part I prices an isolated model call and states the statistical limits of verification. Parts II, III, and IV build closure for the three exposures a single call cannot manage on its own: state carried across turns, authority over external systems, and a horizon over which errors compound. Part V changes the policy weights without expanding authority, since fine-tuning alters which trajectories the model proposes but grants no new access. Part VI multiplies all three exposures across sub-agents. Invariant closure anchors the table, because it marks the one thing computation cannot certify for itself, the task contract that defines acceptance. The exposures also interact; persisting state over a long horizon requires durable write-ahead logging, and delegation carries state and authority across agent boundaries.



Table 1: Fifteen Principles and What They Predict: Each principle appears in its teaching home with the H·S·A exposure it primarily addresses, its core equation or governing statement, and the design consequence that form predicts. Symbols carry the meanings given where each equation is derived. The exposure column is a lens rather than a partition, and each prediction holds under the assumptions its owning chapter states.













#
Principle
Part
Primary exposure
Core equation or statement
What it predicts




\(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)
Invariant closure
Introduction
All three (closure)
\(\Pr(\text{success})=(1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}\) for unchecked steps; bounds enforced below the model, acceptance on evidence above it, under a contract only authorized principals adopt
Unchecked reliability decays exponentially in \(\TurnHorizon\); a check turns a detected violating step into a rejected attempt; a truncated payload becomes a diagnosable rejection; no model output relaxes its own acceptance criteria


\(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)
Output-bound latency
I
None (prices the call)
\(\PerTokenDecodeTime \ge \Parameters\,\ElementStorageSize/\Bandwidth\) per output token when weight reads dominate
Generation time grows with output length; a shorter proposal cuts latency when decode dominates the call


\(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)
The verification asymmetry
I
Closure evidence
\(\VerifierPrecision=\dfrac{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)}{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}\)
More candidates raise coverage, not selection accuracy; at a low valid rate \(\ValidCandidateRate\), a small \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) fills the passing set, or the rewarded set under RL, with invalid candidates


\(\ref{pri-vol3-attention-working-set}\)
Context is a selected working set
II
State
\(\SystemInstructionTokenCount+\ToolDeclarationTokenCount+\TaskStateTokenCount+\ObservationTokenCount\le \ContextWindow-\OutputLimit\)
Every schema or log token displaces evidence; fitting the window does not establish decision quality


\(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)
Attention state is derived from the token prefix
II
State
\(\KvCacheBytesPerToken=2\LayerCount \KvHeadCount \AttentionHeadDimension \ElementStorageSize\) bytes held per token; reuse ends at the first changed token
One volatile field early in the prompt forfeits reuse of everything after it; placing stable material first where the task and request format permit increases potential prefix reuse.


\(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)
Authority stays with the source
II
State
Use entry \(\DerivedMemoryEntry\) at generation \(\QueryWorkspaceGeneration\) only if \(\MemoryEntryBirthGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry)\le \QueryWorkspaceGeneration<\MemoryEntryDeathGeneration(\DerivedMemoryEntry)\) and access permits
Stale or unpermitted records pass on retrieval score alone; source checks, refresh, or exclusion can lower \(\StaleSupportRate\), while a cache hit alone supplies no freshness evidence


\(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)
The typed action contract
III
Authority
Dispatch only a schema-valid, authorized call whose precondition the endpoint enforces with the mutation
A read-then-write race stays open until the endpoint checks the expected version at application


\(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)
Settlement before retry
III
Authority, with horizon
\(\DuplicateEffectProbability=(1-\RequestLossProbability)\,\ReplyLossProbability\,(1-\RequestLossProbability)\) under blind retry
The duplicate rate tracks the reply-loss rate almost one for one; rare per call becomes routine per day across a fleet


\(\ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}\)
Containment beneath the model
III
Authority
\(\text{admit}(\ProposedAccess,\CapabilityGrant,\AccessAttemptTime)\iff\text{authentic}(\CapabilityGrant)\land \ProposedAccess.\text{op}\in \GrantRights\land \ProposedAccess.\text{target}\sqsubseteq \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant\land \GrantCondition(\ProposedAccess)\land \AccessAttemptTime<\GrantExpiryTime\); flows dispatch only if labels permit
Reach is bounded by the envelope, whatever the model complies with; injected text cannot widen a flow label; teardown leaves external effects in place


\(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)
Trajectory-level encapsulation
IV
Horizon
Admit only if actual + reserved + proposed + finalization reserve \(\le\) allowance; derived grants only narrow
A loop that passes every per-call limit still halts at the dispatch ceiling or deadline; per-child ceilings alone would let \(\WorkerCount\) children spend \(\WorkerCount\) times the budget


\(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)
Intent before effect
IV
Horizon, with authority
\(\ValidatedProposalEvent\prec \AdmissionDecisionEvent\prec \IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\prec \ExternalDispatchAction\prec \EvidenceRecordEvent\); \(\ExpectedIrreversibleLoss=\sum_\PlanAction \Pr(\text{bad}\ \PlanAction)\,\text{consequence}(\PlanAction)\,(1-\ActionRecoverableFraction)\)
Under complete mediation, a crash before the flush leaves no effect, and after it the log names every operation that needs settlement; past the pivot only forward recovery remains


\(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\)
Causal and statistical release evidence
IV
Closure evidence
\(\TasksPerComparisonArm\approx 2(\SignificanceCriticalQuantile+\StatisticalPowerQuantile)^2\,\PooledAcceptanceProbability(1-\PooledAcceptanceProbability)/\TargetAcceptanceDifference^2\)
Halving the detectable difference quadruples the tasks per arm, so a small suite cannot rank close systems


\(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)
Verified trajectory post-training
V
None moved
\(\MaskedFinetuningLoss=-\frac{1}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\sum_t \PositionLossMask_{t}\log \Policy(\SequenceToken_t\mid \TokenPrefix)\) over admitted targets
A passing task check does not make every action a target; the active-token fraction sets the supervision each trajectory supplies


\(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)
The coordination tax
VI
All three, multiplied
\(\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount)=\dfrac{1}{(1-\ParallelFraction)+\ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount+\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)}\), judged on acceptance, elapsed time, and \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\)
The serial fraction caps speedup at \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\); growing overhead makes added agents slower; delegation pays only when its acceptance or deadline gain justifies its cost multiple


\(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-goodput}\)
Trajectory goodput and the accepted task
VI
All three, priced
\(\CostPerAcceptedTask=\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\); \(\ConcurrentTrajectories=\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\) per resource
Raising acceptance can cut cost more than cheaper tokens; long tool waits raise held sandboxes in proportion, and the mean alone does not give deadline capacity






These principles bound every performance optimization. KV cache prefix reuse saves the same compute whether or not the cached text still describes the live service, so a reused prefix holding a stale diagnostic snapshot is cheap and wrong at once; freshness has to come from the source’s read or version contract, never from the cache. A smaller, faster model has economic value only if its acceptance rate and tail latency still meet the service level objective. Post-training and delegation remain elective interventions, justified only by matched comparison and cost-per-accepted-task accounting.


↩︎ Cost per accepted task, measured under a declared contract, checker, and environment, as the unit for comparing configurations is established in Cost per Accepted Task.

Checkpoint 20.1: Reading the principle table as a design tool
The equations in the principle table give numbers for sizing and evaluating real architectures.

Horizon budget: Using equation 1.1, what per-step violation rate keeps the chance of any unchecked violation over \(\TurnHorizon\) turns below a target violation probability, and how must that rate change when \(\TurnHorizon\) doubles?
Acceptance vs. price: By equation 1.2, compare cutting the cost per attempt by a fraction \(\RelativeImprovementFraction\) with raising acceptance by the same relative fraction. Which lowers cost per accepted task more, and why does a token discount that touches only part of the attempt cost lose ground to the acceptance gain?
Pass rate vs. acceptance: A change raises the verifier’s pass rate but leaves acceptance under protected checks unchanged. Which two rows of the principle table explain why cost per accepted task does not fall?



The table states what each mechanism guarantees in general. A single incident shows what it takes for all of them to hold at once.



A database service triggers a query-latency alert shortly after a configuration change. An automated remediation agent inspects telemetry, correlates logs, and proposes reverting to the previous known-good settings. The human operator approves the rollback, but the configuration endpoint drops the network connection before returning an acknowledgment. Whether the mutation took effect is now unknown, the classic dilemma of a lost acknowledgment in a distributed system, and no fluent explanation from a language model can resolve it. If the runtime treats the timeout as a failure and retries under a fresh operation identifier, it risks executing the mutation twice. If it assumes success, it risks closing an incident while degraded queries continue to affect production. If it simply halts, it leaves a live production change unverified, with no one accountable for reconciling it. Each failure mode arises by default when every component satisfies its local contract and no component owns the boundary between them. The end-to-end argument that grounded the closure evidence levels (The invariant closure principle) applies to this single incident. An intermediate success report from a tool or a model call cannot establish acceptance, and only the principal holding the task contract can verify completion against direct evidence from the service.



Horizon, state, and authority return together, and the runtime closes each on one trajectory.
This incident, incident_42 on database service db_primary_01, is a workload of the remediation agent (Four lighthouse workloads), the book’s irreversible actor, which operates over a bounded horizon, mutates shared production state, and exercises real authority over a live service. Its single trajectory, from diagnostic telemetry through operator approval, dispatch, and acceptance, anchors the rest of the chapter. At every transition the criterion is the same. The system must durably and verifiably record what it proposed, what permissions were granted, what effects occurred, what evidence validates the outcome, and which principal bears ongoing responsibility. In this architecture, the managed database service owns its active configuration, the runtime orchestrator owns execution and control decisions, and the accepting authority verifies whether post-remediation evidence satisfies the delegated operational contract. One named human principal, operations_owner_42, is accountable both for any operation the runtime cannot settle and for the service once the incident is accepted. The runtime’s settlement process, a runtime component rather than a person, reconciles uncertain operations on that owner’s behalf.


The incident lifecycle begins under incident_contract_v1, which grants bounded diagnostic read access and sets gates for proposing, approving, and validating configuration mutations. Because initial privileges are observational only, the runtime provisions read_scope_42 to query authorized service endpoints so that telemetry gathering cannot inadvertently trigger state changes or be coerced into production writes. Throughout this trace, identifiers such as read_scope_42 denote durable local record keys rather than opaque cryptographic hashes.
Next, the context manager gathers the initial latency alert, recent time-series metrics, active configuration parameters, and relevant runbook sections into an auditable manifest, context_manifest_42. Every observation in this manifest records its originating source, a version tag when available, and a precise ingestion timestamp. The retrieved runbook suggests a memory-pool misconfiguration, but it might describe a previous software deployment. By diffing the runbook recommendations against the active production configuration (config_v7) and current telemetry, the agent formulates a diagnostic hypothesis. Additional diagnostic queries, constrained by the task’s remaining call budget, must corroborate this hypothesis against alternative explanations such as downstream network congestion or disk saturation.
When the diagnostic evidence converges on a known regression, the model emits change_request_42, which specifies the target configuration keys, the desired values, and the expected baseline version config_v7. Under the incident change policy, an authorized human operator reviews the proposed diff and issues approval_42. This record binds the operator’s identity to the request identifier, the target host, the exact payload parameters, the prerequisite baseline config_v7, and an expiration window. The approval records permission for that exact payload and nothing broader; it does not perform the mutation. The model drafts the operational rationale, but it cannot grant itself execution authority. An approval granted minutes before execution is an earlier check, and complete mediation (definition \(\ref{dfn-complete-mediation}\)) requires a fresh one at the moment of use. Before network dispatch, the runtime action gate therefore rechecks the operator’s authorization, compares the payload with the approval’s digest, checks the expiration deadline and resource quotas, and evaluates the runtime preconditions. If an operator revokes the ticket or the model generates an altered proposal, the original approval no longer matches and cannot silently apply to a mutated repair payload.


↩︎ Rechecking an approved request’s digest, expiry, budget, and authorization at the dispatch boundary is established in Dispatch-time rechecks.
Even a thorough pre-dispatch check leaves a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) race if a peer operator changes the settings between the gate check and the write. The endpoint closes this window with the conditional update of Conditional updates, an atomic expected-version check. It applies the change only if the live version still matches config_v7 and otherwise rejects it, returning the task for re-diagnosis. The endpoint also makes the write idempotent in the sense of definition \(\ref{dfn-idempotent-action}\). It deduplicates requests by an operation identity bound to the caller, target, and payload, and it keeps that identity for longer than the maximum client retry horizon, so a replayed request inside the window is recognized rather than reapplied. A read-only operation-status lookup completes the endpoint contract. These guarantees must live in the endpoint itself, since a client tool schema can declare an invariant but only the server can enforce it.
Before transmitting the RPC, the runtime appends an intent record for op_42 to a write-ahead journal at the durability boundary chosen for the deployment, together with its obligation registration, which names the corrective-action template, the preconditions it must satisfy, and the accountable owner, operations_owner_42. Once both are persistent on disk, the runtime dispatches the request with operation identity op_42 and expected version config_v7.


↩︎ Deduplication by an operation identity bound to caller, target, and payload is established in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
The endpoint’s response is then lost in transit, and the runtime sees a socket timeout. This is the lost-acknowledgment problem that opened Recovering After Partial Effects, and the timeout yields no information about execution state. The network may have dropped the outbound packet, the endpoint may still be executing the transaction, or the endpoint may have committed the write and lost the acknowledgment on the way back. Instead of retrying blindly or declaring failure, the runtime logs the status of op_42 as unknown and hands it to the settlement process, which issues an authorized status query against the endpoint’s operation registry rather than a second mutating RPC.
In the successful branch of this scenario, the lookup confirms that op_42 committed the requested payload, transitioning the database configuration to config_v8. The immutable operation identity binds this remote confirmation to the local dispatch record, resolving the ambiguity even if the original RPC was delayed in transit. If the lookup instead returns an empty record or meets a transient outage, the settlement process cannot conclude that the mutation failed, because the original request might still be queued in the network. In that branch the status stays unknown, kept in its obligation registration as an open obligation of operations_owner_42 rather than lost when the process terminates.


↩︎ Registering the recovery obligation alongside the forward intent, before dispatch, is established in Obligation registration.
Confirming that config_v8 committed settles the mutation but not the incident. The context manager retires the stale config_v7 snapshot and assembles fresh telemetry under live load. Assume that latency percentiles and error budgets over an observation window, health_window_42, meet the thresholds in incident_contract_v1 and that the policy checks pass. An authorized principal or automated gatekeeper then signs acceptance_42, which binds together the original incident contract, the operator approval, the settled operation identifier, the new active configuration version (config_v8), and the validated metric window. Only then is the incident formally closed under contract for the evaluated duration. Monitoring the service after the window passes to operations_owner_42, the same owner who would have held op_42 had its status stayed unknown.
Seen from above, this one incident has crossed nearly every part of the book (figure 1). The adopted contract came first; the loop that diagnosed the regression was assembled from the model call, context, tools, and sandbox of Parts I to III; the harness of Part IV wrapped every step; and acceptance rested on external evidence rather than the agent’s report. Learning and delegation never entered, because neither was needed to close this task.






Figure 1: One Trajectory Through the Whole System: A task contract, defined in the introduction and adopted at the specification boundary that Part VII closes on, governs a live loop in which context assembly (Part II) feeds a model call (Part I) whose proposal becomes a validated, authorized tool call run in a sandbox (Part III), with the observation returning to context as data. The harness (Part IV) wraps every step with budgets, the approval gate, the durable log, and recovery. Acceptance rests on scoped external evidence rather than the agent’s report; learning (Part V) and scale (Part VI) are optional lifecycle choices.



The audit chain summarized in table 2 enables an independent auditor or site reliability engineer to reconstruct the causal lineage of the incident without relying on a language model’s retrospective self-report. Structured records also expose gaps at once. A successful completion token from a model call cannot settle the network status of op_42, and an unanchored telemetry snapshot lacking a verified observation window cannot validate an acceptance claim.



Table 2: Owners and Records Along One Trajectory: The incident’s consequential transitions remain auditable through explicit owners and linked records. An unresolved outcome remains a recorded obligation rather than disappearing when execution stops.










Transition
Owner
Record it leaves




Task admitted
Runtime under the delegated contract
incident_42, incident_contract_v1, limits, and read_scope_42


Evidence selected
Context manager and diagnostic tools
context_manifest_42 with source, version, time, and omissions


Change proposed and approved
Model proposes; authorized operator decides
change_request_42 and its bound approval_42


Change admitted and dispatched
Runtime action gate and operation journal
Durable op_42 intent, obligation registration, and dispatch record

Settlement process for operations_owner_42
Source outcome for op_42, confirming config_v8 or preserving uncertainty


Incident accepted
Designated accepting principal with runtime checks
acceptance_42, health_window_42, and residual duty assigned to operations_owner_42









The diagnostic reads assembled in the context manifest also expose the trajectory to untrusted text, because production telemetry is rarely sterile. A log entry or issue tracker comment fetched under the read grant can carry an indirect prompt injection, instructions written to exfiltrate database credentials to an external server. The payload enters the agent’s context through an authorized diagnostic read, yet the untrusted text inherits none of the operator’s administrative authority. An agent that acted on it would be the confused deputy of definition \(\ref{dfn-confused-deputy}\), spending the operator’s grant on the attacker’s intent. Structured provenance tags and XML delimiters help the model separate ingested data from instructions, but model comprehension is not a security boundary. Isolation outside the model runtime must govern what a schema-valid tool call can execute with legitimate system privileges.


↩︎ Indirect prompt injection, delivered through an observation the agent reads rather than by the interacting user, is established in Prompt injection entry points.
In this scenario, an attempted exfiltration meets several independent barriers. If the manipulated model emits a tool call directed to an unauthorized external IP address, the runtime action gate blocks dispatch, because the read grant permits queries only against the named diagnostic endpoints and an arbitrary address is not among them. Independently of that grant, the sandbox’s egress policy drops unsanctioned outbound sockets at the network layer regardless of what code or parameters the agent generates. The read grant says which services the task may ask; the egress policy says which hosts any process may reach. Allowing unrestricted outbound connections would create an exfiltration channel even with local filesystems mounted read-only.


↩︎ Network egress enforcement placed outside the guest’s control boundary is established in Enforcement outside the guest.
The harder case uses only permitted operations. A diagnostic query to an endpoint inside the read grant can carry a database connection string in one of its arguments, and both the tool and the destination are allowed. The dispatch release check of equation 9.3 catches it. The credential carries a confidentiality label whose recipient set excludes the telemetry service, the label propagates into the query string built from it, and the reference monitor rejects dispatch because the recipient is not in that set. Layered constraints thus bound the blast radius of a successful injection, at the gate, at the network layer, and on the data itself.
When the action gate intercepts an unauthorized or malformed action, it appends the rejection to the audit journal as an undispatched intent. An operation that has already crossed into production is a different matter, because terminating the sandbox does not undo an external state change; the operations owner must determine from the audit log which side effects materialized and select the compensating action. If an adversarial prompt leads the model to assert that latency has normalized, the runtime ignores the assertion, since model output never substitutes for telemetry verified across the health window. The same ownership boundaries that handle component outages handle adversarial attacks.
The remediation trajectory terminates with a single model and a single runtime controller. Mining the trace for post-training or delegating sub-problems to sub-agents are later, optional decisions (section 20.5.2, section 20.7); neither optimization alters the authorization invariants required to dispatch the rollback or the empirical evidence demanded to seal the acceptance record. What governed every gate along the trace, before any diagnostic query or rollback ran, is the incident’s task contract.




When the latency alert fires, the runtime starts a diagnostic workflow, not an open-ended authorization to modify the production database. An unconstrained loop could restore query throughput by disabling secondary index updates or relaxing integrity constraints, trading durability for speed. The deployment therefore grounds the workflow in an adopted task contract that separates the desired service outcome from the mechanisms an agent may use to reach it.


Before dispatching any diagnostic query or rollback on the database, the runtime must know which settings may change, which endpoints may be read, and which metric window closes the ticket. The five contract components bind the incident to an identified service, explicit permission boundaries, and named decision authorities (table 3).


↩︎ The five-part task contract governing an agentic workload is established in The five-part task contract.

The goal states process constraints as well as target metrics, because whether an outcome is acceptable depends on how it was reached. Here the constraints are an approval binding and a version precondition, and the contract places the precondition in the endpoint. An endpoint without an atomic expected-version check cannot host this workflow safely, however often the runtime re-reads the baseline configuration, because a concurrent write can still land between the last read and the update. The observation bounds are equally strict. Under the read grant the agent may query telemetry from designated endpoints but not customer rows, payload logs, or external destinations, and tool output arrives truncated and flagged, with the full output kept in a separate log. A filter that strips known keys cannot prove an output free of sensitive data or injected instructions, so protection comes from limiting what the agent reads, where its context flows, and which endpoints receive its output.


↩︎ Head-and-tail byte budgets and explicit truncation notices for tool output are established in Bounded output capture.



The introduction placed the remediation agent at a horizon of tens of turns, mutable shared production state (\(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and changes that cannot always be compensated (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)), and this incident sits exactly there. Each exposure sets an obligation. Diagnosis needs finite allowances for model and tool calls, live service state needs source-aware tracking, and the step from diagnostic reads to a production change needs an explicit escalation of authority. The envelope attached to the incident contract applies the harness’s trajectory budgets: caps on turns, wall-clock time, observation size, disk, and spend, with the liability of each admitted call reserved in advance and a reserve kept for the health check and recovery.


↩︎ Multi-dimensional budget vectors and the advance reservation of each admitted call’s liability are established in Budgets and Ceilings.
Priced on the remediation workload profile used for this lighthouse in Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype, one attempt on this incident runs about 10 turns and costs $20.45: $0.15 of model calls, $0.10 of telemetry queries and change tools, $0.20 for the health-window check, and $20 of on-call review for the approval. At 70 percent acceptance, each accepted incident costs $29.21 (equation 1.2). The model accounts for 0.7 percent of the attempt, while operator approval takes 97.8 percent of the money and 50 percent of the 30-minute time to mitigate. This profile sets a threshold for additional diagnosis rather than establishing superiority over a fixed workflow. If all other expected attempt costs remain unchanged, doubling the model-call charges raises attempt cost by its existing model share, 0.7 percent. The added calls lower cost per accepted task only if acceptance rises by a greater relative fraction under the same contract and latency limits; that gain must be measured.
The same profile shows where the danger lies. A wrong change, proposed in 4 percent of attempts and costing $12,000 when it fully commits, carries an expected irreversible loss of $480 per attempt if no check stands ahead of the write (equation 12.5), about 23× the cost of the attempt itself. For this workload, then, the envelope’s caps on turns and spend matter less than its gates: the approval binding, the expected-version check, and the health window that bounds how long a wrong change runs before anyone reverses it. The contract also makes idempotency, request deduplication, and an operation-status lookup prerequisites for admitting any remediation workload, so that a timeout leads the runtime to ask the endpoint for the operation’s state rather than issue a duplicate mutation (section 20.6).



Suppose the run reaches its deadline while the status of the rollback is still being reconciled. Extending the deadline because the model predicts imminent success violates the envelope, and marking the operation failed fabricates an unverified outcome. The runtime instead halts further admission, logs the expiration, and preserves the pending operation identifier with its reconciliation quota, while the operations owner remains responsible for the orphaned operation. Staying within the turn and token limits proves nothing about recovery either, because resource accounting and acceptance are separate boundaries: mutating the service, verifying its health, and closing the ticket are distinct milestones that each require their own evidence. Sizing those limits is therefore a trade-off between blast radius and completion rate, since tighter ceilings bound exposure at the risk of halting a viable repair, whereas looser ones grant latitude that requires broader human oversight. Even within a well-sized envelope, however, those checks hold only if the state and evidence feeding each step stay aligned as the service changes underneath the run.

Before the mitigation, the context manifest selects diagnostic evidence describing the old configuration. Once the endpoint confirms that the rollback applied the new configuration, any prompt that still presents the old configuration as active state gives the model an incorrect basis for its next decision. The earlier observation remains true, but its role has changed; it no longer describes the live system and serves instead as historical evidence of the trajectory.


That role change is easy to miss when derived stores and serving caches sit between the database and the next prompt. A cached summary or vector index that still reports the old configuration after the rollback commits misleads the next turn even though the KV cache for the old prompt tokens remains mathematically valid. To keep those guarantees separate, the incident’s records occupy distinct roles in an evidence chain. The configuration service is the source record, the runtime operation log is the event log of decisions, approvals, and settlement status, model-written incident summaries are agent-written memory, and diagnostic vector indices are derived retrieval indexes. The context manifest is none of these; it is the working-context view assembled for the next model call. No derived role can override the source, and the operation log attests only to the events it durably wrote, not to an external effect it has not verified (The Trajectory Log).


↩︎ Source records, event logs, agent-written memory, and derived indexes as roles in an evidence chain are established in Record roles.
When the source confirms the new configuration, context assembly updates the active configuration entry, keeps the old record only where it justifies the remediation step, and invalidates derived artifacts that depend on the superseded version, such as diagnostic summaries and precomputed runbook excerpts. If the retrieval index lags, the runtime issues an authorized direct read, and if no read is possible the manifest records the omission rather than presenting stale data as current.


↩︎ Withdrawing a staged observation’s authority over current state when its source changes is established in Context Invalidation.
The serving system judges validity by a different rule. KV cache tensors computed for tokens describing the old configuration remain valid representations of those tokens whatever the service now holds, so substituting evidence for the new configuration ends prefix reuse at the first changed token and leaves the unchanged prefix reusable. Prefix coherence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)) governs computational reuse and source authority (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)) governs semantic freshness, and a cache hit establishes only the first. Freshness checks at prompt time also cannot freeze the service while the model deliberates, which is why the endpoint’s expected-version check at application remains the final guard.


↩︎ Reuse of KV state only over an exact token prefix computed under the same weights and execution parameters is established in Prefix compatibility.
Provenance follows the same separation. The runtime records which endpoint supplied each observation under the read grant, its timestamp and version, any filtering applied, and the model request that consumed it, and these host-verified events stay distinct from the model’s hypotheses about the cause of the alert. Text read from a trusted store, including an instruction injected into a log stream, gains no authority by being stored there. Permissions are evaluated against capability grants, and observed data remains passive payload.



In the source-to-context example, storage and serving each operate within their local specifications while the agent as a whole acts on stale evidence. Delegation makes the final row concrete without changing the acceptance contract. A worker may receive a subset of the read grant, a reusable capability, but a consumable allowance cannot be copied the same way; concurrent workers reserve against one shared budget rather than each receiving an independently spendable quota (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)). With these records in place, an auditor can reconstruct what the runtime observed, what it proposed, what authority it held, and what state the external world committed. Turning that evidence into an admissible next action, whether settling an ambiguous request or dispatching a compensating repair, falls to the execution and recovery boundary.




The incident trace resolved its lost reply with a single status query, and it could do so only because every piece of state that query needed was persisted before the network dropped the reply. Three properties made each step admissible: durability that covers the declared failure domain, evidence states the runtime keeps apart, and obligations that outlive the process that created them.


The trace wrote the intent for the rollback and its obligation registration before the request left (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)), binding the operation to its request, approval, endpoint contract, reservation, and accountable owner. Registering the obligation only after a response would have left exactly the gap the lost reply exposed, an active remote mutation with no durable record of who must reconcile it. The ordering is a database write-ahead log applied to an external effect, with one difference that shapes everything after it. A database’s recovery manager can redo or undo a logged update itself. The runtime can neither redo nor undo the endpoint’s mutation: the log tells it which operation to ask about, and only the endpoint can answer. The acknowledgment must also cover the declared failure domain, since a local fsync does not survive the loss of the storage device, and the execution gate withholds dispatch when that acknowledgment is missing or ambiguous. Recording intent commits the system to track the operation, not to execute it, so a pause or a revoked authority can still withhold the unsent request.


↩︎ Durable intent, the admitted operation acknowledged by storage that survives the declared failure domain before dispatch, is established in Durable Intent Before Dispatch.



Neither the expired timer nor the surviving intent log can say which of the trace’s three outcomes occurred. Because the agent’s local log and the external configuration service cannot share one atomic transaction, recovery from a lost reply depends on guarantees at the endpoint, and issuing an idempotent status query rather than a fresh mutation is settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)). Once correlated evidence confirms that the endpoint applied the new configuration, dependent tasks may consume the result, and any later replay of the same operation must conform to the endpoint’s repeat contract and pass admission checks again. Settling the operation does not complete acceptance, which still needs service-health evidence. The operation’s budget reservation also stays open until settlement, because a charge for remote work can arrive after its reply, as the canceled child with a late bill showed in Spending Governance.



In this incident, the database configuration is restorable selected state, because the endpoint keeps the old version and a further versioned write can return to it. The queries the service answered while a wrong configuration was live are a different matter, a commitment that cannot be undone. That is why the health window, not a later rollback, limits the damage of a wrong change. To separate those cases before any mutation leaves the harness, a recovery contract asks three things of every effect before dispatch: its target state, the recovery action available under the task’s authority, and the evidence that would show recovery worked.
Even a write that restores the old configuration is a compensating step in the sense of the trajectory saga (definition \(\ref{dfn-trajectory-saga}\)). It is a new forward action that observers may see half-applied, not an erasure of the first. It needs current credentials, approval, and preconditions checked against the live service, the same admission the typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)) applies to any forward action. Because the operation was itself a rollback, restoring the old configuration would reinstate the one the incident was opened against, so the useful correction after a wrong rollback is usually a newly diagnosed change. Compensations can themselves stall or fail partially. Rolling back a local workspace cannot reverse an external configuration change, just as a network cancellation request cannot guarantee that the remote endpoint stopped executing. Until an authorized successor acknowledges the handoff, every residual obligation stays with the operations owner.


↩︎ Restoring selected state, compensating a known effect, and managing a commitment that cannot be undone are established as recovery contracts in Recovery contracts.
Stopping a run must preserve admitted work in the same way. A semantic watchdog that halts a stalled loop can mistake legitimate polling of a pending status for a livelock, so the harness backs it with a hard dispatch ceiling. A hold then suspends new speculative dispatches, preserves every admitted operation, and lets only separately authorized settlement and recovery work proceed.

Checkpoint 20.2: Auditing the incident's action boundary
Each prompt names a failure at the action boundary; decide which record or check must catch it.

Changed precondition: approval_42 names config_v7, but another operator changes the configuration before application. Which check must prevent the stale proposal from applying, and who may authorize a revised change?
Retry exposure: The log contains the intent for op_42, but no response. If some fraction of lost replies hide an applied change, what fraction of fresh-identity retries duplicate the change, and which endpoint guarantee brings that fraction to zero?
Missing obligation: A design registers the recovery obligation only after receiving success. Identify the failure interval this leaves uncovered and the record and owner that must survive it.
Unresolved exit: The follow-up allowance expires while status remains unknown. Which operation, financial liability, and handoff records must remain even though this continuation ends?



Because every failure in this trace is anchored to a defined boundary and an accountable owner, the record also shows where the next safeguard belongs. Choosing that safeguard is itself a decision that needs evidence.




An execution trace supports a more precise question than whether the agent needs a larger model. If the context manifest still presents the old configuration as current after settlement confirms the new one, the defect lies in state selection. If the runtime blindly retries the rollback after a timeout, the defect lies in outcome handling and the endpoint’s recovery contract. Further training might change how often the model reaches these paths, but new weights cannot supply a missing state transition or make a non-idempotent retry safe.
Intervention selection pairs an attributed failure with a targeted remedy, and the intervention ladder orders the candidates by cost and reversibility. Context and retrieval, tool interfaces, and runtime control come before changes to model weights, which are reserved for residual failures that evidence traces to the model’s behavior rather than to a missing record or check. The ordering is a default justified by cost, not a sequence every failure must climb; an authorization bypass points directly to a runtime enforcement repair.


↩︎ The intervention ladder ordering candidate remedies by operational cost and reversibility is established in The intervention ladder.


Placing a failure on that ladder requires more than reading the execution log, because a trace records only the path the run took. To isolate which layer caused a failed run of this incident, the engineer reconstructs the saved input, tool contract, runtime state, and outcome. The engineer then varies one suspected factor at a time in a counterfactual replay. Supplying the new configuration in the staged context tests whether stale state misled the model, and replacing a generic timeout with an explicit pending status tests whether the tool interface hid an in-flight operation. Once a single change repairs the failure on replay, the candidate fix is evaluated across the affected task suite alongside regression checks on unrelated workloads. Adapting model weights reshapes which actions the model proposes; it never relieves the runtime of enforcing contracts, budgets, or security boundaries. Both must show their gains on the deployment distribution, and a sandboxed reward evaluator can still be gamed or miss edge cases of the task.


↩︎ Reward hacking, which exploits the gap between a verifiable reward and the intended task, is established in The score and the intended outcome.
Delegation lies outside the ladder. Partitioning a task across agents changes topology, ownership boundaries, and communication overhead rather than repairing a failed component, and a workload with cleanly decoupled subtasks may warrant it without any training. The baseline is a capable single controller with selective retrieval and parallel tool calls, and the comparison must charge the redundant contexts, serialization across dependencies, and reconciliation that make up the coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)). Diagnostic sub-agents reading logs in parallel could shorten triage for this incident, with no worker permitted to apply production changes, but only if the serial share and integration overhead pass the screen of equation 18.1. Diagnosis accounts for only 20 percent of this incident’s time to mitigate, while operator approval takes 50 percent and applying and verifying the change takes the rest. Because parallel sub-agents can compress only that 20 percent diagnostic window while approval and verification remain in the serial fraction of equation 18.1, the screen is hard to pass, which is why this incident closed without delegation.


↩︎ Benchmarking a multi-agent design against a single controller with matched tools, budgets, and concurrency limits is established in Matched comparison conditions.
An intervention that improves reliability must also pay for itself. A one-time investment in data, training, and evaluation is recovered only after enough tasks have run for the per-task saving to repay it (equation 19.8), and the comparison holds only while both configurations accept the same share of tasks. Choosing an intervention therefore combines attribution, matched comparison, and end-to-end cost accounting, while authority and acceptance stay outside the configuration being changed. Once a remedy is chosen, the remaining question is what evidence supports releasing the changed configuration within its declared envelope.


↩︎ The break-even task volume of an adaptation investment is established in Payback of an adaptation investment.




An incident record links an approved configuration change to an observed service outcome, but the link does not imply general correctness. The engineer must still establish which claims the record supports, which enforcement mechanisms make those claims trustworthy, and which failure modes remain unaddressed. That work takes the form of an empirical safety case: an inspectable, structured argument that specific claims hold within a defined operating envelope, not a certificate that the agent behaves correctly under all reachable conditions.1

Each case connects three elements: a claim states a specific operational property such as authorization validity or idempotency, an argument explains how the architecture and runtime mechanisms enforce that property, and evidence backs the argument with audit logs, telemetry windows, regression suites, and operator review traces. As assurance-case methodology emphasizes (Lipson 2013), citing a governance tool or testing practice is not enough; the case must show enforcement, coverage, and relevance to the artifact actually deployed, and it records assumptions and counterexamples so that reviewers can see where the argument stops.

An agent’s diagnostic report can point engineers to anomalous telemetry or inconsistent logs, but it cannot prove its own successful execution. A recorded operator sign-off counts as evidence only where the contract requires it, and human review has its own failure modes and blind spots, so it needs the same provenance and scope checks as an automated assertion.



The three claims of table 7 concern one execution. Releasing the configuration that handled it is a population question, answered by the staged offline, shadow, and canary evidence of Staged Releases under causal and statistical release evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\)). In that comparison this incident counts as a single trial, and halving the detectable difference between two configurations quadruples the tasks per arm (equation 13.3), so one incident cannot settle a release. Had the rollback stayed unknown at the observation cutoff, that trial would count as unresolved even if latency later recovered, because healthy telemetry on one service does not settle an outstanding effect.
Staged exposure carries the limit the incident showed. Stopping a canary, revoking its tokens, or draining its traffic halts only future dispatches; a request the endpoint has already applied, as it applied the rollback before the reply was lost, persists with its settlement owner. A release safety case therefore documents how partially executed work is contained and settled rather than assuming that rolling back a container image restores world state.

An incident trace does not automatically belong in a learning pipeline. If an engineer proposes extracting a segment as a training record, the training admission predicates decide whether its context, targets, permissions, and provenance qualify. An unresolved or aborted trace is not a negative example because a lost reply or an expired deadline can halt a trajectory after the model proposed the right repair, and penalizing that action trains the policy against valid proposals. Validation suites must also stay out of the training loop, because repeatedly selecting policies against the same evaluation set erodes its statistical validity (Dwork et al. 2015). Here the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) meets release evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\)). Once a verification metric becomes a training loss or reward, it loses its standing as an independent assessment. This is Goodhart’s law in the form How search exploits imperfect checks met it under search and The score and the intended outcome met it under training. Optimization concentrates on the verifier’s blind spots, so release evidence must come from checks the optimization never observed.

Updating model weights or prompts produces a new configuration that needs fresh release evidence, not an endorsement inherited from past incidents. A weight update also invalidates serving state, since KV tensors computed under the old weights are not valid for the new model even when the prefix text is identical. The safety case therefore binds to the exact configuration scheduled for deployment, and the resolution of this incident remains an audit of one execution, not a clearance for later versions.

Checkpoint 20.3: Defend the incident's acceptance
Each prompt tests whether a piece of evidence supports the claim it is attached to.

Claim scope: Which records establish that the approved change applied, and why is acceptable latency alone insufficient?
Missing evidence: If operation status remains unavailable, what must stay unresolved and who retains responsibility?
Evidence quality: How can a model report or human review contribute without becoming independent proof of every claimed property?
Evidence volume: A team can afford only twice as many release tasks per arm. By equation 13.3, by what factor does the smallest difference it can detect shrink, and is that enough to rank two configurations that differ by a few points?
Changed configuration: Why do stopping candidate admissions and preserving the same prompt establish neither reversal of earlier effects nor compatibility of old KV state with new weights?



An inspectable safety case makes the acceptance decision transparent and lists its residual risks, including states outside the measurement window, shifting workloads, and unverified edge cases, as explicit design constraints. A case that names its limits is the only kind a reviewer can check.




The safety case for this incident establishes a bounded claim, that an approved configuration change produced acceptable service behavior under a declared contract. Even with every policy boundary enforced, every tool call sandboxed, and every transition logged, three systems questions remain open: how completely acceptance criteria capture service health, how to stay consistent when production state changes during deliberation, and how far the audit trail supports causal attribution.
Acceptance criteria are incomplete. The telemetry from the health window satisfies the latency and error thresholds of the incident contract, yet a service can meet those two metrics while exhausting background worker pools, corrupting downstream records, or leaking memory. Rubric-guided reviews can catch some of these regressions, but human and model judges have blind spots of their own. Tamper-proofing a check stops an agent from modifying its own evaluation without making the specification complete. Coverage grows only as unmodeled failure modes are found and written into the contract, and searching many candidate actions against an incomplete check overfits the search to the proxy.


↩︎ Calibrating rubric-based human and model judges, whose shared mistakes survive high agreement, is established in Calibration of qualitative judgment.
Concurrent state drift imposes a second limit, because production services do not pause while an agent deliberates. While the agent fetches telemetry, runs model calls, or waits for approval, traffic shifts, autoscalers adjust capacity, and peer services deploy schema updates. An expected-version check at the write keeps an approved change off a mutated baseline, but a rejected mutation only restarts the loop, since the agent must re-read state, revise its diagnosis, and seek a fresh approval. When churn is fast or deliberation is slow, the agent can livelock, spending its step and token budgets on retries that never land. Designing protocols that balance evidence freshness, lock granularity, and deliberation latency within bounded incident budgets remains an open systems challenge.
Causal attribution is narrower than the execution record, because an audit log establishes temporal order, not cause. That the rollback applied the new configuration just before the health window recorded healthy telemetry does not prove the change resolved the incident; a transient network bottleneck, an upstream dependency, or a client retry storm may have cleared on its own. Controlled comparisons, fault-injection tests, and dependency analysis can support a causal claim where operations allow them.
A second attribution problem arises inside long trajectories, which this incident is too short to show. When a trajectory fails only at its final acceptance check, the postmortem faces two distinct questions. The first is locating the earliest observable mismatch, which is a replay problem: where retained inputs and boundary records support reconstruction, comparing the run step by step against a reference execution finds that divergence under a declared equivalence relation, even though divergence alone does not prove which action caused the failure. Showing which step was responsible, meaning that a different choice there would have passed, is a counterfactual problem whose search space is every untaken branch. That counterfactual search space grows as the branching factor raised to the task horizon \(\TurnHorizon\), the same exponent that drives the reliability decay of equation 1.1. It is the credit-assignment problem of Baselines and credit assignment seen from the debugging side, with one terminal verdict and every turn a candidate for blame. With an illustrative four candidate actions per step over a fifty-step task, that space spans \(4^{50} \approx 10^{30}\) paths, far beyond any practical replay budget.
Passing checks every five steps can change this arithmetic. If check coverage establishes that the defect occurred after the last passing check, and the window’s state is isolated and safely restorable, the search covers a single five-step window of \(4^{5} = 1,024\) alternatives, about 20 minutes of replay at 1.2 s per check. Without those two conditions, the investigation must keep earlier steps and external changes as possible causes.


↩︎ Replaying a recorded run to its first divergence point is established in Locating a Divergence.
Digital systems, the scope of this book, routinely produce effects that cannot be restored: spent compute and API budgets, third-party financial transactions, messages sent to people, and credentials leaked to external logs. Physical actuation adds sensing, kinematics, continuous dynamics, and hard real-time deadlines, which lie beyond this book’s scope. Software agents are nonetheless not confined to reversible simulation. Both kinds of system act across the causal boundary into a world whose state cannot be rolled back by terminating a process, and in both the engineer must catalog what state can be observed, what actions can be controlled, what effects can be restored, and which residual risks escalate to an accountable human principal.
These boundaries define the scope of an automated acceptance decision and the residual duties it leaves behind, and setting that scope is an engineering responsibility. Models and runtimes can propose plans, run diagnostic checks, and optimize candidate actions, but they cannot assume organizational accountability. Deciding which failure modes are acceptable, which invariants must hold, and which operational risks require human oversight remains the non-delegable duty of authorized system architects.



Suppose an incident model proposes shortening the observation window so that the database service can be declared recovered sooner. The model can state the trade-offs, draft the revised acceptance predicate, and identify supporting metrics, yet none of that alters the incident contract. Until the authorized contract owner adopts a revision through the change-management policy, the runtime evaluates the incident against the existing criteria. Helping to formulate a decision is different from holding the authority to make it binding.
Brooks separated the essential difficulty of conceptualizing complex software entities from the accidental difficulty of expressing them in a particular programming language or machine environment (Brooks 1987). In incident management, producing a configuration change is the accidental part; deciding which service behaviors count as recovery, and which risks the change introduces, is the essential work. An agent can generate a valid configuration payload while the recovery criteria remain poorly specified, and faster payload generation does nothing to resolve that ambiguity.

Brooks, Frederick P. 1987. “No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering.” Computer 20 (4): 10–19.
The boundary does not confine language models to syntax. An agent can propose requirements, weigh design trade-offs, expose inconsistent assumptions across services, or draft fault-injection tests, all of which is conceptual work, and its value depends on the verifiable evidence and arguments it produces. If a fraction of specification and review remains unaided by models, that work acts as the serial fraction in the Amdahl bound of equation 18.1, here with one human and one model rather than many workers. A task whose specification and review require half of the original effort cannot finish more than twice as fast, however quickly the model produces everything else, so end-to-end turnaround stays dominated by deliberate human specification and review.
The specification boundary applies the task contract of The five-part task contract to revisions of that contract, separating candidate proposal from authoritative adoption. The organization responsible for a service decides who may approve changes to its goals, permissions, and acceptance conditions, and the runtime enforces those policies. An agent gains no governance authority by authoring a new contract, and it cannot enlarge its own permissions or relax its evaluation when a task becomes difficult. This is invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) applied to the contract itself; the model can no more alter its own acceptance criteria than certify its own execution trace.
Approval bindings and acceptance records enforce the boundary in practice, because the agent cannot create either by declaring it. An agent that finds a real flaw in the criteria can trigger an authorized review, and the review records which contract governed the attempted execution and which evidence supports any revised claim, so that an unmet condition is never silently replaced by a more lenient one. Even a valuable contract revision proposed by an agent governs production only after it passes that formal adoption process.
The same boundary governs tests. An agent-written test suite has real value even when the model also drafted the implementation, but both can encode the same mistaken requirement. Candidates are therefore judged against the adopted contract, protected regression suites, live observations, and qualified human review, and agreement between a generated candidate and its co-generated tests never counts as independent verification. Across code, tests, and contracts alike, agents can support accountable decisions about bounded tasks, while deciding what those tasks mean remains the responsibility of the system’s owners.



Accepting an automated remediation safely depends on keeping four concerns apart: capability, enforcement, evidence, and accountability. Even when the model proposes an accurate diagnosis and a valid fix, each answers a different question, and conflating them lets a locally successful component close the task before the environment has verified the result.

Fallacy: A sufficiently capable model removes the need for explicit runtime boundaries.
Deploying a more capable model improves diagnostic accuracy and produces fewer malformed actions, but training suppresses the rate of violating proposals without driving it to zero. Over multi-step operational horizons, compound probability amplifies whatever residual risk remains, as captured by equation 1.1. Even with a residual violation rate of only 0.1 percent per step, 4.9 percent of 50-turn trajectories generate at least one violating proposal. Across 10,000 daily trajectories in production, that tiny fraction yields roughly 488 hazardous proposals each day. Explicit runtime boundaries determine whether each proposal is safely intercepted or permitted to produce side effects on live infrastructure. In the incident, even an accurate restoration proposal still requires strict approval bindings and version checks; model confidence can never authorize the rollback.


Pitfall: Treating passing checks as proof of the entire completion claim.



An accurate check shrinks the invalid share from 70 percent to about one in nine, not to zero.
Observing acceptable service latency does not prove that an approved operation occurred, because external traffic might have simply subsided. Conversely, confirming that a configuration change took effect does not guarantee that the service has returned to healthy operation. A valid completion certificate, such as the acceptance record, must assemble evidence of both correct execution and restored service behavior, alongside all mandatory policy checks. Passing a check is also weaker assurance than the check’s accuracy suggests, because under verifier precision (equation 3.3) the base rate dominates. If only 30 percent of proposed candidate actions are valid, a verifier that misses 10 percent of valid proposals while mistakenly passing 5 percent of invalid ones still leaves 11.5 percent of its passing set invalid. This is the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) in numbers; high nominal accuracy does not ensure correctness when candidate quality is low. A defensible safety case therefore documents the scope and blind spots of each check and assigns an owner to any residual monitoring.


Fallacy: An intervention is justified because it is the next rung of the intervention ladder.
The intervention ladder organizes mitigation strategies by ascending operational cost and decreasing reversibility, but stepping to the next rung does not ensure that the action addresses the underlying defect. A stale context entry, an unconstrained retry loop, and an inaccurate model diagnosis call for different remedies, and escalating to a heavier mechanism adds cost whether or not it fixes the problem. For example, adapting a smaller model (priced in Payback of an adaptation investment) demands a one-time investment in data, training, and evaluation that is recovered only over a large volume of reviews, and the payback period lengthens in proportion when review volume falls short of plan. That investment yields zero return if the operational failure actually resided in prompt context or the retry policy. Interventions should follow directly from attributed cause, comparative outcome evidence, and total lifecycle costs; model fine-tuning and operational delegation remain specialized tools rather than automatic defaults.


Pitfall: Allowing the component producing a result to redefine the conditions for accepting it.
A model can identify an unstated requirement, draft a new integration test, or propose revising an impractical service-level objective, but it never holds the authority to shorten the health window, expand its own permissions, or certify its own completion claim. Redefining acceptance to declare success early also carries a statistical penalty, because halving the observation window halves the metric samples. For approximately independent measurements, this reduction widens the confidence interval on the service latency estimate by a factor of 1.41. The revised claim then rests on weaker evidence at the moment the incident is hardest to verify. Modifying acceptance criteria requires explicit sign-off from the designated system authority, backed by an audit record detailing which contract version governs the work. Delegating automated reasoning or execution to an agent never transfers the ultimate responsibility for accepting the result.




The incident connects the book’s components through one concrete task rather than an abstract reference architecture. Context assembly supplies telemetry and logs with verifiable provenance and freshness, so the foundation model can propose a grounded diagnosis and configuration rollback. The action boundary admits that proposal only after validating its approval and version precondition. Durable logs record the intent before dispatch and track the unresolved outcome across the lost reply, until service telemetry and policy checks verify recovery against the contract. Each component satisfies a local specification, and the end-to-end integrity of the system comes from the records, checks, and ownership chains that bind them together. Table 8 summarizes the quantitative relations that govern an agentic execution trajectory, linking the compounding error of unchecked steps to the economics of verification, retry safety, and parallel delegation.
