Adapting model weights reshapes which actions the model proposes; it never relieves the runtime of enforcing contracts, budgets, or security boundaries. Supervised fine-tuning imitates demonstrated recovery paths, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards optimizes behavior through exploration. Both must show their gains on the deployment distribution, and a sandboxed reward evaluator can still be gamed or miss edge cases of the task.


↩︎ Reward hacking, which exploits the gap between a verifiable reward and the intended task, is established in The score and the intended outcome.
Delegation lies outside the ladder. Partitioning a task across agents changes topology, ownership boundaries, and communication overhead rather than repairing a failed component, and a workload with cleanly decoupled subtasks may warrant it without any training. The baseline is a capable single controller with selective retrieval and parallel tool calls, and the comparison must charge the redundant contexts, serialization across dependencies, and reconciliation that make up the coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)). Diagnostic sub-agents reading logs in parallel could shorten triage for this incident, with no worker permitted to apply production changes, but only if the serial share and integration overhead pass the screen of equation 18.1. Diagnosis accounts for only 20 percent of this incident’s time to mitigate, while operator approval takes 50 percent and applying and verifying the change takes the rest. Because parallel sub-agents can compress only that 20 percent diagnostic window while approval and verification remain in the serial fraction of equation 18.1, the screen is hard to pass, which is why this incident closed without delegation.


↩︎ Benchmarking a multi-agent design against a single controller with matched tools, budgets, and concurrency limits is established in Matched comparison conditions.
An intervention that improves reliability must also pay for itself. A one-time investment in data, training, and evaluation is recovered only after enough tasks have run for the per-task saving to repay it (equation 19.8), and the comparison holds only while both configurations accept the same share of tasks. Choosing an intervention therefore combines attribution, matched comparison, and end-to-end cost accounting, while authority and acceptance stay outside the configuration being changed. Once a remedy is chosen, the remaining question is what evidence supports releasing the changed configuration within its declared envelope.


↩︎ The break-even task volume of an adaptation investment is established in Payback of an adaptation investment.

title: 20 Conclusion
text:
An incident record links an approved configuration change to an observed service outcome, but the link does not imply general correctness. The engineer must still establish which claims the record supports, which enforcement mechanisms make those claims trustworthy, and which failure modes remain unaddressed. That work takes the form of an empirical safety case: an inspectable, structured argument that specific claims hold within a defined operating envelope, not a certificate that the agent behaves correctly under all reachable conditions.1
1 Goal Structuring Notation (GSN): Kelly and Weaver (2004) presented a graphical notation for safety arguments that represents the claims being asserted, the strategies that decompose them, the operational context and assumptions under which they hold, and the empirical evidence that supports them. Structuring an argument explicitly uncovers claims lacking supporting evidence or unverified operational assumptions, which are the gaps that table 7 is designed to expose. 
Kelly, Tim, and Rob Weaver. 2004. The Goal Structuring Notation: A Safety Argument Notation.

Lipson, Howard. 2013. Assurance Cases Overview. Software Engineering Institute, Carnegie Mellon University.
Each case connects three elements: a claim states a specific operational property such as authorization validity or idempotency, an argument explains how the architecture and runtime mechanisms enforce that property, and evidence backs the argument with audit logs, telemetry windows, regression suites, and operator review traces. As assurance-case methodology emphasizes (Lipson 2013), citing a governance tool or testing practice is not enough; the case must show enforcement, coverage, and relevance to the artifact actually deployed, and it records assumptions and counterexamples so that reviewers can see where the argument stops.


Showing that the rollback restored latency on the database during the health window does not prove that the remediation agent is safe to run on arbitrary database incidents. Table 7 scopes the safety case for this incident to the mediated database change and its observed outcome, combining runtime records with the validation suites a production case requires so that each row states what the case must verify rather than asserting that every offline test ran during the live incident.



Table 7: An Incident Safety Case in Three Claims: Mechanisms, records, and assumptions support different parts of the argument. Evidence sufficient for one claim does not automatically establish the others.











Scoped claim
Argument and owner
Supporting evidence
Assumptions and residual uncertainty




The mediated change to db_primary_01 requires approval for the exact request and current preconditions
The action gate checks approval_42 against change_request_42, its target, desired settings, expected config_v7, and validity conditions before dispatch
The approval and admission records, together with tests of missing, expired, mismatched, and stale approvals
The argument depends on controlled access paths and endpoint enforcement; an unrelated privileged operator or bypass is outside this particular gate’s claim


The lost response does not justify issuing a fresh duplicate change
The settlement process preserves op_42 for operations_owner_42 and reconciles through the endpoint’s operation-status and deduplication contract
Durable intent and obligation registration recorded before dispatch; the lost-response status; the later source confirmation that op_42 applied config_v8
The endpoint must honor the stated identity, atomic version check, and retention contract, including delayed requests; unavailable status leaves the operation unresolved rather than proving failure


The incident meets incident_contract_v1 under the recorded acceptance scope
The acceptance owner checks the applied configuration, required change-policy conditions, and the declared service measurement window
acceptance_42 references op_42, config_v8, health_window_42, required checks, and the authorized adopter
Measurements cover the named service and window, not every future condition; they do not prove the model’s diagnosis, and post-window monitoring remains with operations_owner_42






An agent’s diagnostic report can point engineers to anomalous telemetry or inconsistent logs, but it cannot prove its own successful execution. A recorded operator sign-off counts as evidence only where the contract requires it, and human review has its own failure modes and blind spots, so it needs the same provenance and scope checks as an automated assertion.



The three claims of table 7 concern one execution. Releasing the configuration that handled it is a population question, answered by the staged offline, shadow, and canary evidence of Staged Releases under causal and statistical release evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\)). In that comparison this incident counts as a single trial, and halving the detectable difference between two configurations quadruples the tasks per arm (equation 13.3), so one incident cannot settle a release. Had the rollback stayed unknown at the observation cutoff, that trial would count as unresolved even if latency later recovered, because healthy telemetry on one service does not settle an outstanding effect.
Staged exposure carries the limit the incident showed. Stopping a canary, revoking its tokens, or draining its traffic halts only future dispatches; a request the endpoint has already applied, as it applied the rollback before the reply was lost, persists with its settlement owner. A release safety case therefore documents how partially executed work is contained and settled rather than assuming that rolling back a container image restores world state.


↩︎ Tripwires that stop admission, and rollback that leaves transmitted requests and changed objects in place, are established in Operational tripwires.



An incident trace does not automatically belong in a learning pipeline. If an engineer proposes extracting a segment as a training record, the training admission predicates decide whether its context, targets, permissions, and provenance qualify. An unresolved or aborted trace is not a negative example because a lost reply or an expired deadline can halt a trajectory after the model proposed the right repair, and penalizing that action trains the policy against valid proposals. Validation suites must also stay out of the training loop, because repeatedly selecting policies against the same evaluation set erodes its statistical validity (Dwork et al. 2015). Here the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) meets release evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\)). Once a verification metric becomes a training loss or reward, it loses its standing as an independent assessment. This is Goodhart’s law in the form How search exploits imperfect checks met it under search and The score and the intended outcome met it under training. Optimization concentrates on the verifier’s blind spots, so release evidence must come from checks the optimization never observed.

Dwork, Cynthia, Vitaly Feldman, Moritz Hardt, Toniann Pitassi, Omer Reingold, and Aaron Roth. 2015. “The Reusable Holdout: Preserving Validity in Adaptive Data Analysis.” Science 349 (6248): 636–38. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aaa9375.

↩︎ The admission predicates for a training record, covering record fidelity, permitted use, process and outcome conditions, and target suitability, are established in Admission predicates.

Updating model weights or prompts produces a new configuration that needs fresh release evidence, not an endorsement inherited from past incidents. A weight update also invalidates serving state, since KV tensors computed under the old weights are not valid for the new model even when the prefix text is identical. The safety case therefore binds to the exact configuration scheduled for deployment, and the resolution of this incident remains an audit of one execution, not a clearance for later versions.

Checkpoint 20.3: Defend the incident's acceptance
Each prompt tests whether a piece of evidence supports the claim it is attached to.

Claim scope: Which records establish that the approved change applied, and why is acceptable latency alone insufficient?
Missing evidence: If operation status remains unavailable, what must stay unresolved and who retains responsibility?
Evidence quality: How can a model report or human review contribute without becoming independent proof of every claimed property?
Evidence volume: A team can afford only twice as many release tasks per arm. By equation 13.3, by what factor does the smallest difference it can detect shrink, and is that enough to rank two configurations that differ by a few points?
Changed configuration: Why do stopping candidate admissions and preserving the same prompt establish neither reversal of earlier effects nor compatibility of old KV state with new weights?



An inspectable safety case makes the acceptance decision transparent and lists its residual risks, including states outside the measurement window, shifting workloads, and unverified edge cases, as explicit design constraints. A case that names its limits is the only kind a reviewer can check.

title: 20 Conclusion
text:
The safety case for this incident establishes a bounded claim, that an approved configuration change produced acceptable service behavior under a declared contract. Even with every policy boundary enforced, every tool call sandboxed, and every transition logged, three systems questions remain open: how completely acceptance criteria capture service health, how to stay consistent when production state changes during deliberation, and how far the audit trail supports causal attribution.
Acceptance criteria are incomplete. The telemetry from the health window satisfies the latency and error thresholds of the incident contract, yet a service can meet those two metrics while exhausting background worker pools, corrupting downstream records, or leaking memory. Rubric-guided reviews can catch some of these regressions, but human and model judges have blind spots of their own. Tamper-proofing a check stops an agent from modifying its own evaluation without making the specification complete. Coverage grows only as unmodeled failure modes are found and written into the contract, and searching many candidate actions against an incomplete check overfits the search to the proxy.


↩︎ Calibrating rubric-based human and model judges, whose shared mistakes survive high agreement, is established in Calibration of qualitative judgment.
Concurrent state drift imposes a second limit, because production services do not pause while an agent deliberates. While the agent fetches telemetry, runs model calls, or waits for approval, traffic shifts, autoscalers adjust capacity, and peer services deploy schema updates. An expected-version check at the write keeps an approved change off a mutated baseline, but a rejected mutation only restarts the loop, since the agent must re-read state, revise its diagnosis, and seek a fresh approval. When churn is fast or deliberation is slow, the agent can livelock, spending its step and token budgets on retries that never land. Designing protocols that balance evidence freshness, lock granularity, and deliberation latency within bounded incident budgets remains an open systems challenge.
Causal attribution is narrower than the execution record, because an audit log establishes temporal order, not cause. That the rollback applied the new configuration just before the health window recorded healthy telemetry does not prove the change resolved the incident; a transient network bottleneck, an upstream dependency, or a client retry storm may have cleared on its own. Controlled comparisons, fault-injection tests, and dependency analysis can support a causal claim where operations allow them.
A second attribution problem arises inside long trajectories, which this incident is too short to show. When a trajectory fails only at its final acceptance check, the postmortem faces two distinct questions. The first is locating the earliest observable mismatch, which is a replay problem: where retained inputs and boundary records support reconstruction, comparing the run step by step against a reference execution finds that divergence under a declared equivalence relation, even though divergence alone does not prove which action caused the failure. Showing which step was responsible, meaning that a different choice there would have passed, is a counterfactual problem whose search space is every untaken branch. That counterfactual search space grows as the branching factor raised to the task horizon \(\TurnHorizon\), the same exponent that drives the reliability decay of equation 1.1. It is the credit-assignment problem of Baselines and credit assignment seen from the debugging side, with one terminal verdict and every turn a candidate for blame. With an illustrative four candidate actions per step over a fifty-step task, that space spans \(4^{50} \approx 10^{30}\) paths, far beyond any practical replay budget.
Passing checks every five steps can change this arithmetic. If check coverage establishes that the defect occurred after the last passing check, and the window’s state is isolated and safely restorable, the search covers a single five-step window of \(4^{5} = 1,024\) alternatives, about 20 minutes of replay at 1.2 s per check. Without those two conditions, the investigation must keep earlier steps and external changes as possible causes.


↩︎ Replaying a recorded run to its first divergence point is established in Locating a Divergence.
Digital systems, the scope of this book, routinely produce effects that cannot be restored: spent compute and API budgets, third-party financial transactions, messages sent to people, and credentials leaked to external logs. Physical actuation adds sensing, kinematics, continuous dynamics, and hard real-time deadlines, which lie beyond this book’s scope. Software agents are nonetheless not confined to reversible simulation. Both kinds of system act across the causal boundary into a world whose state cannot be rolled back by terminating a process, and in both the engineer must catalog what state can be observed, what actions can be controlled, what effects can be restored, and which residual risks escalate to an accountable human principal.
These boundaries define the scope of an automated acceptance decision and the residual duties it leaves behind, and setting that scope is an engineering responsibility. Models and runtimes can propose plans, run diagnostic checks, and optimize candidate actions, but they cannot assume organizational accountability. Deciding which failure modes are acceptable, which invariants must hold, and which operational risks require human oversight remains the non-delegable duty of authorized system architects.

title: 20 Conclusion
text:
Suppose an incident model proposes shortening the observation window so that the database service can be declared recovered sooner. The model can state the trade-offs, draft the revised acceptance predicate, and identify supporting metrics, yet none of that alters the incident contract. Until the authorized contract owner adopts a revision through the change-management policy, the runtime evaluates the incident against the existing criteria. Helping to formulate a decision is different from holding the authority to make it binding.
Brooks separated the essential difficulty of conceptualizing complex software entities from the accidental difficulty of expressing them in a particular programming language or machine environment (Brooks 1987). In incident management, producing a configuration change is the accidental part; deciding which service behaviors count as recovery, and which risks the change introduces, is the essential work. An agent can generate a valid configuration payload while the recovery criteria remain poorly specified, and faster payload generation does nothing to resolve that ambiguity.

Brooks, Frederick P. 1987. “No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering.” Computer 20 (4): 10–19.
The boundary does not confine language models to syntax. An agent can propose requirements, weigh design trade-offs, expose inconsistent assumptions across services, or draft fault-injection tests, all of which is conceptual work, and its value depends on the verifiable evidence and arguments it produces. If a fraction of specification and review remains unaided by models, that work acts as the serial fraction in the Amdahl bound of equation 18.1, here with one human and one model rather than many workers. A task whose specification and review require half of the original effort cannot finish more than twice as fast, however quickly the model produces everything else, so end-to-end turnaround stays dominated by deliberate human specification and review.
The specification boundary applies the task contract of The five-part task contract to revisions of that contract, separating candidate proposal from authoritative adoption. The organization responsible for a service decides who may approve changes to its goals, permissions, and acceptance conditions, and the runtime enforces those policies. An agent gains no governance authority by authoring a new contract, and it cannot enlarge its own permissions or relax its evaluation when a task becomes difficult. This is invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) applied to the contract itself; the model can no more alter its own acceptance criteria than certify its own execution trace.
Approval bindings and acceptance records enforce the boundary in practice, because the agent cannot create either by declaring it. An agent that finds a real flaw in the criteria can trigger an authorized review, and the review records which contract governed the attempted execution and which evidence supports any revised claim, so that an unmet condition is never silently replaced by a more lenient one. Even a valuable contract revision proposed by an agent governs production only after it passes that formal adoption process.
The same boundary governs tests. An agent-written test suite has real value even when the model also drafted the implementation, but both can encode the same mistaken requirement. Candidates are therefore judged against the adopted contract, protected regression suites, live observations, and qualified human review, and agreement between a generated candidate and its co-generated tests never counts as independent verification. Across code, tests, and contracts alike, agents can support accountable decisions about bounded tasks, while deciding what those tasks mean remains the responsibility of the system’s owners.

title: 20 Conclusion
text:
Accepting an automated remediation safely depends on keeping four concerns apart: capability, enforcement, evidence, and accountability. Even when the model proposes an accurate diagnosis and a valid fix, each answers a different question, and conflating them lets a locally successful component close the task before the environment has verified the result.

Fallacy: A sufficiently capable model removes the need for explicit runtime boundaries.
Deploying a more capable model improves diagnostic accuracy and produces fewer malformed actions, but training suppresses the rate of violating proposals without driving it to zero. Over multi-step operational horizons, compound probability amplifies whatever residual risk remains, as captured by equation 1.1. Even with a residual violation rate of only 0.1 percent per step, 4.9 percent of 50-turn trajectories generate at least one violating proposal. Across 10,000 daily trajectories in production, that tiny fraction yields roughly 488 hazardous proposals each day. Explicit runtime boundaries determine whether each proposal is safely intercepted or permitted to produce side effects on live infrastructure. In the incident, even an accurate restoration proposal still requires strict approval bindings and version checks; model confidence can never authorize the rollback.


Pitfall: Treating passing checks as proof of the entire completion claim.



An accurate check shrinks the invalid share from 70 percent to about one in nine, not to zero.
Observing acceptable service latency does not prove that an approved operation occurred, because external traffic might have simply subsided. Conversely, confirming that a configuration change took effect does not guarantee that the service has returned to healthy operation. A valid completion certificate, such as the acceptance record, must assemble evidence of both correct execution and restored service behavior, alongside all mandatory policy checks. Passing a check is also weaker assurance than the check’s accuracy suggests, because under verifier precision (equation 3.3) the base rate dominates. If only 30 percent of proposed candidate actions are valid, a verifier that misses 10 percent of valid proposals while mistakenly passing 5 percent of invalid ones still leaves 11.5 percent of its passing set invalid. This is the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) in numbers; high nominal accuracy does not ensure correctness when candidate quality is low. A defensible safety case therefore documents the scope and blind spots of each check and assigns an owner to any residual monitoring.


Fallacy: An intervention is justified because it is the next rung of the intervention ladder.
The intervention ladder organizes mitigation strategies by ascending operational cost and decreasing reversibility, but stepping to the next rung does not ensure that the action addresses the underlying defect. A stale context entry, an unconstrained retry loop, and an inaccurate model diagnosis call for different remedies, and escalating to a heavier mechanism adds cost whether or not it fixes the problem. For example, adapting a smaller model (priced in Payback of an adaptation investment) demands a one-time investment in data, training, and evaluation that is recovered only over a large volume of reviews, and the payback period lengthens in proportion when review volume falls short of plan. That investment yields zero return if the operational failure actually resided in prompt context or the retry policy. Interventions should follow directly from attributed cause, comparative outcome evidence, and total lifecycle costs; model fine-tuning and operational delegation remain specialized tools rather than automatic defaults.


Pitfall: Allowing the component producing a result to redefine the conditions for accepting it.
A model can identify an unstated requirement, draft a new integration test, or propose revising an impractical service-level objective, but it never holds the authority to shorten the health window, expand its own permissions, or certify its own completion claim. Redefining acceptance to declare success early also carries a statistical penalty, because halving the observation window halves the metric samples. For approximately independent measurements, this reduction widens the confidence interval on the service latency estimate by a factor of 1.41. The revised claim then rests on weaker evidence at the moment the incident is hardest to verify. Modifying acceptance criteria requires explicit sign-off from the designated system authority, backed by an audit record detailing which contract version governs the work. Delegating automated reasoning or execution to an agent never transfers the ultimate responsibility for accepting the result.

title: 20 Conclusion
text:
The incident connects the book’s components through one concrete task rather than an abstract reference architecture. Context assembly supplies telemetry and logs with verifiable provenance and freshness, so the foundation model can propose a grounded diagnosis and configuration rollback. The action boundary admits that proposal only after validating its approval and version precondition. Durable logs record the intent before dispatch and track the unresolved outcome across the lost reply, until service telemetry and policy checks verify recovery against the contract. Each component satisfies a local specification, and the end-to-end integrity of the system comes from the records, checks, and ownership chains that bind them together. Table 8 summarizes the quantitative relations that govern an agentic execution trajectory, linking the compounding error of unchecked steps to the economics of verification, retry safety, and parallel delegation.



Table 8: Key Equations of the Conclusion: Each relation prices one term of an accepted task: unchecked reliability, cost, payback, check precision, retry exposure, irreversible loss, release evidence, delegation, and concurrency. Symbols carry the meanings given where each relation is derived.










Equation
What it bounds or decides
Where derived




\(\Pr(\text{success})=(1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}\)

equation 1.1


\(\CostPerAcceptedTask=\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]/\AcceptanceProbability\)
Charges every rejected attempt to the accepted ones, so raising acceptance can cut cost more than cheaper tokens
equation 1.2

equation 19.8


\(\VerifierPrecision=\dfrac{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)}{\ValidCandidateRate(1-\VerifierFalseRejectionRate)+(1-\ValidCandidateRate)\,\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate}\)

Retrying Uncertain Actions

Expected loss from actions without adequate reversal, which sets how much approval, checking, and compensation an action warrants
equation 12.5


\(\TasksPerComparisonArm\approx 2(\SignificanceCriticalQuantile+\StatisticalPowerQuantile)^2\,\PooledAcceptanceProbability(1-\PooledAcceptanceProbability)/\TargetAcceptanceDifference^2\)

equation 13.3

Delegation speedup, capped at \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) and reversed once coordination overhead grows faster than the parallel share shrinks
equation 18.1


\(\ConcurrentTrajectories=\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\)
Concurrent trajectories, and therefore the sessions, sandboxes, and cached state a workload holds at once
equation 19.4







Key Takeaways: Own every transition, bound every claim

Every consequential transition requires an explicit owner and a durable record: The request, decision, side effect, and resulting evidence must remain structurally linked throughout the trajectory. An unknown outcome is never a license to retry blindly; an ambiguous operation retains its human or system owner rather than fabricating a premature success or failure.
The contract, not a mechanism catalog, defines system boundaries: Task horizon, mutable state, and delegated authority dictate where a workload is vulnerable, and the formal contract determines which guardrails to deploy. Every telemetry record and intermediate artifact retains its provenance, authority level, and expiration window, ensuring that stale cached data never masquerades as fresh environmental evidence.
Interventions must follow attributed evidence, prioritizing the lowest-cost remedy: Prefer lower-cost, reversible remedies when they address the attributed failure; initiate fine-tuning or model changes only when evidence supports them. Compare candidate mitigations under identical task constraints while accounting for development, inference, verification, and recovery costs. Model fine-tuning and multi-agent delegation must justify themselves with measurable end-to-end gains rather than architectural ambition.
Claims must remain bounded by verifiable evidence, while ultimate adoption remains with human principals: A passing verification check supports acceptance strictly within its specified domain, with residual uncertainty and environmental assumptions made explicit. Models can synthesize specifications, generate test cases, and draft operational contracts, but designated human owners must ratify the governing contracts and acceptance procedures, and they retain accountability for whatever residual risks remain.






Unchecked success decays exponentially as the horizon grows.
This book opened with two foundational pieces of arithmetic, and every subsystem analyzed across these chapters addresses one of them. The first is horizon compounding (equation 1.1). With a per-step correctness rate of 99 percent, an unchecked trajectory succeeds 90.4 percent of the time across 10 turns, but falls to 36.6 percent across 100 turns. Post-training can reduce how often a policy proposes an invalid action, but it cannot drive violations to zero, so invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) stays anchored in mechanisms outside the model at any scale. Admission and verification turn detected violations into rejected attempts, typed action contracts intercept unsafe proposals before they take effect, and watchdogs limit how far an error propagates across turns. Durable intent logging and scoped compensation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) bound the cost of recovery, rolling back sandbox changes directly and compensating external effects through explicit forward operations.



Raising acceptance cuts cost per accepted task more than halving token price.
The second governing relation is the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2), which charges the compute and operational overhead of every rejected attempt to the few that are accepted. At $2.10 per attempt and a baseline 40 percent acceptance rate, each accepted task costs $5.25. Cutting the raw token price in half reduces this effective cost to $3.63, whereas improving task acceptance to 60 percent drives the cost down further to $3.50. The four lighthouses stress different terms of that balance, as Cost per Accepted Task by Archetype priced them. Sandbox holding and tools dominate the repair agent’s cost, research spends most on tokens through its sub-agent fan-out, and support spends most on escalation handoffs while its latency target needs separate capacity checks. Remediation spends most on human approval, and this incident showed why, since approval is most of each attempt’s cost and a wrong change costs far more than any attempt. In each case the intervention is chosen by pricing the work needed to improve the outcome, not by finding the largest cost term. Across all workloads, verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)) applies to the denominator: an attempt counts as accepted only within the explicit bounds validated by an authorized check.
This book began by distinguishing a proposed action from its realized side effect, and a plausible generation from an accepted task. In the incident that distinction ends in an auditable decision. The acceptance record binds the governing contract to the settled change, the passing checks, and scoped telemetry, while the operations owner remains responsible for the service after the window, and evidence that cannot be verified leaves an unresolved disposition rather than a fabricated completion. Each common failure of agent deployments meets a specific guard in this trace. A duplicated change from a blind retry meets the operation identity and settlement query, an incident closed before its change applied meets the acceptance record, and an untracked production change meets the intent log and its accountable owner. An audit trail of what the model proposed, what the action boundary permitted, what effects occurred, what evidence validated the result, and who remains responsible is the real deliverable of an agentic machine learning system.
Every mechanism in this book answers the same limitation, that the model samples stochastic outputs and cannot certify its own correctness. No advance in deep learning removes that uncertainty. What remains to engineer is the surrounding system, the harness and runtime that make a model’s proposals safe to execute, verifiable to accept, and economical to operate at scale.
Prof. Vijay Janapa Reddi, Harvard University

title: 18 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can splitting a task across several agents cost more and deliver less than giving one agent the same resources?
Splitting a task across several agents looks like the natural answer when the work is wide, since each worker can hold a smaller context and pursue its piece in parallel. The split replaces nothing the single agent already had. A capable single controller already runs searches and tests concurrently, keeps its context lean through retrieval and compaction, and holds scoped grants, so delegation must be judged against that baseline rather than against a fragile loop. What delegation adds is a set of boundaries between separately managed trajectories, and each boundary must carry explicitly what one trajectory carried implicitly. A worker can build against an interface that changes before its edit lands, two patches can merge cleanly and still break each other, reviewers that share a model can agree on the same mistake, and a canceled child can leave a container running and a budget half spent. Coordination overhead grows with every worker added, while the serial part of the task caps any speedup the parallel part can buy. Whether to split is therefore a measured decision. A multi-agent design earns its place only when it delivers more accepted tasks per unit of cost, or finishes them sooner in a way the objective values, than a single controller given the same tools and budget. Every handoff multiplies horizon, state, and authority, and the runtime must keep each delegated obligation owned until it settles.

Learning Objectives

Estimate the speedup and useful worker count of a work partition from its serial fraction and coordination overhead

The repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) has so far fixed a connection-pool race, a change confined to one module that a single controller holds comfortably in one context. Its next assignment is wider: migrate an authentication module across a repository, a change that reaches every caller of the module’s interface and is exactly the kind of repair task that tempts a split. The task naturally splits into two coupled changes: revising an internal interface and updating its downstream callers. A single coordinator could retain the entire task, dispatching parallel searches and test runs to collect evidence before synthesizing a unified patch. Alternatively, it could partition the problem, assigning the interface update and caller modifications to separate workers. Each worker operates within a focused context window, editing candidate files and reacting to compiler diagnostics independently. This division introduces an immediate distributed consistency challenge: the caller modifications must remain compatible with the interface that ultimately lands, not merely the snapshot the caller worker read at dispatch.



A fleet multiplies horizon, state, and authority, so every handoff must preserve closure.
The runtime mechanisms established in earlier chapters govern a single execution trajectory at a time. Within that boundary, the harness checks each model and tool invocation against an assigned grant and token budget. Durable execution logs one trajectory’s event history, and failure recovery settles, repairs, or compensates the effects of that one trajectory. Evaluation compares trials of one configuration against another, and curation and post-training improve the policy that drives it. Partitioning the migration preserves these local controls inside each individual worker, but it leaves the coordination space between them unmanaged. A single-agent runtime provides no mechanism to resolve which interface revision the caller worker targets, whether a clean textual merge of two patches preserves semantic correctness, or what consensus among five reviewer agents actually guarantees. Nor does it define who claims an orphaned test container after a coordinator cancels a subtask, or how a parent bounds the authority and compute budget delegated to a child. Without explicit systems controls, every such gap threatens to make the split cost far more than it buys.
Making delegation governable requires runtime controls, and deciding whether it pays requires an empirical framework. The required controls are state records and verification gates owned directly by the runtime rather than left to prompt instructions. They include enforceable task assignments and receipts that separate an agent’s self-reported claims from verified tool evidence. They also include a publication barrier that revalidates cross-module dependencies before any candidate patch merges, clean cancellation paths that account for in-flight work, and authority grants that narrow monotonically at every delegation hop. These mechanisms pair with a measurement discipline that compares each multi-agent design against a single agent holding equivalent parallel tools and resource budgets, and that prices every token consumed by failed, retried, or canceled subtasks.
The migration carries the argument from the decision to split through the final accounting, and each control answers a hazard that the previous one exposes. A screen of serial work against coordination overhead first decides whether a partition can pay at all (section 18.2). Dependency, communication, and supervision structures then fix what may run concurrently and who owns each child (section 18.3), and typed envelopes and receipts fix what crosses each handoff (section 18.4). Once workers run in parallel, guarded publication keeps their edits consistent (section 18.5), and a joint error model shows what agreement among reviewers can and cannot certify (section 18.6). Cancellation, hedging, and credit windows bound the work still in flight (section 18.7), and attenuated grants and atomic reservations bound authority and spending at every hop (section 18.8). A matched comparison against a capable single controller decides whether the whole design earns its tax (section 18.9).



Handing the interface update and the caller update to dedicated workers differs from issuing concurrent model queries, and that difference defines the unit of delegation. A delegated worker owns a bounded child trajectory with its own context window, model-and-tool loop, task contract, and independent lifecycle. Several candidate samples dispatched by one controller, such as the self-consistency votes of test-time compute, are instead parallel calls inside one trajectory. They are the cheapest ensemble an agent can run and also the most correlated, because every sample shares the model, the prompt, and the input’s difficulty, a dependence that section 18.6 quantifies. The architectural shift lies in establishing explicit boundaries between separately managed trajectories, regardless of whether those workers execute on a single host or across a distributed cluster.

The point of comparison throughout this chapter is the capable baseline: the single-agent runtime developed in earlier chapters, which already manages its context window, reserves system resources, verifies proposed tool effects externally, and executes candidate searches and isolated tools concurrently. Delegation retains every one of those operational requirements while introducing new coordination boundaries. The systems question is whether dividing control and context improves a declared task objective enough to justify the overhead of managing them.


When a single agent runs a wide repository migration inside one shared context and one broad authority grant, compiler diagnostics from one module crowd out the prompt needed for the next while every tool call carries permissions for the whole codebase. Context partitioning addresses the prompt growth directly: each worker retains only the material strictly necessary for its subtask. In the migration scenario, the interface worker maintains the target API contract and local unit tests without ingesting the intermediate compiler diagnostics of the caller worker, allowing each subsequent model invocation to process substantially fewer prompt tokens. However, the net token savings depend entirely on the structure of the decomposition. If both workers repeatedly require the full repository commit history, separate contexts duplicate prompt state rather than isolating it, a redundancy the single-agent baseline already avoids through retrieval and compaction.
Delegation also provides separate task ownership. Workers can pursue multi-turn exploratory investigations through iterative tool feedback and local reasoning loops while a central coordinator tracks inter-task dependencies and orchestrates final integration. Assigning task ownership, however, does not eliminate underlying data dependencies. A caller worker that generates code against an outdated interface must still reconcile its implementation once the interface worker finalizes the new contract. True operational independence derives from the causal graph of the task itself, never from cosmetic role descriptions in prompt templates.
Finally, decomposing work across workers enforces task-scoped authority, binding tools, execution capabilities, and resource budgets directly to individual subtasks. For example, a test-runner worker can be granted execution privileges in an isolated container without granting it credentials to publish pull requests or write to production databases. Even so, process isolation does not eliminate trust boundaries. A child worker’s textual output can still inject unvalidated claims or prompt injections into the parent coordinator’s context, and any external mutations it produces must still be verified and settled by the runtime. Splitting the authentication migration across separate interface and caller workers adds work that a single controller never performs: the coordinator spends turns packaging task assignments and reconciling returned diffs, both workers ingest shared repository context, and final integration waits at the join barrier for the slower child to finish. Every delegation boundary incurs this coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)).

Definition 18.1: Coordination tax
Coordination tax is the work and elapsed time a delegated design spends on handoffs rather than on the task: preparing and validating envelopes, delivering context, scheduling children, collecting receipts, and reconciling and integrating their results.

Significance: The tax enters both terms of the cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) (equation 1.2): its tokens and tool time raise \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]\), and the part on the critical path lengthens every attempt against its deadline.
Distinction: While task decomposition aims to reduce makespan by distributing work concurrently, the coordination tax represents the unavoidable friction introduced by that distribution. This tax scales with worker count, communication frequency, and inter-task dependencies.
Common pitfall: Accounting only for the tokens and execution time of successful worker turns. Context re-ingestion, supervisor arbitration turns, failed retries, and abandoned speculative branches all consume model quota and execution budgets.



Coordination tax impacts systems along two distinct dimensions: aggregate resource consumption and end-to-end latency. Duplicated input prompt tokens, redundant tool invocations, and serialize-deserialize cycles increase the total operational cost. Meanwhile, user-perceived delay is governed by makespan, the wall-clock time elapsed from the arrival of a task to the completion and verification of its final artifact. Makespan depends strictly on the operations situated on the critical path. A straggling child worker delays synchronization at the join barrier, while subsequent arbitration and reconciliation turns further inflate the critical path before results can be accepted.
Amdahl’s fixed-work argument1 gives the first screening model (Amdahl 1967). Let \(\SerialReferenceTime\) be the time for a fixed set of operations executed serially, with fraction \(\ParallelFraction\) perfectly divisible among \(\WorkerCount\) equally fast workers and fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) remaining serial. Assume enough resources for that division and let \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) be the additional elapsed overhead, normalized by \(\SerialReferenceTime\). Then
1 Amdahl’s Argument: Amdahl’s 1967 conference paper contains no equation; it argues in prose that the serial housekeeping of a program limits what any number of parallel processors can deliver, and the familiar formula was written down by later authors. The lesson transfers intact to delegation, where planning, integration, and final assessment are the housekeeping that no added worker absorbs.\[\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount)=\frac{\SerialReferenceTime}{\Time(\WorkerCount)}=\frac{1}{(1-\ParallelFraction)+\ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount+\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)}. \tag{1}\]
With no coordination overhead, \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=0\), equation 1 reduces to Amdahl’s law, and the serial term alone caps speedup at \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) for any number of workers. The equation provides a preliminary screening model for a specified work partition. The baseline \(\SerialReferenceTime\) reflects that partition executed sequentially on a single thread of execution, rather than the capable baseline runtime (which already pipelines tool executions and concurrent candidate samplings). In production, an empirical benchmark of the capable baseline must replace \(\SerialReferenceTime\) before finalizing any worker allocation. Within this theoretical formulation, achieving any net speedup over the serial reference requires that:
\[\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)<\ParallelFraction\left(1-\frac{1}{\WorkerCount}\right).\]
The right-hand side represents the theoretical wall-clock time saved by distributing the parallelizable portion across \(\WorkerCount\) workers. Whenever coordination overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) exceeds this threshold, the split task takes longer than serial execution. Furthermore, this inequality constrains execution time alone. Task acceptance rates, token expenditures, and monetary costs enter the trade-off in section 18.9, which gives serializing work and pairwise reconciliation separate coefficients because their remedies differ (section 18.9.3).

Napkin Math 18.1: Screening a proposed work partitionProblem: A hypothetical fixed workload has \(\ParallelFraction=\) 0.80 and assumed normalized overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\WorkerOverheadSlope(\WorkerCount-1)\) with \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=\) 0.02. The resource ceiling permits at most 16 workers. Which integer count minimizes modeled elapsed time?
Math: Evaluating the denominator of equation 1 for each permitted count, four workers require 0.460 of the serial reference time. The minimum occurs at 6 workers, requiring 0.433, a 2.3× speedup. Eight workers increase the ratio to 0.440, because the shrinking parallel term \(\ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount\) no longer pays for the added overhead. Halving the overhead coefficient to 0.01 moves the optimum to 9 workers and the speedup to 2.7×.
Systems insight: The serial fraction sets the ceiling and the overhead sets the useful fleet size. No worker count beats \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)=\) 5× here, and the best count sits near \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\), so halving the per-worker overhead \(\WorkerOverheadSlope\) adds 3 workers but only 0.4 of speedup. Shrinking the serial planning and integration work is the larger lever.


A reduction in modeled makespan does not automatically justify a multi-agent architecture. Production systems optimize under varied constraints: one automated migration service may seek to maximize accepted pull requests prior to a nightly release window subject to a strict token budget, whereas another prioritizes minimizing the total cost per accepted migration. Trading latency for computational overhead is justified only against an explicit, pre-declared optimization objective, and the decision framework of section 18.9 charges that objective for retries and failed executions as well. Before sizing a worker pool, an engineer must map the causal dependency graph of the workload to see which subtasks can run concurrently and what evidence each downstream join requires. Those dependencies govern the coordination topology.




In the authentication migration (migration_task_01), the interface worker and the caller worker can inspect the baseline snapshot (repo_base_01) in parallel, yet the caller’s patch still depends on the interface definitions that its peer is actively modifying. Routing both workers through a single supervisor does not eliminate that underlying causal dependency. A runtime architecture that naively treats the supervisor’s message-routing graph as the true dependency graph will prematurely accept and publish a caller patch built on stale interface assumptions.
To build reliable multi-agent systems, engineers must distinguish three separate structural graphs that govern execution:

The dependency graph defines causal precedence by recording which artifacts, decisions, or validation checks must complete before downstream work can safely proceed.
The communication topology defines the network paths, protocols, and message envelopes through which agents exchange information.
The supervision tree defines operational ownership over agent lifecycles, governing fault isolation, resource reservations, and cancellation cascades.

Because a supervisor frequently manages children whose outputs depend causally on one another, runtime engines must maintain these three structures independently. Conflating message delivery with causal dependency or lifecycle ownership leads directly to race conditions, orphaned processes, and corrupted state.


When migration_task_01 splits work across agents, the runtime must decide whether subtasks and candidate artifacts pass through a central coordinator, stream along staged queues, land in a shared store, or route directly between peer workers (table 2). The most prevalent pattern is the supervisor-worker topology (frequently termed orchestrator-worker). In this model, a centralized coordinator decomposes an incoming task, dispatches subtasks to subordinate workers, and synthesizes their returned receipts. This design directly mirrors the contract net protocol2 originally developed for distributed problem solving (Smith 1980). In production systems, these foundational topologies frequently compose. For example, a supervisor might dispatch parallel analytical investigations, stream their candidate patches through a staged validation pipeline, and persist intermediate progress within a shared task store.
2 Contract Net Protocol: In Smith’s 1980 protocol, a manager node announces a task, idle contractor nodes submit bids, and the manager awards the contract to a chosen bidder, which may subcontract in turn. The award represents the conceptual ancestor of the typed task envelope: it fixes which agent owns the subtask and what structured receipt must return, eliminating the ambiguity inherent in prompt-level delegation.

Each coordination topology makes different trade-offs regarding where state accumulates and where synchronization occurs. A supervisor concentrates integration logic and validation evidence at a single coordinator, requiring compact, structured receipts to prevent prompt context exhaustion. A pipeline structures execution as a sequence of discrete transformations, keeping each stage’s working context tightly focused while streaming items concurrently across stages. By contrast, a shared blackboard3 decouples agents entirely by externalizing coordination into a centralized artifact and task store (Erman et al. 1980). In an actor architecture, originally formulated by Hewitt, Bishop, and Steiger, agents maintain completely isolated private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing to explicit addresses (Hewitt et al. 1973). Both blackboards and actor meshes shift the coordination burden toward explicit conflict resolution, distributed ordering, and bounded mailbox management.
3 Blackboard Architecture: The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system of the 1970s coordinated independent knowledge sources that never communicated directly with one another, interacting solely by posting and reading hypotheses on a shared global data structure. Its central scheduling challenge, deciding which pending contribution to evaluate next, reappears whenever agent workers claim tasks from a shared operational store.Message counts scale with the communication graph and its interaction protocol. If each of \(\WorkerCount\) participants transmits an update to every other participant during an execution round, the network must handle \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\) directed deliveries. With an average payload size of \(\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens per delivery, that single round consumes \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens across the system. In contrast, a supervisor managing \(\WorkerCount\) workers requires only \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries per round (one dispatch envelope and one receipt per worker), consuming \(2\WorkerCount{}\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens. The full mesh thus scales quadratically, transmitting \((\WorkerCount-1)/2\) times more messages per round than the centralized coordinator.
Raw transmission volume measures network traffic, not what the receiving models must ingest. In a fully connected mesh where each agent appends every incoming peer message to its prompt history, ingested tokens per round grow as \(\mathcal{O}(\WorkerCount^2)\). The append-only re-send of equation 2.9 compounds that growth across rounds, because each later prompt carries every earlier delivery. Even in a centralized topology, verbose receipts, iterative deliberation rounds, or frequent status polling against a blackboard store can exhaust context windows and inflate inference budgets. Across the four arrangements of figure 1, the supervisor’s round costs \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries and the actor mesh up to \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\), while the pipeline and blackboard replace direct deliveries with bounded queues and versioned claims that the runtime must police. An arrangement therefore keeps context windows bounded only when each handoff carries the specific inputs and checks a subtask requires, and deciding when those handoffs may fire belongs to the dependency graph.

Dispatching subtasks before their prerequisites are verified wastes tokens on stale assumptions or stalls worker slots behind unfinished upstream steps. To schedule concurrent work safely, the runtime models task precedence as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), \((\DependencyGraphVertexSet,\DependencyGraphEdgeSet)\). Each vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex \in \DependencyGraphVertexSet\) represents a bounded unit of execution, either an autonomous agent trajectory or a deterministic runtime validation check. A directed edge \((\PredecessorGraphVertex,\DependencyGraphVertex) \in \DependencyGraphEdgeSet\) indicates that vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex\) requires a declared precondition satisfied by vertex \(\PredecessorGraphVertex\), such as an emitted code artifact, a validated test report, or an explicit authorization token. A status message signaling task completion satisfies an incoming edge only when accompanied by verifiable output receipts.
A vertex becomes dependency-ready once every prerequisite predecessor condition has been verified. Dependency readiness alone does not trigger execution, however. The runtime dispatcher must additionally verify execution authority, allocate an active worker slot, and secure a bounded token and financial budget reservation. If a predecessor fails or emits invalid artifacts, the control plane either halts downstream successors or transitions execution to an explicit recovery branch. Loops and iterative refinement cycles enter the graph as unrolled, bounded attempts. Because graph acyclicity guarantees only the absence of logical dependency loops, the underlying runtime remains responsible for detecting dynamic deadlocks arising from shared resource locks, exhausted thread pools, or saturated queues.
To estimate the theoretical limits of parallel scheduling, assume each vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex\) occupies one interchangeable worker slot for a fixed duration \(\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex)\), encompassing both model inference latency and external tool execution. Let \(\WorkerCount\) represent the pool of available parallel worker slots. Under these assumptions, aggregate slot-work \(\AggregateSlotWork\) totals every vertex’s duration, and critical-path duration \(\CriticalPathDuration\) is the length of the longest dependency chain, the same critical path that trace analysis measures from recorded spans, here computed from assumed durations:
\[
\AggregateSlotWork=\sum_{\DependencyGraphVertex\in \DependencyGraphVertexSet}\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex),\qquad
\CriticalPathDuration=\max_{\pi\in\operatorname{Paths}(\DependencyGraphVertexSet,\DependencyGraphEdgeSet)}\sum_{\DependencyGraphVertex\in\pi}\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex).
\tag{2}\]
Any valid schedule’s total makespan \(\ScheduleFinishTime\) must satisfy the dual lower bounds
\[
\ScheduleFinishTime\ge\max\left(\frac{\AggregateSlotWork}{\WorkerCount},\CriticalPathDuration\right).
\tag{3}\]
The aggregate work bound \(\AggregateSlotWork/\WorkerCount\) reflects the capacity constraint, since \(\WorkerCount\) parallel worker slots cannot complete \(\AggregateSlotWork\) total units of execution time in less than \(\AggregateSlotWork/\WorkerCount\), regardless of schedule structure. The critical-path bound \(\CriticalPathDuration\) reflects the causal precedence constraint, since sequential dependencies cannot be parallelized, and it establishes a lower bound on latency even with infinite worker slots.4 In production environments, resource contention, queuing overhead, payload serialization, and trajectory retries expand the overall makespan well beyond these theoretical minimums unless explicitly incorporated into vertex durations \(\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex)\) and graph edges.
4 Greedy List Scheduling: Graham established that any list schedule which never leaves a worker slot idle while a dependency-ready vertex waits completes within a factor of \(2-1/\WorkerCount\) of the optimal makespan. Graham also demonstrated that such schedules can suffer counterintuitive timing anomalies where adding worker slots or reducing individual task durations actually increases overall completion time (Graham 1969). A runtime dispatcher that greedily schedules ready work is therefore near-optimal relative to the theoretical bound in equation 3, and an observed latency regression after expanding worker pools does not necessarily indicate a scheduler implementation bug.
Graham, Ronald L. 1969. “Bounds on Multiprocessing Timing Anomalies.” SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 17 (2): 416–29. https://doi.org/10.1137/0117039.

When a coordinator fixes every subtask before execution begins, workers cannot branch when they uncover an undocumented dependency. Conversely, letting a model spawn children at will can turn a simple query into dozens of redundant trajectories. A static plan resolves this trade-off toward predictability by specifying its stages, conditional branches, validation checkpoints, and retry bounds ahead of execution. Because all artifact dependencies and message routes are declared upfront, operators can inspect handoffs statically and verify safety invariants before dispatch. With enforced per-node work limits, bounded attempts, and stated service or deadline assumptions, the declared graph supports worst-case resource and execution bounds. A termination deadline does not guarantee accepted completion or immediate settlement of external work.
In contrast, dynamic spawning provisions child agents at runtime in response to intermediate observations. For example, during a repository migration, a worker analyzing call sites might uncover an undocumented dependency and request an isolated sub-investigation. While the model proposes this subtask dynamically, the runtime control plane must evaluate and admit it under the prevailing task contract. Dynamic spawning allows systems to adapt flexibly to open-ended workloads, but it introduces non-deterministic execution graphs. When an unconstrained model decides how many child agents to spawn and when to spawn them, combinatorial fan-out can quickly overwhelm system capacity and inflate execution costs.

War Story 18.1: Unbounded fan-out in a multi-agent research system (2025)Context: Anthropic’s engineering team described building an autonomous research system where a lead orchestrator plans an investigation, spawns parallel subagents to search for evidence, and synthesizes their findings (Hadfield et al. 2025).
Mechanism: The lead agent possessed unconstrained authority to determine subagent fan-out. In early prototype versions, the model routinely spawned 50 subagents even for simple queries, searched endlessly for nonexistent sources, and allowed subagents to degrade coordination by flooding one another with excessive updates.
Impact: The engineering team reports that autonomous agents typically consume about 4× more tokens than standard conversational interactions, while multi-agent systems consume roughly 15× more. Although the multi-agent configuration outperformed a single agent by 90.2 percent on the team’s internal research evaluation, the unconstrained fan-out incurred disproportionate resource expenditure on straightforward tasks.
Fix: The team embedded explicit scaling heuristics into the orchestrator’s prompt, instructing the model to calibrate subagent allocation to query complexity, allocating a single agent for direct fact retrieval and scaling upward only for open-ended synthesis. Furthermore, the orchestrator was structured to wait synchronously for each dispatched subagent batch to conclude before initiating subsequent steps, simplifying state synchronization at the cost of pipeline parallelism.
Systems lesson: Dynamic fan-out is an architectural resource-allocation problem that cannot rely on model self-restraint alone. While prompt-based heuristics guide model proposals, the runtime control plane must enforce hard admission limits on tree breadth, recursion depth, and aggregate budget reservations. These limits directly bound the token consumption in the effective cost metric \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).


Uncontrolled fan-out illustrates the necessity of formal admission control in multi-agent architectures. Prompt instructions alone cannot curb subtask generation, because an unconstrained model can still propose redundant branches or trigger cascading worker requests. Allocating each child a budget fraction smaller than the parent’s remaining funds also fails to protect the system, as a burst of concurrent siblings can issue overlapping claims that collectively exceed available capacity. The runtime admission controller must atomically reserve each child’s maximum potential liability against the shared task budget before dispatching execution, an invariant that section 18.8 formalizes across hierarchical delegation trees. Production runtimes must independently enforce four distinct bounds: fan-out breadth (maximum children per parent), concurrent active slots (maximum parallel executions), recursion depth (maximum delegation layers), and absolute deadlines. A shallow tree can still exhaust resources through excessive breadth, while a strict concurrency cap can still permit an unbounded sequence of sequential worker allocations.

Beyond resource management, dispatching a child agent establishes lifecycle ownership. A child’s running trajectory, pending tool invocations, and uncommitted side effects typically outlive the ephemeral model call that spawned it. The supervision tree defines how the runtime isolates faults and manages recovery when a child encounters an unrecoverable failure. Following the supervision trees of Erlang/OTP (Open Telecom Platform),5 systems formalize recovery through explicit, per-supervisor restart strategies (Armstrong 2003, 2007):
5 Erlang Supervision Trees: Erlang emerged from a telephone-switching research program initiated in 1981, established on the design principle that systems should allow failing processes to crash cleanly while a designated supervisor restores known-good state, rather than attempting defensive error handling locally (Armstrong 2003). In agentic systems, this principle is even more vital: allowing a confused agent trajectory to attempt local recovery within a contaminated context window frequently compounds its errors, whereas a supervisor restart provisions a clean execution context from recorded inputs.
Armstrong, Joe. 2003. “Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors.” PhD thesis, Royal Institute of Technology (KTH).

Armstrong, Joe. 2007. “A History of Erlang.” Proceedings of the Third ACM SIGPLAN Conference on History of Programming Languages (HOPL III), 6-1-6-26. https://doi.org/10.1145/1238844.1238850.

Under a one_for_one policy, the supervisor restarts only the failed child agent while allowing sibling workers to continue uninterrupted. This strategy is ideal for embarrassingly parallel or loosely coupled subtasks, such as searching disjoint documentation sources, where workers share no mutable intermediate state.
Under a one_for_all policy, the failure of any single child triggers the supervisor to terminate and restart all sibling workers within that supervision group. This approach is needed for tightly coupled collaborative tasks where partial artifacts become invalid upon peer failure. For example, if an interface worker crashes and restarts with an altered API contract, any partial implementation generated by a concurrent caller worker is invalidated.

The two policies differ in blast radius (figure 2): one failure under one_for_one costs a single fresh attempt and its reservation, whereas under one_for_all it discards the progress of every coupled sibling and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs. To prevent degenerate retry storms under either policy, supervision trees enforce a restart intensity bound, the maximum number of restarts permitted within a sliding time window. When a child agent repeatedly fails and breaches this threshold, the supervisor ceases local restarts, aborts its remaining subordinates, and escalates the failure upward to its own parent supervisor. In an agentic system, a restart must never continue from the failed worker’s corrupted or circular context window. Instead, the runtime treats each restart as a freshly admitted attempt. It provisions a clean context initialized from recorded input artifacts and acquires a fresh budget reservation. Whenever it aborts sibling processes under one_for_all or escalation, it also invokes the structured cancellation and cleanup protocols of section 18.7.






Figure 2: Restart Policies in a Supervision Tree: Under the one-for-one policy (a), only the failed worker restarts, as a newly admitted attempt with its own reservation, while its siblings continue. Under the one-for-all policy (b), the supervisor stops the coupled siblings through the cancellation protocol and restarts the whole group from recorded inputs, because the caller’s partial work has lost its meaning. Either supervisor that exceeds its declared restart intensity stops restarting and escalates the failure to its parent.

A coordination topology fixes how work, messages, and lifecycle ownership cross agent boundaries, but routing and supervision alone do not specify what a child is allowed to do once it starts. Without an explicit contract on each handoff, a worker can still read stale inputs, touch files outside its scope, or return a long narrative in place of verifiable evidence. Every boundary crossing therefore requires a formal task envelope that states what artifacts the worker receives, what tools and tokens it may consume, and what typed receipt it must return.




A message asking worker_caller_01 to “update the callers” leaves critical engineering boundaries unspecified: the target interface version, the files permitted to change, the resource budget, and the acceptance criteria for completion. If the worker fills those gaps from its own interpretation of the prompt, that interpretation becomes the de facto contract. While a workflow dependency edge dictates when a child task may begin, the task envelope defines what that child is permitted to read, modify, spend, and return. Delegation therefore requires a typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)) that extends across the agent boundary. It works much like a typed interface in a classic remote procedure call, which establishes formal argument types, return values, and failure semantics before execution begins (Birrell and Nelson 1984).

Definition 18.2: Typed task envelope
A typed task envelope is a versioned assignment record binding a child task to identified inputs, a scoped authority grant, resource and lifecycle limits, completion requirements, and a bounded return format.

Significance: The runtime validates task boundaries before admitting work and verifies returned artifacts against required evidence. In addition, capping the return payload prevents runaway worker outputs from flooding the coordinator’s context window on subsequent execution turns.
Distinction: The envelope defines an operational, enforceable contract for execution and resources; the natural-language prompt merely describes the objective within those constraints.
Common pitfall: Mistaking a syntactically valid envelope for proof of authorization or successful execution. Both authorization and task completion require verification against authoritative state records maintained outside the worker’s control.





If a parent passes a subtask in free-form prose or embeds mutable budget numbers directly inside the child’s prompt, the child can misread its scope or rewrite its own limits. When delegating a subtask, the parent agent proposes the work, but the execution runtime authenticates the parent-child relationship, resolves the authority grant, and locks the resource reservation. In the task envelope shown in listing 1, field identifiers point to immutable registry records rather than embedding raw, unverified data. The referenced acceptance contract specifies expected caller behavior, exact test suite versions, the execution environment, and any required human reviews prior to final acceptance.
