The write-set record reflects the diff actually produced in the isolated workspace rather than the worker’s conversational recollection of what it modified. Similarly, the dependency record captures observed file reads, loaded package versions, configuration files, and external environment flags, bounded by explicit tracing coverage. The checker report records the exact candidate hash, the test command, the container environment, and the exit status. This record carries the evidence-scope rule of the tool boundary across the delegation boundary. A single call’s observation confirmed only what that call measured. A check result here establishes an outcome for one identified candidate hash, checker, and environment, and authorizes nothing beyond it. If the runtime cannot produce or verify every piece of mandatory evidence, the return status transitions to evidence_unavailable rather than complete.


↩︎ The evidence-scope rule, under which an observation confirms only what its tool measured during that invocation, is established in Complete mediation.
The usage record accounts for charged and reserved work across tokens, wall-clock time, and tool invocations. The settlement record distinguishes a stop acknowledgment, confirmed resource release, and unresolved background operations with retained owners. A complete return and the final settlement of every operation are therefore distinct statuses. This separation matters when the parent cancels an execution branch (section 18.7), ensuring that task termination does not leave orphaned background processes or dangling locks. Optional prose explanations may be shortened or omitted when space is constrained, with the omission explicitly recorded, while required identities, statuses, and evidence references pass intact. If the mandatory structural fields alone exceed receipt_bytes, the runtime generates an explicit payload-size failure rather than returning a truncated record.



Instead of inlining an entire repository tree into a child task’s context prompt, the parent passes an immutable repository reference (base_ref). The worker then issues targeted read queries to fetch only the source files relevant to its assignment. However, this pass-by-reference pattern yields net token savings only when the child inspects a small fraction of the code base. If the worker iteratively fetches broad directory trees, the combined cost of reference overhead, tool invocation tokens, and repeated context re-reads across turns can quickly outstrip the cost of an upfront payload. Passing a shared base reference also amortizes KV-cache prefill across parallel workers, but only when their prompt prefixes align.


↩︎ Prompt prefix alignment and KV-cache prefill amortization are established in Preserving an exact prefix.

Napkin Math 18.3: Price the reads after the handoffProblem: Each of 6 children receives either a 48,000-token repository slice or a 350-token reference envelope followed by 3,600 tokens of retrieved content. With all other inputs equal, no cache discount, and a hypothetical $3 per million input tokens, how much repository-delivery input does the reference save?
Math: Pasting costs 6 \(\times\) 48,000 \(=\) 288,000 tokens, or $0.864. The reference costs 6 \(\times\) (350 \(+\) 3,600) \(=\) 23,700 tokens, or $0.071, a 12.2× reduction. If every child instead reads the full slice, the reference design consumes 290,100 tokens and loses its saving.
Systems insight: The efficiency of reference passing depends entirely on read selectivity rather than the pointer mechanism alone. In this configuration, each child inspects only 7.5 percent of the slice, keeping reference passing economical until reads exceed 47,650 tokens. Effective multi-agent system design therefore pairs pointer handoffs with precise task scoping and indexing.


Once execution concludes, the receipt hands the parent coordinator an isolated candidate, its base version, and runtime-recorded evidence. Those records, not the absence of overlapping files, decide whether candidates can merge safely, because two patches that touch disjoint files can still break each other when integrated.




In migration_task_01, both worker_interface_01 and worker_caller_01 branch from the same baseline commit, repo_base_01, to edit their respective files. When the interface worker finishes first, the integration service accepts its patch as repo_head_02. Because the caller worker modifies a different file, a standard three-way textual merge succeeds cleanly without merge conflicts. The caller’s patch, however, still targets the obsolete interface. Modifying separate files prevented a textual collision, but it left the semantic dependency behind the caller’s code unchecked.
Optimistic concurrency control (OCC) resolves this tension by letting each agent work privately against a snapshot and validating every publication prerequisite before the shared branch changes (Kung and Robinson 1981). A transaction runs a read phase against private copies, a validation phase that checks whether concurrent commits invalidated anything it read, and a write phase that commits only after validation succeeds. The expected-version check at the tool boundary is that validation applied to a single file. The scheme pays when conflicts are rare, because it trades lock waiting for occasional discarded work. A worker’s read phase, however, spans minutes of model generation and tool execution rather than the brief life of a database transaction, so a failed validation discards real inference spend. Its prerequisites include dependency freshness and acceptance evidence as well as unchanged files. Instead of holding a repository lock while an agent deliberates, the runtime decouples private execution from integration, which exposes parallelism and converts conflicts into the coordination tax of candidate revalidation and occasional discarded work.

↩︎ Conditional updates that commit only while the target still matches its expected version are established in Conditional updates.



Operating multiple agents within a single shared working directory introduces three immediate failure modes. A lost update occurs when two workers inspect the same file, deliberate over multiple inference turns, and serialize their writes back to disk. The later write silently replaces the earlier contribution, and the operating system reports no error because both writes were valid. A torn dependency read emerges when an agent executes tests while a peer is actively modifying related files, for example by evaluating code after a new interface has landed but before the caller has been updated. The test runner executes against an incoherent intermediate state that no agent ever intended to propose. Finally, tool-lock contention strikes when concurrent build tools or version-control commands collide on local metadata locks, such as Git’s .git/index.lock. One worker crashes on a locked index even when the underlying edits target entirely disjoint directories.



Shared writes pass even odds at five workers, long before a fleet feels large.
These collisions manifest surprisingly early as agent concurrency grows. Suppose a repository contains \(\RepositoryFileCount\) files and each of \(\WorkerCount\) workers modifies \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\) distinct files, chosen uniformly and independently at random. Worker \(\EarlierWorkerCount+1\) avoids overlapping with all preceding workers only if it selects its \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\) files exclusively from the \(\RepositoryFileCount-\EarlierWorkerCount \WorkerWrittenFileCount\) files that earlier workers left untouched. The probability that all \(\WorkerCount\) write sets remain pairwise disjoint is therefore
\[
\Pr(\text{no shared write})=\prod_{k=1}^{\WorkerCount-1}\frac{\binom{\RepositoryFileCount-\EarlierWorkerCount \WorkerWrittenFileCount}{\WorkerWrittenFileCount}}{\binom{\RepositoryFileCount}{\WorkerWrittenFileCount}}\approx\exp\left(-\frac{\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\WorkerWrittenFileCount^2}{2\RepositoryFileCount}\right).
\tag{4}\]
Equation 4 is the birthday bound6 generalized to multi-file write sets. When \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\) is small relative to \(\RepositoryFileCount\), each of the \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)/2\) worker pairs compares \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount^2\) file choices against the \(\RepositoryFileCount\) repository files, so the exponent grows quadratically with both the worker count \(\WorkerCount\) and the write-set size \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\). Because the exponent scales with the number of worker pairs rather than linearly with the worker count, collision odds mount rapidly. In a hypothetical repository of 1,000 files where each worker touches 10 files, even 2 concurrent workers collide with probability 9.6 percent. At 5 workers, a write collision becomes more likely than not, and scaling to 8 workers drives the collision probability to 94.4 percent. In practice, uniform random access is an illustrative baseline that can understate risk when writes cluster. Actual agent modifications heavily cluster around package manifests, central routing tables, and shared configuration files. Rigorous workspace isolation is therefore an architectural prerequisite for multi-agent coordination, rather than a performance tuning knob reserved for large worker pools.
6 Birthday Bound: The classical birthday problem calculates the number of people required before two share a birthday. The answer, twenty-three people for even odds across 365 days, often surprises newcomers because the number of potential pairs grows quadratically with group size. Systems designers exploit this same relation to size hash tables and cryptographic identifiers. In multi-agent execution, each worker represents an individual and the repository files represent the calendar, with collision probability amplified because each worker samples \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount\) distinct files simultaneously rather than a single day.Providing each worker with an isolated workspace establishes a stable snapshot baseline and an unshared scratchpad for local modifications. When a worker finishes, the runtime therefore receives an immutable candidate artifact (identified by a cryptographic commit hash) rather than a reference to a mutable filesystem directory. Runtimes implement this isolation through two main mechanisms. Linked Git worktrees allocate a dedicated working tree, index, and HEAD pointer for each agent while sharing underlying object storage in .git/objects. Copy-on-write filesystems provide block-level cloning and zero-copy snapshots governed by runtime pooling lifecycles and reset contracts.


↩︎ Copy-on-write provisioning, which copies only what a task writes over a read-only base, is established in Copy-on-write provisioning.
Neither filesystem mechanism provides security on its own. If an agent executes arbitrary shell commands with unrestricted filesystem permissions, it can traverse parent directories, access peer worktrees, or corrupt the shared Git directory. A robust architecture therefore pairs workspace isolation with an external sandbox and a mediated tool gateway. The gateway confines filesystem writes to the assigned worktree, strips integration credentials, and allocates ephemeral ports and temporary directories for test suites. Furthermore, discarding a worktree cleanly recycles local ephemeral state, but it cannot revoke side effects that an external service has already accepted.



When a worker signals completion, the centralized integration service evaluates the returned execution receipt. The service resolves runtime.base_ref and runtime.candidate_ref, verifies cryptographic commit lineage, and independently derives the modified file paths rather than trusting a worker-reported write set. Beyond commit hashes, the service inspects runtime.dependencies_ref, which records the exact source versions, environmental flags, and file reads underpinning the candidate. Reliable dependency tracking requires runtime instrumentation of mediated filesystem calls, lockfiles, and configuration manifests; subjective, model-generated self-reports cannot be trusted for correctness. Furthermore, negative dependencies require careful tracking: an agent’s code generation may depend on the absence of a conflicting file, meaning that recording only positive file reads yields incomplete dependency graphs. Whenever dependency tracking is partial or ambiguous, the integration service treats an empty dependency manifest as unknown rather than disjoint, triggering a fresh revalidation of the candidate against the current branch head.
Let the commit content hashes \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\), \(\WorkerCandidateCommitHash\), and \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) identify the worker’s base, its returned candidate, and the integration head captured for this attempt. The protocol has four steps, which listing 3 condenses into the control flow of an integration service.

Revalidate dependencies: Compare dependency versions between \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\) and \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\). Pairwise disjoint file sets demonstrate only textual independence. If a referenced interface or schema changed on the main branch, the runtime must revise or regenerate the candidate before attempting integration.
Build the candidate: Construct an immutable integration candidate \(\IntegrationCandidateCommitHash\). If \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) still matches \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\), the candidate is the worker’s own commit \(\WorkerCandidateCommitHash\) (the fast-forward path). If the head advanced, the service stages a private merge commit combining \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) and \(\WorkerCandidateCommitHash\). Should textual or structural conflicts arise, the service may dispatch a bounded reconciliation task to an agent. The resulting merge artifact is treated as a fresh candidate proposal, subject to the full validation pipeline.
Check the exact candidate: Every integration candidate must pass the scope and quality checks mandated by migration_accept_v1 within the protected assessment sandbox of Grader isolation. Under the evidence-scope rule, verification tests executed on the worker’s private branch do not validate the newly synthesized merge candidate. Acceptance criteria must be evaluated directly on the exact commit hash \(\IntegrationCandidateCommitHash\).
Publish with an expected-head update: Advance the target ref if and only if the current branch pointer still equals the captured \(\IntegrationHeadCommitHash\) and all publication guards remain satisfied. These guards verify active grant authorization, unrevoked task status, comprehensive dependency tracking, and fresh acceptance test evidence. In Git, the low-level update-ref command with an expected old object hash guarantees an atomic compare-and-swap. The runtime sequences authorization guards with this atomic ref update to eliminate race conditions between token revocation and publication, while external dependencies are anchored by their action-time version contracts.

If a concurrent writer advances the branch head before the atomic ref update executes, the integration attempt aborts. Rather than blindly retrying the update against the new head, the service loops back to step 1, revalidating all dependencies against the updated state. If the publication command returns an ambiguous network outcome or timeout, the service must query the authoritative repository log before attempting a retry, preventing duplicate commits. Figure 3 assembles three ingredients: private worktrees over shared repository storage, a staged merge that is textually clean even though the caller relies on the interface as of \(\WorkerBaseCommitHash\), and the four-step gate whose moved-head exit returns to revalidation. Table 4 then follows the caller worker’s patch across each decision boundary.



Listing 3: Guarded Integration of a Worker Candidate: The service revalidates dependencies against the captured head, checks the exact candidate, and publishes with an expected-head update under the task’s publication guard.


def integrate(repo, task, receipt, contract, max_attempts):
    for attempt in range(max_attempts):
        head = repo.read_ref(TARGET)                          # h_head for this attempt
        stale = changed_dependencies(receipt.dependencies_ref, receipt.base_ref, head)
        if stale:
            return request_revision(task, stale, head)        # regenerate, then return
        if head == receipt.base_ref:
            candidate = receipt.candidate_ref                 # fast-forward case
        else:
            candidate = stage_merge(head, receipt.candidate_ref)
            if candidate is None:
                return request_reconciliation(task, head)     # another proposal
        evidence = run_protected_checks(contract, candidate)  # binds this exact candidate
        if not evidence.accepted:
            return reject(task, candidate, evidence)
        with publication_guard(task) as guard:                # cancellation, grants, lineage
            if not guard.eligible:
                return withdrawn(task)
            outcome = repo.update_ref(TARGET, candidate, expected=head)
        if outcome.uncertain:
            return reconcile_publication(task, candidate)     # never blind-retry the effect
        if outcome.applied:
            return published(task, candidate, evidence)
        # head moved: loop back to dependency validation for the new head
    return unresolved(task, reason="integration_attempts_exhausted")

Publication (c) therefore revalidates dependencies at the captured head, checks the exact integration candidate, and advances the target only if the head is unchanged and the publication guard holds. A moved head returns the attempt to validation, and every other exit returns an explicit status.

Repeated invalidations quickly erode the efficiency gains of parallel delegation. If several agents continuously update overlapping dependencies, workers spend more compute discarding stale rollouts and reconciling candidates than generating productive code. Runtimes mitigate this through bounded retries, exponential backoff, and serialized commit queues, transitioning exhausted attempts into explicitly unresolved task states. However, when invalidation rates remain persistently high, the architectural remedy lies in work decomposition rather than concurrency tuning. Structuring the task graph to sequence interface migrations ahead of dependent caller tasks eliminates the cross-worker hazard entirely, achieving higher net throughput with fewer wasted agent turns.



Repository staging isolates and buffers only local repository state. A failed Git integration rolls back local commits, but it cannot undo mutations already executed on shared relational databases, physical test rigs, or external payment gateways. External resources operate under their own conditional-update and ownership semantics.
When managing unmergeable stateful resources (a live database migration lock, a dedicated test bench, or an embedded hardware debugger), the runtime must decide precisely when to enforce mutual exclusion. A pessimistic lease acquires an exclusive, time-bounded grant before an agent begins work, and the coordinator reclaims an expired grant so that a stalled holder cannot keep the resource indefinitely. Conflicting workers block until the lease holder releases the lock or times out, avoiding conflict-driven discarded work while the lease remains valid, but agent concurrency collapses into serialized execution. Conversely, optimistic control maximizes parallel execution by deferring conflict checks until publication. If validation fails, however, the runtime discards the entire execution trajectory, while any external side effects already dispatched to outside systems remain irreversible. This irreversibility governs the architectural division: optimistic concurrency control excels for private, discardable working trees, whereas the non-mergeable exclusive resources considered here require exclusion established at the target resource before issuing commands. Checking lease validity inside the runtime before dispatching a command is not enough on its own, because an agent stalled by rate limits or slow inference can outlive its lease while a previously dispatched write is still in transit. Each leased resource therefore needs the resource-side fencing token of Availability and ownership, which stamps every lease transfer with a monotonically increasing generation number and rejects any write carrying an older generation. While the generation number fences out stale holders after a lease changes hands, a duplicate of the same operation sent by the current holder remains a separate hazard that the runtime settles through its operation identity under settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)). Delegation links these mechanisms whenever a supervisor restarts a failed or stalled worker under the policies of section 18.3.4, because the old attempt and the replacement attempt are siblings targeting the same external resource. Before the supervisor releases the replacement worker to issue commands, the runtime must advance the lease generation at the resource itself so that any late write from the superseded sibling is rejected at the destination.

Guarded publication provides a robust concurrency framework for serializing concurrent state transitions. Its scope, however, is limited to structural and dependency consistency; OCC does not establish semantic correctness. If multiple workers inherit the same flawed assumptions from a shared planner, each worker can satisfy every step of the guarded publication protocol and cleanly commit a flawed patch to the repository.




Adding a panel of five model reviewers to migration_task_01 to check semantic correctness before publication exposes the same shared-assumption hazard. All five reviewers may endorse worker_caller_01’s patch because they share the mistaken assumption that the legacy interface remains available, accumulating approvals without ever verifying the underlying dependency. This synchronized breakdown illustrates a correlated failure, in which the reviewers fail on the same inputs. When individual agents share systemic blind spots, consensus among them is informative only up to the limits of their joint error distribution.


Two classical foundations in fault tolerance appear to promise the opposite. Condorcet’s jury theorem (Condorcet, Marquis de 1785) states that if independent voters are each correct with probability above one half, the probability that a majority vote is correct approaches one as voters are added. In computer engineering, N-modular redundancy applies the identical arithmetic to hardware, masking a faulty replica through majority voting circuits (Neumann 1956). Both guarantees rest on a basic premise: that individual voters or components fail independently given the ground truth. Software engineering discovered during the 1980s that this premise breaks down in practice. Independently developed program versions failed on identical inputs far more frequently than statistical independence predicted7 (Knight and Leveson 1986). Table 6 contrasts the physical roots of independence in hardware redundancy with the fragile assumptions underlying model reviewer ensembles.

Language models trained on overlapping web-scale data face this exact vulnerability: benchmark evaluations across hundreds of models show heavily correlated errors, with the strongest correlation appearing among the largest and most capable models (Kim et al. 2025).

To quantify how correlation degrades redundancy, consider a binary review process evaluating candidate artifacts known to violate an acceptance criterion. Let \(\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j=1\) denote the event where reviewer \(\ReviewerIndex\) erroneously approves an invalid candidate, with marginal false-approval probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\) over this candidate population. If an ensemble of \(\WorkerCount\) reviewers makes independent errors with identical probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\), their total number of false approvals \(\FalseApprovalCount\) follows a binomial distribution. For an odd ensemble size \(\WorkerCount\), a faulty majority forms with probability
\[
\Pr(\FalseApprovalCount>\WorkerCount/2)=\sum_{k=(\WorkerCount+1)/2}^{\WorkerCount}\binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability^\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)^{\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}.
\]
Statistical independence must always be stated relative to the information held fixed. Repeated, independently sampled calls to a single model on one fixed input prompt can be conditionally independent. However, candidate defects vary widely in real workloads: some bugs are subtle and intricate, whereas others are straightforward. A challenging candidate is difficult for every reviewer. Across the broader candidate population, individual reviewer errors become positively correlated. Furthermore, multi-agent debate protocols introduce an intentional communication channel where agents revise their answers after inspecting peer conclusions (Du et al. 2023). This deliberate coupling introduces a secondary layer of dependence on top of shared task difficulty.
A latent-propensity model makes this shared difficulty explicit. Eckhardt and Lee originally introduced this framework to explain coincident software failures (Eckhardt and Lee 1985), assigning each candidate input an intrinsic propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity \in [0, 1]\) of causing a randomly chosen version to fail. In an agent review setting, draw a candidate with false-approval propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\). Conditional on \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\), each reviewer independently issues an erroneous approval with probability \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\). Reviewers share the candidate’s intrinsic difficulty, even though their individual sampling realizations remain independent. On a candidate of propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\), two distinct reviewers therefore err together with probability \(\FalseApprovalPropensity^2\). Averaging across the candidate population gives a marginal false-approval rate of \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=\mathbb{E}[\FalseApprovalPropensity]\) and a joint error probability of \(\mathbb{E}[\FalseApprovalPropensity^2]\), so subtracting \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability^2\) leaves a pairwise covariance equal to \(\operatorname{Var}(\FalseApprovalPropensity)\), which divides by the marginal Bernoulli variance \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)\) to give the correlation coefficient \(\CorrelationCoefficient\):
\[
\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=\mathbb{E}[\FalseApprovalPropensity],\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}(\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_i,\ReviewerFalseApprovalIndicator_j)=\operatorname{Var}(\FalseApprovalPropensity),\qquad
\CorrelationCoefficient=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\FalseApprovalPropensity)}{\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)}\quad(\PeerReviewerIndex\ne \ReviewerIndex).
\]
To model this variation analytically, assume \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)\), a flexible density on \([0,1]\) with positive shape parameters \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape\) and \(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape\). Its mean is \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape/(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)\), and for reviewers who share \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\) the pairwise correlation works out to \(1/(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape+1)\), so a small \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape\) means candidates differ widely in difficulty and errors correlate strongly. Setting the mean to the marginal rate and the correlation to the target gives \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape=\CorrelationCoefficient^{-1}-1\), which implies \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape=\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(\CorrelationCoefficient^{-1}-1)\) and \(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape=(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)(\CorrelationCoefficient^{-1}-1)\) for \(0<\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability<1\) and \(0<\CorrelationCoefficient<1\). Compounding the conditional binomial distribution over this beta prior yields the beta-binomial probability for \(\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount\) false approvals:
\[
\Pr(\FalseApprovalCount=\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount)=\binom{\WorkerCount}{\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount}\frac{\mathrm{B}(\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount+\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\WorkerCount-\FalseApprovalOutcomeCount+\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)}{\mathrm{B}(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape,\PropensityPriorRejectionShape)},
\]
where \(\mathrm{B}\) denotes the beta function. A stipulated marginal error rate and pairwise correlation do not uniquely determine the full joint distribution, and the beta family represents an idealized model for shared difficulty. Consequently, any production deployment must empirically measure its joint error distribution directly on domain-specific candidates.

How often does a majority falsely approve if their errors are independent, and how often under the beta mixture at \(\CorrelationCoefficient=0.40\)?
Math: Summing the binomial masses for three or more false approvals gives 5.79 percent under independent errors. The beta-binomial masses with \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape=\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability(\CorrelationCoefficient^{-1}-1)\) and \(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape=(1-\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability)(\CorrelationCoefficient^{-1}-1)\) give 16.68 percent. The mixture’s majority improves only slightly on a single reviewer’s marginal rate \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability\), and a unanimous false approval is about 122 times as likely as independence predicts. Before adding reviewers to an ensemble, estimate \(\CorrelationCoefficient\) empirically on known-invalid candidates. When correlation is high, spending additional token budget on more reviewers of the same type yields diminishing returns. That budget is better spent on independent, deterministic validation checks. These calculations condition on the candidate being invalid; the overall probability that an approved candidate is invalid also depends on the prevalence of invalid candidates in the workload.


The mixture model also bounds what ensemble scaling can achieve. Conditional on a candidate’s propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\), the weak law of large numbers implies that the fraction of reviewers falsely approving converges to \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\) as the ensemble grows. Consequently, an arbitrarily large majority vote falsely approves precisely those candidates with \(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2\). Rather than decaying toward zero, majority false approval approaches a nonzero asymptotic floor at \(\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)\).
Under the parameters modeled in the notebook, that floor is 15.0 percent. At 15 reviewers, independent errors would reduce majority false approvals to 0.42 percent, whereas the beta mixture leaves the error rate stalled at 15.6 percent. At five reviewers the mixture moves probability to the extremes, so a candidate is approved by no one or by a majority far more often than independence predicts. Tripling the committee from five to 15 reviewers of the same kind triples review spend yet lowers majority false approval only from 16.68 percent to 15.6 percent, because the remaining errors concentrate on candidates that every such model finds difficult.

In an automated workflow such as migration_task_01, five reviewers that all repeat the assumption that the old interface remains available provide essentially a single effective observation. Their consensus should not trigger an automatic merge; instead, it should trigger an end-to-end integration check that evaluates the modified caller alongside the updated callee interface. A protected, deterministic check supplies ground-truth evidence that model reviewers cannot fabricate. A compiler establishes whether the candidate compiles cleanly under the target configuration, and a regression test suite confirms that specified functional behaviors remain intact. If an untrusted worker agent modifies a test suite to bypass a signature verification check, the test may pass while completely failing to validate the security property. This vulnerability is why authoritative evaluation suites must remain isolated behind a protected grading boundary. Even so, deterministic validation remains bounded by test suite coverage gaps and flawed formal specifications.
Classical distributed quorum protocols cannot rescue a review ensemble plagued by correlated errors. When a large language model (LLM) outputs well-formed, plausible, yet incorrect evidence, it produces a fail-plausible fault rather than a fail-stop crash. In the unsigned-message protocol model, Byzantine agreement guarantees consensus despite arbitrary faults only while faulty participants remain strictly below one third of the ensemble8 (Lamport et al. 1982). Because reviewers that share training distributions, system prompts, or upstream reasoning summaries fail together, correlated errors can push the faulty fraction past that one-third threshold regardless of replica count. Requiring each reviewer to inspect primary evidence before viewing peer conclusions (information isolation) removes direct peer influence. Distinct model architectures, diversified prompts, and separate evidence sources lower \(\CorrelationCoefficient\) only as far as empirical measurement on known-invalid candidates demonstrates.
8 Byzantine Bound: The replica bound fixes how large a faulty fraction a protocol tolerates, not why replicas fail; the one-third limit applies to unsigned messages, and digital signatures relax it (Lamport et al. 1982). Classical deployments seek to keep simultaneous faults below that bound through physical diversity, running distinct code bases on separate hardware in different administrative domains. Model reviewers drawn from common model families, or trained on overlapping web-scale data, lack that isolation by default.

Consensus among worker agents must never be confused with authoritative execution privilege. Reviewer agreement provides an informative heuristic signal within the bounds defined by an orchestration workflow. Merging code, publishing artifacts, broadening task scopes, or bypassing gate checks requires explicit capability grants issued by a privileged control plane. Even unanimous approval from the five reviewers in migration_task_01 only advances the candidate to the integration gate, where the runtime still checks its scope, dependencies, and publication grant before updating the branch.

Checkpoint 18.2: Interpreting concurrent results and agreement

Clean merge vs. valid change: Why do disjoint write paths leave the caller patch unvalidated after an interface change, and which record lets the integration service decide?
Collision estimate: A repository has 2,000 files and each worker writes 10. Using equation 4, roughly how many workers make a shared write more likely than not? Should the runtime isolate workers at that size?
Reviewer budget: Majority false approval is 16.68 percent at five reviewers and levels off near 15.0 percent. Should the system provision ten more reviewers of the same kind, or one protected test, and why?
Approval vs. authority: Distinguish a worker’s approval, a scoped protected-test result, and permission to publish the candidate.



Validation evidence also carries a finite lifetime while asynchronous workers execute in parallel. If an upstream orchestrator rejects an intermediate candidate patch or alters its task plan, downstream worker agents may continue computing on stale state. Robust agent runtimes must invalidate and reject superseded work while properly terminating and accounting for in-flight child processes.




Suppose the supervisor cancels migration_task_01 while worker_interface_01 awaits an external test job and worker_caller_01 finishes generating a candidate patch. Even if the caller’s patch passes its local validation checks after the supervisor initiates cancellation, the runtime must ensure that the patch remains strictly unpublishable. Meanwhile, an external testing service may have already accepted the interface worker’s test request, incurring resource and billing charges that remain unsettled long after the worker process halts. In single-agent execution, a cancellation signal interrupts a local loop or an outstanding remote inference call. In a multi-agent system, that control boundary must span an entire hierarchy of distributed descendants.


↩︎ Pause and cancellation of a single trajectory, applied at turn boundaries and by streaming cancellation, are established in Control Actions.
To enforce cancellation across a fleet of workers, the runtime records the affected subtree, its current control generation, and the rationale for stopping. Authoritative dispatch and publication gates consult this record along the serialized path that admits new work. In distributed agent systems, closing admission, terminating execution, and releasing resources are three distinct milestones, each demanding its own independent evidence. Everything admitted before the cancellation stays under the settlement rule of failure recovery, now applied across the entire subtree. An operation admitted before the stop preserves its identity, execution status, and assigned owner until its outcome and associated financial charges settle. No cancellation signal, authorization revocation, timeout, or queue purge can retroactively erase that obligation.


↩︎ The settlement rule, which keeps an operation’s reservation and record until evidence establishes its outcome, is established in Effects Outside a Shared Transaction.


When a parent task is canceled, a grandchild worker that has not yet received the stop signal can keep calling tools and publishing results under the parent’s delegated authority. The cancellation context tree prevents that leak without introducing a fourth graph structure. It is the supervision tree of section 18.3.4 seen from the control plane, with the same parent-child ownership edges, each annotated with the control generation of the ancestor that governs the child. A child’s delegation lineage is its path from that tree’s root. Cancellation proceeds in two steps across the runtime’s graphs. First, the runtime traces delegation lineage rather than data-dependency edges to determine which active workers must lose their authority and budget. Because execution mandates and resource allowances flow down the supervision tree, revoking an ancestor immediately strips every descendant in that subtree of eligibility to run tools or publish results. Second, once that subtree is marked ineligible, the runtime inspects the data-dependency graph to see which tasks outside the canceled subtree were waiting on its outputs. Any downstream continuation that required an artifact from the canceled subtree can no longer satisfy its preconditions and is invalidated, whereas sibling or downstream tasks that treated the canceled child as an optional speculative branch continue undisturbed.

Definition 18.3: Hierarchical cancellation context tree
Hierarchical cancellation context tree is a runtime-owned delegation structure that links each child to the ancestor control decisions governing its continued execution and result publication.

Significance: It identifies which descendants must lose eligibility when an ancestor stops and which outstanding operations still need an owner.
Distinction: Propagating a stop request changes control policy; confirming remote termination, resource release, and effect settlement requires separate evidence.
Common pitfall: Treating a canceled parent record as proof that every child, external job, and charge has ended.



The ordering of events at each admission and publication gate dictates the precise boundary of cancellation. Suppose an admission gateway accepts worker_interface_01’s test operation, logs its unique operation identity along with its resource reservation, and begins transmitting the request. If the parent task cancels before a reply arrives, that test operation remains admitted and must proceed through the settlement protocol. However, any subsequent request from either child that arrives at that gateway after the cancellation decision is serialized will be rejected immediately. Result publication follows the exact same linear order. The integration path must re-verify task eligibility at the atomic publication boundary: if the cancellation commits first, it blocks publication of any patch, regardless of whether that patch passed every local check. If publication commits before the cancellation is serialized at the boundary, the resulting state change stands as a durable modification that the recovery contract must handle.
Under this architecture, a supervisor can authoritatively report that its gateways deny new work and reject publications without falsely claiming that a disconnected or remote worker process has already halted. A remote enforcement gateway that loses connectivity to the central control plane must fail closed. If a gateway instead relies on cached authorization tokens, it operates under an explicit stale-authorization window and cannot guarantee immediate, subtree-wide revocation (section 18.8).



Closing a local client stream does not confirm that a remote model provider has ceased generation, and killing a local worker process leaves requests accepted by external services in flight. Because local termination and remote completion are asymmetric across distributed boundaries, the runtime must dispatch explicit stop requests to each reachable execution service, with each acknowledgment certifying only its specific operational scope (table 7). An executor’s process-level or infrastructure confirmation always outranks an agent’s self-reported claim that it has halted.

For an outstanding test request, the runtime retains the operation identity, execution attempt history, resource reservation, and external job handle while actively reconciling status. If the external test service eventually delivers a late result, that response can settle the operation’s outcome and finalize its billing without reactivating the canceled task trajectory. If the external outcome remains indeterminate, the runtime transfers the operation to a designated settlement owner. The execution receipt preserves these audit records through runtime.settlement_ref, ensuring they survive any context-window summarization or lineage compaction.
Cleanup operations cannot execute under the revoked worker’s authority; the runtime must provision a separately scoped administrative credential and a protected resource allowance. Furthermore, tearing down an allocated environment is itself an asynchronous operation with an uncertain outcome. Scratch workspace or container deletion must block until all relevant filesystem writers have terminated and required diagnostic artifacts have been safely archived. An asynchronous background sweeper reconciles registered physical allocations against these pending evidentiary obligations before unlinking directories or recycling sandbox containers.

Waiting for every worker drops on-time odds below half by seven workers.
Beyond handling failures and user aborts, cancellation is a primitive for speculative execution and latency management. When an agent workflow fans out across multiple subtasks, waiting for every parallel worker exposes the entire system to stragglers, the tail-at-scale problem (Dean and Barroso 2013). Consider \(\WorkerCount\) parallel workers with independent and identically distributed completion times \(\WorkerCompletionTime_i\) required to produce an admissible result. If \(\WorkerCompletionDistribution(\TimeInstant)=\Pr(\WorkerCompletionTime_i\le \TimeInstant)\) represents the cumulative probability of a single worker finishing within time \(\TimeInstant\), an all-results barrier, which requires every worker to complete, achieves a deadline completion probability of
\[\Pr\bigl(\max_i \WorkerCompletionTime_i\le \TimeInstant\bigr)=\WorkerCompletionDistribution(\TimeInstant)^{\WorkerCount}.\]
Because the barrier needs every worker’s admissible result, each added worker multiplies the deadline probability by another factor \(\WorkerCompletionDistribution(\TimeInstant)<1\), so it decays geometrically as the fan-out \(\WorkerCount\) grows. This is the same geometric decay that horizon compounding (equation 1.1) applies across turns, now applied across workers. In production systems, correlated queueing delays, shared rate limits, and unequal prompt lengths break the idealized independent model, so deadline probabilities must be measured under the shared serving conditions. However, if the task contract permits any \(\RequiredResultCount\) interchangeable admissible results out of \(\WorkerCount\) replicas, the probability of meeting the deadline becomes
\[\Pr(\WorkerCompletionTime_{(k)}\le \TimeInstant)=\sum_{j=k}^{\WorkerCount}\binom{\WorkerCount}{\FinishedWorkerCount} \WorkerCompletionDistribution(\TimeInstant)^\FinishedWorkerCount[1-\WorkerCompletionDistribution(\TimeInstant)]^{\WorkerCount-\FinishedWorkerCount},\]
where \(\WorkerCompletionTime_{(k)}\) denotes the arrival time of the \(\RequiredResultCount\)th admissible result. This \(\RequiredResultCount\)-of-\(\WorkerCount\) stopping rule applies strictly to interchangeable outputs, such as parallel candidate retrieval or redundant reasoning paths. In the migration scenario, by contrast, the system requires both the interface update and the caller refactor; no majority of completed caller patches can stand in for a missing interface patch.

Napkin Math 18.5: A completion contract changes the barrierProblem: A hypothetical read-only analysis task permits any 6 interchangeable admissible results from 8 workers. Each worker independently has a 90 percent probability of returning such a result within 10 s of dispatch, including its checks. What is the probability of having sufficient results by that deadline, compared with waiting for every worker?
Math: Requiring every result gives \(\WorkerCompletionDistribution(\TimeInstant)^{\WorkerCount}\), or 43.05 percent. Summing the binomial probabilities for 6 through 8 completions gives 96.19 percent.
Systems insight: An all-results barrier multiplies the deadline probability by \(\WorkerCompletionDistribution(\TimeInstant)\) for every worker added; at this per-worker rate it drops below even odds at 7 workers. Where the contract permits interchangeable results, a \(\RequiredResultCount\)-of-\(\WorkerCount\) stopping rule recovers most of the lost probability. Where it does not, the fan-out itself must shrink or the per-worker tail must be cut. The workers still running after the rule fires consume resources until cancellation takes effect, and that work belongs in the cost account.


Hedging9 mitigates tail latency by dispatching a redundant replacement attempt after a specified delay while the original worker continues running, subsequently accepting whichever admissible result completes first (Dean and Barroso 2013). Hedging functions smoothly for read-only analyses and sandboxed candidate patches where a single runtime publication gate arbitrates the winner and cancels redundant runners. However, speculative hedging introduces acute hazards if an agent executes external mutating actions. Unless the destination service implements a strict duplicate-effect or idempotency contract, a trailing or canceled worker can execute irreversible side effects before its cancellation signal is processed. A hedge of a mutating action is a retry issued before the first attempt has settled, which settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)) forbids unless both attempts carry one operation identity that the endpoint deduplicates. Furthermore, speculative attempts consume real token allowances and concurrency slots; dispatching hedges into a congested inference cluster amplifies queue depth and prolongs the very tail latencies the mechanism was intended to truncate.
9 Hedged Requests: Dean and Barroso’s recipe defers the second request until the first has been outstanding longer than the 95th-percentile expected latency, which bounds the extra load to roughly the fraction of requests that are that slow. For agents the delay matters more than for storage reads, because each hedge is a full model trajectory with its own reservation, and a hedge issued too early doubles spend on the common case to shorten the rare one.

Even when every child agent stays within its own token budget, a rate mismatch between stages of a pipeline can still destabilize the workflow. A fast producer that emits candidate changes faster than a downstream reviewer or test runner can drain them fills the queue between the two stages. As that backlog grows, candidates wait longer before inspection, so the repository state they were built against moves underneath them while they sit in line.
Consider an upstream agent that lists files and emits candidate diffs at \(\ArrivalRate =\) 5 items per second. A downstream reviewer model generates a 500-token critique for each item at a decode speed of 40 tokens per second, yielding an effective service rate of only \(\ServiceRate =\) 0.08 items per second. In an unconstrained queue, the backlog expands at the net rate \(\ArrivalRate - \ServiceRate\). After 10 minutes, the queue accumulates 2,952 unreviewed items, and a newly submitted diff faces an estimated queue wait of 10.2 hours. Long before process memory is exhausted, the queued items become obsolete, because the repository state they reference has diverged, reproducing between agents the stale-observation failure that context invalidation guards against inside one trajectory. Per-agent token budgets fail to prevent this collapse because each individual candidate item is inexpensive to generate.


↩︎ Context invalidation, which withdraws observations that a later change has made stale, is established in Context Invalidation.
A finite credit window prevents this divergence by bounding the number of admitted, in-flight items, much as an aggregate budget caps token expenditure. It is the same mechanism that bounds staged records in trajectory collection. A producer transmits only while it holds a credit the consumer issued for free capacity, so congestion delays the producer but never overflows a buffer. Let \(\CreditWindowCapacity\) denote the fixed credit capacity of the channel, \(\FreeCreditCount\) the unallocated credits held by the producer, and \(\OutstandingItemCount\) the outstanding admitted items currently circulating in the pipeline. The runtime enforces the structural invariant:
\[\FreeCreditCount+\OutstandingItemCount=\CreditWindowCapacity,\qquad \FreeCreditCount\ge0,\quad \OutstandingItemCount\ge0.\]


↩︎ Collection credits, which bound staged trajectories between generation and verification, are established in Collection credits and staging reserves.
Under this discipline, admitting a new work item requires the producer to acquire and attach an available credit. That credit remains tied to the item while it traverses the network, waits in downstream queues, undergoes evaluation, or reserves output buffer space. The runtime returns the credit to the producer’s pool only when the item reaches a designated capacity-release boundary. Credit returns are processed atomically and with at-most-once semantics. A lost return silently shrinks the window, and a duplicated one inflates it, so network disconnections trigger a recount of outstanding credits against the authoritative runtime state rather than granting producers a fresh batch of credits.
Beyond protecting buffer memory, credit windows provide a sizing model for mean residence at a sustained service rate. Little’s law (theorem \(\ref{thrm-05-littles-law}\), equation 5.7) states that the mean number of items held equals their admitted rate times their mean residence. Applying it to a saturated window takes one mapping. The items held are the outstanding ones, \(\OutstandingItemCount=\CreditWindowCapacity\). The window admits a new item only when the consumer drains one, so the admitted rate is the drain rate \(\ServiceRate\), not the producer’s offered rate \(\ArrivalRate\). Dividing the items held by the admitted rate gives a mean residence of \(\CreditWindowCapacity/\ServiceRate\). With a window of \(\CreditWindowCapacity =\) 8 credits in the pipeline above, a diff that would have waited 10.2 hours behind the unbounded backlog instead resides in the window for 100 seconds on average. A hard freshness requirement additionally needs admission timestamps, deadline checks before service, and bounded service times if timely service must be guaranteed. When credits are exhausted, the producer yields execution instead of flooding the pipeline with artifacts destined to be obsolete upon inspection. Furthermore, if each in-flight payload is constrained to at most \(\DataVolume\) bytes, total memory occupancy cannot exceed \(\CreditWindowCapacity\DataVolume\). This demonstrates why payload return bounds (section 18.4) serve as admission-control parameters rather than mere prompt formatting conventions.
Exhausting data credits, however, must never starve control-plane traffic. Signals such as cancellation commands, credit reconciliation messages, execution status receipts, and financial settlement records travel over reserved out-of-band control channels. The runtime must reject new task admissions whenever doing so would risk exhausting the execution slots reserved for downstream consumers and cleanup handlers. Otherwise, upstream producers waiting for credits will block the very consumers needed to release them, deadlocking the system. Finally, releasing a channel credit must not be conflated with releasing an external resource or refunding a financial commitment. Credit reclamation restores pipeline capacity, whereas financial settlement accounts for external cost.
Together, cancellation trees and credit windows bound the volume and financial exposure of in-flight work while keeping control paths responsive, and the credit window sets mean residence under the stated service rate. Neither control, however, decides which operations a child is allowed to propose while it runs. Enforcing those limits across a delegation tree depends on the authority model at each node: what capabilities each descendant holds, how its allowance is reserved, and how fresh its lineage must be when checked at a remote gateway (section 18.8).




Suppose worker_caller_01, an agent authorized only to update selected caller functions, spawns a new child task to inspect upstream source code and designates the root orchestrator as that child’s parent. If the runtime naively resolves authority from the client-supplied parent identifier, the inspection child inherits the root’s global authority, including publication credentials intended exclusively for the release integration service. The delegation tree (the supervision tree’s parent-child edges, along which grants now flow) has itself manufactured a confused deputy (definition \(\ref{dfn-confused-deputy}\)). The runtime resolved authority from a name the requester supplied, the parent identifier that the child chose for itself. Similarly, two sibling workers dispatched concurrently might both observe the parent’s uncommitted budget before either issues an external call, overdrawing the task’s shared financial or token allowance. Task cancellation exposes a matching temporal hazard: a descendant grant that was perfectly valid when minted must admit no further work once the runtime revokes an ancestor in its lineage.
Scoped grants and credential brokering establish where authority resides within isolated execution environments. Multi-agent architectures extend this foundation through attenuated delegation: every hop down the task hierarchy passes authority no broader than the delegator’s existing authority. This model enforces the principle of least privilege (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975) with capabilities (definition \(\ref{dfn-capability}\)). The authority therefore travels in the reference a child holds rather than being looked up from the identity it claims, and confinement survives concurrent spending and ancestor state transitions. While a model may propose spawning a child task and suggest its scope, the runtime supervisor alone assigns the child’s identity, issues its attenuated grant, commits its resource reservation, and binds its lifecycle.

Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.


Passing a parent’s full credential or unreserved budget balance to a child lets a single compromised subtask modify unrelated files or spend the entire task allowance. To keep each hop narrower than the one above it, a delegation tree applies the containment relation \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant)\) established in Narrowing delegated authority at every hop. In a multi-agent tree the relation governs concrete operations executed on underlying system resources, rather than superficial labels such as tool names or directory prefixes that an agent might attempt to manipulate. For example, an inspection child task may hold permission to inspect a specific interface file, but it must possess no rights to modify caller source files, exfiltrate repository data, or access the parent broker’s credentials for external repositories. The execution boundary enforces these perimeter restrictions directly; the child environment starts without inheriting broader host credentials or open file handles.
Runtimes can implement these bindings using either protected internal kernel handles or cryptographically verifiable bearer tokens. Chained-caveat tokens let a holder attenuate its grant locally without contacting an issuer, because each added restriction extends a keyed hash chain that the holder cannot unwind (Birgisson et al. 2014). Because the runtime supervisor, never the generative model, binds the resulting capability to the specific task execution context, a compromised or malfunctioning worker cannot forge a parent lineage or substitute a token belonging to another task.
Permissions and consumable budgets require different delegation rules. Permissions are not depleted by use, so they can be shared: a parent that delegates read access retains its own ability to read. Consumable budgets, by contrast, are depletable resources that must be partitioned rather than duplicated, ensuring that each unit of currency or token quota is spent at most once. The admission control gate must therefore ensure that no unit of budget is created from nothing or spent twice anywhere in the delegation hierarchy. Before dispatching a child task, the runtime atomically reserves the child’s admitted liability against the shared allowance, accounting for all concurrent siblings and the parent’s own outstanding work. This atomic reservation prevents two sibling workers from racing to commit the same remaining balance. It is the shared-allowance rule of trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) applied across a tree, under which concurrent holders reserve against one allowance and a derived allowance only narrows. If a child subsequently subdivides its allowance among its descendants, it creates a nested sub-budget that can never exceed its own allocation, not an independent pool that can be charged separately.


↪ The settlement rules developed in Budget conservation across descendants decide when a delegated allocation’s unspent backing returns to the parent and count a late bill once.



In a distributed multi-agent system, revocation cannot depend on promptly delivering push notifications to every running child. A robust architectural pattern assigns each task node in the runtime a monotonic generation counter and an operational state (such as active, canceled, or completed). When a grant is issued, the runtime binds it cryptographically to the complete root-to-holder lineage path, recording the exact generation counter of each ancestor at the moment of delegation. Revoking an ancestor marks that node ineligible or advances its generation counter. Node restarts must monotonically advance or preserve generation counters rather than resetting to zero, which would inadvertently revive expired or revoked grants.
When an agent submits an operation to the API gateway, the admission check verifies the grant’s cryptographic integrity, scope, and expiration while querying the current lifecycle status and generation of every ancestor in the bound lineage path. If any ancestor has been canceled or its generation has advanced, the gateway rejects the descendant’s request immediately, even if the leaf worker has not yet received a cancellation signal and still considers itself active. Traversing a lineage path of depth \(\ell\) requires \(\mathcal{O}(\ell)\) ancestor lookups at admission time, whereas advancing an ancestor’s generation number invalidates the entire subtree of descendant grants in \(\mathcal{O}(1)\) time without rewriting individual token payloads. Gateway caches or indexed summaries can shorten those admission lookups at the cost of cache-invalidation rules, and table 8 traces how the check behaves across migration_task_01 without assuming that cancellation messages arrive everywhere at once.

Enforcing cancellation semantics requires an unambiguous, linearizable ordering point. Under a strict freshness policy, revocation updates and admission checks share an authoritative global order: once a revocation is committed, no subsequent admission check within that scope may evaluate against stale policy state. Because local signature verification and expiry checks establish only that a grant was valid when issued, a replicated gateway that cannot verify current ancestor state must fail closed, withholding admission from new operations.
Alternatively, systems that prioritize availability over strict consistency may permit distributed gateways to evaluate requests against cached ancestor state for a declared interval. This engineering trade-off introduces a stale-policy window, the bounded interval in which an already-revoked grant may still be accepted by an out-of-date gateway. The system designer must explicitly bound this window to account for cache invalidation propagation, token refresh intervals, clock skew assumptions, and network partition timeouts. Furthermore, revocation must actively sever all mediation pathways, including revoking open writable file handles held by running processes. Any operations already admitted to external systems prior to revocation remain governed by transactional settlement rules.



During execution, a worker may discover that completing its objective requires an operation that exceeds its delegated authority. Rather than terminating or attempting privilege escalation, the worker submits an authorization request. An approval binds to the exact operation it authorizes, never to a model’s explanation of it (Action-bound approval), and the runtime recomputes that binding and rechecks its preconditions at dispatch (Dispatch-time rechecks). For a delegated publication, the bound operation names the originating task (migration_task_01), the content hash of the candidate artifact, the destination reference, and its base-version preconditions, so a candidate altered by a single byte after approval needs a fresh decision.
Delegation changes where the request goes and what the recheck must cover. The worker cannot widen its own grant, and attenuation forbids its parent from granting more than the parent holds. The runtime therefore collects such requests in a bounded approval queue, deduplicates repeated submissions from siblings, and routes each to the task owner rather than to an intermediate parent whose own grant could not cover the operation. Any rationale a root or worker model attaches remains unverified commentary. At dispatch, the recheck extends from the operation to its lineage: current grants, every ancestor’s lineage generation, and the remaining budget must still permit the action, so an ancestor cancellation committed after approval blocks it as surely as a changed candidate does. Passing validation tests in migration_accept_v1, obtaining operator approval, and executing the privileged publication remain three distinct, non-fungible events.

Checkpoint 18.3: Bounding work, authority, and spending after a split

Cancellation scope: The supervisor cancels migration_task_01 after the gateway admitted worker_interface_01’s test operation but before its reply arrives. Which statements can the runtime make truthfully now, and which must wait for further evidence?
Barrier vs. quorum: At a per-worker on-time probability of 90 percent, why can a 6-of-8 stopping rule rescue a read-only analysis but not the two-part migration?
Hedging a mutation: Why is a hedged copy of a mutating tool call a retry before settlement, and what must both attempts share before the runtime may issue it?
Credit window: The reviewer drains 0.08 items per second. What window keeps the modeled mean residence under one minute, and which messages must travel outside the data credits?
Joint allowances and revocation: Two siblings each receive less than the parent’s remaining allowance. What must the runtime do so they cannot jointly overdraw it, and what happens at a remote gateway that cannot confirm an ancestor’s current generation?



Delegation controls conserve authority and spending, distinguish cancellation from completed cleanup, and separate administrative approval from verified success. These safeguards make task decomposition governable. Whether splitting a task across multiple agents is actually useful, however, remains a separate empirical question, answerable only by measurement against a strong single-agent baseline.




When benchmarking the authentication migration (migration_task_01), granting parallel tool execution to the multi-agent supervisor while artificially restricting the single controller to serial execution measures a baseline handicap rather than the true benefit of delegation. A rigorous evaluation compares the supervisor against a single controller that already dispatches parallel searches and tests, beginning with an objective declared in advance, such as minimizing cost per accepted task subject to a deadline, or maximizing completed tasks within a fixed operating budget. The coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) then appears in three measurements read together: accepted-task rate, elapsed wall-clock time, and cost per accepted task. While a Pareto improvement across all three dimensions is ideal, it is rarely achieved. In practice, delegating work across agents represents an explicit trade of computational cost for lower latency. This trade-off is justified only when the engineering objective values latency reduction and the solution satisfies all quality and budget constraints.


Comparing a multi-agent fleet against a single-turn prompt or a controller with lower tool concurrency credits delegation for resources the single agent was never allowed to use. A fair evaluation applies the matched-budget comparison established in Matched-budget comparison, which fixes the task distribution, criteria, and resource envelope before policies are compared. It also uses an equally capable baseline, an iterative single controller with parallel tool execution, rather than an isolated, single-turn model call. For delegation, the matched envelope must also fix starting fixtures, evidence access, and identical concurrency limits on both model calls and tool executions. Because either policy may terminate early, unconsumed budget represents an operational outcome rather than an experimental discrepancy. If a delegated design also alters underlying model selections or prompt formulations, the trial evaluates a compound bundle of variables, so isolating the architectural impact of delegation requires a controlled ablation. Finally, acceptance must be scored on the integrated end-to-end task rather than on worker subtasks, because an interface update that passes its local unit tests still fails the migration if the accompanying caller patch introduces breaking signature incompatibilities.



Every attempted task must remain in the evaluation denominator; tasks that encounter timeouts, unhandled errors, or indeterminate verdicts cannot be discarded from the benchmark. When the operational contract treats late delivery as an outage, on-time acceptance must be recorded as a distinct metric alongside gross completion. End-to-end latency spans the full execution envelope, measured continuously from task arrival through task decomposition, sub-agent dispatch, intermediate reconciliation, final integration, and automated assessment. Calculating median latency solely over accepted tasks introduces severe survival bias by filtering out prolonged failures. Systems evaluation therefore tracks latency across all arrivals. A task still running at the observation cutoff is right-censored: its latency is known only to exceed the cutoff, so it enters the latency distribution as a lower bound rather than being dropped. This is the same refusal to discard unresolved outcomes that keeps pending and unknown verdicts in the evaluation denominator (The four-verdict rule).
Cost accounting must encompass the complete system boundary: supervisor orchestration, retrieval queries, verification suites, merge conflict reconciliation, failed exploratory attempts, canceled speculative branches, and environment cleanup. Token expenditures must distinguish input and output tokens at their respective market prices, while concurrent tool invocations must be billed by aggregate worker execution time, which frequently exceeds the wall-clock span of the critical path. The effective cost per accepted task divides this full cohort spend by the accepted count under the same matched-budget accounting, so an architecture with no accepted solutions still reports its spend and the zero count. The token inflation documented in war story 18.1 illustrates why rigorous cost accounting is needed before committing to a multi-agent deployment.

Napkin Math 18.6: How much acceptance a token multiple must buyProblem: A delegated multi-agent architecture consumes tokens at the ratios reported for the research system: 15× the token volume of a standard chat interaction, compared to 4× for an autonomous single agent. Assuming a constant price per token, how much must task acceptance improve for delegation to break even on cost per accepted task, and over which baseline success rates is break-even mathematically achievable?
Math: Let \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\) be the token multiple, delegated tokens per attempt over single-agent tokens per attempt. Following equation 1.2, with cost proportional to tokens, the delegated cost per accepted task divided by the single-agent cost per accepted task is \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\,\SingleAgentAcceptanceProbability/\MultiAgentAcceptanceProbability\). With \(\DelegationTokenMultiple=\) 15× \(/\) 4× \(=\) 3.75×, economic break-even requires that \(\MultiAgentAcceptanceProbability =\) 3.75× \(\cdot\, \SingleAgentAcceptanceProbability\). Because probability is bounded (\(\MultiAgentAcceptanceProbability \le 1\)), break-even is possible only when the single-agent baseline achieves \(\SingleAgentAcceptanceProbability \le\) 26.7 percent. Even if the reported evaluation score gain of 90.2 percent translated directly into an acceptance rate multiplier of 1.90×, the effective cost per accepted task would remain 2.0× that of the single-agent baseline.
Systems insight: When delegation multiplies token consumption by a factor of \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\), it reduces effective cost \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) if and only if it scales task acceptance by more than \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\). At an expansion ratio of 3.75×, this economic efficiency can materialize only on difficult tasks where the single agent succeeds less than 26.7 percent of the time. On workloads where a single agent already succeeds reliably, delegation cannot be justified by cost efficiency. It must be justified as a purchase of reduced wall-clock latency or broader search coverage, valued explicitly by the system’s operational requirements.








Coherency cost turns added workers into lost capacity past the peak.
A matched trial is expensive, so before running one a team must decide which worker counts deserve a trial at all. The fixed-work scaling model of equation 1 does not replace that benchmarking; its role is to guide the search by identifying promising worker counts. Varying the worker count alters resource contention, sub-task dispatch boundaries, and inter-agent reconciliation costs simultaneously. Consequently, any empirical overhead curve holds strictly within the evaluated range and serves as a hypothesis beyond it. To reason about scaling limits systematically, classical systems engineering separates everything that keeps a fleet from ideal division into work that serializes (undivided planning, and any overhead that queues at a single resource) and pairwise reconciliation. These two mechanisms require different architectural remedies.

Theorem 18.1: Universal scalability law
For a fixed amount of work divided among \(\WorkerCount\) equally capable workers, Gunther’s universal scalability law (USL) (Gunther 2008) gives the relative capacity, the speedup over one worker, as equation 5, with its peak at equation 6.
\[
\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount)=\frac{\WorkerCount}{1+\ContentionCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)+\CoherencyCoefficient \WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)}
\tag{5}\]
\[
\WorkerCount^*=\sqrt{\frac{1-\ContentionCoefficient}{\CoherencyCoefficient}}
\tag{6}\]

Contention (\(\ContentionCoefficient\)): The share of work that serializes, including undivided planning, final assessment, and queueing at single resources such as the supervisor or the integration queue.
Coherency (\(\CoherencyCoefficient\)): The cost of pairwise reconciliation. Each of the \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\) ordered worker pairs may exchange state, re-read a peer’s output, or resolve a conflicting change, the same count as the mesh round in section 18.3.
Amdahl’s law (\(\CoherencyCoefficient=0\)): Capacity saturates at \(1/\ContentionCoefficient\) and never declines.
Retrograde region (\(\WorkerCount>(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\CoherencyCoefficient\)): A positive \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) makes added workers harmful, not merely useless. Capacity peaks at \(\WorkerCount^*\) and falls below one, slower than a single worker, past this count. With the screening notebook’s \(\ContentionCoefficient=\) 0.20 and \(\CoherencyCoefficient=\) 0.02, every count from 41 workers up finishes later than the serial reference.



Dividing both the numerator and denominator of equation 5 by \(\WorkerCount\) yields \(1/[\ContentionCoefficient+(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\WorkerCount+\CoherencyCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)]\). This expression matches equation 1 directly when setting the parallel fraction \(\ParallelFraction=1-\ContentionCoefficient\) and the overhead function \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\CoherencyCoefficient(\WorkerCount-1)\). In elapsed-time terms, \(\ContentionCoefficient\) captures fixed serial work whose duration does not change as workers are added, whereas the screen’s linear penalty \(\WorkerOverheadSlope\) plays the role of \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) by capturing any elapsed delay that grows in proportion to \(\WorkerCount-1\). Multiplying top and bottom by \(\WorkerCount\) turns that linear elapsed-time penalty into the quadratic term \(\CoherencyCoefficient\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\) in the denominator of equation 5. Two very different physical mechanisms can produce that same algebraic term. True pairwise state reconciliation generates \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\) interactions across the fleet, and when that quadratic aggregate work is shared evenly across the \(\WorkerCount\) concurrent workers, each worker experiences an elapsed delay proportional to \(\WorkerCount-1\). However, a central supervisor that sequentially processes one extra dispatch or receipt for each additional worker also adds an elapsed delay proportional to \(\WorkerCount-1\), without any peer-to-peer communication at all. A fitted value of \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) therefore flags an elapsed overhead that scales with worker count, and engineers must still inspect traces to see whether the culprit is pairwise worker reconciliation or per-worker queuing at the coordinator. Applying the notebook’s assumed parameters, equation 6 places the continuous theoretical optimum at 6.3 workers, which evaluates to the discrete optimum of 6 workers identified in the screening notebook.
