The architectural remedy depends on the measured source of overhead. Supervisor queue time, dependency invalidations, and reconciliation work help distinguish serial processing from cross-worker dependency work, and a matched trial that changes one mechanism can test the diagnosis. A verified serial bottleneck may benefit from pipelining supervisory prompts, sharding shared integration queues, or asynchronous event loops. When dependency reconciliation dominates, a partition that reduces cross-agent synchronization may instead pay. Interface refactoring coupled to caller implementations provides one such dependency hazard; a research query with independent search paths provides a contrasting partition.

Lighthouse 18.1: Research agent (orchestrator-worker fan-out)Workload: The research agent addresses open-ended, breadth-first queries. A lead orchestrator decomposes the inquiry into independent search paths, dispatches read-only subagents to retrieve and analyze external sources, and synthesizes their condensed findings. The builders of one production research system report that this breadth-first regime is where delegation helps most, in contrast to coding tasks whose tight interdependencies leave less work to run in parallel (Hadfield et al. 2025).
Scenario coefficients: Suppose lead-agent planning and final synthesis serialize \(\ContentionCoefficient=\) 0.10 of total execution, while subagents operate almost entirely without cross-communication (\(\CoherencyCoefficient=\) 0.002). Evaluating the scalability model yields an optimal fan-out of 21 subagents achieving 5.5× relative capacity. In contrast, the code repair agent’s high coherency limits its configuration to 6 workers at 2.3× capacity. Under these assumptions, the research partition permits a 3.5× wider effective worker fan-out. (These stylized coefficients illustrate the scaling regime rather than measured telemetry.)
Local constraint: Low coherency overhead permits wider fan-out under the supplied model, but token expenditure and context trust can still constrain deployment. At fixed per-worker work, token consumption scales linearly with fan-out, so the economic break-even threshold analyzed in notebook 18.6 may cap deployment before the modeled capacity peak \(\WorkerCount^*\). Furthermore, because worker receipts incorporate uncurated text from external web APIs, the bounded receipt protocol of section 18.4 limits returned context and keeps worker claims separate from runtime evidence. Source-derived fields and summaries remain untrusted inputs whose proposed uses require the security checks established for the tool boundary.
Systems insight: Under the supplied coefficients, the research partition supports wider fan-out than the repair partition. Dependency traces can establish whether interface isolation addresses the repair workload’s overhead; matched outcome and cost measurements determine whether wider research fan-out earns its additional spend. Admission controls bound that spend independently of the modeled capacity gain.


In production systems, empirical engineering inverts this analytical workflow. Rather than postulating coefficients, engineers conduct targeted benchmarking trials across a small set of practical worker counts (for example, \(\WorkerCount \in \{1, 2, 4\}\)) to estimate \(\ContentionCoefficient\) and \(\CoherencyCoefficient\). The resulting model fit projects the empirical capacity peak \(\WorkerCount^*\), identifying the next candidate configuration to benchmark. A large fitted coherency parameter \(\CoherencyCoefficient\) warrants inspecting traces and testing targeted interventions. Redesigning the task decomposition is justified when that evidence confirms that dependency reconciliation dominates; the coefficient alone does not establish the remedy.



Once the scalability fit has nominated a configuration, the matched trial decides whether it earns its tax. Consider the evaluation results for a representative cohort of software migration tasks patterned after migration_task_01, evaluated under identical automated test suites (migration_accept_v1). Both configurations operate under identical constraints: matching tool and model concurrency limits, identical sandbox permissions, and equivalent token and financial ceilings. The experiment isolates the delegation architecture itself (how work is decomposed, dispatched, and integrated) rather than what the runtime allows.

Every pitfall below comes from treating a delegation boundary as a guarantee that the runtime never actually enforced. Splitting work across agents does not by itself speed up completion, prevent semantic conflicts, decorrelate reviewer errors, or settle in-flight operations when a parent stops. Each of those assumptions carries a measurable cost in latency, token spend, or broken repository state.

Fallacy: More workers necessarily improve the task outcome.
Adding parallel workers introduces synchronization overhead, resource contention, and coordination traffic that quickly erode parallel speedup. In the fixed-partition screen (notebook 18.1), deploying eight workers consumes 0.440 of the serial execution time, compared to 0.433 achieved at an optimal configuration of 6 workers. Beyond this point, coherency cost dominates: under the universal scalability law with those same coefficients, scaling out to 41 workers runs slower than executing the workload on a single agent. Furthermore, economic cost escalates even when latency stalls. A multi-agent delegation multiple of 3.75× in token consumption pays for itself only on difficult tasks that an isolated single agent completes less than 26.7 percent of the time. Rather than assuming that parallelism is beneficial, system designers must benchmark candidate topologies under identical token budgets and time ceilings against a declared task objective.


Pitfall: Treating a clean merge as evidence that concurrent changes remain compatible.
A successful textual merge only verifies that concurrent workers avoided line collisions in shared files, leaving cross-file semantic dependencies completely unvalidated. Across a repository of 1,000 files where each worker performs 10 edits, two concurrent workers touch completely disjoint files 90.4 percent of the time. As a result, nearly every pair of concurrent patches merges cleanly from the perspective of version control, even when a caller and an interface worker introduce mutually incompatible API contracts. Coordination systems must validate semantic dependencies and test candidate integration trees within an isolated environment before guarded publication (section 18.5).


Fallacy: Agreement among reviewers proves correctness.
Consensus among language-model reviewers reflects the correlation of their errors rather than an objective proof of correctness. When multiple reviewer agents share underlying model families, prompt templates, or reasoning biases, their mistakes correlate positively. For instance, five reviewers with an individual false-approval rate of 20 percent would reach an erroneous majority verdict only 5.79 percent of the time under strict statistical independence. Under the assumed beta mixture, in which reviewers share each candidate’s difficulty, that false-majority rate jumps to 16.68 percent. Adding more reviewers of the same kind cannot eliminate this shared bias, because error rates quickly level off near an irreducible floor of 15.0 percent (section 18.6). Production architectures must treat subjective reviewer voting as an advisory signal and isolate it strictly from deterministic, guarded verification checks.


Pitfall: Closing the parent task and releasing its reservations as soon as cancellation is requested.
A cancellation request immediately closes admission for new subtasks, but active execution, external tool calls, and downstream token charges drain asynchronously. Discarded work is not a rounding error. In the delegation of table 9, failed attempts and canceled speculative branches account for $6 of $18 in delegated spend, and that table is complete only because every one of those charges stayed owned until it settled. If the parent task releases its accounting context and budget allocations the moment cancellation is requested, the trailing operations continue running without an owner, and their charges land outside any budget as untracked spend and leaked resources. Robust orchestrators close admission at the entry gates, broadcast cancellation signals downstream, and maintain accounting context and state reservations until all active operations, diagnostic evidence, and billing charges have fully settled under the settlement rule.


Fallacy: If each worker usually finishes on time, the fan-out usually finishes on time.
Synchronizing multiple concurrent workers behind an all-results barrier compounds tail latency exponentially. Because every worker must complete before the barrier can lift, the overall probability of on-time completion multiplies each individual worker’s success rate. With an individual on-time probability of 90 percent per worker, a fan-out of 8 workers completes within the deadline only 43.05 percent of the time, and barrier success falls below even odds once the fleet reaches 7 workers (section 18.7). Where the system contract accepts interchangeable or quorum-based results, implementing a stopping rule restores 96.19 percent. Where every subtask is strictly required, the orchestrator must reduce fan-out width to keep tail latency bounded.




Delegation turns one trajectory into several. Every boundary it adds must carry explicitly what a single trajectory carried implicitly: the inputs a worker may rely on, the authority and allowance it may spend, the evidence it must return, and the obligations that outlive it. The runtime, not the workers, owns those boundaries. It separates claims from execution records, revalidates dependencies before anything publishes, treats agreement among similar reviewers as one correlated signal, and keeps every admitted operation owned until it settles.
Whether those boundaries are worth building is a measurement question. Delegation lowers cost per accepted task only when it raises acceptance by more than it multiplies spend; otherwise it must be bought as reduced wall-clock time or broader coverage that the declared objective explicitly values. Key Takeaways: Delegation must earn and preserve its boundaries

Coordination overhead sets the useful fleet size: Serial execution constraints cap parallel speedup at \(1/\ContentionCoefficient\), while pairwise reconciliation costs cause effective system throughput to fall beyond \(\WorkerCount^*=\sqrt{(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\CoherencyCoefficient}\). Shrinking serial planning and integration overhead raises the scalability ceiling far more than merely shaving latency off individual handoffs. Empirical profiling across realistic workloads, rather than casual inspection of isolated agent trajectories, must calibrate these parameters.
Task dependencies govern completion makespan: Communication topologies, scheduling precedence, and fault-supervision hierarchies address distinct systems requirements. Once a schedule attains its critical-path bound, further latency reductions require shortening that path; before it does, additional slots or reduced contention may also shorten runtime. Furthermore, any agent endowed with recursive delegation authority requires hard runtime limits on fan-out, nesting depth, and aggregate token reservations.
Delegation handoffs require explicit runtime contracts: A handoff envelope must establish immutable task inputs, granted execution authority, resource budgets, and required evidence before worker execution begins. The returned receipt must strictly isolate ground-truth execution records from the worker’s unverified self-assessment, truncating narrative explanations rather than audit telemetry whenever context limits bind.
Disjoint writes do not guarantee semantic compatibility: Non-overlapping file edits establish only that parallel workers avoided concurrent modification conflicts; they do not prove that combined changes preserve system-wide behavioral invariants. Safe publication requires revalidating dependencies against the latest branch head, testing the integrated candidate in isolation, and advancing branch pointers through conditional atomic updates.
Correlated reviewer errors impose an irreducible accuracy floor: When automated reviewers evaluate an intrinsically challenging artifact, shared model blind spots cause their errors to correlate, preventing majority-voting failure rates from dropping to zero. Beyond this floor, spending additional tokens on reviewers of the same kind yields negligible benefit. Runtimes must instead incorporate independent checks, such as deterministic test suites or static analyzers, because peer consensus cannot manufacture authoritative correctness.
Resource obligations outlive parent caller lifecycles: Canceling a parent agent halts the dispatch of new downstream tasks, but it does not automatically terminate remote tool operations, network sockets, or asynchronous child processes already in flight. Each in-flight bound has its own mechanism. Credit windows bound the volume of queued work and support mean-residence sizing. Attenuated grants and atomic reservations bound authority and spend. The settlement record, not cancellation or credit release, keeps every admitted effect owned until its outcome and charges settle.
Multi-agent execution must outperform a capable single-agent baseline: A meaningful evaluation benchmarks multi-agent architectures against an equally optimized single-agent controller provisioned with identical parallel tool access, context allowances, and wall-clock budgets. System accounting must price every failed attempt, speculative invocation, and rollback, justifying multi-agent coordination only when the resulting increase in task success or latency reduction offsets its marginal token overhead.



The coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) manifests in the serialized handoffs, validation barriers, and residual dependencies that remain after decomposing a task. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) mandates that these architectural boundaries maintain strict external validation and effect gating, ensuring that peer consensus among models is never mistaken for authoritative execution rights. Finally, trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) extends from one trajectory to a tree of them. Every child is a separately owned trajectory whose derived grants only narrow, whose consumable allowance is reserved against its ancestors’ shared allowance, and whose unsettled side effects remain accounted for by the runtime after its parent stops.



The question of when dividing computational work yields a net speedup is older than autonomous software agents. Gene Amdahl’s 1967 argument established that serial execution fractions strictly cap the speedup achievable by adding processors (Amdahl 1967). Two years later, Ronald Graham showed that while greedy list scheduling lands close to the theoretical dependency bound, adding parallel resources can paradoxically increase total completion time (Graham 1969). Neil Gunther later unified these dynamics in the universal scalability law, introducing a pairwise coherency penalty to explain how crosstalk and contention turn throughput saturation into outright performance collapse (Gunther 2008). Across successive computing generations, systems architects repeatedly found that coordination overhead and coherency penalties, rather than the raw supply of workers, dictate practical scale.

Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.

Erman, Lee D., Frederick Hayes-Roth, Victor R. Lesser, and D. Raj Reddy. 1980. “The Hearsay-II Speech-Understanding System: Integrating Knowledge to Resolve Uncertainty.” ACM Computing Surveys 12 (2): 213–53. https://doi.org/10.1145/356810.356816.

Hewitt, Carl, Peter Bishop, and Richard Steiger. 1973. “A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence.” Proceedings of the 3rd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI), 235–45.
Distributed artificial intelligence confronted the handoff problem in the 1970s. The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system coordinated independent, opportunistic knowledge sources through a shared blackboard (Erman et al. 1980). Carl Hewitt’s actor model abandoned shared memory entirely, giving each autonomous agent private local state and routing interactions through addressed messages (Hewitt et al. 1973). Reid Smith formalized structured delegation in the Contract Net Protocol, turning task announcement, bidding, and award into an explicit, typed exchange between a manager and prospective contractors (Smith 1980).
Over the following decades, classical distributed systems research supplied the precise operational controls that multi-agent architectures require today. Kung and Robinson introduced optimistic concurrency control, permitting workers to execute tentatively against private workspace copies and validate isolation before committing (Kung and Robinson 1981). Birrell and Nelson established typed remote procedure calls with explicit failure semantics, replacing unstructured message passing with formal client-server contracts (Birrell and Nelson 1984). Gray and Cheriton solved distributed state synchronization and lock management through time-bounded leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989). Joe Armstrong formalized supervision trees within Erlang, demonstrating how structured hierarchies and crash-only semantics allow runtimes to restart failed processes from clean, known states (Armstrong 2003). Finally, object-capability systems eliminated ambient authority by embedding access rights directly into object references rather than relying on global identity checks (Dennis and Van Horn 1966; Hardy 1988), an approach later extended through cryptographically attenuable tokens with chained caveats (Birgisson et al. 2014).

Kung, H. T., and John T. Robinson. 1981. “On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 6 (2): 213–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/319566.319567.

Dennis, Jack B., and Earl C. Van Horn. 1966. “Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations.” Communications of the ACM 9 (3): 143–55. https://doi.org/10.1145/365230.365252.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.

Birgisson, Arnór, Joseph G. Politz, Úlfar Erlingsson, Ankur Taly, Michael Vrable, and Mark S. Miller. 2014. “Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats for Decentralized Authorization in the Cloud.” Proceedings of the Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS).

Condorcet, Marquis de. 1785. Essai Sur l’application de l’analyse à La Probabilité Des décisions Rendues à La Pluralité Des Voix. Imprimerie Royale.

Neumann, John von. 1956. “Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components.” In Automata Studies, edited by Claude E. Shannon and John McCarthy, vol. 34. Annals of Mathematics Studies. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400882618-003.

Eckhardt, Dave E., and Larry D. Lee. 1985. “A Theoretical Basis for the Analysis of Multiversion Software Subject to Coincident Errors.” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-11 (12): 1511–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1985.231895.
Redundancy followed a parallel trajectory of high theoretical promises followed by sobering empirical corrections. The Condorcet jury theorem (Condorcet, Marquis de 1785) and John von Neumann’s multiplexed majority organs (Neumann 1956) demonstrated that aggregating independent votes can synthesize near-perfect reliability from noisy components. Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease proved the rigorous mathematical bounds of Byzantine fault tolerance. Agreement in the unsigned-message protocol model survives arbitrary, even malicious, faults only while fewer than one third of participants are faulty (Lamport et al. 1982). However, the independence premise behind probabilistic majority-voting guarantees collapsed when applied to software. John Knight and Nancy Leveson demonstrated experimentally that independently written programs fail coincidentally on the same edge cases far more often than chance predicts (Knight and Leveson 1986). Dave Eckhardt and Larry Lee provided the analytical explanation: complex problem domains harbor intrinsically difficult input regions that induce correlated failures across diverse implementations (Eckhardt and Lee 1985).
Modern language-model systems have revived every one of these designs at the same time. Self-consistency uses majority voting across sampled reasoning paths (Wang et al. 2023), multi-agent debate structures iterative argumentation across model instances (Du et al. 2023), and conversational frameworks coordinate role-playing agents over structured communication graphs (Wu et al. 2023). In production, orchestrator-worker patterns have delivered capability gains on breadth-first research tasks, and their builders report roughly 15× the token consumption of a chat interaction to get them (Hadfield et al. 2025). Systematic empirical analyses of multi-agent failures reveal that the field has re-encountered classical distributed failure modes: ill-defined task boundaries, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification bottlenecks that silently propagate errors rather than catching them (Cemri et al. 2025).

Wang, Xuezhi, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, and Denny Zhou. 2023. “Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models.” The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations.

Du, Yilun, Shuang Li, Antonio Torralba, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, and Igor Mordatch. 2023. “Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models Through Multiagent Debate.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2305.14325.

Wu, Qingyun, Gagan Bansal, Jieyu Zhang, Yiran Wu, Beibin Li, Erkang Zhu, Biyi Gao, et al. 2023. AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation.

Hadfield, Jeremy, Barry Zhang, Kenneth Lien, Florian Scholz, Jeremy Fox, and Daniel Ford. 2025. How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System. Anthropic Engineering Blog.

The Contract Net Protocol (Smith 1980). The foundational text on structured delegation. Smith frames task distribution as a typed, negotiated protocol, showing that the essential elements of modern task envelopes, from capability announcements to formal awards, were established long before language models existed.
An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming (Knight and Leveson 1986). The landmark controlled experiment that disproved the assumption of independent software failures. This paper provides the standard methodological blueprint for evaluating whether an ensemble of redundant agent reviewers yields genuine reliability gains or merely inflates inference cost.
Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors (Armstrong 2003). Armstrong’s doctoral dissertation detailing the architecture of Erlang. It articulates the operational rationale for supervision trees, fail-stop process isolation, and restart strategies, mapping directly to how orchestrators should manage the lifecycles and blast radiuses of child agent trajectories.
A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions (Gunther 2008). Gunther derives the universal scalability law directly from queueing models. The derivation clarifies the physical distinction between contention and coherency, explaining why serial bottlenecks and cross-agent communication require different architectural fixes.
Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (Cemri et al. 2025). An extensive empirical taxonomy analyzing real-world multi-agent failure traces. It serves as a field catalog of the specification gaps, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification failures that production runtime environments must actively prevent.


Smith, Reid G. 1980. “The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Distributed Problem Solving in a Distributed Processor.” IEEE Transactions on Computers C-29 (12): 1104–13.

Gunther, Neil J. 2008. “A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:0808.1431.

Cemri, Mert, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A. Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, Rishabh Tiwari, Kurt Keutzer, et al. 2025. Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?



Every figure given below is a hypothetical problem input, not a measurement of a real system. Each problem ends in a design decision, and the calculation exists to justify it.

Choosing the lever in a worker-count screen (Basic). A fixed work partition has divisible fraction \(\ParallelFraction=0.9\) and normalized overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\WorkerOverheadSlope(\WorkerCount-1)\) with \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.01\). The resource ceiling permits at most \(20\) workers, and each added worker adds roughly the same token spend.

Using equation 1, compute the normalized elapsed time at \(\WorkerCount=4\), \(8\), and \(16\), the integer count that minimizes it, and the speedup at that count. Compare the count with \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\).
Two proposals compete for the same engineering effort: halving the per-worker overhead to \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.005\), or halving the serial work so that \(\ParallelFraction=0.95\). Compute the best integer count and its speedup under each proposal.
Decide which proposal to fund once worker spend is counted, and state which proposal alone can ever deliver a speedup above \(10\times\).

Hot files in a shared workspace (Basic). A repository holds \(\RepositoryFileCount=5{,}000\) files, and each worker writes \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount=20\) of them, chosen uniformly and independently.

Using equation 4, compute the probability of at least one shared write for \(\WorkerCount=2\) and \(\WorkerCount=4\) workers, both exactly and by the exponential approximation. Find the smallest fleet for which a shared write is more likely than not.
Each worker also edits one shared dependency manifest with probability \(0.3\), independently of its other writes. For four workers, compute the probability that at least two edit the manifest, and the probability of any shared write at all.
A colleague proposes a single shared working directory for four workers because “collisions are under 40 percent.” Decide, and name the two hazards of section 18.5 that remain even when no two workers write the same file.

Sizing a credit window for staleness (Basic). A producer emits candidate items at \(\ArrivalRate=2\) items per second. A consumer model writes a \(400\)-token critique of each item at \(50\) output tokens per second, and each returned record occupies at most \(\DataVolume=8{,}192\) bytes. An item is useful only if the consumer begins serving it within \(60\) s of admission. For initial sizing, screen a saturated credit window by requiring its modeled mean residence to be no greater than this interval; assume negligible transport time and full utilization at the stated service rate.

Compute the consumer’s service rate \(\ServiceRate\), the backlog of an unbounded queue after five minutes, and the wait of the newest item behind that backlog.
Using the full-window mean residence \(\CreditWindowCapacity/\ServiceRate\), find the largest integer window \(\CreditWindowCapacity\) that passes this sizing screen and its payload bound \(\CreditWindowCapacity\DataVolume\). Does passing the screen establish that every item begins service before its freshness deadline?
Find the minimum number of identical consumers needed to keep pace with the producer and the largest shared window that passes the same mean-residence screen at their aggregate service rate. State how admission timestamps and a freshness check before service should handle an item that has waited too long. Explain why cancellation and settlement traffic must not draw on these data credits.

A fourth slot or a shorter vertex (Intermediate). A migration plan has a shared specification \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\) (\(30\) s); four module refactors \(\DependencyGraphVertex_2\) through \(\DependencyGraphVertex_5\) (\(60\), \(60\), \(90\), and \(40\) s), each depending only on \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\); and an integration check \(\DependencyGraphVertex_6\) (\(50\) s) depending on all four refactors. Each vertex occupies one interchangeable slot, with no other delays.

Compute \(\AggregateSlotWork\) and \(\CriticalPathDuration\) from equation 2, and the lower bound of equation 3 for \(\WorkerCount=2\), \(3\), and \(4\) slots.
By assigning the four refactors to slots, find the shortest achievable makespan for each \(\WorkerCount\). Explain why the bound is not attained at \(\WorkerCount=2\).
The team currently runs \(\WorkerCount=3\) and can afford either a fourth slot or engineering that shortens \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) to \(60\) s. Decide, and state what shortening \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) buys once the fourth slot exists.

Pricing deadline coverage (Intermediate). Under matched resource ceilings, a single controller spends an expected \(\$0.40\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.60\), and \(40\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. A delegated configuration spends \(\$0.90\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.80\), and \(72\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. Spend includes failed attempts and canceled branches, and cost is proportional to tokens.

Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for both configurations from equation 1.2, and their ratio.
Find the token multiple \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\), the delegated acceptance that would restore break-even on \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), and the largest single-controller acceptance for which break-even is possible at all.
Per \(100\) attempts, compute the marginal cost of each additional on-time acceptance. One service values an on-time accepted migration at \(\$1\), another at \(\$5\). Decide which configuration each should run.

Hedged lookups for the support agent (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The support agent answers a refund-eligibility question by dispatching three read-only lookups in parallel: the customer record, the order history, and the governing policy clause. All three are required. Each lookup attempt independently returns an admissible result within \(1\) s with probability \(0.70\) and within \(2\) s with probability \(0.95\). The service target is that at least \(95\) percent of answers have all three results within \(2\) s. Assume \(1{,}000\) sessions dispatch their three initial lookups simultaneously. The lookup pool has \(4{,}000\) slots, and each launched attempt retains its reservation until the \(2\) s observation cutoff, even if its result arrives earlier. An attempt that has not returned an admissible result remains outstanding until that cutoff. Treat the stated completion probabilities as unchanged by load when calculating a policy without admission blocking.

Compute the probability that all three results arrive within \(2\) s without hedging. Explain why the \(\RequiredResultCount\)-of-\(\WorkerCount\) stopping rule of section 18.7 does not rescue this fan-out.
Compare two hedging policies: duplicating every lookup at dispatch, and starting a replacement only for a lookup still outstanding at \(1\) s, which must then itself return within the remaining \(1\) s. Assuming every proposed hedge is admitted, compute the per-lookup and all-three probabilities within \(2\) s. For each policy, compute both expected slot demand and the largest possible slot demand before the cutoff.
Decide whether either calculation establishes that the policy meets the deadline target within the hard slot limit. Propose an admission rule for delayed hedges, and explain why deadline acceptance must be evaluated again when the rule can deny replacements. Contrast the binding constraint here with the coherency limit on the repair agent’s migration, and state what must hold before the same hedging could be applied to issuing the refund itself.

Bounding a remediation delegation tree (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The remediation agent is restoring a degraded checkout service. Its root grant permits reading metrics and logs for checkout and scaling the checkout deployment between \(4\) and \(12\) replicas; it permits no configuration writes. The root’s remaining allowance is \(\$50\), of which \(\$5\) is a protected finalization reserve and \(\$6\) is already reserved for the root’s own outstanding work. The model proposes three children, each with a \(\$20\) allowance, “less than the parent’s remaining \(\$50\)”: a metrics worker that reads checkout metrics, a log worker that reads logs for checkout and payments, and a capacity worker that scales checkout between \(4\) and \(16\) replicas.

State which proposed grants violate \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant)\) and how to narrow them. Compute the worst-case liability if each child’s allowance is copied from the parent’s balance, and which children atomic reservation admits if they are dispatched in the order listed. Find the largest equal allowance that admits all three. The capacity worker then proposes two scale workers at \(\$8\) each; state which the runtime admits and repair the split.
An operator takes over and the runtime cancels the root at \(\TimeInstant=0\). Both scale workers are active, and each submits at most one scale step every \(5\) s to a remote gateway. Under a cached-authorization policy the gateway trusts a lineage record for up to \(18\) s, with a \(2\) s clock-skew allowance. Under a strict policy it looks up the current status and generation of each of the \(3\) nodes in a scale worker’s lineage at \(4\) ms per lookup. Compute the stale-policy window, the most scale steps it can admit after cancellation, and the strict policy’s added latency as a fraction of the step interval. Choose a policy for scale steps and one for metric reads, and state what the strict policy costs if the authoritative store is unreachable for \(30\) s.
Under the policy chosen in part (b), the cost record at cancellation shows: the metrics worker settled \(\$4\) and stopped; the log worker settled \(\$9\), and a log-export job it started before cancellation is still unresolved with a bounded liability of \(\$3\); the first scale worker settled \(\$2\) and was confirmed terminated; the second scale worker settled nothing, and a node-pool scale-up it started before cancellation has an unknown outcome with a bounded liability of \(\$5\); the root’s own work settled \(\$4\). Compute the allowance the runtime may release now, the amount still held, and the release a “cancellation refunds all reservations” rule would claim. A follow-up remediation task needs a \(\$20\) allowance. Decide whether to admit it now, and state who owns the two open operations and what that owner must retain.

Buying evidence past a correlated floor (Advanced). Reviewers each falsely approve a known-invalid candidate with marginal probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=0.10\), and their errors follow the beta mixture of section 18.6 with \(\CorrelationCoefficient=0.30\). The release rule requires that an invalid candidate be approved with probability at most \(0.01\). A reviewer call costs \(\$0.20\). A protected regression test costs \(\$0.50\) and passes an invalid candidate with probability \(0.05\), assumed independent of the candidate’s reviewer propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\).

Compute the beta parameters \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape\) and \(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape\), and the majority false-approval probability for three reviewers under independent errors and under the mixture.
Compute the mixture’s majority false approval for seven reviewers and the floor \(\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)\), numerically. Decide whether any number of reviewers of this kind can meet the release rule.
Price two designs per candidate: seven reviewers under majority vote, and three reviewers plus the protected test, with approval requiring both a reviewer majority and a passing test. Compute each design’s false-approval probability and choose one.
Critique the assumption that the test is independent of \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\). Name a mechanism from this chapter that would correlate the test with the reviewers, and state the measurement that must precede release.

Fitting the scalability law before choosing a fan-out (Advanced, critique and redesign). Trials of a repair-migration partition under matched resources measure relative capacity \(\text{Speedup}(2)=1.835\) and \(\text{Speedup}(4)=2.878\). The serial reference takes \(40\) minutes, and the service requires completion within \(11\) minutes. The expected cost of an attempt grows with worker count as \(\$1.00+\$0.30(\WorkerCount-1)\), and acceptance does not change with \(\WorkerCount\).

Rearrange equation 5 so that it is linear in \(\ContentionCoefficient\) and \(\CoherencyCoefficient\), fit both coefficients from the two measurements, and compute \(\WorkerCount^*\) from equation 6, the best integer count and its capacity, and the smallest count that runs slower than one worker.
A trial at \(\WorkerCount=8\) measures \(2.90\). Compare it with the fitted prediction, and state what the gap implies about using the fit outside the measured range.
The team proposes deploying the best integer count from part (a). Critique the proposal against the deadline. For this calculation, suppose two proposed redesigns have the following responses: sharding the integration queue halves \(\ContentionCoefficient\), and repartitioning the migration so interface changes land before caller work begins halves \(\CoherencyCoefficient\). For each, find the smallest worker count that meets the deadline, if any, and its cost per attempt, and recommend a design under these assumptions. State what trace or matched intervention evidence would establish the assumed coefficient responses in a deployment.



What’s Next: From coordination to costWhen is the time saved by delegation worth its additional resource use? This chapter answered for one stated workload, charging failed attempts and canceled branches to the accepted tasks they served. That accounting is a special case of a question every deployment faces, for one agent or many. The next chapter opens with the repair team offered a model whose tokens cost a tenth as much and asks why the switch can still raise the price of every repair that ships. Answering it means counting what each accepted task costs across all its attempts, how context reuse, retries, and model choice change that cost, and how concurrent trajectories compete for capacity. The same account then prices delegation itself, without dropping the reservations and unresolved obligations established here.

title: 18 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can splitting a task across several agents cost more and deliver less than giving one agent the same resources?
Splitting a task across several agents looks like the natural answer when the work is wide, since each worker can hold a smaller context and pursue its piece in parallel. The split replaces nothing the single agent already had. A capable single controller already runs searches and tests concurrently, keeps its context lean through retrieval and compaction, and holds scoped grants, so delegation must be judged against that baseline rather than against a fragile loop. What delegation adds is a set of boundaries between separately managed trajectories, and each boundary must carry explicitly what one trajectory carried implicitly. A worker can build against an interface that changes before its edit lands, two patches can merge cleanly and still break each other, reviewers that share a model can agree on the same mistake, and a canceled child can leave a container running and a budget half spent. Coordination overhead grows with every worker added, while the serial part of the task caps any speedup the parallel part can buy. Whether to split is therefore a measured decision. A multi-agent design earns its place only when it delivers more accepted tasks per unit of cost, or finishes them sooner in a way the objective values, than a single controller given the same tools and budget. Every handoff multiplies horizon, state, and authority, and the runtime must keep each delegated obligation owned until it settles.

Learning Objectives

Estimate the speedup and useful worker count of a work partition from its serial fraction and coordination overhead
Calculate makespan bounds from a task’s dependency graph to decide whether added slots or shorter tasks pay
Design bounded receipts and credit windows that cap returned context and payload occupancy, and size mean residence under an explicit freshness policy
Apply shared-write collision estimates to justify private workspaces and dependency revalidation before publication
Calculate majority false approval under correlated reviewer errors to choose between more reviewers and a different check
Evaluate fan-out completion rules and hedging under deadline, capacity, and duplicate-effect constraints
Apply spawn limits, restart policies, attenuated grants, and atomic reservations to bound a delegation tree’s fan-out, authority, and spending
Evaluate delegation against a capable single-controller baseline using a declared objective and matched resource ceilings

title: 18 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
The repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) has so far fixed a connection-pool race, a change confined to one module that a single controller holds comfortably in one context. Its next assignment is wider: migrate an authentication module across a repository, a change that reaches every caller of the module’s interface and is exactly the kind of repair task that tempts a split. The task naturally splits into two coupled changes: revising an internal interface and updating its downstream callers. A single coordinator could retain the entire task, dispatching parallel searches and test runs to collect evidence before synthesizing a unified patch. Alternatively, it could partition the problem, assigning the interface update and caller modifications to separate workers. Each worker operates within a focused context window, editing candidate files and reacting to compiler diagnostics independently. This division introduces an immediate distributed consistency challenge: the caller modifications must remain compatible with the interface that ultimately lands, not merely the snapshot the caller worker read at dispatch.



A fleet multiplies horizon, state, and authority, so every handoff must preserve closure.
The runtime mechanisms established in earlier chapters govern a single execution trajectory at a time. Within that boundary, the harness checks each model and tool invocation against an assigned grant and token budget. Durable execution logs one trajectory’s event history, and failure recovery settles, repairs, or compensates the effects of that one trajectory. Evaluation compares trials of one configuration against another, and curation and post-training improve the policy that drives it. Partitioning the migration preserves these local controls inside each individual worker, but it leaves the coordination space between them unmanaged. A single-agent runtime provides no mechanism to resolve which interface revision the caller worker targets, whether a clean textual merge of two patches preserves semantic correctness, or what consensus among five reviewer agents actually guarantees. Nor does it define who claims an orphaned test container after a coordinator cancels a subtask, or how a parent bounds the authority and compute budget delegated to a child. Without explicit systems controls, every such gap threatens to make the split cost far more than it buys.
Making delegation governable requires runtime controls, and deciding whether it pays requires an empirical framework. The required controls are state records and verification gates owned directly by the runtime rather than left to prompt instructions. They include enforceable task assignments and receipts that separate an agent’s self-reported claims from verified tool evidence. They also include a publication barrier that revalidates cross-module dependencies before any candidate patch merges, clean cancellation paths that account for in-flight work, and authority grants that narrow monotonically at every delegation hop. These mechanisms pair with a measurement discipline that compares each multi-agent design against a single agent holding equivalent parallel tools and resource budgets, and that prices every token consumed by failed, retried, or canceled subtasks.
The migration carries the argument from the decision to split through the final accounting, and each control answers a hazard that the previous one exposes. A screen of serial work against coordination overhead first decides whether a partition can pay at all (section 18.2). Dependency, communication, and supervision structures then fix what may run concurrently and who owns each child (section 18.3), and typed envelopes and receipts fix what crosses each handoff (section 18.4). Once workers run in parallel, guarded publication keeps their edits consistent (section 18.5), and a joint error model shows what agreement among reviewers can and cannot certify (section 18.6). Cancellation, hedging, and credit windows bound the work still in flight (section 18.7), and attenuated grants and atomic reservations bound authority and spending at every hop (section 18.8). A matched comparison against a capable single controller decides whether the whole design earns its tax (section 18.9).

title: 18 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Handing the interface update and the caller update to dedicated workers differs from issuing concurrent model queries, and that difference defines the unit of delegation. A delegated worker owns a bounded child trajectory with its own context window, model-and-tool loop, task contract, and independent lifecycle. Several candidate samples dispatched by one controller, such as the self-consistency votes of test-time compute, are instead parallel calls inside one trajectory. They are the cheapest ensemble an agent can run and also the most correlated, because every sample shares the model, the prompt, and the input’s difficulty, a dependence that section 18.6 quantifies. The architectural shift lies in establishing explicit boundaries between separately managed trajectories, regardless of whether those workers execute on a single host or across a distributed cluster.


↩︎ Self-consistency, which samples several reasoning paths and returns the plurality answer, is established in Choosing a selection rule.
The point of comparison throughout this chapter is the capable baseline: the single-agent runtime developed in earlier chapters, which already manages its context window, reserves system resources, verifies proposed tool effects externally, and executes candidate searches and isolated tools concurrently. Delegation retains every one of those operational requirements while introducing new coordination boundaries. The systems question is whether dividing control and context improves a declared task objective enough to justify the overhead of managing them.


When a single agent runs a wide repository migration inside one shared context and one broad authority grant, compiler diagnostics from one module crowd out the prompt needed for the next while every tool call carries permissions for the whole codebase. Context partitioning addresses the prompt growth directly: each worker retains only the material strictly necessary for its subtask. In the migration scenario, the interface worker maintains the target API contract and local unit tests without ingesting the intermediate compiler diagnostics of the caller worker, allowing each subsequent model invocation to process substantially fewer prompt tokens. However, the net token savings depend entirely on the structure of the decomposition. If both workers repeatedly require the full repository commit history, separate contexts duplicate prompt state rather than isolating it, a redundancy the single-agent baseline already avoids through retrieval and compaction.
Delegation also provides separate task ownership. Workers can pursue multi-turn exploratory investigations through iterative tool feedback and local reasoning loops while a central coordinator tracks inter-task dependencies and orchestrates final integration. Assigning task ownership, however, does not eliminate underlying data dependencies. A caller worker that generates code against an outdated interface must still reconcile its implementation once the interface worker finalizes the new contract. True operational independence derives from the causal graph of the task itself, never from cosmetic role descriptions in prompt templates.
Finally, decomposing work across workers enforces task-scoped authority, binding tools, execution capabilities, and resource budgets directly to individual subtasks. For example, a test-runner worker can be granted execution privileges in an isolated container without granting it credentials to publish pull requests or write to production databases. Even so, process isolation does not eliminate trust boundaries. A child worker’s textual output can still inject unvalidated claims or prompt injections into the parent coordinator’s context, and any external mutations it produces must still be verified and settled by the runtime. Table 1 separates these opportunities from capabilities already present in the baseline.



Table 1: What Delegation Adds: The comparison preserves the capable single-controller runtime and identifies the extra boundaries a coordinated design must justify.










Dimension
One controller already provides
Delegation adds




Parallel work
Concurrent candidate calls and tools
Independently managed, multi-turn subtask trajectories


Context
Retrieval, compaction, and selective observations
Separate working contexts and explicit return boundaries


Authority and isolation
Scoped grants and sandboxed execution
Descendant grants and lifecycle relationships to enforce


State and evidence
Versioned artifacts and checks on proposed changes
Cross-worker dependency validation and integrated-result assessment


Resource control
Admission, reservations, deadlines, and settlement
Aggregate obligations across descendants and their communication









Splitting the authentication migration across separate interface and caller workers adds work that a single controller never performs: the coordinator spends turns packaging task assignments and reconciling returned diffs, both workers ingest shared repository context, and final integration waits at the join barrier for the slower child to finish. Every delegation boundary incurs this coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)).

Definition 18.1: Coordination tax
Coordination tax is the work and elapsed time a delegated design spends on handoffs rather than on the task: preparing and validating envelopes, delivering context, scheduling children, collecting receipts, and reconciling and integrating their results.

Significance: The tax enters both terms of the cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) (equation 1.2): its tokens and tool time raise \(\mathbb{E}[\AttemptCost]\), and the part on the critical path lengthens every attempt against its deadline.
Distinction: While task decomposition aims to reduce makespan by distributing work concurrently, the coordination tax represents the unavoidable friction introduced by that distribution. This tax scales with worker count, communication frequency, and inter-task dependencies.
Common pitfall: Accounting only for the tokens and execution time of successful worker turns. Context re-ingestion, supervisor arbitration turns, failed retries, and abandoned speculative branches all consume model quota and execution budgets.



Coordination tax impacts systems along two distinct dimensions: aggregate resource consumption and end-to-end latency. Duplicated input prompt tokens, redundant tool invocations, and serialize-deserialize cycles increase the total operational cost. Meanwhile, user-perceived delay is governed by makespan, the wall-clock time elapsed from the arrival of a task to the completion and verification of its final artifact. Makespan depends strictly on the operations situated on the critical path. A straggling child worker delays synchronization at the join barrier, while subsequent arbitration and reconciliation turns further inflate the critical path before results can be accepted.
Amdahl’s fixed-work argument1 gives the first screening model (Amdahl 1967). Let \(\SerialReferenceTime\) be the time for a fixed set of operations executed serially, with fraction \(\ParallelFraction\) perfectly divisible among \(\WorkerCount\) equally fast workers and fraction \(1-\ParallelFraction\) remaining serial. Assume enough resources for that division and let \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) be the additional elapsed overhead, normalized by \(\SerialReferenceTime\). Then
1 Amdahl’s Argument: Amdahl’s 1967 conference paper contains no equation; it argues in prose that the serial housekeeping of a program limits what any number of parallel processors can deliver, and the familiar formula was written down by later authors. The lesson transfers intact to delegation, where planning, integration, and final assessment are the housekeeping that no added worker absorbs.\[\text{Speedup}(\WorkerCount)=\frac{\SerialReferenceTime}{\Time(\WorkerCount)}=\frac{1}{(1-\ParallelFraction)+\ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount+\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)}. \tag{1}\]
With no coordination overhead, \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=0\), equation 1 reduces to Amdahl’s law, and the serial term alone caps speedup at \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)\) for any number of workers. The equation provides a preliminary screening model for a specified work partition. The baseline \(\SerialReferenceTime\) reflects that partition executed sequentially on a single thread of execution, rather than the capable baseline runtime (which already pipelines tool executions and concurrent candidate samplings). In production, an empirical benchmark of the capable baseline must replace \(\SerialReferenceTime\) before finalizing any worker allocation. Within this theoretical formulation, achieving any net speedup over the serial reference requires that:
\[\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)<\ParallelFraction\left(1-\frac{1}{\WorkerCount}\right).\]
The right-hand side represents the theoretical wall-clock time saved by distributing the parallelizable portion across \(\WorkerCount\) workers. Whenever coordination overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) exceeds this threshold, the split task takes longer than serial execution. Furthermore, this inequality constrains execution time alone. Task acceptance rates, token expenditures, and monetary costs enter the trade-off in section 18.9, which gives serializing work and pairwise reconciliation separate coefficients because their remedies differ (section 18.9.3).

Napkin Math 18.1: Screening a proposed work partitionProblem: A hypothetical fixed workload has \(\ParallelFraction=\) 0.80 and assumed normalized overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\WorkerOverheadSlope(\WorkerCount-1)\) with \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=\) 0.02. The resource ceiling permits at most 16 workers. Which integer count minimizes modeled elapsed time?
Math: Evaluating the denominator of equation 1 for each permitted count, four workers require 0.460 of the serial reference time. The minimum occurs at 6 workers, requiring 0.433, a 2.3× speedup. Eight workers increase the ratio to 0.440, because the shrinking parallel term \(\ParallelFraction/\WorkerCount\) no longer pays for the added overhead. Halving the overhead coefficient to 0.01 moves the optimum to 9 workers and the speedup to 2.7×.
Systems insight: The serial fraction sets the ceiling and the overhead sets the useful fleet size. No worker count beats \(1/(1-\ParallelFraction)=\) 5× here, and the best count sits near \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\), so halving the per-worker overhead \(\WorkerOverheadSlope\) adds 3 workers but only 0.4 of speedup. Shrinking the serial planning and integration work is the larger lever.


A reduction in modeled makespan does not automatically justify a multi-agent architecture. Production systems optimize under varied constraints: one automated migration service may seek to maximize accepted pull requests prior to a nightly release window subject to a strict token budget, whereas another prioritizes minimizing the total cost per accepted migration. Trading latency for computational overhead is justified only against an explicit, pre-declared optimization objective, and the decision framework of section 18.9 charges that objective for retries and failed executions as well. Before sizing a worker pool, an engineer must map the causal dependency graph of the workload to see which subtasks can run concurrently and what evidence each downstream join requires. Those dependencies govern the coordination topology.

title: 18 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
In the authentication migration (migration_task_01), the interface worker and the caller worker can inspect the baseline snapshot (repo_base_01) in parallel, yet the caller’s patch still depends on the interface definitions that its peer is actively modifying. Routing both workers through a single supervisor does not eliminate that underlying causal dependency. A runtime architecture that naively treats the supervisor’s message-routing graph as the true dependency graph will prematurely accept and publish a caller patch built on stale interface assumptions.
To build reliable multi-agent systems, engineers must distinguish three separate structural graphs that govern execution:

The dependency graph defines causal precedence by recording which artifacts, decisions, or validation checks must complete before downstream work can safely proceed.
The communication topology defines the network paths, protocols, and message envelopes through which agents exchange information.
The supervision tree defines operational ownership over agent lifecycles, governing fault isolation, resource reservations, and cancellation cascades.

Because a supervisor frequently manages children whose outputs depend causally on one another, runtime engines must maintain these three structures independently. Conflating message delivery with causal dependency or lifecycle ownership leads directly to race conditions, orphaned processes, and corrupted state.


When migration_task_01 splits work across agents, the runtime must decide whether subtasks and candidate artifacts pass through a central coordinator, stream along staged queues, land in a shared store, or route directly between peer workers (table 2). The most prevalent pattern is the supervisor-worker topology (frequently termed orchestrator-worker). In this model, a centralized coordinator decomposes an incoming task, dispatches subtasks to subordinate workers, and synthesizes their returned receipts. This design directly mirrors the contract net protocol2 originally developed for distributed problem solving (Smith 1980). In production systems, these foundational topologies frequently compose. For example, a supervisor might dispatch parallel analytical investigations, stream their candidate patches through a staged validation pipeline, and persist intermediate progress within a shared task store.
2 Contract Net Protocol: In Smith’s 1980 protocol, a manager node announces a task, idle contractor nodes submit bids, and the manager awards the contract to a chosen bidder, which may subcontract in turn. The award represents the conceptual ancestor of the typed task envelope: it fixes which agent owns the subtask and what structured receipt must return, eliminating the ambiguity inherent in prompt-level delegation.


Table 2: Coordination arrangements and runtime obligations: While routing patterns structure message handoffs, the execution runtime must enforce result validity, resource boundaries, and state consistency across agent boundaries.











Arrangement
How work crosses a boundary
Useful when
Obligation that remains




Supervisor–worker
A coordinator assigns subtasks and collects bounded receipts
A task has separable investigations and an explicit integration decision
Bound dispatch, returned context, and the coordinator’s own work


Pipeline
Each stage receives the artifacts and evidence its predecessor is required to provide
Later work depends on a sequence of transformations or checks
Preserve stage preconditions and bound queues between stages


Shared blackboard
Workers claim tasks and publish versioned artifacts through a shared store
Different workers can contribute as dependencies become available
Enforce claim ownership, publication rules, and dependency validity


Actor messaging
Workers hold local state and exchange addressed messages
Responsibilities require ongoing asynchronous interactions
Define delivery, duplicate handling, ordering, and bounded mailboxes






Each coordination topology makes different trade-offs regarding where state accumulates and where synchronization occurs. A supervisor concentrates integration logic and validation evidence at a single coordinator, requiring compact, structured receipts to prevent prompt context exhaustion. A pipeline structures execution as a sequence of discrete transformations, keeping each stage’s working context tightly focused while streaming items concurrently across stages. By contrast, a shared blackboard3 decouples agents entirely by externalizing coordination into a centralized artifact and task store (Erman et al. 1980). In an actor architecture, originally formulated by Hewitt, Bishop, and Steiger, agents maintain completely isolated private state and communicate exclusively via asynchronous message passing to explicit addresses (Hewitt et al. 1973). Both blackboards and actor meshes shift the coordination burden toward explicit conflict resolution, distributed ordering, and bounded mailbox management.
3 Blackboard Architecture: The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system of the 1970s coordinated independent knowledge sources that never communicated directly with one another, interacting solely by posting and reading hypotheses on a shared global data structure. Its central scheduling challenge, deciding which pending contribution to evaluate next, reappears whenever agent workers claim tasks from a shared operational store.Message counts scale with the communication graph and its interaction protocol. If each of \(\WorkerCount\) participants transmits an update to every other participant during an execution round, the network must handle \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\) directed deliveries. With an average payload size of \(\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens per delivery, that single round consumes \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens across the system. In contrast, a supervisor managing \(\WorkerCount\) workers requires only \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries per round (one dispatch envelope and one receipt per worker), consuming \(2\WorkerCount{}\MeanDeliveryPayloadLength\) tokens. The full mesh thus scales quadratically, transmitting \((\WorkerCount-1)/2\) times more messages per round than the centralized coordinator.
Raw transmission volume measures network traffic, not what the receiving models must ingest. In a fully connected mesh where each agent appends every incoming peer message to its prompt history, ingested tokens per round grow as \(\mathcal{O}(\WorkerCount^2)\). The append-only re-send of equation 2.9 compounds that growth across rounds, because each later prompt carries every earlier delivery. Even in a centralized topology, verbose receipts, iterative deliberation rounds, or frequent status polling against a blackboard store can exhaust context windows and inflate inference budgets. Across the four arrangements of figure 1, the supervisor’s round costs \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries and the actor mesh up to \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\), while the pipeline and blackboard replace direct deliveries with bounded queues and versioned claims that the runtime must police. An arrangement therefore keeps context windows bounded only when each handoff carries the specific inputs and checks a subtask requires, and deciding when those handoffs may fire belongs to the dependency graph.






Figure 1: Four Coordination Arrangements: Each panel shows where work crosses a boundary. A supervisor sends envelopes down and collects receipts, a pipeline passes artifacts through bounded queues, a blackboard mediates claims and versioned publications through a shared store, and actors exchange addressed messages through mailboxes. One supervisor round costs \(2\WorkerCount\) deliveries and a full mesh round \(\WorkerCount(\WorkerCount-1)\). Each topology imposes specific runtime obligations for bounding queues, isolating concurrent state, and verifying result correctness.






Dispatching subtasks before their prerequisites are verified wastes tokens on stale assumptions or stalls worker slots behind unfinished upstream steps. To schedule concurrent work safely, the runtime models task precedence as a directed acyclic graph (DAG), \((\DependencyGraphVertexSet,\DependencyGraphEdgeSet)\). Each vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex \in \DependencyGraphVertexSet\) represents a bounded unit of execution, either an autonomous agent trajectory or a deterministic runtime validation check. A directed edge \((\PredecessorGraphVertex,\DependencyGraphVertex) \in \DependencyGraphEdgeSet\) indicates that vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex\) requires a declared precondition satisfied by vertex \(\PredecessorGraphVertex\), such as an emitted code artifact, a validated test report, or an explicit authorization token. A status message signaling task completion satisfies an incoming edge only when accompanied by verifiable output receipts.
A vertex becomes dependency-ready once every prerequisite predecessor condition has been verified. Dependency readiness alone does not trigger execution, however. The runtime dispatcher must additionally verify execution authority, allocate an active worker slot, and secure a bounded token and financial budget reservation. If a predecessor fails or emits invalid artifacts, the control plane either halts downstream successors or transitions execution to an explicit recovery branch. Loops and iterative refinement cycles enter the graph as unrolled, bounded attempts. Because graph acyclicity guarantees only the absence of logical dependency loops, the underlying runtime remains responsible for detecting dynamic deadlocks arising from shared resource locks, exhausted thread pools, or saturated queues.
To estimate the theoretical limits of parallel scheduling, assume each vertex \(\DependencyGraphVertex\) occupies one interchangeable worker slot for a fixed duration \(\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex)\), encompassing both model inference latency and external tool execution. Let \(\WorkerCount\) represent the pool of available parallel worker slots. Under these assumptions, aggregate slot-work \(\AggregateSlotWork\) totals every vertex’s duration, and critical-path duration \(\CriticalPathDuration\) is the length of the longest dependency chain, the same critical path that trace analysis measures from recorded spans, here computed from assumed durations:
\[
\AggregateSlotWork=\sum_{\DependencyGraphVertex\in \DependencyGraphVertexSet}\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex),\qquad
\CriticalPathDuration=\max_{\pi\in\operatorname{Paths}(\DependencyGraphVertexSet,\DependencyGraphEdgeSet)}\sum_{\DependencyGraphVertex\in\pi}\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex).
\tag{2}\]
Any valid schedule’s total makespan \(\ScheduleFinishTime\) must satisfy the dual lower bounds
\[
\ScheduleFinishTime\ge\max\left(\frac{\AggregateSlotWork}{\WorkerCount},\CriticalPathDuration\right).
\tag{3}\]
The aggregate work bound \(\AggregateSlotWork/\WorkerCount\) reflects the capacity constraint, since \(\WorkerCount\) parallel worker slots cannot complete \(\AggregateSlotWork\) total units of execution time in less than \(\AggregateSlotWork/\WorkerCount\), regardless of schedule structure. The critical-path bound \(\CriticalPathDuration\) reflects the causal precedence constraint, since sequential dependencies cannot be parallelized, and it establishes a lower bound on latency even with infinite worker slots.4 In production environments, resource contention, queuing overhead, payload serialization, and trajectory retries expand the overall makespan well beyond these theoretical minimums unless explicitly incorporated into vertex durations \(\VertexSlotTime(\DependencyGraphVertex)\) and graph edges.
4 Greedy List Scheduling: Graham established that any list schedule which never leaves a worker slot idle while a dependency-ready vertex waits completes within a factor of \(2-1/\WorkerCount\) of the optimal makespan. Graham also demonstrated that such schedules can suffer counterintuitive timing anomalies where adding worker slots or reducing individual task durations actually increases overall completion time (Graham 1969). A runtime dispatcher that greedily schedules ready work is therefore near-optimal relative to the theoretical bound in equation 3, and an observed latency regression after expanding worker pools does not necessarily indicate a scheduler implementation bug.
Graham, Ronald L. 1969. “Bounds on Multiprocessing Timing Anomalies.” SIAM Journal on Applied Mathematics 17 (2): 416–29. https://doi.org/10.1137/0117039.

↩︎ Trace-based measurement of the critical path is established in Span overlap and latency attribution.

Math: Summing the node durations as in equation 2 gives 275 s of aggregate slot-work. Dividing by the slot count gives the work term in equation 3, 68.75 s. The paths \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\to \DependencyGraphVertex_2\to \DependencyGraphVertex_5\to \DependencyGraphVertex_7\) and \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\to \DependencyGraphVertex_3\to \DependencyGraphVertex_5\to \DependencyGraphVertex_7\) tie for the critical path.
