Key Takeaways: Delegation must earn and preserve its boundaries

Coordination overhead sets the useful fleet size: Serial execution constraints cap parallel speedup at \(1/\ContentionCoefficient\), while pairwise reconciliation costs cause effective system throughput to fall beyond \(\WorkerCount^*=\sqrt{(1-\ContentionCoefficient)/\CoherencyCoefficient}\). Shrinking serial planning and integration overhead raises the scalability ceiling far more than merely shaving latency off individual handoffs. Empirical profiling across realistic workloads, rather than casual inspection of isolated agent trajectories, must calibrate these parameters.
Task dependencies govern completion makespan: Communication topologies, scheduling precedence, and fault-supervision hierarchies address distinct systems requirements. Once a schedule attains its critical-path bound, further latency reductions require shortening that path; before it does, additional slots or reduced contention may also shorten runtime. Furthermore, any agent endowed with recursive delegation authority requires hard runtime limits on fan-out, nesting depth, and aggregate token reservations.
Delegation handoffs require explicit runtime contracts: A handoff envelope must establish immutable task inputs, granted execution authority, resource budgets, and required evidence before worker execution begins. The returned receipt must strictly isolate ground-truth execution records from the worker’s unverified self-assessment, truncating narrative explanations rather than audit telemetry whenever context limits bind.
Disjoint writes do not guarantee semantic compatibility: Non-overlapping file edits establish only that parallel workers avoided concurrent modification conflicts; they do not prove that combined changes preserve system-wide behavioral invariants. Safe publication requires revalidating dependencies against the latest branch head, testing the integrated candidate in isolation, and advancing branch pointers through conditional atomic updates.
Correlated reviewer errors impose an irreducible accuracy floor: When automated reviewers evaluate an intrinsically challenging artifact, shared model blind spots cause their errors to correlate, preventing majority-voting failure rates from dropping to zero. Beyond this floor, spending additional tokens on reviewers of the same kind yields negligible benefit. Runtimes must instead incorporate independent checks, such as deterministic test suites or static analyzers, because peer consensus cannot manufacture authoritative correctness.
Resource obligations outlive parent caller lifecycles: Canceling a parent agent halts the dispatch of new downstream tasks, but it does not automatically terminate remote tool operations, network sockets, or asynchronous child processes already in flight. Each in-flight bound has its own mechanism. Credit windows bound the volume of queued work and support mean-residence sizing. Attenuated grants and atomic reservations bound authority and spend. The settlement record, not cancellation or credit release, keeps every admitted effect owned until its outcome and charges settle.
Multi-agent execution must outperform a capable single-agent baseline: A meaningful evaluation benchmarks multi-agent architectures against an equally optimized single-agent controller provisioned with identical parallel tool access, context allowances, and wall-clock budgets. System accounting must price every failed attempt, speculative invocation, and rollback, justifying multi-agent coordination only when the resulting increase in task success or latency reduction offsets its marginal token overhead.



The coordination tax (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-coordination-tax}\)) manifests in the serialized handoffs, validation barriers, and residual dependencies that remain after decomposing a task. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) mandates that these architectural boundaries maintain strict external validation and effect gating, ensuring that peer consensus among models is never mistaken for authoritative execution rights. Finally, trajectory-level encapsulation (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-encapsulation}\)) extends from one trajectory to a tree of them. Every child is a separately owned trajectory whose derived grants only narrow, whose consumable allowance is reserved against its ancestors’ shared allowance, and whose unsettled side effects remain accounted for by the runtime after its parent stops.

title: 18 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
The question of when dividing computational work yields a net speedup is older than autonomous software agents. Gene Amdahl’s 1967 argument established that serial execution fractions strictly cap the speedup achievable by adding processors (Amdahl 1967). Two years later, Ronald Graham showed that while greedy list scheduling lands close to the theoretical dependency bound, adding parallel resources can paradoxically increase total completion time (Graham 1969). Neil Gunther later unified these dynamics in the universal scalability law, introducing a pairwise coherency penalty to explain how crosstalk and contention turn throughput saturation into outright performance collapse (Gunther 2008). Across successive computing generations, systems architects repeatedly found that coordination overhead and coherency penalties, rather than the raw supply of workers, dictate practical scale.

Amdahl, Gene M. 1967. “Validity of the Single Processor Approach to Achieving Large Scale Computing Capabilities.” Proceedings of the April 18-20, 1967, Spring Joint Computer Conference on - AFIPS ’67 (Spring), AFIPS ’67 (spring), 483–85. https://doi.org/10.1145/1465482.1465560.

Erman, Lee D., Frederick Hayes-Roth, Victor R. Lesser, and D. Raj Reddy. 1980. “The Hearsay-II Speech-Understanding System: Integrating Knowledge to Resolve Uncertainty.” ACM Computing Surveys 12 (2): 213–53. https://doi.org/10.1145/356810.356816.

Hewitt, Carl, Peter Bishop, and Richard Steiger. 1973. “A Universal Modular ACTOR Formalism for Artificial Intelligence.” Proceedings of the 3rd International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI), 235–45.
Distributed artificial intelligence confronted the handoff problem in the 1970s. The Hearsay-II speech-understanding system coordinated independent, opportunistic knowledge sources through a shared blackboard (Erman et al. 1980). Carl Hewitt’s actor model abandoned shared memory entirely, giving each autonomous agent private local state and routing interactions through addressed messages (Hewitt et al. 1973). Reid Smith formalized structured delegation in the Contract Net Protocol, turning task announcement, bidding, and award into an explicit, typed exchange between a manager and prospective contractors (Smith 1980).
Over the following decades, classical distributed systems research supplied the precise operational controls that multi-agent architectures require today. Kung and Robinson introduced optimistic concurrency control, permitting workers to execute tentatively against private workspace copies and validate isolation before committing (Kung and Robinson 1981). Birrell and Nelson established typed remote procedure calls with explicit failure semantics, replacing unstructured message passing with formal client-server contracts (Birrell and Nelson 1984). Gray and Cheriton solved distributed state synchronization and lock management through time-bounded leases (Gray and Cheriton 1989). Joe Armstrong formalized supervision trees within Erlang, demonstrating how structured hierarchies and crash-only semantics allow runtimes to restart failed processes from clean, known states (Armstrong 2003). Finally, object-capability systems eliminated ambient authority by embedding access rights directly into object references rather than relying on global identity checks (Dennis and Van Horn 1966; Hardy 1988), an approach later extended through cryptographically attenuable tokens with chained caveats (Birgisson et al. 2014).

Kung, H. T., and John T. Robinson. 1981. “On Optimistic Methods for Concurrency Control.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 6 (2): 213–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/319566.319567.

Birrell, Andrew D., and Bruce Jay Nelson. 1984. “Implementing Remote Procedure Calls.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 2 (1): 39–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/2080.357392.

Gray, Cary G., and David R. Cheriton. 1989. “Leases: An Efficient Fault-Tolerant Mechanism for Distributed File Cache Consistency.” Proceedings of the Twelfth ACM Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 202–10. https://doi.org/10.1145/74850.74870.

Dennis, Jack B., and Earl C. Van Horn. 1966. “Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations.” Communications of the ACM 9 (3): 143–55. https://doi.org/10.1145/365230.365252.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.

Birgisson, Arnór, Joseph G. Politz, Úlfar Erlingsson, Ankur Taly, Michael Vrable, and Mark S. Miller. 2014. “Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats for Decentralized Authorization in the Cloud.” Proceedings of the Network and Distributed System Security Symposium (NDSS).

Condorcet, Marquis de. 1785. Essai Sur l’application de l’analyse à La Probabilité Des décisions Rendues à La Pluralité Des Voix. Imprimerie Royale.

Neumann, John von. 1956. “Probabilistic Logics and the Synthesis of Reliable Organisms from Unreliable Components.” In Automata Studies, edited by Claude E. Shannon and John McCarthy, vol. 34. Annals of Mathematics Studies. Princeton University Press. https://doi.org/10.1515/9781400882618-003.

Eckhardt, Dave E., and Larry D. Lee. 1985. “A Theoretical Basis for the Analysis of Multiversion Software Subject to Coincident Errors.” IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering SE-11 (12): 1511–17. https://doi.org/10.1109/TSE.1985.231895.
Redundancy followed a parallel trajectory of high theoretical promises followed by sobering empirical corrections. The Condorcet jury theorem (Condorcet, Marquis de 1785) and John von Neumann’s multiplexed majority organs (Neumann 1956) demonstrated that aggregating independent votes can synthesize near-perfect reliability from noisy components. Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease proved the rigorous mathematical bounds of Byzantine fault tolerance. Agreement in the unsigned-message protocol model survives arbitrary, even malicious, faults only while fewer than one third of participants are faulty (Lamport et al. 1982). However, the independence premise behind probabilistic majority-voting guarantees collapsed when applied to software. John Knight and Nancy Leveson demonstrated experimentally that independently written programs fail coincidentally on the same edge cases far more often than chance predicts (Knight and Leveson 1986). Dave Eckhardt and Larry Lee provided the analytical explanation: complex problem domains harbor intrinsically difficult input regions that induce correlated failures across diverse implementations (Eckhardt and Lee 1985).
Modern language-model systems have revived every one of these designs at the same time. Self-consistency uses majority voting across sampled reasoning paths (Wang et al. 2023), multi-agent debate structures iterative argumentation across model instances (Du et al. 2023), and conversational frameworks coordinate role-playing agents over structured communication graphs (Wu et al. 2023). In production, orchestrator-worker patterns have delivered capability gains on breadth-first research tasks, and their builders report roughly 15× the token consumption of a chat interaction to get them (Hadfield et al. 2025). Systematic empirical analyses of multi-agent failures reveal that the field has re-encountered classical distributed failure modes: ill-defined task boundaries, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification bottlenecks that silently propagate errors rather than catching them (Cemri et al. 2025).

Wang, Xuezhi, Jason Wei, Dale Schuurmans, Quoc Le, Ed Chi, Sharan Narang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, and Denny Zhou. 2023. “Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models.” The Eleventh International Conference on Learning Representations.

Du, Yilun, Shuang Li, Antonio Torralba, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, and Igor Mordatch. 2023. “Improving Factuality and Reasoning in Language Models Through Multiagent Debate.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2305.14325.

Wu, Qingyun, Gagan Bansal, Jieyu Zhang, Yiran Wu, Beibin Li, Erkang Zhu, Biyi Gao, et al. 2023. AutoGen: Enabling Next-Gen LLM Applications via Multi-Agent Conversation.

Hadfield, Jeremy, Barry Zhang, Kenneth Lien, Florian Scholz, Jeremy Fox, and Daniel Ford. 2025. How We Built Our Multi-Agent Research System. Anthropic Engineering Blog.

The Contract Net Protocol (Smith 1980). The foundational text on structured delegation. Smith frames task distribution as a typed, negotiated protocol, showing that the essential elements of modern task envelopes, from capability announcements to formal awards, were established long before language models existed.
An Experimental Evaluation of the Assumption of Independence in Multiversion Programming (Knight and Leveson 1986). The landmark controlled experiment that disproved the assumption of independent software failures. This paper provides the standard methodological blueprint for evaluating whether an ensemble of redundant agent reviewers yields genuine reliability gains or merely inflates inference cost.
Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors (Armstrong 2003). Armstrong’s doctoral dissertation detailing the architecture of Erlang. It articulates the operational rationale for supervision trees, fail-stop process isolation, and restart strategies, mapping directly to how orchestrators should manage the lifecycles and blast radiuses of child agent trajectories.
A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions (Gunther 2008). Gunther derives the universal scalability law directly from queueing models. The derivation clarifies the physical distinction between contention and coherency, explaining why serial bottlenecks and cross-agent communication require different architectural fixes.
Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail? (Cemri et al. 2025). An extensive empirical taxonomy analyzing real-world multi-agent failure traces. It serves as a field catalog of the specification gaps, uncoordinated handoffs, and verification failures that production runtime environments must actively prevent.


Smith, Reid G. 1980. “The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Distributed Problem Solving in a Distributed Processor.” IEEE Transactions on Computers C-29 (12): 1104–13.

Gunther, Neil J. 2008. “A General Theory of Computational Scalability Based on Rational Functions.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:0808.1431.

Cemri, Mert, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A. Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, Rishabh Tiwari, Kurt Keutzer, et al. 2025. Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?

title: 18 Multi-Agent Coordination
text:
Every figure given below is a hypothetical problem input, not a measurement of a real system. Each problem ends in a design decision, and the calculation exists to justify it.

Choosing the lever in a worker-count screen (Basic). A fixed work partition has divisible fraction \(\ParallelFraction=0.9\) and normalized overhead \(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)=\WorkerOverheadSlope(\WorkerCount-1)\) with \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.01\). The resource ceiling permits at most \(20\) workers, and each added worker adds roughly the same token spend.

Using equation 1, compute the normalized elapsed time at \(\WorkerCount=4\), \(8\), and \(16\), the integer count that minimizes it, and the speedup at that count. Compare the count with \(\sqrt{\ParallelFraction/\WorkerOverheadSlope}\).
Two proposals compete for the same engineering effort: halving the per-worker overhead to \(\WorkerOverheadSlope=0.005\), or halving the serial work so that \(\ParallelFraction=0.95\). Compute the best integer count and its speedup under each proposal.
Decide which proposal to fund once worker spend is counted, and state which proposal alone can ever deliver a speedup above \(10\times\).

Hot files in a shared workspace (Basic). A repository holds \(\RepositoryFileCount=5{,}000\) files, and each worker writes \(\WorkerWrittenFileCount=20\) of them, chosen uniformly and independently.

Using equation 4, compute the probability of at least one shared write for \(\WorkerCount=2\) and \(\WorkerCount=4\) workers, both exactly and by the exponential approximation. Find the smallest fleet for which a shared write is more likely than not.
Each worker also edits one shared dependency manifest with probability \(0.3\), independently of its other writes. For four workers, compute the probability that at least two edit the manifest, and the probability of any shared write at all.
A colleague proposes a single shared working directory for four workers because “collisions are under 40 percent.” Decide, and name the two hazards of section 18.5 that remain even when no two workers write the same file.

Sizing a credit window for staleness (Basic). A producer emits candidate items at \(\ArrivalRate=2\) items per second. A consumer model writes a \(400\)-token critique of each item at \(50\) output tokens per second, and each returned record occupies at most \(\DataVolume=8{,}192\) bytes. An item is useful only if the consumer begins serving it within \(60\) s of admission. For initial sizing, screen a saturated credit window by requiring its modeled mean residence to be no greater than this interval; assume negligible transport time and full utilization at the stated service rate.

Compute the consumer’s service rate \(\ServiceRate\), the backlog of an unbounded queue after five minutes, and the wait of the newest item behind that backlog.
Using the full-window mean residence \(\CreditWindowCapacity/\ServiceRate\), find the largest integer window \(\CreditWindowCapacity\) that passes this sizing screen and its payload bound \(\CreditWindowCapacity\DataVolume\). Does passing the screen establish that every item begins service before its freshness deadline?
Find the minimum number of identical consumers needed to keep pace with the producer and the largest shared window that passes the same mean-residence screen at their aggregate service rate. State how admission timestamps and a freshness check before service should handle an item that has waited too long. Explain why cancellation and settlement traffic must not draw on these data credits.

A fourth slot or a shorter vertex (Intermediate). A migration plan has a shared specification \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\) (\(30\) s); four module refactors \(\DependencyGraphVertex_2\) through \(\DependencyGraphVertex_5\) (\(60\), \(60\), \(90\), and \(40\) s), each depending only on \(\DependencyGraphVertex_1\); and an integration check \(\DependencyGraphVertex_6\) (\(50\) s) depending on all four refactors. Each vertex occupies one interchangeable slot, with no other delays.

Compute \(\AggregateSlotWork\) and \(\CriticalPathDuration\) from equation 2, and the lower bound of equation 3 for \(\WorkerCount=2\), \(3\), and \(4\) slots.
By assigning the four refactors to slots, find the shortest achievable makespan for each \(\WorkerCount\). Explain why the bound is not attained at \(\WorkerCount=2\).
The team currently runs \(\WorkerCount=3\) and can afford either a fourth slot or engineering that shortens \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) to \(60\) s. Decide, and state what shortening \(\DependencyGraphVertex_4\) buys once the fourth slot exists.

Pricing deadline coverage (Intermediate). Under matched resource ceilings, a single controller spends an expected \(\$0.40\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.60\), and \(40\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. A delegated configuration spends \(\$0.90\) per attempt with \(\AcceptanceProbability=0.80\), and \(72\) of every \(100\) attempts are accepted by the deadline. Spend includes failed attempts and canceled branches, and cost is proportional to tokens.

Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for both configurations from equation 1.2, and their ratio.
Find the token multiple \(\DelegationTokenMultiple\), the delegated acceptance that would restore break-even on \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), and the largest single-controller acceptance for which break-even is possible at all.
Per \(100\) attempts, compute the marginal cost of each additional on-time acceptance. One service values an on-time accepted migration at \(\$1\), another at \(\$5\). Decide which configuration each should run.

Hedged lookups for the support agent (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The support agent answers a refund-eligibility question by dispatching three read-only lookups in parallel: the customer record, the order history, and the governing policy clause. All three are required. Each lookup attempt independently returns an admissible result within \(1\) s with probability \(0.70\) and within \(2\) s with probability \(0.95\). The service target is that at least \(95\) percent of answers have all three results within \(2\) s. Assume \(1{,}000\) sessions dispatch their three initial lookups simultaneously. The lookup pool has \(4{,}000\) slots, and each launched attempt retains its reservation until the \(2\) s observation cutoff, even if its result arrives earlier. An attempt that has not returned an admissible result remains outstanding until that cutoff. Treat the stated completion probabilities as unchanged by load when calculating a policy without admission blocking.

Compute the probability that all three results arrive within \(2\) s without hedging. Explain why the \(\RequiredResultCount\)-of-\(\WorkerCount\) stopping rule of section 18.7 does not rescue this fan-out.
Compare two hedging policies: duplicating every lookup at dispatch, and starting a replacement only for a lookup still outstanding at \(1\) s, which must then itself return within the remaining \(1\) s. Assuming every proposed hedge is admitted, compute the per-lookup and all-three probabilities within \(2\) s. For each policy, compute both expected slot demand and the largest possible slot demand before the cutoff.
Decide whether either calculation establishes that the policy meets the deadline target within the hard slot limit. Propose an admission rule for delayed hedges, and explain why deadline acceptance must be evaluated again when the rule can deny replacements. Contrast the binding constraint here with the coherency limit on the repair agent’s migration, and state what must hold before the same hedging could be applied to issuing the refund itself.

Bounding a remediation delegation tree (Intermediate, second-lighthouse transfer). The remediation agent is restoring a degraded checkout service. Its root grant permits reading metrics and logs for checkout and scaling the checkout deployment between \(4\) and \(12\) replicas; it permits no configuration writes. The root’s remaining allowance is \(\$50\), of which \(\$5\) is a protected finalization reserve and \(\$6\) is already reserved for the root’s own outstanding work. The model proposes three children, each with a \(\$20\) allowance, “less than the parent’s remaining \(\$50\)”: a metrics worker that reads checkout metrics, a log worker that reads logs for checkout and payments, and a capacity worker that scales checkout between \(4\) and \(16\) replicas.

State which proposed grants violate \(\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ChildCapabilityGrant)\subseteq\GrantAllowedAccesses(\ParentCapabilityGrant)\) and how to narrow them. Compute the worst-case liability if each child’s allowance is copied from the parent’s balance, and which children atomic reservation admits if they are dispatched in the order listed. Find the largest equal allowance that admits all three. The capacity worker then proposes two scale workers at \(\$8\) each; state which the runtime admits and repair the split.
An operator takes over and the runtime cancels the root at \(\TimeInstant=0\). Both scale workers are active, and each submits at most one scale step every \(5\) s to a remote gateway. Under a cached-authorization policy the gateway trusts a lineage record for up to \(18\) s, with a \(2\) s clock-skew allowance. Under a strict policy it looks up the current status and generation of each of the \(3\) nodes in a scale worker’s lineage at \(4\) ms per lookup. Compute the stale-policy window, the most scale steps it can admit after cancellation, and the strict policy’s added latency as a fraction of the step interval. Choose a policy for scale steps and one for metric reads, and state what the strict policy costs if the authoritative store is unreachable for \(30\) s.
Under the policy chosen in part (b), the cost record at cancellation shows: the metrics worker settled \(\$4\) and stopped; the log worker settled \(\$9\), and a log-export job it started before cancellation is still unresolved with a bounded liability of \(\$3\); the first scale worker settled \(\$2\) and was confirmed terminated; the second scale worker settled nothing, and a node-pool scale-up it started before cancellation has an unknown outcome with a bounded liability of \(\$5\); the root’s own work settled \(\$4\). Compute the allowance the runtime may release now, the amount still held, and the release a “cancellation refunds all reservations” rule would claim. A follow-up remediation task needs a \(\$20\) allowance. Decide whether to admit it now, and state who owns the two open operations and what that owner must retain.

Buying evidence past a correlated floor (Advanced). Reviewers each falsely approve a known-invalid candidate with marginal probability \(\MarginalFalseApprovalProbability=0.10\), and their errors follow the beta mixture of section 18.6 with \(\CorrelationCoefficient=0.30\). The release rule requires that an invalid candidate be approved with probability at most \(0.01\). A reviewer call costs \(\$0.20\). A protected regression test costs \(\$0.50\) and passes an invalid candidate with probability \(0.05\), assumed independent of the candidate’s reviewer propensity \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\).

Compute the beta parameters \(\PropensityPriorApprovalShape\) and \(\PropensityPriorRejectionShape\), and the majority false-approval probability for three reviewers under independent errors and under the mixture.
Compute the mixture’s majority false approval for seven reviewers and the floor \(\Pr(\FalseApprovalPropensity>1/2)\), numerically. Decide whether any number of reviewers of this kind can meet the release rule.
Price two designs per candidate: seven reviewers under majority vote, and three reviewers plus the protected test, with approval requiring both a reviewer majority and a passing test. Compute each design’s false-approval probability and choose one.
Critique the assumption that the test is independent of \(\FalseApprovalPropensity\). Name a mechanism from this chapter that would correlate the test with the reviewers, and state the measurement that must precede release.

Fitting the scalability law before choosing a fan-out (Advanced, critique and redesign). Trials of a repair-migration partition under matched resources measure relative capacity \(\text{Speedup}(2)=1.835\) and \(\text{Speedup}(4)=2.878\). The serial reference takes \(40\) minutes, and the service requires completion within \(11\) minutes. The expected cost of an attempt grows with worker count as \(\$1.00+\$0.30(\WorkerCount-1)\), and acceptance does not change with \(\WorkerCount\).

Rearrange equation 5 so that it is linear in \(\ContentionCoefficient\) and \(\CoherencyCoefficient\), fit both coefficients from the two measurements, and compute \(\WorkerCount^*\) from equation 6, the best integer count and its capacity, and the smallest count that runs slower than one worker.
A trial at \(\WorkerCount=8\) measures \(2.90\). Compare it with the fitted prediction, and state what the gap implies about using the fit outside the measured range.
The team proposes deploying the best integer count from part (a). Critique the proposal against the deadline. For this calculation, suppose two proposed redesigns have the following responses: sharding the integration queue halves \(\ContentionCoefficient\), and repartitioning the migration so interface changes land before caller work begins halves \(\CoherencyCoefficient\). For each, find the smallest worker count that meets the deadline, if any, and its cost per attempt, and recommend a design under these assumptions. State what trace or matched intervention evidence would establish the assumed coefficient responses in a deployment.



What’s Next: From coordination to costWhen is the time saved by delegation worth its additional resource use? This chapter answered for one stated workload, charging failed attempts and canceled branches to the accepted tasks they served. That accounting is a special case of a question every deployment faces, for one agent or many. The next chapter opens with the repair team offered a model whose tokens cost a tenth as much and asks why the switch can still raise the price of every repair that ships. Answering it means counting what each accepted task costs across all its attempts, how context reuse, retries, and model choice change that cost, and how concurrent trajectories compete for capacity. The same account then prices delegation itself, without dropping the reservations and unresolved obligations established here.

title: 16 Trajectory Fine-Tuning
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can training on a useful recovery record teach the model to repeat the mistake instead of the correction?
While prompt engineering and runtime guardrails guide an off-the-shelf model, fine-tuning modifies the neural network weights directly, embedding specialized decision policies and tool calling conventions into model parameters. However, training on multi-turn trajectories requires strict separation between agent proposals and external environment observations, so that imitation loss applies only to selected policy responses while environment feedback remains conditioning context. Naive fine-tuning can teach a policy to fabricate its own tool results or overfit to static workspace layouts, degrading general reasoning and error recovery. Systems engineering governs how datasets are partitioned, how loss masks are applied, and how updated checkpoints are validated against regression suites before deployment. An update is worth releasing only when closed-loop task acceptance improves under the same runtime that still bounds every proposal the model makes, however far its training loss has fallen.

Learning Objectives

Assign agent behavior to weights, context, or runtime, and decide when a failure warrants a weight change
Construct model inputs that preserve intended conditioning and price per-invocation serialization in training tokens
Map admitted response spans to causal token targets, observation masks, and termination policy
Compare loss weighting and construct batches without unintended cross-example dependencies
Calculate imitation regret bounds on reference and learner states to decide when on-policy labeling pays
Calculate preference margins and gradient weights, and distinguish what a comparison measures from task acceptance
Select behavior sources and parameter artifacts using explicit resource and version accounting
Evaluate a versioned policy for release on closed-loop acceptance, cost per accepted task, and schema transfer, while preserving runtime enforcement



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗






Fine-tuning reshapes each model call but leaves every exposure to the runtime.
Consider a recovery demonstration admitted by the curation pipeline for the repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) into repair_demonstrations_v1. During the recorded session, the agent generated a malformed edit proposal that the runtime validator refused prior to tool dispatch. In response to the failure notification, the model inspected the tool schema, generated a corrected edit, and produced candidate patch ws_r20. From this multi-turn trajectory, the target-selection policy recovery_targets_v1 marks three assistant turns as supervised targets: the schema inspection request (e3), the corrected edit (e4), and the scoped final summary (e6). The malformed proposal (e2) and the runtime’s refusal remain in the input history as conditioning context. The member that entered the corpus is the redacted view trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, and the corpus manifest binds it to those role assignments, its lineage, and its split membership.
The raw event log of an admitted record is not yet in a form a training loop can safely ingest, because it interleaves model generations, runtime observations, and tool responses in the order they occurred. If a data loader treats every assistant message as a supervised target, it computes loss on the malformed edit proposal alongside the correction and reinforces the initial mistake. If the training pipeline computes loss across all sequence tokens indiscriminately, the model spends parameter capacity predicting deterministic environment replies, such as compiler diagnostics or directory listings, that it will never emit during inference. Finally, if the batching pipeline packs multiple trajectories into a shared context window without attention masking, self-attention heads attend across sample boundaries and leak private workspace contents into unrelated training examples. Standard cross-entropy loss fails silently under each of these mistakes. The training loss falls steadily as the optimizer fits the data, hiding the corrupted behavior from offline metrics. While curation contracts decide which actions show desirable behavior and evaluation contracts measure the deployed agent, neither specifies how to turn a multi-turn execution trace into isolated, causal gradient updates.
The path from an admitted record to an evaluated policy update begins with a question curation leaves open, namely which parts of the repair behavior belong in weights at all (section 16.2). The answer fixes what the data pipeline must protect. Serialization reconstructs each model input exactly as the agent received it (section 16.3), loss masking places the gradient on the selected responses and nowhere else (section 16.4), and batching shares buffers without letting examples read one another or skew one another’s weight (section 16.5). Masking and batching guard directly against those three silent failures, and serialization guards the premise both rely on, that each prefix is the one the model actually saw.
A faithful loader still trains on recorded prefixes, and the deployed policy acts on prefixes its own choices produce. Exposure bias prices that gap over the horizon and decides when labeling the learner’s own states pays (section 16.6), and schema robustness asks the same question of the tool interfaces the policy is shown (section 16.7). The remaining sections vary the update itself along three independent choices. The first is the objective, where preference optimization contrasts valid alternatives that imitation cannot rank (section 16.8). The second is the behavior source, where distillation moves a costlier configuration’s behavior into a cheaper one (section 16.9). The last is the parameter artifact, where adapters change what a run must store (section 16.10). Closed-loop evaluation decides whether any of them earned a release (section 16.11), and a training manifest for the repair policy assembles the whole chain (section 16.12).



Before turning an admitted record such as trace_r19_01_redacted_v1 into a weight update, engineers must decide whether the failure it repaired belongs in the model’s parameters at all. Fine-tuning a model to work around a missing prompt instruction or a broken tool schema bakes a temporary workaround into billions of weights, only for the behavior to break again the next time the interface changes. Modifying model weights is an expensive, high-blast-radius change reserved for behavioral failures that survive cheaper fixes. The intervention ladder orders changes by cost and reversibility, so engineers test prompt, schema, and runtime fixes before spending compute on parameter updates, while diagnostic evidence can justify a direct weight update when the policy itself is at fault. Verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) requires curation to tie recorded evidence to a declared learning use and separate admissible targets from contextual or rejected actions. While this ordering is the default because of cost and blast radius, fine-tuning also pays when moving stable procedural guidance into the weights costs less than resending a long instructional prefix on every turn (section 16.9).


↩︎ The intervention ladder, which orders context, schema, runtime, and parameter interventions by cost and reversibility, is established in The intervention ladder.
Once diagnostic evidence justifies a parameter update, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adjusts trainable model parameters to maximize the conditional likelihood of selected target tokens given their causal prefix context. When processing trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, the training loop must follow the recovery sequence defined in recovery_targets_v1 rather than computing loss over every recorded token. The model must see the historical context and tool outputs that justify a chosen action, yet the data pipeline must exclude later steps that would reveal future observations or solutions ahead of time. Trajectory fine-tuning therefore inherits two data contracts: a target-selection contract that designates which tokens contribute to the loss gradient, and a conditioning contract that governs what causal history the model sees when generating those tokens.
The two contracts separate learning improved behavior from overfitting an idiosyncratic run. In an error-recovery trajectory, the behavioral goal is teaching the model to inspect an updated schema after a refusal, issue a properly formed corrective call, and interpret what the runtime verification check establishes. Memorizing the file paths of a specific test fixture or predicting hard-coded test outputs lowers training loss without teaching generalizable recovery skills. Whether the updated policy transfers these habits to unfamiliar environments and new tasks is what section 16.11 measures, and keeping the update generalizable starts with deciding which parts of agent behavior live in weights versus the prompt and runtime.


If a fine-tuned repair agent memorizes an API signature in its parameters instead of reading the prompt, a routine tool-interface change, such as adding a required parameter or revoking a permission, immediately breaks the deployed policy. Every response the agent generates combines the model’s static weights with the dynamic context window assembled for that call, and fine-tuning updates only the weights. Engineers therefore divide agent behavior across three architectural homes, summarized in table 1:

Procedure is behavior that stays stable across tasks and changes slowly, such as inspecting diagnostic output before modifying source code or checking unresolved issues before reporting completion. Procedure is what model weights can reliably absorb.
Contracts are the dynamic operational facts that vary across deployments, user sessions, and individual turns, such as API tool definitions, schema requirements, environment parameters, and granted permissions. Contracts belong in the prompt context; a model that memorized an earlier schema will keep emitting obsolete arguments when an interface changes.
Enforcement covers the invariants that must hold even when the model proposes an invalid or adversarial action, such as schema validation, authorization checks, sandbox containment, and execution timeouts. Enforcement stays in the deterministic runtime harness under invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).




Table 1: Responsibilities of Weights, Context, and Runtime: Weights hold procedure, context holds the current contract, and the runtime enforces that contract whatever the model proposes.










Home
Intended responsibility
Consequence for fine-tuning




Weights
Learned procedures and response tendencies, including tool selection and recovery behavior
Update the proposal distribution, then measure whether the changed behavior helps under the declared task conditions


Context
Current task facts, tool schemas, observations, and represented scope
Supply the information the policy needs now; do not rely on memorized versions as the authority for current facts or permissions


Runtime
Validation, authorization, containment, resource controls, and evidence collection
Preserve enforcement independently of the learned policy; a model’s predicted result is not an observed external effect






Relying on parameters to store interface contracts makes a deployment brittle, because a revoked permission stays revoked regardless of how often the action appeared in past training demonstrations. Fine-tuning cannot replace dynamic contracts; what it can teach is the habit of reading and following whichever contract the context window supplies.
This boundary disproves the view that fine-tuning only moves the prompt into the weights. Only the procedural parts of a prompt (structured reasoning guidelines, diagnostic checklists, or few-shot error-recovery examples) belong in the parameters, where they save token overhead on every turn (section 16.9). The contractual parts must stay in the prompt context, because omitting them forces the model to guess the current execution environment. The deterministic checks that enforce authorization and boundary invariants cannot live in either prompts or weights, because a probability distribution over tokens cannot guarantee an invariant.
Fine-tuning changes the policy’s proposal distribution: which tools it requests, how thoroughly it inspects diagnostic evidence, and which execution paths it tries. Those shifts change task success rates, end-to-end latency, and token use, yet every proposed action still runs inside the horizons, state transitions, and authority boundaries enforced by the runtime harness. This separation is the proposal boundary of The Model Call Boundary. Training reshapes what the policy proposes, while the runtime decides which actions may execute, and that boundary governs every adaptation choice that follows.



Deciding that a recovery habit belongs in the weights still leaves a team to choose whether to imitate single corrections or rank competing repairs, whether to train on recorded logs or collect fresh trajectories, and whether to ship a full checkpoint copy or a lightweight adapter. Treating “fine-tuning” as a single knob obscures which decision is responsible when an update overfits or exceeds its memory budget, so the pipeline separates adaptation along three independent axes:

Training Objective: The loss function that defines the learning signal. Supervised imitation maximizes the likelihood of curated target demonstrations, whereas preference methods such as direct preference optimization (section 16.8) adjust weights by contrasting preferred trajectories against dispreferred alternatives under an explicit ranking rule.
Behavior Source: Where the demonstrations and conditioning inputs come from. Traces may be collected from instrumented production runs and filtered by offline verification, generated by a teacher configuration with privileged context or a larger search budget (section 16.9), labeled on the states the learner itself reaches, or constructed by injecting faults the recordings never contained (section 16.6.2).
Parameter Artifact: Which weights the run updates and stores. Teams can update all model parameters directly or train compact adapter matrices, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules, that attach to a frozen base checkpoint (section 16.10).

Because these three choices are independent, they combine freely; a deployment can, for example, train a low-rank adapter with a preference objective on synthetic teacher demonstrations. Whichever combination a team chooses, the run still trains on trajectory records converted into model inputs, so the first pipeline step is reconstructing the input prefix and conditioning window for each selected response.




In the admitted repair demonstration trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, the corrected edit (e4) makes sense only as a response to the malformed proposal (e2), the runtime refusal, and the schema inspection (e3) that preceded it. A training loader that strips out the refusal changes the problem the subsequent correction answered, and a loader that places the later passing test check (e5) before the edit leaks future evidence that the model did not have when proposing the patch. While curation selects which model completions to reinforce, serialization must reconstruct the exact prompt and observation history that prompted them, including any runtime redactions (such as synthetic placeholders substituted for private file paths), so the training example matches the context the model actually saw.


Runtime event logs record state transitions across the harness, but an event log alone does not show what was inside the model’s context window at a given call. System prompts change, tool schemas update between versions, and earlier messages are often summarized or truncated to fit token budgets. To reconstruct each call’s input faithfully, the training pipeline reads the delivered-input manifests, which record the exact messages, tool definitions, summaries, and bounded observations sent to the model along with their schema versions.


↩︎ The delivered-input manifest that records the exact payload sent to the model, rather than mutable paths or references, is established in The log event schema.
When an example requires historical fidelity, the loader serializes the selected invocation directly from its delivered-input manifest, preserving partial buffers, truncated outputs, and execution errors rather than substituting a cleaner result obtained later in the run. When a pipeline instead transforms an example deliberately, such as shortening prompts for context distillation (section 16.9), it applies the reviewed transformation to both the prompt and the paired response, keeps the parent trace reference, and rechecks schema compatibility. Chat templates differ across model families, and even checkpoints from the same base model often format tool schemas, parallel calls, or message boundaries differently. Rendering a trajectory with delimiters that do not match the serving parser teaches the policy a syntax that production will reject. A serialized dataset artifact therefore records the tokenizer version, template configuration, tool-formatting schema, and response-boundary policy alongside the token arrays, because the message sequence and its rendering configuration together form the model input.

The training pipeline packages this rendered dataset as serialization_v1, whose manifest pairs the admitted execution records with the active rendering configuration and maps every selected response span to its token offsets. Because tokenization, template formatting, and string redaction can shift token boundaries (for example, when leading whitespace merges into an adjacent special token), the pipeline re-verifies all token offsets against the rendered token array and decodes completed examples to check task prompts, tool bindings, span boundaries, and end-of-sequence markers. If an example fails boundary alignment or drops content, the pipeline discards the record rather than patching it with synthetic filler.
Role delimiters define protocol syntax, but they carry no runtime authority: if a model emits text that mimics a <|tool|> delimiter, that text is still model output under the tokenizer’s grammar, and the serialization pipeline never promotes unverified generations into environment observations. Once the template fixes how each turn is rendered, the pipeline still has to decide whether a multi-turn trajectory can be stored as a single rendered sequence or must be split into separate per-invocation examples.

Because the repair agent’s runtime compacts history once the working set crosses its watermark, a turn delivered after compaction saw a summary digest rather than the raw earlier turns that a single concatenated transcript would place before it. A single concatenated transcript is a faithful training example only when the serving runtime appends every turn without pruning earlier steps, compacting intermediate context, or dropping reasoning scratchpads to save KV-cache memory. Whenever serving prunes or compacts history between steps so that later causal prefixes no longer match a growing transcript, the loader must serialize each invocation as its own training example containing that call’s exact delivered prefix.


↩︎ Watermark-triggered compaction, which replaces earlier turns with a digest between invocations, is established in Context Compaction.
Serializing each call separately carries the same triangular token cost that already priced an append-only trajectory at serving time (equation 2.9), now paid in stored training tokens. If a trajectory spans \(\TurnHorizon\) turns and each turn adds roughly \(\TurnAppendLength\) tokens, the example for turn \(\TurnIndex\) spans about \(\TurnIndex\,\TurnAppendLength\) tokens. Serializing all \(\TurnHorizon\) invocations separately stores \(\TurnAppendLength\,\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon+1)/2\) tokens, compared with \(\TurnHorizon\,\TurnAppendLength\) tokens for a single transcript. That is an expansion factor of \((\TurnHorizon+1)/2\), which over a stipulated 30-turn horizon multiplies the stored token volume by 15.5×. An agent’s history-retention policy therefore directly governs training storage and compute. The same fidelity rule applies to the model’s own reasoning text. If serving drops an earlier turn’s rationale before the next call, the reconstructed prefix for that call omits it too. Whether retained rationale is trained as a target or kept as context is a separate masking choice (section 16.4.4).
With serialization_v1 assembled, the pipeline has the tokenized sequences, their conditioning prefixes, and the response spans selected during curation. The next step is deciding which token positions contribute to the training loss, because computing cross-entropy over an entire multi-turn sequence would penalize the model for failing to predict tool outputs and user messages.




In serialization_v1, the token array for the repair trajectory still contains the prompt, the malformed proposal e2, the runtime refusal, the returned schema, and the check summary e5 alongside the selected responses e3, e4, and e6. A loader that selects every assistant token trains the model on the malformed proposal e2 alongside its correction e4, undoing curation, while a loader that computes loss across all tokens trains the policy to predict environment replies. Serialization turns the interaction into tokens; the loss mask decides which of those tokens drive gradient updates.


Let \(\SerializedTrainingExample=(\SequenceToken_1,\ldots,\SequenceToken_{\SequenceLength})\) be one serialized example, with an initial context or boundary token at \(\SequenceToken_1\), and let \(\EligibleTargetPositionSet\subseteq\{2,\ldots,\SequenceLength\}\) contain the policy-token positions selected for imitation. Which positions belong to \(\EligibleTargetPositionSet\) depends on the admitted response spans and the training objective rather than token authorship alone. With the binary mask \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=\IndicatorFunction\{\TokenIndex\in\EligibleTargetPositionSet\}\) and \(\PositionLossMask_1=0\), the mean masked cross-entropy for an example with at least one selected target is
\[\MaskedFinetuningLoss(\ModelParameters)=-\frac{1}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}\log\Policy(\SequenceToken_t\mid \TokenPrefix),\qquad \ActiveTargetTokenCount=\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}>0. \tag{1}\]
Each selected token is predicted from the recorded prefix \(\TokenPrefix\), which includes earlier actions, observations, and admitted mistakes, rather than from fresh rollouts sampled during training. This regime is teacher forcing1 (Williams and Zipser 1989), and it lets recovery prefixes that contain earlier failures serve as conditioning context whenever the trajectory satisfies the curation contract.
1 Teacher Forcing: Williams and Zipser (1989) named the technique for recurrent networks, feeding the recorded target back as the next input instead of the network’s own output. Because every prefix is recorded rather than generated, a causal model computes all of an example’s next-token predictions in one parallel forward pass, which is why imitating a trajectory costs one pass per example rather than one sampled rollout per decision.
Williams, Ronald J., and David Zipser. 1989. “A Learning Algorithm for Continually Running Fully Recurrent Neural Networks.” Neural Computation 1 (2): 270–80. https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1989.1.2.270.

Definition 16.1: Observation loss masking
Observation loss masking excludes supplied observations from the direct token-prediction loss while retaining the permitted observation context needed to train selected policy responses.

Significance: Focuses the optimization objective on the policy’s conditional distribution \(\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})\), so verbose environment output cannot dilute the gradient on policy actions regardless of how much context observations occupy (notebook 16.1 quantifies this dilution).
Distinction: Masked tokens stay in the input context and participate in self-attention; only their next-token loss terms are zeroed. Policy authorship alone does not make a token a target, because refused attempts or unsafe actions are also masked even when emitted in the assistant role.
Common pitfall: Selecting an entire multi-turn tool exchange only because the tool call succeeded, which trains the model to predict external environment responses.



A deployed agent trajectory interleaves two different generators: the agent policy and the external environment. Training without observation masking forces one set of weights to fit both distributions at once:

The agent policy \(\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})\), which maps prior observations and instructions to tool calls or answers.
An environment dynamics model \(\EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\TrajectoryState_{t+1}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t}, \TrajectoryAction_{t})\), which predicts the outputs returned by shells, databases, or remote APIs.

Because real tools run during deployment and return actual outputs, spending model capacity to predict environment returns is wasted work, and supervising the environment distribution causes two concrete failures:

Loss dilution: Under token-averaged cross-entropy, unmasking expands the denominator from \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\) to all \(\SequenceLength-1\) causal prediction terms (every stored position after the initial boundary). Each decision token’s gradient weight shrinks by the ratio of selected targets to predicted positions (computed in notebook 16.1), while the rest of the loss budget goes to file paths, stack traces, compiler dumps, and JSON payloads. Repetitive boilerplate pulls the average loss down, while novel stack traces or file contents dominate the gradient; in either case, the average stops measuring the policy.
Role confusion: When trained to predict the tokens that follow a tool call, the policy learns that tool outputs continue the same autoregressive stream. At serving time, it can keep generating past its own tool call and write a fabricated tool result instead of emitting the stop token that hands control back to the runtime. Because the runtime rejects unauthenticated observations (section 16.3), those fabricated tokens are discarded, wasting output budget and stalling the turn.

The prompt, task statement, refused proposal, rejection message, and tool result carry \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\) and stay as conditioning context, where gradients from later selected targets still update the weights that encode them.

Observation masking prevents both loss dilution and role confusion at the objective level, while closed-loop trials verify that the trained model stops at tool boundaries. Realizing that masked objective in code requires aligning every mask bit \(\PositionLossMask_{t}\) with the exact prediction step that generates token \(\SequenceToken_t\).



An off-by-one shift between input tokens and target masks silently corrupts every tool boundary in a corpus, masking the first token of each selected response while training the policy to predict the first token of the following tool observation. Many training frameworks shift labels by one position inside their own loss function, so shifting them once in the loader and a second time in the loss misaligns every target mask across the dataset. In a causal autoregressive model,2 the hidden state at input position \(\TokenIndex-1\) produces the logits that predict token \(\SequenceToken_t\), so the loader must pair the logits at \(\TokenIndex-1\) with target label \(\SequenceToken_t\) and target mask \(\PositionLossMask_{t}\) rather than with the mask of input token \(\SequenceToken_{t-1}\) (table 4). Checking the aligned labels and masks on a short synthetic example before launching a run catches this bug immediately.

Even within the model-generated share of a trajectory, masking out a chain-of-thought scratchpad during training while expecting the deployed policy to act without any scratchpad at serving time trains the model on conditioning context it will not have in production. When a dataset includes intermediate reasoning traces or tool-use plans alongside tool calls, the loader must therefore choose among three masking regimes (table 7) that match how the model will be served. Supervising the rationale trains the model to generate its own reasoning before invoking tools. Retaining the rationale under a loss mask treats the reasoning as supplied conditioning context, training the model to act on plans provided by an external orchestrator or user. Stripping the rationale entirely changes the conditional distribution so the policy acts from context alone.
Formally, given context prefix \(\TurnContext_{t}\), rationale tokens \(\RationaleTokens\), and action tokens \(\ResponseActionTokens=(\ResponseActionTokens_1,\ldots,\ResponseActionTokens_n)\), response-only supervision fits the conditional distribution \(\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \RationaleTokens, \ActionTokenPrefix)\). If the production serving environment does not supply \(\RationaleTokens\), the deployed model instead evaluates \(\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \ActionTokenPrefix)\). Because those are distinct conditional distributions, omitting rationale at serving time is a distillation step that must be evaluated directly against the unconditioned target.

At serving time, either an external planner or the policy’s own autoregressive decoder supplies the reasoning text. Whether a response carries rationale or only a tool call, its mask must also handle how the turn ends. To teach an agent when to yield control, the training loss must include the authentic policy-generated stop token (such as <|eom_id|> or <|im_end|>) at the end of each complete selected response, rather than confusing it with host delimiters that mark incoming tool payloads. Without direct supervision on the stop token, the policy can keep generating past the end of a valid tool call until it hits the output limit, returning TRUNCATED instead of COMPLETED so the runtime’s quarantining rule withholds the proposal.

Appending a synthetic end-of-turn token to a response cut short by a context window or timeout is the training-side twin of the hazard the quarantining rule blocks at serving time, where a truncated rm -rf argument still parses as a complete and broader command. The training-side version is worse, because a policy that has learned to emit the terminator after a partial command produces a COMPLETED status, which the quarantining rule admits. When a turn was truncated in the recorded trace, the loader has two sound options:

Conservative exclusion: Mask the truncated turn entirely (\(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\)) while keeping earlier complete turns in the trajectory.
Prefix-only supervision: Supervise the valid initial tokens of the truncated turn up to the truncation point, and omit any terminating token.

Whenever trajectories undergo truncation, sliding-window packing, or template changes, the data pipeline recomputes target masks and checks that \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount > 0\). Automated assertions verify the first token of each agent response, the closing turn terminator, the transition into tool observations, refused recovery attempts, and truncated turns before the serialized dataset enters the training loop.

With per-example loss masking in place, the loader separates conditioning context from imitation targets inside each sequence. Training at scale, however, combines trajectories of widely varying lengths into batches across device buffers, and the batching pipeline must preserve that per-example contract without leaking context across examples or silently skewing their weights.




Consider a batch where a 30-turn debugging and code-repair trace shares a training buffer with a brief, one-turn file lookup. Under an ordinary lower-triangular causal mask, the lookup can attend directly to the repair trace’s intermediate file contents and tool outputs, context that the lookup policy will never have at serving time. Under token averaging, the multi-turn repair trace also outweighs the brief lookup by the ratio of their active target tokens.
Constructing a batch of variable-length trajectories therefore pairs two systems choices: how much gradient weight each trajectory receives in the batch loss, and how multiple sequences share physical buffer memory without leaking context across sequence boundaries. Sequence packing is only a memory layout; a faithful implementation keeps both the declared loss weighting and each example’s isolated predictive context.


Let a batch contain \(\BatchSize\) examples, where example \(\BatchExampleIndex\) has stored length \(\SequenceLength^{(\BatchExampleIndex)}\) (including context) and \({\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex}>0\) selected target tokens under the mask of section 16.4, with mean masked negative log-likelihood \(\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}\). The two standard batch objectives weight the long repair trace and the one-turn file lookup differently:
\[\TokenAveragedBatchLoss=
\sum_{\BatchExampleIndex=1}^{\BatchSize}\frac{{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_{\BatchExampleIndex}}{\sum_{k=1}^{\BatchSize}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}_k}\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}, \tag{2}\]
\[\ExampleAveragedBatchLoss=\frac{1}{\BatchSize}\sum_{\BatchExampleIndex=1}^{\BatchSize}\LossFunction_{\BatchExampleIndex}. \tag{3}\]
Token averaging in equation 2 gives equal weight to every selected token loss, whereas example averaging in equation 3 gives equal weight to every example mean. Both count only selected targets, never context or padding, and any record with no selected targets is excluded from both objectives. Because a serialized example may be a single invocation rather than a full task, example averaging equalizes serialized records rather than underlying tasks, while token averaging weights each record in proportion to its active target count.
The difference becomes critical when per-invocation serialization splits one multi-turn interaction into separate training records. If one of \(\BatchSize\) initial examples is split into \(\TurnHorizon\) per-invocation records while every other example stays unsplit, example averaging raises that trajectory’s share of the batch loss from \(1/\BatchSize\) to \(\TurnHorizon/(\BatchSize-1+\TurnHorizon)\), giving it \(\TurnHorizon\) times the weight of each unsplit example. Under token averaging, the trajectory’s aggregate share stays unchanged as long as its selected targets are partitioned disjointly across the \(\TurnHorizon\) records. Even though the record for a later turn repeats earlier assistant responses inside its conditioning prefix, the loader masks those earlier responses (\(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\)) and sets \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=1\) only on that invocation’s final response, so repeating prefix context does not repeat active targets. A corpus mixture specified in selected target tokens, the unit in which Records, stored tokens, and selected targets fixes class shares, therefore reaches the parameter update unchanged only under token averaging. Example averaging, or a per-invocation split that leaves earlier assistant turns unmasked and selects the same target twice, changes the realized mixture (table 8).
