11 Catastrophic Forgetting: McCloskey and Cohen (1989) showed that a connectionist network trained sequentially on a new task can lose an earlier one almost entirely, because both share the same weights. A repair-trained policy shares its weights with every other behavior the agent still needs, so retention is measured on the release’s required task set rather than assumed from a narrow training corpus.
McCloskey, Michael, and Neal J. Cohen. 1989. “Catastrophic Interference in Connectionist Networks: The Sequential Learning Problem.” Psychology of Learning and Motivation 24: 109–65. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0079-7421(08)60536-8.
Even a repair update that improves acceptance at lower \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) can degrade the other tasks the deployment serves if weight updates overwrite broader skills. Testing capability retention checks that specializing the weights on repair traces has not degraded those non-repair tasks, using a regression suite drawn from the agent’s full operational scope rather than generic language benchmarks alone. When performance drops on non-repair tasks, engineers check both the serving template and the training mixture before attributing the drop to catastrophic forgetting11 (McCloskey and Cohen 1989), and re-evaluate any mitigation, such as mixing in general trajectories, lowering the learning rate, or switching to a LoRA adapter, on the same five-part scorecard.



To attribute changes on those five measurements to the weight update rather than to a coincidental prompt or schema edit, the release protocol varies one factor at a time under the fixture contract of Task fixtures. Each comparison pins task fixtures, acceptance criteria, resource budgets, and random seeds across repeated trials, binding every score to an artifact manifest that records the checkpoint or adapter hash, base model hash, tokenizer version, serialization template, decoding parameters, and harness commit.
The leakage controls of Evaluation leakage govern contamination here as well. Re-prompted attempts, redacted traces, and paraphrased variants inherit their source task’s split. Checkpoints and tuning mixtures are selected on validation splits alone. A test suite whose failures were fed back into training or prompt tuning has become development data and must be replaced by a fresh split. Benchmarking on familiar repositories or APIs reflects legitimate deployment requirements, but a claim that the fine-tuned policy generalizes demands held-out schema and environment families.
Controlled ablations compare the fine-tuned checkpoint against the incumbent policy, as well as against the prompt-engineering, schema-refactoring, and runtime-guardrail alternatives prioritized by the intervention ladder. Because the candidate and the incumbent can run on the same tasks, the comparison is a paired one, and the paired-outcome discipline (an interval on the difference, never two overlapping single-arm intervals) applies unchanged. Reading several ablations at once adds one correction beyond a single pair. If each comparison is tested at the same significance level, the chance that at least one of them shows a false win grows with their number, so the per-comparison level must be tightened. Dividing it by the number of comparisons is the simplest such rule. A release claim resting on one seed or one favorable run is a sample of one.


↩︎ Paired comparison of two configurations on the same tasks, with intervals on the difference and the rule for splitting trials between new tasks and repeats, is established in Statistical Evaluation Rigor.
While a lower common validation loss confirms that training optimized the intended objective, only closed-loop task acceptance, recovery resilience, and load-tested serving configurations provide defensible release evidence. A fine-tuned candidate enters the same declared release gate as any other change (The declared decision rule), approved for an exact artifact hash and operating envelope under principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\). Even after a fine-tuned model passes release qualification, external safety boundaries remain non-negotiable: runtime schema validators, permission sandboxes, token budgets, and supervisory recovery monitors must remain active in production. Assembling the scope, serialization, masking, batching, coverage, and release decisions into one auditable training manifest turns an admitted recovery record into a deployable policy candidate.




The recovery record that opened the chapter can now become a training artifact. The behavior to teach is narrow. When the runtime refuses an invalid tool proposal, the policy should inspect the schema, issue a corrected invocation that satisfies the interface, and end with a bounded report. Consider an illustrative supervised fine-tuning run that ingests repair_demonstrations_v1 to produce candidate policy trained_policy_v1. That artifact is a set of weights, distinct from ws_r20, the workspace the demonstration produced.
Each of the three adaptation choices is settled by evidence the chapter has already developed. The objective is imitation because the record supplies a demonstrated correction, not an admissible comparison; e2 and e4 were produced under different information, so they cannot form a preference pair (section 16.8). The behavior source is the admitted recovery corpus. It covers the malformed-argument refusal the recording happened to contain, not the version conflict that section 16.6 showed a policy trained on it would meet. That uncovered state is therefore the first candidate for a labeling round or a fault-injected record, and the first evaluation of trained_policy_v1 must include trials that reach it. The artifact is a full-parameter update, chosen for two reasons the chapter has developed. The repair policy is a single role, so none of the multi-role sharing that makes adapters attractive applies yet. The lesson is also a new recovery behavior, the kind for which a small rank is not known in advance to suffice, so the full update serves as the reference that any later adapter candidate must match. The choice has a price. On the hypothetical model of notebook 16.5, it keeps 128 GB of parameter state where an adapter run would keep 16.13 GB. A rank sweep whose adapter matches the full update’s paired acceptance, or a second role that must share the base, would flip the decision toward the adapter, which would then be a different candidate with its own evidence. Changing any one of the three choices produces a configuration that needs its own evidentiary trail.

The mask and the serialization follow directly from the earlier sections. target_mask_v1 selects the policy-response spans of e3 (the schema query), e4 (the corrected tool call), and e6 (the final report), each with its authentic end-of-turn token. The malformed proposal and its pre-dispatch refusal at e2, the schema returned to e3, and the check summary at e5 carry \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\); they stay in the prefix as conditioning and receive no direct loss (table 2). Selecting e2 would teach the malformed call, and selecting the returned schema or e5 would teach the policy to write tool results instead of requesting them. Whether serialization_v1 may use one concatenated transcript or must serialize each selected invocation separately depends on whether the runtime compacted history between e2 and e6. If it did not, each selected response’s prefix is a prefix of one transcript and a single example is faithful. The manifest records which case held, from the delivered-input manifests, rather than assuming it, because a record that crossed the watermark would need one example per invocation at up to \((\TurnHorizon+1)/2\) the stored tokens (section 16.3.3). If the run packs these examples with others, block-diagonal attention and per-example label shifts keep each example’s context its own (section 16.5).
The release gate for trained_policy_v1 follows from the lesson it was meant to learn. Lower held-out loss on the repair corpus shows only that the objective was optimized. Promotion needs budgeted task acceptance on held-out repair tasks under the same runtime and fixtures as the incumbent, compared as paired trials, with \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) reported for both so that a slower but more reliable candidate is credited correctly. Because the lesson is “consult the delivered schema,” the most direct test is schema-following accuracy and parametric recall error on a renamed-argument set: a candidate whose PRE rises there may be relying on the recorded interface rather than the delivered schema. The gate also needs trials that reach the version-conflict state the corpus does not cover, and a retention suite for the agent’s other required tasks. A candidate missing any of these measurements is held, however its loss compares (section 16.11).
Even when the evaluations justify a staged release, the proposal boundary stays where it was. Fine-tuning makes the policy’s proposals more reliable without making the model an execution authority. The runtime keeps enforcing schema validation, least-privilege tool permissions, process isolation, and hard timeout budgets, and the agent’s final report remains a claim the harness checks against workspace artifacts. The manifest is what turns one admitted recovery into a reproducible, auditable policy update; the runtime is what keeps that update’s mistakes bounded.



A fine-tuning pipeline can optimize its nominal loss objective with complete numerical fidelity while departing from the intended operational behavior. In agent systems, where training corpora interweave multi-turn plans, tool invocations, and environment feedback, subtle flaws emerge at the interfaces between admitted evidence, context assembly, loss masking, and deployment evaluation. Each of the following mistakes produces a concrete failure mode, and each carries a quantifiable engineering penalty illustrated in this chapter’s worked examples.

Fallacy: Every model response in an accepted trajectory is a desirable training target.
When an agent successfully recovers from an error, the recorded trajectory necessarily contains the initial flawed or refused proposal alongside the eventual correction. That initial misstep is essential as conditioning context, because it explains why the correction was required, but it is the one action the policy must never learn to emit. In the inventory of notebook 16.1, the refused positions number 160 tokens, 20 percent as many as the 800 selected response targets. An unselective mask over all assistant turns therefore puts 160 of the 960 response positions to work reproducing the malformed call. That share is a minority of the response weight, yet all of it rewards the refused proposal directly, in every recovery record that contains one. Systems must instead implement target admission masks (section 16.4): retain rejected proposals and environment observations in the prefix context so the agent learns to condition on failure signals, but restrict direct imitation loss to admitted response targets.


Pitfall: Treating efficient batching as a change with no learning consequences.
Packing multiple variable-length trajectories into a single contiguous buffer raises occupancy, but it alters training dynamics unless the execution kernel accounts for sequence boundaries. In notebook 16.2, sequence packing raises token occupancy from 19.1 percent to 76.6 percent. However, applying a standard causal attention mask across that packed buffer allows subsequent examples to attend across episode boundaries to unrelated earlier sequences. Loss normalization alters optimization just as profoundly: standard token-level averaging gives the long example 32× the short one’s weight, whereas per-example averaging weights both examples equally. Always configure block-diagonal attention with per-example position coordinates and reset label shifts (section 16.5), explicitly declare loss reduction semantics, and verify real execution throughput on target accelerator kernels before claiming a speedup.


Fallacy: Recovery examples and schema perturbations make a fine-tuned agent robust to the states it will meet.
Synthesized recovery trajectories and perturbed schemas broaden training coverage, but they do not provide a blanket guarantee against distribution shift. Theoretical bounds on policy regret depend on where state error rates are evaluated. Over an execution horizon of 30 steps with a 2 percent per-step disagreement rate, theorem 16.1 bounds excess cost at 18 units on reference demonstration states, but at 0.6 units on states generated by the learner itself. Furthermore, that tighter bound holds only while the disadvantage of each individual deviation remains near one, a condition that fails as soon as one unexpected tool error can spoil the rest of the task. Robust agent systems require sampling and labeling states actually reached by the learner, maintaining end-to-end coherence between schema transformations, tool calls, and parser observations (section 16.7), and stress-testing the policy under held-out operational shifts.


Pitfall: Reading a preference pair’s logistic score as the probability that the preferred repair succeeds.
The implicit reward margin computed in direct preference optimization reflects pairwise discrimination on historical data, not absolute operational success. In notebook 16.4, identical trajectory log-probabilities yield a logistic score of 0.646 at \(\PreferenceScale=\) 0.2, yet that score rises to 0.769 when the preference scale doubles to \(\PreferenceScale=\) 0.4. A metric that shifts this much with an optimization hyperparameter measures relative fitting margin rather than task competence. Furthermore, that margin can widen because the objective suppresses the dispreferred trajectory rather than improving the execution likelihood of the preferred one. Reliable acceptance rates cannot be read off training curves; they must be measured directly through closed-loop environment trials (section 16.11).


Fallacy: Training a small fraction of the parameters shrinks training memory in proportion.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning cuts the number of updated weights to a small fraction, but accelerator memory does not scale down linearly with the parameter fraction. In notebook 16.5, low-rank adapters account for 0.10 percent of total model parameters, yet the training job still requires 12.6 percent of the parameter-associated memory consumed by a full fine-tuning run. This 7.9× reduction is governed by bytes per parameter across base and adapter states rather than the parameter count alone. The frozen base weights must remain resident in memory throughout forward and backward passes, accounting for 99.2 percent of what remains, while dynamic activation buffers and workspace memory scale with sequence length for both approaches. Dimension adapter training hardware by accounting for frozen base representations and empirically measured activation peaks (section 16.10).


Pitfall: Promoting the artifact with the lowest recorded loss.
Selecting an agent checkpoint based purely on validation loss conflates prefix prediction with closed-loop execution competence. In notebook 16.1, an unmasked causal evaluation averages across 16,383 prediction terms per example. Tool outputs that the policy never emits occupy 77.1 percent of the stored input. In contrast, a selective objective evaluates only the 800 target positions where the model generates actions. A checkpoint with lower overall loss may simply fit the repetitive parts of that environment text more tightly without improving decision quality. Even when measured exclusively on action tokens, offline likelihood improvements do not guarantee that the policy will avoid deadlocks or handle schema variations during execution. Always qualify production candidates by measuring scoped task acceptance, effective cost \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), schema compliance, and retained foundational capabilities (section 16.11), while maintaining strict runtime validation checks regardless of training performance.




Trajectory fine-tuning changes the policy itself, and every decision in this chapter serves one requirement, that the update teach the lesson curation admitted and nothing else. A trajectory mixes the policy’s responses with the environment’s replies, so a loss computed over the wrong positions, under the wrong prefixes, or with the wrong batch weighting can fall while the behavior it teaches drifts. Even a faithful update is fitted on recorded prefixes. Its value is settled only by closed-loop evidence on the states the policy reaches on its own, under the same runtime that bounds every proposal it makes.

Key Takeaways: Preserve the lesson from record to release

Weights hold procedure, never contracts: Training changes what the policy proposes, not what the runtime permits. Stable procedure can move into the weights, while schemas, permissions, and any guidance that changes faster than a training and evaluation cycle stay in context, and enforcement stays in the runtime.
A trajectory has two authors; train one: Observations stay in the input as context but receive no direct loss. An unmasked average dilutes each selected target by the inverse of its selected share of predicted positions, 20.5× in the worked inventory, and teaches the policy to invent tool results.
A loader can change the lesson without changing the loss: Later evidence in a prefix, a shifted label, or a causal mask across packed examples each redefines the prediction problem. Normalization is a choice too, since token averaging gives a long trajectory 32× the weight of a short one in the worked batch.
Where error is measured sets the horizon penalty: The same 2 percent disagreement over 30 steps bounds excess cost at 18 units on reference states and 0.6 on learner states when the deviation disadvantage is bounded by one. Long-horizon agents therefore need labels on the states they actually visit.
A preference score measures one comparison: A pair’s logistic score moves with \(\PreferenceScale\) and can rise by suppressing the dispreferred record, so it measures fit to that comparison, never the probability that a repair is accepted.
Adapters cut state by bytes, not parameter fraction: Training 0.10 percent of the parameters still keeps 12.6 percent of the parameter state, because the frozen base stays resident. The lever is the frozen base’s representation, not the adapter rank.
Release on closed-loop acceptance, not loss: A candidate is promoted on task acceptance, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), schema behavior, and retained capability under its full serving configuration. Rollback selects an earlier policy for future work and leaves effects already dispatched to settlement and compensation.



Verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) now has a concrete implementation obligation at the token level: preserve useful conditioning while aligning the objective with the selected predictions, rather than equating every recorded policy token with a target. At the record level, it connects the admitted lesson to a versioned update whose usefulness remains an evaluation question. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) stays outside that update, which is why the proposal boundary holds from the first training example to the release decision.



The core mechanism of this chapter is older than language models. Williams and Zipser named teacher forcing in 1989, training recurrent networks by feeding the recorded target back as the next input (Williams and Zipser 1989). At about the same time, ALVINN learned road following as a supervised mapping from camera images to a steering direction (Pomerleau 1988), the template for what control researchers came to call behavioral cloning. Both generations met the same obstacle. A policy trained on recorded prefixes is run on its own, and its first error moves it into inputs the recording never showed. Ross and Bagnell turned that obstacle into a quadratic bound in 2010 (Ross and Bagnell 2010), and DAgger answered it the following year by labeling the states the learner itself visits (Ross et al. 2011). Sequence-generation research reached the same diagnosis independently, with scheduled sampling (Bengio et al. 2015) and the name exposure bias (Ranzato et al. 2016).

Preference learning has a statistical root. Bradley and Terry’s 1952 model of paired comparisons (Bradley and Terry 1952) underlies the reward models that Christiano and colleagues fit to human comparisons of agent behavior (Christiano et al. 2017), and InstructGPT combined supervised demonstrations with such a reward model to align a language model (Ouyang et al. 2022). DPO then showed that the separate reward model and reinforcement learning stage could be folded into a classification loss on policy/reference log ratios (Rafailov et al. 2023), the form this chapter extends from responses to selected trajectory spans.
The cost of adaptation has its own lineage. Model compression (Buciluă et al. 2006) and knowledge distillation (Hinton et al. 2015) made a large model’s behavior a training signal for a cheaper one, and context distillation applied the same idea to a prompt (Askell et al. 2021). Adapter modules (Houlsby et al. 2019), low-rank adaptation (Hu et al. 2021), and quantized frozen bases (Dettmers et al. 2023) shrank what each adaptation stores and trains, while the systems accounting of mixed-precision training (Micikevicius et al. 2018) and ZeRO (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) made the per-parameter memory of that training explicit. Agent fine-tuning joined these threads once models emitted tool calls inside interleaved reasoning and action traces (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023), and trajectories generated by stronger models became training data for smaller ones (Chen et al. 2023; Zeng et al. 2023). What changes for agents is the environment: a trajectory has two authors, which is why masking, serialization, and on-policy coverage become engineering obligations rather than details.

For further reading, six works trace this lineage from behavioral cloning to modern trajectory post-training:

Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell’s DAgger paper (Ross et al. 2011) states both regret bounds of theorem 16.1 and the reduction to online learning behind them; it is the shortest route to seeing why where error is measured matters more than how small it is.
Rafailov and colleagues’ DPO paper (Rafailov et al. 2023) derives the preference loss from a reference-regularized objective, and reading the derivation shows exactly which assumptions a trajectory-span surrogate relaxes.
Ouyang and colleagues’ InstructGPT paper (Ouyang et al. 2022) documents a complete demonstration-then-preference pipeline, including the human evaluations that compared the model after each stage.
Hu and colleagues’ LoRA paper (Hu et al. 2021) motivates low-rank updates and reports experiments on which matrices to adapt and at what rank, the knobs this chapter says to set by evaluation.
Rajbhandari and colleagues’ ZeRO paper (Rajbhandari et al. 2020) itemizes training memory by owner and precision, the same inventory discipline notebook 16.5 applies to an adapter run.
Krell and colleagues’ packing paper (Krell et al. 2021) treats packing as an equivalence to prove rather than a throughput trick, the stance the chapter’s packed-versus-separate logit test takes.

Every given below is a hypothetical problem input chosen for round arithmetic, not a measurement of any system. Each problem asks for a calculation and the training or release decision it supports.

Per-invocation serialization under a token budget (Basic). The serving policy of the repair agent omits earlier generated text before each later invocation, so every turn of a trajectory becomes its own training example (section 16.3). Assume that the delivered prefix at each turn still grows by approximately \(\TurnAppendLength\) tokens despite the omitted generated text. Trajectories run \(\TurnHorizon=40\) turns, each turn adds about \(\TurnAppendLength=500\) tokens, the corpus holds 2,000 admitted trajectories, and the run may store at most 200 million training tokens.

Compute the stored tokens per trajectory under per-invocation serialization and under a single transcript, and the expansion factor between them.
Compute how many complete trajectories fit the budget under each serialization, and what fraction of the corpus the per-invocation run can use.
Name the serving-side change that would make a single transcript a faithful example, and state what the training pipeline must verify before relying on it.

Target count and dilution (Basic). A serialized repair example stores 2,000 prompt and schema tokens, 18,000 observation tokens, and 1,500 policy-response tokens. Of the response tokens, 300 belong to a refused proposal that curation retains as context only. The prompt and schema count includes the initial boundary; no preceding external seed is supplied. The example has no rationale and no padding.

Compute \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\) under equation 1, the selected share of the stored input, and the factor by which an unmasked token average would dilute each selected target’s coefficient.
A loader instead selects every policy-response token. Compute the fraction of the imitation weight that lands on the refused proposal, and state what behavior that weight trains.
A colleague expects masking to cut this example’s training compute by the dilution factor from part (a). Explain why the saving is far smaller, and identify the only work a loader can skip at masked positions.

Normalization and segmentation (Basic). A batch holds one long repair trajectory with 6,000 selected targets and 15 short file-lookup examples with 200 selected targets each.

Compute the long trajectory’s share of the batch objective under token averaging (equation 2) and under example averaging (equation 3).
Serialization instead splits the long trajectory into 20 per-invocation examples of 300 selected targets each, every example selecting only its own turn’s response. Recompute both shares.
The short lookups exercise a capability the release must retain. Choose a normalization and a segmentation, and state what the choice costs the long task’s influence on the update.

Packing and the cross-example work a kernel can skip (Intermediate). Ten independent examples have stored lengths of 16,384, 8,192, 6,144, 4,096, 4,096, 2,048, 2,048, 1,024, 1,024, and 512 tokens. Each buffer holds 16,384 positions.

Compute the occupancy of a padded batch that allocates the maximum length to every row.
Pack the examples by first-fit decreasing, placing each example, longest first, in the first buffer with room. Report the buffers, the packed occupancy, and the factor by which packing reduces allocated positions.
For the buffer holding the 8,192-, 6,144-, and 2,048-token examples, compute the fraction of causal score entries (the lower triangle, diagonal included) that block-diagonal attention (equation 4) sets to \(-\infty\). Explain what that fraction means for a variable-length attention kernel, and why the mask, not the skipped work, is the correctness requirement.

When on-policy labeling pays (Intermediate). Offline imitation of the repair agent reaches a disagreement rate of \(\ReferenceStateDisagreementRate=0.01\) on reference states over a horizon of \(\TurnHorizon=50\) decision steps. Three DAgger rounds would each collect 400 trajectories that run the full horizon and label all 50 visited states of each, and each label costs $0.05 to obtain and $0.25 to verify by a sandbox continuation. After aggregation, the retrained policy’s disagreement on its own states is \(\LearnerStateDisagreementRate=0.02\), and one deviation followed by reference recovery costs at most \(\DeviationDisadvantage=2\).

Compute both bounds of theorem 16.1, their ratio, and the reference-state error offline imitation would need to match the learner-state bound.
Compute the labeling cost of the three rounds, and the horizon at which the reference-state bound saturates at its cap.
A remediation step for the remediation agent changes live configuration with no adequate reversal, so one deviation there can spoil the rest of the task. Recompute the learner-state bound with \(\DeviationDisadvantage=\TurnHorizon\) at the same \(\LearnerStateDisagreementRate\), and state whether further labeling or a runtime mechanism should carry that step’s reliability.

Reading preference margins (Intermediate). Two checkpoints trained with equation 7 at \(\PreferenceScale=0.1\) are compared on one admitted repair pair. On the selected spans, the reference log-probability sums are \(-22\) for the preferred record and \(-24\) for the dispreferred one. Checkpoint A assigns \(-20\) and \(-25\); checkpoint B assigns \(-23\) and \(-30\). The sums exclude a shared 1,000-token prefix with identical conditioning, whose inclusion would add \(+0.5\) to each record’s score under either checkpoint.

Compute each checkpoint’s scores \(\PreferredReferenceRelativeScore\) and \(\DispreferredReferenceRelativeScore\), margin \(\PreferenceMargin\), pair loss, saturation factor \(\SigmoidFunction(-\PreferenceMargin)\), and full gradient coefficient \(\PreferenceScale\SigmoidFunction(-\PreferenceMargin)\).
Show that including the shared prefix leaves every quantity in part (a) unchanged.
A team proposes promoting checkpoint B because its pair loss is lower. Critique the proposal from the scores, and name the measurement that decides between the checkpoints.

Sizing an adapter run on a fixed memory budget (Intermediate). A hypothetical base model has 20 billion parameters. The run attaches rank-32 adapters to four matrices in each of 48 layers, and each adapted matrix has 6,144 input and 6,144 output coordinates. Use the chapter’s convention of 16 bytes of state per trainable parameter and 2 bytes per frozen parameter, with decimal GB. The accelerator offers 48 GB, of which 16 GB is reserved for activations and workspace.

Compute the adapter parameter count, its fraction of the base, and the parameter state of full fine-tuning and of the adapter run. Decide whether either fits the remaining budget.
Store the frozen base at 4 bits per parameter plus 0.5 bits per parameter of quantization metadata. Recompute the adapter run’s parameter state, decide whether it fits, and compute what doubling the rank would add.
Five agent roles each need their own adaptation. With every weight stored at 2 bytes per parameter, compare five full-weight copies with one shared base plus five adapters, and state what the shared base does not provide between roles.

Context distillation for the support agent (Advanced). The support agent runs short sessions under concurrency, so its binding constraint is per-turn input and response latency rather than the long observations that dominate the repair corpus. Each turn’s input carries a 3,000-token procedural checklist, a 1,500-token refund policy that changes weekly, and about 1,500 tokens of conversation and customer record. Sessions average four turns, and the deployment serves 2 million sessions per month. Input tokens cost $2 per million, and a cached prefix is billed at one tenth of that rate. Each redistillation, a training run plus the release evaluation, costs $15,000, and the checklist is revised once a month.

Using table 1, decide which of the three input segments may be distilled into the weights and which must stay in context.
Compute the monthly input tokens and spend that distilling the checklist removes, first with no prefix caching and then with the stable prefix always billed at the cached rate. Compute the net monthly saving after redistillation in each case, and the number of checklist revisions per month at which the uncached saving reaches zero.
Decide whether to distill under each serving configuration. State what must be measured, rather than inferred from the token reduction, before claiming a latency gain, and contrast the constraint that decides this case with the one that governs masking for the repair agent.

Critique a release proposal (Advanced). A team proposes promoting a fine-tuned repair policy on the following evidence. Its all-token training loss fell. On 500 closed-loop trials each, the baseline was accepted in 60 percent of trials at a mean attempt cost of $1.20, and the candidate in 66 percent at $1.50. On familiar interfaces, schema-following accuracy rose from 0.92 to 0.95. On a renamed-argument test set, the baseline scored an SFA of 0.90 with a PRE of 0.02, and the candidate an SFA of 0.81 with a PRE of 0.12.

Compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) for each policy in the per-attempt form of equation 1.2, and the largest mean attempt cost at which the candidate would match the baseline.
Using a normal approximation for independent trials, compute the standard error of the difference in acceptance rates and the difference measured in standard errors.
Interpret the pattern in SFA and PRE, and redesign the release gate. Name what the decision should be now, which measurements must be added or repeated, and which training change to test first.
Suppose the two arms in fact ran on the same 500 tasks. State what record the paired comparison of section 16.11 needs beyond the two acceptance rates, and explain how the count of discordant tasks could make the difference in part (b) more or less convincing than the independent-trials calculation suggests.



What’s Next: From admitted responses to reward-scored interactionWhen a task offers an outcome check but no demonstrated response for each decision, the adaptation framework must evolve beyond supervised imitation and static comparisons. Every update in this chapter needed a demonstrated or compared response, so the version conflict that trained_policy_v1 never saw could be taught only by labeling that state or injecting it. Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards starts from that checkpoint and lets the repair agent’s acceptance check score fresh attempts on the states the policy reaches by itself, turning each verdict into a weight update. The check then stops being only a release gate and becomes the objective. That shift raises questions this chapter’s objectives never posed: whether the reward resists the shortcuts optimization will find, how one terminal verdict assigns credit across many turns, how rollout records stay faithful to the policy that sampled them, and what the rollout and verifier fleet costs. Containment and closed-loop release evidence apply as before.

title: 16 Trajectory Fine-Tuning
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can training on a useful recovery record teach the model to repeat the mistake instead of the correction?
While prompt engineering and runtime guardrails guide an off-the-shelf model, fine-tuning modifies the neural network weights directly, embedding specialized decision policies and tool calling conventions into model parameters. However, training on multi-turn trajectories requires strict separation between agent proposals and external environment observations, so that imitation loss applies only to selected policy responses while environment feedback remains conditioning context. Naive fine-tuning can teach a policy to fabricate its own tool results or overfit to static workspace layouts, degrading general reasoning and error recovery. Systems engineering governs how datasets are partitioned, how loss masks are applied, and how updated checkpoints are validated against regression suites before deployment. An update is worth releasing only when closed-loop task acceptance improves under the same runtime that still bounds every proposal the model makes, however far its training loss has fallen.

Learning Objectives

Assign agent behavior to weights, context, or runtime, and decide when a failure warrants a weight change
Construct model inputs that preserve intended conditioning and price per-invocation serialization in training tokens
Map admitted response spans to causal token targets, observation masks, and termination policy
Compare loss weighting and construct batches without unintended cross-example dependencies
Calculate imitation regret bounds on reference and learner states to decide when on-policy labeling pays
Calculate preference margins and gradient weights, and distinguish what a comparison measures from task acceptance
Select behavior sources and parameter artifacts using explicit resource and version accounting
Evaluate a versioned policy for release on closed-loop acceptance, cost per accepted task, and schema transfer, while preserving runtime enforcement

title: 16 Trajectory Fine-Tuning
text:
Fine-tuning reshapes each model call but leaves every exposure to the runtime.
Consider a recovery demonstration admitted by the curation pipeline for the repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) into repair_demonstrations_v1. During the recorded session, the agent generated a malformed edit proposal that the runtime validator refused prior to tool dispatch. In response to the failure notification, the model inspected the tool schema, generated a corrected edit, and produced candidate patch ws_r20. From this multi-turn trajectory, the target-selection policy recovery_targets_v1 marks three assistant turns as supervised targets: the schema inspection request (e3), the corrected edit (e4), and the scoped final summary (e6). The malformed proposal (e2) and the runtime’s refusal remain in the input history as conditioning context. The member that entered the corpus is the redacted view trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, and the corpus manifest binds it to those role assignments, its lineage, and its split membership.
The raw event log of an admitted record is not yet in a form a training loop can safely ingest, because it interleaves model generations, runtime observations, and tool responses in the order they occurred. If a data loader treats every assistant message as a supervised target, it computes loss on the malformed edit proposal alongside the correction and reinforces the initial mistake. If the training pipeline computes loss across all sequence tokens indiscriminately, the model spends parameter capacity predicting deterministic environment replies, such as compiler diagnostics or directory listings, that it will never emit during inference. Finally, if the batching pipeline packs multiple trajectories into a shared context window without attention masking, self-attention heads attend across sample boundaries and leak private workspace contents into unrelated training examples. Standard cross-entropy loss fails silently under each of these mistakes. The training loss falls steadily as the optimizer fits the data, hiding the corrupted behavior from offline metrics. While curation contracts decide which actions show desirable behavior and evaluation contracts measure the deployed agent, neither specifies how to turn a multi-turn execution trace into isolated, causal gradient updates.
The path from an admitted record to an evaluated policy update begins with a question curation leaves open, namely which parts of the repair behavior belong in weights at all (section 16.2). The answer fixes what the data pipeline must protect. Serialization reconstructs each model input exactly as the agent received it (section 16.3), loss masking places the gradient on the selected responses and nowhere else (section 16.4), and batching shares buffers without letting examples read one another or skew one another’s weight (section 16.5). Masking and batching guard directly against those three silent failures, and serialization guards the premise both rely on, that each prefix is the one the model actually saw.
A faithful loader still trains on recorded prefixes, and the deployed policy acts on prefixes its own choices produce. Exposure bias prices that gap over the horizon and decides when labeling the learner’s own states pays (section 16.6), and schema robustness asks the same question of the tool interfaces the policy is shown (section 16.7). The remaining sections vary the update itself along three independent choices. The first is the objective, where preference optimization contrasts valid alternatives that imitation cannot rank (section 16.8). The second is the behavior source, where distillation moves a costlier configuration’s behavior into a cheaper one (section 16.9). The last is the parameter artifact, where adapters change what a run must store (section 16.10). Closed-loop evaluation decides whether any of them earned a release (section 16.11), and a training manifest for the repair policy assembles the whole chain (section 16.12).

title: 16 Trajectory Fine-Tuning
text:
Before turning an admitted record such as trace_r19_01_redacted_v1 into a weight update, engineers must decide whether the failure it repaired belongs in the model’s parameters at all. Fine-tuning a model to work around a missing prompt instruction or a broken tool schema bakes a temporary workaround into billions of weights, only for the behavior to break again the next time the interface changes. Modifying model weights is an expensive, high-blast-radius change reserved for behavioral failures that survive cheaper fixes. The intervention ladder orders changes by cost and reversibility, so engineers test prompt, schema, and runtime fixes before spending compute on parameter updates, while diagnostic evidence can justify a direct weight update when the policy itself is at fault. Verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) requires curation to tie recorded evidence to a declared learning use and separate admissible targets from contextual or rejected actions. While this ordering is the default because of cost and blast radius, fine-tuning also pays when moving stable procedural guidance into the weights costs less than resending a long instructional prefix on every turn (section 16.9).


↩︎ The intervention ladder, which orders context, schema, runtime, and parameter interventions by cost and reversibility, is established in The intervention ladder.
Once diagnostic evidence justifies a parameter update, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) adjusts trainable model parameters to maximize the conditional likelihood of selected target tokens given their causal prefix context. When processing trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, the training loop must follow the recovery sequence defined in recovery_targets_v1 rather than computing loss over every recorded token. The model must see the historical context and tool outputs that justify a chosen action, yet the data pipeline must exclude later steps that would reveal future observations or solutions ahead of time. Trajectory fine-tuning therefore inherits two data contracts: a target-selection contract that designates which tokens contribute to the loss gradient, and a conditioning contract that governs what causal history the model sees when generating those tokens.
The two contracts separate learning improved behavior from overfitting an idiosyncratic run. In an error-recovery trajectory, the behavioral goal is teaching the model to inspect an updated schema after a refusal, issue a properly formed corrective call, and interpret what the runtime verification check establishes. Memorizing the file paths of a specific test fixture or predicting hard-coded test outputs lowers training loss without teaching generalizable recovery skills. Whether the updated policy transfers these habits to unfamiliar environments and new tasks is what section 16.11 measures, and keeping the update generalizable starts with deciding which parts of agent behavior live in weights versus the prompt and runtime.


If a fine-tuned repair agent memorizes an API signature in its parameters instead of reading the prompt, a routine tool-interface change, such as adding a required parameter or revoking a permission, immediately breaks the deployed policy. Every response the agent generates combines the model’s static weights with the dynamic context window assembled for that call, and fine-tuning updates only the weights. Engineers therefore divide agent behavior across three architectural homes, summarized in table 1:

Procedure is behavior that stays stable across tasks and changes slowly, such as inspecting diagnostic output before modifying source code or checking unresolved issues before reporting completion. Procedure is what model weights can reliably absorb.
Contracts are the dynamic operational facts that vary across deployments, user sessions, and individual turns, such as API tool definitions, schema requirements, environment parameters, and granted permissions. Contracts belong in the prompt context; a model that memorized an earlier schema will keep emitting obsolete arguments when an interface changes.
Enforcement covers the invariants that must hold even when the model proposes an invalid or adversarial action, such as schema validation, authorization checks, sandbox containment, and execution timeouts. Enforcement stays in the deterministic runtime harness under invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)).




Table 1: Responsibilities of Weights, Context, and Runtime: Weights hold procedure, context holds the current contract, and the runtime enforces that contract whatever the model proposes.










Home
Intended responsibility
Consequence for fine-tuning




Weights
Learned procedures and response tendencies, including tool selection and recovery behavior
Update the proposal distribution, then measure whether the changed behavior helps under the declared task conditions


Context
Current task facts, tool schemas, observations, and represented scope
Supply the information the policy needs now; do not rely on memorized versions as the authority for current facts or permissions


Runtime
Validation, authorization, containment, resource controls, and evidence collection
Preserve enforcement independently of the learned policy; a model’s predicted result is not an observed external effect






Relying on parameters to store interface contracts makes a deployment brittle, because a revoked permission stays revoked regardless of how often the action appeared in past training demonstrations. Fine-tuning cannot replace dynamic contracts; what it can teach is the habit of reading and following whichever contract the context window supplies.
This boundary disproves the view that fine-tuning only moves the prompt into the weights. Only the procedural parts of a prompt (structured reasoning guidelines, diagnostic checklists, or few-shot error-recovery examples) belong in the parameters, where they save token overhead on every turn (section 16.9). The contractual parts must stay in the prompt context, because omitting them forces the model to guess the current execution environment. The deterministic checks that enforce authorization and boundary invariants cannot live in either prompts or weights, because a probability distribution over tokens cannot guarantee an invariant.
Fine-tuning changes the policy’s proposal distribution: which tools it requests, how thoroughly it inspects diagnostic evidence, and which execution paths it tries. Those shifts change task success rates, end-to-end latency, and token use, yet every proposed action still runs inside the horizons, state transitions, and authority boundaries enforced by the runtime harness. This separation is the proposal boundary of The Model Call Boundary. Training reshapes what the policy proposes, while the runtime decides which actions may execute, and that boundary governs every adaptation choice that follows.



Deciding that a recovery habit belongs in the weights still leaves a team to choose whether to imitate single corrections or rank competing repairs, whether to train on recorded logs or collect fresh trajectories, and whether to ship a full checkpoint copy or a lightweight adapter. Treating “fine-tuning” as a single knob obscures which decision is responsible when an update overfits or exceeds its memory budget, so the pipeline separates adaptation along three independent axes:

Training Objective: The loss function that defines the learning signal. Supervised imitation maximizes the likelihood of curated target demonstrations, whereas preference methods such as direct preference optimization (section 16.8) adjust weights by contrasting preferred trajectories against dispreferred alternatives under an explicit ranking rule.
Behavior Source: Where the demonstrations and conditioning inputs come from. Traces may be collected from instrumented production runs and filtered by offline verification, generated by a teacher configuration with privileged context or a larger search budget (section 16.9), labeled on the states the learner itself reaches, or constructed by injecting faults the recordings never contained (section 16.6.2).
Parameter Artifact: Which weights the run updates and stores. Teams can update all model parameters directly or train compact adapter matrices, such as low-rank adaptation (LoRA) modules, that attach to a frozen base checkpoint (section 16.10).

Because these three choices are independent, they combine freely; a deployment can, for example, train a low-rank adapter with a preference objective on synthetic teacher demonstrations. Whichever combination a team chooses, the run still trains on trajectory records converted into model inputs, so the first pipeline step is reconstructing the input prefix and conditioning window for each selected response.

title: 16 Trajectory Fine-Tuning
text:
In the admitted repair demonstration trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, the corrected edit (e4) makes sense only as a response to the malformed proposal (e2), the runtime refusal, and the schema inspection (e3) that preceded it. A training loader that strips out the refusal changes the problem the subsequent correction answered, and a loader that places the later passing test check (e5) before the edit leaks future evidence that the model did not have when proposing the patch. While curation selects which model completions to reinforce, serialization must reconstruct the exact prompt and observation history that prompted them, including any runtime redactions (such as synthetic placeholders substituted for private file paths), so the training example matches the context the model actually saw.


Runtime event logs record state transitions across the harness, but an event log alone does not show what was inside the model’s context window at a given call. System prompts change, tool schemas update between versions, and earlier messages are often summarized or truncated to fit token budgets. To reconstruct each call’s input faithfully, the training pipeline reads the delivered-input manifests, which record the exact messages, tool definitions, summaries, and bounded observations sent to the model along with their schema versions.


↩︎ The delivered-input manifest that records the exact payload sent to the model, rather than mutable paths or references, is established in The log event schema.
When an example requires historical fidelity, the loader serializes the selected invocation directly from its delivered-input manifest, preserving partial buffers, truncated outputs, and execution errors rather than substituting a cleaner result obtained later in the run. When a pipeline instead transforms an example deliberately, such as shortening prompts for context distillation (section 16.9), it applies the reviewed transformation to both the prompt and the paired response, keeps the parent trace reference, and rechecks schema compatibility. Table 2 shows how the curated responses in the running repair demonstration map to their conditioning evidence; in the rendered training example, each row also carries the system instructions and active tool definitions delivered at that turn.



Table 2: Inputs and Selected Responses in the Repair Demonstration: Each row pairs a reviewed response with evidence available to condition it.










Selected response
Relevant conditioning evidence
Response content selected by curation




e3
Earlier delivered task context and the malformed e2 proposal with its pre-dispatch refusal
Request to inspect the available schema


e4
The corresponding returned schema and the retained context supporting the edit
Corrected edit with its version condition


e6
The candidate-specific check summary delivered at e5 and retained evidence for the report’s scope
Final report of the supported result and limitations






The refusal at e2 shows that runtime validation caught the malformed proposal before dispatch, so no tool ran on the host. Because the check summary at e5 arrived only after the agent issued the corrected edit, it can condition the final report at e6 but cannot appear in the prefix for e4. Selecting the schema request at e3 likewise trains the model’s query tokens while leaving the returned schema as an external observation, so that loss masking in the next stage can separate model decisions from environment replies.



Once the delivered messages for e3, e4, and e6 are reconstructed, the loader must turn those structured message objects (system instructions, user prompts, assistant reasoning, tool calls, and environment returns) into the exact token sequence the model expects at serving time. Chat templates differ across model families, and even checkpoints from the same base model often format tool schemas, parallel calls, or message boundaries differently. Rendering a trajectory with delimiters that do not match the serving parser teaches the policy a syntax that production will reject. A serialized dataset artifact therefore records the tokenizer version, template configuration, tool-formatting schema, and response-boundary policy alongside the token arrays, because the message sequence and its rendering configuration together form the model input.
In schematic form, a multi-turn tool-calling example looks like the sequence below. The delimiter strings are illustrative placeholders, since each model family defines its own special tokens. The system segment gives the task contract and tool definitions. The assistant segment emits a reasoning trace followed by two parallel tool calls with unique identifiers. Each tool segment returns an observation bound to its call identifier.
<|system|> task contract; schemas for read_file(target_uri), run_tests(target) <|end|>
<|user|> Fix the connection-pool leak in src/pool.py <|end|>
<|assistant|> <|reasoning|> Reproduce the failure, then read the module. <|end_reasoning|>
  <|call id=c1|> {"name": "read_file", "arguments": {"target_uri": "src/pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
  <|call id=c2|> {"name": "run_tests", "arguments": {"target": "tests/test_pool.py"}} <|end_call|>
<|end_turn|>
<|tool id=c2|> FAILED test_release: pool exhausted <|end|>
<|tool id=c1|> ...file contents... <|end|>
<|assistant|> ...
In this sequence, c2 finishes before c1, and because the runtime delivers observations in arrival order, the listing places the c2 reply first to match the prompt the model actually received on its next turn. The call identifiers keep each observation bound to its original call regardless of arrival order. Re-sorting the replies into call order (c1, then c2) for tidiness would invent a prompt the model never saw, and reordering calls whose arguments or observations depend on one another changes the causal problem into a synthetic transformation that needs its own validation. The <|end_turn|> token marks where the policy handed control back to the runtime loop, while all tokens between <|tool|> and <|end|> are external observations.
The training pipeline packages this rendered dataset as serialization_v1, whose manifest pairs the admitted execution records with the active rendering configuration and maps every selected response span to its token offsets. Because tokenization, template formatting, and string redaction can shift token boundaries (for example, when leading whitespace merges into an adjacent special token), the pipeline re-verifies all token offsets against the rendered token array and decodes completed examples to check task prompts, tool bindings, span boundaries, and end-of-sequence markers. If an example fails boundary alignment or drops content, the pipeline discards the record rather than patching it with synthetic filler.
Role delimiters define protocol syntax, but they carry no runtime authority: if a model emits text that mimics a <|tool|> delimiter, that text is still model output under the tokenizer’s grammar, and the serialization pipeline never promotes unverified generations into environment observations. Once the template fixes how each turn is rendered, the pipeline still has to decide whether a multi-turn trajectory can be stored as a single rendered sequence or must be split into separate per-invocation examples.


↩︎ The rule that model output is a proposal carrying no authority until the runtime validates it is established in The Model Call Boundary.



Because the repair agent’s runtime compacts history once the working set crosses its watermark, a turn delivered after compaction saw a summary digest rather than the raw earlier turns that a single concatenated transcript would place before it. A single concatenated transcript is a faithful training example only when the serving runtime appends every turn without pruning earlier steps, compacting intermediate context, or dropping reasoning scratchpads to save KV-cache memory. Whenever serving prunes or compacts history between steps so that later causal prefixes no longer match a growing transcript, the loader must serialize each invocation as its own training example containing that call’s exact delivered prefix.


↩︎ Watermark-triggered compaction, which replaces earlier turns with a digest between invocations, is established in Context Compaction.
Serializing each call separately carries the same triangular token cost that already priced an append-only trajectory at serving time (equation 2.9), now paid in stored training tokens. If a trajectory spans \(\TurnHorizon\) turns and each turn adds roughly \(\TurnAppendLength\) tokens, the example for turn \(\TurnIndex\) spans about \(\TurnIndex\,\TurnAppendLength\) tokens. Serializing all \(\TurnHorizon\) invocations separately stores \(\TurnAppendLength\,\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon+1)/2\) tokens, compared with \(\TurnHorizon\,\TurnAppendLength\) tokens for a single transcript. That is an expansion factor of \((\TurnHorizon+1)/2\), which over a stipulated 30-turn horizon multiplies the stored token volume by 15.5×. An agent’s history-retention policy therefore directly governs training storage and compute. The same fidelity rule applies to the model’s own reasoning text. If serving drops an earlier turn’s rationale before the next call, the reconstructed prefix for that call omits it too. Whether retained rationale is trained as a target or kept as context is a separate masking choice (section 16.4.4).
With serialization_v1 assembled, the pipeline has the tokenized sequences, their conditioning prefixes, and the response spans selected during curation. The next step is deciding which token positions contribute to the training loss, because computing cross-entropy over an entire multi-turn sequence would penalize the model for failing to predict tool outputs and user messages.

title: 16 Trajectory Fine-Tuning
text:
In serialization_v1, the token array for the repair trajectory still contains the prompt, the malformed proposal e2, the runtime refusal, the returned schema, and the check summary e5 alongside the selected responses e3, e4, and e6. A loader that selects every assistant token trains the model on the malformed proposal e2 alongside its correction e4, undoing curation, while a loader that computes loss across all tokens trains the policy to predict environment replies. Serialization turns the interaction into tokens; the loss mask decides which of those tokens drive gradient updates.


Let \(\SerializedTrainingExample=(\SequenceToken_1,\ldots,\SequenceToken_{\SequenceLength})\) be one serialized example, with an initial context or boundary token at \(\SequenceToken_1\), and let \(\EligibleTargetPositionSet\subseteq\{2,\ldots,\SequenceLength\}\) contain the policy-token positions selected for imitation. Which positions belong to \(\EligibleTargetPositionSet\) depends on the admitted response spans and the training objective rather than token authorship alone. With the binary mask \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=\IndicatorFunction\{\TokenIndex\in\EligibleTargetPositionSet\}\) and \(\PositionLossMask_1=0\), the mean masked cross-entropy for an example with at least one selected target is
\[\MaskedFinetuningLoss(\ModelParameters)=-\frac{1}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}\log\Policy(\SequenceToken_t\mid \TokenPrefix),\qquad \ActiveTargetTokenCount=\sum_{t=2}^{\SequenceLength}\PositionLossMask_{t}>0. \tag{1}\]
Each selected token is predicted from the recorded prefix \(\TokenPrefix\), which includes earlier actions, observations, and admitted mistakes, rather than from fresh rollouts sampled during training. This regime is teacher forcing1 (Williams and Zipser 1989), and it lets recovery prefixes that contain earlier failures serve as conditioning context whenever the trajectory satisfies the curation contract.
1 Teacher Forcing: Williams and Zipser (1989) named the technique for recurrent networks, feeding the recorded target back as the next input instead of the network’s own output. Because every prefix is recorded rather than generated, a causal model computes all of an example’s next-token predictions in one parallel forward pass, which is why imitating a trajectory costs one pass per example rather than one sampled rollout per decision.
Williams, Ronald J., and David Zipser. 1989. “A Learning Algorithm for Continually Running Fully Recurrent Neural Networks.” Neural Computation 1 (2): 270–80. https://doi.org/10.1162/neco.1989.1.2.270.
In the running repair trajectory, target_mask_v1 maps the reviewed response spans onto the token array of serialization_v1, separating target positions from conditioning context (table 3). Because changing a tokenizer vocabulary, chat template, or text transformation can shift token boundaries, the pipeline regenerates and checks masks against the final serialized tokens rather than copying offsets from an earlier stage.



Table 3: Loss Masking by Token Segment: The loss mask specifies which serialized tokens generate gradient updates. It acts as an optimization filter rather than an attention barrier or provenance record.










Token segment
Target policy for this imitation objective
What remains as conditioning input




Prompt and supplied tool contracts
\(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\)
The actual task, current interfaces, and supplied constraints


Selected policy response
\(\PositionLossMask_{t}=1\) on its admitted target positions
Earlier tokens of the response and its available prefix


Unselected policy response, including the refused proposal
\(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\)
History needed to interpret a selected correction

\(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\)
Delivered results, errors, and evidence available before the next response


Optional authorized rationale

Retained rationale remains visible whether or not it is selected


Termination boundary

When an example has no selected targets (\(\ActiveTargetTokenCount=0\)), the loss in equation 1 is undefined, so the loader must drop the example or route it to a declared fallback rather than counting it as a completed demonstration. How examples of different lengths are weighted against one another inside a batch is a separate choice developed in section 16.5.

Definition 16.1: Observation loss masking
Observation loss masking excludes supplied observations from the direct token-prediction loss while retaining the permitted observation context needed to train selected policy responses.

Significance: Focuses the optimization objective on the policy’s conditional distribution \(\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})\), so verbose environment output cannot dilute the gradient on policy actions regardless of how much context observations occupy (notebook 16.1 quantifies this dilution).
Distinction: Masked tokens stay in the input context and participate in self-attention; only their next-token loss terms are zeroed. Policy authorship alone does not make a token a target, because refused attempts or unsafe actions are also masked even when emitted in the assistant role.
Common pitfall: Selecting an entire multi-turn tool exchange only because the tool call succeeded, which trains the model to predict external environment responses.



A deployed agent trajectory interleaves two different generators: the agent policy and the external environment. Training without observation masking forces one set of weights to fit both distributions at once:

The agent policy \(\Policy(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t})\), which maps prior observations and instructions to tool calls or answers.
An environment dynamics model \(\EnvironmentTransitionDistribution(\TrajectoryState_{t+1}\mid \TrajectoryState_{t}, \TrajectoryAction_{t})\), which predicts the outputs returned by shells, databases, or remote APIs.

Because real tools run during deployment and return actual outputs, spending model capacity to predict environment returns is wasted work, and supervising the environment distribution causes two concrete failures:

Loss dilution: Under token-averaged cross-entropy, unmasking expands the denominator from \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\) to all \(\SequenceLength-1\) causal prediction terms (every stored position after the initial boundary). Each decision token’s gradient weight shrinks by the ratio of selected targets to predicted positions (computed in notebook 16.1), while the rest of the loss budget goes to file paths, stack traces, compiler dumps, and JSON payloads. Repetitive boilerplate pulls the average loss down, while novel stack traces or file contents dominate the gradient; in either case, the average stops measuring the policy.
Role confusion: When trained to predict the tokens that follow a tool call, the policy learns that tool outputs continue the same autoregressive stream. At serving time, it can keep generating past its own tool call and write a fabricated tool result instead of emitting the stop token that hands control back to the runtime. Because the runtime rejects unauthenticated observations (section 16.3), those fabricated tokens are discarded, wasting output budget and stalling the turn.

The full repair record selects three responses (e3, e4, and e6). In the simplified view of figure 1, which omits the schema request e3 and its returned schema, only two of the seven segments shown (the corrected tool call and the final response) carry \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=1\) and receive direct imitation loss. The prompt, task statement, refused proposal, rejection message, and tool result carry \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\) and stay as conditioning context, where gradients from later selected targets still update the weights that encode them.






Figure 1: Observation Loss Masking: The mask over a simplified view of the serialized repair example that omits the schema request (selected) and its returned schema (context). Of the segments shown, only the corrected tool call and the final response carry \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=1\) and receive a direct loss term. The prompt, task, refused proposal, rejection message, and tool result carry \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\), yet every one of them is still read through attention, so gradients from later selected targets update the parameters that encode it. Selecting only policy responses fits the policy’s conditional distribution; unmasking the observations would also ask the same weights to fit the environment’s.



Observation masking prevents both loss dilution and role confusion at the objective level, while closed-loop trials verify that the trained model stops at tool boundaries. Realizing that masked objective in code requires aligning every mask bit \(\PositionLossMask_{t}\) with the exact prediction step that generates token \(\SequenceToken_t\).



An off-by-one shift between input tokens and target masks silently corrupts every tool boundary in a corpus, masking the first token of each selected response while training the policy to predict the first token of the following tool observation. Many training frameworks shift labels by one position inside their own loss function, so shifting them once in the loader and a second time in the loss misaligns every target mask across the dataset. In a causal autoregressive model,2 the hidden state at input position \(\TokenIndex-1\) produces the logits that predict token \(\SequenceToken_t\), so the loader must pair the logits at \(\TokenIndex-1\) with target label \(\SequenceToken_t\) and target mask \(\PositionLossMask_{t}\) rather than with the mask of input token \(\SequenceToken_{t-1}\) (table 4). Checking the aligned labels and masks on a short synthetic example before launching a run catches this bug immediately.
2 Causal Self-Attention: Causal masking in Transformer decoders restricts each token from attending to subsequent positions (Vaswani et al. 2017). The same triangular structure enforces the label shift: the network predicts \(\SequenceToken_t\) using only the representation formed at \(\TokenIndex-1\).
Vaswani, Ashish, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. 2017. “Attention Is All You Need.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30: 5998–6008.



Table 4: The Causal Label Shift at a Tool Boundary: Target selection applies to the predicted token rather than the input token driving the hidden state. Exact boundary encodings depend on the serialized chat template.










Logits computed from a prefix ending at…
Next-token label
Target mask




The final supplied prompt token
First token of a selected policy response
\(1\)


The final content token of that selected response
Its authentic policy-generated end token
\(1\)


The end token before a delivered tool observation
First token of that observation
\(0\)






Let \(\VocabularyTokenLogit_{t-1,\VocabularyToken}\) denote the logit for vocabulary token \(\VocabularyToken\) produced from \(\TokenPrefix\), using an ordinary softmax and no label smoothing. Differentiating equation 1 gives
\[\frac{\partial\MaskedFinetuningLoss}{\partial \VocabularyTokenLogit_{t-1,\VocabularyToken}}=\frac{\PositionLossMask_{t}}{\ActiveTargetTokenCount}\left(\Policy(\VocabularyToken\mid \TokenPrefix)-\IndicatorFunction\{\VocabularyToken=\SequenceToken_t\}\right).\]
When \(\PositionLossMask_{t}=0\), the prediction at position \(\TokenIndex-1\) contributes zero direct gradient, yet token \(\SequenceToken_t\) still shapes later representations through causal self-attention, so gradients from later active targets update the weights that read it. The model conditions on tool outputs without spending capacity trying to generate them, which carries verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) down to individual token positions.






Observations fill 77.1 percent of the input; the loss sits on 4.9 percent.
Because every masked observation token still passes through self-attention, zeroing its loss term removes almost none of the forward-pass compute. The number of selected positions \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\) sets the denominator of the loss and the gradient weight on each target token, whereas the full stored sequence length \(\SequenceLength\) sets the attention and projection FLOPs. Comparing \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\) against the \(\SequenceLength-1\) causal prediction terms gives the dilution factor an unmasked loss would suffer, while \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount/\SequenceLength\) gives the fraction of stored positions that carry a target. Notebook 16.1 computes both quantities under two target policies on the same serialized trajectory.

Napkin Math 16.1: Stored tokens and selected targetsProblem: A hypothetical serialized example has the segment counts in table 5. Its curation record excludes some policy-response positions from imitation while retaining them as context. If the optional rationale is either selected or kept as context only, how many positions receive direct loss, what fraction of the stored input do they occupy, and by how much would an unmasked loss dilute each of them?

Variables: Exactly 160 of the other-policy-response positions belong to the refused proposal and stay context; every other response position is selected. The rationale is reviewed for either target policy, both policies see the same input, the initial position belongs to the prompt, and there is no padding.
Math: The disjoint segments sum to 16,384 stored tokens, of which observations occupy 77.1 percent. Removing the refused positions leaves 960 \(-\) 160 \(=\) 800 selected response targets, and selecting the rationale adds 1,400 more. The first stored boundary has no preceding-position prediction, so an unmasked causal average divides by 16,383 prediction terms instead of \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\). Each selected target’s coefficient therefore shrinks by 16,383/800, a factor of 20.5× (7.4× when the rationale is selected). Under each target policy, table 6 sets \(\ActiveTargetTokenCount\) against the stored input it is drawn from.



Table 6: Two Target Policies on One Input: Excluding a segment from the objective does not shorten the conditioning sequence.

Result: Both masks place the whole loss on a small minority of stored positions and leave the context identical; they differ only in whether the rationale is a target.
Systems insight: Because the dilution factor scales inversely with the selected fraction of predicted positions, it expands rapidly as environment interactions accumulate. Doubling the observation volume while holding response lengths constant escalates dilution from 20.5× to 36.3×. Consequently, observation masking becomes increasingly essential as agents tackle deep, tool-intensive reasoning traces. Masking, however, yields negligible reductions in FLOPs: every masked token must still pass through causal attention layers to form context for subsequent predictions. Only the final language model head projection and cross-entropy loss computation can be bypassed at masked positions.


Recorded repair trajectories show that the hypothetical inventory’s proportions are realistic. Figure 2 splits the transcripts of five published agent configurations on the same repository-repair tasks (Jimenez et al. 2024) by the role that produced each message.














Figure 2: Observations Dominate Recorded Trajectories: Share of transcript characters by the role that produced them, pooled over every run of each configuration and counting each message once. Prompt covers the system message, demonstrations, and task statement; observations are tool and environment output; model output is everything the model generated, the only region from which training targets can be selected. Characters stand in for tokens because the configurations use different tokenizers. Trajectories from Jimenez et al. (2024) submissions.


Jimenez, Carlos E., John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan. 2024. “SWE-Bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).


Across the 5 configurations and 2,100 runs, observations make up 56 to 72 percent of the transcript, and model output only 12 to 31 percent. These shares count each message once. Serializing one example per invocation repeats the growing prefix in every example, so the observation share of the stored training input is larger still, approaching the inventory’s proportion. The mask is therefore not a refinement applied to a few verbose tool calls; in recorded repair work it decides the fate of most of the sequence.



Even within the model-generated share of a trajectory, masking out a chain-of-thought scratchpad during training while expecting the deployed policy to act without any scratchpad at serving time trains the model on conditioning context it will not have in production. When a dataset includes intermediate reasoning traces or tool-use plans alongside tool calls, the loader must therefore choose among three masking regimes (table 7) that match how the model will be served. Supervising the rationale trains the model to generate its own reasoning before invoking tools. Retaining the rationale under a loss mask treats the reasoning as supplied conditioning context, training the model to act on plans provided by an external orchestrator or user. Stripping the rationale entirely changes the conditional distribution so the policy acts from context alone.
Formally, given context prefix \(\TurnContext_{t}\), rationale tokens \(\RationaleTokens\), and action tokens \(\ResponseActionTokens=(\ResponseActionTokens_1,\ldots,\ResponseActionTokens_n)\), response-only supervision fits the conditional distribution \(\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \RationaleTokens, \ActionTokenPrefix)\). If the production serving environment does not supply \(\RationaleTokens\), the deployed model instead evaluates \(\Policy(\ResponseActionTokens_j\mid \TurnContext_{t}, \ActionTokenPrefix)\). Because those are distinct conditional distributions, omitting rationale at serving time is a distillation step that must be evaluated directly against the unconditioned target.



Table 7: Rationale Treatment Changes Targets or Inputs: The choice requires a compatible serving protocol and evaluation, not a universal model-size threshold.










Treatment
Input and direct targets
Serving question to evaluate




Select reviewed rationale
Retain \([\TurnContext_{t},\RationaleTokens,\ResponseActionTokens]\); selected \(\RationaleTokens\) and \(\ResponseActionTokens\) positions receive loss
Does generated rationale improve the declared outcomes enough to justify its output and latency cost?

Retain \([\TurnContext_{t},\RationaleTokens,\ResponseActionTokens]\); only selected \(\ResponseActionTokens\) positions receive loss
How will appropriate rationale become available, and how do errors in it affect the response?
