The paired comparison, diagnostic experiment, and sequential monitor answer different questions and cannot substitute for one another. A coherent release record brings them together with their fixtures, limits, and residual obligations so that the resulting decision can be inspected.

title: 14 Operating Agents
text:
In a paired evaluation cohort, candidate_v2 accepted more tasks than baseline_v1, while an isolated diagnostic probe pointed toward an effective observation-interface repair. Taken on their own, these indicators seem encouraging, but neither outcome satisfies a sound engineering release gate. The two results also concern different configurations. The 150-pair cohort compared candidate_v2 as submitted, and the worked trial of pool_repair_01 that produced ws_r19 sits outside that cohort. The interface repair changes candidate_v2’s observation adapter, so the configuration it would produce is a revision that needs its own paired evaluation; the probe is evidence about the defect, not about the revision’s cohort performance. Evaluating an agentic system requires an accountable evidence trail. Before routing production traffic to a new candidate, engineers determine which claims have verified empirical support, which operational obligations remain unresolved, and what follow-up experiment the data actually justifies.


When an individual trial verdict, a paired cohort comparison, and a diagnostic probe sit in separate reports without their provenance, scope, and operational boundaries attached, a positive result on the localized probe can easily be mistaken for missing regression checks or fleet-wide superiority evidence. A structured decision record prevents those disparate experimental results from being conflated by bringing the worked individual trial, the paired cohort comparison, and the diagnostic interface experiment together in one place (table 8). Rather than duplicating bulky workspace snapshots, the record links directly to immutable, content-addressed artifacts and explicitly logs when trace payloads, token charges, or downstream verdicts remain unavailable.



Table 8: An integrated evaluation record: Each field identifies what the evidence supports and which decision it constrains. Missing or pending evidence remains visible rather than becoming an implicit pass.










Evidence record field
Entry or required reference
Decision consequence




Task, fixture, and criteria
pool_repair_01, pool_fixture_v1, repair_accept_v1; record permitted effects, required checks, budgets, and residual-duty conditions
The verdict concerns this declared task contract, not unrestricted correctness.


Trial and artifact identity
The worked trial, configuration candidate_v2, artifact ws_r19; preserve grader and check versions
Do not confuse a trial, system configuration, source artifact, or historical operation.


Individual trial verdict
Targeted check passed; required regression evidence remains pending in An Interim Repair Evaluation Record
Do not accept the trial merely because one check passed. Preserve other established failures or unknowns independently.


Paired comparison
The complete task-pair record and candidate-minus-baseline interval from Statistical Evaluation Rigor, with its prespecified degradation margin
The worked comparison does not establish noninferiority; favorable marginal counts do not override that result.


Resources and unresolved duties
Account for all started generation, grading, tools, and declared finalization; retain actual charges and outstanding liability separately
A pending final bill is not zero cost. Whether sufficient bounded evidence satisfies a criterion follows the stated contract.


Capture and privacy
Retained trace boundaries, payload availability, sampling probabilities, delayed verdicts, drops, and authorized evidence access
Diagnostic completeness and population representativeness require evidence; redacted bytes cannot be claimed available for exact replay.


Diagnosis and regression
The controlled observation-interface experiment and its fixture-specific regression tests
Support a scoped intervention hypothesis without labeling the model or interface the sole possible cause. Its repeated fixture runs are not additional independent tasks in the paired cohort.


Release disposition
Retain the baseline; no live promotion of this candidate on the current evidence
Further work needs a stated question and planned evidence collection, not an automatic increase in traffic.









Promoting candidate_v2 on the current evidence would ship a configuration whose trial-level regression checks are unfinished, whose interface repair has been tested on only one saved prefix, and whose paired comparison interval still crosses the degradation threshold. The decision record leaves those three engineering obligations open, each at a different layer of the evaluation stack.

Trial-level verification: The targeted repair in ws_r19 passed its immediate assertion, but its full regression suite and final resource accounting remain pending. Engineers cannot mark an individual trial successful while side effects and outstanding token bills remain unquantified.
Component-level diagnosis: The observation-interface modification proved effective on continuations from one saved prefix of pool_repair_01, but success from a single prefix does not demonstrate generalized capability. Validating the interface repair requires testing across diverse environments and workloads.
Cohort-level release gate: The paired comparison across the task cohort yielded a confidence interval that spans the noninferiority threshold. The next comparison needs a preregistered paired sample designed for the anticipated gain, discordance, tolerance, and power.

Inspecting a single execution trace in greater detail resolves none of these three obligations. A granular trace can explain why an agent failed a specific step, but it cannot substitute for missing regression suites, multi-fixture validation, or cohort-wide statistical significance. Collecting that missing evidence under an established protocol is also distinct from altering the evaluation question itself. When a candidate fails to clear a deployment threshold, engineers may feel tempted to prune difficult tasks, drop incomplete trials, expand token budgets mid-flight, or tune task selection criteria. While these adjustments reliably inflate raw acceptance rates, they distort the operational meaning of the benchmark. Such post hoc filtering measures an artificially sanitized workload rather than genuine system capability. When task specifications, resource constraints, or operational boundaries legitimately change, the engineering team must record a revised evaluation protocol and test the configuration against a fresh, independent sample.



Even if candidate_v2 ran faster or cheaper than baseline_v1, a release gate cannot let a gain in latency or cost override an inconclusive acceptance comparison where the lower limit of the paired interval drops below the permissible degradation threshold \(-\NoninferiorityTolerance\). That empirical evidence establishes neither noninferiority nor superiority: the interval does not rule out the specified unacceptable loss, and it does not establish that candidate_v2 is inferior either. An inconclusive observed interval also does not by itself determine the study’s planned power. The planning count in Paired outcome comparison is about 217 paired evaluations if the observed advantage persists, and even that count clears the gate with only roughly even odds. A powered next sample therefore uses the paired-variance planning approximation in Statistical Evaluation Rigor, with its gain, discordance, and tolerance fixed in advance.
In production environments, engineering teams guard against wishful thinking by encoding deployment policies into explicit, declared decision rules. A release gate is formulated as a logical conjunction of independent criteria, each anchored to concrete empirical evidence:
\[\ShipDecision=\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\PairedDifferenceLowerLimit>-\NoninferiorityTolerance\right]\wedge
\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\CandidateTrajectoryGoodput\ge(1-\GoodputRelativeTolerance)\,\BaselineTrajectoryGoodput\right]\wedge
\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\CandidateTailCompletionTime\le \CompletionDeadline\right]\wedge
\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\CandidateViolationCount=0\right]. \tag{5}\]
Each predicate in equation 5 enforces a distinct operational requirement:

Paired noninferiority (\(\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\PairedDifferenceLowerLimit>-\NoninferiorityTolerance\right]\)): The lower bound of the confidence interval for the paired acceptance difference, \(\PairedDifferenceLowerLimit\), must exceed the allowed degradation margin \(-\NoninferiorityTolerance\). Clearing it supports, at the interval’s stated nominal confidence, the claim that the candidate does not degrade task completion by more than the tolerance.
Goodput preservation (\(\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\CandidateTrajectoryGoodput\ge(1-\GoodputRelativeTolerance)\,\BaselineTrajectoryGoodput\right]\)): Candidate trajectory goodput \(\CandidateTrajectoryGoodput\) must match baseline goodput \(\BaselineTrajectoryGoodput\) within a declared relative tolerance \(\GoodputRelativeTolerance\), evaluated across matched traffic profiles, workloads, and compute capacity.
Tail-latency constraint (\(\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\CandidateTailCompletionTime\le \CompletionDeadline\right]\)): The empirical 99th-percentile task completion time \(\CandidateTailCompletionTime\) across the evaluation cohort must not exceed the operational ceiling \(\CompletionDeadline\). This bound serves as a cohort-level service-level objective rather than a per-task watchdog timeout.
Zero-violation tripwire (\(\IndicatorFunction\!\left[\CandidateViolationCount=0\right]\)): The count of verified safety or contract violations \(\CandidateViolationCount\), such as unauthorized data modifications, privilege escalations, or uncontained tool executions, must equal zero. A single verified breach trips the gate immediately. Engineers must note, however, that observing zero violations within an evaluation cohort demonstrates only the absence of detected failures on that specific sample; it does not constitute a mathematical proof of absolute safety.

Certain operational metrics serve as diagnostic triggers rather than binary gates. For example, if a behavioral-drift metric such as the tool-distribution divergence in equation 1 crosses its declared alert threshold, the gate pipeline routes the candidate to manual engineering review rather than failing it outright. A significant change in tool usage frequency is not necessarily an anomaly; it often represents the exact behavioral modification intended by an interface or prompt redesign.
Because the release rule is a strict boolean conjunction, a failure in any single predicate yields \(\ShipDecision = 0\). Exceptional tail latency, lower token expenses, or an unblemished safety record cannot compensate for an inconclusive or degraded task acceptance rate. At the same time, the gate enforces only the predicates explicitly written into its formula. Any failure mode the conjunction does not monitor passes through it, as war story 14.1 showed.
For the worked candidate the first predicate already fails, so the gate returns zero without evaluating the goodput, latency, and violation terms, none of which the worked evidence measures for candidate_v2. The decision is to retain baseline_v1 in production and withhold live traffic from candidate_v2. The engineering team’s immediate next steps are to complete the pending regression runs for ws_r19, reconcile open token and tool expenditures, and pre-register an appropriately powered sample size before collecting further paired comparison data.
Automated gates evaluate these conditions deterministically, yet the underlying metrics reflect varying degrees of statistical uncertainty. A release evaluation report must therefore label each criterion with its precise operational status: satisfied, failed, or inconclusive under the declared evidence rule. Furthermore, individual 95 percent confidence intervals evaluated across separate operational metrics do not compound into an overall 95 percent system guarantee. When \(\TestFamilySize\) statistical predicates are each allowed probability \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\) of a wrong verdict, the chance that at least one of them is wrong is bounded only by \(\TestFamilySize\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\), since the probability of any error is at most the sum of the individual error probabilities. It approaches that bound when the individual errors rarely coincide. That combined probability is the family-wise error rate, and the simplest control divides the allowed error among the tests, testing each predicate at \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel/\TestFamilySize\). Production evaluation protocols must document their family-wise error accounting, specifying how they control for multiple hypothesis tests and for repeated peeking across sequential evaluation checkpoints.

Checkpoint 14.4: Defend the evaluation decision

Evidence scope: Why does the targeted pass for ws_r19 not accept its trial while the required regression result is pending? Why is a recovered result for ws_r18 not a replacement?
Comparison: Why can a candidate have more accepted trials in the paired sample without clearing the prespecified noninferiority rule?
Diagnosis: What does a successful observation-interface intervention on one fixture support, and what broader claim still needs evaluation?
Next step: Using the paired-comparison notebook’s planning formula, how many task pairs would center the expected lower limit on the tolerance if the true gain were hypothesized to be half the observed one? Which discordance and power assumptions would a powered plan also need? How can the evaluation harness prevent repeated testing or selective exclusions from altering the claimed decision rule?



An agent evaluation pipeline exists to produce an auditable decision, recorded immutably, that identifies the exact configuration under test, establishes what the empirical evidence proves, authorizes the next operational step, and transparently logs every duty that remains open. Skipping any link in that chain turns an operational measurement into a misleading release signal.

title: 14 Operating Agents
text:
Even an apparently thorough operational record can answer the wrong engineering question. The failure modes below break the link between operational evidence and deployment readiness, and each exacts a measurable cost in operational stability, exposure, or diagnostic visibility.

Pitfall: Relying on uniform head sampling to keep examples of rare failures.
Head sampling makes a retention decision at request ingestion, long before the agent’s final execution outcome is known (section 14.3). Because severe regressions and edge-case agent failures are inherently rare, uniform head sampling discards the vast majority of critical failure traces. At a 10 percent sampling rate, an intermittent failure mode that occurs 5 times across an evaluation run leaves no detailed trace 59 percent of the time, blinding engineers during root-cause debugging. Systems should instead employ tail sampling keyed to task outcomes and anomalous step traces. Engineers should retain a small, fixed uniform control sample to validate aggregate rates, while computing production failure rates from complete, lightweight accounting telemetry rather than sampled execution traces.


Fallacy: A small canary fraction limits the damage a regression can do.
For regressions that automated monitors track, the total blast radius depends on the sample count required to achieve statistical confidence rather than the traffic split percentage (section 14.5). In the reference monitor, a decision needs the same expected number of labeled tasks at any allocation (notebook 14.3), so the measured regression costs about 7 excess failures at a 5 percent allocation and about 11 at full allocation. A small fraction trims only the failures among tasks admitted while labels are pending, and it stretches the time to a decision to 15.58 h. A small traffic fraction limits damage only for unmonitored hazards or qualitative failures that human operators spot manually. Automated deployment systems must therefore enforce hard circuit-breaker limits and absolute failure thresholds that operate independently of the canary traffic fraction.


Pitfall: Treating a clean diagnostic run or a rollback as closing the incident.
A successful diagnostic run demonstrates stability only within the narrow confines of its specific test fixture (section 14.4.3). Statistically, observing 20 accepted runs out of 20 diagnostic executions still leaves the true failure rate as high as 16 percent at 95 percent confidence. Furthermore, rolling back candidate code or throttling traffic merely prevents new failures; it cannot retract state mutations, external tool invocations, or corrupted database records that the agent already generated. Teams must maintain regression monitoring, enforce bounded exposure limits, and retain designated recovery owners until all asynchronous downstream effects have fully settled.


Pitfall: Reading a successful span or a zero exit code as a passed task.
Span status records how one operation ended, not whether the task met its contract (section 14.2.2). A test process can exit cleanly while its output shows failed assertions, and a client span can end in a timeout while the candidate still produces a valid patch from cached context. A dashboard that counts green spans as accepted work therefore reports activity rather than acceptance, and the gap widens exactly when verdicts arrive late, after the execution spans have closed. Traces should carry a reference to the task verdict rather than a copy of it, and every acceptance figure should come from the accounting record, where pending and unknown verdicts stay in the denominator.


Fallacy: A configuration that clears every term of the release gate is safe to release.
A conjunctive gate enforces exactly the predicates written into it and nothing else (section 14.6.3). A regression in a property no criterion measures clears every term, and no sequential monitor stops it, because none is watching that property. The sycophancy rollback of war story 14.1 followed offline evaluations and an A/B test that both looked good. Zero observed violations in a cohort also bound the violation rate only as tightly as the cohort’s size allows. A passed gate supports the scoped claim its predicates state, and the canary’s allocation, the hard tripwires, and a recovery owner for every outstanding effect remain the protection against what the gate does not measure.

title: 14 Operating Agents
text:
An agent configuration that acts on live work produces evidence that no offline comparison collects, and operating it well means deciding in advance which of that evidence to keep and what each piece can establish. A trace binds model calls, tool executions, and checks to their trial, but a span’s status is not a task verdict, and summing overlapping spans overstates elapsed time that only the critical path explains. Retention keeps rare failures only when selection waits for verdicts, while the accounting record, which is never sampled, supplies every population rate. A postmortem separates the findings each boundary supports and tests an explanation by intervening on a saved prefix, so its conclusions hold for that fixture and need broader evaluation before they support a release. Staged exposure then trades calendar time against harms the monitor does not measure, and a rollback stops new admission without settling what the candidate already did. The worked case ends where the evidence does. The interface repair is supported on its fixture, the offline comparison remains inconclusive, and the declared gate returns zero, so baseline_v1 stays in production while the team collects the evidence the decision record names as missing.
The quantitative decisions developed across this chapter rely on the mathematical relationships summarized in table 9. Each formulation either sizes the operational evidence required to support a claim or translates that evidence into a scoped promotion decision.



Table 9: Key equations of agent operations: Each relation holds under the sampling, independence, and labeling assumptions stated where it is derived; none replaces the acceptance contract, the four-verdict rule, or the accounting record.

Key Takeaways: Keep operational evidence scoped to what it shows

A trace correlates; it does not authorize or accept: Spans bind model calls, tool executions, and checks to their trial and artifact, and the critical path through their dependencies, not the sum of their durations, explains elapsed time. A diagnostic trace may be sampled or truncated, so it never replaces the durable recovery log or the task verdict.
Retention decides what diagnosis can see: Uniform head sampling before a run completes systematically misses rare failure modes. Conversely, verdict-aware retention prioritizes intermittent bugs but skews raw telemetry distributions. Population failure rates come from complete accounting records; estimates from diagnostic samples require appropriate inclusion probabilities and reweighting.
A postmortem tests an explanation by intervening: Findings stay separated by boundary (interface defect, model response, runtime refusal), and a hypothesis is tested by a controlled branch from a saved prefix, not by rereading telemetry. Its conclusion holds for that fixture; broader claims need the evaluation of a revised configuration.
Canary allocation and monitoring control different harms: Sequential hypothesis testing, such as Wald’s SPRT, sets the expected sample count needed to reach a decision on a measured regression. Reducing the canary allocation primarily extends the time needed to collect that evidence while lowering the exposure rate to unmonitored harms. Unmonitored failure modes bypass statistical canary monitors entirely and require hard operational tripwires. Furthermore, rolling back routing terminates only incoming traffic; repairing external mutations and state corruption requires explicit recovery mechanisms.
A release is a decision record, not a scorecard: A production release gate mandates satisfying every declared acceptance criterion simultaneously. Superior performance on task accuracy cannot compensate for regressions in tail latency, budget breaches, or safety violations. Inconclusive trials must never be converted into default approvals, and rigorous experimental protocols require fixing hypotheses, sample sizes, and decision thresholds before collecting evaluation data.



Enforcing causal and statistical release evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-release-evidence}\)) requires a release protocol to specify its task criteria, operational boundaries, exposure policy, and statistical uncertainty explicitly. By tying release gates directly to structured execution traces and paired counterfactual baselines, systems engineers ensure that promotion decisions rest on reproducible evidence with stated limits rather than on summary scorecards.

title: 14 Operating Agents
text:
The statistics of staged release are older than electronic computing. During World War II, Abraham Wald developed the sequential probability ratio test (SPRT) to optimize industrial quality inspection, showing that deciding acceptance or rejection dynamically as evidence accumulates minimizes the expected sample size relative to fixed-horizon trials (Wald 1945).

Lamport, Leslie. 1978. “Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System.” Communications of the ACM 21 (7): 558–65. https://doi.org/10.1145/359545.359563.

Fonseca, Rodrigo, George Porter, Randy H. Katz, Scott Shenker, and Ion Stoica. 2007. “X-Trace: A Pervasive Network Tracing Framework.” 4th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI), 271–84.

Kohavi, Ron, Roger Longbotham, Dan Sommerfield, and Randal M. Henne. 2009. “Controlled Experiments on the Web: Survey and Practical Guide.” Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery 18 (1): 140–81. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10618-008-0114-1.

Johari, Ramesh, Pete Koomen, Leonid Pekelis, and David Walsh. 2017. “Peeking at A/B Tests: Why It Matters, and What to Do about It.” Proceedings of the 23rd ACM SIGKDD International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining, 1517–25. https://doi.org/10.1145/3097983.3097992.

OpenAI. 2025b. Sycophancy in GPT-4o: What Happened and What We’re Doing about It. OpenAI blog.
The telemetry required to diagnose multi-turn agent execution draws directly from distributed systems observability. Lamport established that asynchronous events across decoupled components admit only a partial order unless system metadata explicitly captures their causal links (Lamport 1978). Fonseca et al. (2007) extended this principle to modern network architectures with X-Trace, propagating deterministic task contexts across diverse protocol layers and administrative domains to reconstruct complete end-to-end execution paths. In the same years, production web services transformed deployment validation into continuous experimentation: Kohavi et al. (2009) codified online controlled experiments with staged canary deployments as standard release gates. Sigelman et al. (2010) then proved in Dapper that distributed tracing could operate continuously at production scale by decoupling span collection from the critical path and employing aggressive head-based sampling to bound runtime overhead to negligible levels. Google’s site reliability engineering practice established the blameless postmortem, institutionalizing structured incident postmortems as essential operational records for diagnosing systemic failures (Beyer et al. 2016). When engineering teams began monitoring live experimentation dashboards in real time, Johari et al. (2017) proved that repeated significance testing inflates false-positive rates far above the nominal level, establishing why sequential testing bounds, the descendants of Wald’s test, must govern automated canary rollouts. Agent releases add what Wald’s inspection lines did not face: labels that arrive hours after admission, tasks whose effects outlive the decision, and harms that no monitored metric records, the gap that the 2025 sycophancy rollback exposed (OpenAI 2025b).
Further reading.

Wald, “Sequential Tests of Statistical Hypotheses” (Wald 1945): The original derivation of the sequential probability ratio test, its approximate decision boundaries, and its average sample number, providing the mathematical foundation for staged canary deployments and early-stopping test monitors.
Sigelman et al., “Dapper” (Sigelman et al. 2010): The foundational architecture of production distributed tracing under strict overhead budgets, examining the sampling policies and trace contexts that enable fine-grained post-hoc diagnosis.
Kohavi, Tang, and Xu, Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments (Kohavi et al. 2020): A practitioner’s guide to randomized experimentation in production systems, covering assignment units, sample-ratio mismatches, and the statistical pitfalls that invalidate live rollout decisions.
Beyer et al., Site Reliability Engineering (Beyer et al. 2016): The practitioner’s account of operating production services, including the blameless postmortem and the release engineering that agent operations extend from people to components.


Wald, Abraham. 1945. “Sequential Tests of Statistical Hypotheses.” The Annals of Mathematical Statistics 16 (2): 117–86. https://doi.org/10.1214/aoms/1177731118.

Kohavi, Ron, Diane Tang, and Ya Xu. 2020. Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments: A Practical Guide to A/B Testing. Cambridge University Press. https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108653985.

title: 14 Operating Agents
text:
Each problem states its constraints and ends in a decision about what the evidence supports or what to collect next. Givens are hypothetical unless stated otherwise, and every interval is a nominal 95 percent interval with \(\IntervalNormalQuantile=1.96\).
1. Where the time went (Basic). A repair-agent timing trial records these spans on one host clock, in seconds after segment start. Retrieval runs 0.0 to 1.2, a model call proposing checks 1.2 to 4.0, targeted tests 4.0 to 13.0, a static lint check 4.0 to 7.5, a dependency audit 4.0 to 10.0, and a model call synthesizing the report 14.0 to 17.0. The three checks are independent of one another, synthesis waits for all three, and the enclosing segment ends at 17.5. (a) Compute the sum of the leaf span durations and the critical-path duration, and find how much of the 17.5 s segment the spans leave unattributed. (b) A cache cuts the targeted tests to 5.0 s with everything else unchanged. Compute the new critical path and the saving, and name the span that now limits the check phase. (c) A routing change instead halves both model calls. Compute its saving, compare it with part (b), and state which assumption about the unattributed intervals both estimates share. (d) Decide which change to fund first if each costs the same to build, and name the controlled measurement that must confirm the saving before it is claimed.
2. A retention budget for rare failures (Intermediate). A repair fleet runs 20,000 evaluation trials per day, each with a 2 MB (decimal) permitted trace body. At the selection boundary, 3 percent of trials have failed a criterion, 1 percent remain pending or unknown, and the rest are ordinary accepted trials. One failure mode occurs 8 times per week, and downstream diagnostic storage is capped at 1.5 GB per day. (a) Compute the daily volume of full retention and of uniform head sampling at \(\HeadSamplingProbability=2\) percent, and the probability that head sampling keeps no detailed trace of the rare mode in a week. (b) Compute the daily volume of tail selection that keeps every failed and unresolved trial plus a 1 percent random control sample of ordinary trials, and check it against the cap. (c) Design a selection policy within the cap that keeps every failed trial. State the sampling rates for unresolved and ordinary trials, the inclusion probabilities the record must keep, and one change to the trace body that would relax the cap. (d) An analyst reports the fraction of retained traces under the policy of part (b) that failed as the fleet’s failure rate. Compute the reported value, and name the record the failure rate must come from.
3. Drift in shadow execution (Intermediate). A shadow run of the revised repair configuration records its tool calls over four categories, read, test, lint, and edit. The baseline distributes its calls as 0.40, 0.30, 0.10, and 0.20, and the candidate as 0.30, 0.45, 0.05, and 0.20. Two independent baseline samples of the same size differ by a Jensen–Shannon divergence of 0.004 nats. (a) Compute \(\JensenShannonDivergence\) between baseline and candidate with equation 1, in nats, and express it as a fraction of its maximum, \(\ln 2\). (b) Release policy routes a candidate to engineering review when its divergence exceeds three times the baseline-versus-baseline value. Decide whether this candidate is routed, and whether the decision would change under a five-times rule. (c) The candidate is the paginated observation interface, which retrieves remaining results instead of guessing. Explain why more test calls and fewer reads may be the intended change, and state which measurement, not the divergence, decides whether the shift is an improvement. (d) The shadow copies also read from a production ticketing service. Name three effects such reads can have and the declarations the shadow design must make before it mirrors any input.
4. Postmortem of a wrong refund answer (Advanced). The support agent tells a customer that a purchase is refundable within 60 days, while the current policy allows 30. The retained trace holds three records. The raw retrieval result contains two policy passages, the current version and a superseded one, each with an effective date; the delivered context contains both passages with the effective dates removed by the observation adapter; and the answer quotes the superseded passage. The team restores a compatible saved prefix ending just before the retrieval call and runs 40 fresh continuations in each of three branches, holding the model configuration, sampling settings, prompt, and a policy-grounded reference check fixed; every run reaches a known verdict. Branch A keeps the original adapter and yields 18 wrong answers. Branch B delivers the effective dates and yields 3 wrong answers. Branch C removes the superseded passage from the index, so only the current version is retrieved, and yields none. Release policy requires the Wilson upper limit on the support agent’s per-session wrong-answer rate to be at most 2 percent. (a) For each claim, state whether the retained record alone, a regression replay of the captured result without a model call, or only the intervention can establish it: the adapter removes effective dates; the model received both passages; the missing dates contributed to the wrong answer. (b) Compute each branch’s wrong-answer rate with its Wilson interval. Decide whether the data support the claim that delivering effective dates reduces wrong answers from this prefix, and whether 40 runs per branch distinguish branch B from branch C. (c) Compute how many consecutive correct continuations a fix would need before its Wilson upper limit met the release policy, and the corresponding lower confidence bound on five-session consistency from branch C’s upper limit at 40 runs, assuming independent recurrences from this same saved prefix. (d) A teammate reports a fourth branch that delivers the dates and also lowers the sampling temperature to zero, with 40 of 40 correct, and proposes shipping it as the fix. Critique the proposal, choose a corrective change, and write the postmortem record’s lines for established findings, tested change, and remaining questions.
5. Size a canary against a deadline (Advanced). A repair-agent canary monitors acceptance with the SPRT of equation 2, comparing \(\HypothesizedAcceptanceProbability_0=0.80\) with \(\HypothesizedAcceptanceProbability_1=0.70\) at design targets \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel=0.05\) and \(\HypothesisTestFalseNegativeRate=0.10\). Eligible tasks arrive regularly at 40 per hour, each label arrives 2 hours after admission when the regression suite finishes, and under \(\HypothesizedAcceptanceProbability_1\) the planning target is an approximate expected decision time of at most 24 hours from the first admission. Separately, a harm the monitor does not measure occurs in 0.5 percent of candidate tasks, and release policy requires the candidate to run for 7 days at its allocation before any wider release. (a) Compute \(\SprtUpperLogBoundary\), \(\SprtLowerLogBoundary\), \(\SprtExpectedLogIncrement_1\), and the no-overshoot \(\mathbb{E}_1[\SprtStoppingSampleCount]\). (b) Find the smallest allocation \(\CanaryAllocationFraction\) that meets that expected-time target. (c) Compute the expected excess failures from the measured regression at that \(\CanaryAllocationFraction\) and at \(\CanaryAllocationFraction=25\) percent. (d) If the allocation continues for all seven days, compute the expected count of unmeasured harms over the 7-day period at both allocations. Choose \(\CanaryAllocationFraction\) and justify it from parts (b) through (d). Explain why this exposure calculation is not an instruction to keep admitting the candidate after a degradation alarm. (e) A teammate proposes replacing the SPRT with a fixed-sample test rerun after every new label, stopping at the first value below 0.05. Critique the proposal.
6. Critique a release report (Advanced). A team asks to promote a repair-agent candidate with the following evidence. The candidate accepted 78 percent of tasks and the baseline 72 percent, reported as a 6-point gain. The baseline ran on 100 tasks sampled last month, and the candidate on 100 newly sampled tasks. The team dropped 12 candidate trials whose regression suites had not finished, so the candidate accepted 69 of the remaining 88. Report quality counted as accepted when an LLM judge scored it at least 4 of 5, justified by 90 percent raw agreement with a second judge. The failure rate in the release notes was computed from tail-sampled traces. (a) Under the four-verdict rule, bound the candidate’s accepted fraction of its admitted cohort, and state what the 6-point claim becomes. (b) Using equation 13.3 with \(\PooledAcceptanceProbability=0.75\), a 5 percent two-sided significance target, and 80 percent power, compute the tasks per independent arm needed to detect a 6-point difference. (c) Redesign the comparison as paired. Assuming a discordant fraction \(\DiscordantPairFraction=0.15\), an anticipated gain of 3 points, and \(\NoninferiorityTolerance=2\) points, find the number of task pairs at which the normal-approximation lower limit \(\EstimatedPairedAcceptanceDifference-\IntervalNormalQuantile\sqrt{(\DiscordantPairFraction-\EstimatedPairedAcceptanceDifference^2)/\EvaluationSampleCount}\) clears \(-\NoninferiorityTolerance\) if the gain holds. Contrast this expected-limit-centering count with the fixed-variance normal planning count at 80 percent power, using power quantile 0.84. Both calculations assume the stated gain and discordance; the powered count approximates a normal gate rather than calibrating the exact paired-score interval. (d) Identify the remaining defects in the report and write a defensible protocol: which criteria the automated gate enforces, which measurements the judge must carry, and which conditions the team must declare before collecting data.

What’s Next: From operational evidence to curated trajectoriesOperation leaves a qualified record: verdicts held in the accounting record, traces retained with their inclusion probabilities, and a postmortem that separated an interface defect from a model behavior and a runtime refusal. Trajectory Curation uses that record to guide diagnosis, admission, and corpus design, and its first decision is triage. The truncated-observation failure that the postmortem traced largely to the observation adapter belongs in an interface fix, not in a corpus. A logged success is not automatically a useful demonstration, and a failure is not automatically a policy defect. Preserve criterion and configuration provenance, unresolved evidence, and the separation between development data and held-out evaluation. Curation turns that qualified record into a learning-data decision.

title: 12 Failure Recovery
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can an agent that records every step it takes still leave the world half changed?
A durable record tells a restarted agent what it intended and what it observed, but the record does not change the world. A provisioning request whose reply was lost may have created a billed environment or nothing at all, and no amount of replay settles which. Restoring a workspace snapshot resets local files, while the remote environment the agent created keeps running and keeps charging. Recovery therefore begins where recording ends, with decisions made on incomplete evidence. A runtime that reads a timeout as failure sends a second request and can leak a second resource, and one that reads it as success builds on an effect that may never have happened. Some effects can be undone only by a new operation that can itself fail, and some cannot be undone at all, so the cheapest place to stop a bad change is before the step that commits it. Other failures raise no error. A trajectory can alternate between two edits for dozens of turns, every call returning success and every health check green, while each turn resends a longer context and the bill grows faster than the turn count. Retries that every layer grants on its own allowance multiply against a dependency that is already failing, so one slow service can stall the shared worker pool. A warning in the prompt does not contain any of these hazards, because the model may ignore advice that a runtime bound would enforce. The runtime must record the cleanup it owes before it acts and keep unknown outcomes owned rather than guessed. It must weigh another attempt against unwinding by the cost still ahead rather than the cost already spent, and halt work that makes no progress at the gate where new actions are admitted. Over a long horizon, the authority an agent has already exercised becomes a set of obligations the runtime must settle.

Learning Objectives

Select among retry, repair, compensation, and escalation by an effect’s evidence state first, then admission, then expected cost
Register compensations before forward dispatch and order their execution with a dependency-based cleanup graph
Compare one bounded forward repair against compensation and rebuilding, in time and dollars, at the same endpoint
Analyze how checks placed before an irreversible commitment reduce expected loss while cleanup and residual duties remain
Construct progress detectors and price detection latency against a cumulative budget ceiling
Design dependency containment with a single retry owner, scoped circuit breakers, and a capped worker share
Design an incident containment order that limits blast radius while preserving evidence and cleanup
Evaluate recovery policies by accepted tasks, residual obligations, and unresolved outcomes rather than local status



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗






Over a long horizon, authority becomes a recovery problem for the runtime.
When a replacement worker takes over the repair agent’s failed connection-pool repair (Four lighthouse workloads), it reconstructs the execution log and restores the candidate workspace snapshot ws_r18. The surviving history records an intent to run test_r18, but contains no evidence confirming whether the test passed, failed, or ever ran. As Resuming a Trajectory demonstrated, the worker cannot treat missing evidence as a clean slate; it must retain that uncertainty alongside the unresolved liability. State reconstruction recovers the factual foundation of the execution, but facts alone do not dictate the next step. The runtime’s recovery policy must decide whether to wait for delayed evidence, attempt a targeted repair of the candidate snapshot, or abort the task entirely.
Now expand the scope of the repair to include an external side effect. Besides the unresolved test_r18, which remains a separate operation whose outcome is still owed, the repair provisions an isolated, temporary integration-test environment and runs a new integration suite against ws_r18 inside it. The agent’s authorization grant covers this ephemeral environment and nothing else. Production deployments, public network routing, payment processing, and the deletion of unrelated cloud resources remain strictly beyond its authority.
If a network timeout or process crash drops the provisioning reply, the worker faces an immediate impasse: it cannot know whether the remote environment was successfully allocated or never created.1 Suppose instead that telemetry confirms creation, but the integration suite subsequently crashes. Rolling back the local workspace to snapshot ws_r18 resets internal state, yet the external environment remains active and billing charges continue to accumulate. Local rollback does not undo distributed side effects. Reclaiming those external resources requires an explicit compensating cleanup operation, followed by concrete evidence that the operation satisfied its declared postconditions.
1 Lost acknowledgment: Gray named this the generals paradox in his 1978 notes on database operating systems: over a channel that can lose messages, no finite exchange lets both parties know that the last message arrived (Gray 1978). Fischer, Lynch, and Paterson later proved that in a fully asynchronous system no deterministic consensus protocol can guarantee termination while preserving agreement and validity if even one process may crash, since a crashed process cannot be told apart from a slow one (Fischer et al. 1985). A tool-call timeout inherits the same ambiguity, which is why the settlement rule keeps the outcome unknown rather than guessing. 
Gray, Jim. 1978. “Notes on Data Base Operating Systems.” In Operating Systems: An Advanced Course. Springer. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-08755-9_9.

Fischer, Michael J., Nancy A. Lynch, and Michael S. Paterson. 1985. “Impossibility of Distributed Consensus with One Faulty Process.” Journal of the ACM 32 (2): 374–82.
Durable logs, checkpoints, and deterministic replay reconstruct what the runtime intended and what it observed. That historical reconstruction provides the evidence for recovery, but passive logs cannot alter the outside world. An execution log does not tear down an orphaned test cluster, resolve a lost network acknowledgment, or evaluate whether a subsequent attempt justifies its operational cost.


↩︎ Durable logs, checkpoints, and deterministic replay are established in Durable Execution.
Complicating matters further, agent failures frequently manifest without throwing runtime exceptions. An agent trajectory can issue structurally valid tool calls while drifting into destructive patterns: alternating indefinitely between two conflicting edits, bombarding a degraded testing service with aggressive retries, or attempting to transmit private credentials after parsing an untrusted document. Every network call returns a successful status, every worker health check reports green, yet the agent either makes zero forward progress or actively threatens system integrity.
The recovery architecture records every compensating cleanup obligation before dispatching the operation that produces an external side effect. When an operation is interrupted, the runtime evaluates the surviving evidence alongside projected forward costs and ignores sunk expenses. It then chooses whether to retry the operation, repair the proposal within a bound, run compensating actions that unwind external side effects, or hand control to an authorized human operator. Furthermore, the architecture bounds ongoing executions even when no component raises an explicit error. By intercepting actions at the admission gate where new tool calls are scheduled, the runtime halts unproductive loops, throttles retries against saturated dependencies, and quarantines suspicious behaviors. It does not rely on prompt warnings that an agent model might overlook or ignore.
Section 12.2 demonstrates why the environment service and runtime log in this workflow share no atomic commit boundary, carrying forward from the harness the two rules that govern every subsequent recovery decision. Section 12.3 translates these invariants into an executable saga pattern, tracking compensation obligations as explicit, dependency-ordered records. Where an execution encounters partial failure, section 12.4 formalizes how to evaluate the marginal cost of forward repair against backward unwinding, while section 12.5 governs the critical transition across irreversible commitment points.
To address failures that emerge without explicit error signals, the runtime introduces three containment boundaries. Progress watchdogs identify trajectory stagnation and oscillatory loops (section 12.6). Dependency controls insulate shared backend services from retry cascades (section 12.7). Automated quarantine policies isolate suspected security incidents (section 12.8). Finally, section 12.9 unites these control loops in a recovery worksheet for a degraded connection-pool repair, detailing the fault-injection test harness required to verify recovery correctness under real-world failures.



When the integration suite crashes inside the temporary test environment, rolling back the agent runtime’s local database cannot reach across the network to deallocate the remote virtual machine. Even if the cloud provider’s environment service executes internal database transactions with strict ACID guarantees, its database and the runtime’s execution log commit in separate administrative domains with no shared atomic boundary. Inside a single database or a tightly coupled cluster, a locking transaction holds exclusive locks until commit or abort, and two-phase commit coordinates an atomic decision across cooperating resource managers (Gray 1981). In two-phase commit, each participant first prepares by writing the recovery state needed to either commit or abort on command, and then holds its locked resources in that prepared state until the coordinator announces the global decision. Agent tool workflows break both requirements of that protocol. First, the external endpoints an agent invokes commit each request on receipt and rarely expose a prepare phase or accept the agent runtime as their transaction coordinator. Second, even where internal services do cooperate, a prepared participant must keep its resources locked while waiting for the coordinator, and a coordinator crash while participants are prepared prolongs that wait until recovery completes. Holding database locks or reserved capacity across model generation, long integration tests, or asynchronous human review would stall competing work for unacceptable periods. Across the independently administered services in this workflow, recovery therefore relies on tentative operations, explicit cancellations, and idempotent exchanges rather than assuming a shared transaction (Helland 2007).
2 Compensating transaction: Gray’s 1981 travel-agent example had this exact structure (Gray 1981). Because each flight or hotel reservation commits at an independent organization, canceling the itinerary requires executing a compensating transaction. Gray proposed that each nested step return the name and parameters of its compensator for the parent coordinator to log, falling back to human intervention as a last resort. However, Gray’s coordinator logs the compensator only after the forward step successfully returns. A trajectory saga must instead record the recovery obligation before dispatching the request over the network, because a dropped connection or lost acknowledgment would otherwise leave unmanaged side effects with no corresponding recovery record. 
Gray, Jim. 1981. “The Transaction Concept: Virtues and Limitations.” Proceedings of the Seventh International Conference on Very Large Data Bases (VLDB) 7: 144–54.
When atomic rollback across independent boundaries is impossible, systems must rely on compensation:2 a forward-executing operation that establishes acceptable postconditions after a prior effect has already committed. Compensation does not erase history or restore the universe to its pristine pre-transaction state. For example, releasing a cloud-hosted development environment deallocates its virtual compute instances and stops active billing meters. The provisioning event, network ingress logs, and financial charges already accrued remain permanent, and the teardown request itself may fail on an unreachable network. To structure multi-step workflows without global isolation, Garcia-Molina and Salem introduced the saga pattern for long-lived transactions (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). Rather than treating the entire trajectory as a single atomic unit, a saga partitions execution into a sequence of smaller, independently committed steps. It pairs each forward step with a compensating action designed to mitigate its side effects if a later step fails.


↪ Two-phase commit’s blocking behavior and the original saga abstraction are developed in Classical Transaction Background.
Compensation is not the only recovery strategy. Apart from a plain retry of an operation whose repeat contract permits one, an agent runtime chooses among three families of response:

Compensation: execute explicit counteracting operations to neutralize partial side effects.
Forward repair: preserve valid intermediate artifacts, such as a successfully compiled binary or a provisioned database schema, and adjust subsequent steps rather than discarding completed progress.
Escalated handoff: halt autonomous dispatch and transfer unresolved obligations, active resource handles, and diagnostic logs to an authorized human operator.

The runtime balances available evidence against projected forward costs to choose among these alternatives; capital and compute time already expended are sunk costs that must not distort future recovery decisions. Whichever path it selects, two rules that the harness already enforces govern the choice, and recovery is where both are tested hardest.
The settlement rule governs what the runtime may believe about an external effect. The harness stated it as a rule about the operation table: withdrawing an operation’s observation eligibility never settles the operation, and only authenticated, correlated evidence does. Recovery needs the rule in a sharper form, as three mutually exclusive evidence states for every dispatched operation: established, established absent, or unknown. An outcome begins as unknown, and only evidence correlated with that specific operation, interpreted through the target endpoint’s contract, can move it to established or established absent. A dropped TCP acknowledgment, an HTTP gateway timeout, an asynchronous accepted-but-pending status, or a status query that returns nothing while the original request may still be in transit all leave the outcome unknown. An unknown outcome keeps its liability reservation against the task budget, keeps a durable record with a named owner, and blocks any forward action that presupposes either success or failure. The runtime may repeat the dispatch only when the endpoint’s verified repeat contract makes re-execution safe, which is settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)).


↩︎ The settlement rule, which separates observation eligibility from settling the operation, is established in The Trajectory Record.
The admission check governs what the runtime may do next. Every candidate operation passes the same predicates the harness applies to ordinary work, whether it is forward progress, a retry, an environment repair, a status probe, or a cleanup action. The predicates are valid authority and approval, satisfied dependencies, available capacity, and enough time before the deadline. They also require a reservation whose bounded liability fits beside actual consumption, outstanding liability from unsettled operations, and the protected finalization reserve. The check is re-evaluated at the dispatch boundary immediately before transmission, so a plan-time approval or an earlier durable intent cannot override a later administrative hold, a revoked token, or a depleted budget. Recovery operations receive no exemption. Organizational liability for remote infrastructure does, however, outlive the agent’s reasoning loop, so administrative cleanup backed by independent operational credentials can still pass admission and decommission orphaned resources long after model-directed continuation has ended.


↩︎ The admission check and the finalization reserve it protects are established in Transition guards and the admission check.
A naive undo stack, such as a reversed list of tool invocations that maps server creation to server deletion, is too brittle to satisfy either the settlement rule or the admission check. In-flight operations fail asynchronously, remote endpoints drop responses, and partial writes leave external resources in states that cannot be resolved by replaying inverse functions with original arguments. Instead, the runtime must persist a structured recovery obligation before allowing any request to cross the network boundary. This obligation captures correlation identifiers, parent-child causal links, parameter snapshots, timeout thresholds, and settlement state, providing the durable bookkeeping needed to handle partial failure without leaking resources. The trajectory saga pattern formalizes this durable record of obligations.



When the repair worker dispatches its request to provision the temporary test environment, the remote service may allocate the virtual machine and start billing even if a network partition drops the return acknowledgment before it reaches the runtime. That lost reply breaks the binary assumption of a classical database saga, which coordinates a long-lived transaction across independent services by assuming that each local step either commits cleanly or aborts cleanly and reports which one happened. In an agent trajectory, the runtime can be left with an active cleanup obligation for a remote resource whose endpoint-assigned identifier has not yet arrived. A saga for agent tool calls therefore cannot merely log completed steps after they return; it must durably register each recovery obligation before dispatch and explicitly track what the runtime does not yet know.

Definition 12.1: Trajectory saga
Trajectory saga is a recovery pattern that durably records constituent tool actions and coordinates compensating actions when established external effects must be remediated, while explicitly preserving unresolved outcomes and inter-action dependencies.

Significance: Enables systematic recovery across independent external tools and services that share no common distributed transaction boundary.
Distinction: Compensation represents new forward execution that produces its own observable outcome, rather than an atomic rollback or physical reversal of the environment.
Common pitfall: Deferring cleanup registration until after receiving a successful forward response, creating a crash window where external resources leak without any durable record of their recovery obligation.



In its classical formulation, a saga consists of a sequence of separately committed forward steps \(\SagaForwardStep_1, \dots, \SagaForwardStep_n\), each paired with a compensating step \(\SagaCompensatingStep_i\) that the runtime executes if downstream failures require remediating earlier effects (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). A forward action that produces no external side effect requires no compensation. When every forward step succeeds, the saga completes execution as \(\SagaForwardStep_1, \dots, \SagaForwardStep_n\). If step \(\SagaForwardStep_k\) fails, a linear saga unwinds by executing compensating actions in reverse order:
\[\SagaForwardStep_1, \dots, \SagaForwardStep_{k-1}, \SagaFailedForwardStep, \SagaCompensatingStep_k, \SagaCompensatingStep_{k-1}, \dots, \SagaCompensatingStep_1, \tag{1}\]
where \(\SagaCompensatingStep_k\) runs only when evidence confirms that the failed step actually produced an external effect. If the outcome of \(\SagaForwardStep_k\) remains unknown, the runtime’s settlement rules keep the obligation for \(\SagaCompensatingStep_k\) open rather than guessing. While equation 1 models an idealized sequential workflow, non-linear trajectories require a generalized directed cleanup graph. Each compensating step \(\SagaCompensatingStep_i\) is itself an independent, separately committed operation with its own execution outcome; an unwind can stall partway through, leaving certain compensations settled while others remain pending or in flight.


Registering a compensating step before dispatching the forward action creates an immediate addressing problem: when the worker sends a provisioning request, the cloud service has not yet created the environment or returned the handle needed to tear it down. Waiting until the reply arrives to log the cleanup would open a crash window in which a dropped connection orphans a live, billed environment with no local recovery record; the runtime instead durably registers a cleanup template before forward dispatch and binds the target identifier when evidence arrives. In our temporary test-infrastructure workflow, let provision_test_env_r18 be the stable logical operation that provisions an isolated test environment, and let release_test_env_r18 be its corresponding cleanup operation, a distinct logical identity that remains stable across retries and restarts. Neither identity should be confused with the endpoint-generated environment identifier. That system handle, denoted env_r18_01 in a successful provisioning run, becomes known to the runtime only after correlated response evidence settles the forward operation.
The pre-dispatch cleanup template records the exact forward operation and payload, authorized capability scope, execution preconditions, dependencies, and an explicit rule for binding the returned environment identifier once it arrives. Appended directly to the write-ahead log alongside the forward admission record, this registration shares the forward attempt’s storage acknowledgment and resource reservation, avoiding the overhead and complexity of an independent state machine. Registering the cleanup before the effect it cleans up applies intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) to the recovery obligation itself.


↩︎ The durable intent record written before dispatch is established in Durable Intent Before Dispatch.
The resulting template binds cleanup to the specific environment instantiated by this provisioning operation, rather than relying on transient metadata like display names. Durably registering this template establishes a binding commitment for future recovery rather than asserting that the resource already exists. When an acknowledgment is lost following dispatch, an idempotent result-recovery probe may retrieve the missing outcome. For a mutating tool without endpoint deduplication, this is the probe that the tool contract of equation 7.1 ships beside its actuate and compensate routines. The template registered here instantiates that contract’s compensate routine for one specific, bound resource. If probing is unsupported or inconclusive, settlement rules mandate that the operation remain open with an assigned recovery owner. A naive runtime might query the external service, observe that the environment is absent, and prematurely close the cleanup record on the assumption that creation failed. Doing so creates a race condition. If the original provisioning request was merely delayed in transit, the remote service may instantiate the environment seconds later, leaving an orphaned resource that accrues compute charges indefinitely without any controlling process. If the endpoint supports explicit request cancellation, the runtime can invoke that contract to terminate the pending creation, provided the endpoint guarantees that canceled requests will not take effect downstream.


↪ Result recovery, as distinct from repeated execution, is developed in Repetition and Result Recovery.



Once env_r18_01 is bound and a failed integration run triggers release_test_env_r18, the runtime must verify that teardown succeeded even though the external world cannot be rewound to its state before provisioning. Rather than checking for an impossible physical reversal, the runtime checks whether the compensating action has re-established a declared set of postconditions while leaving outside side effects to their own lifecycles.

Definition 12.2: Semantic compensation
Semantic compensation is an independent forward action designed to establish declared application postconditions following an earlier side effect, without claiming to erase execution history or restore every dimension of the external environment.

Significance: Provides a verifiable, checkable objective for recovery when exact physical or historical reversal is impossible.
Distinction: Releasing a temporary environment terminates its active allocation; it does not un-send network packets, erase system audit logs, or refund consumed compute charges.
Common pitfall: Treating an endpoint’s asynchronous acceptance response as proof that declared postconditions have been achieved when only request receipt has occurred.



In our running example, the compensation contract stipulates that the task-owned environment must no longer be allocated and that no active integration test may still depend on it, requiring any diagnostic artifacts to be transferred to durable storage prior to deallocation. The contract also defines what evidence the endpoint must supply to demonstrate successful release. Because final billing charges often settle asynchronously hours after an environment is torn down, the runtime decouples the physical resource obligation from financial settlement.
Formally, let \(\PreForwardEnvironmentState\) represent the state of the environment prior to executing forward step \(\SagaForwardStep\), and let \(\CompensatedEnvironmentState\) denote the state after executing \(\SagaForwardStep\) followed by its compensating action \(\SagaCompensatingStep\). Because physical time cannot be reversed and side effects alter audit trails and financial balances, \(\CompensatedEnvironmentState\) and \(\PreForwardEnvironmentState\) inevitably differ. Compensation guarantees equivalence only with respect to an explicitly declared set of postcondition predicates \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\). The compensation succeeds if and only if both states agree on every predicate in \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\):
\[\CompensatedEnvironmentState \equiv_{\CompensationPostconditionSet} \PreForwardEnvironmentState \iff \forall \CompensationPostcondition \in \CompensationPostconditionSet:\ \CompensationPostcondition(\CompensatedEnvironmentState) = \CompensationPostcondition(\PreForwardEnvironmentState). \tag{2}\]
Here, predicates such as “the environment is allocated” and “an admitted test depends on it” belong to \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\), and both evaluate to false in \(\PreForwardEnvironmentState\) and \(\CompensatedEnvironmentState\). In contrast, billing records and audit histories lie outside \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\), which is why financial reconciliation requires an independent settlement lifecycle. A compensation contract claims to satisfy only the predicates explicitly declared in \(\CompensationPostconditionSet\); unmodeled side effects remain unaddressed.
Compensation inevitably operates on an environment that has moved on. External services or human operators may have observed the intermediate state, consumed compute seconds cannot be un-billed, and concurrent processes can alter cleanup preconditions. For instance, if a peer workflow has attached to the temporary environment for joint debugging, the originating agent cannot unilaterally destroy the resource simply because its own plan stalled. The runtime’s admission control boundary must inspect live ownership and active dependency graphs at the moment of compensation, rather than blindly following stale planning text.
Local workspace restoration plays a complementary but narrower role. A compatible checkpoint restores only the local workspace projection managed directly by the runtime. Checkpoints cannot reset remote cloud environments, running external daemons, dispatched batch jobs, or accrued service charges. Those external side effects demand semantic compensation. When recovery requires both local rollback and remote compensation, the runtime orchestrates both mechanisms, verifying the independent outcome of each path before declaring the system recovered.


↩︎ Checkpoint restoration, which reinstates the record and workspace without re-executing external actions, is established in Consistent recovery boundaries.



Because cleanup actions cross the same external tool boundaries as forward actions, they encounter the same failure modes: network drops, rate limits, and remote service outages. Consequently, every compensating operation must pass admission control, and its intent must be durably committed before dispatch. When retrying a failed cleanup call, the runtime assigns each transport attempt a unique attempt identifier, while release_test_env_r18 continues to designate the persistent logical operation. Retries adhere to the endpoint’s repeat contract. The stable logical key ensures that duplicate deletion requests execute safely without targeting a different resource if the external system reuses names or identifiers.


↩︎ Stable operation identities, with a fresh attempt identity for each retry under the endpoint’s repeat contract, are established in Operation identity and endpoint contracts.
The coordinator retires a compensation entry only upon receiving verifiable outcome evidence, rather than assuming success simply because a remote call returned without a transport error. If a release call times out, three states remain possible: the environment may be gone, it may still be undergoing deallocation, or it may remain allocated. The settlement rules keep all three possibilities open. Furthermore, cleanup actions consume quota and wall-clock execution budget; a timed-out call refunds nothing. If cleanup cannot progress further within its assigned budget, the obligation stays on record with its accumulated evidence and an assigned escalation owner. In this way, a failed agent trajectory can terminate safely without masking unresolved external leaks.
Preregistered cleanup templates execute under the supervision of the trusted runtime coordinator without invoking another model inference step. This separation enforces least-privilege control: even if the model’s forward execution authority is revoked following an anomaly or budget exhaustion, a narrowly scoped cleanup grant remains accessible to the coordinator to tear down provisioned resources. If remediation requires operations beyond this pre-authorized grant, the runtime does not guess; it halts and issues an explicitly owned handoff. Later authenticated evidence or manual operator actions can settle the obligation without restarting the obsolete agent trajectory.



Tearing down env_r18_01 the moment a failure is detected would sever an integration test that is still running inside it and destroy diagnostic logs before they are copied to durable storage, whereas deleting an unrelated local scratch directory need not wait for either step. A simple last-in, first-out (LIFO) unwind stack is adequate only when an agent executes a strictly linear sequence and every cleanup precondition follows that reverse order. When an agent invokes tools concurrently, triggers asynchronous background tasks, or branches across speculative plans, recovery requires tracking explicit causal dependencies in a directed cleanup graph \((\CleanupGraphVertexSet,\CleanupGraphEdgeSet)\), where each vertex represents an admitted cleanup operation and a directed edge
\[\SagaCompensatingStep_j \rightarrow \SagaCompensatingStep_k\]
signifies that compensating operation \(\SagaCompensatingStep_j\) must establish its declared settlement conditions before \(\SagaCompensatingStep_k\) is permitted to dispatch. Declared cleanup dependencies must form a directed acyclic graph (DAG); cyclical dependencies represent contradictory recovery requirements that demand explicit operator intervention rather than an arbitrary stack ordering.
In our temporary environment scenario, confirming that the test process has stopped (or canceling it and verifying termination) and preserving diagnostic test artifacts outside the sandbox are both predecessors of release_test_env_r18 in \((\CleanupGraphVertexSet,\CleanupGraphEdgeSet)\). Removing the unrelated local scratch directory forms an independent vertex with no edges to the environment release, provided no active test or pending evidence collection depends on it. The cleanup graph answers what must happen first, settlement rules determine what has been empirically verified, and admission control determines which operations may run next. The graph cannot be sequenced until provisioning evidence has bound its target, which is why figure 1 draws the release ordering beneath the registration step it depends on.






Figure 1: Registration Before Dispatch, Release After Evidence: The forward lane records the cleanup obligation before provision_test_env_r18 is sent, and binds env_r18_01 only when correlated evidence arrives; a lost reply leaves the obligation open with an owner instead of guessing a target. The dashed link shows the binding supplying the target of the registered cleanup. In the cleanup lane, release_test_env_r18 waits for its predecessors, and its own outcome either closes the obligation or remains owned, so no path ends in an assumed clean state.



Structuring cleanup as a DAG isolates failures and enables concurrent unwinding. An unresolved or failed cleanup node blocks only its transitive dependents in \((\CleanupGraphVertexSet,\CleanupGraphEdgeSet)\); independent recovery subgraphs can proceed immediately once their predecessors settle, their preconditions hold, and they clear admission control. Executing independent cleanup actions in parallel reduces overall recovery latency.
The cleanup graph enforces ordering without erasing historical accountability. Settled nodes retain their verification evidence, while failed or ambiguous nodes remain bound to their assigned owners. While an authorized administrator may deliberately accept residual risk to unblock downstream execution, the system never silently records an unconfirmed release as clean.



If an agent creates a cloud test sandbox during a common trajectory prefix before branching into three candidate test configurations, tearing down that sandbox when Candidate B fails would sabotage the active experiments in Candidates A and C. During tree search or multi-candidate exploration, branch ancestry tracks where model execution diverged, but it reveals nothing about which external resources each branch still claims.
The runtime therefore decouples resource ownership from logical branch history by tracking effects and cleanup obligations through reference-counted dependency graphs. When the runtime abandons a speculative branch, it reclaims only those resources owned exclusively by that branch, once its outstanding work has settled or stopped cleanly. Shared resources remain allocated until all surviving dependencies permit release. Furthermore, if an abandoned branch dispatched a provisioning request whose outcome remains unknown, that request stays recorded in the durable operation table; pruning a branch from the scheduler does not erase an unresolved external obligation.
Restoring a branch’s local workspace or context window does not rewind the external environment to the branch point, and evidence gathered from an abandoned candidate cannot be assumed valid for a sibling branch merely because they share an ancestor. During counterfactual execution, local workspaces can be rolled back to earlier checkpoints, but external networks, databases, and billing meters cannot. Enforcing this distinction ensures that speculative branch pruning never silently discards external recovery duties.


↩︎ Counterfactual branches, which replay a recorded prefix and then require fresh observations, are established in Counterfactual branches.

Checkpoint 12.1: Compensation obligations and dependency scope
Compensation is registered before dispatch and settled by evidence afterward. Each prompt places an obligation on one side of that boundary.

Registration: Provisioning returns its resource identifier only after creation. What must be recorded before dispatch, and what can be bound only afterward?
Unknown creation: Why does an empty resource lookup not justify closing cleanup while a provisioning request may still be delayed?
Cleanup outcome: Release is accepted but completion is unconfirmed. Which resource and charge obligations remain, and what evidence could settle each?
Cleanup graph: Draw the graph for four nodes: end the test, preserve artifacts, release the environment, delete unrelated private scratch. Which nodes can run in parallel, and which one waits if ending the test stays unresolved?
Branch scope: Two branches share an environment. Why does abandoning one branch not authorize releasing it or discarding its unresolved operations?



While semantic compensation systematically remediates partial effects, unwinding external work is not always the right response to a fault. When earlier steps have already built healthy, reusable state and a subsequent step fails before touching it, tearing those resources down wastes time and budget that a bounded in-place fix could preserve. Deciding whether to unwind or repair in place requires comparing the expected cost of forward correction against the expense of backward unwinding and rebuilding.




Take the branch in which provisioning evidence did arrive. The separately authorized operation provision_test_env_r18 has settled, binding the temporary integration-test environment env_r18_01. Before dispatching the integration test, the runtime validates the proposed test configuration and rejects it because a field requiring an integer contains a string. The candidate workspace remains ws_r18, and no integration test has started. Releasing the environment through release_test_env_r18 would discard expensive, fully functional preparation. Conversely, a bounded correction of the configuration can restore readiness without rebuilding the environment from scratch.
This situation differs from the unresolved test_r18 intent that the replacement worker recovered. When the runtime rejects a proposal before dispatch, it establishes definitive evidence that the executor never launched the action. A missing result under the settlement rule provides no such assurance; the operation might have succeeded, failed, or stalled midway through execution.
In dependable system design, forward recovery modifies the current state or repairs a proposed action to restore an admissible path toward completing the task. By contrast, backward recovery returns the system to an earlier saved state. The classical dependability taxonomy formalizes these strategies as rollforward and rollback, where rollback restores a previously captured checkpoint (Avizienis et al. 2004).3 Forward repair, the response family named earlier, is the agent runtime’s form of forward recovery, which keeps valid intermediate artifacts and corrects the proposal that failed. In an agentic system, restoring a workspace checkpoint performs backward recovery for the local filesystem and memory state that the checkpoint covers. External systems, however, rarely support true rollback, and compensation sits across the divide. In intent it is backward recovery, because it moves the environment back toward the pre-effect predicates of equation 2. In execution it is forward, a new operation with its own outcome, which is why the trajectory saga definition calls it new forward execution. It achieves semantic equivalence rather than physical restoration.
