The supervisor admits as many as standby permits, then prioritizes queued tasks over rebuilding the reserve. It can restore 2 instances concurrently, each taking exactly 15 ms to become ready under that concurrency. Assume sufficient execution slots for all tasks, no other arrivals, no lease returns during the calculation, and no restore failures. Handoff and dispatch time are negligible in this model; the restore interval includes the required readiness work.
Math: Initial admission consumes the reserve, leaving 12 − 4 = 8 tasks waiting. The workers serve those tasks in 4 rounds of 15 ms, so the last admission occurs at 60 ms. Rebuilding the original reserve takes another 2 rounds. The pool has its full reserve again at 90 ms, while all 12 admitted leases remain active. Admitting the burst finishes allocating the environments, but the trajectories themselves continue executing.
For an illustrative memory allowance at that final state, suppose immutable resident pages consume 1,000 MB shared across the pool. Each active instance has 64 MB of additional private resident state, and each standby has 8 MB. The resulting 16 instances each require 8 MB for monitor, page-table, and control state. Reserve another 256 MB of headroom. The budget is in decimal megabytes and sums the exact byte quantities.
1,000 MB shared + 768 MB active-private + 32 MB standby-private + 128 MB control + 256 MB headroom = 2,184 MB.
The private-state terms include resident writable workspace pages, so the workspace is charged once. Host and broker services, storage caches, disk, and accelerator memory sit outside this pool-residency allowance. Transient restore buffers must fit within the stated headroom, and enforcement uses exact byte counts.
Systems insight: The standby reserve governs instantaneous admission capacity, while restoration concurrency dictates queue drainage rate. The last admission waits \(\lceil (\BurstArrivalCount - \StandbyReserveCount)/\RestoreWorkerCount \rceil \, \InstanceReplenishTime\) for a burst of \(\BurstArrivalCount\) tasks, a reserve of \(\StandbyReserveCount\), and \(\RestoreWorkerCount\) restore workers. Using 4 workers instead of 2 therefore cuts the wait from 60 ms to 30 ms, provided restores do not slow under the added concurrency. Each added standby admits one more task immediately and costs 8 MB of idle private memory. The trace is deterministic; a different arrival pattern needs its own calculation.


An exhausted reserve must trigger explicit queueing, deferral, or rejection signals; it must never license the supervisor to lease an unreset or unverified sandbox to bypass admission bottlenecks. Admission control must also track physical resource headroom across active execution and background restoration. Instances awaiting teardown or memory scrubbing continue to occupy host memory and hypervisor tracking tables without providing usable standby capacity. Delays in resetting expired leases therefore represent hidden capacity drains that operators must measure alongside restore latency and trajectory duration.

Checkpoint 8.2: Sizing and reclaiming a pool
The pool equations and the reset contract answer each of these.

Active-lease estimate: Arrivals double while trajectories become half as long. Estimate the change in mean active leases, and name which term of equation 6 moves.
Reserve sensitivity: A cold boot replaces snapshot restore and takes an order of magnitude longer. Estimate \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\) from the inputs of Notebook 8.3 and compare the minimum reserves that meet the request-level miss target at the baseline and tenfold lead times.
Reset coverage: A reclaimed instance passed a scan for leftover files, but a daemon from the previous lease still holds a socket. Which state domain of table 7 failed, and may the instance return to standby?








↪ Repeated runs, confidence intervals, and paired comparisons for agents evaluated on this substrate are developed in Statistical Evaluation Rigor.

Jimenez, Carlos E., John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan. 2024. “SWE-Bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
When an evaluation harness or a reinforcement-learning rollout loop runs thousands of candidate patches against a repository’s native test suite, any leftover file from a prior attempt or any writable test script lets a candidate pass by corrupting the grader rather than fixing the bug. Benchmarks such as SWE-bench (Jimenez et al. 2024) and training rollout pools therefore rely on the same pooled sandbox lifecycle as production traffic. A pinned baseline snapshot and a verified reset prevent cross-attempt contamination, while read-only mounts keep the test harness outside the agent’s writable scope and leave the runner only bounded scratch storage and controlled logging channels. Even so, an evaluation team must separate execution containment from test quality. A clean sandbox guarantees that the test suite started from a known baseline. It does not guarantee that the tests cover the bug, or that external dependencies, non-deterministic timers, and floating-point drift will produce identical scores across runs. Whether the pool serves production, evaluation, or training, its guarantee has the same shape. It provides a contained execution with task-local continuity starting from a verified baseline. What happens inside that boundary, including which permitted channels the code uses and what it sends through them, lies outside that guarantee. A sandbox that passes every reset check can therefore still host a task that discloses what it was allowed to read.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
Robust containment requires both a sound enforcement boundary and sufficient host capacity to sustain that boundary under load. When deploying agent sandboxes, engineering teams often confuse practical filtering heuristics with architectural guarantees, or mistake microbenchmark startup latencies for the true operational cost of isolation.

Fallacy: Removing dangerous names removes the process’s authority.
Stripping dangerous symbols from an execution namespace hides convenient entry points, but it leaves the underlying runtime authority intact (section 8.3). Reachable object graphs, open file descriptors, and native extensions remain within the interpreter’s shared address space. For example, a caller can traverse an ordinary reference like total.__globals__ to retrieve the supervisor’s unredacted module namespace from an allowed helper function. Rice’s theorem rules out a sound and complete semantic classifier for unrestricted programs; it does not cause this reachable-reference escape or prohibit conservative safe subsets. While a specialized, deliberately restricted language can enforce safety invariants through its own formal semantics, executing untrusted code inside the supervisor’s process forces both into a single failure domain. True containment and resource limits must be enforced by the host operating system outside that interpreter process.


Pitfall: Choosing an envelope from a platform label alone.
Architectural labels like “container” or “microVM” specify virtualization mechanisms, not actual security boundaries (section 8.5). While a container shares the host kernel and a microVM interposes a guest kernel beneath a hypervisor monitor, the true blast radius depends on how the runtime environment is configured: filesystem mounts, virtualized devices, egress network routes, control groups, and trusted helper daemons. The same user-space kernel changed its trusted file-access path between releases without changing its name (section 8.5.1), and a microVM given a writable host mount or an unfiltered network route exposes exactly what its label suggests it hides. Systems engineers must evaluate the complete execution configuration against specific threat models and operational workloads. Lower startup latency indicates a lighter initialization path, not stronger isolation.


Fallacy: The cost of strong isolation is its startup latency.
Snapshot restoration reduces guest startup overhead to milliseconds, 15 ms in the chapter’s illustrative profile. However, boot latency is rarely the dominant infrastructure expense. The primary cost of sandboxing stems from cumulative memory residency across the lease horizon. At an arrival rate of 2 trajectories per second and lease durations of 300 s, the pool averages 600 active leases. Even with copy-on-write page sharing, mean active guest pages plus the configured reserve occupy roughly 39.0 GB, compared to the 322.1 GB required by isolated private images (Notebook 8.3). Sandbox provisioning must be budgeted by memory-seconds per trajectory, a quantity that scales directly with the lease hold time \(\LeaseHoldTime\), rather than evaluated solely by boot time.


Pitfall: Treating an allowed destination as approval of everything sent there.
A network egress rule restricts traffic to approved remote endpoints, but it cannot verify whether the payload in a request body is safe (table 6). Credential brokering keeps long-lived tokens and secret keys outside the guest environment while still allowing sandboxed code to request operations against authorized services. Under this design, an agent can use an approved outbound channel to exfiltrate private task data or modify remote state without ever extracting a credential or escaping the sandbox envelope. Preventing this residual abuse is an information-flow and semantic authorization challenge, rather than a perimeter-bypass flaw in the network sandbox.


Fallacy: An empty workspace proves that a used envelope is ready for another tenant.
Files represent only one of the four state domains cataloged in table 7. Even if a cleanup script successfully wipes every file, lingering processes from double-forked daemons, abstract Unix domain sockets, kernel keyring credentials, or modified environment search paths continue persisting. Any leftover artifact across these state domains compromises the next tenant. Multi-tenant recycling demands an explicit reset contract that accounts for every state domain an incoming lease could inspect, destroys or reinitializes that state to a known golden baseline, and validates isolation before reassignment. Moreover, no local cleanup protocol can undo external side effects already committed to remote APIs during the lease.


Pitfall: Sizing the standby reserve from a restore time measured on an idle host.
Determining standby pool capacity from initialization benchmarks gathered on an unloaded system severely underestimates provisioning requirements. Reserve sizing is governed by the traffic intensity parameter \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\), where the request-level miss probability under the stated replenishment policy follows a steep Poisson tail. In the chapter’s illustrative profile, the selected reserve of 2 instances satisfies a 0.1 percent request-level miss objective only as long as snapshot restore completes in under 22 ms. If initialization degrades by a factor of 10×, as an unoptimized cold boot can, the required reserve jumps to 4 instances. Under burst traffic, concurrent VM restoration, host cache contention, and lazy demand paging across copy-on-write regions degrade \(\InstanceReplenishTime\) precisely when capacity is most critical. Sizing calculations must measure initialization latency under the target concurrency of the anticipated burst rather than in quiescent conditions (Notebook 8.4).

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
A sandbox is an enforceable contract defining the boundaries of execution. It specifies precisely which hardware and operating system resources untrusted code can touch, which platform components form the trusted computing base, and how long both the execution environment and its delegated privileges endure. Because these limits are enforced beneath the executing process, the boundary never depends on model compliance. However, strong isolation introduces concrete operational costs: every admitted trajectory incurs startup latency, memory footprint, and environment reset overhead. In the chapter’s README attack scenario, containment succeeds through architectural enforcement rather than prompt adherence. The injected command cannot read the host’s credentials or open a route to an unapproved destination, although the same instructions can still misuse a channel the task was permitted, as the submit_report request showed.
In the connection-pool repair scenario, this architecture preserves candidate patches and test artifacts while denying the agent access to the host account or the mutable state of concurrent tasks. The evaluation harness keeps validation suites outside the writable workspace, giving the test runner bounded scratch storage. This separation protects the integrity of gathered evidence, even though accepting the repair requires end-to-end evaluation beyond the targeted regression checks run against candidate r18. Table 8 summarizes the mathematical foundations established across the chapter, connecting access authorization and boundary overhead to the queueing models that govern warm-pool capacity.



Table 8: Key equations of agent sandboxing: Each relation formalizes an access decision or provisioning boundary; the final four equations size warm sandbox pools from arrival rate, task horizon, and environment restore latency.

\(\StandbyReserveCount \ge \ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime + \StockoutNormalQuantile\sqrt{\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime}\)

\(\PoolResidentMemory = \TemplateSharedMemory + \ActiveLeaseCount \LeaseDirtyMemory + \StandbyReserveCount \StandbyInstanceMemory\)
Guest pages for mean active leases and configured standby
equation 6


\(\lceil (\BurstArrivalCount - \StandbyReserveCount)/\RestoreWorkerCount \rceil \, \InstanceReplenishTime\)
Wait of the last admission in a burst drained by \(\RestoreWorkerCount\) restore workers
section 8.8.3







Key Takeaways: Containment includes reach and lifetime

Execution environments define blast radius: Tool declarations specify intended interfaces, but the execution environment determines the files, sockets, and memory addresses a process can actually touch. The blast radius of an agent action spans everything its running code can read, mutate, exfiltrate, or consume. Consequently, robust isolation must be enforced by the operating system or hypervisor beneath the process.
In-process filtering cannot guarantee isolation: Code executing inside the supervisor’s runtime can reach the supervisor’s objects through attribute traversal and subclass walks, and native libraries share its address space and identity. The shown escape follows from shared object reach. A process or virtual machine boundary can govern that reach, while a purpose-built language can instead bound its operands, operations, and cost by construction.
Capabilities bound reach to what the task was handed: A capability binds authority to an unforgeable reference with an enforced lifetime instead of to ambient user identity. Attenuation can narrow a grant but never widen it, and deriving a child leaves the parent usable until the runtime withdraws it. Brokers let code request credentialed operations without holding the secret.
Envelope selection balances isolation against performance: Containers, user-space kernels, microVMs, and bytecode runtimes place trust boundaries at different system layers and pay the system-call tax on different calls. A call-heavy build favors a guest kernel over an emulating one. Retaining an envelope for the trajectory amortizes setup when the within-task trust policy permits reuse. A policy that requires fresh state between calls can justify per-call setup even when it dominates useful work.
Permitted egress channels create exfiltration risks: Network policies restrict unapproved endpoints, but permitted traffic, including API requests, artifact uploads, and DNS queries, can still carry sensitive task state outward. Once transport-level isolation is in place, safeguarding sensitive data becomes an information-flow tracking challenge.
Trajectory duration dictates pool capacity: By Little’s law, active sandbox leases scale with arrival rate and total trajectory length rather than individual tool execution time. Copy-on-write memory sharing can reduce the resident footprint of concurrent agent workloads. Strict reset contracts must scrub compute, storage, and network state before an instance returns to the standby pool.



Enforcing containment beneath the model (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}\)) ensures that execution boundaries remain intact regardless of model instructions or prompt injection attempts. This boundary complements the typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)), separating the admission of a tool request from the confinement of the code that fulfills it. Under invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)), these guarantees must reside below the model, in the supervisor and the envelope it configures, rather than in prompting guidelines. Ultimately, any isolation boundary protects only the specific resources its enforcement mechanisms monitor and reset across successive tool invocations.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
Running a stranger’s program on a machine that holds something valuable is the oldest problem in operating-system protection. In the 1960s, multiprogrammed mainframes forced systems designers to isolate mutually suspicious users sharing a single CPU and physical memory. Dennis and Van Horn addressed this challenge by introducing capabilities: unforgeable tokens that bundle the identity of an object with the explicit rights granted to operate on it (Dennis and Van Horn 1966). This design departed from ambient, identity-based permissions. Lampson’s access matrix (Lampson 1974) then placed capability lists and access control lists in one model. To enforce such policies, Anderson established the concept of the reference monitor, a compact, tamper-proof mechanism that must mediate every access request between a subject and an object (Anderson 1972). Saltzer and Schroeder subsequently synthesized these insights into an enduring canon of security design principles, establishing least privilege, complete mediation, and fail-safe defaults as non-negotiable engineering requirements (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). These principles apply directly to tool execution in agent runtimes, where tool code must never inherit the broad ambient authority of the host environment. Furthermore, Lampson recognized early that even when direct access is barred, confinement can fail through subtle covert channels that no designer intentionally provisioned (Lampson 1973). Hardy’s confused deputy (Hardy 1988) later gave ambient authority’s characteristic failure its name, and it reappears whenever an agent invokes external tools using ambient platform credentials.

Dennis, Jack B., and Earl C. Van Horn. 1966. “Programming Semantics for Multiprogrammed Computations.” Communications of the ACM 9 (3): 143–55. https://doi.org/10.1145/365230.365252.

Anderson, James P. 1972. Computer Security Technology Planning Study. ESD-TR-73-51. Deputy for Command; Management Systems, Electronic Systems Division, Air Force Systems Command.

Kivity, Avi, Yaniv Kamay, Dor Laor, Uri Lublin, and Anthony Liguori. 2007. Kvm: The Linux Virtual Machine Monitor.

Kamp, Poul-Henning, and Robert N. M. Watson. 2000. Jails: Confining the Omnipotent Root.
Each isolation envelope examined in this chapter descends from decades of mechanism design. Popek and Goldberg (1974) established the formal requirements for efficient, recursive virtualization, proving that all sensitive processor instructions must trap when executed in an unprivileged mode so that a virtual machine monitor can intercept and emulate them. For decades, commodity architectures like x86 violated these conditions because certain sensitive instructions failed silently rather than trapping. Hardware vendors resolved this deficit only when Intel (VT-x) and AMD (AMD-V) introduced hardware-assisted virtualization extensions with dedicated guest execution modes (Uhlig et al. 2005). Building on these CPU extensions, KVM integrated hypervisor capabilities directly into the Linux kernel, turning guest virtual machines into standard schedulable threads (Kivity et al. 2007). Along a parallel track, systems researchers pursued in-process isolation to eliminate hardware context-switching overhead. Wahbe and colleagues introduced software fault isolation (SFI), rewriting untrusted binary instructions to enforce memory safety within a single address space (Wahbe et al. 1993), an approach that WebAssembly later standardized into a portable, verifiable bytecode (Haas et al. 2017). Between hardware virtualization and language runtimes lies the shared-kernel lineage. System-call interposition initially promised lightweight confinement for unmodified binaries (Goldberg et al. 1996). Garfinkel, however, systematically cataloged the traps and pitfalls of user-level mediation, demonstrating how time-of-check to time-of-use races and incomplete kernel semantics inevitably compromise user-space monitors (Garfinkel 2003), which pushed security mediation back into the kernel. Concurrently, FreeBSD Jails partitioned a single kernel among mutually untrusted tenants (Kamp and Watson 2000), establishing the shared-kernel foundation that Linux namespaces and control groups later expanded into modern container runtimes. Capsicum proved that capability discipline could be retrofitted onto standard UNIX processes by restricting system calls and mediating access exclusively through file descriptors (Watson et al. 2010).
Multi-tenant cloud platforms subsequently transformed isolation into an engineering economics problem. Running untrusted, short-lived functions at high multi-tenant density exposed the memory footprint and startup latencies of conventional hypervisors. This friction drove the development of lightweight virtual machines that could boot in tens of milliseconds, matching container agility while preserving hardware-level isolation (Manco et al. 2017). Firecracker pushed this optimization further by stripping away legacy PC devices such as ACPI tables, IDE controllers, and PCI buses in favor of a minimal virtio device model and a lean, memory-safe implementation tailored specifically for transient workloads (Agache et al. 2020). To eliminate guest boot overhead entirely, systems engineers elevated microVM snapshotting and state restoration into a precise latency-engineering discipline. They found that the page faults that bring a restored guest’s memory in from disk dominate its startup, and they cut those faults by prefetching the working set each function touches (Ustiugov et al. 2021).

Manco, Filipe, Costin Lupu, Florian Schmidt, Jose Mendes, Simon Kuenzer, Sumit Sati, Kenichi Yasukata, Costin Raiciu, and Felipe Huici. 2017. “My VM Is Lighter (and Safer) Than Your Container.” Proceedings of the 26th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles (SOSP), 218–33. https://doi.org/10.1145/3132747.3132763.

Greshake, Kai, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. “Not What You’ve Signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection.” Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, 79–90. https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985.
Agent systems inherit this entire architectural foundation, but they overturn a core operational assumption. In conventional serverless platforms, an untrusted author uploads fixed code in advance, and the runtime executes that code across isolated, stateless invocations. In an agent runtime, by contrast, the untrusted author sits directly inside the execution loop: an autonomous model generates and executes code dynamically at each step of an iterative trajectory. This code is steered by external, untrusted content retrieved from web pages, databases, or third-party tools, content that an adversary can deliberately manipulate through indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al. 2023). Furthermore, while a serverless function discards its environment after a brief invocation, an agent maintains a mutable, stateful environment across an extended multi-step problem-solving sequence. This persistent lifecycle turns state isolation, residual-data scrubbing, and network egress control from occasional provisioning tasks into continuous operational requirements.

Saltzer and Schroeder (1975), The Protection of Information in Computer Systems. The classical foundation of security engineering. It defines the core principles of least privilege, complete mediation, economy of mechanism, and fail-safe defaults. Reading it today reveals how directly five-decade-old operating system principles govern modern agent sandbox design.
Lampson (1973), A Note on the Confinement Problem. A landmark three-page paper that defines confinement and formalizes how untrusted programs leak information across covert channels. This analysis provides the conceptual framework for modern egress filtering, rate limiting, and residual-state scrubbing in agent sandboxes.
Hardy (1988), The Confused Deputy. An influential case study demonstrating how ambient authority causes security boundaries to collapse when a privileged service executes tasks on behalf of an unprivileged requester. It remains the canonical justification for capability-based security, demonstrating why agent tools must receive scoped authorization tokens rather than ambient platform credentials.
Popek and Goldberg (1974), Formal Requirements for Virtualizable Third Generation Architectures. The foundational formalization of trap-and-emulate virtualization. It defines the precise conditions under which sensitive instructions must trap, establishing the theoretical guarantees that allow modern hypervisors and microVM boundaries to contain arbitrary guest code.
Garfinkel (2003), Traps and Pitfalls. An indispensable catalog of failure modes in user-level system-call mediation, analyzing race conditions, path aliasing, and the difficulty of tracking kernel state from user space. It remains an essential checklist for evaluating sandboxes built from ptrace or seccomp filters.
Agache et al. (2020), Firecracker. The production architecture of a minimalist microVM monitor built in Rust for dense multi-tenant workloads. Read it for the concrete engineering trade-offs among device surface, boot latency, and memory overhead that dictate how to size and manage an agent sandbox pool.


Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.

Agache, Alexandru, Marc Brooker, Andreea Florescu, Alexandra Iordache, Anthony Liguori, Rolf Neugebauer, Phil Piwonka, and Diana-Maria Popa. 2020. “Firecracker: Lightweight Virtualization for Serverless Applications.” Proceedings of the 17th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 20), 419–34.

title: 8 Agent Sandboxes
text:
All givens below are hypothetical problem inputs, not measurements of any product. Decimal units apply throughout these problems (1 GB is \(10^9\) bytes and 1 KB is \(10^3\) bytes), while configured guest memory in the worked notebooks is a binary capacity quoted in conventional megabytes, so a problem’s answer need not reproduce a notebook value digit for digit.
Problem 1 (Basic): Splitting a repair grant across test shards. A repair task holds \(\RepairCapabilityGrant = (\GrantRights=\{\text{read}, \text{write}, \text{execute}\},\ \mathcal{O}_\CapabilityGrant=\texttt{repo/},\ \GrantCondition,\ \GrantExpiryTime=\GrantIssueTime_0 + 900\,\text{s})\), where \(\GrantCondition\) binds use to this task and carries an aggregate budget of 600 CPU-seconds. The controller proposes three children for parallel test shards: \(\TestsDirectoryShardGrant = (\{\text{read}, \text{execute}\},\ \texttt{repo/tests/},\ 250\ \text{CPU-s},\ \GrantIssueTime_0 + 600\,\text{s})\), \(\WholeRepositoryShardGrant = (\{\text{read}, \text{execute}\},\ \texttt{repo/},\ 200\ \text{CPU-s},\ \GrantIssueTime_0 + 1200\,\text{s})\), and \(\SourceWriteShardGrant = (\{\text{read}, \text{write}\},\ \texttt{repo/src/},\ 200\ \text{CPU-s},\ \GrantIssueTime_0 + 600\,\text{s})\). (a) Apply the component-wise attenuation check to each child and decide which may be issued. (b) The parent keeps 150 CPU-seconds for its own work. Decide whether the valid children fit the aggregate budget, and whether they would still fit if \(\WholeRepositoryShardGrant\) were corrected to expire at \(\GrantIssueTime_0 + 900\,\text{s}\). (c) At \(\GrantIssueTime_0 + 700\,\text{s}\) a shard holding \(\TestsDirectoryShardGrant\) requests execute on repo/tests/run.sh. Evaluate equation 1 term by term and state the verdict.
Problem 2 (Basic): Resident memory of a repair pool. A platform admits repair trajectories at \(\ArrivalRate = 0.25\ \text{s}^{-1}\), each holding its lease for \(\LeaseHoldTime = 1600\,\text{s}\). The shared template occupies 0.5 GB, each active lease writes 96 MB of private pages, three standby instances hold 16 MB each, and a full private guest image would be 0.5 GB. The pool host has 64 GB for sandbox residency. (a) Compute \(\ActiveLeaseCount\) and \(\PoolResidentMemory\) by equation 6, and compare with private images. (b) Trajectories double in length. Recompute \(\PoolResidentMemory\) and decide whether the host still fits. (c) If it does not, find the largest admission rate the host supports at the longer horizon and state the admission policy that enforces it.
Problem 3 (Basic): Paying the system-call tax on a build. An untrusted dependency build performs 30 s of useful computation and issues \(2 \times 10^{6}\) system calls, of which \(5 \times 10^{4}\) touch a virtual device. Take these per-call costs as givens. A shared-kernel container pays \(\PrivilegeTrapTime = 0.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) and \(\SystemCallFilterTime = 0.05\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) on every call. A user-space kernel pays \(0.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) trap, \(1.5\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) emulation, and \(2.0\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) switch on every call. A microVM pays a \(0.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) native trap on ordinary calls and \(5.1\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{s}\) in total on each device call. (a) Using equation 3, compute each envelope’s added time and its overhead relative to the useful work. (b) Find the system-call count at which the user-space kernel’s overhead reaches 10 percent. (c) The build holds no credentials but runs code nobody reviewed. Choose the envelope and justify the choice by both cost and trusted components.
Problem 4 (Intermediate): Guard checks for the remediation agent. The remediation agent attaches a model-written guard to each proposed configuration change, such as p99_ms < 400 and error_rate < 0.01. The supervisor, which holds the agent’s production-change credentials, evaluates the guard on 500 service samples per second, with a 10 ms deadline per sample and a budget of 0.5 CPU cores for guard checks. Three options are available. The first is an in-process evaluator for a purpose-built expression language whose only operands are the supplied metric values and numeric literals. The language offers arithmetic, comparisons, and, and or, with no attribute access, subscripts, calls, or loops, and at most 200 syntax nodes at no more than 0.2 µs each. The others are a fresh bytecode sandbox per sample (0.5 ms setup) and a fresh microVM per sample (20 ms setup). (a) Compute each option’s worst-case time per sample and the CPU cores it consumes, and decide which options meet the deadline and the budget. (b) The agent asks for a matches(line, pattern) operator over log lines of up to 200 characters. A backtracking matcher can take \(2^\AdversarialInputLength\) steps of 10 ns on an adversarial \(\AdversarialInputLength\)-character input. A linear-time automaton matcher, with patterns capped at 100 states, takes at most one 10 ns step per state per character. Compute the backtracking time on a 40-character line and the longest input that stays within the evaluator’s 40 µs bound, then the linear matcher’s worst case and the resulting CPU cores. Decide which matcher, if either, may run inside the supervisor, and explain why the supervisor cannot simply stop a runaway match. (c) The agent next proposes replacing guards with a model-written Python script that parses the last minute of logs through a native parsing library, running once per minute with 2 s of useful work. Test the script against each condition that made the guard safe to evaluate in-process, choose its envelope and whether to start one per run under a 10 percent setup cap, and state which authority that envelope may hold.
Problem 5 (Intermediate): Per-document envelopes for the research agent. The research agent parses 400 retrieved pages while answering one question, each parse needing 2 ms of useful work and no filesystem or network access. The task requires mutable parser and module state from each independently hostile page to be inaccessible to the next; sharing a trusted read-only baseline is permitted. The options are a fresh bytecode sandbox per page (0.5 ms setup), a fresh microVM per page (20 ms setup), or one microVM retained for the whole question (20 ms setup once). (a) Compute the elapsed setup plus work for each option and each option’s setup share of a fresh call. (b) For a cap of \(\SetupShareCap = 10\) percent, compute the minimum per-call work for each fresh-per-call option. (c) The retained microVM is fastest. Apply the stated freshness requirement to decide whether the retained microVM is eligible, and decide which option to deploy even though it misses the 10 percent cap.
Problem 6 (Intermediate): Sizing the reserve under load, not at idle. A repair pool receives offered Poisson requests at \(\ArrivalRate = 0.5\ \text{s}^{-1}\) under the no-loss, constant-lead-time replenishment policy of section 8.8.3, with a request-level miss target \(\StockoutProbabilityTarget = 10^{-3}\). Snapshot restore takes 40 ms on an idle host but 200 ms at the restore concurrency a burst produces. (a) For each restore time, compute \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\) and the smallest reserve whose Poisson tail at or above the reserve meets the target. (b) Find the largest \(\InstanceReplenishTime\) each of the reserves one and two tolerates. (c) Evaluate the normal approximation of equation 5 at the loaded mean, explain why its answer should not be trusted here, and decide the reserve to provision.
Problem 7 (Intermediate): Draining a burst of repair tasks. A continuous-integration trigger releases forty repair tasks at once into a pool holding eight standby instances. With up to four concurrent restore workers each restore takes 25 ms; with eight workers restores contend and each takes 40 ms. Queued tasks take precedence over rebuilding the reserve, and each standby holds 16 MB of private memory. (a) Compute the last admission’s wait and the time at which the reserve of eight is rebuilt with four workers. (b) The platform requires every task in such a burst to start within 100 ms. Decide whether doubling the workers meets the requirement. (c) Find the smallest reserve that meets it with four workers, its standing memory cost, and the time at which that larger reserve is rebuilt.
Problem 8 (Intermediate): When copy-on-write stops paying. An evaluation host starts sixty-four workspaces from a 6 GB pinned base; each task writes 150 MB of edits and build outputs, and the shared drive sustains 5 GB/s. (a) Compute provisioning payload and drive-time lower bounds for full private copies and for a copy-on-write view. (b) The test suite then modifies a 3 GB database fixture in place once per task, and the storage copies whole files on first write. Recompute the copy-on-write payload and its advantage over full copies. (c) Redesign the fixture’s storage so that the advantage returns, given that the tests touch 2,000 blocks of 64 KB. Compute the resulting payload, drive time, and advantage, and name one alternative that avoids copying altogether.
Problem 9 (Advanced): Admission latency for the support agent. The support agent runs each customer session in its own sandbox. At peak it receives offered Poisson sessions at \(\ArrivalRate = 40\ \text{s}^{-1}\) under the same no-loss, constant-lead-time replenishment policy, so eventual admitted throughput equals that rate. Each admitted lease lasts \(\LeaseHoldTime = 45\,\text{s}\), and a customer waiting for a sandbox counts against a 1 s first-response budget. Two provisioning paths exist: snapshot restore at 50 ms, or cold boot at 1.5 s. Use \(\StockoutProbabilityTarget = 10^{-3}\), a 0.5 GB template, 24 MB of private pages per active session, and 16 MB per standby. (a) Compute \(\ActiveLeaseCount\) and, for each path, \(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime\), the reserve from equation 5, and the smallest reserve from the exact Poisson tail at or above the reserve. (b) Compute \(\PoolResidentMemory\) for each path and the relative margin \(\StockoutNormalQuantile\sqrt{\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime}/(\ArrivalRate \InstanceReplenishTime)\). (c) Compare with Problem 2. Identify which term binds the repair pool and which binds the support pool, and recommend a provisioning path and reserve conditional on the declared policy. State why the miss target alone does not prove the 1 s end-to-end response budget, and identify the remaining response-work and waiting-time evidence needed.
Problem 10 (Advanced): Critique a rate-limited resolver. A design review proposes letting repair guests resolve any name under the package mirror’s domain subtree, limited to 20 queries per second, and claims the limit “bounds exfiltration.” Each query name can carry 120 base32 characters of attacker-chosen labels (5 bits each), and a trajectory lasts 1200 s. A legitimate dependency install needs about 400 lookups. (a) Compute the channel’s payload per query, its rate at the limit, the time to leak a 40 KB file, and the total a trajectory could leak. (b) Compute the query budget per trajectory that would hold leakage below 1 KB, and compare it with the install’s legitimate lookups. (c) State what the rate limit actually bounds, then redesign name resolution so the guest’s lookups stop being a channel while installs still work, and say which residual channel the redesign leaves.
Problem 11 (Advanced): Suspend the sandbox while the model deliberates. Extend Problem 2 at the doubled horizon (\(\LeaseHoldTime = 3200\,\text{s}\)). Each trajectory runs forty turns, and 70 percent of every lease is spent waiting for model calls. A proposal suspends the guest to the shared 5 GB/s drive at the start of each model call and resumes it after, writing and then reading its 96 MB of private pages every turn; suspended guests hold no host memory. (a) Compute the admission rate the 64 GB host supports with suspension, the admission rate at which the drive saturates, and the resulting gain over Problem 2(c). (b) Compute the lower bound on added resume latency per turn and per trajectory, and choose an operating admission rate that leaves the drive 20 percent headroom for provisioning traffic. (c) The binding constraint has moved. Name it, and list the reset-contract and authority conditions a suspended guest must satisfy (which work may be running, what happens to its broker sessions, and where its image may go) before the proposal can ship.

What’s Next: From contained code to a defended agentThe submit_report request that passed every boundary in this chapter is not an isolated gap. The same README text can persuade the model to place a private test fixture in the query of a permitted package search. The query reaches an approved registry, the broker keeps its credential, and the code never leaves its envelope, yet the registry receives information the task was never authorized to share. The README can also claim that the test suite passed, and no envelope stops the agent from recording that claim as evidence. Agent Security opens with these attacks through permitted operations and builds the runtime checks that decide which data may cross an approved boundary and which sources may justify a consequential decision.

title: 6 Long-Term Memory
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why does an agent that can search everything it has ever stored still act on the wrong facts?
A context window holds the working state of one model call, and retained attention state only accelerates computation over that same prefix. Neither decides what an agent should still know across sessions, system restarts, or extended operational horizons. Providing an agent with persistent memory requires an external storage architecture that can index varied experiences, retrieve relevant historical context without polluting active prompts, and resolve conflicting observations over time. However, semantic vector retrieval alone provides no temporal guarantees. Stale facts, superseded code versions, and contradicted preferences score just as highly in cosine similarity as fresh ground truth. The runtime must therefore treat every stored memory as a fallible claim that carries its provenance, the versions for which it holds, and an explicit path to invalidation. Reliability depends on keeping persistent state behind explicit consistency rules rather than trusting the model to reconcile contradictory historical evidence.

Learning Objectives

Classify persistent records by their source, evidential role, and relationship to derived search representations
Specify a retrieval contract that bounds access, returned content, resource use, and required freshness
Choose among pre-staged evidence, a direct read, and model-directed search from how much of the need the task names
Select retrieval methods for an information need, use a bandwidth floor to screen exact vector scans against a latency budget, and estimate multi-hop evidence against a serialized-token budget
Design a memory write policy for admission, correction, supersession, expiry, and deletion that keeps derived summaries from perpetuating a withdrawn claim
Explain version-aware exclusion and fallback without mistaking removal of stale candidates for complete fresh retrieval
Evaluate cross-session memory policies by task outcomes, update behavior, and total resource cost



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



Consider the repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) working on its connection-pool defect across several sessions. When the initial session terminates, the subsequent run must reconstruct the operational state: the candidate source tree at revision r18, the diagnostic failure observed at r17, the passing run of test_waiter_notified_on_return, the integration checks that remain unresolved, and an operational note indicating where to resume execution. None of this state survives inside a transient context window once the process exits. Persisting only the final summary message discards critical supporting evidence. Conversely, retaining raw message transcripts without explicit scope creates confusion. An agent reading an unannotated log can easily mistake an earlier failure under r17 for an error in the new candidate patch.



Durable State, closed by checking each retrieved record against its source.
Standard runtime mechanisms do not bridge this gap. Context engineering selects among information already staged for a single model call, while the inference serving system maintains key-value (KV) attention cache state purely to accelerate that computation. Although a prefix cache can outlive an individual request, it remains a derived acceleration structure for a compatible prompt prefix (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)), regardless of the storage medium holding it. Long-term memory addresses a different systems problem, preserving information that must govern decisions across distinct invocations. A durable memory system must explicitly resolve what records to retain, how to index and retrieve them efficiently, and how to update or invalidate them when external sources change. In the formal framing of The H·S·A Exposure Space, these records constitute durable State (\(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), persisting across session boundaries.
Architecting persistent memory for an agent requires solving three interconnected systems problems. First, the data model must establish explicit record roles that keep external sources, tool observations, and agent-authored notes strictly differentiated, ensuring that subsequent sessions recognize what evidence each record supports. Second, the system requires a retrieval contract. Regardless of the candidate generation mechanism, every read must report its query scope, the snapshot versions it admitted, and whether the search terminated cleanly or degraded under resource budgets. Third, the storage engine needs a write lifecycle that admits, updates, supersedes, expires, and deletes records while propagating those mutations to downstream indexes and summaries.
The chapter takes these problems in the order a read depends on them. Record roles come first (section 6.2), because every later indexing, retrieval, and invalidation policy depends on knowing what authority a stored record carries. The retrieval contract (section 6.3) then fixes what any read must specify and report, whatever index sits behind it, and the choice between pre-staged and model-directed retrieval (section 6.4) decides which component formulates the query. Three method sections match index structures to information needs, moving from names and syntax (section 6.5) through learned representations and fused rankings (section 6.6) to chains of related evidence (section 6.7). The write path (section 6.8) and storage invalidation (section 6.9) keep the store and its derived indexes truthful as sources change, and the final section (section 6.10) judges a complete memory policy by the tasks it helps finish across sessions.



When a multi-session repair agent stores repository source files, test execution logs, and its own progress notes in a single undifferentiated memory pool, a later session can easily treat an unverified hypothesis or an old r17 test log as current ground truth about the code. Those artifacts play different roles in the repair. The repository source defines what the code looks like at a given commit. An execution log records how a test behaved under specific runtime parameters against that commit. A progress note records only where the previous session planned to resume work. Retrieval strategies, cache validation, and deletion policies all depend on keeping these operational roles distinct.


Separating those roles begins with where each artifact originates. Version-controlled repositories, production databases, system configurations, and user profiles exist outside the agent’s execution loop, whereas raw environment observations, tool output traces, progress summaries, and speculative heuristics are produced during execution on top of those external sources, and search indexes are derived from both. Grouping all of them under the single label “agent memory” obscures the boundary between a verifiable source and a derived claim. Table 1 categorizes these records by their architectural role in the evidence chain.



Table 1: Roles of persistent records: These are roles in an evidence chain, not a hierarchy of storage devices or universal levels of trust. One record can serve more than one role.










Record role
Example
What a later use must preserve




Source record
src/pool.py at a specified revision; the user’s stated scheduling preference
The designated source, applicable version or scope, and access conditions


Observation or event log
The outcome of test_waiter_notified_on_return under recorded source, test, and configuration
What was observed, when, and under which conditions; gaps in the retained history


Agent-written memory
A progress note, session summary, or proposed repair lesson
Supporting records, uncertainty, intended scope, and the policy for correction or removal


Derived retrieval index
Search entries over source files, logs, or notes
Which source generation produced the entry and how changes affect its use






A source of record is the designated authoritative origin for a specific claim. For example, the Git tree serves as the source of record for a file’s contents at a particular commit hash, while an authenticated user message serves as the source of record for that user’s operational constraints. Establishing a source of record defines where any downstream assertion must be validated. It confers evidential provenance rather than correctness. A repository commit may harbor a regression, and an inline code comment may contain unauthorized instructions. Under the principle that authority stays with the source (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)), authority describes an evidentiary relationship between a claim and its origin, never an unconstrained permission grant. When an agent’s generated output drifts from its source of record, the output still binds whoever deployed the agent, as one tribunal made explicit in the case that follows. For a memory system, the further question is what happens when such an answer is kept and read again.

War Story 6.1: A support chatbot contradicts its policy page (2024)Context: In November 2022, following the death of his grandmother, passenger Jake Moffatt consulted the customer-support chatbot on Air Canada’s website regarding bereavement fares (Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia 2024). Air Canada’s formal bereavement policy, published on a separate page of the website, explicitly prohibited retroactive bereavement fare adjustments once travel was completed.
Mechanism: The chatbot erroneously informed Moffatt that he could purchase regular-fare tickets immediately and submit a bereavement refund claim within 90 days of ticket issuance, directly contradicting the airline’s published policy. When Moffatt submitted his claim, Air Canada denied it based on the static policy page. Before the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal, Air Canada argued that the chatbot was an independent legal entity responsible for its own actions.
Impact: The tribunal rejected Air Canada’s argument, finding that the chatbot was an integral component of Air Canada’s website and that the airline remained liable for all information published through it. Finding Air Canada liable for negligent misrepresentation, the tribunal ordered the airline to pay CA$650.88 in damages (representing the difference between the full fare and the bereavement rate), alongside interest and statutory tribunal fees.
Fix: The tribunal dismissed the assertion that customers must independently reconcile conflicting guidance across different website pages, holding that the airline was responsible for all information on its website, whether a static page or a chatbot supplied it.
Systems lesson: A generated response is a derived artifact, yet users and legal frameworks treat it as an authoritative corporate commitment. The engineering remedy is to stage the versioned source of record into the model call and constrain the answer to claims that text supports, which is the job of the retrieval contract developed below. Model fluency provides neither evidentiary validity nor legal protection.



Civil Resolution Tribunal of British Columbia. 2024. Moffatt v. Air Canada, 2024 BCCRT 149. CanLII.
Through the taxonomy of table 1, the published policy page functioned as the source of record, while the chatbot’s generated response was a derived artifact that diverged from ground truth. If a customer-support system logs its previous dialogue turns to inform future responses, those conversational turns become agent-written memory. They document past interactions, but they never constitute organizational policy. A store that kept the chatbot’s wrong answer and retrieved it for the next bereavement question would repeat the error with the apparent weight of precedent, unless the record carried its role as a derived answer and a link to the policy version it claimed to reflect.
Observation logs capture empirical execution history. When an agent tests a connection pool, an execution log showing a failure at revision r17 remains valid diagnostic history even after revision r18 resolves the bug. The subsequent passing run confirms that the specific reproducer succeeded under that exact environment configuration. An execution log provides primary evidence of what the system observed during a run, rather than proving the universal validity of any underlying program assertion. Retaining this historical record across machine restarts or worker failures requires durable persistence guarantees.


↪ Durable, replicated logs that survive worker and machine failures are developed in The Trajectory Log.
Agent-written memory synthesizes raw observations into structured artifacts for future execution steps, taking the form of scratchpad notes, session summaries, or learned heuristics. Condensing raw traces prevents repetitive computation and conserves context window capacity. However, summarization introduces its own failure modes, because compression can strip vital boundary conditions or fabricate causal explanations. For instance, the observation that the targeted reproducer passed at r18 is strictly justified by the execution log. In contrast, the generalized claim that connection-pool timeouts always stem from missed thread notifications asserts a universal rule that a single test execution cannot substantiate. Storing an unsupported generalization in a persistent database creates compounding errors in subsequent planning steps.
This divergence mirrors the foundational distinction from cognitive psychology (Tulving 1972) that agent architectures have adopted. Episodic memory captures discrete, time-stamped events anchored to specific execution contexts. Semantic memory stores generalized knowledge, rules, and abstractions extracted across multiple episodes. Procedural memory complements both by preserving executable workflows, tool scripts, and operational runbooks. In the terms of table 1, observation logs and episode summaries are episodic records, generated lessons and reference facts are semantic records, and reusable repair workflows represent procedural records. In an engineered system, semantic and procedural records are therefore derived artifacts whose epistemic validity depends entirely on the fidelity and scope of the underlying episodic records.

Tulving, Endel. 1972. “Episodic and Semantic Memory.” In Organization of Memory, edited by Endel Tulving and Wayne Donaldson. Academic Press.
A retrieval index serves as an auxiliary acceleration structure for locating information across storage tiers. Whether an index stores term postings, learned vector embeddings, or graph edges over source files, logs, and agent notes (structures this chapter develops in turn), an index only locates candidate records. When a search query matches an index entry, a high similarity score demonstrates lexical or semantic affinity to the query string, but provides no assurance of operational applicability to the current task. Operational applicability depends on whether the referenced record matches the current system state, schema revision, and environment constraints.



Consider the state of a code-repair agent immediately after it writes revision r18. If its vector or keyword index was generated from revision r17, a retrieval query for src/pool.py will return the unpatched file. While that record remains an accurate historical reflection of r17, serving it as current context leads the model to believe the bug persists, prompting redundant or conflicting edits. The staleness that context invalidation guards against thus extends beyond the active prompt into the persistent storage tiers that feed subsequent inference calls.


↩︎ Context invalidation, which withdraws a staged observation’s authority over current state once its source changes, is established in Context Invalidation.
Precomputing search indexes eliminates the need to scan large repositories or execution histories during inference. However, this optimization incurs an ongoing synchronization cost. Every update to a source file requires indexing new content and invalidating or evicting obsolete embeddings. Executing these updates synchronously blocks read or write operations, while background asynchronous indexing opens a lag window in which the index still answers from r17 although the file is already at r18. A query that arrives inside that window needs an explicit rule for what it may return, which section 6.9.2 supplies.
Conversational agents meet the same consistency problem in user state. A user who said “Schedule no meetings before 10:00 AM” later says “before 11:00 AM.” The two directives are nearly identical as text, yet their intent is mutually exclusive. A store that treats the second as a duplicate keeps the stale behavior, and one that appends it without retiring the first leaves a contradiction in every later prompt. Telling a complementary fact from a superseding one requires explicit lifecycle metadata, which the write path (section 6.8) supplies and carries to every derived index, alongside validation, time-to-live (TTL) expiration, and cascade deletion.
The read side comes first, because lifecycle metadata protects the agent only if every read reports it. A retrieval interface must therefore return candidate text alongside the provenance, version, and completeness information on which safe execution depends.




Diagnosing the connection pool’s stalled waiter requires both the current implementation in src/pool.py and the test telemetry associated with test_waiter_notified_on_return. A search across repository history can easily return both an r17 test failure and an r18 reproducer pass. While both records are genuine, they answer distinct questions: one documents the defect that triggered the investigation, whereas the other evaluates a candidate patch. Before choosing an index structure or a similarity metric, a system must specify what the agent’s next decision demands and what guarantees a returned record actually establishes.

Definition 6.1: Retrieval contract
A retrieval contract specifies the information requested, the permitted scope and resource limits of the read, and the provenance, applicability, and completion information returned with its results.

Significance: It ensures a bounded search result remains interpretable before that result enters the next model invocation. A misread or misattributed result exacts a double penalty in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2): its tokens consume prompt budget and inference cost during the attempt, while the mistaken decision it induces drives down the acceptance probability.
Distinction: Ranking algorithms merely score and order candidate items under a specific relevance heuristic. The retrieval contract establishes authorization boundaries, version constraints, serialization budgets, and explicit completion semantics.
Common pitfall: Mistaking an empty result or a truncated scan for definitive proof that the requested data does not exist.



This contract applies uniformly whether the agent executes an index search, a relational database query, or a direct filesystem read; it mandates no single storage layout or similarity threshold. It divides the work among three parties (figure 1). The runtime sets the request’s bounds, the retrieval service checks access and searches within them, and the result envelope reports status, provenance, and limitations before the runtime stages any evidence for the next model call.






Figure 1: The Retrieval Contract: The runtime sets the request’s scope, version requirement, and limits; the model may propose search terms but cannot widen those bounds. The retrieval service checks access, searches, and excludes inapplicable versions, and the envelope reports what was searched and whether the operation completed, returned a partial result, or was unavailable. Only then does the runtime stage selected evidence, with its source and version labels, within the payload budget.





A raw information need such as “find the notification logic” underspecifies the retrieval operation. It leaves undefined whether the caller requires the active workspace, an earlier Git revision, or a diff between them. It says nothing about which repositories the principal may access. It also ignores how many tokens the caller’s remaining context window can accommodate. As summarized in table 2, framing retrieval as a bounded request separates these operational constraints from the underlying index mechanics.

A version requirement differs from a wall-clock freshness heuristic. An index entry for revision r17 remains invalid as current r18 source code even if an indexing worker refreshed it seconds ago. Wall-clock TTLs merely trigger periodic reindexing, whereas explicit version tokens establish whether a cached representation strictly matches its underlying source snapshot. When the retrieval service cannot fulfill the requested version from its precomputed index, it must either fall back to an authorized direct read of the primary store or return an explicit incomplete status. Section 6.9 develops this trade-off once the index itself can lag its source.
Similarly, result-count, payload-size, and compute limits constrain different dimensions of system resource consumption. Ten complete source files consume far more serialized tokens than ten function docstrings, yet returning a single item might still require scanning millions of candidate records. The payload limit protects the caller’s downstream context window, search-work budgets (such as graph traversal caps or posting-list scan limits) constrain retrieval service compute, and execution deadlines prevent the agent runtime from blocking indefinitely. Client timeouts must also propagate cancellation signals to the underlying storage engines. Uncancelled background queries continue to consume backend resources and inflate total execution cost.



Returning bare text snippets from a search leaves the caller unable to tell whether the matches came from r17 or r18, or whether zero hits meant the symbol was absent from the repository or the query timed out halfway through the index. To keep search outcomes interpretable, a production retrieval service wraps matching records in a result envelope that specifies the repository scope and snapshot revision actually searched, the terminal execution status, and any operational constraints that qualify the results:

complete confirms that the declared search algorithm ran to conclusion under its stated semantics. It is a mechanical guarantee about the search performed, not a claim to have found every relevant fact.
partial indicates that the operation halted before exhaustive evaluation, explicitly recording the abort reason (such as an expired deadline, an unavailable index partition, or an output payload cap).
unavailable signals that the retrieval subsystem failed to return usable data, whether due to network partitions, authorization failures, or service crashes.

When an operation yields partial results or truncates output to respect payload limits, the envelope provides an opaque continuation cursor so subsequent bounded requests can resume paging without re-executing the entire query. Together with the terminal status, that cursor and envelope decide what the runtime may infer when a query returns zero hits, a rule this chapter calls the absence rule. An empty result proves nonexistence if and only if a fully completed exhaustive scan produced it, and even then only within the scanned scope and revision snapshot. A completed literal string search across the repository showing that a symbol does not occur in revision r18 meets this standard. A truncated or partial scan that returns zero matches proves nothing, because the target may reside in an unvisited partition. An approximate index (section 6.6.2) offers no absence guarantee even when it completes, because it deliberately skips most of the candidate space to save work. A result set that lacks the relevant record may reflect that skipped region rather than the record’s absence from the corpus.
At the item level, every returned record carries structured metadata alongside its raw content: a persistent URI or path, byte or line ranges, the exact source commit or snapshot identifier, and a content hash of the returned bytes. When an item represents an empirical observation, such as a test execution log, the record must document the runtime configuration, environment variables, test revision, and terminal outcome. If an item stores a derived lesson or summary synthesized by an agent in an earlier session, its envelope must link to the primary records supporting that inference and flag its status as a derived model output. If the retrieval engine attaches a relevance score, it must name the algorithm that produced it (a lexical ranking function, a vector similarity, or a learned reranker, each developed later in this chapter). Ranking scores exist on their algorithm’s internal scale; systems must not treat them as calibrated probabilities.



Listing 1: A serialized result envelope: The response-level fields report what was searched and how the search ended; each item carries its role, location, version, and hash beside its content. Symbolic values stand for settings and contents chosen by the runtime; the field names do not prescribe a storage API.

scope: {workspace: repair, principal: repair-agent, source_snapshot: r18}

    path: src/pool.py
    lines: [a, b]
    revision: r18
    content_hash: h18
    score: {method: lexical_rank, value: s}
    content: <slice of the return path>
  - role: observation
    test: test_waiter_notified_on_return
    revision: r17
    configuration: c17
    outcome: failed
    content: <recorded failure trace>



In the connection-pool repair task, the staged payload might pair a slice of src/pool.py from revision r18 with an error trace recorded under revision r17, as in listing 1. The fields outside the two content bodies count against the payload budget just as the bodies do. The r17 trace explains why the repair was initiated, but it provides zero evidence regarding the behavior of the r18 candidate. By packaging each record in an explicit envelope, the retrieval subsystem preserves these applicability distinctions across the boundary between persistent storage and the working context. Envelope labels, however, record provenance without certifying veracity. A cryptographic content hash verifies only that the byte sequence matches a specific snapshot. It does not validate the factual correctness of the text. Similarly, categorizing a record as user input or agent-written memory confers no administrative authority on any instructions embedded within that content.


↩︎ The scope rule and the untrusted span are established in Preserving source and scope.



Piping top-ranked retrieval hits straight from the search backend into the prompt lets uncalibrated similarity scores, stripped version labels, and uncounted metadata wrappers overrun the context budget or slip stale r17 excerpts into an r18 decision. The agent runtime, never the retrieval backend or a raw ranking score, therefore decides which records enter the downstream prompt: it selects evidence for the immediate decision, keeps the source and version tags needed to interpret each item, and accounts for the full serialized token footprint. Staging is where invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) reaches the durable read boundary. The bound below the model is mechanical, because a runtime rule rather than the model or the ranker decides what is admitted. The version labels the runtime preserves are the evidence a later acceptance check needs to tell an r17 observation from an r18 one. Even after those checks, retrieved records remain untrusted spans when fetched from a local repository, because serialization that separates them from system instructions cannot stop the model from following text embedded in a record body, the hazard known as prompt injection.


↪ Indirect prompt injection, delivered through retrieved documents and other observations an agent reads, is developed in Prompt injection entry points.
Accurate payload accounting must measure the entire serialized envelope, including wrapper tags, source paths, version identifiers, and status headers, alongside the raw text bodies. Underestimating this structural overhead leads directly to context exhaustion. The token count in notebook 6.1 shows how metadata overhead changes the number of complete records an agent can stage within a fixed prompt allocation.

Napkin Math 6.1: Making room for retrieved evidenceProblem: A hypothetical model call permits 32,768 tokens in total. Reserving 2,048 tokens for generation leaves the remainder for input. If baseline system prompts, tool schemas, and conversation history occupy 24,576 tokens, how many complete retrieval records can the prompt accommodate?
Math: The retrieval allowance is \(32,768 - 2,048 - 24,576 = 6,144\) tokens. Assume a 128-token response envelope and records that each contain 512 body tokens plus 64 metadata tokens, giving 576 tokens per record.
The maximum number of complete records that fit is 10. Staging these records alongside their envelope consumes \(128 + 10 \times 576 = 5,888\) tokens, leaving a remainder of 256 tokens, too few to hold another complete record.
A naive sizing policy that accounts only for raw document bodies would admit 12 records. When serialized with metadata and envelopes, however, those records require 7,040 tokens, overshooting the allocated retrieval budget by 896 tokens.
Systems insight: Metadata and envelope framing consume context capacity just as surely as document bodies. In this configuration, each record dedicates 64 of its 576 tokens to provenance, causing a body-only heuristic to overcommit the prompt by 2 records. The runtime must reserve capacity for output tokens and the global envelope first, then admit \(\lfloor(\text{allowance} - \text{envelope})/(\text{body} + \text{metadata})\rfloor\) records, remembering that every token assigned to system instructions or tool definitions shrinks the retrieval allowance one for one.


Because subword tokenizers (such as Byte-Pair Encoding) merge tokens across string boundaries, tokenizing text fragments in isolation and summing their counts yields an inaccurate total. Runtimes must measure token lengths on the final, fully serialized prompt structure using the target model’s tokenizer. When a critical record exceeds the remaining budget, the runtime must not silently truncate the text. Instead, it should stage a syntactically coherent excerpt with explicit truncation markers, defer the item to a subsequent retrieval pass, or return an opaque handle that the model can resolve on demand.
Every staged token also incurs concrete inference engine overhead beyond occupying space in the context window. Retrieved context must be processed through the model’s compute-intensive prefill phase and then pinned in accelerator memory as key-value (KV) cache tensors for the duration of the generation cycle or prefix cache retention window. Staging more records increases the token volume that the serving engine must process and retain, although the resulting prefill latency depends on the model, prefix reuse, and serving configuration. Every retained token counts against the resident-fit bound of the serving node’s KV pool, so a generous staging policy reduces how many trajectories the node can serve concurrently.


↩︎ The per-sequence footprint of key-value cache state, and how it limits the number of sequences a node can serve concurrently, is established in The Footprint of Retained Attention State.

Checkpoint 6.1: Interpreting a bounded result
Each question presents a retrieval outcome; decide what operational conclusions it licenses.

Stale excerpt: A query for current source returns an r17 excerpt after the workspace reaches r18. Which historical diagnostic inferences remain valid, and what must happen before the excerpt informs an r18 edit?
Deadline vs. completion: A search reaches its deadline with no matches. Which status does it return, and which conclusion that a completed literal scan of the same snapshot would support is unavailable here?
Payload estimate: If per-record metadata doubled from the value in notebook 6.1, how many complete records would fit the same allowance, and what must the runtime measure before dispatching the call?



The retrieval contract establishes the operational bounds, provenance requirements, and payload limits for each read, but it leaves open an architectural question, namely which component formulates the query. A runtime can predict needed evidence and pre-stage it before invoking the model, or it can equip the agent with search tools to probe the store interactively as discoveries unfold.




Predicting every file the repair agent will need before invoking the model either stuffs the prompt with irrelevant code or misses a helper dependency that becomes visible only after reading the first stack frame. Forcing the model to search interactively for files the task already named, however, wastes an entire inference turn on a predictable lookup. Two retrieval architectures divide this work differently. In a pre-staged architecture, the runtime predicts which artifacts will be necessary (such as src/pool.py, tests/test_pool.py, and a stack trace from a prior run) and injects them directly into the prompt before model execution begins. In an agentic architecture, the runtime equips the model with bounded text search, file reading, and symbol-navigation tools, allowing the agent to locate notification logic, inspect the test harness, and follow cross-file references as intermediate discoveries dictate. Both architectures operate over the same underlying storage systems and share identical security boundaries. They differ in when the information need is resolved and which component formulates the retrieval queries.
Pre-staging implements standard retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), where the host system selects external documents and packages them alongside the prompt before inference begins (Lewis et al. 2020). By contrast, agentic retrieval delegates query formulation to the model during the execution loop, interleaving environment observations with subsequent reasoning and action steps (Yao et al. 2023). Autonomous systems designed for repository-scale software engineering (Jimenez et al. 2024) rely on this interactive loop, because search and navigation commands shaped for code inspection prove far more adaptable than a single, static set of top-\(\RetrievalCutoffCount\) retrieved passages staged up front (Yang et al. 2024). Rather than mutually exclusive alternatives, these two patterns represent complementary policies operating over the same underlying data stores.

Jimenez, Carlos E., John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan. 2024. “SWE-Bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Yang, John, Carlos E Jimenez, Alexander Wettig, Kilian Lieret, Shunyu Yao, Karthik Narasimhan, and Ofir Press. 2024. “SWE-Agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems.
That trade-off sets the operating envelope of each policy. When the required files are known from the task description or project layout, pre-staging them into the initial prompt avoids spending a full model turn on discovery. When a failing assertion in tests/test_pool.py names an internal helper whose definition resides in another module, model-directed search lets that intermediate observation shape the next query instead of guessing the transitive dependency graph up front. Interactive exploration, however, introduces its own failure modes: an agent can chase unpromising leads, issue redundant searches across familiar directories, or stop probing before gathering enough evidence to verify a fix.
Before introducing an auxiliary index, such as an inverted text index or a vector store, an engineer should benchmark against a live-source baseline. Bounded substring searches and direct file reads inspect the target workspace directly on disk, introducing no external index that can lag behind ongoing edits. When a problem description already specifies exact filenames or literal error strings, these live-source primitives often supply all the retrieval capability the agent requires. Direct filesystem access, however, presents distinct systems trade-offs. Live reads observe whichever version of a file exists at the exact moment of execution. If concurrent processes modify the workspace, separate reads executed across successive turns can straddle modifications and observe inconsistent snapshots. Furthermore, raw literal searches locate character matches without semantic awareness, failing to distinguish an active symbol definition from an obsolete comment or an unrelated log message. An auxiliary index justifies its memory footprint, construction time, and synchronization overhead only when it earns them back. It measurably amortizes repetitive scanning costs across long trajectories, resolves vocabulary mismatches through semantic embeddings, or accelerates traversal over structural relationships such as call graphs derived from abstract syntax trees (ASTs). An evaluation must charge the cost of building and refreshing the index directly against its query-time savings. The chapter prices that charge at its end, once lexical, dense, and graph indexes are in hand (notebook 6.5).
When an agent probes its environment, the runtime can optimize query execution through parallelism. A single model turn can emit several independent tool calls that the runtime batches or executes concurrently across threads. Only queries that strictly depend on earlier observations must block for sequential resolution. Table 3 summarizes the core trade-offs between runtime pre-staging and model-directed probing.
