def completed_candidate(envelope):
    if envelope["status"] != "COMPLETED":
        raise ValueError("Response is not a completed candidate")
    # Syntax, permission, and task evidence remain unchecked.
    return envelope["payload"]



Incomplete payloads go to a diagnostic log with its own storage and access limits, keeping the partial byte stream and stop_reason for debugging. “Repairing” a truncated fragment by appending guessed arguments or closing braces invents a new candidate that the model never completed, and such patched fragments must never be marked COMPLETED.



Waiting for a four-thousand-token response to finish before checking its structure wastes seconds of accelerator time when the first key violates the tool schema. Streaming delivers response fragments over the connection as generation proceeds, letting the runtime inspect prefixes early, provided its parser follows the provider’s framing protocol rather than assuming each network chunk holds one token. When an arriving prefix violates the required format, the stream monitor stops waiting immediately instead of buffering the rest of an unusable reply. Because generation is still in flight, the monitor checks whether the prefix can still be completed into a valid structure, not whether it is already complete.
Rejection and cancellation are distinct events. When the stream monitor spots a structural violation, the runtime sets the status to REJECTED and sends a cancel request to the service. When an operator or runtime policy aborts a compliant stream before completion, the runtime marks the status CANCELED. A local deadline that expires before completion maps instead to TRANSPORT_FAILURE (table 2), after which the runtime may also send a cancel request. Keeping the partial payload out of tool dispatch is a local guarantee the host enforces in all three cases. Stopping the remote decode loop and freeing accelerator memory, however, depends on the serving engine honoring the cancel signal; merely closing a client socket does not prove that remote decoding stopped.
Consider a call with an output allowance of 4,096 tokens whose stream validator detects a schema violation at step \(\RejectionDecodeStep =\) 96. The runtime’s part of the response finishes at once. It records the rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The service’s part depends on whether that request is honored (figure 3).






Figure 3: Reject, Then Cancel: The runtime’s stream validator advances a parser state as each prefix arrives and holds the output rather than acting on it. At step 96 the proposal introduces a key outside the schema, so the runtime records a rejection, discards the partial proposal, and sends a cancel request. The runtime outcomes on the left hold regardless of the service; the service outcomes on the right hold only if the service receives and honors the cancel request.



The skipped-step count shown is an upper bound that requires provider cooperation. If the serving engine processes the cancellation promptly, it skips up to \(\OutputLimit - \RejectionDecodeStep =\) 4,000 autoregressive decode steps. In the reference unbatched deployment, each plain autoregressive decode step reads the model weights from accelerator memory, so the step takes at least the weight bytes divided by the memory bandwidth; for the reference deployment of section 2.8, that floor is 21.075 ms per generated token. At that reference floor, skipping all these steps avoids 84.3 s of estimated decode work. An honored cancellation also frees the request’s slot among the requests the serving engine decodes together and releases the call’s KV-cache allocations. If the remote service fails to honor the cancellation, the host runtime still quarantines the rejected payload locally, but the remote service may continue generating up to its token allowance.
Nonstreaming calls apply the same status gate once the whole response arrives. Streaming moves the check earlier in the call so the runtime can reject bad prefixes and reclaim resources sooner, without relaxing the rule that incomplete prefixes never run. Either way, the status gate settles only whether a complete candidate arrived. A COMPLETED read_file proposal can still name a missing file or a path outside the workspace, so the next question is what each subsequent check on that candidate actually proves.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
Passing the status gate admits a completed proposal to the candidate path, whether that proposal is the initial read_file("src/pool.py") request or the connection-pool patch the repair agent emits on the next turn. Neither high token probability nor schema conformance determines whether the runtime can safely act on either candidate: a well-formed read_file request can still target a missing or unauthorized path (section 2.2.2), and a candidate patch can parse cleanly, compile against existing headers, and pass a sequential unit test while leaving the underlying race condition untouched. Because each verification check answers a narrow question rather than certifying overall task satisfaction, the runtime must track what each gate actually proves and what it leaves open.


A model often assigns high probability to an obsolete or nonexistent file path because that path matches common directory naming patterns in its training corpus. Autoregressive generation scores tokens by how well they fit training data and prompt context, not by whether a path exists on disk, whether the caller has permission to read it, or whether an edited function preserves a lock invariant.
Checking a candidate therefore means pairing each required property with the tool or gate that actually tests it. For a read_file proposal, a schema validator checks that the payload has only allowed keys and a string-valued path. Passing that check proves schema conformance, provided the validator implements the schema dialect faithfully and inspects the exact object passed to execution. Proving that the target file exists requires checking the filesystem, and proving permission requires checking the task’s capability grant against the host policy.
Static checks and dynamic tests likewise establish different claims. A compiler checks types and syntax under fixed flags, while a linter flags suspect patterns with static rules. Dynamic tests run concrete code paths and check runtime assertions, so a passing single-threaded checkout test says nothing about how the connection pool behaves under concurrent contention.


↩︎ The closure evidence levels, from self-report and static checks through visible and sealed tests to formal proof, are established in The invariant closure principle.
8 Complete Mediation: One of the design principles that Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) set out for protection systems: every access to every object is checked against current authority at the moment of access, not remembered from an earlier decision. The tool handler applies the same rule to a model’s proposal, so a path validated when the request was composed is checked again when the read executes, closing the gap in which the grant or the file could have changed. 
Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.
Because each check covers only its own scope, the runtime must treat model output as untrusted data rather than executable control flow. A candidate tool call stays passive data until an authorized tool handler validates and dispatches it, checking permissions at the moment of access8 regardless of what the model claims about its own rights. Running an untrusted code patch likewise executes arbitrary machine instructions and belongs inside an isolated sandbox even during early test runs.



Asking a model to review or refine its own patch can catch surface syntax mistakes or missing edge cases, yet self-review is just another generation step drawn from the same weights and conditioned on the same incomplete context. When the model starts from a mistaken assumption about an API or lock protocol, prompting it to critique its own answer usually repeats that assumption rather than catching it. Re-prompting does not create an independent check: across reasoning benchmarks, models asked to grade and revise their own answers without new external evidence rarely improve accuracy and often turn right answers into wrong ones (Huang et al. 2024).

Huang, Jie, Xinyun Chen, Swaroop Mishra, Huaixiu Steven Zheng, Adams Wei Yu, Xinying Song, and Denny Zhou. 2024. “Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Zheng, Lianmin, Wei-Lin Chiang, Ying Sheng, Siyuan Zhuang, Hao Wu, Yonghao Zhuang, Zi Lin, et al. 2023. “Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36: 46595–623.
Refining a candidate and certifying a property must therefore stay separate. A model’s critique can guide the next search step, but external tools (compilers, linters, sandboxed test runners, and kernel permission checks) must supply the evidence for the properties they test. No model critique, whether from the generator itself or from a separate learned judge (a second model prompted or trained to score the first model’s output), carries authority to clear a security boundary or approve a release. When a pipeline uses a learned judge to rank or filter candidates, the runtime should treat its verdicts as noisy scores with measurable false-accept rates and known biases, such as favoring longer answers or particular list positions (Zheng et al. 2023). Even when a check returns a passing verdict, a conditional-probability calculation shows how much defect risk remains when the checker itself can pass a defective patch.

Systems Perspective 2.1: What a passing verdict leaves unresolvedLet \(\CandidateDefectRate\) denote the defect rate, the share of generated patches that violate a specified behavioral property (a local symbol here, distinct from the per-turn error rate of horizon compounding), and let \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) denote the checker’s false-accept rate, the probability that it passes a defective patch. Suppose \(\CandidateDefectRate =\) 18 percent, \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate =\) 0.65, and the checker passes valid patches with probability 0.85. Bayes’ rule gives the fraction of defective patches among the passing results:
\[\Pr(\text{Defective} \mid \text{PASS}) = \frac{\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate \cdot \CandidateDefectRate}{\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate \cdot \CandidateDefectRate + \Pr(\text{PASS} \mid \text{Valid}) \cdot (1 - \CandidateDefectRate)} \tag{4}\]
Substituting the assumed rates gives \(\frac{0.65 \times 0.18}{(0.65 \times 0.18) + (0.85 \times (1 - 0.18))}\approx 14.37\%\). The defect share among passing patches falls only from 18 percent to 14.37 percent, because the checker rejects 35 percent of defective patches while also rejecting 15 percent of valid ones. The lever is \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\): a checker with half the false-accept rate, 0.325, lowers the residual to 7.7 percent. Repeating the same check buys no such guarantee, because its behavior on the surviving candidates is correlated with the first pass. Every defective patch that passes also inflates the apparent acceptance probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2).
A sound checker for the exact property drives \(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\) to zero under its assumptions. Determinism alone does not supply soundness, and soundness for schema membership does not extend to patch behavior. The residual in equation 4 is one minus the precision \(\VerifierPrecision\) of a passing verdict in the verification asymmetry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-verification-asymmetry}\)), written there with valid-candidate rate \(\ValidCandidateRate = 1 - \CandidateDefectRate\) and false-reject rate \(\VerifierFalseRejectionRate = 1 - \Pr(\text{PASS} \mid \text{Valid})\). That principle holds that producing a candidate, selecting it, and establishing that it satisfies the task are different events, and it yields a design rule. Select each validation gate for the specific property it establishes and its false-accept rate, and let the task contract determine what residual defect rate the system can tolerate.





Running full end-to-end integration tests or sandboxed reproduction scripts on every model output is orders of magnitude more expensive than parsing JSON or running a static linter. The runtime therefore stages candidate checks from cheapest to most expensive, rejecting malformed or unauthorized requests early before spending compute on behavioral tests. Ordering checks by cost improves throughput, yet each gate tests a different property rather than a tighter approximation of overall correctness. Table 3 lists these four layers along with what each costs and what its passing result leaves open.



Table 3: Scoped candidate checks: A passing result supports a named claim, not every property needed for task acceptance. The runtime preserves these distinctions when composing the checks.












Verification layer
Gate mechanism
Property or evidence
Cost to account for
Limit of the claim




Syntax and schema
Parser and schema validator
Required fields, supported types, and declared value constraints
Parsing and validation
Does not establish permission or correct values beyond the schema


Authorization
Task permission check and enforcing tool handler
Requested operation and target fall within the current grant
Policy lookup and mediation
Permission does not establish that the operation serves the goal


Static analysis
Compiler, type checker, or linter
Properties covered by the selected analysis and configuration
Analysis of the candidate and its dependencies
Coverage depends on the checker and language assumptions


Behavioral evaluation
Controlled execution and designated tests
Observed outcomes for the exercised inputs and conditions
Environment preparation and execution
Passing cases do not establish untested behavior






Consider how this pipeline handles an inspection request versus a patch. Behind the status gate of section 2.5, a read_file proposal needs only the first two rows of table 3 before dispatch, because reading the file supplies an observation for the next turn rather than finishing the repair. When evaluating a proposed patch, by contrast, the pipeline checks patch syntax and target paths, applies the diff in an isolated scratch workspace, and runs the required unit and stress tests. Final acceptance follows the task contract’s evidence standard, escalating to human review when automated checks cannot settle safety or correctness.
Every layer in table 3 inspects tokens the model has already emitted. Even when a streaming monitor aborts a broken response early, the offending token has already been chosen, and recovering still requires another call. For the first layer of that cascade, syntax and schema conformance, the runtime knows the legal structure before decoding begins and can enforce it inside the sampler itself.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
If the repair agent’s read_file("src/pool.py") call omits the closing quotation mark before emitting an end-of-turn token, the schema validator in table 3 catches the malformed JSON and blocks dispatch, but recovering still costs another full round of queueing, prefill, and decoding. Because the request already declares the tool schema ahead of time, the inference engine does not need to wait for an illegal token to arrive at the parser; it can mask out every vocabulary token that would violate the required syntax at each decode step, so a syntax error cannot be sampled in the first place.

Definition 2.3: Grammar-constrained decoding
Grammar-constrained decoding restricts next-token selection during autoregressive generation to tokens whose decoded text preserves a viable prefix of a target formal grammar.

Significance: Dynamic token masking guarantees that any completed generation sequence strictly satisfies the structural grammar, eliminating syntax errors at the model boundary when the constraint parser covers the target schema.
Distinction: Post-generation validation inspects an already emitted sequence and discards invalid payloads after full generation. Constrained decoding actively shapes the vocabulary distribution at every generation step. Even so, neither approach verifies whether a syntactically correct payload contains sensible parameter values or possesses valid execution permissions.
Common pitfall: Mistaking a viable prefix for a completed data structure. If token limits, request timeouts, or connection failures truncate generation early, the emitted sequence remains an unfinished prefix that cannot be safely dispatched.





If a model emits an unquoted identifier or a stray comma after {"path":, the entire JSON payload breaks and no later token can repair it. To block illegal tokens before they are sampled, the constraint engine keeps a running parse state synchronized with the sequence generated so far. For a schema expecting a string-valued path parameter, once {"path": appears in the buffer, the grammar allows optional whitespace followed by an opening quotation mark, and forbids unquoted booleans, numbers, or bare identifiers. When the generator emits {"path":"src/, the text is a viable prefix:9 although incomplete as a JSON document, it can still be completed into a valid object by later string and delimiter tokens. Constrained decoding admits a candidate token only if it can extend the current prefix toward an accepting grammar state.
9 Legal (Viable) Prefix: The viable-prefix concept comes from classical compiler theory. The LR parsers introduced by Knuth (1965) read input strings left to right and report an error at the first symbol that cannot extend the prefix into any valid sentence of the language. A grammar mask applies the same property constructively, pruning invalid tokens from the vocabulary before sampling instead of catching syntax errors after generation finishes. 
Knuth, Donald E. 1965. “On the Translation of Languages from Left to Right.” Information and Control 8 (6): 607–39. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-9958(65)90426-2.
At generation step \(\TokenIndex\), let \(\DecodingConstraintState_t\) represent the parser’s internal state, including nested scope tracking for recursive structures. Let \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\) denote the set of vocabulary tokens whose decoded strings maintain a viable prefix under the target grammar. Because modern language models operate on subword tokens rather than individual characters, a single token can span multiple characters, punctuation marks, or whitespace segments (for example, a single token .py"} that finishes the extension, closes the string, and closes the object). The engine must therefore simulate the parser across the token’s full decoded byte sequence to confirm that every character transition is valid.
For each token index \(\MaskTokenIndex\) in vocabulary \(\TokenVocabulary\), the constraint engine constructs an additive logit mask:
\[\LogitMaskEntry_i(\DecodingConstraintState_t) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \in \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \\ -\infty & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \notin \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \end{cases}\]
Adding this mask to the unnormalized logit vector \(\LogitVector_t\) produces the filtered logit vector \(\MaskedLogitVector_t = \LogitVector_t + \LogitMask(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\). At unit temperature, the resulting softmax distribution becomes
\[\SoftmaxOutputProbability_{t, i} = \frac{\exp(\MaskedTokenLogit_{t, i})}{\sum_{j \in \TokenVocabulary} \exp(\MaskedTokenLogit_{t, j})} = \begin{cases} \frac{\exp(\OutputLogit_{t, i})}{\sum_{k \in \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)} \exp(\OutputLogit_{t, k})} & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \in \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \\ 0 & \text{if } \MaskTokenIndex \notin \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t) \end{cases} \tag{5}\]
Setting the logits of invalid tokens to \(-\infty\) forces their sampling probabilities to zero, renormalizing the distribution entirely across viable continuations. Once the sampler draws a token from this restricted set, the engine consumes that token’s characters and advances the parser to state \(\DecodingConstraintState_{t+1}\). This formulation assumes that \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\) remains nonempty and that the sampling configuration respects the mask. The engine applies the mask before top-\(\TopTokenSampleCount\) or nucleus truncation so that these filters select among legal continuations. If an implementation instead truncates first and no retained token belongs to \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\), the serving runtime must raise an explicit constraint-satisfaction error rather than silently disabling the mask. Positive finite temperature rescales the remaining probabilities without removing their support.
Recomputing \(\ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\) from scratch at every step would cost a scan of the whole vocabulary per token. For a regular grammar or a flat tool schema with a finite state space, engines compile the schema once into a finite-state automaton whose states each carry a precomputed mask \(\LogitMask(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\), so that each step is a table lookup followed by a state transition (Willard and Louf 2023). When a grammar allows recursive nesting, such as nested JSON objects or parenthesized expressions, a pushdown stack tracks the open scopes at runtime while precomputed masks still accelerate the lexical transitions at each state. Incremental parsing of this kind yields syntactically valid output even for a language as structured as SQL (Scholak et al. 2021). The automaton in figure 4 is compiled for a query tool with two fields, query and limit, rather than for read_file, and the masking mechanism is identical.






Figure 4: Grammar-Constrained Decoding: A tool schema compiles once into an automaton whose states each carry a token mask. At every step the mask sets illegal tokens to \(-\infty\) before normalization, so only a legal continuation can be drawn, and the drawn token advances the automaton. The logit values are illustrative: a fluent but illegal continuation can outscore the legal one and still receive zero probability. A precomputed per-state mask suits a finite-state constraint; nested structures need additional parser state. The strip along the bottom lists what the mask leaves unchecked.



The resulting guarantee is conditional. The mask keeps every prefix viable, and the engine disallows the end-of-sequence (<eos>) token while required fields or closing delimiters remain unwritten, so an output that ends normally belongs to the enforced language. Nothing in the mask makes generation end normally within its token budget.


↪ The automaton behind the token mask, and the induction showing that a constrained output ending in a permitted end token belongs to the grammar, are developed in Finite-state constrained decoding.
Consider what happens when an inference request hits its maximum output token limit while emitting arguments, leaving the decoding buffer at {"path":"src/po. The string is a viable prefix under the schema, yet the envelope reports status: TRUNCATED, and the quarantining rule of section 2.5.2 applies. A heuristic repair parser that appends the closing quote and brace would fabricate the call read_file("src/po"), which the model never finished and which names a file nobody asked for. The mask governs which tokens can appear; it never promotes an interrupted generation to a completed one.



Grammar masking moves the first row of table 3 into generation and leaves every other row where it was. A masked {"path":"src/pool.py"} still names a file that may not exist or may lie outside the grant, because the mask operates strictly on the textual representation and never queries repository state or security policy. Property by property, the mask’s own reach is narrow (table 4).



Table 4: Reach of the grammar mask: A completed constrained output establishes membership in the enforced output language. Every other property keeps the check it needed without the mask.










Verification dimension
What the grammar mask establishes
Evidence still required




Syntactic conformance
All of it for the enforced grammar, once generation accepts
A COMPLETED status, since a legal prefix may be unfinished


Schema completeness
Only the constraints its compiler supports, at accepting completion
A final validation pass against the authoritative schema


Referential integrity
Nothing
Observation of the named resource in the relevant environment


Semantic invariants
Nothing
Checks or judgments covering the task property


Authorization bounds
Nothing; generated text grants no authority
A runtime permission decision for the proposed operation






How much a grammar mask guarantees depends on the grammar it compiles. Enforcing a general JSON grammar guarantees only RFC 8259 syntax (balanced braces, legal numbers, and escaped strings) without restricting keys or value types. Compiling a specific JSON Schema into the constraint engine goes further, enforcing required fields, distinguishing integers from floats, and restricting strings to declared regular expressions or enumerations.
Even a schema-aware mask has limits when a schema uses features that cannot be compiled into a finite-state or pushdown automaton. Keywords that enforce cross-field conditionals (if/then/else), unique array elements, or arbitrary lookahead often exceed what precomputed token masks support. Whenever an engine drops unsupported schema keywords, has a bug in its grammar compiler, or parses types differently from the downstream consumer, the guarantee stops holding. The runtime should therefore document which schema features its mask enforces and still run a final check against the authoritative schema before dispatch. Under invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)), logit masking is a mechanical bound below the model: it enforces syntax without the model’s cooperation while leaving authorization and semantic checks above the model.
A strict schema can also force a model to guess when context is missing. If a schema requires a path string with no alternative branch, every completed output must supply a path even when the prompt gives no clue which file to inspect. Stripping out every token outside that single object shape leaves the model no way to report that information is missing, so it must invent a plausible path to reach an accepting parser state.
Adding an explicit unknown variant or a structured error branch to the schema avoids that forced guessing and lets the model report missing context cleanly. Those branches are semantic choices inside the payload, distinct from transport statuses and tool errors. They make an honest report possible without forcing one, since the model can still guess a path when unknown is available, or pick unknown when the answer is already in the prompt. The runtime therefore handles each branch under the task contract, gathering another observation or asking the user when the model reports uncertainty.



Fine-tuning a model on tool examples makes well-formed arguments likely but still permits rare syntax slips on long contexts, whereas a grammar mask alone forces valid syntax even when the model has no idea which tool or argument fits the task. The two mechanisms work at different layers and complement each other. Supervised fine-tuning (further training on curated example responses, developed in Trajectory Fine-Tuning) and instruction tuning teach models to map prompts onto tool definitions and put high probability on appropriate arguments (Schick et al. 2023). Runtime logit masking fixes the support of the distribution at each step by setting illegal tokens to zero probability. A model tuned for tool use puts high logits on sensible tokens, and the runtime mask guarantees that sampling noise or long-context drift cannot emit broken syntax. Neither replaces the other: training alone gives no hard guarantee against syntax errors, and a grammar mask supplies no domain knowledge about which file path is right.

Schick, Timo, Jane Dwivedi-Yu, Roberto Dessı̀, Roberta Raileanu, Maria Lomeli, Luke Zettlemoyer, Nicola Cancedda, and Thomas Scialom. 2023. “Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36: 68539–51.
Grammar constraints also carry their own costs. Compiling complex regular expressions or nested JSON schemas into deterministic automata consumes CPU time and memory. In dynamic environments where agents construct ad hoc schemas per request, compilation latency can offset the latency saved by avoiding syntax retries. Similarly, tracking parse states and computing masks across large vocabularies (\(|\TokenVocabulary| \ge 128{,}000\) tokens) adds per-token decoding overhead unless supported by precomputed lookup indices or bitmasks applied on the accelerator. Eliminating syntax retries lowers total cost only when compilation, mask memory, and per-token mask work together cost less than the retries they replace.

Checkpoint 2.2: Evaluating schema-constrained decoding
A repair agent uses constrained decoding for file-reading proposals. Its runtime records response kind and invocation status separately.

Completion: If an output ceiling interrupts a legal JSON prefix, can you explain why grammar masking does not permit dispatch of the fragment?
Constraint scope: If a completed request satisfies the schema but names a nonexistent file, can you identify which property was enforced and which observation is still needed?
Response variants: A completed, schema-valid response selects the unknown variant. Decide what the runtime does next, and name the observation it should obtain before calling the model again.
Combined mechanisms: Can you explain why a model trained for tool use can still benefit from runtime masks without either mechanism granting execution authority?



Constrained decoding removes one class of syntax failure before dispatch, but a structurally valid invocation still needs enough budget to finish and external evidence to justify execution. Whether a mask pays for itself, and what any call costs at all, depends on how prompt processing and token generation consume time on the serving hardware.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
On the repair agent’s first turn, reading a long prompt of repository context and tool schemas takes less accelerator time than generating a short reply, yet across a multi-turn repair loop, resending that growing prompt history balloons into hundreds of thousands of input tokens. Counting a call as a single black-box unit, or summing input and output tokens into one unweighted total, hides which phase actually drives latency and cluster work. An invocation contract therefore budgets prompt reading and output generation separately, pricing both a single call’s latency and a multi-turn trajectory’s cumulative input load.
Input length and output length stress distinct subsystems in the inference serving stack. Prompt ingestion exposes many known token positions to parallel matrix computation across the accelerator’s execution units. Conversely, autoregressive token generation executes as a strictly sequential loop, where each new token depends on the hidden state of all preceding positions. Because hardware handles these two phases under different physical constraints, output length is the primary software lever for controlling generation latency. A long prompt, a short reply, or a congested service queue can, however, shift the latency bottleneck elsewhere.


A runtime that records only the total wall-clock time of a slow call cannot tell whether the delay came from a bloated prompt, a backed-up serving queue, or a long reply, yet each cause requires a different fix. To separate them, the runtime measures five non-overlapping phases. They run from the moment it prepares the outbound request to the moment the normalized response is ready for validation. The phases are preparation (context assembly, serialization, and network send), queueing (waiting in the service’s admission queue), prefill (reading the prompt tokens in a parallel forward pass), decode (generating output tokens step by step), and postprocessing (response transfer, deserialization, and schema checks):
\[\CallLatency = \CallPreparationTime + \RequestQueueTime + \PrefillTime + \DecodeInterval + \CallPostprocessingTime \tag{6}\]
Each term in equation 6 is an elapsed time in seconds, measured with timestamps rather than estimated backward from token counts; when network transfer or local preparation overlaps server execution, the spans track non-overlapping intervals so nothing is counted twice. The first generated token needs careful accounting so it is not charged to both prefill and decode. In a standard Transformer, the prefill pass reads the whole prompt and produces the logits from which the first output token is drawn. On the client side, the time from sending the request to receiving that first token is the time to first token (TTFT), and the average spacing between later tokens is the time per output token (TPOT). Serving systems track TTFT and TPOT as separate objectives because prefill and decode contend for the same accelerator compute and memory bandwidth; disaggregated serving systems go further and run prefill and decode on separate accelerator pools so neither stalls the other (Zhong et al. 2024).

Zhong, Yinmin, Shengyu Liu, Junda Chen, Jianbo Hu, Yibo Zhu, Xuanzhe Liu, Xin Jin, and Hao Zhang. 2024. “DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-Optimized Large Language Model Serving.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), July, 193–210.
When TTFT includes sampling and delivering the first token, the remaining decode interval covers only the next \(\OutputLength-1\) tokens in a completion of length \(\OutputLength\). For a streamed reply, adding client-measured TTFT, the \(\OutputLength-1\) inter-token intervals, and final deserialization gives the full call latency without double-counting the first token. Client-measured TTFT is larger than server prefill time because it also includes network transit and queueing, and because servers and networks often batch several streamed tokens into one network chunk, chunk arrival times on the client do not always match per-token step times on the accelerator.
The first-token boundary separates these two measurements in figure 5. The service produces the initial logits during prefill, but the client must still wait for sampling and delivery before its TTFT interval ends.






Figure 5: First-Token Accounting: A schematic timeline separates server prefill from client time to first token. Here K is the total number of output tokens. Prefill supplies the initial logits; only the remaining output tokens require subsequent generation passes. The later tokens arrive together in an illustrative buffered chunk, so client arrivals do not identify individual service steps. Distances are not measured durations.



A client trace can therefore identify a long wait for the first token without establishing how much of that wait the accelerator spent on prefill. Diagnosing the delay requires queueing and execution boundaries from the service, rather than a finer sampling of chunk arrivals.
Capping max_output_tokens bounds how many tokens the model can emit, not how fast the call returns; a congested queue can burn the entire deadline before prefill even starts. Latency benchmarks must therefore record the model, prompt and output lengths, prefix-cache hit rate, and cluster load. Even when a single agent runs one turn at a time, the serving cluster rarely runs that call alone: continuous batching schedules requests at each decode step (Yu et al. 2022), interleaving the agent’s tokens with dozens of other requests.



Counting input and output tokens together hides why a two-hundred-token reply can take longer on the accelerator than an eight-thousand-token prompt. Input processing and output generation hit different hardware bottlenecks, so a baseline work model gives them separate per-token time floors. A dense Transformer with \(\Parameters\) parameters executes approximately \(2\Parameters\) floating-point operations for each token it processes, in prefill and decode alike. What differs is how often the weights must be read. Prefill reads each weight tensor from accelerator memory once per call and reuses it across all \(\SequenceLength\) prompt positions, so a long prompt spreads one weight read over thousands of tokens of arithmetic, and each prompt token costs about \(2\Parameters\) operations at the peak arithmetic rate \(\PeakRate\). Single-stream decode produces one token per step, so it reads every weight once per generated token. Each output token therefore moves the full weight payload of \(\Parameters\,\ElementStorageSize\) bytes (with \(\ElementStorageSize\) bytes per parameter) across a memory interface of bandwidth \(\Bandwidth\), and its arithmetic finishes long before those bytes arrive.
These two regimes are the two limbs of the roofline model (Williams et al. 2009), which bounds attainable throughput by the lesser of the peak arithmetic rate and the memory bandwidth multiplied by the work done per byte moved. Prefill does much work per byte and sits under the arithmetic limb; low-batch decode does little and sits under the bandwidth limb, a split that empirical evaluations of Transformer inference confirm (Pope et al. 2023). The two floors are

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[\PerTokenPrefillTime \approx \frac{2\Parameters}{\PeakRate}, \qquad \PerTokenDecodeTime \ge \frac{\Parameters\,\ElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth} \tag{7}\]
The lowercase symbols are per-token floors. The analytical budget uses the allowances \(\PrefillTime \approx \SequenceLength\,\PerTokenPrefillTime\) and \(\DecodeInterval \approx \OutputLength\,\PerTokenDecodeTime\). Dividing the two floors cancels the parameter count \(\Parameters\):
\[\frac{\PerTokenDecodeTime}{\PerTokenPrefillTime} \approx \frac{\PeakRate \, \ElementStorageSize}{2 \, \Bandwidth} \tag{8}\]
Consider a concrete reference deployment: a dense model with 70.6B parameters stored in 8-bit precision (\(\ElementStorageSize = 1\) byte) on a single accelerator with an 8-bit peak rate of 1,979 TFLOP/s and a memory bandwidth of 3.35 TB/s. Each token costs 141.2 GFLOP of arithmetic, and dividing by the peak rate gives a prefill floor of 71.35 μs per prompt token. Each decode step reads 70.6 GB of weights, and dividing by the bandwidth gives a decode floor of 21.075 ms per generated token. Under equation 8, decoding a single output token therefore takes the same hardware time as ingesting roughly 295 prompt tokens. This asymmetry is the content of output-bound latency (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)), under which each plain, unbatched decode step incurs a full weight read in this model, so output volume can dominate call latency. The ratio reflects weight-dominated, unbatched decode against peak-throughput prefill, not a measured cloud service rate or a commercial billing tier.


↪ Both execution floors and their operating boundaries are developed in Cost Asymmetry Between Input Prefill and Output Generation.
This analytical budget charges each prompt token once at the prefill floor and reserves one decode floor step for each generated token. The first output token receives that allowance even though prefill supplies its initial logits. The budget therefore includes an extra decode-floor step relative to the measured post-TTFT interval, which contains only subsequent generation steps.
The budget is an idealized hardware baseline rather than a substitute for wall-clock measurement: it omits network transit, queueing delay, attention quadratics, and runtime software overhead. It also assumes standard autoregressive generation without speculative decoding. In production, a serving system that batches concurrent client requests, distributes model weights across tensor-parallel accelerators (sharding individual weight matrices across multiple devices), or reuses cached attention state substantially alters the relationship between token count and elapsed time. The analytical estimate is therefore suited to comparing interface formats and output volumes, but certifying a production deadline requires measuring latency directly under realistic serving load.
Applying this baseline to the first repair turn shows how output tokens dominate. A prompt of 8,000 tokens contributes 0.571 s of prefill work, while generating a reply of 200 tokens is charged 4.215 s of decode work. The total call estimate is 4.786 s. Although output constitutes only 2.4 percent of the call’s total tokens, it accounts for 88.1 percent of the modeled hardware time. Pruning redundant output tokens therefore reduces overall latency far more effectively than removing an identical number of prompt tokens. At the same time, an agent benefits from a cheaper invocation only if the model still receives sufficient diagnostic context to generate a correct candidate; engineers must prune verbosity from the output format, not critical evidence from the prompt.



Even when individual turns produce concise outputs, a multi-turn trajectory can still generate a large prompt-ingestion workload. Consider an agent runtime that maintains an append-only execution log and re-transmits the full cumulative history on every invocation. If the initial turn contains \(\BasePromptLength\) prompt tokens and each subsequent turn appends \(\TurnAppendLength\) tokens of combined model output and tool observations, a trajectory spanning a horizon of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns submits:
\[\PromptTokensSent = \sum_{j=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1} \left(\BasePromptLength + \PriorTurnCount\,\TurnAppendLength\right) = \TurnHorizon \BasePromptLength + \TurnAppendLength \frac{\TurnHorizon(\TurnHorizon-1)}{2} \tag{9}\]
prompt tokens in total. The quadratic growth in equation 9 comes from resending the growing history on every turn rather than from an inherent need of multi-turn reasoning. Sliding-window context buffers, trimmed tool outputs, or turn summaries can reduce the tokens sent, and a stateful serving endpoint can hold the conversation on the server to avoid resending the bytes over the network even when attention still spans the full history.



Re-sent input grows with the square of the horizon; prefix reuse keeps fresh prefill linear.
Repeated prompt input need not mean repeated computation. Prefix caching enables the inference engine to retain and reuse previously computed Key-Value (KV) activations for prompt prefixes that remain identical across consecutive requests (Zheng et al. 2024). Reuse holds only for an exact token prefix computed under the same model and serving configuration, so altering an early system instruction or a tool schema forces fresh prefill from that point onward. The full compatibility conditions are developed in Prefix compatibility.
To see how much work prefix reuse saves, suppose the inference service caches earlier prompt prefixes and runs fresh prefill only on the newly appended turn suffix (the model’s previous reply plus the new tool observation). Across all \(\TurnHorizon\) turns, the prompt tokens needing fresh prefill drop to \(\BasePromptLength + (\TurnHorizon-1)\,\TurnAppendLength\). That baseline conservatively assumes the server does not keep the KV state produced during decode; engines that retain decoded KV state as well avoid fresh prefill on the earlier model replies too.

Napkin Math 2.2: The price of an append-only trajectoryProblem: A coding agent runs 30 turns. Its first prompt has 8,000 tokens, each turn appends 1,500 tokens, and each call emits 200 output tokens. Assume that every prompt fits the service’s context limit and that compatible earlier prompt state remains available for reuse. How much input does the trajectory supply, and how does prompt-prefix reuse change its estimated processing work?
Math: Applying the arithmetic series in equation 9 gives \(30\times 8,000+1,500\times\frac{30\times 29}{2}=892,500\) prompt tokens. Total output is \(30\times 200=6,000\) tokens. Without reuse, input therefore accounts for 99.3 percent of the combined input and output token count, although it does not account for that share of processing time.
With prompt-prefix reuse, fresh prefill covers \(8,000+29\times 1,500=51,500\) tokens. Dividing the original input count by this fresh-prefill count gives a 17.3× reduction. At the reference prefill floor, the prefill-work estimate falls from 63.68 s to 3.67 s. Decode work stays at 126.45 s; caching earlier input does not remove the task’s new responses.
Systems insight: Append-only context makes input work grow with the square of the horizon. Doubling the trajectory to 60 turns multiplies re-sent input by 3.5× but fresh prefill under prefix reuse by only 1.9×, because reuse converts quadratic growth into a linear trajectory. Prefix reuse therefore serves as the primary lever for minimizing the input component of \(\AttemptCost\) in the cost per accepted task (equation 1.2), with its value compounding as horizons lengthen. While caching preserves the full decision context without loss of information, cache eviction and cross-worker request routing can dilute these theoretical savings in production.


Even across the multi-turn trajectory above, decode time at the unbatched floor exceeds uncached prefill time, yet on a shared serving cluster uncached prefill can dominate the aggregate hardware work of that same trajectory. The two statements price different accounts. Wall-clock latency governs the responsiveness of a single trajectory. Because each turn depends on the outcome of prior tool executions, an agent cannot parallelize its own dependent turns, and every output token remains a sequential step on the critical path even when the server batches that step with other requests. Computational work, by contrast, sets cluster throughput, hardware provisioning, and aggregate operating cost. When a serving cluster batches dozens of concurrent streams, the weight reads at each decode step are amortized across all active requests in the batch. The amortized service time per decoded token then drops from the memory-bandwidth floor toward the compute-bound arithmetic limit \(2\Parameters/\PeakRate\) of equation 7, the same per-token efficiency as prompt prefill (Cost Asymmetry Between Input Prefill and Output Generation derives the batched-step bound). Once input and output tokens require comparable hardware work per token, total cluster work scales with aggregate token volume, which for an append-only agent is dominated by re-sent prompt history, provided the cluster sustains high batching and has memory for the attention state. Prefix reuse acts directly on that input component, while its effect on end-to-end latency depends on how much the input contributes to the call a consumer waits on.
Which term an engineer should attack therefore depends on who waits for the output, and the repair agent alone cannot show the contrast. Its consumer is a compilation and test pipeline that must wait for a syntactically complete response. The support agent instead streams output tokens to a person reading as they arrive. The consumer requirements determine which latency terms these two illustrated workloads prioritize.

Lighthouse 2.1: Call latency for two lighthousesSupport agent: A customer-operations turn submits an 8,192-token prompt (consisting of policy documentation, customer account history, and recent dialogue) and streams an 150-token response to a human user in a live chat interface. At the chapter’s reference hardware floors, prefill takes 0.58 s and generating the full reply requires 3.2 s. However, token streaming displays the initial words immediately following queueing and prefill; the remaining tokens arrive at approximately 47 tokens per second, faster than a person reads. Under these lengths and streaming rates, TTFT governs how soon the user can begin reading. When 6,144 prompt tokens represent a common prefix of system instructions, organizational policies, and tool definitions shared across all concurrent sessions, prefix caching leaves only 2,048 tokens of fresh prefill, which takes just 0.15 s. In a loaded cluster, admission queueing becomes the dominant contributor to first-token latency.
Repair agent: The initial repair turn commits 88.1 percent of its estimated hardware work to generating a 200-token response. The agent runtime can parse, validate, and execute the generated patch only after receiving the entire payload. Decode duration dominates this repair estimate, making the compactness of the requested code representation its primary optimization lever.
Systems insight: The illustrated support turn prioritizes TTFT because the user can read while the remaining tokens arrive, whereas output volume dominates the illustrated repair call, whose consumer waits for a complete patch. Shortening the support reply does not directly remove queueing or prefill from first-token latency. Caching the repair prompt reduces its input work and input cost, but that saving contributes little to this output-dominated estimate. Different prompt lengths, streaming rates, or serving load can change the binding term; measured phase durations and queueing determine which intervention improves the latency the consumer waits on.


Prefix reuse is not free. A cached prefix occupies accelerator memory that concurrent requests cannot use, and holding it through a long tool wait pins memory that no generation is using. Eviction discards only derived attention state, never the context itself, so the runtime can rebuild the prompt from its own logs at the cost of fresh prefill. Which evidence the model sees and whether its attention state is worth keeping are therefore separate decisions.


↪ The choice to keep, move, or drop attention state held through a tool wait is developed in Paused-State Policies.
Billed dollars form a third account, separate from latency and hardware work. Providers bill uncached input, cached input, and output tokens at different rates, and on-premise hardware amortizes fixed costs across utilization, so token-count ratios do not translate directly into dollars; Pricing prefix cache hits prices a whole trajectory under such tariffs. The per-call estimate is one building block of a task budget that also carries failed tool executions, retries, validation runs, and idle reservations during tool waits.

Checkpoint 2.3: Pricing calls and trajectories
A call’s token count and its elapsed execution time quantify distinct facets of the overall system budget.

Measurement boundary: If the time to first token already accounts for sampling and delivering the initial token, how many subsequent token-generation intervals remain in a completed completion of length \(\OutputLength\)?
Horizon estimate: If an agent trajectory triples to 90 turns under fixed \(\BasePromptLength\) and \(\TurnAppendLength\), estimate the growth factor for uncached re-sent input vs. fresh prefill under prefix caching. Which term dictates whether scaling to longer trajectories remains computationally viable?
Reuse assumptions: How does the analytical work estimate change if the inference server evicts the cached prefix from accelerator memory during a blocking tool execution?
Cost denominator: Why does an overwhelming majority of input tokens fail to produce an equivalent majority of financial cost when providers bill cached input and generated output at starkly different rates?
Interface estimate: A full-file replacement requires 1,850 output tokens, whereas a localized diff requires only 80. At the reference decode floor, which interface alternative can realistically operate within a 15 s latency deadline? Why is this analytical roofline model insufficient on its own to guarantee real-world service-level agreement (SLA) compliance?



Breaking down a call’s cost shows two main sources of waste: generating unchanged output tokens that the tool interface does not need, and recomputing prompt prefixes that the server could reuse. Cutting that waste helps only when the resulting output still solves the task, because a short diff that fails to apply or a cached prompt that produces a broken edit wastes the entire call. Choosing an output interface therefore requires comparing candidate accuracy, failure modes, and total resource spend under the same task budget.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
When the repair agent proposes a fix to the connection-pool locking logic in src/pool.py, its output payload does not need to repeat the entire source file. The model could emit a fully rewritten file, or it could target a specific code block and emit only the replacement text. Emitting a localized edit consumes far fewer generation tokens by omitting unchanged code, but it creates an operational dependency: the execution runtime must locate the exact target coordinates in the target file. The interface therefore determines both the computational cost of generating a candidate and the operational preconditions required for the runtime to apply it.
High schema parse rates alone cannot validate an interface design. A whole-file replacement might parse into valid JSON yet arrive long after the service deadline because the model spent tens of seconds generating unchanged lines. Conversely, a compact diff might arrive in about 2.3 s yet fail to match its target anchors against current repository state. Neither outcome delivers an accepted repair. A rigorous empirical comparison must track the model call’s completion status, account for all compute resources consumed across retries, and validate the resulting artifact against uniform acceptance criteria.


When a patch interface fails in production by timing out on long files, missing its target lines, or breaking JSON syntax, teams often swap the entire prompt format at once and cannot tell whether edit granularity, wire framing, or decoding constraints caused the failure. Because those three choices are independent, diagnosing a failure or comparing designs requires varying one dimension at a time.
The first choice, edit granularity, sets how much text the model must emit to describe a change. At one end, a whole-file format returns the entire file, regenerating hundreds of untouched lines alongside the edit. At the other end, a localized edit supplies only a target locator and the replacement lines. An anchored search-and-replace block, for instance, gives an exact snippet of source text to find and the new text to substitute; if that anchor snippet is missing from the file or appears more than once, the runtime cannot apply the edit uniquely. Rewriting the whole file avoids anchor mismatches, but forces the runtime to check that the model did not accidentally delete unrelated functions or overwrite concurrent edits.
Regardless of which granularity the interface chooses, serialization framing remains an independent decision. Either edit size can be wrapped in JSON (one schema carrying a path and full file body, another carrying a path, search snippet, and replacement block) or framed with Markdown code fences or unified diff headers. Token overhead comes from the tokenizer’s vocabulary and the wrapper markers, not from whether the outer wrapper is JSON or diff syntax; emitting thousands of tokens for an unchanged file is the price of whole-file granularity, not of JSON.
How the runtime enforces that framing, the constraint mechanism, is independent of both granularity and wire syntax. An engineer can get structured outputs through fine-tuning, few-shot examples in the prompt, or grammar masking during decoding, and can combine them by running a fine-tuned model under a grammar mask. As section 2.7 showed, a grammar mask guarantees grammatical form, not valid targets or working code: it cannot ensure that an anchor snippet exists in the file or that the edit fixes the race condition. Changing serialization and decoding constraints at the same time tests a bundle of choices rather than isolating which change helped.



Giving a brittle diff format free retries whenever its output fails to parse, or dropping timed-out whole-file calls from the denominator, makes a weak interface look more accurate than it is. A fair comparison holds every condition fixed except the interface itself. In the connection-pool repair benchmark, every trial starts from the same repository snapshot and defect description, under the same model weights, sampling parameters, tools, acceptance tests, resource ceilings, and retry policy. Matched budgets do not require equal token consumption, because prompt overhead and response length are properties of the interface under test; they require identical operating limits and accounting rules.


↪ Matched-budget comparison of complete agent policies, charging every initiated trial to the cost per accepted task, is developed in Matched-budget comparison.
Two deadlines bound the comparison. The invocation deadline ends when the runtime receives and normalizes the model’s response. The task deadline also covers parsing, patching, compilation, and tests, and every retry, unparsable output, and failing run draws against it. A benchmark that grants free retries after malformed responses therefore subsidizes the brittle interface.
The harness also records each intermediate stage separately from final acceptance (table 5). Every initiated trial stays in the denominator of the top-level success rate, because discarding unparsable responses or timed-out calls inflates reported accuracy. Conditional rates, such as the share of applied edits that pass tests, remain useful diagnostics when they state their filter explicitly.



Table 5: Interface evaluation measurements: Distinct observations prevent a formatting improvement from being mistaken for a task-level improvement. The same task fixtures, acceptance standard, and resource ceilings govern each design.










Measurement
What the trial records
What it does not establish




Invocation outcome
Completion status, elapsed time, and token usage
That a delivered candidate is valid


Structural validity
Whether a completed payload parses and satisfies the required schema
That its values describe the current environment


Applicability
Whether the authorized edit identifies its target and can be applied to the expected version
That the resulting program repairs the defect


Acceptance evidence
Results of the same required checks on the resulting artifact
Correctness beyond the checks’ coverage


Resource use
All calls and checks charged to the trial, including failed attempts
A benefit unless accepted outcomes justify the expenditure






Latency measurements also need their serving conditions. Cache hits, batching contention, and queueing change observed wall-clock time at fixed prompt and completion lengths, so a few favorable measurements during quiet periods do not establish deadline reliability; tail latency decides deadline violations in shared clusters (Dean and Barroso 2013). The engineering question is whether a representation leaves enough headroom under the tail of the latency distribution to generate and validate a candidate fix.

Dean, Jeffrey, and Luiz André Barroso. 2013. “The Tail at Scale.” Communications of the ACM 56 (2): 74–80.



When a repair call must finish inside a fifteen-second deadline, asking the model to rewrite an entire source file spends almost the whole budget copying unchanged lines before a single test can run. The per-token floors of section 2.8.2 put a concrete price on that unchanged text, and that price falls on edit granularity rather than on the outer wrapper format.



Generating unchanged code, not reading the prompt, pushes the whole file past the deadline.

Napkin Math 2.3: A repair representation under an invocation deadlineProblem: A repair invocation begins with 8,000 baseline context tokens and operates under an invocation deadline of 15 s. Emitting a whole-file replacement requires 350 additional instruction tokens and 1,850 output tokens. Emitting a localized edit requires 120 additional instruction tokens and 80 output tokens. These token counts represent scenario parameters. Using the prefill and autoregressive decoding rates established earlier, which interface representation fits within the simplified service-work budget?
Math: The service-work model charges prompt prefill at 71.35 μs per token and autoregressive decoding at 21.075 ms per token. To isolate inference execution, this baseline calculation omits request serialization, network transit, server-side queueing, and subsequent validation runs. Multiplying each interface’s token profile by these unit costs yields:
\((8,000+350)\times 0.00007135\,\text{s}+1,850\times 0.021075\,\text{s}\approx 39.58\,\text{s}\)
\((8,000+120)\times 0.00007135\,\text{s}+80\times 0.021075\,\text{s}\approx 2.27\,\text{s}\)
The whole-file estimate exceeds the deadline by a wide margin, whereas the localized edit finishes well within the allocated budget. The localized representation provides a 17.5× reduction in estimated service work, with token decoding accounting for 98.5 percent of the whole-file latency. In production, normalized invocation outcomes and observed wall-clock times determine whether the candidate arrived before deadline expiration.
To evaluate downstream yield, consider a second hypothetical scenario where localized edits complete on time with valid syntax, but only 95 percent resolve to an applicable edit on the codebase. Among those applicable edits, assume 60 percent pass the required test suite. The fraction of all initiated trials that yield an accepted repair is:
\(0.95\times 0.60=0.57\)
This 57 percent yield is the product of the applicability rate and the conditional test-pass rate, requiring no independence assumption between stages. Invocations that miss deadlines or emit invalid syntax reduce this end-to-end yield even further.
Systems insight: When output generation threatens an invocation deadline, shrinking representation granularity is the primary engineering lever. Because autoregressive decoding is memory-bandwidth bound, each generated token costs roughly 295 prompt prefill tokens at hardware reference floors (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)). Whole-file generation squanders almost all of its 39.6 s runtime emitting unchanged code, while the localized edit meets the deadline with a 6.6× safety margin. However, compact representations trade decoding latency for applicability risk: localized edits require exact anchor matching, which restricts the passing yield to 57 percent in this scenario. That hypothetical yield forms the acceptance probability \(\AcceptanceProbability\) that governs the amortized cost per accepted task (equation 1.2).


The call deadline acts as a hard filter: under these timing numbers, a whole-file response misses the cutoff before any test can run, so its code quality never comes into play. If the deadline is relaxed past the whole-file duration, the trade-off flips toward applicability and patch accuracy. With a generous time budget, a localized edit format that frequently misses stale anchors or ambiguous line ranges can lose to a whole-file format that applies cleanly every time.

Checkpoint 2.4: Reconsidering the interface when conditions change
The repair interface must be reassessed whenever the workspace state or resource budget shifts.

Applicability: If the source file changes after the prompt is assembled, which measurement in the benchmark pipeline changes, and what preconditions must the runtime verify before applying either representation?
Deadline: If the invocation deadline doubles while token lengths and accounting rates stay fixed, which representations fit the budget, and how do you distinguish that analytical estimate from an empirical completion guarantee?
Serialization: If the localized edit is encoded as a JSON object rather than plain text delimiters, which latency benefits survive and which token counts must be re-profiled?
Admission: How do you distinguish a COMPLETED but malformed request from a syntactically valid but TRUNCATED request? Which specific check prevents each from triggering downstream tool execution?
Acceptance evidence: If an edit applies cleanly and passes a sequential test suite, what additional runtime evidence does a race-condition task still require before acceptance?



Interface benchmarking joins the call contract to the cost of the call. The request specifies the context and output allowances; the normalized response confirms whether the model delivered a completed payload before the deadline; and tiered evaluation metrics determine whether the proposed mutation reliably solves the task within resource constraints. Assuming that a valid schema implies an applicable patch, or that a fast diff implies defect-free code, collapses these stages into one and hides which of them failed.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
A code repair request can return promptly yet name the wrong file, or return the right patch long after its latency budget has expired. In autonomous execution loops, engineers frequently conflate distinct operational boundaries, confusing inference execution with total round-trip latency, syntactic validity with semantic correctness, and transport success with task completion. These failures expose several persistent mistaken assumptions about the model call.

Fallacy: One model response has a fixed cost.
Output length drives most of the execution time in the unbatched interface comparison. At its reference hardware floors, decoding a single output token takes far longer than reading a prompt token in parallel. Regenerating a whole file takes 39.6 s, whereas emitting a localized patch for the same bug takes 2.3 s, a 17.5× speedup that comes almost entirely from generating fewer tokens (section 2.8). Engineers must therefore budget input and output tokens separately rather than treating a model call as a fixed unit of work. Wall-clock budgets must also cover queueing and network transit; setting max_output_tokens caps how many tokens the model generates, not when the reply arrives.


Pitfall: Treating a completed invocation as a completed task.
A status of COMPLETED says only that the serving engine finished generating tokens within the call’s limits; it does not mean the output is right or even usable. In the interface comparison, every localized edit finished on time, yet only 57 percent of those trials produced patches that passed the repair checks. Conversely, a call cut off at the token ceiling can still leave a syntactically valid file path, which is why the runtime must check completion status before acting on the payload. Every call record needs two separate facts: whether a complete candidate arrived from the service, and whether independent checks confirm that it satisfies the task contract.


Fallacy: Valid JSON means a safe and correct tool call.
A JSON object passes schema validation whenever its fields match the declared types, whether the payload is safe, authorized, or sensible. A tool call with a string path passes schema checks whether that path names the intended file, a stale file, or a sensitive directory outside the workspace. As table 3 shows, schema validation checks structure, while permission gates and task checks govern safety and correctness. The same gap holds for behavioral checks: a test runner with a false-accept rate of 0.65 on defective patches still leaves 14.37 percent of its passing candidates defective under the assumed rates. Even under grammar-constrained decoding, a call cut off at the token limit remains an unfinished fragment even though every token emitted before truncation was legal.


Pitfall: Collapsing every unsuccessful outcome into the same retry.
Retrying a failed call with the exact same request repeats the cause of the failure when the fault is not transient. If a whole-file request misses a 15 s deadline, resending the identical prompt spends another 39.6 s of estimated work only to time out again, while the first call may still be running and billed on the server, since a local timeout leaves the remote outcome unknown. Likewise, a call that hits max_output_tokens will truncate at the same limit on retry, and a safety refusal will refuse again. Instead of treating every failure like a dropped packet, the runtime should route on the normalized status: bounded backoff for transient service faults, a larger output allowance or more compact output format for truncation, and a fresh file read when an edit anchor fails to match. Recovery actions and evidence develops which recovery action fits each failure class.



↪ The idempotency rules that decide when a timed-out call may be repeated are developed in Retrying Uncertain Actions.

Fallacy: Greedy decoding makes a served call reproducible.
Greedy selection fixes the token choice for a given logit vector, but the serving infrastructure computes that vector, and two distinct causes can change it. The first operates even on a healthy serving path, where batch-dependent floating-point reduction order shifts closely contested logits in their least significant bits, enough to flip an argmax and redirect every later token. The second is a change to the serving path itself. In war story 2.1, misrouting and a miscompiled top-\(\TopTokenSampleCount\) operation changed model outputs for identical requests, affecting 16 percent of one model’s requests at peak impact, so an identical prompt succeeded on one attempt and failed on the next. Pinning the temperature addresses neither cause. Systems engineers should record the model revision and serving configuration with every invocation, and replay recorded responses whenever the goal is to reproduce downstream runtime behavior deterministically.

Each of these traps blurs two separate runtime records: token usage measures spend, completion status tracks whether generation finished, schema validation checks form, and acceptance tests check the result. Keeping those records separate lets higher-level loops compose single model calls without mistaking a clean response envelope for a working repair.

title: 2 The Foundation Model
text:
A repair agent interacts with a foundation model through a bounded request-response contract. The request bundles messages, tool schemas, token and time limits, and sampling settings into a serialized payload without handing any execution authority to the model. On the way back, the normalized status envelope separates completed proposals from truncated, refused, or failed calls, leaving the runtime to authorize side effects and verify results against the task contract. That division of work is invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) applied to a single model call, the baseline that every later chapter builds on. Table 6 summarizes the quantitative relations governing model invocations, tracking admission constraints, generation dynamics, verification limits, and trajectory-level resource scaling.



Table 6: Key equations of the model call: Each relation holds only under the assumptions stated where it is derived, such as a combined input-and-output window, weight-dominated unbatched decode, or a reusable prefix that stays resident.










Equation
What it bounds or decides

\(\SequenceLength \le \ContextWindow - \OutputLimit\)

equation 1


\(\Pr(\OutputTokenSequence \mid \InputTokenSequence) = \prod_{t=1}^{\OutputLength} \Pr(\OutputToken_t \mid \InputTokenSequence, \OutputTokenPrefix)\)
Sequential probability factorization defining token-by-token autoregressive generation
equation 2


\(\Pr(\OutputToken_t = \VocabularyToken \mid \InputTokenSequence, \OutputTokenPrefix) \propto \exp\left(\OutputLogit_{t, \VocabularyToken} / \SamplingTemperature\right)\)
Temperature scaling trading sample diversity against distribution concentration
equation 3


\(\Pr(\text{Defective} \mid \text{PASS}) = \frac{\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate \CandidateDefectRate}{\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate \CandidateDefectRate + \Pr(\text{PASS} \mid \text{Valid})(1 - \CandidateDefectRate)}\)
Residual defect probability among candidate outputs accepted by a fallible checker

\(\SoftmaxOutputProbability_{t, i} \propto \exp(\OutputLogit_{t, i})\) for \(\MaskTokenIndex \in \ValidTokenSet(\DecodingConstraintState_t)\), else \(0\)

\(\CallLatency = \CallPreparationTime + \RequestQueueTime + \PrefillTime + \DecodeInterval + \CallPostprocessingTime\)
