INT4: 4-bit integer; lower integer precisions follow the same uppercase INTn pattern (for example, INT3, INT2)






Tokens count what a call reads and writes, and serving throughput is reported in tokens per second.
Turns count the steps of a trajectory, and the horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) is measured in turns.
Dollars per accepted task normalize spend by the results that passed acceptance, not by attempts or requests.
Trajectory goodput (\(\TrajectoryGoodput\)) is reported as accepted tasks per unit of elapsed time; goodput per dollar uses total included cost as its denominator.
Byte-seconds measure memory held over time, such as attention state kept resident during a tool wait.




Common collision points in ML Systems literature arise when a single letter is standard in both machine learning and computer systems. As a general principle, machine learning conventions take precedence for single letters, while systems concepts receive subscripts or multi-letter symbols:










Symbol
ML Meaning
Systems Meaning
Book Convention




\(\BatchSize\)
Batch Size
Bandwidth
Batch Size. Use \(\Bandwidth\) for bandwidth.


\(\Glyph{D}\)
Dataset Size
Data Volume
Dataset Size. Use \(\DataVolume\) for bytes moved and \(\SearchDepth\) for a search depth limit.


\(\Parameters\)
Parameters
Peak FLOP/s
Parameters. Use \(\PeakRate\) for peak rate.




The agentic conventions that follow apply the same precedence rule. Every recurring symbol keeps a single meaning across this book, and local symbols are declared explicitly where they appear.



Agentic systems borrow notation from machine learning, systems, and control, so several letters arrive with more than one meaning. Where those traditions collide, the bare letter belongs to one recurring quantity and subscripts, font weight, or explicit level indices distinguish the rest:









Symbol
Other common meanings
Convention in this book




\(\Glyph{\tau}\)
Temperature; a threshold; an interval
Bare \(\Glyph{\tau}\) is a trajectory. A subscripted \(\Glyph{\tau}\) is a scoped quantity named where it is used, such as the sampling temperature \(\Glyph{\tau_{\text{temp}}}\). A time window is \(\Glyph{T_{\text{win}}}\), and the checkpoint interval is \(\CheckpointInterval\).


\(\Glyph{H}\)
Attention heads; hidden size
\(\Glyph{H}\) is the horizon in turns. Heads use \(\AttentionHeadCount\) and \(\KvHeadCount\); hidden size uses \(\Glyph{d}\).


\(\Glyph{S}\)
The State exposure
Bare \(\Glyph{S}\) is sequence length. State is written only with a level, \(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\).


\(\Glyph{A}\)
Advantage; action sets
Authority is written only with a level, \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\). Advantage is \(\Glyph{\hat{A}}\); action sets are \(\Glyph{\mathcal{A}_{\text{prop}}}\) and \(\PermittedActions\).


\(\Glyph{P}\)
Prompt length; precision; a predicate; a count
\(\Glyph{P}\) is parameter count, as in the shared table, and a subscripted \(\Glyph{P}\) is a power. Prompt length is \(\Glyph{S}\), a grant’s condition predicate is \(\GrantCondition\), a worker count is \(\WorkerCount\), and a named probability is a lowercase \(\Glyph{p}\), as in \(\DuplicateEffectProbability\).


\(\Glyph{p}\)
Any probability
Bare \(\Glyph{p}\) is a probability named where it is used. The per-attempt pass probability \(\AttemptPassProbability\) and the valid-candidate rate \(\ValidCandidateRate\) are different events; a workload-level acceptance probability carries a subscript, as \(\AcceptanceProbability\) does.


\(\Glyph{N}\)
Device count; a sample size
Bare \(\Glyph{N}\) counts what the text names: a candidate pool \(\CandidatePoolSize\), a cohort of initiated tasks \(\InitiatedTasks\), or a local count. Counts that recur carry a subscript, as \(\AcceptedTasks\) and \(\WorkerCount\) do, and the break-even task volume is \(\BreakEvenTaskCount\).


\(\Glyph{B}\)
A budget
\(\Glyph{B}\) is batch size. The trajectory budget is bold \(\TrajectoryBudget\), the reasoning budget is \(\Glyph{B_{\text{reason}}}\), and a dollar budget is a \(\CostCeiling\).


\(\Glyph{C}\)
A fourth taxonomy axis; a grant or commit
There is no \(\Glyph{C}\) axis; closure evidence levels are named in words. Costs carry subscripts (\(\TaskCost\), \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), \(\CostCeiling\)), and the task contract is \(\TaskContract\). A capability grant is \(\Glyph{\Gamma}\), and a commit is named by its content hash, as in \(\Glyph{h_{\text{base}}}\).


\(\Glyph{M}\)
A worker or agent count
The \(\Glyph{M}\) root is memory, always subscripted (\(\KvCacheMemory\), \(\Glyph{M_{\text{total}}}\)). A worker or agent count is \(\WorkerCount\).


\(\Glyph{\lambda}\)
Arrival rate; failure rate
Arrival rate is the shared \(\ArrivalRate\), or \(\TrajectoryAdmissionRate\) when counted in trajectories, and failure rate is \(\TurnFailureRate\). Bare \(\Glyph{\lambda}\) is the learning chapters’ trace decay or a local function defined where it is used.


\(\Glyph{\mu}\)
A mean; a friction coefficient
\(\ServiceRate\) is the per-server service rate. A mean carries a subscript, as \(\Glyph{\mu_R}\) does, or is a local statistical mean defined where it is used.


\(\Glyph{\rho}\)
Utilization; a recoverable fraction
Server utilization is the shared \(\ServingUtilization\), and the recoverable fraction of an action is \(\ActionRecoverableFraction\). Bare \(\Glyph{\rho}\) is a local ratio, such as a correlation, defined where it is used.


\(\Glyph{L}\)
Little’s law occupancy; loss; latency
Little’s law is written in the shared form \(\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate\,\RequestTimeInSystem\) for requests, with service time \(\RequestServiceTime\) and queue wait \(\RequestQueueTime\); other held resources use \(\ConcurrentTrajectories\)-style occupancies. Loss is \(\LossFunction\), and latency is a subscripted time such as \(\CallLatency\).


\(\Glyph{\mathcal{G}}\)
The goal; a graph
\(\Glyph{\mathcal{G}}\) is trajectory goodput. The goal is \(\Glyph{g}\) in the loop and \(\TaskContractGoal\) in the task contract; a graph is named by its vertex and edge sets, \((\Glyph{V}, \Glyph{E})\).


\(\Glyph{\mathcal{E}}\)
Evidence or event sets
\(\Glyph{\mathcal{E}}\) is the environment, and \(\TaskEnvironment\) its specification in the task contract. Accepted influences on an operation are \(\AcceptedInfluences(\ProposedOperation)\).


\(\Glyph{h}\)
A commit hash
\(\CoordinationOverhead(\WorkerCount)\) is the coordination overhead, always written with its argument, and \(\Glyph{h}_k\) is the interaction history in the learning chapters. Commit content hashes carry text subscripts, as in \(\Glyph{h_{\text{base}}}\) and \(\Glyph{h_{\text{head}}}\).


\(\Glyph{\epsilon}\)
A small constant; a tolerance
\(\PerStepErrorRate\) is the per-step error rate of horizon compounding. Other error rates carry subscripts (\(\VerifierFalseAcceptanceRate\), \(\StaleSupportRate\)), and a stability constant or a stockout target is local.


\(\pi\)
Peak arithmetic rate
The policy is \(\Policy\); a local derivation that writes a fixed policy as bare \(\pi\) says so where it does. Peak arithmetic rate is \(\PeakRate\) from the shared table.


\(\Glyph{\alpha}\), \(\Glyph{\beta}\)
Test error rates; bandwidth; regularization weights
\(\AcceptanceFraction\) is the acceptance fraction, and a significance level is \(\StatisticalSignificanceLevel\). Bandwidth is \(\Bandwidth\) from the shared table. A Type II error rate, a draft token’s relative cost, and the preference and divergence weights written \(\Glyph{\beta}\) are local and defined where used.


\(\Glyph{\kappa}\)
Cohen’s kappa; a coherency coefficient
\(\Glyph{\kappa}(\Glyph{x})\) is a confidentiality label. Cohen’s kappa is local to the evaluation chapter’s agreement analysis, and the scalability law’s coherency coefficient is \(\CoherencyCoefficient\).


\(\Glyph{K}\)
Top-\(\Glyph{k}\); sample count
\(\Glyph{K}\) is output length in tokens. Sample counts use lowercase \(\Glyph{k}\), as in pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\); the repair cap \(\RepairCap\) and the reinforcement-learning chapter’s continuation count \(\ContinuationCount\) are declared in their rows.

title: Author’s Note
text:
Author’s Note

When an AI answers a question, the interaction is over. When an AI takes an action, the real engineering has only just begun.
A prompt-and-response model in a stateless, text-only interaction is an oracle behind glass: it answers when spoken to, carries no action privileges, and leaves no session state for the next call. Once you give that intelligence tools, memory, and a delegated goal, however, it ceases to be an oracle. It becomes an actor.
My curiosity about agentic systems began during a National Science Foundation (NSF) workshop on AI efficiency. As someone whose work has long focused on benchmarking and quantitative systems evaluation, including the initialization of MLPerf, I found myself asking a basic systems question: how do we benchmark and evaluate the efficiency of these actors?
At the algorithmic and application layers, the community has introduced a vibrant lexicon of techniques: “prompt engineering,” “prompt chaining,” “in-context reflection,” and “agentic workflows.” These ideas are genuinely creative and impactful. They show us what is possible when models interact iteratively with task environments. As a computer systems architect, however, I found myself asking a complementary question: what machine is required to build, benchmark, and scale these ideas? When you hear these exotic-sounding terms at the application level, what is the actual system you have to construct underneath?
To measure and engineer these workflows, we have to break them down to their fundamentals. Viewed from first principles, an agentic system is not an alien artifact. It is a machine built around a foundation model, and its parts are ones a systems engineer recognizes:

The foundation model reads a context and proposes the next action.
Agent memory decides what each call sees and keeps what must outlast the session.
Tools carry approved proposals into the environment under scoped permissions, with sandboxes containing the reach of executable code.
The agent runtime mediates proposals, records execution, and coordinates recovery or escalation when something goes wrong.

Taken together, these parts form a single architectural map that I call the Stochastic Computer. That map shows how the pieces fit at a glance, after which each subsystem must be engineered on its own terms, because a foundation model does not behave like deterministic logic and a context window does not behave like a hardware cache.
Yet this machine carries a profound systems twist: it is stochastic. A deterministic program repeats its result when its inputs and execution conditions remain fixed. A sampling foundation model can propose a different action under the same context. Even when generation is repeatable, the proposal can still be wrong. Repeated success is no substitute for bounding what the next action may reach.
I experienced this firsthand while drafting these chapters. Working alongside an autonomous coding assistant with direct terminal access, the agent took an unexpected turn and executed an rm -f directly in the directory containing my active edits. Then, late at night and out of habit, I committed and pushed the changes upstream. Days of work across a holiday weekend were gone.
A computer systems professor should know better than to give an unconstrained actor raw effector privileges without an isolated sandbox, or to push a tree without reading the diff. That is the trap. Autonomy is convenient until it makes a change that cannot be undone. The task needed only reversible authority over a disposable working copy of my files, and the environment granted irreversible authority over my sole authoritative workspace (The H·S·A Exposure Space).
Reliability has always required more than debugging individual components. When the component proposing actions is learned, we must also account for proposals that look plausible while violating the task. We cannot rely on human vigilance or prompt cleverness alone to guarantee safety. The runtime around the model must bound what each call sees, contain what each action can reach, preserve the records needed for recovery, and escalate when an effect cannot be safely repaired.
I write these chapters as a student of a discipline in motion. Putting this book together, shuttling between Cambridge and Zurich, has been my way of distilling the durable first principles that will still govern these systems a decade from now: the three exposures of horizon, state, and authority and the closure the runtime builds against them. I hope you find it helpful.
— Vijay Janapa Reddi
Cambridge, Massachusetts & Zurich, Switzerland
2026

title: Agentic Machine Learning Systems
text:
Vijay Janapa Reddi

October 26, 2026




  
    This is a working volume. Agentic machine learning systems turn model inference into a stateful control loop that observes, decides, acts, verifies, and adapts. The managed trajectory, rather than the isolated request, is the central unit of engineering.
    The volume builds an agentic system in the order its dependencies impose (model, memory, tools, runtime, measurement, learning, and scale) and treats unsettled mechanisms as open design questions rather than fixed doctrine.
  

  
    
    Agentic Machine Learning Systems
    Vijay Janapa Reddi
  


What You Will Learn

The book opens with an introduction that defines the agentic system, its unit of work (the trajectory), and the three exposures an agent adds beyond a single model call: horizon, state, and authority. Seven parts then build the system in order.

  Part I: The Model. The foundation model and test-time compute.
  Part II: Agent Memory. Context engineering, KV cache management, and long-term memory.
  Part III: Tool Use. Tool calling, agent sandboxes, and agent security.
  Part IV: The Agent Runtime. The agent harness, durable execution, failure recovery, agent evaluation, and operating agents.
  Part V: Learning from Trajectories. Trajectory curation, trajectory fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.
  Part VI: Agents at Scale. Multi-agent coordination and agent economics.
  Part VII: Synthesis. One trajectory through every part, and the specification boundary.


Prerequisites

Readers should be familiar with foundation models and large language models, including prompting and token generation, and with software systems concepts such as APIs, state management, concurrency, and process isolation. Programming experience and undergraduate-level probability provide the remaining foundations. The book assumes no earlier volume of this series and develops the agentic and serving concepts it needs.

title: Preface
text:
This book is for senior undergraduates and beginning graduate students in computer science and computer engineering who are taking a course on agentic machine learning systems, and for practicing engineers who build, operate, or evaluate agents. It is written for the engineer who has watched an agent demonstration succeed. That engineer now has to ship a system that carries delegated work to an accepted result, day after day, without deleting the wrong directory, looping until a budget runs out, or reporting success on a task it never finished.
The reader should understand foundation-model prompting and token generation and be comfortable with software systems, including APIs, state, concurrency, and process isolation. This book is self-contained and assumes no prior machine learning systems course. It develops agentic concepts where they are first used and derives the serving-cost relationships needed to reason about agent workloads without requiring accelerator microarchitecture or fleet-scale training.



A reasonable engineer might look at the current wave of agent demonstrations and ask a skeptical question. Is agentic machine learning a systems discipline with durable principles, or a collection of framework wrappers, prompt templates, and API glue that will be rewritten next year?
The skepticism is fair. Much of what is written about agents concerns surface choices, such as a framework’s abstractions, a persona in a system prompt, or a ten-line loop that looks impressive in a demonstration and fails under real workloads. Those choices change every few months. What does not change is the engineering problem underneath them.
A single model call reads a context and returns a proposal. By itself, the call neither executes that proposal nor establishes whether it satisfies the task. An agent puts that call inside a loop. The loop runs for many turns, carries state from one turn to the next, and turns approved proposals into edits, commands, queries, and messages that affect the environment. Each of those departures adds exposure beyond an isolated call, and each fails in its own way. A long loop compounds small errors and can run without advancing. Carried state overflows the context, goes stale, or contradicts itself. Actions leak data, repeat when a timeout hides whether they ran, or cannot be undone. The model cannot close any of these exposures by itself, because its proposal grants no authority and its self-report is insufficient evidence of success. The closure has to come from the machine built around it.
This book teaches how to design, measure, and improve that machine. Its central question is what a delegated task needs around a foundation model to produce a result supported by the required evidence. Readers should leave able to decide when a fixed workflow suffices and when a model-directed loop earns its added cost, what memory, tools, and runtime that loop requires, how to show that it works, and when changing the model or adding agents is worth the price.



The unit of engineering in this book is the trajectory, the ordered record of one delegated task’s execution. It holds what the model saw on each turn, what it proposed, what the runtime did with the proposal, and what came back. Accuracy on a single call is not the measure of an agentic system. The measure is whether trajectories reach results that meet the task’s acceptance standard, supported by evidence independent of the model’s self-report, and at what cost in turns, tokens, seconds, and dollars.
Three exposures describe how far a task departs from a single model call, and the book calls them H·S·A. Each axis captures one dimension along which a delegated loop accumulates risk beyond a stateless request:

Horizon is how many turns the trajectory runs, and so how long errors have to compound and how much can go wrong between the start and the result.
State is what the task carries from one turn to the next, from nothing, through the context window and a sandboxed workspace, to durable state that outlives the session or is shared beyond it.
Authority is what the task may do to the world through its tools, from read access, which can still leak, to irreversible external actions such as a payment or a production migration.

Closure is not a fourth exposure, but the runtime’s answer to the three. Under the invariant closure principle, runtime mechanisms enforce named bounds (such as resource limits and permitted access) under stated assumptions, whereas independent checks supply evidence for the completion properties they cover. Making a check deterministic or protecting it from modification keeps that evidence sound without making its coverage complete, and while instructions or fine-tuning can improve the model’s proposals, neither replaces runtime enforcement. Higher exposure along any axis therefore demands stronger mechanical boundaries and a stricter acceptance standard. The introduction develops the three exposures, the principle, and the forms of evidence that can stand behind a claim that a task is done.
Two relations quantify these obligations throughout the book. Horizon compounding is the decay of reliability over unchecked turns. If each of \(\TurnHorizon\) sequential turns is correct independently with probability \(1-\PerStepErrorRate\) and nothing checks them, the task succeeds with probability \((1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}\). Cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), charges every attempt, failed ones included, to the tasks that meet their acceptance standard, and so states what a mechanism is worth in the unit the task cares about.
Four recurring workloads, each bound by a different exposure, keep the argument concrete. A repair agent that fixes a defect in an isolated working copy over a long horizon is the running example in every chapter. A research agent that reads untrusted sources, a remediation agent whose actions on production systems can be irreversible, and a support agent that serves many short interactive sessions at once return wherever the repair agent cannot exercise a constraint. A mechanism that is central for one of these workloads can be pure overhead for another, which is why the book prices mechanisms against a workload rather than ranking them in the abstract. That pricing and exposure framework sets the order in which the book constructs the system.



The book builds understanding in dependency order: model, memory, tools, runtime, measure, learn, scale. Each part adds responsibilities that the preceding material prepares the reader to evaluate. This teaching sequence is not a requirement to deploy every mechanism. When an agent fails, a related ordering governs the response. The intervention ladder ranks remedies by cost and reversibility. Once a failure is attributed to a measured cause, changes to context, to tools and their schemas, and to runtime control come before changes to the model’s weights. Weight changes are reserved for the failure that survives the earlier rungs, and they are made only on evidence that the change helps. The ladder is a default order rather than a sequence every failure must climb, and The intervention ladder develops it.
Before the seven parts begin, Introduction defines the agentic system and the trajectory, names the fail-plausible faults that make agents hard to trust, states the invariant closure principle, and turns a task into a contract. Along the horizon, state, and authority axes, it shows how to judge the runtime responsibilities a workload requires, when a fixed workflow suffices over a model-directed loop, and how the subsystems fit into a single architectural map:

Part I: The Model studies the component every agent is built around through a single call. The Foundation Model establishes what a call reads, returns, and costs, and why its output is a proposal the runtime must check rather than a result. Test-Time Compute asks when longer reasoning, additional candidates, or check-and-revise rounds improve the selected result within a bounded budget, and what evidence supports accepting it.
Part II: Agent Memory governs the state exposure. Context Engineering decides what each call sees under a fixed budget, KV Cache Management prices what holding that context costs in the serving system, and Long-Term Memory governs what persists across sessions and returns only through retrieval.
Part III: Tool Use governs the authority exposure. Tool Calling separates proposal validation, authorization, dispatch, and evidence of the resulting effect, including cases where a timeout leaves the outcome uncertain. Agent Sandboxes bounds the reach of executing code, while Agent Security addresses how untrusted information can misuse otherwise legitimate access.
Part IV: The Agent Runtime governs the horizon exposure. The Agent Harness runs the loop under budgets and approvals, Durable Execution preserves progress across stated failure conditions, and Failure Recovery chooses among repair, compensation, containment, and escalation. Agent Evaluation measures the whole single-agent system and establishes the evidence needed to judge later learning and scaling decisions, and the part ends with Operating Agents, which traces, diagnoses, and stages the release of a configuration on live work.
Part V: Learning from Trajectories changes model behavior when evaluation justifies that intervention; it does not replace the runtime’s boundaries. Trajectory Curation decides when a failure warrants changing the weights at all, then selects and prepares records for different learning objectives, including demonstrations of recovery. Trajectory Fine-Tuning teaches behavior from those records, and Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards optimizes against verifiable rewards while examining the limits and protection of the reward checks.
Part VI: Agents at Scale multiplies all three exposures. Multi-Agent Coordination splits a task across agents only when the coordination pays for itself, and Agent Economics prices and provisions agents per accepted task.
Part VII: Synthesis follows a production incident-remediation task through the system in Conclusion. It ends at the specification boundary, where defining success, judging whether the evidence is sufficient, and answering for the result stay with the engineer.

Reference appendices collect material that supports the chapters without interrupting them. Together they supply the mathematical background, the inference cost derivations behind the book’s serving estimates, the distributed-state guarantees behind durable execution and coordination, a reference architecture, typed tool interfaces, a failure taxonomy, and a glossary.



The book is written to be read in order. Each chapter uses only ideas introduced earlier in the book or defined where they appear, and each owns its concepts, so a mechanism is taught once and cited afterward. Every chapter opens with the agent problem it solves, introduces the mechanism as the answer to that problem, and closes with a summary and a handoff to the next chapter. Classical systems ideas, such as write-ahead logs, compensating transactions, idempotency keys, and capabilities, appear where they are the real engineering, introduced as the fix for an agent failure rather than as a lesson in their own right.
Readers with a particular role can weight their reading after the introduction. Engineers who build serving and execution infrastructure will lean on the chapters covering the model, the KV cache, sandboxes, durable execution, and economics. Engineers who build agent platforms will focus on context engineering, tool calling, security, the harness, failure recovery, evaluation, operations, and multi-agent coordination. Researchers and post-training teams will concentrate on the model, test-time compute, evaluation, and all of Part V. None of these emphases removes the prerequisites established by earlier chapters, so every path begins with Introduction and ends with Conclusion.
These dependencies divide the book into a core systems sequence and an optional post-training branch (figure 1). Because the detailed test-time compute and post-training methods (Test-Time Compute and Part V) branch off the core path without blocking Part VI or the conclusion, a course on building and operating agents can follow the core sequence alone. A course on post-training keeps that branch and still needs Parts I through IV beneath it, because Trajectory Curation starts from the evidence that Agent Evaluation defines and Operating Agents retains.

Because the book focuses on the durable engineering of agentic systems, several adjacent topics lie outside its scope. First, it is not a prompt-engineering guide: prompts matter, but the runtime treats them as one assembled input and never relies on a prompt instruction where a mechanical check is possible. Nor is it a tutorial for any specific agent framework, protocol implementation, or model provider, or a leaderboard of this year’s models and benchmarks, which appear only as cited examples of a general technique or evaluation method. At the hardware layer, the text leaves accelerator microarchitecture to other works and develops only the serving relationships an agent engineer needs (such as how prompt processing differs from output generation and when shared-prefix reuse saves work, with full derivations in the appendix). Finally, the book covers software agents that act through tools on digital systems; agents that act on the physical world raise distinct control and safety problems outside its scope.



Frameworks, protocols, and model weights will change, some of them before this book reaches print. The text therefore emphasizes the ideas that survive those changes. These include the trajectory as the unit of work, the three exposures and the closure against them, the separation between a model that proposes and a runtime that decides, and the discipline of measuring before changing anything. Current protocols and systems appear throughout to make the ideas concrete, but the principles stand independently of any vendor or tool. Where a question is still open, such as how best to evaluate systems that act or how to structure an agent’s long-term memory, the book says so and presents the question as an open problem rather than a settled method.



Readers should be comfortable with:

working familiarity with foundation models, including prompting and autoregressive token generation;
computer systems fundamentals, including processes, memory, file systems, and networking;
basic distributed systems concepts, including remote calls, failure, and consistency;
undergraduate probability; and
programming in Python or another modern language.

Deeper study of operating systems, databases, or computer security helps, but the book explains how the systems mechanisms it uses apply to agent workloads. Readers who want more background on how machine learning systems are built and served can find it in Introduction to Machine Learning Systems, which this book does not assume.

title: Preface
text:
This book is for senior undergraduates and beginning graduate students in computer science and computer engineering who are taking a course on agentic machine learning systems, and for practicing engineers who build, operate, or evaluate agents. It is written for the engineer who has watched an agent demonstration succeed. That engineer now has to ship a system that carries delegated work to an accepted result, day after day, without deleting the wrong directory, looping until a budget runs out, or reporting success on a task it never finished.
The reader should understand foundation-model prompting and token generation and be comfortable with software systems, including APIs, state, concurrency, and process isolation. This book is self-contained and assumes no prior machine learning systems course. It develops agentic concepts where they are first used and derives the serving-cost relationships needed to reason about agent workloads without requiring accelerator microarchitecture or fleet-scale training.

title: Preface
text:
A reasonable engineer might look at the current wave of agent demonstrations and ask a skeptical question. Is agentic machine learning a systems discipline with durable principles, or a collection of framework wrappers, prompt templates, and API glue that will be rewritten next year?
The skepticism is fair. Much of what is written about agents concerns surface choices, such as a framework’s abstractions, a persona in a system prompt, or a ten-line loop that looks impressive in a demonstration and fails under real workloads. Those choices change every few months. What does not change is the engineering problem underneath them.
A single model call reads a context and returns a proposal. By itself, the call neither executes that proposal nor establishes whether it satisfies the task. An agent puts that call inside a loop. The loop runs for many turns, carries state from one turn to the next, and turns approved proposals into edits, commands, queries, and messages that affect the environment. Each of those departures adds exposure beyond an isolated call, and each fails in its own way. A long loop compounds small errors and can run without advancing. Carried state overflows the context, goes stale, or contradicts itself. Actions leak data, repeat when a timeout hides whether they ran, or cannot be undone. The model cannot close any of these exposures by itself, because its proposal grants no authority and its self-report is insufficient evidence of success. The closure has to come from the machine built around it.
This book teaches how to design, measure, and improve that machine. Its central question is what a delegated task needs around a foundation model to produce a result supported by the required evidence. Readers should leave able to decide when a fixed workflow suffices and when a model-directed loop earns its added cost, what memory, tools, and runtime that loop requires, how to show that it works, and when changing the model or adding agents is worth the price.

title: Preface
text:
The unit of engineering in this book is the trajectory, the ordered record of one delegated task’s execution. It holds what the model saw on each turn, what it proposed, what the runtime did with the proposal, and what came back. Accuracy on a single call is not the measure of an agentic system. The measure is whether trajectories reach results that meet the task’s acceptance standard, supported by evidence independent of the model’s self-report, and at what cost in turns, tokens, seconds, and dollars.
Three exposures describe how far a task departs from a single model call, and the book calls them H·S·A. Each axis captures one dimension along which a delegated loop accumulates risk beyond a stateless request:

Horizon is how many turns the trajectory runs, and so how long errors have to compound and how much can go wrong between the start and the result.
State is what the task carries from one turn to the next, from nothing, through the context window and a sandboxed workspace, to durable state that outlives the session or is shared beyond it.
Authority is what the task may do to the world through its tools, from read access, which can still leak, to irreversible external actions such as a payment or a production migration.

Closure is not a fourth exposure, but the runtime’s answer to the three. Under the invariant closure principle, runtime mechanisms enforce named bounds (such as resource limits and permitted access) under stated assumptions, whereas independent checks supply evidence for the completion properties they cover. Making a check deterministic or protecting it from modification keeps that evidence sound without making its coverage complete, and while instructions or fine-tuning can improve the model’s proposals, neither replaces runtime enforcement. Higher exposure along any axis therefore demands stronger mechanical boundaries and a stricter acceptance standard. The introduction develops the three exposures, the principle, and the forms of evidence that can stand behind a claim that a task is done.
Two relations quantify these obligations throughout the book. Horizon compounding is the decay of reliability over unchecked turns. If each of \(\TurnHorizon\) sequential turns is correct independently with probability \(1-\PerStepErrorRate\) and nothing checks them, the task succeeds with probability \((1-\PerStepErrorRate)^{\TurnHorizon}\). Cost per accepted task, \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\), charges every attempt, failed ones included, to the tasks that meet their acceptance standard, and so states what a mechanism is worth in the unit the task cares about.
Four recurring workloads, each bound by a different exposure, keep the argument concrete. A repair agent that fixes a defect in an isolated working copy over a long horizon is the running example in every chapter. A research agent that reads untrusted sources, a remediation agent whose actions on production systems can be irreversible, and a support agent that serves many short interactive sessions at once return wherever the repair agent cannot exercise a constraint. A mechanism that is central for one of these workloads can be pure overhead for another, which is why the book prices mechanisms against a workload rather than ranking them in the abstract. That pricing and exposure framework sets the order in which the book constructs the system.

title: Preface
text:
The book builds understanding in dependency order: model, memory, tools, runtime, measure, learn, scale. Each part adds responsibilities that the preceding material prepares the reader to evaluate. This teaching sequence is not a requirement to deploy every mechanism. When an agent fails, a related ordering governs the response. The intervention ladder ranks remedies by cost and reversibility. Once a failure is attributed to a measured cause, changes to context, to tools and their schemas, and to runtime control come before changes to the model’s weights. Weight changes are reserved for the failure that survives the earlier rungs, and they are made only on evidence that the change helps. The ladder is a default order rather than a sequence every failure must climb, and The intervention ladder develops it.
Before the seven parts begin, Introduction defines the agentic system and the trajectory, names the fail-plausible faults that make agents hard to trust, states the invariant closure principle, and turns a task into a contract. Along the horizon, state, and authority axes, it shows how to judge the runtime responsibilities a workload requires, when a fixed workflow suffices over a model-directed loop, and how the subsystems fit into a single architectural map:

Part I: The Model studies the component every agent is built around through a single call. The Foundation Model establishes what a call reads, returns, and costs, and why its output is a proposal the runtime must check rather than a result. Test-Time Compute asks when longer reasoning, additional candidates, or check-and-revise rounds improve the selected result within a bounded budget, and what evidence supports accepting it.
Part II: Agent Memory governs the state exposure. Context Engineering decides what each call sees under a fixed budget, KV Cache Management prices what holding that context costs in the serving system, and Long-Term Memory governs what persists across sessions and returns only through retrieval.
Part III: Tool Use governs the authority exposure. Tool Calling separates proposal validation, authorization, dispatch, and evidence of the resulting effect, including cases where a timeout leaves the outcome uncertain. Agent Sandboxes bounds the reach of executing code, while Agent Security addresses how untrusted information can misuse otherwise legitimate access.
Part IV: The Agent Runtime governs the horizon exposure. The Agent Harness runs the loop under budgets and approvals, Durable Execution preserves progress across stated failure conditions, and Failure Recovery chooses among repair, compensation, containment, and escalation. Agent Evaluation measures the whole single-agent system and establishes the evidence needed to judge later learning and scaling decisions, and the part ends with Operating Agents, which traces, diagnoses, and stages the release of a configuration on live work.
Part V: Learning from Trajectories changes model behavior when evaluation justifies that intervention; it does not replace the runtime’s boundaries. Trajectory Curation decides when a failure warrants changing the weights at all, then selects and prepares records for different learning objectives, including demonstrations of recovery. Trajectory Fine-Tuning teaches behavior from those records, and Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards optimizes against verifiable rewards while examining the limits and protection of the reward checks.
Part VI: Agents at Scale multiplies all three exposures. Multi-Agent Coordination splits a task across agents only when the coordination pays for itself, and Agent Economics prices and provisions agents per accepted task.
Part VII: Synthesis follows a production incident-remediation task through the system in Conclusion. It ends at the specification boundary, where defining success, judging whether the evidence is sufficient, and answering for the result stay with the engineer.

Reference appendices collect material that supports the chapters without interrupting them. Together they supply the mathematical background, the inference cost derivations behind the book’s serving estimates, the distributed-state guarantees behind durable execution and coordination, a reference architecture, typed tool interfaces, a failure taxonomy, and a glossary.

text:
The book is written to be read in order. Each chapter uses only ideas introduced earlier in the book or defined where they appear, and each owns its concepts, so a mechanism is taught once and cited afterward. Every chapter opens with the agent problem it solves, introduces the mechanism as the answer to that problem, and closes with a summary and a handoff to the next chapter. Classical systems ideas, such as write-ahead logs, compensating transactions, idempotency keys, and capabilities, appear where they are the real engineering, introduced as the fix for an agent failure rather than as a lesson in their own right.
Readers with a particular role can weight their reading after the introduction. Engineers who build serving and execution infrastructure will lean on the chapters covering the model, the KV cache, sandboxes, durable execution, and economics. Engineers who build agent platforms will focus on context engineering, tool calling, security, the harness, failure recovery, evaluation, operations, and multi-agent coordination. None of these emphases removes the prerequisites established by earlier chapters, so every path begins with Introduction and ends with Conclusion.

title: Preface
A Note on AI Assistance
text:
A Note on AI Assistance






NoteWorking draft



This text is an evolving working draft. As I collect ideas and organize this material, these chapters represent an active work in progress. While I develop each section carefully from foundational literature and verified computation cells, I have not yet reached the stage of stress-testing these frameworks with external domain experts. I am sharing this draft openly to organize my thoughts and invite early community feedback as the curriculum takes shape.


This book is released as an open-access, living textbook; it is not yet under contract with a commercial publisher. Unlike established engineering disciplines with decades of teaching consensus, the field of agentic systems is young, fast-moving, and fluid. Because systems architectures for autonomous machine learning are moving week by week, I am sharing these chapters as an open research notebook rather than holding them back for a multi-year publishing cycle.
Every textbook begins with collecting ideas, organizing scattered concepts, and structuring outlines: deciding what needs to be a chapter, what belongs in a section, and what not to cover. In developing this text, I used artificial intelligence to help explore how to structure the pieces together, discover relevant literature, and organize the resulting curriculum.
In this book, I frame agent trajectories through the H·S·A exposures of horizon, state, and authority, examining how mechanical bounds and evidence of task completion support reliable execution around probabilistic foundation models. To explore this framework, I used an agentic approach to write about agentic systems. I collaborated with multi-agent workflows to brainstorm taxonomies, explore alternative structural framings, and debate architectural trade-offs. To test whether the explanations were clear, I prompted agent personas with diverse student backgrounds to probe where my explanations broke down, reveal conceptual blind spots, and help me work backward to clarify the exposition. I pushed the methodology further by running simulated panels of domain specialists (systems architects, runtime developers, and benchmark evaluators) to critique draft chapters from multiple perspectives before human review.
Yet simulated feedback and AI-assisted drafting can never replace human engineering. An early attempt to run an unconstrained multi-step agentic pipeline to write sections of this book failed decisively, showing firsthand why autonomous agents cannot replace human synthesis. Setting up context boundaries, execution sandboxes, and alignment guardrails to help models collaborate constructively provided immediate, practical insight into the exact systems challenges this book analyzes.
A textbook is fundamentally a distillation; the primary credit belongs to the researchers whose papers made the foundational discoveries and whose work populates our bibliography. At the same time, tools do not write textbooks. Assembling those discoveries into a coherent, teachable systems narrative requires demanding labor, late nights, and iterative rewriting: defining the abstractions, constructing executable models, and refining the text. Authorship means assuming that responsibility by curating the material with integrity and serving as the human point of contact when a reader finds an error or an engineer offers a critique.
While the embedded computation cells execute and the automated test suite checks reference hygiene, no automated check substitutes for scrutiny from the community building and teaching these systems. I encourage readers, practitioners, and researchers to read critically, report flaws on GitHub, and help sharpen these arguments as the book matures. That division of labor holds with special force when the subject itself is autonomous: the tool can propose, and the tool can simulate, but only the human engineer can ratify and take responsibility.

title: 1 Introduction
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why can a model that generates a fluent, correct action still fail to complete an autonomous task?
The difference between answering a prompt and completing a delegated task marks the boundary of agentic machine learning systems. A foundation model can propose the exact line of code needed to fix a race condition, yet the repository remains broken until software inspects the source tree, applies the patch, runs regression tests, and verifies the outcome. Delegating autonomous work therefore requires building an engineered machine around the model, not merely selecting capable weights. That machine resembles a complete computer, with components that compute, remember, act on the external world, supervise execution, recover from faults, and learn from experience. However, its central processing element differs fundamentally from any classical processor: it is an autoregressive model whose outputs are stochastic proposals rather than deterministic execution. A fluent proposal can be subtly wrong, and the model cannot vouch for its own correctness. The surrounding system exists to contain that reality. The runtime determines what data the model perceives, bounds the actions it may execute, persists critical state across interruptions, and verifies whether the task actually succeeded. Every decision consumes computational time and monetary budget that only accepted outcomes justify. Building an agentic system is thus an exercise in systems engineering: sizing the runtime machinery to the horizon, state, and authority that the task demands.

Learning Objectives

Trace the architectural evolution from predictive and generative machine learning to autonomous agentic systems
Explain why a model’s stochastic proposals require an external runtime to close the interaction loop, and trace one turn through the runtime’s six phases
Analyze which isolated-request assumptions a multi-turn trajectory breaks, and why the runtime accounts for cost, state, and authority per trajectory
Classify a delegated task by horizon, state, and authority to identify its systems engineering obligations
Distinguish mechanically enforced sandbox bounds from the external evidence that catches plausible but wrong results before task acceptance
Calculate unchecked task reliability and cost per accepted task across multi-turn horizons, and use them to decide between a fixed workflow and a model-directed loop
Specify a five-part task contract that separates goal, environment, permitted actions, observations, and completion criteria



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



A prediction service returns a score, a conversational assistant proposes a patch, and an agentic system applies and checks that patch under delegated authority. These three deployment arrangements trace the progression from predictive pipelines through conversational foundation models to autonomous workloads. They overlap historically: predictive models can participate in feedback loops, and a foundation model can serve any of the three arrangements. The engineering distinction is who controls the actions and checks the outcome, as three representative arrangements illustrate:

Predictive Machine Learning Systems: A predictive model maps a supplied input to a structured output (\(\ExampleLabel = \ModelPredictor(\ModelInput)\)), as in image classification, recommendation ranking, or fraud scoring. Application code supplies the input and consumes the returned score, so the serving call needs no conversational memory or tool loop, even when the application feeds its scores into a broader process. Systems engineering concentrates on serving throughput, memory layout, and batch latency.
Generative Foundation Models: Large autoregressive transformers trained on internet-scale corpora generate open-ended text, code, and multimodal tokens. In standard conversational deployment, however, the interaction remains open-loop and human-mediated. A developer working with a conversational assistant acts as the runtime controller, issuing a prompt, inspecting the response, copying code into an editor, running commands in a terminal, and pasting compiler errors and stack traces back into the prompt window. The model generates candidate tokens; the human provides the execution environment, carries working memory across turns, diagnoses failures, and verifies correctness.
Agentic Machine Learning Systems: Agentic systems replace the human in the inner control loop with a software runtime. Instead of requesting advice, a user delegates an end-to-end objective: clone a software repository, reproduce a reported defect, synthesize a candidate fix, run the full test suite in an isolated sandbox, iterate until regressions clear, and return a verified patch. The foundation model shifts from an advisory partner to an action-proposing component inside an active feedback loop.

Replacing the human operator in the interaction loop with a software runtime defines an agentic system and shifts what engineering optimizes (table 1).



Table 1: Three Eras of Machine Learning Systems: The representative arrangements differ in who closes the interaction loop. The predictive serving call returns a score without an autonomous tool loop, the conversational arrangement relies on a person to act on the response, and the agentic arrangement delegates that loop to a runtime. This changes the metric the system is engineered against.

Definition 1.1: Agentic system
Agentic system is an autonomous software system in which a runtime places a foundation model in a closed control loop with context, state, tools, and an environment, dispatching the model’s authorized proposals and returning their environmental observations to subsequent calls until the task is accepted, halted, or escalated.

Significance: The unit of systems optimization shifts from the isolated model call to the complete task trajectory. Unchecked errors compound exponentially across sequential turns (section 1.6), and every attempt, accepted or aborted, is charged to the task’s cost per accepted result.
Distinction: In conversational interfaces, a human executes tools, verifies output, and bridges state between turns. In an agentic system, software executes these operations under delegated authority, meaning the model’s output is strictly a proposal that holds no standing authority of its own.
Common pitfall: Treating agency as a capability inherent to the model’s weights. A more capable model produces more accurate candidate actions, but permission enforcement, sandbox isolation, durable state persistence, and completion verification belong entirely to the surrounding software runtime.



Production traffic shows how rapidly that third arrangement has overtaken the volume of isolated prompts. Across a multi-provider inference gateway serving more than 200,000 production teams (Vercel 2026), the share of requests ending in a tool call nearly doubled over six months, rising from 11.4 percent to 22.2 percent. Because each tool-using turn carries accumulated history and environment output, those 22.2 percent of requests already consumed 58.9 percent of all production tokens (up from 31.6 percent), or 5.0× as many tokens per request as calls without tools. Figure 1 tracks the aggregate token volume, total inference spend, and average price per token over the following five months on the same gateway.














Figure 1: Cheaper Tokens Fuel an Agentic Volume Surge: Monthly production token volume, total inference spend, and average price per token across a multi-provider inference gateway, each indexed to 100 in April 2026. All three series share a common baseline so their divergence is directly comparable: while the per-token price index falls below half of its starting level by September, token volume climbs nearly eightfold and pulls total inference spend to more than three times its April level. Data from Vercel (2026).


Vercel. 2026. AI Gateway Production Index.


As the average price per token fell by 57 percent (to an index of 43.3), teams did not pocket the savings on a fixed request volume; they deployed multi-turn loops that consumed 7.9× as many tokens (reaching 790.8) and raised total expenditure 3.4× (to 342.7). Lower per-token prices made multi-step delegation affordable, and multi-step delegation in turn broke the assumptions of isolated-request serving. An isolated-request service accounts for each call separately, retains no task state after the response, and treats an HTTP 200 status as success. None of those conventions holds when a delegated task spans dozens of dependent steps, accumulates context and serving state between calls (the attention key-value cache retained for the growing prefix, so that the next turn need not recompute it, can occupy gigabytes of accelerator memory), and triggers side effects that permanently alter external systems. Turning a model’s candidate output into a completed task therefore requires examining everything that must happen between a useful proposal and an accepted outcome.



That gap between a model response and a finished job is concrete when an engineering team delegates a repository repair: diagnosing and fixing an intermittent race condition in a distributed key-value store.1 A foundation model2 can inspect the issue description and propose an edit to the connection-pool locking logic. Emitting that patch text, however, leaves the repository untouched. Resolving the defect requires an agent to locate the relevant source files, draft an edit, execute compilers and test runners inside an isolated environment, interpret diagnostic logs when a build fails, and verify that the resulting code satisfies the repository’s regression test suite.
1 Repository Repair as a Benchmark Task: SWE-bench established repository repair as a standard benchmark for agentic systems: each instance pairs a real GitHub issue with the unit and integration tests from the patch that fixed it (Jimenez et al. 2024). A candidate patch is evaluated by whether those tests pass after application. The model is never permitted to inspect the evaluation tests directly, ensuring that acceptance rests on independent, untampered evidence rather than self-reported success. 
Jimenez, Carlos E., John Yang, Alexander Wettig, Shunyu Yao, Kexin Pei, Ofir Press, and Karthik Narasimhan. 2024. “SWE-Bench: Can Language Models Resolve Real-World GitHub Issues?” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
2 Foundation Model: Bommasani and colleagues introduced the term in 2021 to describe models trained on large, diverse datasets at scale that can be adapted to an expansive range of downstream tasks (Bommasani et al. 2021). Because a foundation model is general-purpose, its weights encode neither the security permissions nor the specific acceptance criteria of a given production task; those boundaries must be defined and enforced by the surrounding runtime. 
Bommasani, Rishi, Drew A. Hudson, Ehsan Adeli, Russ Altman, Simran Arora, Sydney von Arx, Michael S. Bernstein, et al. 2021. “On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2108.07258.
An agentic system comes into existence when software closes this interaction loop. Rather than relying on an engineer to copy prompts and error traces back and forth, the surrounding software feeds the foundation model an objective alongside fresh environmental observations and captures the model’s proposed action. It then dispatches that action and returns structured execution feedback to guide the next decision.
The surrounding software, the runtime, enforces the boundary between what the model proposes and what the environment executes. All execution authority resides with the runtime. Because a model outputs only text or token streams, generating an operation’s name confers no permission to run it. The runtime parses the proposed action, checks that it complies with current access policies, and dispatches the call through a designated tool. A tool provides a structured interface to an environmental action, such as reading file contents, editing source code, running a shell command, or running a test suite. The part of the runtime that drives this loop is often called the agent harness, and The Agent Harness develops it as a component of the runtime rather than a separate system. In the conversational arrangement of figure 2 (panel A), a developer carries every command and every error by hand; in the agentic arrangement (panel B), the runtime dispatches only the actions it grants and routes verifier evidence back to itself rather than trusting the model’s account of what happened.






Figure 2: A Person or a Runtime Closes the Loop: In the conversational arrangement (A), the model answers and the developer runs every tool and carries each error back by hand. In the agentic arrangement (B), the runtime assembles context, receives the model’s proposal, and dispatches only actions it grants; the model holds no authority, and verifier evidence returns to the runtime rather than to the model’s own report.



Panel B is the arrangement this book engineers. A capable model served by an optimized inference engine supplies proposals, but it cannot manage its own execution authority, maintain state across tool failures, or verify its actions against external reality. Those responsibilities fall on the surrounding software, so engineering an agent is the discipline of designing, securing, and operating the closed-loop system around the model. Analyzing and building that system requires four foundational instruments:

The Stochastic Computer: An architectural map that relates the parts of an agentic system to the parts of a classical computer and marks where the comparison fails (section 1.3).
The H·S·A Exposure Space: An analytical coordinate system that measures how far a delegated task departs from stateless model inference along three operational dimensions: execution horizon (\(\TurnHorizon\)), persistent state (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)), and external authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)) (section 1.4).
The Invariant Closure Principle: A governance rule stipulating that safety and security invariants must be mechanically enforced by the runtime below the model, while task acceptance must be verified against independent evidence above the model (section 1.5). Below the model means between its proposal and the environment, where the runtime decides what may execute; above it means between the finished result and whoever accepts it, where the runtime decides what counts as done.
Horizon Reliability and Cost Arithmetic: Mathematical relations that quantify how single-step error rates compound across multi-turn trajectories, showing how retry budgets and recovery mechanisms set the true compute cost per accepted task (section 1.6).

Section 1.4 also places four recurring reference workloads, which the book calls lighthouses, in the exposure space; the repair task is one of them. Once all four instruments are in hand, section 1.7 follows the repair task turn by turn to show where each one acts, and section 1.8 maps the instruments onto the structure of the book.



Repairing the connection-pool race condition requires more than a model call: the system must hold source files and test logs in working and persistent memory, invoke compilers and test runners that read and modify the workspace, supervise which commands may run, and improve future repairs from recorded runs. A classical computer organizes the same requirements, which makes it a convenient map of how the subsystems of an agentic system fit together.
The stochastic computer names that map (figure 3).3 Its upper band is the live execution loop of a single task, and its lower band acts across tasks. In the live band, the foundation model plays the processor. Context and external stores play the memory hierarchy, from the active context window to long-term retrieval indices. Tools play input and output. The agent runtime plays the operating system, scheduling model calls, mediating every privileged operation, and enforcing access control. Across tasks, learning from recorded runs plays the role of recompiling a program from measurements of its earlier executions, refining the model’s policy without changing the runtime’s safety boundaries. Coordinating many agents mirrors scale-out across a network, where agents divide one workload and contend for shared state and resource limits.
3 The Stored-Program Organization: Von Neumann’s 1945 draft report on the EDVAC partitioned a computer into central arithmetic, central control, memory, and input/output organs (Neumann 1945). In von Neumann’s architecture, central control holds the absolute authority to fetch and execute instructions. In an agentic system, that authority is deliberately inverted: authority resides strictly within the surrounding runtime, while the learned model only proposes actions. Trust is decided outside the processor.

Figure 3: The Stochastic Computer as an Architectural Map: The agent stack structured around traditional computing layers (marked with ≈). The live execution loop (top) executes one task trajectory turn by turn. The across-task loop (bottom) compiles evaluated trajectories into updated model policies and coordinates multi-agent scale. While the architectural analogy provides intuition, the chapters develop each subsystem through its own rigorous systems mechanisms.



The analogy breaks at the processor, and that break defines the discipline of agentic systems engineering. A conventional processor executes instructions deterministically, so that identical machine state yields repeatable, auditable execution. A foundation model samples tokens from a distribution learned during training and conditioned on the observations supplied in its context, and that conditioning guarantees neither that the observations are complete and current nor that the proposed action is correct. Its outputs are candidate proposals, not certified computations. A response can be fluent yet factually wrong, or syntactically correct yet semantically destructive, and nothing in the generated text can vouch for its own validity.
A classical kernel trusts the processor to execute instructions faithfully. An agentic runtime cannot trust the model even to report its own status, since a model may report a successful return code that no tool returned, or actions it never took. The runtime therefore closes the control loop independently, enforcing permissions mechanically below the model and verifying results against external evidence above it (section 1.5.2). Memory diverges as sharply. A processor addresses memory directly, whereas the context presented to a model is a selective, lossy projection of the environment’s state. Authoritative state resides in external databases, filesystems, and version-control trees, and the context holds only a transient working representation of it.
The map therefore marks where classical systems guarantees carry over and where new mechanisms are required. The engineering problem is the deterministic runtime around the model (context management, execution sandboxes, and verification) that lets a model whose proposals may be wrong drive reliable autonomous work. Not every workload needs the same runtime defenses, however, so sizing that runtime starts by measuring how far a delegated task departs from a single model call.






Agents depart from a single model call along horizon, state, and authority.
A single model call reads a static prompt, returns one completion, and leaves the outside world untouched. When a runtime instead stretches execution across dozens of turns, carries files and memory forward, and invokes tools that modify external systems, a single mistaken proposal can compound across steps, corrupt shared state, or trigger an irreversible outage. Sizing the runtime’s defenses to a task therefore starts from the book’s central runtime artifact, the trajectory, which records the complete sequence of steps the runtime must govern.

Definition 1.2: Trajectory
Trajectory is the ordered sequence of recorded states, proposed actions, runtime decisions, and observations through which one delegated task proceeds, from its initial context to its ultimate acceptance, termination, or escalation.

Significance: The trajectory length defines the operational horizon \(\TurnHorizon\), which governs how compounding errors degrade system reliability. Its complete span (encompassing rejected actions, retries, and failed branches) establishes the true accounting boundary when computing cost and latency per accepted task.
Distinction: While a conversational transcript captures the tokens exchanged between a model and a user, a trajectory preserves the full causal history of execution. It records which action proposals the runtime approved, modified, or rejected, alongside the raw observations returned by external tools, linking every decision to the exact evidence available at that step.
Common pitfall: Preserving only the final deliverable. Storing just the accepted patch or completed document hides the computational cost of discarded attempts, masks transient faults, and discards the intermediate verification evidence that justified accepting the work.



In compact notation, the trajectory is
\[\Trajectory = (\TrajectoryState_0, \TrajectoryAction_0, \TrajectoryObservation_1, \TrajectoryState_1, \TrajectoryAction_1, \TrajectoryObservation_2, \dots, \TrajectoryState_{\TurnHorizon})\]
where \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) is the recorded state available at decision step \(\TurnIndex\), \(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\) is the action the model proposes, and \(\TrajectoryObservation_{t+1}\) is the observation returned by the execution environment. Each transition from \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) to \(\TrajectoryState_{t+1}\) is one turn: one model call paired with the runtime’s mediation of the resulting proposal. The notation establishes a total ordering across interactions, where each \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) reflects the runtime’s partially observed view of the broader environment. The repair trajectory that section 1.7.1 follows turn by turn shows why the runtime must manage cost, state, and authority over this whole sequence rather than per call.
Each trajectory \(\Trajectory\) departs from an isolated model call along three operational dimensions: how many turns \(\TurnHorizon\) execution continues, what state \(\TrajectoryState_{t}\) persists across steps, and what external side effects the actions \(\TrajectoryAction_{t}\) can trigger. This book models these dimensions as the Horizon, State, and Authority (H·S·A) exposure space.

Definition 1.3: H·S·A exposure space
H·S·A exposure space is the three-dimensional coordinate system quantifying how far a delegated task departs from an isolated model call: its horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) measured in sequential turns, the state \(\StateExposureLevel_0\) through \(\StateExposureLevel_3\) carried between invocations, and the authority \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) through \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) exercised over external systems.

Significance: Each axis identifies a concrete operational exposure that the runtime must bound. Horizon determines how rapidly unverified errors compound, state dictates the working memory and durable artifacts carried forward, and authority establishes the maximum blast radius of an errant action. Later divisions of this book systematically address how to close these exposures: Part II governs state, Part III controls authority, and Part IV bounds horizon.
Distinction: A coordinate in this space describes the exposure a task carries, which is a property of the task and its environment. The runtime’s validation gates, sandboxes, and compensating operations are its response to that exposure, which section 1.5 develops as closure. Closure is what the runtime builds; the coordinate is where the task sits.
Common pitfall: Inferring authority from syntax or command names alone. Authority reflects the operational consequence of an action within its specific environment; an identical file deletion is discardable inside an ephemeral sandbox, but irreversible when executed directly against an unversioned production datastore.



Horizon \(\TurnHorizon\) tracks the length of execution in sequential turns. Every additional turn gives the agent another chance to invoke a tool with bad arguments, act on stale observations, or drift from the goal. Section 1.6 shows mathematically how unchecked step-level error rates compound into severe task-level failure rates across long sequences. Turn count and wall-clock latency are distinct budgets that require separate limits. A three-turn workflow that triggers a large remote build cluster can run for hours, whereas a hundred-turn in-memory code refactoring completes in seconds. Production runtimes must meter both, bounding turns to restrict error compounding and bounding wall-clock time to release compute and network resources.
State (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\)) describes the data, memory, and workspace artifacts that persist across turns. At \(\StateExposureLevel_0\), the system is stateless, carrying no task context past a single call; stepping to \(\StateExposureLevel_1\) adds conversational working state, including the tokenized context window and inference-tier serving state such as cached key-value (KV) attention pairs. Once the agent modifies task-local working artifacts within an isolated workspace (such as a private source tree, an ephemeral container, or an in-memory scratchpad), it reaches \(\StateExposureLevel_2\). \(\StateExposureLevel_3\) covers execution that reads or writes durable shared state outliving the task session, such as an authoritative database, a shared object store, or a central code repository. Because realistic workloads routinely span several tiers at once, this classification establishes what data the runtime must checkpoint or isolate, sets cache invalidation boundaries, and decides which storage system remains authoritative when local scratchpad views diverge.
Authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\)) defines the blast radius of actions delegated to the task. At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\), access is strictly read-only, although exfiltration remains a risk if retrieved secrets leak into output text. Stepping up to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_1\) permits mutations, but confines them entirely to a disposable workspace where unintended modifications carry zero external impact. At \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_2\), actions affect external systems, yet every mutating operation pairs with an explicit compensating transaction4 executed under verified preconditions and a separate retry policy that prevents duplicate effects. Finally, \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) covers non-compensable actions (such as modifying unversioned production records, issuing financial transactions, or publishing public communications) for which no automated reversal exists. Authority reflects the operational consequence within the specific execution environment rather than command syntax. Because a trusted runtime mediates every action against an explicit per-task capability grant, restricting this grant provides the first and most cost-effective line of defense before deploying complex validation machinery.5
4 Compensating Transactions: Garcia-Molina and Salem introduced sagas for long-lived distributed transactions where holding locks across the entire workflow is impractical: a saga consists of a sequence of local transactions, each paired with a compensating transaction that semantically undoes earlier steps if the overall workflow aborts (Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987). Compensation is an active forward recovery action rather than an atomic rollback; concurrent processes can observe intermediate states, and the compensating action itself may fail. An \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_2\) capability grant therefore requires an executable compensation handler before dispatching the initial mutating effect. 
Garcia-Molina, Hector, and Kenneth Salem. 1987. “Sagas.” Proceedings of the 1987 ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data, 249–59. https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742.
5 Least Privilege and Complete Mediation: Saltzer and Schroeder’s protection principles state that every program should run with the smallest set of privileges needed to complete its task (least privilege), and that every access to every object should be checked for authority (complete mediation) (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). Checking capability grants on every tool call applies both principles to a non-deterministic model whose proposals cannot be trusted on their own. Restricting the task’s initial capability grant remains the most dependable way to limit damage when runtime verification checks fail to catch an unsafe request.

The coordinate space in figure 4 maps agentic workloads across three operational exposure axes: horizon (\(\TurnHorizon\), turns along the horizontal), authority (\(\AuthorityExposureLevel_0\) to \(\AuthorityExposureLevel_3\) on the vertical), and carried state (\(\StateExposureLevel_0\) to \(\StateExposureLevel_3\) on the depth axis). This space serves as an analytical lens rather than a rigid taxonomy: two workloads occupying the same cell may still demand different runtime controls if their data sensitivity, tool reliability, or failure thresholds differ. Changing the execution environment can shift a task into a completely different cell even when its foundation model and turn horizon remain identical, as shown in example 1.1. The four workloads plotted in the space are the book’s lighthouse workloads, described in section 1.4.1.
