title: 5 KV Cache Management
text:
Most KV-cache failures in production agent deployments come from two mistakes. The first is treating an instantaneous memory-fit count as a throughput guarantee while idle tool waits hold slots for tens of seconds. The second is treating a fast prefix-cache hit as proof that the underlying environment state is still current. Each fallacy and pitfall below pairs the failure mode with its concrete cost on the reference node.

Fallacy: Model size, not retained context, decides how many sequences a node can serve.
Static model weights consume a fixed footprint allocated at initialization, leaving a 526.0 GB pool dedicated to dynamic attention state on the reference node. While model parameters establish the initial baseline headroom, the active context length of running sequences governs dynamic memory consumption. Holding the model constant, that memory pool accommodates 195 unshared sequences when context is kept to 8,192 tokens, but capacity plunges to just 12 concurrent sequences once context expands to 131,072 tokens (section 5.2). Retained context length serves as the primary operational lever governing system concurrency, and the agent harness dictates that length through its prompt construction, tool history, and conversation buffering. Swapping in a smaller model only increases concurrent serving capacity to the extent that it reduces the per-token memory footprint \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) or frees up additional accelerator memory for the KV pool.


Pitfall: Reserving every request’s maximum context.
Allocating contiguous memory upfront for each request’s worst-case context length severely throttles system throughput through internal fragmentation. When a serving system sizes every slot for a 32,768-token cap while requests average a final length of only 2,048 tokens, barely 6.25 percent of the allocated memory actually holds valid attention state upon completion. Under this static reservation regime, the reference pool can admit only 48 concurrent sequences. In contrast, paged virtual memory allocation dynamically allocates physical blocks on demand, giving the final-length snapshot estimate of approximately 780 over the same physical memory (section 5.4). Systems should allocate memory blocks incrementally as tokens arrive during prefill and generation, reserving the output allowance the admission controller promises, as the capacity notebook does, rather than the full context cap.


Fallacy: Compatible cached attention state proves that its evidence is current.
Prefix caching operates strictly at the level of token identifiers and model configurations, without semantic awareness of environment state or external reality. On the reference node, a prefix match on the agent repair loop’s 4,096-token invariant prompt saves roughly 169 ms of prefill computation per turn (section 5.5). The inference engine achieves that speedup regardless of whether those cached tokens reflect stale diagnostics from revision 17 (r17) or up-to-date observations from the current repository source. Prefix match compatibility only confirms that the token sequence and attention architecture match bit-for-bit. Determining whether an earlier r17 failure supports a claim about revision 18 (r18) requires semantic validation in the agent harness before serializing the prompt. Updating the prompt with fresh r18 observations breaks prefix reuse at the first modified token and forfeits part of that computational saving. That forfeited saving is the correct price of grounding the next decision in current evidence (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)). Under that principle, no cached, staged, or derived copy supersedes the designated source for the claim it represents, which here is the repository at r18.



↪ Every staged or cached claim is validated against a designated source of record, whose role is developed in Record roles.

Pitfall: Always moving paused state out of accelerator memory.
Blindly offloading KV cache blocks to host memory whenever an agent pauses to execute an external tool wastes interconnect bandwidth and inflates resumption latency. Evacuating the 10.74 GB attention state for a paused repair agent requires 42 ms of link transfer, which adds 21 ms of overhead before the model can resume generation. When the memory pool contains plenty of free blocks, this offload latency provides zero benefit to the system. Conversely, under heavy contention, offloading that same state frees valuable high-bandwidth accelerator memory for 44.98 s across an extended 45 s tool invocation (section 5.7). Serving schedulers must evaluate eviction dynamically based on uniquely reclaimable blocks, active queue pressure, and expected resumption deadlines. An external tool call marks an opportunity for scheduling decisions rather than an automatic eviction trigger.


Fallacy: A resident-fit count is a throughput guarantee.
Calculating how many concurrent request snapshots fit into physical accelerator memory establishes an instantaneous capacity limit, not a sustained throughput guarantee. The reference node fits 41 unshared repair trajectories in memory simultaneously. However, if those sessions hold their memory allocations across an idle 45 s tool pause, the node sustains a maximum of only 0.82 turns/s from memory alone. If the engine instead releases those memory slots during the pause, the memory-only throughput bound rises to 8.2 turns/s (notebook 5.4). Memory fit dictates maximum concurrency (\(\MeanSlotOccupancy\)), but Little’s law (\(\MeanSlotOccupancy = \ArrivalRate \MeanHoldTime\)) dictates that arrival throughput (\(\ArrivalRate\)) is governed equally by mean residence time (\(\MeanHoldTime\)). When agent turns involve long execution pauses or queueing delays, residence time inflates and throughput collapses even though memory looks full. Occupancy stays high, but most of the resident state is idle, so the turn rate is low. Schedulers must validate admission against offered traffic distributions, burst arrivals, and latency targets rather than relying on static slot counts.


Pitfall: Treating KV storage as the authoritative task record.
The KV cache is a hardware-bound optimization artifact, not a durable system of record. Dropping the 10.74 GB repair state from accelerator memory costs approximately 1.3 s of prefill compute to rebuild from raw tokens, and it forfeits zero evidence needed by the task. Retaining or serializing KV cache tensors preserves only intermediate, activation-level computation tied to a specific hardware layout, model architecture, and numerical precision. It does not record the authoritative code revisions, environment observations, or validation evidence that govern an agent’s task progression. Systems must persist trajectory history, tool outputs, and verification state in a durable application runtime. The KV cache should always be treated as an ephemeral, recomputable cache over that authoritative token log, reproducible up to floating-point differences across distinct implementations.

title: 5 KV Cache Management
text:
Retained key-value (KV) attention state is a cache of intermediate computation. Like any cache, its cost has two parts, capacity and residency. Capacity is the bytes it occupies in high-bandwidth memory, which grow with the model’s tensor geometry and the active sequence length. Allocation decides how many of those bytes do useful work, since coarse blocks strand bytes in internal fragmentation and branches that do not share a common prefix store it twice. Residency is how long a sequence holds those bytes. It is what turns capacity into throughput, because an agent blocked on a tool call still occupies accelerator memory, and every byte it holds is a byte another request cannot use. Every memory management policy examined in this chapter (paged block tables, tree-based prefix eviction, offloading, and recomputation) trades memory footprint against recomputation work and scheduling delay. Cache mechanisms manage physical storage, but they cannot assess whether cached tokens remain semantically valid; context validity stays the responsibility of the agent harness and the context it supplies. Table 7 summarizes the primary analytical relations used throughout this chapter to size, share, schedule, and reclaim key-value cache storage.



Table 7: Key equations: Each relation holds under the chapter’s assumptions of full causal attention, uniform layer geometry, and tensor payload that excludes allocator metadata.










Equation
What it bounds or decides
Where derived




\(\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount \cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \ElementStorageSize\), \(\; \KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\)
Bytes retained per token and per sequence; retained sequence length serves as the primary capacity driver
equation 1


\(0 \le \KvBlockTailWaste \le \KvBlockSize - 1\)
Per-sequence internal fragmentation slack in paged allocation; dictates the capacity impact of block size \(\KvBlockSize\)
section 5.4


\(\PrefixHitRate = \sum_{i} \ReusedPrefixLength^{(\WorkloadRequestIndex)} / \sum_{i} \PromptLength^{(\WorkloadRequestIndex)}\)
Effective prefix hit rate: the proportion of prompt tokens served directly from reusable cached state
equation 2

Chunked prefill admission budget alongside active decodes; controls inter-token generation latency
equation 3

Crossover ratio determining whether paused state is restored faster via interconnect reload or local recomputation

Maximum resident concurrency \(\BatchSize\) under block quantization, memory headroom, and a shared prefix
equation 6

Theoretical upper bound on capacity gain from prefix sharing in large memory pools with shared fraction \(\SharedPrefixFraction\)
section 5.8.1


\(\MeanSlotOccupancy = \ArrivalRate \MeanHoldTime\)
Turn throughput sustained by a fixed pool of resident slots (via Little’s law)
equation 7


\(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\)
Residency tax factor: capacity lost when sequences occupy memory slots during idle tool waits
section 5.8.2







Key Takeaways: Managing derived attention state

Retained length is the capacity knob: With model weights occupying a static allocation, resident capacity scales inversely with retained sequence length, falling from 195 sequences at 8,192 tokens down to 12 sequences at 131,072 tokens on the reference node. A context length that easily satisfies the model architecture’s maximum context window can still quickly exhaust the serving node’s physical memory pool.
Physical blocks, not logical references, consume capacity: Paged attention rounds private sequence state up to fixed-size blocks, whereas identical prefix sequences share physical blocks through reference counting. Reclaiming a finished trajectory frees only those physical blocks whose reference count drops to zero, ensuring active sequences and asynchronous transfer operations remain protected.
Prefix reuse requires both structural compatibility and memory availability: Matching token prefixes permit KV cache reuse only when the corresponding physical blocks remain resident and accessible under tenant-isolation rules. A cache hit guarantees neither the freshness of underlying external data nor the semantic validity of the trajectory; preserving cache affinity must never prevent an agent harness from invalidating stale context.
Retention policies and compute schedulers manage complementary resources: Chunked prefill schedules incoming prompt tokens alongside active decodes to prevent high latency spikes during token generation. Similarly, each way of handling a paused agent trajectory (retaining its blocks in accelerator memory, offloading them to host RAM or secondary storage, or recomputing them on demand) exchanges memory footprint for interconnect bandwidth and resumption latency. The optimal strategy depends on the link bandwidth and the expected wait duration.
Idle tool waits impose a severe residency tax on throughput: Static resident-fit bounds govern instantaneous occupancy rather than sustained request throughput. Holding physical cache blocks resident while an agent waits on external tools or human feedback depresses sustainable turn throughput by the residency tax factor \(1 + \ToolTime/\ModelTime\). Production admission and eviction policies must therefore optimize for end-to-end task completion rates and tail latency rather than raw accelerator memory utilization.



Attention state derived from the token prefix (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-prefix-coherence}\)) enables the serving engine to reuse previous computation rather than evaluating redundant prompt tokens. Precise block tracking and residency accounting quantify the trade-off between retaining that state and freeing high-bandwidth memory for active generation. Throughout these optimizations, authority stays with the source (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)): an inexpensive continuation never justifies serving an obsolete observation when the underlying system or environment has changed.

title: 5 KV Cache Management
text:
Almost every memory management technique in this chapter resolves an architectural problem that time-sharing operating systems encountered decades ago. When early programs outgrew physical core memory, the Manchester Atlas one-level store introduced paging (Kilburn et al. 1962). An address translation table mapped a program’s contiguous virtual address space onto scattered physical page frames, freeing programmers from managing manual overlays and allowing memory to allocate without contiguous physical reservations. Decoupling virtual addresses from physical layout promptly exposed new systems trade-offs. Randell (1969) formalized the distinction between internal fragmentation (storage lost inside rounded-up allocations) and external fragmentation, where free memory sits stranded between allocations. Belady (1966) demonstrated that optimal offline page replacement requires clairvoyant knowledge of future memory references, establishing that practical online policies must rely on heuristics. When memory pressure mounted, time-sharing systems routinely collapsed into thrashing, spending virtually all cycles swapping pages rather than executing user code. Denning’s working-set model clarified the dynamics of this failure and proved that the only dependable remedy was admission control. That meant admitting fewer concurrent processes rather than swapping pages more aggressively (Denning 1968a, 1968b). Operating systems also pioneered fine-grained memory sharing. The TENEX system introduced copy-on-write sharing so that multiple processes could reference identical pages safely until one attempted a mutation (Bobrow et al. 1972), while Morrison’s PATRICIA trees indexed strings through shared prefixes (Morrison 1968). Denning (1970) gathered these foundations into the virtual-memory discipline that computer systems curricula teach to this day.

Kilburn, Tom, David B. G. Edwards, Michael J. Lanigan, and Frank H. Sumner. 1962. “One-Level Storage System.” IRE Transactions on Electronic Computers EC-11 (2): 223–35. https://doi.org/10.1109/TEC.1962.5219356.

Vaswani, Ashish, Noam Shazeer, Niki Parmar, Jakob Uszkoreit, Llion Jones, Aidan N. Gomez, Lukasz Kaiser, and Illia Polosukhin. 2017. “Attention Is All You Need.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 30: 5998–6008.
Modern inference serving collided with these identical capacity limits when the autoregressive Transformer architecture made each generated token attend to key and value tensors from all prior tokens (Vaswani et al. 2017). Early efforts mitigated this growth by modifying the neural network architecture itself. Multi-query attention (Shazeer 2019) and grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al. 2023) reduced the memory footprint by sharing key-value heads across multiple query heads. In parallel, Pope et al. (2023) developed an analytical framework showing that accelerator memory capacity and memory bandwidth, rather than floating-point compute throughput, impose the primary bottleneck on context length and batch concurrency.
Subsequent innovations in serving systems recapitulated the operating-systems lineage directly. Orca introduced iteration-level scheduling, enabling fine-grained preemption and dynamic batching where requests join and leave running batches on individual token boundaries (Yu et al. 2022). PagedAttention adapted classical virtual paging directly to key-value cache management, using block tables and copy-on-write mechanisms to eliminate external fragmentation and reclaim the memory previously wasted by reserving contiguous worst-case sequence lengths (Kwon et al. 2023). SGLang introduced radix-tree prefix caching with leaf-first eviction, enabling structural cache reuse across independent requests that share common system prompts or few-shot exemplars (Zheng et al. 2024). To prevent lengthy prompt ingestions from stalling generation, Sarathi introduced chunked prefill, bounding the latency spikes that prefill operations impose on active decode iterations (Agrawal et al. 2023). Finally, DistServe and Splitwise extended this decoupling across physical hardware nodes through phase disaggregation, placing the prefill and decode stages on separate, specialized worker pools (Patel et al. 2024; Zhong et al. 2024).

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.

Agrawal, Amey, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2023. “SARATHI: Efficient LLM Inference by Piggybacking Decodes with Chunked Prefills.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2308.16369, August.

Patel, Pratyush, Esha Choukse, Chaojie Zhang, Aashaka Shah, Íñigo Goiri, Saeed Maleki, and Ricardo Bianchini. 2024. “Splitwise: Efficient Generative LLM Inference Using Phase Splitting.” 2024 ACM/IEEE 51st Annual International Symposium on Computer Architecture (ISCA), 118–32. https://doi.org/10.1109/isca59077.2024.00019.

Zhong, Yinmin, Shengyu Liu, Junda Chen, Jianbo Hu, Yibo Zhu, Xuanzhe Liu, Xin Jin, and Hao Zhang. 2024. “DistServe: Disaggregating Prefill and Decoding for Goodput-Optimized Large Language Model Serving.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), July, 193–210.

Gao, Bin, Zhuomin He, Puru Sharma, Qingxuan Kang, Djordje Jevdjic, Junbo Deng, Xingkun Yang, Zhou Yu, and Pengfei Zuo. 2024. “Cost-Efficient Large Language Model Serving for Multi-Turn Conversations with CachedAttention.” 2024 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (USENIX ATC 24), 111–26.

Qin, Yeqi, Yufan Shen, Zeyu Shi, Chen Sun, Wei Wang, Xiao Wang, Xiaobo Wang, et al. 2024. Mooncake: A KVCache-Centric Disaggregated Architecture for LLM Serving.

Xiao, Guangxuan, Yuandong Tian, Beidi Chen, Song Han, and Mike Lewis. 2024. “Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).

Zhang, Zhenyu, Sheng Shen, Derek Zhiyuan Cheng, Xingli Dong, and Kurt Keutzer. 2023. “H2O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36.
Agent workloads introduce the memory dilemma at the center of this chapter: execution state that idles during tool execution and subsequently resumes. When an agent invokes an external tool, its execution thread pauses while waiting for external API responses or environment feedback. During this idle window, the retained KV cache ties up expensive accelerator high-bandwidth memory. Work on tool interception formalized this challenge by framing KV cache lifecycle management around three primary operations. These were keeping the state resident in device memory, swapping it to host memory or storage, and dropping it entirely to recompute upon resumption (Abhyankar et al. 2024). This trade-off balances idle memory capacity against host-to-device transfer bandwidth and compute recomputation costs. Multi-turn serving systems such as CachedAttention and Mooncake expanded this design space into multi-tier memory hierarchies, paging dormant KV caches out to host DRAM and disaggregated solid-state storage clusters (Gao et al. 2024; Qin et al. 2024). Lossy approximation techniques pursued an alternative path, trading mathematical fidelity for reduced memory footprints through attention sinks (Xiao et al. 2024) and score-based eviction policies (Zhang et al. 2023). However, whether lossy cache approximation can reliably preserve the intricate, long-range dependencies required across extended agent trajectories remains an open systems and modeling challenge.
For readers seeking to trace the lineage from classical memory management to agent serving infrastructure, six works are especially illuminating:

Denning (1970) provides the foundational survey of paging, replacement algorithms, and locality of reference, showing how modern KV-cache management problems mirror classical virtual memory challenges transposed onto a new architectural storage unit.
Denning (1968a) introduces the working-set model, establishing the formal link between program locality and resource allocation. It provides the theoretical foundation for admission control, explaining why multi-tenant model servers must reject or queue requests when aggregate memory demand exceeds physical accelerator capacity.
Pope et al. (2023) develops an analytical model for large-model inference, demonstrating rigorously how attention head sharing, tensor partitioning, and memory bandwidth dictate whether a deployment is bounded by arithmetic throughput or memory capacity.
Kwon et al. (2023) introduces PagedAttention, adapting classical operating system paging, virtual block tables, and copy-on-write mechanisms to eliminate KV cache fragmentation in serving engines. It serves as an exemplary case study in translating classical systems principles to modern accelerator architectures.
Zheng et al. (2024) structures prompt cache management through radix trees, treating token prefix reuse as a first-class scheduling and eviction problem in multi-turn and agentic serving workloads.
Abhyankar et al. (2024) formalizes the tool-wait problem in agent workloads, quantifying the engineering trade-offs among retaining, swapping, and discarding KV cache state during external tool execution.


Denning, Peter J. 1970. “Virtual Memory.” ACM Computing Surveys 2 (3): 153–89. https://doi.org/10.1145/356580.356581.

Denning, Peter J. 1968a. “The Working Set Model for Program Behavior.” Communications of the ACM 11 (5): 323–33. https://doi.org/10.1145/363095.363141.

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, et al. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with Pagedattention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26.

Zheng, Lianmin, Liangsheng Ying, Zhenghao Yin, Cody Hao Liu, Eric Yu, Prakhar Patel, Zhipeng Yang, Anthony K. Joseph, and Ion Stoica. 2024. “SGLang: Efficient Execution of Structured Language Model Programs.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2312.07104, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2312.07104.

Abhyankar, Reyna, Zijian He, Vikranth Srivatsa, Hao Zhang, and Yiying Zhang. 2024. “InferCept: Efficient Intercept Support for Augmented Large Language Model Inference.” Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML), Proceedings of machine learning research, vol. 235: 81–95.

Unless a problem states otherwise, use the hypothetical reference deployment in table 8. Its values are problem inputs chosen for round arithmetic, not measurements of any system. Take GB as \(10^9\) bytes, count \(2\Parameters\) weight operations per processed token, and model one engine iteration over \(\ForwardPassTokenCount\) token positions with the chapter’s weight-only estimate, \(\WeightOnlyStepTime(\ForwardPassTokenCount) = \max\left(5\;\text{ms},\; 2 \Parameters \ForwardPassTokenCount / \AttainableComputeRate\right)\).

1. Sizing retained state for a session target (Basic). An operator must hold 200 unshared sessions resident at once, each retaining 16,384 tokens.

Compute \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) from equation 1, the payload \(\KvCacheMemory\) of one session, and the resident-fit bound in the pool.
A multi-head variant of the same model stores 64 key-value heads per layer instead of 8. Compute its fit, and explain why no allocator policy can recover the difference.
Two proposals would meet the target: storing KV at one byte per element, or having the harness cap retained context. Find the longest retained length that meets the target at two bytes per element. Then argue which proposal to try first and what evidence each must produce before it ships.

2. When paging pays (Basic). Static reservation sizes every request for a cap of 8,192 tokens. The request population’s mean final length is 3,072 tokens.

What fraction of a reservation holds state at completion, and how many reservations fit in the pool?
Paged allocation uses 32-token blocks, and final lengths have uniformly distributed remainders modulo the block size. Estimate the mean tail waste per sequence, its share of allocated KV memory, and the final-length snapshot count estimated by dividing the pool by the mean allocation. Repeat for 256-token blocks. Does this estimate alone determine live admission capacity?
If the mean final length rose to 7,000 tokens under the same cap, how much of paging’s capacity advantage over static reservation would remain? Name one benefit of block allocation that does not depend on the length distribution.

3. Moving one field (Basic). A session sends four requests of 6,000 prompt tokens each. The first 4,500 tokens are invariant instructions and tool schemas, except for a request timestamp serialized after the first 300 tokens. The service reuses only complete 256-token blocks; the first request finds nothing cached, and each later request finds the earlier state resident, compatible, and permitted.

Compute \(\PrefixHitRate\) from equation 2 over the four requests.
Recompute it after the harness moves the timestamp to follow the invariant prefix.
For layout (b), how much weight-only prefill does each hit avoid, and how much more would a service that also reuses partial tail blocks avoid? Which change should the team make first?

4. Choosing a chunk budget (Intermediate). Forty-eight requests are decoding when an 8,000-token uncached prompt arrives.

If the engine runs the prompt as one unit, what gap between tokens do the ongoing decodes see?
The ongoing streams must see at most 25 ms between tokens. Using equation 3 with one position per decode, find the largest budget \(\IterationTokenBudget\) and chunk size that meet the target, the number of iterations the prompt needs, and the time until its prefill completes.
Ignoring the smaller final chunk, show that prefill completion is approximately \(\left(2 \Parameters \UncachedPromptLength/\AttainableComputeRate\right) \cdot \Time / \left(\Time - 2 \Parameters \lvert\DecodeRequestSet\rvert / \AttainableComputeRate\right)\) for an inter-token target \(\Time\) above the weight-read floor, where \(\UncachedPromptLength\) is the uncached prompt length. Find the tightest \(\Time\) that still completes the prompt within 500 ms.
Explain why a target approaching \(2 \Parameters \lvert\DecodeRequestSet\rvert / \AttainableComputeRate\) is unworkable, and propose a design change for a service whose streams need 8 ms between tokens while new prompts need their prefill within 500 ms.

5. Reload, recompute, and a return burst (Intermediate).

Evaluate equation 4 for the reference deployment. How much faster is reload than recomputation, and why does the answer not depend on retained length?
Below what sustained link bandwidth would recomputation become the faster way back?
Forty paused sessions of 32,768 tokens each return at the same instant. Compute each session’s state, its isolated reload time, the reload completion time of the last session when reloads share the full aggregate link rate, and the time to recompute all forty sequentially from weight work alone.
Each returning session must be restored within 250 ms. How many of the forty meet that target if reloads share the link fairly, and how many if they are served one at a time in arrival order at the full link rate? Propose two design changes that would serve the rest.

6. Shared prefix and residence time (Intermediate). Requests carry 24,576 prompt tokens and an output allowance \(\OutputLimit = 1{,}024\). A block-aligned common prefix of 16,384 tokens is compatible and shareable across all of them. Blocks hold \(\KvBlockSize = 16\) tokens, and the planner withholds headroom \(\KvPoolHeadroomFraction = 0.10\). Each turn generates for 4 s and then waits 36 s for a tool.

Using equation 6, compute the usable blocks and the resident-fit bound without and with sharing. Compare the gain with \(1/(1-\SharedPrefixFraction)\).
The operator wants memory to sustain 10 turns/s. Using the shared fit and equation 7, what rate does keeping state through the wait sustain, and how many resident slots would the target require under that policy?
Instead, each paused turn moves its private blocks to host memory and reloads them when the tool returns, while the common prefix stays resident for the other requests. Compute the memory-bound rate, the host-link traffic at 10 turns/s, and the restoration delay per turn. Is the link the binding resource?

7. Fan-out over a shared source bundle (Advanced). The research agent retrieves a 60,000-token bundle of source documents and fans the question out to 12 workers. Each worker’s input is the bundle followed by a 2,000-token private instruction, and each may generate up to 3,000 tokens. A synthesis call then reads the bundle followed by all 12 worker outputs. Ignore block rounding and headroom.

A contiguous allocator deep-copies the bundle’s state into every worker. How much KV state does it copy? Compute the KV footprint of one question with and without block sharing, and how many questions each policy keeps resident in the pool.
A developer serializes each worker’s private instruction before the bundle so that the model reads its task first. What happens to the shared footprint in (a), and what layout serves both goals?
For the synthesis call, how much weight-only prefill does a hit on the bundle avoid, and how much new prefill remains? Contrast the constraint that binds this workload with the one that binds the repair agent in this chapter.
A platform team proposes reusing the bundle’s KV state across different users’ questions that retrieve the same documents. State the conditions under which that reuse is compatible, available, and permitted, and explain why a hit says nothing about whether the documents are current or trustworthy.

8. Paused state through a human approval (Advanced). The remediation agent proposes a production change and waits for human approval. During a major incident, 60 trajectories await approval at once. Each retains 20,000 tokens: an 8,000-token invariant prefix, identical and shareable across trajectories, followed by 12,000 tokens of incident-specific diagnostics. Each turn generates for 6 s, approval takes 10 minutes, and the host can hold 1 TB of parked state.

Under the keep policy, what share of the pool do the 60 trajectories hold without sharing and with the prefix shared, and what residency tax does the approval wait impose?
Suppose the private blocks move to host memory and the shared prefix stays resident. Compute the host footprint, and compare the time to restore 20 trajectories whose approvals arrive together by reload with the time to recompute their private regions sequentially.
Before acting on an approval, the harness must re-observe production state (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)), and the refreshed observations replace the diagnostics from token 8,000 onward. How much of the parked state remains usable? Recommend a paused-state policy, and say how the recommendation changes if refreshed observations were only appended after the existing diagnostics.
Compared with the repair agent, what binds this workload, and how large is its restoration cost relative to the wait?


What’s Next: From reusable computation to durable informationDropping the r18 request’s attention state forfeits no evidence, because the serving engine can rebuild it from the token log. The repair’s next session still needs that evidence once this serving session ends: the candidate at r18, the r17 failure, the passing reproducer, and the integration checks that remain unresolved. KV state can itself be moved or serialized, so storage location alone does not separate a cache from a memory. The unresolved problem is which information should persist, how it is identified and updated as its sources change, and how a later session retrieves evidence appropriate to its task. Long-Term Memory develops that durable-information contract.

title: 7 Tool Calling
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why does a tool call that parses cleanly still need a runtime between it and the world?
A tool call is the first point at which a model’s output can change something outside the conversation. A proposal that parses cleanly can still name a target the task was never granted, act on a file that has changed since the model read it, or repeat an operation whose first attempt already took effect. Generating the call therefore cannot be what authorizes it. The runtime must stand between proposal and effect, validating each call against its schema, checking it against the grants the task holds, dispatching it, and recording what is actually known about the result. That record is often incomplete. A request that times out may have been lost, may still be running, or may have succeeded without a delivered reply, and a blind retry can restart healthy workers or apply the same change twice. The outcome has to stay explicitly unknown until the runtime settles it, rather than be filled in by the model’s account or the runtime’s optimism. What returns to the model is itself a design decision. A log far longer than the next call can hold must be cut down without hiding the line that matters, and a job that outlives one turn must report back without being mistaken for a finished one. Tool calling keeps the model a proposer and leaves authority with the runtime, which exercises it only on evidence it can check.

Learning Objectives

Trace a proposed tool call through validation, authorization, dispatch, and a correlated observation into the next model call
Design a tool descriptor that separates structural validation from action-time preconditions enforced with the effect
Distinguish tool discovery and connectivity from the grants required to invoke an operation
Select blind retry, endpoint deduplication, or reconciliation for an uncertain effect from operation semantics and loss rates
Design bounded observations that preserve execution status, omission information, and the scope of available evidence
Compare waiting and resumption strategies for long-running tools by detection delay, inference cost, and retained supervision
Evaluate toolkit granularity by context cost, cost per accepted task, and enforced reach across structured, general-purpose, and computer-use interfaces



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗



An agent asked to restart a container on a staging server, the kind of infrastructure change the remediation agent (Four lighthouse workloads) makes, emits a short tool call. The host runtime checks the call against the tool’s schema, confirms that this session may restart that container, and sends POST /containers/srv-stage-04/restart. Two seconds later the socket times out. The request may be lost, delayed, still executing, or completed without a delivered reply. A retry could restart healthy workers, and the first attempt can still take effect after the timeout.



The Authority axis, closed at the tool boundary by mediating every proposed call.
Nothing about this failure is exotic. The repair agent meets the same questions on every turn of the connection-pool repair. It reads src/pool.py, replaces text derived from the version it read, runs the test suite, and receives a log far longer than the next model call can hold. Each step is a tool call, and each can be rejected, left running, completed without a reply, or answered with more output than the model should see.
The pieces built so far do not settle these questions. Messages and tool definitions gave the model a structured way to propose a call. The memory chapters already relied on tools to read sources, search indexes, and update records without examining what happens between a proposal and its result. A retrieval result identifies the version it observed, but whether the file still has that version when a later edit commits is an action-time precondition that something must enforce. A proposal names an operation and its arguments. It does not decide whether this task may run the operation, whether an earlier attempt already ran it, or what the next model call should receive.
The runtime’s tool boundary is the path between a proposed call and the environment it would change. The boundary validates each proposal, checks it against the task’s grants, dispatches it, tracks what is known about its effect, and returns a bounded observation matched to the call. Throughout, it keeps apart the three things the timeout blurs: what the model proposed, what effect the operation had, and what evidence the runtime holds about either. The chapter follows one call from proposal to observation, then widens to effects whose outcome stays uncertain, to output too large to return whole, to jobs that outlive a model turn, and finally to the catalog of tools the model sees.


↩︎ The separation of proposal, effect, and observation is established in Why the runtime manages the trajectory, not the single call.



When the socket times out on restart_container, a runtime that drops the failed call from history or reports it as a clean failure invites the next model turn to issue a duplicate restart. Listing 1 shows the staging restart as one turn of the loop, in a provider-neutral form. The runtime reports what it knows about this attempt, and the next model call receives that result together with the earlier request and proposal.



Listing 1: One turn of the tool-call loop: A call identifier correlates the proposed call with its result. The next model call receives the timeout as an unknown effect, not as evidence that the restart did not happen.


[
  {"role": "user",
   "content": "Stage-04 is serving a stale config. Restart it."},
  {"role": "assistant",
   "content": [
     {"type": "tool_call", "id": "call_1", "name": "restart_container",
      "arguments": {"container_id": "srv-stage-04"}}]},
  {"role": "tool",
   "content": [
     {"type": "tool_result", "call_id": "call_1",
      "content": {"transport_status": "timeout", "effect_status": "unknown"}}]}
]



The runtime correlates each result with its corresponding call using an explicit identifier rather than message order alone. That identifier establishes message lineage across asynchronous turns, but correlation alone does not resolve whether the target service completed the requested mutation. Preventing duplicate restarts requires an operational contract for idempotency, developed in section 7.5. Even if the subsequent model turn assumes that the service recovered, the runtime preserves the underlying uncertainty. It authorizes a retry only when idempotent semantics, an endpoint deduplication contract, or reconciliation evidence that also rules out a still-delayed attempt supports it. Fresh evidence that the container looks unchanged is not enough on its own (section 7.5.1).


Between the tool_call and tool_result messages of listing 1 lies the runtime’s mediation path. If the runtime piped a model’s proposed call straight to an execution backend and piped the raw output straight back into the prompt, an unauthorized call would mutate the host and an unbounded log would overflow the next context window. Instead, once the inference engine emits a structured invocation block at the model-side call surface, execution passes entirely to the runtime, which mediates the round trip between the proposed call and the next turn’s observation across the four coordinated stages of figure 1: argument validation, policy authorization, dispatch with outcome tracking, and observation shaping.


↩︎ The six-phase turn lifecycle, whose validation, execution, and observation phases these four stages refine, is established in The six phases of a turn.
Request validation parses proposed arguments against the tool’s declared schema, verifying required fields, data types, value ranges, and relational invariants among parameters. Dynamic constraints that depend on volatile environment state cannot be settled at this boundary. The system must evaluate them at the execution boundary rather than inferring them from historical context. Next, operation authorization verifies the active session’s security grants and access policies against the targeted resource, for read operations as well as state mutations, and admits the call against its concurrency budgets and rate limits.
Following authorization, dispatch submits the permitted operation to the underlying execution provider while outcome tracking maintains execution identity and status. This tracking distinguishes among pre-dispatch rejections, active background tasks, successfully reported results, and unconfirmed execution states. A transport timeout indicates only that the runtime exceeded its waiting deadline, leaving the remote execution state unconfirmed. Finally, observation shaping maps the raw return value back to the originating call identifier, truncating payloads to fit context budgets, sanitizing terminal escape sequences, and tagging the output with accurate status metadata. If log output must be truncated, the payload explicitly discloses the omission; if a system returns an asynchronous job ticket, observation shaping reports it as an acknowledgment rather than a completed effect.
Certain validation checks must execute at the remote endpoint because safety requires atomicity with the state change itself. For example, an edit conditioned on a source version requires the version check to occur in lockstep with the update. Consequently, the host runtime and the remote endpoint each enforce their respective boundaries. The endpoint checks access independently, even for requests that the host runtime already cleared. This division is the end-to-end argument applied to system protection. An authorization check that depends on private endpoint state can be finalized only at that endpoint, which makes preliminary host-level checks useful optimizations rather than authoritative substitutes (Saltzer et al. 1984).






Figure 1: The tool-call loop: Validation and authorization can reject a proposed call before dispatch. For a dispatched call, the runtime tracks the available outcome and shapes the return into a bounded observation matched to its call identifier. An unknown effect remains unknown in that observation.



When the serving interface returns native structured call blocks, the runtime extracts the proposed operation and arguments directly. When a model emits proposals within unstructured free text, the runtime must first detect and parse those fragments before validation can proceed. Constrained decoding eliminates syntactic parsing failures by enforcing grammar rules directly during token generation. However, syntax alone never establishes operational safety. Whether the target resource exists, whether the observed version remains current, and whether the current session holds execution privileges remain runtime checks that no decoding grammar can verify.



Just as a decoding grammar cannot verify execution privileges, a system-prompt instruction to touch only staging containers or read only inside /workspace places no barrier between a hallucinated or prompt-injected tool call and the host operating system. Securing the tool interface rests on complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), the protection principle that already required the tool handler of Why token likelihood cannot replace checks to check a validated path again when the read executes. At the tool boundary, mediation must govern both reads and mutations. Emitting a tool name does not grant the model ambient runtime authority, nor does receiving an observation make external data trusted.

Definition 7.1: Complete mediation
Complete mediation requires every proposed access to pass through an enforced authorization boundary before it reaches the protected resource. In an agent runtime, the return path is also mediated so that observations enter context under explicit access, payload, and status contracts.

Significance: A valid-looking call cannot bypass the checks governing what the session may read, change, or disclose.
Distinction: Schema validation establishes structural admissibility, not permission. Observation normalization establishes a usable representation, not the truth of its contents or immunity to prompt injection, attacker-controlled content that attempts to redirect the model.
Common pitfall: Treating a prompt instruction such as “never delete production data” as an access barrier. The runtime must enforce the restriction even when the model proposes the prohibited action.



Stating complete mediation as a policy does not by itself guarantee that every tool route honors it. Anderson formalized the architectural mechanism required to make that guarantee hold across every access path: the reference monitor (Anderson 1972).

Definition 7.2: Reference monitor
Reference monitor is the enforcement component through which every access to a protected resource passes. It must be tamper-proof, always invoked, and small enough to verify. In an agent runtime, the host’s validation and authorization path is the reference monitor for proposed tool calls, and each endpoint’s access check is a second monitor for the resources that endpoint owns.

Significance: The three requirements turn complete mediation from an intention into a checkable property of the runtime’s structure.
Distinction: The policy specifies permitted accesses, whereas the reference monitor provides the non-bypassable mechanism that evaluates and enforces those rules on every attempt.
Common pitfall: Adding a tool route that does not pass through the monitor, such as an unrestricted shell with network access beside a checked file adapter, which makes the adapter’s checks advisory.



These three requirements dictate concrete architectural choices at the tool boundary. Tamper-proofing ensures that neither generated model tokens nor untrusted data ingested from external systems can alter the authorization rules enforced by the runtime. Always-invoked mandates that every operational path pass through the monitor without exception. Exposing an unrestricted shell runner alongside a sandboxed file tool, for example, undermines the protection boundary, because the agent can bypass file restrictions by issuing shell commands. Finally, verifiability requires policy decisions to be deterministic, auditable software checks. Although an auxiliary classifier or guardrail model can score operational risk, probabilistic inference cannot be verified in the strict systems sense; the monitor itself must enforce deterministic access boundaries.
Two operational rules follow directly from complete mediation. The grant rule establishes that execution authority derives solely from the session’s active security grants, re-evaluated on every invocation. Read operations demand the same rigorous mediation as state mutations, because returning private records discloses sensitive data even when environment state remains unchanged. Nothing the model sees or emits enlarges those grants, whether a schema-valid call or a tool description claiming broad permission; later sections apply the rule to each new artifact they introduce. The evidence-scope rule establishes that an observation confirms only the specific metric or condition measured by the tool during that invocation. Reporting that an operating system process exited with code zero confirms only process termination; it does not prove overall task completion, which remains a distinct judgment governed by invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)). Raw output text also remains untrusted data even after the runtime strips terminal formatting and normalizes metadata; observations supply empirical evidence of state, but they carry no ambient authority to dictate subsequent actions.



When a single model response proposes reading src/pool.py and patching src/pool.py in the same batch, dispatching both calls in parallel yields non-deterministic results depending on which thread reaches the file first. When batched operations are strictly read-only and independent, such as reading three distinct source files, the runtime can dispatch them concurrently and correlate each returned observation with its respective call identifier. A failure in one read does not invalidate concurrent reads that succeeded. Every call in the batch must still pass validation and authorization individually and draw from a shared resource and rate-limit budget.
When tools declare a trustworthy resource footprint, the explicit read set \(\ToolCallReadSet_i\) and write set \(\ToolCallWriteSet_i\) of each call \(\ToolCallIndex\), the runtime can check whether batched mutations and reads interfere. Calls \(\ToolCallIndex\) and \(\PeerToolCallIndex\) may run concurrently when neither writes state the other reads or writes, \(\ToolCallWriteSet_i \cap (\ToolCallReadSet_j \cup \ToolCallWriteSet_j) = \emptyset\) and \(\ToolCallWriteSet_j \cap \ToolCallReadSet_i = \emptyset\), which are Bernstein’s conditions for noninterference (Bernstein 1966). Reads of two different files pass both conditions; a read and an edit of src/pool.py fail the first, because the edit writes the file the read reads. This guarantee, however, relies entirely on the completeness of footprint declarations; any hidden side effect or undeclared shared dependency invalidates the concurrency guarantee.

Bernstein, Arthur J. 1966. “Program Analysis for Parallel Processing.” IEEE Transactions on Electronic Computers EC-15 (5): 757–62. https://doi.org/10.1109/PGEC.1966.264565.
Operations with opaque side effects, such as arbitrary shell commands, have unknown footprints. In such cases, the runtime must either isolate the execution environment, serialize calls conservatively, or reject batched execution in favor of fine-grained tools. When operations have causal dependencies, those ordering constraints must come from the workflow policy or an explicit dependency graph. The sequential order of tokens generated by the model is not reliable evidence of intended execution order. Batching also does not imply atomicity; a batch forms a transaction only when the underlying tool substrate explicitly provides transactional all-or-nothing rollback semantics.
The runtime can also govern whether the model proposes an action. Using serving-level tool-choice control, the runtime can configure tool calling as optional, mandate that the model invoke at least one tool, restrict selection to a specific named operation, or forbid tool execution altogether. Orchestration engines use these constraints to guide execution phases, for instance forcing a diagnostic read before permitting an edit, or disallowing tool calls to force a final textual summary. Tool-choice controls, however, only shape model generation; under the grant rule, forcing a tool choice confers no operational authorization. Executing each stage of this mediated round trip requires an unambiguous request representation, establishing a strict operational boundary between static schema validation and dynamic preconditions verified at dispatch time.




When the repair agent finishes inspecting revision r17 of src/pool.py and proposes a patch to produce r18, that boundary between static validation and dispatch-time checks becomes concrete. Before applying the modification to the workspace, the host runtime must resolve four questions: which tool operation the model selected, what its arguments denote, whether the current task possesses the authority required to execute the mutation, and whether src/pool.py still matches the revision r17 state on which the model based its proposal. A well-formed JSON payload satisfies syntactic structure, but syntax alone cannot answer these operational questions.
A tool descriptor defines an operation’s functional purpose, input parameters, expected return values, and execution side effects. Within that descriptor, the argument schema codifies machine-checkable constraints: required fields, primitive types, permitted enumerations, and supported size bounds. These specifications serve two distinct audiences: natural-language descriptions guide the language model in selecting and parameterizing tools, while the surrounding runtime and downstream service endpoints validate and enforce the interface contract.


Even when every field passes JSON type checking, unstated edge cases in a descriptor can destroy workspace state: if a file-replacement tool leaves unspecified whether an empty replacement string is a no-op or a zero-byte write, a model attempting to leave src/pool.py unchanged will wipe the file. A tool such as conditional_replace_file, which replaces a single file in the task’s designated workspace and commits the change only if that file still matches the expected source version, must therefore state exact semantic invariants alongside its types. The path field resolves strictly relative to the designated workspace rather than an arbitrary host location, expected_version identifies the baseline source revision the model inspected, and replacement supplies the complete replacement content encoded in the endpoint’s documented format, with an empty string explicitly defined to truncate the file to zero bytes.
Full file replacement keeps this precondition example transparent, though production runtimes often prefer line-anchored patches or structured diffs to minimize token generation overhead. The interface comparison in Comparing Output Interfaces shows that localized edits reduce generated output while still demanding the same coordination between precondition verification and atomic mutation. Listing 2 illustrates the machine-checkable argument structure for that contract. The request payload contains neither a credential token nor a privilege flag through which the model might expand its access rights, and the host runtime independently binds the invocation to the task’s authorized execution context.



Listing 2: Conditional file replacement arguments: The schema describes the request’s structure. Its descriptions do not implement path confinement, authorization, or atomic version checking.


{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["path", "expected_version", "replacement"],
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "path": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "File path relative to the designated workspace."
    },
    "expected_version": {
      "type": "string",
      "minLength": 1,
      "description": "Source version returned with the inspected file."
    },
    "replacement": {
      "type": "string",
      "description": "Complete replacement text, written as UTF-8."
    }
  }
}



The descriptor’s result contract requires equal precision. A completed replacement reports the affected path and its newly assigned revision token. A version conflict explicitly reports that the target diverged and the replacement was not applied. The runtime must also distinguish deterministic client errors (malformed arguments or insufficient authority) from indeterminate transport failures where the endpoint’s state remains unknown after a dropped connection. A comprehensive descriptor models all four outcomes, including network timeouts where no acknowledgment arrives.
Precise field names and descriptions eliminate avoidable ambiguity during generation. For example, a file-reading tool should state whether its offset argument counts bytes, characters, or lines. Similarly, a timeout parameter must state its measurement units and specify whether it bounds connection establishment, remote execution, or end-to-end response delivery. While clear documentation guides the model toward valid parameters, the execution runtime must programmatically enforce all defaults, enumeration sets, and numerical bounds. Explicit tool documentation measurably improves the reliability of generation. Patil et al. (2023) demonstrated that models trained to condition tool invocations on retrieved API documentation invent nonexistent operations and hallucinate invalid arguments far less frequently than models relying solely on unconditioned prompting.



If generation halts at the output token limit or a client disconnection in the middle of a replacement string and a permissive parser closes the JSON object or accepts a partial payload, executing that call writes a half-finished src/pool.py to disk. Before parsing any arguments, the runtime therefore verifies that the model produced a completed candidate under the invocation contract defined in The Invocation Contract and aborts immediately on a truncated response. Once execution status confirms a complete output, the runtime parses the candidate and validates its arguments against the tool’s registered JSON schema before performing any domain checks.
In this replacement example, omitting expected_version or supplying a numeric path fails structural validation immediately. Setting "additionalProperties": false in listing 2 likewise causes the parser to reject hallucinated arguments such as force or recursive. However, structural conformance resolves only syntax. Verifying whether the path resides within the task’s assigned sandbox, and determining whether the target still contains the inspected source revision, require distinct evaluation steps. As summarized in table 1, the runtime enforces these guarantees across layered boundaries.

A string formatted as a file path does not constitute a confined resource reference.1 The tool implementation must canonicalize and resolve the target inside the authorized workspace, accounting for symlinks, directory traversal escapes, and path alias changes that could redirect the operation. Similarly, declaring replacement as a string does not bound its encoded memory footprint. Production adapters enforce explicit byte-size limits on incoming payloads, bound the volume of captured diagnostic output, and apply strict execution timeouts. Static schema validation handles input syntax, whereas dynamic state verification, path confinement, and resource throttling remain runtime obligations. Schema Rules for Tool Definitions supplies a bounded edit descriptor along with schema rules for required fields, size limits, explicit units, and variant semantics.

A tool adapter that validates src/pool.py and then reopens the path by name inherits the same window: a symbolic link swapped in between turns a permitted edit into an edit elsewhere. Resolving the path once and operating on the resolved object, rather than re-resolving the string, is what closes it.

Grammar-guided decoding does not change this division of labor. A token-level mask removes syntax errors before the candidate exists, but it cannot resolve a filesystem reference, evaluate an access policy, or compare a version tag with the file’s current revision. The host runtime validates the materialized request, and the endpoint verifies dynamic preconditions at the moment the effect happens. This separation instantiates the typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)). The contract admits a call to the environment only after validation, precondition, and authorization checks, with the version precondition enforced together with the mutation rather than during an earlier read.


↩︎ The structural guarantee of grammar-guided decoding, and the reference and permission checks it leaves open, are established in What a grammar mask guarantees.



An earlier read confirmed only that src/pool.py matched revision r17 at the instant of observation. If another agent or background process modifies src/pool.py while the model is generating its patch, applying an unconditioned write silently overwrites those intervening changes. The expected_version parameter binds the retrieval contract of The Retrieval Contract directly to the mutation contract enforced here so that this lost-update race cannot succeed. To prevent the lost update, the storage service must verify the expected version and commit the replacement as a single atomic conditional update, the storage equivalent of a hardware compare-and-swap (CAS) primitive.2 In this example, the workspace source service executes the entire sequence inside a single coordination boundary: it resolves the target file, verifies that its current revision matches expected_version, writes the new content, and publishes the resulting revision token. Decomposing this sequence into non-atomic operations (reading the revision, verifying it in user space, then issuing a write) reopens a race window where concurrent writers can intervene. The atomic conditional update closes this time-of-check to time-of-use gap.
2 Optimistic Validation Under Contention: The expected-version check is commit-time validation from optimistic concurrency control, applied to one file. What is new at the tool boundary is the price of a conflict: each failed validation costs the agent a fresh read and a new proposal, paid in model turns rather than in microseconds. 
↩︎ Why context engineering cannot close the refresh-to-execute race, and leaves the revision check to the tool boundary, is established in Detecting change and bounding uncertainty.

This execution branch yields two distinct operational outcomes:

If the current source revision remains r17, the update commits the replacement and returns r18, identifying the new revision produced by the edit.
If another writer modified the source first, the version check fails. The service rejects the replacement, leaves the storage state unaltered, and returns an explicit version-conflict status.

Following a conflict, the runtime directs the agent to perform an authorized read of the updated source file and synthesize a fresh proposal, rather than blindly overwriting the intervening modifications. This concurrency guarantee holds only as long as all mutations route through the shared coordination boundary. If external processes or unmanaged scripts modify files directly on disk, bypassing the version service, version tokens offer no protection and the endpoint cannot ensure integrity. Dry-run previews follow the identical principle. A dry run confirms that a proposed patch applies cleanly against revision r17 at the moment of evaluation, but it establishes no lock on that revision. The runtime must re-verify all preconditions, permissions, and version tokens when executing the live write.
Receiving a successful r18 confirmation verifies that the file modification committed to disk, but it does not establish that the underlying connection-pool bug has been resolved. Demonstrating functional correctness requires empirical validation. A subsequent passing run of test_waiter_notified_on_return is evidence that the patch fixes the exercised case of the race, while broader task acceptance continues to follow the project’s verification suite. At the network layer, a dropped reply leaves the caller uncertain whether the server committed the edit or failed before processing the payload. The retry and idempotency contracts analyzed in section 7.5 resolve this operational uncertainty.



If a rejected tool call returns only "Error: operation failed", the model guesses blindly on its next turn. If a permission denial dumps the host directory tree and environment variables to explain why a path was refused, the error message itself leaks unauthorized state. When an operation fails, the runtime must return a structured, bounded diagnostic that isolates the failure condition without leaking information beyond the task’s authorized grants. A structural rejection should identify the missing expected_version property. A concurrency conflict should state that revision r17 has been superseded. Permission rejections, by contrast, must refuse access cleanly without exposing directory structures or path hints that an agent might probe. The runtime logs whether a rejection originated locally during client-side schema validation or remotely at the service endpoint, allowing downstream decision logic to distinguish between an unattempted proposal and a failed remote mutation. Clear, bounded diagnostics give the model the exact evidence needed to synthesize a valid revision, which must then traverse the same validation pipeline.
The descriptor, its layered checks, and its diagnostics together define one tool’s contract, and every check so far has assumed that the runtime already holds that contract and knows which endpoint implements it. In a real deployment the contract arrives from elsewhere: a repository server, another team’s service, a vendor’s integration. How the runtime learns which operations exist, and why learning that an operation exists confers nothing, is the next problem. How many of the discovered descriptors to stage on each turn is a separate budget question that section 7.9 takes up.




In practice, a tool implementation such as conditional_replace_file can live in several environments: an in-process adapter compiled into the application, a standalone background daemon, or a remote microservice managed by another team. Before the model can propose a valid call, the host runtime must determine which operations that endpoint exposes and how to encode their arguments. This discovery phase supplies that interface metadata. Under the grant rule, however, learning that an operation exists confers no authority to execute it. Discovery defines interface syntax, whereas authorization governs execution rights.


When building a self-contained agent with a small, static set of tools, registering local functions directly in-process is simple and fast. However, when multiple host applications must connect to independently maintained tool services, custom point-to-point integration quickly becomes impractical. The underlying challenge is combinatorial. Without a shared interface, \(\HostRuntimeCount\) host runtimes integrating \(\ToolServiceCount\) tool services require up to \(\HostRuntimeCount \times \ToolServiceCount\) bespoke adapters. Standardizing on a common protocol reduces this burden to \(\HostRuntimeCount + \ToolServiceCount\) implementations, allowing each side to build to the specification once.



A shared protocol turns pairwise adapters into one implementation per side.
Decoupling tools across a protocol boundary also provides fault isolation. When a tool runs in a separate process, a memory leak, segmentation fault, or unhandled blocking call crashes only the tool server rather than tearing down the primary agent orchestration loop. Even so, protocol standardization does not eliminate engineering responsibilities. Integrators must still define tool semantics, audit version compatibility, and enforce security policies. Local in-process plugins and out-of-process tool servers represent deliberate deployment trade-offs rather than mutually exclusive or evolutionary stages.
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) exemplifies this architecture. MCP structures integrations across three distinct entities: a host application (such as an interactive environment or agent runtime), clients that manage connections, and servers that expose capabilities. The host runs one client per connected server, and each client speaks the protocol on the host’s behalf. Servers can run as local child processes or as remote network services. This architectural division clarifies integration responsibilities rather than prescribing a specific execution sandbox (Model Context Protocol 2025).
Each deployment model matches different operational demands. A local child process keeps filesystem operations adjacent to the working copy and simplifies process lifecycle management. Conversely, a remote service can centralize credential storage, connection pooling, and backend access without replicating sensitive configurations across every host machine. Both options, however, introduce distinct failure modes and resource boundaries. An unconfined local process still reaches whatever local filesystem it is granted, while a severed network link can leave an in-flight operation executing invisibly on a remote server. The choice between them follows where resource governance and policy enforcement belong, weighing transport latency against tool execution duration rather than presuming any transport topology is universally superior.



Connecting a host client to multiple servers raises an immediate routing hazard: if two connected servers both advertise an apply_patch operation and the host dispatches calls by bare function name, an untrusted server can silently shadow the repository’s patch tool. Even though MCP separates discovery from execution through two primary wire operations (tools/list to discover available tool definitions and tools/call for execution3), the host must bind each discovered definition to its specific server instance and local policy before exposing it. On the wire, each definition advertises a unique name, a natural-language description, and a JSON Schema governing accepted arguments; an invocation names the target tool and supplies a matching argument dictionary. These messages establish the mechanics of interface exchange rather than a task’s execution rights. The MCP tools specification (Model Context Protocol 2025) defines these message formats and mandates server-side input validation and access controls.

To trace where policy boundaries sit during execution, consider a repository server advertising two illustrative operations: read_source and apply_patch. A concrete integration sequence proceeds through several verification checkpoints:

The host’s client queries tools/list, and the host admits each returned schema only if its own policy allows it (for example, because the server and its version are on an allowlist), binding each admitted schema explicitly to that server instance and its locally governed tool policy so no other server can shadow it.
The host determines which admitted definitions to expose in the model context for the connection-pool repair task.
When the model proposes an operation, the host runtime validates the arguments against the schema and verifies task-level authorization before transmitting the request.
Upon receiving tools/call, the endpoint independently verifies the request against the underlying operating system permissions and data access controls it manages.

For the connection-pool repair, discovering that apply_patch exists leaves the permitted edit paths and the expected-version preconditions unchanged. The guarantee of atomic, conditional updates derives entirely from the server implementation, never from an encouraging function name. If an endpoint fails to provide conditional-update guarantees, the runtime must reject it as incompatible with the task’s safety contract.



Just as an encouraging function name proves nothing about atomicity, a discovered apply_patch description that states “approved for all workspaces” or embeds instructions to steer the model is an untrusted external input, not an authorization grant. A description returned during discovery might accurately summarize an operation, omit critical failure modes, or attempt to redirect model behavior, and even an authenticated server can supply a misleading description because verifying a server’s identity does not imply endorsing every claim it emits.
Filtering which tools appear in the model prompt narrows the attack surface, but catalog filtering alone cannot replace per-call enforcement. Task grants evolve dynamically, and call arguments select specific resources at runtime. Authorizing an agent to inspect src/pool.py does not permit it to read unrelated credentials or transmit private source code to an external service. Defense in depth also requires the server or backing service to enforce its own perimeter rather than assuming every client performs flawless checks. Host authorization and endpoint authorization protect different assets and operational domains; neither supersedes the other. On the return path, protocol framing cleanly differentiates a tool result payload from a system message, but it does not disarm adversarial text within the payload. When ambient credential reach serves as the sole barrier between discovery and side effects, adversarial text in a tool result can steer the agent across repository boundaries (war story 7.1).
