Math: Dividing each confirmed-disclosure count in table 4 by the attacked-episode count gives 20 percent for A and 5 percent for B, a relative reduction of 75 percent. In the stipulated scenario where every unresolved outcome in both arms is a disclosure, the rates rise to 25 percent and 15 percent, and the reduction falls to 40 percent. Even that figure is not the least favorable comparative reduction, because unresolved episodes in the baseline arm A could have been clean while unresolved episodes in the defended arm B could all have leaked. The worst-case bound on B’s relative improvement therefore compares B’s upper disclosure fraction with A’s confirmed lower fraction. On benign work, B accepts 10 fewer repairs per 100, which equals its extra false blocks. The attacked cohort shows the same cost. B completes 55 legitimate repairs under attack against A’s 65, although fewer of its attacked episodes end in disclosure or an unresolved outcome. The reason is that its release check also blocks searches the repair itself needed. At equal cost per attempt, equation 1.2 scales with \(1/\AcceptanceProbability\), so B’s cost per accepted benign repair is 12.5 percent higher than A’s before counting its own label and check work.
Systems insight: Policy B achieves an apparent 75 percent reduction in observed disclosures, but it does so at the cost of a 12.5 percent increase in effective cost per accepted benign task, driven entirely by its elevated false-block rate. Two engineering levers govern this trade-off. First, refining the false-block policy recovers benign acceptance one-for-one without sacrificing the integrity of the release check. Second, reducing evaluation uncertainty is as important as tuning the policy itself: in the scenario where unresolved outcomes in both arms are disclosures, Policy B’s apparent relative advantage falls from 75 percent to 40 percent. Finally, Policy B’s remaining confirmed disclosures pinpoint concrete failure modes (untracked data dependencies, misclassified release boundaries, or policy bypasses) that engineers must diagnose in audit traces before clearing the system for deployment.





A fixed collection of injected README payloads provides a reproducible regression test during development, but an attacker whose first fixture query is blocked by Policy B’s release check will not keep submitting the same canned phrasing. Certifying system robustness demands adaptive evaluation that actively probes the boundaries of policy enforcement, systematically varying injection channels, summary representations, retrieval contexts, tool signatures, and network endpoints while holding the underlying legitimate task constant. Red-teaming must also test structural bypasses alongside natural-language trickery. These scenarios include injecting boolean literals (such as spoofing a tests_passed: true field) to subvert status parsers, reusing expired capability handles across task sessions, and mounting time-of-check to time-of-use attacks where an approval request mutates before dispatch. Evaluating against these diverse attack patterns tests whether the architecture’s security contracts hold under stress rather than whether a model happens to recognize a specific prompt phrasing.
Because stochastic decoding and distributed tool environments introduce execution variance, red teams must run repeated independent trials and report comprehensive confidence intervals alongside raw counts and tested strategies. A common pitfall in empirical defense papers is treating zero observed attacks as proof of invulnerability. Observing zero successes across a finite sample bounds the attack-success rate, but never proves it is zero. For example, if a defense experiences zero compromises across 100 independent trials, the 95 percent confidence upper bound on its true attack-success rate remains 3.0 percent, closely matching the classical rule-of-three11 estimate of \(3/\AttackedTrialCount\). Translating such benchmark figures into production risk estimates requires explicit modeling of adversary capability, attack prevalence, and shifting operational workloads. Naively multiplying an empirical attack-success rate by total monthly request volume provides an illusion of precision without modeling attacker incentives. The non-negotiable systems requirement here is transparently declaring the outcome boundary, trial protocol, and empirical uncertainty.
11 Rule of Three: With no successes in \(\AttackedTrialCount\) independent trials, the 95 percent upper bound \(\Pr(\text{success})\) solves \((1-\Pr(\text{success}))^\AttackedTrialCount = 0.05\), so \(\Pr(\text{success}) = 1 - 0.05^{1/\AttackedTrialCount} \approx \ln(20)/\AttackedTrialCount \approx 3/\AttackedTrialCount\). Hanley and Lippman-Hand drew attention to the rule for clinical studies that report zero adverse events (Hanley and Lippman-Hand 1983). Inverted, it tells a security team how many clean attacked episodes a release target demands, about three divided by the tolerable attack-success rate. 
Hanley, James A., and Abby Lippman-Hand. 1983. “If Nothing Goes Wrong, Is Everything All Right? Interpreting Zero Numerators.” JAMA 249 (13): 1743–45.

↪ Repeated-run design and confidence intervals for agent outcome rates are developed in Statistical Evaluation Rigor.


Zero successes in n trials still allow an attack rate near 3/n.



Checkpoint 9.3: Interpreting a defense report
A proposed defense lowers observed fixture disclosures but blocks more legitimate searches and leaves several endpoint results unresolved.

Outcome boundary: Which records distinguish proposed misuse, a block before dispatch, confirmed harm, and an unresolved outcome?
Denominators: Why must a refused or timed-out attacked task remain in its eligible cohort, and how should unresolved effects be reported?
Utility: Which benign and attacked completion measures would distinguish useful protection from simply disabling the search tool?
Adaptation: How can an evaluation test a poisoned summary retrieved in a later session without contaminating other trials or treating a fixed attack set as a universal guarantee?
Zero-success bound: A defense shows no disclosures in 50 attacked episodes. Estimate the upper bound on its attack-success rate at the level used above, and decide whether the report supports release for a task that tolerates at most 1 percent.

title: 9 Agent Security
text:
Each of these design mistakes conflates evidence established at one operational boundary with authorization or trust at another. They persist because they readily pass superficial tests: a model successfully rejects a known exploit string, or an audit log records fewer observed disclosures. In each case, however, the runtime system’s true enforcement mechanisms, its evidence and release checks, remain unexamined.

Fallacy: A guardrail classifier in front of the agent eliminates prompt injection.
An input screening classifier is itself a learned function over text. Attackers can therefore evade it through paraphrasing, character encodings, or by splitting malicious payloads across multiple external documents and conversational turns (Zou et al. 2023). An adaptive adversary optimizes prompts against the guardrail model just as systematically as against the agent itself. For example, EchoLeak passed a production classifier by formatting its malicious instructions as commentary addressed to the human reader (war story 9.1). Furthermore, multi-document agent workflows compound even negligible false-negative rates. A classifier that misses only 5 percent of individual malicious payloads still leaves 4.9 percent of research tasks exposed to at least one payload when the agent consumes 100 documents per task (notebook 9.1). Targeted attacker adaptation pushes this miss rate higher. Input screening filters low-effort noise and reduces the load on downstream controls, but architectural security depends on rigorous runtime release and evidence checks.


Pitfall: Exempting read and search tools from disclosure checks.
Systems engineers often assume that read and search operations are inherently safe because retrieving data leaves the remote index unmodified. However, every read request transmits query parameters, HTTP headers, or lookup keys across a trust boundary, making read-oriented tools effective channels for data exfiltration. In the hypothetical comparison of section 9.9, which illustrates the method rather than measuring any system, an authorization policy that validated only the tool name and destination endpoint disclosed sensitive fixtures in 20 percent of attacked episodes. In contrast, enforcing an explicit release check on the data payload embedded within each query reduced the disclosure rate to 5 percent. Every outbound tool call is a potential communication channel; runtime policies must inspect the data entering each request and verify that its release to the specified destination is authorized.


Fallacy: Safety post-training makes the model immune to injection.
Safety alignment trains models to recognize and refuse overtly malicious requests, such as generating exploit code or hate speech. Indirect prompt injection, however, masks its malicious intent as an ordinary, benign step within an authorized task, such as formatting a database query or running a local diagnostic. An attacker directly exploits the model’s core instruction-following capability, deliberately pitting its helpfulness against its safety guardrails. Wei and colleagues identified these competing objectives as a primary cause of safety-training failures (Wei et al. 2023). While post-training can reduce attack success under standard benchmark protocols, fine-tuned weights cannot enforce a hard security boundary that the model itself cannot cross. Systems engineers must enforce authority delegation and data release checks within the execution runtime beneath the model.

Wei, Alexander, Nika Haghtalab, and Jacob Steinhardt. 2023. “Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 36. https://doi.org/10.52202/075280-3508.


Pitfall: Cleaning retained state by deleting the raw injection.
Deleting an offending input document or message from disk does not purge its influence from the agent. In multi-turn systems, intermediate inferences quickly propagate into summaries, distilled execution lessons, and queued tool proposals that preserve the attacker’s intent long after the raw injection is removed (section 9.8). Remediating corrupted state demands rigorous provenance tracking: developers must withdraw the tainted source, trace its causal dependencies across every derived record, and treat the broader retained memory as suspect whenever those dependencies cannot be cleanly isolated.


Fallacy: A valid scalar extracted by a separate reader is trusted evidence.
Parsing unstructured model output into a typed scalar, such as the extracted boolean claimed_tests_passed: true, verifies syntactic structure rather than operational authenticity. Constraining data to a schema does not elevate an untrusted source into an authoritative one. Under the formal dispatch model of equation 3, an assertion whose provenance traces to unverified external text lies outside the set of authorized influences. The runtime must reject such claims during evidence checking, no matter how cleanly structured the parser’s output appears. Authoritative evidence must originate directly from a designated execution runner and remain strictly scoped to the automated checks that runner independently conducted.


Pitfall: Treating a lower attack-success rate as a complete security result.
An empirical attack-success rate provides an incomplete measure of security on its own. The observed rate depends heavily on the adversary’s search budget, the target threat model, and the specific test harness configuration, all while omitting the operational costs imposed by the defense. In the hypothetical comparison of section 9.9, an apparent 75 percent reduction in observed disclosures falls to 40 percent in the scenario where unresolved evaluation runs in both arms are disclosures. The least favorable comparative reduction instead uses the defended arm’s upper rate and the baseline’s confirmed lower rate. Furthermore, achieving that protection came with a 12.5 percent increase in cost per accepted benign repair. Observing zero successful attacks in a finite test suite does not close the question either: recording zero breaches across 100 trials still leaves an upper confidence bound as high as 3.0 percent. Robust evaluations must report statistical confidence bounds, account explicitly for unresolved outcomes, and measure benign task utility alongside attack mitigation.

title: 9 Agent Security
text:
Agent security centers on influence rather than traditional access control: which party’s content steered an execution proposal, where data embedded in that proposal may travel, and which sources can legitimately justify the resulting state mutation. A language model cannot answer these questions for itself because it processes control instructions and untrusted data within a single, undifferentiated token stream. The runtime environment must track this provenance instead. It maintains records that trace every value across extraction, summarization, long-term memory, and handle references, enforcing policy checks directly on the concrete operation and recipient at dispatch time. Because exposure compounds with every document ingested and every interaction turn executed, these runtime checks must fire unconditionally on every transaction, rather than selectively when an input appears suspicious.
The quantitative foundation of agent security rests on seven governing relations. Two exposure relations estimate how often a task encounters an attacker-controlled payload, three information-flow label rules govern dispatch decisions, and two accounting rules measure defense overhead and bound empirical evaluation guarantees. Table 5 summarizes these relationships.



Table 5: Key equations of agent security: Exposure relations quantify payload arrival rates, label rules govern which operations the runtime admits, and accounting rules price defense overhead while bounding empirical test guarantees.

section 9.9







Key Takeaways: Preserve authority and evidence across influence

Injection borrows authority it never acquires: Attacker-controlled content hijacks the reasoning loop to propose operations that the runtime executes under legitimate task credentials. Authentic transport channels and natural-language plausibility provide zero authorization guarantees; the runtime must verify whether the accumulated provenance of an instruction justifies exercising the task’s delegated capabilities at dispatch.
A callable tool is not a permitted effect: Permission to invoke an API does not grant blanket authority over all arguments, target destinations, or data disclosures. Effective permission is the strict intersection of requester grants, task-scoped limits, and service-side authorization, enforced directly at the concrete endpoint the call reaches.
Every query is outbound data: Read and search tools transmit their arguments across external interfaces, meaning exfiltration requires neither a sandbox breakout nor an unauthorized API call. Enforcing confidentiality requires release checks on the actual parameters and resolved payload destinations, including data referenced through typed handles.
Well-formed is not true: Isolating input parsing inside a dedicated reader model reduces raw prompt exposure for the primary planner, but structuring untrusted text into schema-compliant fields does not make the content truthful. A schema-valid boolean remains an unverified external assertion. Trustworthy acceptance evidence requires deterministic verification inside an isolated environment, ensuring that external influence cannot masquerade as an authenticated test pass.
Labels outlive the text that set them: Provenance and confidentiality labels attach to information rather than syntax, propagating downstream through summaries, episodic memory, and reference handles. Stripping the original injection string from the active context window does not purge the contamination. Endorsement marks an exact value and version as fit for a specific control decision, and declassification explicitly permits an outbound release; neither transformation occurs as a byproduct of string parsing or model summarization.
Approval binds an action, not a narrative: Trustworthy approval must bind immutably to the exact operation, target destination, and parameter payload that the runtime dispatches. Any modification to the payload invalidates prior consent and requires a fresh decision. Furthermore, approval cannot validate an unverified source claim, nor can it grant capabilities beyond the approver’s own authority boundary.
Protection is priced in accepted tasks: Defensive filtering imposes an economic cost that must be measured against end-to-end task completion. False-positive blocks inflate the effective cost per accepted task (\(\CostPerAcceptedTask\)) just as severely as failed model trajectories or costly repair loops. A rigorous evaluation must report unauthorized disclosures, unresolved execution failures, and benign task drop rates alongside attack-success metrics. When evaluating rare exploit events, the rule of three establishes that observing zero breaches across \(\AttackedTrialCount\) independent trials only bounds the 95 percent attack-success rate to approximately \(3/\AttackedTrialCount\).



Enforcing containment beneath the model (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-zero-trust-sandboxing}\)) and invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) relocates authorization and information-flow tracking from the probabilistic model into deterministic runtime infrastructure. The runtime enforces this guarantee through baseline release and evidence checks at dispatch, supplemented only by separately authenticated decisions bound to the exact value, version, and authorized use. The evidence check is also authority staying with the source (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)) made enforceable against an adversary, since a README can describe a test result but only the runner’s record can be accepted as one. No input filter, schema sanitizer, or model-generated label can substitute for these external runtime invariants.

title: 9 Agent Security
text:
The problem of a program misusing ambient authority on behalf of an untrusted request predates language models by half a century. In a foundational 1972 planning study for the U.S. Air Force, Anderson introduced the concept of the reference monitor, a tamper-proof, universally invoked validation mechanism through which every resource access must pass (Anderson 1972). Three years later, Saltzer and Schroeder articulated the enduring design principles of protected computer systems, establishing complete mediation, least privilege, and fail-safe defaults as prerequisites for dependable software (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). Lampson observed in 1973 that confining an untrusted program is harder than restricting its immediate entry points, because sensitive information can easily escape through covert channels never designed for communication (Lampson 1973). Hardy’s 1988 confused deputy, already met at the tool boundary, named the failure that prompt injection now industrializes (Hardy 1988).

Anderson, James P. 1972. Computer Security Technology Planning Study. ESD-TR-73-51. Deputy for Command; Management Systems, Electronic Systems Division, Air Force Systems Command.
Traditional access control inspects permissions at the perimeter, but it cannot track where data travels after it is read. Information-flow security emerged to close this gap. Bell and LaPadula formalized multilevel confidentiality to prevent sensitive data from leaking into lower-security sinks (Bell and LaPadula 1973), while Biba formulated the mathematical dual for integrity to prevent untrusted inputs from corrupting trusted system state (Biba 1977). Denning synthesized these models by organizing security classes into an algebraic lattice, establishing that the label of any derived value is the join of its constituent inputs (Denning 1976), the operational rule expressed in equation 2. Goguen and Meseguer gave these flow constraints a semantic foundation with noninterference, formalizing the requirement that low-privilege observers must not be able to distinguish whether high-privilege computations occurred (Goguen and Meseguer 1982). Later work made these guarantees practical in software. Myers and Liskov introduced decentralized label models so that individual principals could safely declassify their own data without a centralized arbiter (Myers and Liskov 1998). Newsome and Song demonstrated that dynamic taint tracking could trace untrusted data through commodity binaries at machine-instruction boundaries (Newsome and Song 2005).
Language models reopened these classical security challenges at an entirely new system boundary: the prompt, where executable instructions and passive data share a single channel. Willison identified and named prompt injection in 2022 (Willison 2022). Greshake and colleagues expanded the threat model by demonstrating indirect prompt injection, showing how retrieved context such as web pages, email messages, or database records can carry adversarial instructions directly into an agent’s reasoning loop (Greshake et al. 2023). Zou and colleagues then showed that these adversarial prompts do not rely on clever manual phrasing; gradient-based search algorithms can generate transferable token sequences automatically (Zou et al. 2023). Early defenses attempted to secure the system within the model weights, for example by training models to distinguish between developer instructions and untrusted context (Wallace et al. 2024). Heuristic filtering inside the neural network proved fragile against adaptive attackers, however. Modern system architectures instead enforce isolation outside the model weights. The shift runs from dual-model pipelines that separate untrusted parsing from privileged planning (Willison 2023) to runtimes that attach provenance and permitted-use metadata to values and check that metadata before every tool execution (Debenedetti et al. 2025). The architectural progression mirrors that of classical systems: heuristic content filtering inevitably yields to the strict, external mediation of information flows.

Zou, Andy, Zifan Wang, Nicholas Carlini, Milad Nasr, J. Zico Kolter, and Matt Fredrikson. 2023. Universal and Transferable Adversarial Attacks on Aligned Language Models.

Wallace, Eric, Kai Xiao, Reimar Leike, Lilian Weng, Johannes Heidecke, and Alex Beutel. 2024. The Instruction Hierarchy: Training LLMs to Prioritize Privileged Instructions.

Willison, Simon. 2023. The Dual LLM Pattern for Building AI Assistants That Can Resist Prompt Injection. Personal blog.

Saltzer and Schroeder, “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems” (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). The foundational treatise on secure systems architecture. Its design principles, particularly complete mediation, least privilege, and fail-safe defaults, remain the essential working vocabulary for any enforcement layer, including an agent runtime.
Hardy, “The Confused Deputy” (Hardy 1988). In just three pages, Hardy demonstrates why identity-based access controls fail when a privileged program exercises borrowed authority on behalf of an untrusted client. This dynamic is the central failure mode of an injected agent.
Denning, “A Lattice Model of Secure Information Flow” (Denning 1976). This paper presents the concise mathematical argument for why security labels combine through a lattice join operation. It is essential reading before designing label propagation or dynamic taint tracking in an agent engine.
Greshake et al., “Not What You’ve Signed Up For” (Greshake et al. 2023). The paper that transformed prompt injection into a concrete systems threat model, establishing how untrusted content ingested through retrieval or tool execution can commandeer an agent.
Debenedetti et al., “AgentDojo” (Debenedetti et al. 2024). A benchmark and execution environment that evaluates security mechanisms by measuring task utility alongside attack mitigation success, embodying the evaluation discipline developed in this chapter.
Debenedetti et al., “Defeating Prompt Injections by Design” (Debenedetti et al. 2025). A comprehensive systems design that applies capability architectures and information-flow tracking to an agent runtime, best read with close attention to the utility and flexibility that strict isolation requires sacrificing.


Saltzer, J. H., and M. D. Schroeder. 1975. “The Protection of Information in Computer Systems.” Proceedings of the IEEE 63 (9): 1278–308. https://doi.org/10.1109/proc.1975.9939.

Hardy, Norm. 1988. “The Confused Deputy: (Or Why Capabilities Might Have Been Invented).” ACM SIGOPS Operating Systems Review 22 (4): 36–38. https://doi.org/10.1145/60609.60611.

Greshake, Kai, Sahar Abdelnabi, Shailesh Mishra, Christoph Endres, Thorsten Holz, and Mario Fritz. 2023. “Not What You’ve Signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection.” Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, 79–90. https://doi.org/10.1145/3605764.3623985.

Debenedetti, Edoardo, Jie Zhang, Mislav Balunović, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Marc Fischer, and Florian Tramèr. 2024. “AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS), Datasets and Benchmarks Track 37.

Debenedetti, Edoardo, Ilia Shumailov, Tianqi Fan, Jamie Hayes, Nicholas Carlini, Daniel Fabian, Christoph Kern, Chongyang Shi, Andreas Terzis, and Florian Tramèr. 2025. Defeating Prompt Injections by Design.

title: 9 Agent Security
text:
The problems use the chapter’s notation and mechanisms. All numeric givens are hypothetical problem inputs, not measurements of any system; workload read volumes and approval parameters are those of the chapter’s lighthouse profiles.
Problem 1 (Basic): A read budget behind a screen. A repair task reads external documents in which a fraction \(\DocumentPayloadFraction\) = 0.5 percent independently carry a payload. The team wants at most 10 percent of tasks to meet a payload before any release or evidence check fires.

With equation 1, compute \(\Pr(\text{exp})\) for a task that reads 40 documents.
Find the largest \(\TaskReadCount\) that meets the target.
A screening classifier misses 10 percent of payloads. Find the new largest \(\TaskReadCount\), and state what the screen changes about the runtime’s release check and what it leaves unchanged.

Problem 2 (Basic): Labels on a derived query. A repair planner’s context holds three records. A public issue has \(\IntegrityProvenance = \{\texttt{issue\_12}\}\) and no recipient restriction. A private configuration has \(\IntegrityProvenance = \{\texttt{config}\}\) and \(\ConfidentialityLabel = \{\text{runner}, \text{reviewer}\}\). A protected-runner log has \(\IntegrityProvenance = \{\text{runner}\}\) and \(\ConfidentialityLabel = \{\text{runner}, \text{reviewer}, \text{dashboard}\}\). The planner emits a message \(\LabeledRecord\).

Compute \(\IntegrityProvenance(\LabeledRecord)\) and \(\ConfidentialityLabel(\LabeledRecord)\) with equation 2.
Apply equation 3 to three proposals. One posts \(\LabeledRecord\) to the public issue tracker. Another submits \(\LabeledRecord\) to the internal review service, whose task policy accepts any source. A final proposal records \(\LabeledRecord\) as a test pass, whose \(\AcceptedInfluences(\ProposedOperation)\) is \(\{\text{runner}\}\). For each, name the condition that fails or state that both hold.
Redesign the acceptance path so that a test pass can be recorded without weakening the evidence check.

Problem 3 (Basic): How many clean episodes a release needs. A release rule requires that the 95 percent upper bound on the attack-success rate be at most 0.5 percent.

Using the zero-success bound of section 9.9, find the smallest number of attacked episodes with zero observed successes that meets the rule, and compare it with the rule-of-three estimate.
The team reports zero disclosures in 200 attacked episodes. Compute the upper bound this supports.
The same report excludes 3 episodes whose endpoint outcome was unresolved at the horizon. Critique the exclusion and compute the conservative outcome fraction once they are restored. Decide whether the restored report supports the release rule, and explain why unresolved outcomes cannot be treated as clean trials in the zero-success calculation.

Problem 4 (Intermediate): Pricing a release check. Two policies run the same repair distribution with 200 attacked and 200 benign episodes each. Policy A checks the search operation and destination only; Policy C adds typed fixture handles and a release check. Table 6 records the outcomes.



Table 6: Outcomes for two repair policies: Counts from the same attacked and benign repair episodes under each policy; problem inputs, not measurements.










Outcome count
Policy A
Policy C




Attacked episodes, observed disclosure
30
6


Attacked episodes, unresolved outcome
4
16


Accepted benign repairs
180
171


Benign repairs lost to a false block
8
17







Compute each policy’s observed attack-success rate and its upper disclosure fraction counting unresolved outcomes as disclosures. Find the relative reduction using the observed rates and in the stipulated scenario where unresolved outcomes in both arms are disclosures. Then find the least favorable comparative reduction using A’s confirmed lower rate and C’s upper rate.
At $2 per attempt for both policies, compute \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) per accepted benign repair for each with equation 1.2, and the added monthly cost of C at 10,000 accepted repairs per month.
Assume 100 production tasks per month meet this attack exactly as tested. Find the cost per disclosure above which C pays for itself using the observed rates and in the stipulated both-arms disclosure scenario of part (a). Repeat using the least favorable difference between A’s confirmed lower rate and C’s upper rate.
Name two assumptions in part (c) that the chapter warns a benchmark rate cannot supply, and name the cheapest change to C that would lower its break-even cost without touching the release check.

Problem 5 (Intermediate): Same payload rate, different binding constraint. Transfer the repair analysis to the research agent, which reads 100 untrusted items per task, and the support agent, which reads 6. Both face \(\DocumentPayloadFraction\) = 1 percent, and an exposed task yields a successful injection with probability 10 percent. A successful research injection discloses data worth $20; a successful support injection issues a redirected refund worth $400.

Compute the per-task exposure and the expected loss per task for each agent.
For the support agent, compare two defenses: a screening classifier with miss rate 5 percent, and an effect-scope check that takes the refund amount and account from the case record, which caps a successful injection’s loss at $20. Compute the expected loss per task under each.
An adaptive attacker raises the classifier’s miss rate to 50 percent. Recompute both options and choose one. Explain why the binding constraint for the support agent is consequence rather than exposure, while for the research agent it is the release of what it reads.

Problem 6 (Intermediate): Drawing the sharing domain for a support fleet. Each support session holds 8,192 tokens of context, of which the first 6,144 are a public policy and instruction prefix identical for every customer; the rest is the customer’s private conversation. A replica prefills 10,000 tokens per second. Treat each session as one prefill of its full context, each session as a different customer’s only session, a resident prefix as always hit when its sharing domain permits reuse, and private conversations as never repeated.

Compute prefill tokens per session and replica-hours of prefill per 1,000,000 sessions for three designs. The first design uses a tenant-wide sharing domain for all cached state. The second uses a per-customer domain for all cached state. The last is a split in which the public prefix follows a shared policy while the private suffix is confined to a per-customer domain.
Explain what a customer can learn under the first design by timing candidate prefixes, and why the split design removes that channel at no prefill cost relative to the first.
Name one condition under which the split design still leaks, and the serving-side control that closes it.

Problem 7 (Advanced): Paying for conservative labels. Under the conservative invocation rule, a planner that has read the private fixture taints every later query, so every subsequent search fails the release check. Without the rule, a repair attempt is accepted with probability 90 percent. In 60 percent of tasks the planner reads the fixture before it needs a search, and a task whose searches are all blocked then fails with probability 50 percent. An attempt costs $1.50.

Compute \(\AcceptanceProbability\) under the conservative rule and the resulting rise in \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\).
A redesign routes search construction through a trusted query adapter that reads only public manifest fields and receives no planner output. It adds $0.01 per search and a task makes 3 searches on average. Assuming it restores the original acceptance probability, compute its \(\CostPerAcceptedTask\) and compare the three designs.
A colleague proposes instead that the planner choose which of two public package names the adapter should search. Compute the query’s \(\IntegrityProvenance\) and \(\ConfidentialityLabel\) when that choice depends on the fixture, decide whether it passes equation 3, and state what the adapter must not receive for part (b)’s assumption to hold.

Problem 8 (Advanced): Standing approval for the remediation agent. The remediation agent requests 2 approvals per hour, each costing 10 minutes of an approver paid $120 per hour. Each change follows a diagnosis that reads 10 untrusted alerts and log lines at \(\DocumentPayloadFraction\) = 1 percent. An exposed diagnosis redirects the change’s parameters with probability 10 percent, and a redirected change costs $12,000. A reviewer inspecting the exact represented action catches 90 percent of redirected changes. To save approver time, the team proposes a standing approval: one review per hour authorizes every configuration change to the same service during that hour. The standing review sees no individual change’s parameters, so it catches no redirected change.

Compute the approver cost per hour under per-action approval and under the standing approval.
Compute the expected redirected-change loss per hour under each, and the total hourly cost.
Find the injection success probability below which the standing approval would be cheaper, and explain why that break-even is not a safe basis for the decision.
Propose a redesign that lowers approver cost while keeping the approval bound to the exact represented action, and state which approval fields it must still show.


What’s Next: From security boundaries to trajectory supervisionEvery check in this chapter fires at one dispatch, on one proposal and the labels it carries. None of them decides whether the trajectory should propose again. Suppose the test of candidate r18 is still running when an operator asks to pause and the repair nears its budget. The pending job, the workspace lease, any held approval, and the labels on retained information then need a single owner that keeps the task’s grants, budgets, and outstanding work current as execution continues or someone intervenes. The Agent Harness develops that whole-trajectory supervision, which decides when to call the model, dispatch permitted work, wait, request approval, or stop. Making that supervision survive a crash, and repairing effects already completed, are separate responsibilities developed afterward.

title: 11 Durable Execution
text:
Lecture slides for this chapter












Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why must an agent write down what it is about to do before it does it?
Real agent tasks, such as migrating an enterprise database or debugging a distributed codebase, run for minutes, hours, or days, long enough that process restarts, node preemptions, and rolling updates stop being rare events and become part of the workload. The harness that supervises such a task keeps its control record in the memory of a single worker, and the model’s context holds only a curated transcript, so one crash erases the admitted operations, held reservations, and pending approvals that tell a successor what may happen next. Restarting from the original prompt is worse than slow, because it resamples a stochastic model and may repeat an external effect, such as a deployment or a payment, that has already escaped. Durable execution answers with an ordering discipline inherited from transaction processing. The runtime appends every decision and observation to a log that outlives the worker, makes each intended action durable before dispatching it, and rebuilds control state by folding that history rather than by asking the model again. The log still cannot report what happened to a request whose reply never arrived, and keeping that ambiguity visible instead of guessing it away is what lets state survive a long horizon without corrupting the world the agent acts on.

Learning Objectives

Construct a trajectory log whose fold rebuilds control state without treating recorded claims as world truth
Apply intent-before-dispatch ordering under a declared failure domain, price its acknowledgment, and classify what each crash position lets recovery conclude
Select a checkpoint representation and cadence from write volume, capture pause, and reconstruction cost
Design a resume policy that reconciles outstanding obligations under current ownership within a stage-by-stage latency budget
Distinguish time-travel replay of a recorded projection, harness regression replay, and counterfactual branches by the conclusion each supports
Diagnose the first divergence between two executions from captured inputs, stating what the evidence cannot establish
Design retention policies that keep the bytes each declared recovery, replay, and diagnostic promise requires



Explore the concepts in this chapterThe volume’s concept map, opened on this chapter. Select a concept to read how it connects to ideas in other chapters. Open the full map ↗






Horizon stretches state past one worker’s life, so continuation needs a durable record.
Consider a software repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) that has admitted and dispatched an integration test against ws_r18, a fixed workspace snapshot of candidate patch r18. Before the test runner reports a result, the worker process crashes, or the host suffers a spot preemption (the sudden reclamation of an ephemeral cloud node). A replacement worker cannot simply re-invoke the model with the original prompt. Starting over discards context: the pending test invocation, the active capability tokens and resource reservations, any pause state acknowledged by an operator, and any evidence indicating whether the remote executor accepted, completed, or failed the job. Worse, the original test suite may still be executing on a remote cluster, incurring financial charges and modifying sandbox state, while a newly launched model redundantly dispatches a conflicting command. This crash, with its dispatched but unreported test, is the chapter’s running worksheet, and each section asks what the surviving record says about it.
The agent harness already tracks most of what the replacement worker requires. Its live trajectory record separates pending execution continuations from outstanding external obligations, while its admission checks govern which actions may cross the runtime boundary. In a naive implementation, however, both structures reside exclusively in volatile host memory and vanish the instant the worker fails. The model’s context window cannot substitute for this operational state. A large language model (LLM) context contains only an episodic transcript shaped by bounded observation windows and prompt compaction; it contains no record of in-flight network sockets, admitted capability tokens, or active cloud billing meters. As the execution horizon expands across dozens of turns and long-running external tasks, worker crashes, node preemptions, and rolling updates shift from rare anomalies to operational certainties.


↩︎ The trajectory record that holds pending continuations and outstanding obligations is established in The Trajectory Record.
Surviving mid-trajectory failures requires durable history: an append-only, ordered log of every decision, admitted action, and received observation. With this durable log, a replacement worker can deterministically reconstruct the agent’s state, reconcile side effects that already reached external systems, and safely resume execution under valid authority. That capability names the chapter’s subject. A trajectory has durable execution when a different worker, after any failure the runtime declares it tolerates, can reconstruct the trajectory’s control state and outstanding obligations from surviving records and continue it without losing an effect that already escaped or repeating one unsafely. One ordering rule makes that possible. Under write-ahead durability, the record of an intended action becomes durable before the action is dispatched over the network. The rule is the runtime’s mechanical answer to the horizon and state exposures, a bound placed below the model that no prompt can supply. It carries measurable costs in acknowledgment latency on every dispatch, capture pauses at checkpoints, and reconstruction time on recovery.
The chapter builds the durable runtime in the order a crash demands it. First, the trajectory log (section 11.2) defines the record from which a clean worker rebuilds control state, and durable intent before dispatch (section 11.3) orders that record against external effects while pricing the acknowledgment each failure domain requires. Folding an unbounded log and reconstructing mutated files from scratch would grow too slow over long runs, so checkpoints (section 11.4) bind the control record to workspace snapshots at regular strides. The resume protocol (section 11.5) then turns that reconstructed state into an authorized continuation under a new owner. The same durable records then serve offline debugging. Replay (section 11.6) inspects or tests history without new model calls, divergence localization (section 11.7) finds the earliest boundary where two executions disagree, and retention (section 11.8) decides which of these recovery and replay promises the stored bytes can still keep. Each mechanism answers the central question of the worksheet crash by establishing what the surviving record proves and what ambiguity remains unresolved.



A replacement worker can rebuild the crashed trajectory only from what the failed worker wrote somewhere that outlived it, so the first design question is what outliving it means. If the worker host and its attached disk are destroyed together mid-turn, a replacement on an independent machine can resume only if the acknowledged history was already replicated to independent storage. Durability is therefore meaningful only relative to an explicit fault model that names which failures the stored history must survive. Systems engineers call this boundary a failure domain, the set of faults across which a persistence guarantee holds. Three tiers of increasing severity recur: a process crash that leaves host storage intact, replacement of the worker node while a shared network-attached volume survives, and permanent loss of that storage tier. Each tier demands stronger replication and wider physical fault isolation, and section 11.3.1 prices the acknowledgment each one requires. The crash worksheet targets the strongest tier, in which the acknowledged event history and every artifact required for recovery survive the simultaneous destruction of the worker host and its attached disk. Every durability claim in this chapter is made relative to that contract.


Surviving the failure domain solves where the bytes live, but it leaves open what those bytes must record so the replacement worker never has to ask the model what happened before the crash. Re-prompting the model from its last visible message cannot reconstruct past control state, because stochastic sampling and a changed external environment steer the trajectory down a different path. Instead, the runtime decouples execution state from process lifetime by recording an append-only, chronological history of every decision and observation across the trajectory.

Definition 11.1: Trajectory log
Trajectory log is the append-only, ordered sequence of typed events (including delivered model prompts, returned completions, resource authorizations, control transitions, and observed tool outcomes) from which a deterministic reducer reconstructs an agent trajectory’s control state.

Significance: Recovery folds recorded decisions sequentially rather than re-executing completed turns. A crash late in a long trajectory therefore costs only deterministic replay time. It avoids fresh model invocations, which would re-expose the system to the compounding error rates of equation 1.1 and accumulate redundant token charges against the task attempt budget in equation 1.2.
Distinction: The trajectory record (definition \(\ref{dfn-trajectory-record}\)) is the live in-memory projection that governs the immediate next decision. The trajectory log is the immutable, append-only history from which that record is derived. The context window is the transient, curated token sequence supplied to the model.
Common pitfall: Recording only tool results while omitting operation dispatches. If an admitted tool call crashes mid-execution or drops its network response, the absence of an intent record leaves the recovery worker unaware that an external side effect may already be in flight.



Formally, the log is a sequence
\[\LoggedEventPrefix = [\LoggedEvent_1, \LoggedEvent_2, \dots, \LoggedEvent_j]\]
When an agent refines an earlier hypothesis or encounters an unexpected tool error, it appends fresh evidence to the tail of the log rather than mutating historical records in place.1 The active trajectory record represents an accumulated projection over this append-only stream. Starting from a base state \(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0\), a deterministic reducer applies each recorded event sequentially:
1 Append-Only Log as Primary Record: Rosenblum and Ousterhout’s log-structured file system treated the sequential log as the primary on-disk data structure, boosting write throughput and simplifying crash recovery (Rosenblum and Ousterhout 1992). A trajectory log inherits these exact advantages: append operations never overwrite historical evidence required by future recovery passes, so a recovering worker can reconstruct state by streaming an ordered log rather than untangling conflicting in-place updates. 
Rosenblum, Mendel, and John K. Ousterhout. 1992. “The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 10 (1): 26–52. https://doi.org/10.1145/146941.146943.
\[\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_j = \text{fold}(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0, \LoggedEventPrefix) = \text{apply}(\dots\text{apply}(\text{apply}(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0, \LoggedEvent_1), \LoggedEvent_2)\dots, \LoggedEvent_j)\]
In this formulation, \(\LogPositionIndex\) indexes the durable log sequence boundary rather than the interaction turn \(\TurnIndex\). Given deterministic reducer semantics and complete event payloads, folding reconstructs the precise control state without invoking the foundation model or re-executing external tools. This architecture embodies the classic event sourcing pattern (Kleppmann 2016): historical decisions serve as deterministic inputs to state reconstruction, while unrecorded events remain explicitly unknown. If the latest durable log entry indicates that a test execution was authorized and dispatched, but contains no corresponding completion event, the reconstructed state marks that operation as unresolved (figure 1). For the worksheet crash, the fold keeps the held reservation and the dispatched test_r18 intent, and it invents no outcome for the test.






Figure 1: The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log: The record in runtime memory (top) is lost on a crash; the durable, append-only log (bottom) is not. Folding the logged events through a deterministic reducer, starting from the initial record \(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0\), rebuilds the recorded projection \(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_j\) at boundary \(\LogPositionIndex\) without calling the model or any tool. Because the log ends at the test’s recorded intent with no recorded result, the reconstructed record keeps the admission and reservation and marks the test unresolved rather than inventing its outcome.



Engineers must distinguish the trajectory log from the model’s active context window. Context assembly is selective and ephemeral: prompt compilation filters past interactions, and context compaction periodically replaces verbose command outputs with concise summaries. The trajectory log, by contrast, preserves the exact delivered inputs and operational decisions required by the system’s replay contract. For a truncated observation, the log retains the exact byte slice exposed to the model rather than the full, unpruned output stream emitted by the tool. State reconstruction reproduces only what was durably captured. A compacted summary replays as a summary, and a logged hash of a payload can verify those bytes only while the stored payload itself survives (section 11.8.2 develops this separation of digests from bytes).



If a log entry records only that a tool was called without capturing the worker lease, control epoch, or reservation bound, a replacement worker cannot tell whether a late callback belongs to an invalidated turn or how much budget remains locked. An event log supports reliable recovery only when its schema captures the operational metadata that succeeding workers need to answer those questions. Table 1 groups these event families by their roles during reconstruction. These schemas define logical event boundaries rather than requiring isolated physical storage writes for every individual field. For example, a high-throughput runtime can coalesce authorization checks, budget reservations, and tool dispatch intents into a single batched write transaction, provided the deterministic reducer preserves their causal dependencies. The storage engine must also durably acknowledge the batch before dispatch (the ordering that section 11.3 develops).
Every event envelope contains a trajectory identifier, a unique event identifier, a monotonically increasing sequence_number, schema type and version tags, and tenant or issuer provenance. In addition, the log records the active reducer version alongside the worker lease identity under which appends were accepted. Within this envelope, the sequence_number defines total event ordering, and record_version tracks state machine modifications. The control_epoch is the harness’s control fence, which advances whenever a pause, cancellation, or interruption invalidates in-flight continuations, so an observation stamped with an older epoch cannot advance the current one. A distinct owner_epoch counts grants of trajectory ownership, so that storage can reject appends from a worker whose ownership has passed to another (the fencing mechanism of section 11.5.1). Neither ownership handoffs across workers nor control-epoch increments alter the unique logical identity of an in-flight operation.


↩︎ Epoch fencing, which keeps a stale asynchronous response from advancing the current continuation, is established in Transition guards and the admission check.



Table 1: Trajectory log schema: Event families preserve the control and evidence contract across a crash. The log records observations and decisions, not automatic proof that an external effect settled or a task succeeded.










Event family
Required contents
Reconstruction use




TaskStarted
Task and requester, initial grants and limits, ordinary and finalization deadlines, initial record and workspace references, configuration provenance
Establish the initial scope and accounting contract


ContextBuilt, ModelReplied
Model-call identity, immutable delivered-input manifest and bytes or available references, assembly and request configuration, reply status and payload, raw signals and available provider provenance
Recover what was supplied and observed without resampling the historical invocation


Authorized, BudgetReserved, BudgetSettled
Decision and policy version, invocation or operation identity, reservation bound, actual usage evidence, remaining unresolved liability, protected finalization reserve
Rebuild admission and accounting, not merely a remaining-balance scalar


ToolIntent, ToolResult
Logical operation and transport attempt identities, represented operation and arguments, applicable revision and repeat contract, job handle when known, outcome evidence and observation completeness
Preserve possible dispatch and its evidence; a pending, partial, or timeout result does not establish settlement


ControlChanged, PlanChanged
Control request and issuer, guarded state and grant changes, record and control versions, plan revision and dependencies, observation eligibility, resource and outstanding-obligation owners
Restore the continuation separately from work that remains unresolved


ApprovalRequested, ApprovalResolved
Exact held action and relevant versions, authorized reviewer and decision evidence, expiry, withdrawal or refusal status
Restore the held decision without treating an old approval as current dispatch permission


Compacted, RuntimeInput
Recorded summary and dependencies; clocks, identifiers, policy/configuration inputs, and event-order information captured at the declared replay boundary, where replay substitutes recorded inputs for live ones
Preserve the actual inputs used by context assembly or supervisory decisions


Checkpoint
Exact covered log boundary, compatible record and workspace manifests, required artifact references and integrity information
Select an available base for reconstructing the record and workspace through a later suffix






The software repair worksheet illustrates how these identifiers link distributed lifecycle events. Alongside the workspace snapshot ws_r18, the identifier operation_id=test_r18 designates the logical test suite invocation, while attempt_id=attempt1 tracks the specific network transport attempt. If an asynchronous test executor returns an acknowledgment containing a cluster job identifier such as job_tests_18, that handle correlates future asynchronous callbacks with the original operation. However, a recovering worker can discover this link only if that acknowledgment was durably flushed to the log before the crash. A durable ToolResult may record an active execution state, a timeout, or a completed test report; the reducer interprets these payloads according to their authenticated provenance. If an asynchronous execution finishes after the supervisor has already timed out the enclosing step, the late-arriving ToolResult updates the operation table rather than corrupting an obsolete execution branch.


↩︎ The observation-eligibility protocol that routes late results to the operation table rather than the active turn is established in Late results and observation eligibility.
Capturing model context requires equal diligence regarding immutability. The manifest in ContextBuilt must record the exact tokenized payload or byte stream delivered over the wire, rather than mutable file system paths or external URLs that could mutate before recovery occurs. The log must also capture available inference engine provenance (model checkpoints, serving system versions, and decoding configurations), recording any gaps because hosted model identifiers frequently hide upstream weight updates or inference engine modifications. When execution resumes, the replacement worker can assemble an updated prompt context from recent evidence while preserving the historical invocation records exactly as delivered.
Defining an event schema specifies what state reconstruction requires, but schema definitions alone cannot guarantee that writes reach disk before an agent issues network requests. If a runtime persists a model completion but crashes before flushing the subsequent tool intent, the recovering worker cannot determine whether an external tool call was dispatched, risking duplicate side effects. To resolve this vulnerability, the runtime must enforce strict write-ahead ordering between logging an operational intent and releasing its network dispatch.




In the crash worksheet, the repair worker’s next step is to submit test_r18 against workspace ws_r18. If the harness dispatches that test request across the network and crashes before the ToolIntent record reaches durable storage, a replacement worker folding the surviving log recovers a plan that still says “run the test.” Meanwhile the original job is already executing on the remote cluster and accruing charges. Recording only the eventual result leaves that blind spot open on every call. To prevent duplicate runs and untracked financial liability, the runtime must commit the admitted request and its reservation to persistent storage before that request ever leaves its control.
Recording the admitted request durably before dispatching it is classical write-ahead logging applied to trajectory dispatch. A durable history ensures that recovery can identify every external operation that may have begun, even if network partitions or crashes prevent the worker from ever receiving the reply. Under the runtime’s declared failure model, an external mutation that occurs without a recoverable record of intent is a phantom effect. Eliminating phantom effects requires two guarantees, strict write-ahead ordering in the runtime execution pipeline and a storage substrate that reliably outlives the failures the system claims to tolerate. Together they are the Part IV principle of intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)), whose ordering this section derives (equation 1) and whose storage half it prices.


↪ The database form of write-ahead logging, and why a runtime borrows its ordering but not its control over remote state, is developed in Classical Transaction Background.

Definition 11.2: Durable intent
Durable intent is the immutable record of an admitted operation, capturing its identity, input arguments, a reference to its authorization decision and capability grant, and its budget reservation, acknowledged by storage that survives the declared failure domain before the request is dispatched.

Significance: It converts a crash between dispatch and reply from an untracked phantom effect into an unresolved operation with an explicit owner, at the price of placing one durable acknowledgment on the critical path of every dispatch (table 2).
Distinction: A durable intent records that work may have escaped into the external environment. It does not certify that the remote endpoint committed or executed the work, nor does it mandate that a recovered worker must re-execute it.
Common pitfall: Taking an acknowledgment from storage that shares the failure boundary the design claims to survive, such as writing to a local scratch volume under a system contract that promises resilience against host or volume loss.



The intent references the grant rather than copying a secret into it. A log retained for months and read during replay is the wrong place for a credential, so the secret stays with the credential broker, and a recovered worker obtains a fresh use of it only by passing admission under current ownership.


↩︎ The credential broker, which holds a secret outside the guest and uses it on behalf of an authorized request, is established in Credential brokering.


Suppose the repair worker appends the test_r18 intent with a standard POSIX write() call, observes a successful return, and promptly dispatches the test. The host then suffers an immediate power failure. A successful write() guarantees only that the kernel copied the payload into its page cache; those dirty pages evaporate when the power cuts before writeback to disk. When the replacement worker boots, it finds an empty log, completely unaware that a remote test is already active. A returned write() therefore covers only the first failure domain of section 11.2, a process crash on an intact host, while offering zero protection against host power loss.
This reasoning extends upward through the failure hierarchy. If a worker fails, a replacement process can recover using reattachable block storage, provided that the replacement can mount the disk and read the acknowledged log and artifacts. If the failure domain includes the permanent destruction of the worker’s storage volume, as in cloud environments where spot instances or underlying hardware failures destroy ephemeral disks, the acknowledgment must originate from a storage service outside that volume. Remoteness alone does not satisfy this requirement. An asynchronous replica updated out of band can lag the primary log, leaving the replacement worker with an incomplete history during a failover.
Each step up the failure hierarchy demands a correspondingly stronger persistence barrier. Surviving host power loss requires fsync() or fdatasync(), which returns only after the underlying storage device reports that the data has reached stable media. The two system calls differ in how they handle metadata: fsync() flushes file attributes such as modification timestamps, whereas fdatasync() flushes only the metadata strictly required to read the payload back. For a trajectory log that preallocates its disk files, using fdatasync() eliminates an unneeded disk seek and metadata write per barrier. Even with these system calls, subtle failure modes remain.2 If a drive contains a volatile write cache, it must honor the disk flush command before an acknowledgment truly covers power loss. Alternatively, the write must specify Force Unit Access (a per-write flag that bypasses the drive cache entirely). Even a verified local barrier, however, cannot survive the catastrophic loss of the physical drive or volume. Surviving permanent volume loss requires a replicated storage engine that returns a success acknowledgment only after a quorum of replicas, distributed across distinct failure domains, have committed the record.3 The worksheet requires two durable copies outside the worker volume before dispatch. This chosen placement policy is stronger than the single-volume-loss requirement alone; table 2 lists acknowledgments that satisfy the stated contracts.

A trajectory log inherits the same exposure, so its durability claim should be checked by injecting crashes between every write and barrier, not inferred from the calls it makes.

The implementation must define precisely which failure modes its persistence layer covers, how storage errors surface to the application, and how a replacement worker discovers the complete authoritative history. Underlying storage engines provide the mechanical primitives, but the systems architect must establish the durability contract. When an acknowledgment fails or times out with an ambiguous status, the runtime must hold dispatch and resolve the append according to the storage contract. Resolution means re-reading the authoritative log. If the intent is present, the attempt is admitted but still unsent, so a pause or a failed recheck can still withhold it. If a complete authoritative prefix lacks it, the worker appends it again under the same event identity, which storage deduplicates if the first append did land. Holding back a dispatch during a storage outage may temporarily stall progress, but dispatching before confirmation permanently destroys the evidence required to govern in-flight work after a crash.


↪ Why a durability claim must name both its acknowledgment and the failures it survives, and how durability differs from atomicity and isolation, is developed in Guarantee Boundaries.



If a worker validates a proposal and reserves budget in memory (Transition guards and the admission check) but dispatches the network call before the storage acknowledgment returns, a crash in that gap leaves an untracked phantom effect. Durable execution closes that window by inserting an acknowledged intent write between admission and network release. For an attempt that proceeds to dispatch and later produces an observation, the ordering is
\[
\ValidatedProposalEvent \prec \AdmissionDecisionEvent \prec \IntentAcknowledgmentEvent \prec \ExternalDispatchAction \prec \EvidenceRecordEvent.
\tag{1}\]
In equation 1, \(\ValidatedProposalEvent\) is the validated complete proposal, \(\AdmissionDecisionEvent\) is the admitted authorization and reservation decision, and \(\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\) acknowledges its recoverable ToolIntent and required preceding records under the declared failure domain. The action \(\ExternalDispatchAction\) is dispatch, not endpoint completion. The event \(\EvidenceRecordEvent\) is the later durable recording of received evidence, whose status may still be pending, partial, or unknown. The ordering constrains the events that occur, though an attempt can stop before dispatch or never produce evidence. Its payoff is that the position of a crash in this sequence determines what recovery may conclude (figure 2). A crash before the worker receives \(\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\) means the attempt was never dispatched, though an intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost in transit. Recovery must inspect the complete authoritative prefix to determine whether that intent survived. Once \(\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\) is durable, a crash at any point before adequate outcome evidence \(\EvidenceRecordEvent\) becomes durable leaves an in-doubt action, an admitted operation whose outcome the surviving evidence cannot settle. Because releasing the network request \(\ExternalDispatchAction\) does not write a separate log record, the surviving log looks identical whether the worker crashed just before sending the packet, while the request was in flight, or after recording a pending or timeout observation. That window is the tool layer’s uncertain outcome (definition \(\ref{dfn-uncertain-outcome}\)) seen from the recovery side, and it is what the fold of section 11.2.1 marked unresolved. Only recorded, correlated evidence establishes an outcome.

Where a crash falls determines the recovery state of table 3. Before the worker receives the acknowledgment, dispatch is withheld, but the intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. An absent intent establishes non-dispatch only when the authoritative prefix is complete. Between the acknowledgment and adequate recorded evidence, including a crash before dispatch, the operation is in doubt; a pending or timeout observation leaves it there. After correlated outcome evidence is recorded, the outcome is established within the endpoint’s contract.



In the crash worksheet, the intent names operation_id=test_r18, attempt_id=attempt1, the immutable ws_r18 input, the selected check, and the endpoint’s repeat contract. It references the applicable Authorized and BudgetReserved decisions, together with the requester and task bindings, control_epoch, and owner_epoch under which they were made. The recoverable prefix must reconstruct the admitted reservation itself, rather than merely a remaining balance.
Admission and control stay coordinated while the barrier is pending. An operator pause or an administrative change in authority can still intercept and withhold an admitted but unsent request, because logging a durable intent records permission to dispatch rather than an irrevocable obligation to execute. The harness’s dispatch-time recheck, the last gate before the request leaves, re-evaluates the admitted attempt against current control state without reserving a second batch of budget. If the release mechanism already dispatched the request across the network, subsequent control actions must treat the request as sent. Conversely, a withheld request keeps its entry in the operation table and its reserved budget until verified evidence confirms that no remote side effects or financial liabilities remain.

Foundation model invocations require identical rigor regarding identity and liability. Token generation streams over network sockets, and an interrupted invocation can incur charges on the provider’s bill even if a worker crash prevents the client from ever logging the output. The same ordering therefore covers model calls. The ContextBuilt record and the invocation’s BudgetReserved decision become durable before the request leaves, so a crash mid-stream leaves a logged invocation with no ModelReplied. Recovery treats that invocation as in doubt only for its charge, which it settles from the provider’s usage evidence. The lost reply cannot be reconstructed by replaying the prompt, because stochastic sampling produces a different completion, so recovery discards any partial stream and never replays the call. Any retry is a separately admitted invocation, requiring a fresh invocation identity, validated request and context, current admission checks, and a durable budget reservation before dispatch.

An asynchronously updated read replica cannot satisfy this rule, because the replica cannot distinguish between an operation that was never dispatched and an intent whose log record has not yet arrived across the network. In the crash worksheet scenario, the dispatched test may have failed to reach the service, may still be executing on a remote runner, or may have finished just before the worker crashed. If the executor’s reply accepting the job was never logged, its job handle, job_tests_18, is lost with the worker as well. The in-doubt status reflects runtime uncertainty rather than external failure, and resolving it is a question about the endpoint. Operation identity and endpoint contracts details the endpoint requirements needed to execute a safe repeat: strict identity scoping, immutable payload binding, retention of prior execution results, handling of concurrent in-flight requests, and coordination between state mutations and returned values. A client-provided idempotency key protects only those endpoints that implement these semantics. Probing an endpoint by resource name provides much weaker guarantees, as a matching name might belong to an unrelated operation, while an absent resource could indicate that a delayed initial request is still in transit. For an in-doubt action, durable execution therefore applies settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)) unchanged. The log supplies the operation identity and its evidence, and only the endpoint’s contract or positive outcome evidence licenses another attempt.
