Systems insight: A year of full recovery and replay retention adds under 1 percent to \(\AttemptCost\) in equation 1.2, and the workspace snapshot, not the log, is 93 percent of the bytes. The bill grows linearly with retention months and bytes per turn, so the effective lever is sharing workspace bases by content address across trajectories of the same repository; truncating the log saves almost nothing. Set retention by the recovery and replay promise, because pruning a required artifact forfeits a reconstruction claim to save 0.05 percent of an attempt.





Keeping every event from the start of a trajectory grows the log without bound, even after a published checkpoint at sequence \(\CheckpointLogPosition\) has already captured record_R_ckpt and workspace ws_r18. Yet deleting that earlier prefix while the checkpoint is still staging, or while an audit replay still depends on it, breaks the runtime’s promises. Log compaction reclaims storage capacity safely by retiring the older prefix once a newer published checkpoint preserves the active state and all unresolved operations required by the current recovery contract. The retained suffix of subsequent events must connect seamlessly to the checkpoint’s exact committed sequence boundary. Before pruning any log records or referenced artifacts, the storage layer must verify both conditions: the replacement checkpoint and its dependencies are durable across the declared failure domain, and no active historical replay, auditing, or compliance obligation still depends on the older prefix.
Compaction preserves current recovery while deliberately shortening the historical replay horizon. Downstream systems cannot substitute a later agent context for an earlier one once the original inputs have expired. Similarly, squashing incremental workspace deltas into a single snapshot preserves the latest workspace tree while shedding intermediate revisions. A compaction policy must therefore explicitly define the surviving replay interval. An uncompacted event history grows monotonically with every turn, regardless of how tightly the agent manages its prompt token budget.
Systems engineers must not confuse log compaction with context compaction. Context compaction operates on prompt token budgets: when conversational history approaches model context limits, the runtime condenses prior turns and commits a Compacted event to the log. This event records the exact summary text delivered to subsequent model calls, preserving deterministic replay for future turns. The underlying historical events and payloads that generated the summary remain governed by their own retention policies rather than vanishing when the context window shrinks. Diagnostic telemetry can follow aggressive downsampling or retention rules; in contrast, recovery-critical events and payloads must remain bit-for-bit complete throughout their promised operational lifetime.


↪ Sampling and retention policies for diagnostic traces are developed in Trace Retention and Privacy.



A storage layer can quietly undermine durable execution if its ingestion mechanics treat every duplicate event key as a harmless network retry. When a worker retries a log append after a lost storage acknowledgment, the retried record carries the exact same envelope and payload bytes as the first attempt. If a bug or an unfenced zombie worker instead submits a timeout ToolResult for test_r18 under an event identity or sequence number that the store already holds with verified success evidence, the two writes share a key while disagreeing on what happened. A plain key-uniqueness constraint (such as an ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING clause) cannot tell those two cases apart, so it keeps the stored record and silently hides the conflicting write. Ingestion must instead perform semantic deduplication, comparing the immutable envelope and payload against the stored record under a declared canonical encoding. An identical retry returns an acknowledgment for the existing record. A conflicting payload under the same identity signals an integrity violation or a split-brain failure (two workers both acting as owner), not an idempotent duplicate, so the store must raise an error or record a distinct conflict event that the operation table evaluates. Deduplicating an event insertion, moreover, never deduplicates an external side effect that has already occurred.
The same discipline governs how the engine manages capacity and replication. When disk saturation or transient faults block new commits, the runtime must apply backpressure and stall the trajectory rather than proceed speculatively. A bounded circular buffer may overwrite an older entry only after every recovery and replay contract has released it. Moving older logs to a cheaper cold tier obeys the same completeness rule: the local copy can be retired only after every referenced payload body, not merely its index entry, has arrived and been verified at the destination. Replication across nodes must preserve both prefix completeness and ownership provenance. A follower that receives records out of order may stage them in memory, but it can advertise a recoverable prefix only up to its first sequence gap. Fresh appends must validate the active lease and fencing token to block zombie writes, whereas replicated historical events keep their original worker provenance and timestamps rather than taking on the credentials of the replicating node.
At the physical layer, an append-only event model can sit on any storage engine that guarantees deterministic ordering. Key-value stores built on log-structured merge trees (LSM trees) (O’Neil et al. 1996), for example, index immutable events under composite trajectory and sequence keys. In an LSM tree, storage-level compaction periodically merges the tree’s sorted on-disk files (sorted string tables) to reclaim space and speed reads. Despite the shared name, it is purely physical. It reorganizes bytes without changing the logical sequence of events, so unlike log compaction it never retires evidence. Overwriting an existing event with a newer state representation, by contrast, is a destructive application-level mutation, permissible only when a retention contract authorizes discarding the older evidence, because the order of observations and decisions is the agent’s causal chain.
Each cost derived earlier in the chapter therefore becomes a concrete requirement when selecting or configuring the storage engine. On the write path, the durable-acknowledgment boundary (local disk, quorum fsync, or multi-region replication) sets both the dispatch latency floor of table 2 and the batch wait of equation 2. The engine’s internal write amplification multiplies the snapshot bytes that equation 3 already counts. Its blob-store integration determines whether the payload-before-reference ordering of section 11.8.2 can be enforced in one place. On the recovery path, sequential read throughput governs the suffix read time \(\CheckpointSuffixReadTime\) in equation 7, while atomic compare-and-set support on the owner_epoch determines whether the log itself can reject a stale owner’s appends without an external lock hop.
A single relational or key-value store suffices for modest deployments. At higher throughput, architectures often split into an online recovery store for low-latency point lookups by trajectory and an offline analytical store for columnar scans over historical replays. The analytical copy may lag the primary only while a durable, synchronized copy already satisfies the recovery contract within the declared failure domain, and every additional copy needs its own prefix synchronization, completeness verification, and retention policy.

Checkpoint 11.4: Retention is a recovery promise

Missing dependency: The checkpoint manifest and suffix survive, but ws_r18 is gone. Which reconstruction claim is no longer supported, and why does its digest not repair the loss?
Pruning boundary: A new checkpoint supports current recovery. What else must be checked before deleting the older prefix, and which historical replay promises might be lost?
Replication window: A local intent is acknowledged and its tool request dispatched before the remote copy arrives. Which declared failure domain would make that ordering insufficient?
Conflicting retry: An incoming event has an existing sequence number but different result content. Why must ingestion reject the conflict rather than silently accept the duplicate key?



Retention completes the reconstruction contract by guaranteeing that committed evidence and required artifacts remain accessible after a failure. A storage engine faithfully preserves recorded uncertainties, but determining whether an external operation actually succeeded or produced correct side effects requires active reconciliation. Resolving in-flight ambiguities and reconciling orphan operations belong to effect-recovery policy, not to the storage engine.




Building durable agentic systems demands clarity about what persistent state actually guarantees. The most consequential engineering mistakes confuse a surviving record with evidence it cannot provide, or expend heavy recovery effort where structured logging has already eliminated the need.

Fallacy: Saving the final context window is enough to audit or recover a trajectory.
A model’s final context window represents only the transient view passed to the last inference call, filtered through compaction policies and bounded observation budgets. It omits the operational decision history: which candidate proposals were admitted, which intents became durable, and which raw tool observations arrived and were subsequently summarized away. For example, if a tool returns an exposed credential at turn 7 and a compaction pass replaces that observation with an abstract summary at turn 12, the final context retains no trace of the leak. Comprehensive auditing and reliable crash recovery require the append-only event sequence defined in table 1. From an authoritative log with the required retained payloads, the execution engine can deterministically rebuild each captured past context window, whereas a surviving context window lacks the operational history needed to reconstruct the log.


Pitfall: Checkpointing after every turn to be safe.
Naively snapshotting full agent state after every turn introduces severe latency overhead for minimal operational gain. When turn-by-turn events and workspace mutations are already appended to a durable log, taking a full checkpoint only reduces replay time during recovery, yet it forces execution to pause on every step. In the crash trace of notebook 11.1, checkpointing after each of the 100 turns spends 52 s in cumulative capture and recovery time, compared to 6 s for a 25-turn stride. Engineers should tune this cadence with the logged balance of equation 5, grounding the calculation in the per-turn log reconstruction cost rather than the much slower runtime of live re-execution.


Fallacy: Rerunning the model at temperature zero reproduces a trajectory.
Greedy decoding fixes only the argmax token-selection rule for a given logit distribution, and the serving path that computes those logits is not numerically deterministic (Repetition and replay). Because autoregressive generation conditions every token on all preceding tokens, a single flipped token early in execution steers the entire subsequent trajectory into a different subspace.
Across multi-step agent horizons, trajectory reproduction compounds multiplicatively (equation 1.1). Even under the optimistic assumption that individual greedy calls reproduce their recorded outputs 99 percent of the time, a 30-turn trajectory matches its recording end to end only 74 percent of the time. That estimate ignores external non-determinism such as shifting system clocks, generated identifiers, and mutating external environments. Rerunning an agent prompt creates an entirely new execution trajectory that generates fresh side effects; reliable reproduction requires replaying the exact model completions and tool results recorded in the log.


Pitfall: Using an incomplete replica to conclude that a call was never sent.
In distributed systems, the absence of an event record in a replica does not prove that an action never took place. When recovery logic evaluates whether to re-dispatch an unconfirmed operation after a crash, inspecting an asynchronous read replica or diagnostic log can lead to duplicate side effects. If replication lag delays the arrival of an acknowledged intent, recovery logic reading that replica might incorrectly assume the request was never transmitted, even though the crashed worker had already dispatched the RPC to an external service. Re-dispatching on that false assumption duplicates external mutations. Recovery engines must verify prefix completeness directly against the authoritative, strongly consistent store before treating the absence of an intent as evidence of non-dispatch.


Fallacy: A durable intent, or a newer ownership epoch, makes an unresolved operation safe to settle or repeat.
Writing an intent record before dispatch guarantees that an operation is tracked, but it does not resolve the state of an in-flight network request. When an agent crashes with an operation marked in-flight, a missing response or recorded timeout leaves the physical outcome ambiguous. The crash might have occurred before the packet left the network interface, or after the remote service processed the mutation but before the acknowledgment arrived. Similarly, advancing an ownership epoch fences zombie workers from committing further updates to internal databases, but an epoch token cannot retroactively cancel a request already delivered to an external endpoint. Resolving an unconfirmed operation requires positive evidence obtained through the remote service’s inquiry API, and repeating it requires the endpoint’s idempotency contract. Settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)) applies after a crash exactly as it does after a timeout.


Pitfall: Resuming a recovered trajectory on whichever server is free.
Reconstructing an agent’s memory by folding an event log requires minimal CPU time and consumes no model tokens. Teams often make the mistake of budgeting recovery purely around log deserialization, scheduling the resumed agent on whichever inference node happens to report idle capacity. However, moving to a server without compatible cached state discards KV-cache locality. When the resumed agent issues its next model call, the target accelerator must recompute the attention state across the entire reconstructed context window. For a 32,768-token context on the reference model and accelerator, this cold prefill phase alone imposes a latency floor of roughly 2.3 s, even before accounting for network queueing delays. Prefix-aware dispatch compares the avoided prefill work against queueing, transfer delay, and capacity at eligible workers (equation 7), while preserving the exact prefix during prompt assembly.




Durable execution enforces a strict separation between what an agent runtime can verify locally and what actually transpires across external network boundaries. A runtime knows its own decisions, the dispatches it initiated, and the observations it received, provided each event reached storage provisioned to survive the declared failure domain before any dependent action occurred. What the runtime cannot deduce from internal logs alone is whether a dispatched request that yielded no response took effect in the outside world. Every mechanism examined in this chapter maintains this boundary. Durability must always be stated relative to a specific, named failure domain. Event log reconstruction replaces expensive model re-execution across recorded history. Ambiguous external outcomes remain explicitly assigned to an owner rather than resolved through speculative retries or uncoordinated model invocations. Providing these guarantees incurs concrete, quantifiable systems costs: a write acknowledgment per external dispatch, a brief coordination pause during checkpointing, a prompt prefill during cold resume, and about 1.5 cents per trajectory for a year of retention. Each overhead can be measured, budgeted, and amortized rather than avoided, and table 7 summarizes the governing relations that enforce dispatch ordering and balance checkpoint frequency against resume latency.

Key Takeaways: Preserve the evidence needed to continue

The event log, rather than the LLM context window, serves as the authoritative recovery record: A deterministic reducer folds recorded decisions, delivered inputs, and resource reservations back into the trajectory’s control state. In the event of a crash, recovery incurs the modest CPU cost of local log reconstruction rather than invoking redundant, nondeterministic model turns. The prompt context is merely a transient view assembled from this underlying history, and cannot reconstruct past state on its own.
Durability is meaningful only relative to a declared failure domain: An acknowledgment guarantees persistence only against the specific faults its underlying storage tier is provisioned to survive. Because the runtime must hold external dispatch until the intent is acknowledged, the write latency of that storage layer establishes the performance floor for every dispatch. An absent intent record proves that no dispatch took place only when the surviving log history can be verified as complete.
Fine-grained event logging shifts the checkpoint optimum: Classical checkpoint cadence balances capture overhead against lost execution time. Because replaying a deterministic event log is orders of magnitude cheaper than invoking new model calls, logging each turn lengthens the optimal checkpoint stride by the square root of the re-execution-to-reconstruction cost ratio. In the worked trace, the stride grows by a factor of 14.1×. Because the cost curve is broad and flat around this minimum, choosing a stride within a factor of 2 raises the cadence-dependent overhead by at most 25 percent.
Resuming an agent requires acquiring authorization rather than merely restoring memory: Reconstructed state explains why past decisions occurred, but the ownership lease, the fencing epoch, remaining token allowances, and human approvals govern subsequent actions. Any in-doubt external side effects and financial liabilities transfer intact to the new worker. A worker retaining compatible KV state avoids prefix recomputation, but the placement decision also depends on queueing, transfer delay, and capacity.
Deterministic replay serves a different diagnostic purpose than a live rerun: In regression replay, the test harness feeds recorded inputs back into the agent logic with live tool execution disabled, isolating the exact state boundary where behavior diverges. Conversely, re-running an agent against live models generates an entirely new trajectory; because model sampling and external environments drift, divergences during a rerun cannot isolate where the original execution went wrong.
Retention policies must reflect operational guarantees rather than raw storage costs: Fast crash recovery, regression replay, and post-incident auditing require different artifacts over distinct operational lifetimes. Long-term object storage is inexpensive. In the worked estimate, retaining every recovery and replay input for a full year costs about 0.7 percent of a single attempt. Eagerly pruning intermediate artifacts saves negligible budget while permanently forfeiting the ability to verify or reconstruct past runs.



The principle of intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)) mandates writing an immutable record to durable storage before any external dispatch leaves the host, with durability calibrated against the failure domain the system claims to tolerate. Checkpoints and retained execution artifacts make this internal state reconstructible, while leaving in-doubt external outcomes explicitly visible to recovery supervisors. This discipline preserves the precise evidence that an automated or human recovery decision requires, while leaving the choice of recovery action to a separate policy that reads it. That separation also delineates the mechanical boundary of invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)). The runtime can guarantee that no admitted effect escapes unrecorded and that no settled effect repeats without an explicit idempotency contract. However, local logs alone cannot determine whether an in-doubt external request succeeded across the network, nor can they judge whether a historically recorded action was semantically correct.



Every mechanism in this chapter answers a question that transaction processing confronted first: how a system that crashes mid-update can determine afterward what work had already escaped. In his foundational 1978 notes on database operating systems, Jim Gray established the write-ahead log as the record from which recovery reconstructs committed work, while introducing the two-phase commit protocol to coordinate atomic updates across autonomous resource managers (Gray 1978). As databases moved into main memory, writing that log to stable storage emerged as the primary throughput bottleneck. DeWitt and colleagues addressed this limitation with group commit, amortizing disk synchronization barriers across concurrent transactions (DeWitt et al. 1984). Mohan and colleagues turned write-ahead logging into a comprehensive recovery discipline with ARIES (Mohan et al. 1992). ARIES established the rule of forcing each log record to stable storage before writing the modified page to disk. It also introduced the principle of repeating history on restart: the recovery manager reconstructs the exact state at the crash before undoing uncommitted changes. Gray and Reuter subsequently synthesized the formal transaction model, logging architectures, and crash recovery into a definitive treatise (Gray and Reuter 1992). Modern storage engines took this logic a step further by elevating the log from an auxiliary recovery file to the primary storage structure. Rosenblum and Ousterhout established this design with the Log-Structured File System (LFS), converting all file modifications into sequential append operations (Rosenblum and Ousterhout 1992). O’Neil, O’Neil, and Weikum later adapted that concept to database indexing with the log-structured merge-tree (LSM-tree) (O’Neil et al. 1996), establishing the append-only storage patterns that modern trajectory stores rely on today.

A parallel lineage originated in high-performance computing and distributed systems, where jobs ran for days across fragile clusters and any node failure risked restarting computations from scratch. Young modeled the trade-off between the overhead of writing state snapshots and the cost of lost work, deriving an optimal checkpoint interval that remains the benchmark formula today (Young 1974). When computations spanned multiple communicating processes, capturing state became a distributed consistency problem. Chandy and Lamport solved this by defining snapshot consistency without freezing system execution (Chandy and Lamport 1985). Building on this foundation, the rollback-recovery literature demonstrated that combining periodic state snapshots with an event log of nondeterministic inputs guarantees deterministic replay, eliminating the need to re-execute expensive computations from the beginning (Elnozahy et al. 2002). Distributed environments also required explicit primitives to coordinate ownership and prevent split-brain execution during failover. Gray and Cheriton introduced time-bounded leases so that a crashed lock holder could not permanently block other workers (Gray and Cheriton 1989). Burrows introduced generation-stamped lock sequencers in Chubby, enabling external resources to reject requests from stale or zombie workers (Burrows 2006). Meanwhile, consensus protocols based on replicated state machines, from Lamport’s Paxos (Lamport 1998) to Ongaro and Ousterhout’s Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout 2014), guaranteed that committed log records survive node crashes as long as a quorum persists. Capturing nondeterministic inputs also became a tool for systems debugging, as time-traveling virtual machines recorded external interrupts and network packets to replay operating system states deterministically backward and forward (King et al. 2005).
Agent runtimes synthesize these two lineages, yet they operate under distinct operational constraints that alter what recovery can promise. In an agent loop that interleaves model reasoning with tool invocations (Yao et al. 2023), the dominant nondeterministic event is the model’s generated output. Because stochastic token sampling and remote model endpoints cannot be assumed to reproduce identical outputs upon re-evaluation, the runtime cannot simply restart the agent loop from the beginning; it must log every generated prompt and completion as an immutable event. External tool execution introduces an even sharper departure from classic transaction processing: external endpoints do not participate in two-phase commit. When an agent invokes a web search, dispatches a payment API request, or modifies an external code repository, there is no prepare phase to hold resources in doubt, nor any global rollback coordinator to undo side effects. Large-scale distributed architectures encountered this same boundary decades earlier. Pat Helland articulated why cross-boundary distributed transactions fail at scale, showing that independent entities must instead communicate through idempotent messages, explicit sequence tokens, and compensating workflows (Helland 2007). Modern durable execution frameworks translated these distributed messaging guarantees directly into programming models: Burckhardt and colleagues provided a formal operational semantics for durable workflows that advance persistent progress without re-executing completed side effects (Burckhardt et al. 2021). In an agent architecture, these concepts become three runtime mechanisms: the durable intent that records planned actions before execution, the in-doubt state machine that reconciles unknown tool outcomes before retry, and the separation of historical trajectory reconstruction from live execution against the external world.

Yao, Shunyu, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, and Yuan Cao. 2023. “ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models.” International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
For further reading, six works trace the lineage from database recovery to modern agent runtimes:

Gray and Reuter (1992) remains the definitive foundation for transaction processing, logging architectures, and crash recovery. Its rigorous analysis of what a commit guarantee actually promises, and across which specific failure domains that promise holds, provides the conceptual model for the failure-domain contracts developed throughout this chapter.
Mohan et al. (1992) delivers the complete specification for write-ahead logging and recovery. Studying ARIES clarifies precisely which consistency guarantees depend on owning the underlying storage pages, a structural guarantee database engines take for granted, but one that agent runtimes forfeit when interacting with external tool endpoints.
Elnozahy et al. (2002) organizes decades of distributed checkpointing and message logging research into a coherent taxonomy. The survey highlights why capturing nondeterministic inputs changes what a checkpoint must record, establishing the theoretical basis for deterministic trajectory replay.
Kleppmann (2016) connects classical principles of event sourcing, log replication, and distributed fencing to the realities of production infrastructure. It bridges distributed systems theory and the practical engineering of a scalable trajectory store.
Helland (2007) explains why large-scale distributed systems abandon atomic transactions across autonomous administrative boundaries in favor of idempotent, uniquely identified messages. Its practical reasoning directly anticipates the in-doubt action lifecycle and settlement-before-retry protocols required by agent runtimes.
Burckhardt et al. (2021) provides a formal operational semantics for durable execution and asynchronous workflow runtimes. It establishes how persistent progress can be mathematically specified and verified, showing how runtimes ensure exactly-once execution semantics across process crashes without manual state machine management.


Gray, Jim, and Andreas Reuter. 1992. Transaction Processing: Concepts and Techniques. Morgan Kaufmann.

Mohan, Chandrasekaran, Don Haderle, Bruce Lindsay, Hamid Pirahesh, and Peter Schwarz. 1992. “ARIES: A Transaction Recovery Method Supporting Fine-Granularity Locking and Partial Rollbacks Using Write-Ahead Logging.” ACM Transactions on Database Systems 17 (1): 94–162. https://doi.org/10.1145/128765.128770.

Kleppmann, Martin. 2016. Designing Data-Intensive Applications: The Big Ideas Behind Reliable, Scalable, and Maintainable Systems. O’Reilly Media.

Helland, Pat. 2007. “Life Beyond Distributed Transactions: An Apostate’s Opinion.” Third Biennial Conference on Innovative Data Systems Research (CIDR).

Burckhardt, Sebastian, Chris Gillum, David Justo, Konstantinos Kallas, Connor McMahon, and Christopher S. Meiklejohn. 2021. “Durable Functions: Semantics for Stateful Serverless.” Proceedings of the ACM on Programming Languages 5 (OOPSLA): 1–27. https://doi.org/10.1145/3485510.



Each problem states its constraints and ends in a decision about what to record, when to checkpoint, or how to resume. Givens are hypothetical problem inputs unless a lighthouse profile supplies them, and none describes a particular store, model, or service.
1. Pricing the durable acknowledgment (Basic). A repair worker makes 40 tool dispatches over 40 turns, and each turn otherwise spends 4 s on model and tool work. Its store offers three acknowledgments: a returned write() after 0.02 ms, a returned fdatasync() after 0.4 ms, and a replicated append that a three-replica store acknowledges once two replicas hold the record durably. Measured from the append, the replicas become durable after 1.5, 2.5, and 6.5 ms, and the 1.5 ms replica keeps its copy on the worker’s own volume. For this problem, the worksheet requires both off-volume replicas to hold durable copies before dispatch.
Give the acknowledgment latency that satisfies each of the first two rows of table 2. Under this additional placement policy, identify the required copies and compute the resulting acknowledgment latency. What fraction of the trajectory’s elapsed time does that acknowledgment add? A colleague proposes ordinary majority commitment using the co-located replica and one off-volume replica. Compute the saving, distinguish the single-volume-loss guarantee from the chosen placement policy, and decide whether adopting that policy change satisfies the stated contract.
2. Write amplification of a growing record (Basic). A repair trajectory runs 400 turns, its checkpointed record grows by 64 KB per turn, and a checkpoint is published every 8 turns.
Use equation 3 to compute the bytes written by full snapshots and by deltas, and their ratio. Restore reads at 200 MB/s, and each delta in a chain adds 20 ms of fetch, validation, and application beyond its bytes. Starting from an empty base, compare the time to restore the state at the final checkpoint from one full snapshot and from the chain of deltas. Which representation suits a trajectory that rarely crashes, and which mechanism bounds its weakness?
3. Checkpointing too often (Basic). A long local analysis step inside a trajectory keeps intermediate state that the log does not capture, so a crash forces its work to be re-executed. Each checkpoint pauses execution for 3 s, including durable publication, and work-losing failures arrive on average every 30 minutes.
Compute \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) and the overhead at the optimum from equation 4. The current policy checkpoints every 10 s. Compute its overhead and the factor by which it exceeds the optimum. A second proposal checkpoints every 200 s to cut pause time. Compute its overhead, decide between the two proposals, and explain from the shape of the overhead curve why the comparison depends on the ratio to \(\OptimalCheckpointInterval\) rather than on the direction of the error.
4. Group commit against a dispatch budget (Intermediate). A harness admits 2,000 intents per second, arriving evenly every 0.5 ms. Its replicated store takes 5 ms per durable flush regardless of batch size. A batch starts its flush as soon as it holds its last intent and the store can accept a flush. The dispatch budget allows at most 8 ms from an intent’s arrival to its acknowledgment.
Without batching, with one flush at a time, what intent rate can the store sustain, and what happens to the queue? Find the smallest batch that keeps up, and use equation 2 to compute the steady-state waits of a batch’s first and last arrivals. Does that policy meet the budget, and how much utilization margin does it leave? The store can instead keep two flushes in flight at once. Recompute the smallest batch, its first arrival’s wait, and the amortized storage work per intent. A teammate suggests acknowledging from the page cache and flushing in the background. Evaluate the suggestion against the design rule that closes section 11.3.
5. What logging buys the cadence (Intermediate). A trajectory’s checkpoint write time is \(\CheckpointWriteTime = 0.8\) s, and crashes arrive at failure rate \(\TurnFailureRate = 0.01\) per completed turn. Reconstructing a logged turn costs \(\TurnReconstructionTime = 0.05\) s, and re-executing an unlogged turn costs \(\TurnReexecutionTime = 12\) s.
Compute \(\CheckpointStride^*\) for a fully logged and a fully unlogged trajectory, and their ratio. Show that the per-turn overhead at the optimum is \(\sqrt{2\,\CheckpointWriteTime\,\TurnFailureRate\,\TurnReconstructionTime}\) and evaluate it for the logged case. An audit then finds that 10 percent of turns write workspace files the log does not capture; in a lost suffix each such turn costs \(\TurnReexecutionTime\) and every other turn costs \(\TurnReconstructionTime\). Compute the effective per-turn cost, the new \(\CheckpointStride^*\), and the overhead of keeping the logged stride. Which investment lowers overhead more, retuning the stride or capturing the missing workspace deltas? Justify the choice with the three overheads.
6. Second lighthouse: mass resume for the support agent (Intermediate). The support agent holds many short sessions at once. Each session’s context is 8,192 tokens, of which 6,144 form a policy prefix shared by every session, and a customer takes about 20 s to read a reply and answer. A serving region fails, and 2,000 open sessions must resume on surviving workers. Per session, acquiring ownership takes 20 ms, reading and validating the checkpoint and suffix 15 ms, and folding 5 ms. There is no workspace to restore, because the customer record stays in its system of record, but 10 percent of sessions hold an in-doubt refund whose authorized lookup takes 150 ms. One request prefills at 20,000 tokens/s, and the surviving pool prefills 400,000 tokens/s in aggregate. The failover may add at most 1 s to any customer’s next reply.
Use serial stage execution for the per-session estimate. Apply equation 7 to compute \(\ResumeTime\), excluding queueing, for a clean session and for one with an in-doubt refund, first with a cold prefill and then with the shared prefix already resident on every surviving worker. If every session resumes eagerly with a cold prefill, how long does the pool take to drain the prefill work, and with the shared prefix resident? Treat customers’ next messages as arriving evenly over the following 20 s. Propose a resume policy that meets the 1 s bound, compute its prefill load as a fraction of the pool, and state what it does with the in-doubt refunds. Contrast the binding term with the one that governs the repair trajectory’s resume.
7. Second lighthouse: retention for the research agent (Intermediate). The research agent runs 20 turns and fetches 100 external pages. Per turn it logs 4 KB of event envelopes and 40 KB of delivered, bounded observations. Each fetched page averages 300 KB raw, and the model receives only the bounded observation. Storage costs $0.023 per GB-month, the replay promise is 12 months, and one attempt costs $1.50.
Compute a year’s retention cost for the recovery and replay inputs and for the raw pages, each as a share of the attempt cost. An investigator later asks which text the model received before producing a suspicious citation. Decide whether folding the recorded projection, a harness regression replay, or a fresh rerun of the trajectory establishes the delivered input. Name the earliest boundary to compare and the retained bytes it needs, and explain why neither the raw pages nor the rerun can settle it. State what that evidence cannot establish about the text’s causal influence, and what a controlled new branch would add. Propose retention lifetimes that keep raw pages for 1 month under a diagnostic policy, and compute the annual storage bill for one million trajectories under full retention and under the proposed policy. Explain how the dominant bytes, and the reason for retaining them, differ from the repair trajectory’s in notebook 11.2.
8. An asynchronous replica behind an irreversible actor (Advanced). A fleet of 50 remediation workers each dispatch approved changes at 2 per hour, at random times, after an approval wait of about 15 minutes. Each worker acknowledges intents with a local fdatasync() and ships them to a remote store that lags by 200 ms. After a failure, the replacement reads the remote store and dispatches every approved proposal that lacks an intent. Each worker suffers 2 volume-losing failures per year, and a duplicated change costs $12,000 in expected damage. The alternative acknowledges from a quorum outside the worker’s volume at 6.5 ms per dispatch.
Identify the rules of section 11.3 that the recovery procedure violates, and state the recovery state that operations in the lag window should occupy instead. Treating dispatches as a Poisson process, compute the probability that a failure follows within 200 ms of at least one dispatch, the expected number of such failures per year across the fleet, and the expected annual loss if each produces a duplicate change. Repeat for a network partition that stretches the lag to 60 s. Compute the latency the quorum alternative adds per worker per day, and per change as a fraction of the approval wait. Redesign the acknowledgment and recovery path, and defend why neither acknowledgment latency nor the small expected loss at 200 ms is the right quantity to optimize for this lighthouse.
9. Consolidating a delta chain under a resume deadline (Advanced). A repair trajectory publishes an incremental checkpoint at every stride and, every \(\ConsolidationStride\) checkpoints, consolidates the chain by writing and publishing a new base, which pauses execution for 1.0 s. The chain therefore holds between 1 and \(\ConsolidationStride\) deltas. A restore reads the base in 0.2 s and spends 0.04 s on each delta in the chain. The probability that a restore is needed between two consecutive checkpoints is 0.005.
Write the expected overhead per checkpoint \(\ConsolidationOverheadTime(\ConsolidationStride)\) as a consolidation term plus an expected restore term, taking the chain length at a crash to average \(\ConsolidationStride/2\). Find \(\ConsolidationStride^*\) and \(\ConsolidationOverheadTime(\ConsolidationStride^*)\) by the method of theorem 11.1, and compute the worst-case restore time at \(\ConsolidationStride^*\). Resume now must finish restoring within 2 s in the worst case. Find the largest admissible \(\ConsolidationStride\) and the overhead the deadline costs relative to \(\ConsolidationOverheadTime(\ConsolidationStride^*)\), and check the ratio of the \(\ConsolidationStride\)-dependent terms against the flat-minimum form \((\OptimumMissFactor + 1/\OptimumMissFactor)/2\). When a consolidation publishes a new base, which older deltas and bases may compaction delete, and what must be verified first?

What’s Next: From reconstructing the record to repairing effectsIf the log faithfully records every intent and observation, why can a recovered trajectory still leave the world half changed? Reconstruction restores what the runtime decided and saw, but it cannot settle a test_r18 job whose outcome is still unknown, decide whether revising candidate r18 is worth another attempt, or tear down an environment that a lost reply left running and billing. Failure Recovery turns the recorded evidence and unresolved obligations into recovery policy: retries that an endpoint’s repeat contract permits, bounded forward repair, compensations registered before the effects they undo, and escalation to an operator, together with watchdogs that stop trajectories which fail without raising any error.

title: 11 Durable Execution
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why must an agent write down what it is about to do before it does it?
Real agent tasks, such as migrating an enterprise database or debugging a distributed codebase, run for minutes, hours, or days, long enough that process restarts, node preemptions, and rolling updates stop being rare events and become part of the workload. The harness that supervises such a task keeps its control record in the memory of a single worker, and the model’s context holds only a curated transcript, so one crash erases the admitted operations, held reservations, and pending approvals that tell a successor what may happen next. Restarting from the original prompt is worse than slow, because it resamples a stochastic model and may repeat an external effect, such as a deployment or a payment, that has already escaped. Durable execution answers with an ordering discipline inherited from transaction processing. The runtime appends every decision and observation to a log that outlives the worker, makes each intended action durable before dispatching it, and rebuilds control state by folding that history rather than by asking the model again. The log still cannot report what happened to a request whose reply never arrived, and keeping that ambiguity visible instead of guessing it away is what lets state survive a long horizon without corrupting the world the agent acts on.

Learning Objectives

Construct a trajectory log whose fold rebuilds control state without treating recorded claims as world truth
Apply intent-before-dispatch ordering under a declared failure domain, price its acknowledgment, and classify what each crash position lets recovery conclude
Select a checkpoint representation and cadence from write volume, capture pause, and reconstruction cost
Design a resume policy that reconciles outstanding obligations under current ownership within a stage-by-stage latency budget
Distinguish time-travel replay of a recorded projection, harness regression replay, and counterfactual branches by the conclusion each supports
Diagnose the first divergence between two executions from captured inputs, stating what the evidence cannot establish
Design retention policies that keep the bytes each declared recovery, replay, and diagnostic promise requires

title: 11 Durable Execution
text:
Horizon stretches state past one worker’s life, so continuation needs a durable record.
Consider a software repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) that has admitted and dispatched an integration test against ws_r18, a fixed workspace snapshot of candidate patch r18. Before the test runner reports a result, the worker process crashes, or the host suffers a spot preemption (the sudden reclamation of an ephemeral cloud node). A replacement worker cannot simply re-invoke the model with the original prompt. Starting over discards context: the pending test invocation, the active capability tokens and resource reservations, any pause state acknowledged by an operator, and any evidence indicating whether the remote executor accepted, completed, or failed the job. Worse, the original test suite may still be executing on a remote cluster, incurring financial charges and modifying sandbox state, while a newly launched model redundantly dispatches a conflicting command. This crash, with its dispatched but unreported test, is the chapter’s running worksheet, and each section asks what the surviving record says about it.
The agent harness already tracks most of what the replacement worker requires. Its live trajectory record separates pending execution continuations from outstanding external obligations, while its admission checks govern which actions may cross the runtime boundary. In a naive implementation, however, both structures reside exclusively in volatile host memory and vanish the instant the worker fails. The model’s context window cannot substitute for this operational state. A large language model (LLM) context contains only an episodic transcript shaped by bounded observation windows and prompt compaction; it contains no record of in-flight network sockets, admitted capability tokens, or active cloud billing meters. As the execution horizon expands across dozens of turns and long-running external tasks, worker crashes, node preemptions, and rolling updates shift from rare anomalies to operational certainties.


↩︎ The trajectory record that holds pending continuations and outstanding obligations is established in The Trajectory Record.
Surviving mid-trajectory failures requires durable history: an append-only, ordered log of every decision, admitted action, and received observation. With this durable log, a replacement worker can deterministically reconstruct the agent’s state, reconcile side effects that already reached external systems, and safely resume execution under valid authority. That capability names the chapter’s subject. A trajectory has durable execution when a different worker, after any failure the runtime declares it tolerates, can reconstruct the trajectory’s control state and outstanding obligations from surviving records and continue it without losing an effect that already escaped or repeating one unsafely. One ordering rule makes that possible. Under write-ahead durability, the record of an intended action becomes durable before the action is dispatched over the network. The rule is the runtime’s mechanical answer to the horizon and state exposures, a bound placed below the model that no prompt can supply. It carries measurable costs in acknowledgment latency on every dispatch, capture pauses at checkpoints, and reconstruction time on recovery.
The chapter builds the durable runtime in the order a crash demands it. First, the trajectory log (section 11.2) defines the record from which a clean worker rebuilds control state, and durable intent before dispatch (section 11.3) orders that record against external effects while pricing the acknowledgment each failure domain requires. Folding an unbounded log and reconstructing mutated files from scratch would grow too slow over long runs, so checkpoints (section 11.4) bind the control record to workspace snapshots at regular strides. The resume protocol (section 11.5) then turns that reconstructed state into an authorized continuation under a new owner. The same durable records then serve offline debugging. Replay (section 11.6) inspects or tests history without new model calls, divergence localization (section 11.7) finds the earliest boundary where two executions disagree, and retention (section 11.8) decides which of these recovery and replay promises the stored bytes can still keep. Each mechanism answers the central question of the worksheet crash by establishing what the surviving record proves and what ambiguity remains unresolved.

title: 11 Durable Execution
text:
A replacement worker can rebuild the crashed trajectory only from what the failed worker wrote somewhere that outlived it, so the first design question is what outliving it means. If the worker host and its attached disk are destroyed together mid-turn, a replacement on an independent machine can resume only if the acknowledged history was already replicated to independent storage. Durability is therefore meaningful only relative to an explicit fault model that names which failures the stored history must survive. Systems engineers call this boundary a failure domain, the set of faults across which a persistence guarantee holds. Three tiers of increasing severity recur: a process crash that leaves host storage intact, replacement of the worker node while a shared network-attached volume survives, and permanent loss of that storage tier. Each tier demands stronger replication and wider physical fault isolation, and section 11.3.1 prices the acknowledgment each one requires. The crash worksheet targets the strongest tier, in which the acknowledged event history and every artifact required for recovery survive the simultaneous destruction of the worker host and its attached disk. Every durability claim in this chapter is made relative to that contract.


Surviving the failure domain solves where the bytes live, but it leaves open what those bytes must record so the replacement worker never has to ask the model what happened before the crash. Re-prompting the model from its last visible message cannot reconstruct past control state, because stochastic sampling and a changed external environment steer the trajectory down a different path. Instead, the runtime decouples execution state from process lifetime by recording an append-only, chronological history of every decision and observation across the trajectory.

Definition 11.1: Trajectory log
Trajectory log is the append-only, ordered sequence of typed events (including delivered model prompts, returned completions, resource authorizations, control transitions, and observed tool outcomes) from which a deterministic reducer reconstructs an agent trajectory’s control state.

Significance: Recovery folds recorded decisions sequentially rather than re-executing completed turns. A crash late in a long trajectory therefore costs only deterministic replay time. It avoids fresh model invocations, which would re-expose the system to the compounding error rates of equation 1.1 and accumulate redundant token charges against the task attempt budget in equation 1.2.
Distinction: The trajectory record (definition \(\ref{dfn-trajectory-record}\)) is the live in-memory projection that governs the immediate next decision. The trajectory log is the immutable, append-only history from which that record is derived. The context window is the transient, curated token sequence supplied to the model.
Common pitfall: Recording only tool results while omitting operation dispatches. If an admitted tool call crashes mid-execution or drops its network response, the absence of an intent record leaves the recovery worker unaware that an external side effect may already be in flight.



Formally, the log is a sequence
\[\LoggedEventPrefix = [\LoggedEvent_1, \LoggedEvent_2, \dots, \LoggedEvent_j]\]
When an agent refines an earlier hypothesis or encounters an unexpected tool error, it appends fresh evidence to the tail of the log rather than mutating historical records in place.1 The active trajectory record represents an accumulated projection over this append-only stream. Starting from a base state \(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0\), a deterministic reducer applies each recorded event sequentially:
1 Append-Only Log as Primary Record: Rosenblum and Ousterhout’s log-structured file system treated the sequential log as the primary on-disk data structure, boosting write throughput and simplifying crash recovery (Rosenblum and Ousterhout 1992). A trajectory log inherits these exact advantages: append operations never overwrite historical evidence required by future recovery passes, so a recovering worker can reconstruct state by streaming an ordered log rather than untangling conflicting in-place updates. 
Rosenblum, Mendel, and John K. Ousterhout. 1992. “The Design and Implementation of a Log-Structured File System.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 10 (1): 26–52. https://doi.org/10.1145/146941.146943.
\[\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_j = \text{fold}(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0, \LoggedEventPrefix) = \text{apply}(\dots\text{apply}(\text{apply}(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0, \LoggedEvent_1), \LoggedEvent_2)\dots, \LoggedEvent_j)\]
In this formulation, \(\LogPositionIndex\) indexes the durable log sequence boundary rather than the interaction turn \(\TurnIndex\). Given deterministic reducer semantics and complete event payloads, folding reconstructs the precise control state without invoking the foundation model or re-executing external tools. This architecture embodies the classic event sourcing pattern (Kleppmann 2016): historical decisions serve as deterministic inputs to state reconstruction, while unrecorded events remain explicitly unknown. If the latest durable log entry indicates that a test execution was authorized and dispatched, but contains no corresponding completion event, the reconstructed state marks that operation as unresolved (figure 1). For the worksheet crash, the fold keeps the held reservation and the dispatched test_r18 intent, and it invents no outcome for the test.






Figure 1: The Trajectory Record as a Projection of the Log: The record in runtime memory (top) is lost on a crash; the durable, append-only log (bottom) is not. Folding the logged events through a deterministic reducer, starting from the initial record \(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_0\), rebuilds the recorded projection \(\ProjectedTrajectoryRecord_j\) at boundary \(\LogPositionIndex\) without calling the model or any tool. Because the log ends at the test’s recorded intent with no recorded result, the reconstructed record keeps the admission and reservation and marks the test unresolved rather than inventing its outcome.



Engineers must distinguish the trajectory log from the model’s active context window. Context assembly is selective and ephemeral: prompt compilation filters past interactions, and context compaction periodically replaces verbose command outputs with concise summaries. The trajectory log, by contrast, preserves the exact delivered inputs and operational decisions required by the system’s replay contract. For a truncated observation, the log retains the exact byte slice exposed to the model rather than the full, unpruned output stream emitted by the tool. State reconstruction reproduces only what was durably captured. A compacted summary replays as a summary, and a logged hash of a payload can verify those bytes only while the stored payload itself survives (section 11.8.2 develops this separation of digests from bytes).



If a log entry records only that a tool was called without capturing the worker lease, control epoch, or reservation bound, a replacement worker cannot tell whether a late callback belongs to an invalidated turn or how much budget remains locked. An event log supports reliable recovery only when its schema captures the operational metadata that succeeding workers need to answer those questions. Table 1 groups these event families by their roles during reconstruction. These schemas define logical event boundaries rather than requiring isolated physical storage writes for every individual field. For example, a high-throughput runtime can coalesce authorization checks, budget reservations, and tool dispatch intents into a single batched write transaction, provided the deterministic reducer preserves their causal dependencies. The storage engine must also durably acknowledge the batch before dispatch (the ordering that section 11.3 develops).
Every event envelope contains a trajectory identifier, a unique event identifier, a monotonically increasing sequence_number, schema type and version tags, and tenant or issuer provenance. In addition, the log records the active reducer version alongside the worker lease identity under which appends were accepted. Within this envelope, the sequence_number defines total event ordering, and record_version tracks state machine modifications. The control_epoch is the harness’s control fence, which advances whenever a pause, cancellation, or interruption invalidates in-flight continuations, so an observation stamped with an older epoch cannot advance the current one. A distinct owner_epoch counts grants of trajectory ownership, so that storage can reject appends from a worker whose ownership has passed to another (the fencing mechanism of section 11.5.1). Neither ownership handoffs across workers nor control-epoch increments alter the unique logical identity of an in-flight operation.


↩︎ Epoch fencing, which keeps a stale asynchronous response from advancing the current continuation, is established in Transition guards and the admission check.



Table 1: Trajectory log schema: Event families preserve the control and evidence contract across a crash. The log records observations and decisions, not automatic proof that an external effect settled or a task succeeded.

Reconstruction use

Task and requester, initial grants and limits, ordinary and finalization deadlines, initial record and workspace references, configuration provenance

Rebuild admission and accounting, not merely a remaining-balance scalar

Logical operation and transport attempt identities, represented operation and arguments, applicable revision and repeat contract, job handle when known, outcome evidence and observation completeness
Preserve possible dispatch and its evidence; a pending, partial, or timeout result does not establish settlement

The software repair worksheet illustrates how these identifiers link distributed lifecycle events. Alongside the workspace snapshot ws_r18, the identifier operation_id=test_r18 designates the logical test suite invocation, while attempt_id=attempt1 tracks the specific network transport attempt. If an asynchronous test executor returns an acknowledgment containing a cluster job identifier such as job_tests_18, that handle correlates future asynchronous callbacks with the original operation. However, a recovering worker can discover this link only if that acknowledgment was durably flushed to the log before the crash. A durable ToolResult may record an active execution state, a timeout, or a completed test report; the reducer interprets these payloads according to their authenticated provenance. If an asynchronous execution finishes after the supervisor has already timed out the enclosing step, the late-arriving ToolResult updates the operation table rather than corrupting an obsolete execution branch.


↩︎ The observation-eligibility protocol that routes late results to the operation table rather than the active turn is established in Late results and observation eligibility.
Capturing model context requires equal diligence regarding immutability. The manifest in ContextBuilt must record the exact tokenized payload or byte stream delivered over the wire, rather than mutable file system paths or external URLs that could mutate before recovery occurs. The log must also capture available inference engine provenance (model checkpoints, serving system versions, and decoding configurations), recording any gaps because hosted model identifiers frequently hide upstream weight updates or inference engine modifications. When execution resumes, the replacement worker can assemble an updated prompt context from recent evidence while preserving the historical invocation records exactly as delivered.
Defining an event schema specifies what state reconstruction requires, but schema definitions alone cannot guarantee that writes reach disk before an agent issues network requests. If a runtime persists a model completion but crashes before flushing the subsequent tool intent, the recovering worker cannot determine whether an external tool call was dispatched, risking duplicate side effects. To resolve this vulnerability, the runtime must enforce strict write-ahead ordering between logging an operational intent and releasing its network dispatch.

title: 11 Durable Execution
text:
In the crash worksheet, the repair worker’s next step is to submit test_r18 against workspace ws_r18. If the harness dispatches that test request across the network and crashes before the ToolIntent record reaches durable storage, a replacement worker folding the surviving log recovers a plan that still says “run the test.” Meanwhile the original job is already executing on the remote cluster and accruing charges. Recording only the eventual result leaves that blind spot open on every call. To prevent duplicate runs and untracked financial liability, the runtime must commit the admitted request and its reservation to persistent storage before that request ever leaves its control.
Recording the admitted request durably before dispatching it is classical write-ahead logging applied to trajectory dispatch. A durable history ensures that recovery can identify every external operation that may have begun, even if network partitions or crashes prevent the worker from ever receiving the reply. Under the runtime’s declared failure model, an external mutation that occurs without a recoverable record of intent is a phantom effect. Eliminating phantom effects requires two guarantees, strict write-ahead ordering in the runtime execution pipeline and a storage substrate that reliably outlives the failures the system claims to tolerate. Together they are the Part IV principle of intent before effect (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-intent-before-effect}\)), whose ordering this section derives (equation 1) and whose storage half it prices.


↪ The database form of write-ahead logging, and why a runtime borrows its ordering but not its control over remote state, is developed in Classical Transaction Background.

Definition 11.2: Durable intent
Durable intent is the immutable record of an admitted operation, capturing its identity, input arguments, a reference to its authorization decision and capability grant, and its budget reservation, acknowledged by storage that survives the declared failure domain before the request is dispatched.

Significance: It converts a crash between dispatch and reply from an untracked phantom effect into an unresolved operation with an explicit owner, at the price of placing one durable acknowledgment on the critical path of every dispatch (table 2).
Distinction: A durable intent records that work may have escaped into the external environment. It does not certify that the remote endpoint committed or executed the work, nor does it mandate that a recovered worker must re-execute it.
Common pitfall: Taking an acknowledgment from storage that shares the failure boundary the design claims to survive, such as writing to a local scratch volume under a system contract that promises resilience against host or volume loss.



The intent references the grant rather than copying a secret into it. A log retained for months and read during replay is the wrong place for a credential, so the secret stays with the credential broker, and a recovered worker obtains a fresh use of it only by passing admission under current ownership.


↩︎ The credential broker, which holds a secret outside the guest and uses it on behalf of an authorized request, is established in Credential brokering.


Suppose the repair worker appends the test_r18 intent with a standard POSIX write() call, observes a successful return, and promptly dispatches the test. The host then suffers an immediate power failure. A successful write() guarantees only that the kernel copied the payload into its page cache; those dirty pages evaporate when the power cuts before writeback to disk. When the replacement worker boots, it finds an empty log, completely unaware that a remote test is already active. A returned write() therefore covers only the first failure domain of section 11.2, a process crash on an intact host, while offering zero protection against host power loss.
This reasoning extends upward through the failure hierarchy. If a worker fails, a replacement process can recover using reattachable block storage, provided that the replacement can mount the disk and read the acknowledged log and artifacts. If the failure domain includes the permanent destruction of the worker’s storage volume, as in cloud environments where spot instances or underlying hardware failures destroy ephemeral disks, the acknowledgment must originate from a storage service outside that volume. Remoteness alone does not satisfy this requirement. An asynchronous replica updated out of band can lag the primary log, leaving the replacement worker with an incomplete history during a failover.
Each step up the failure hierarchy demands a correspondingly stronger persistence barrier. Surviving host power loss requires fsync() or fdatasync(), which returns only after the underlying storage device reports that the data has reached stable media. The two system calls differ in how they handle metadata: fsync() flushes file attributes such as modification timestamps, whereas fdatasync() flushes only the metadata strictly required to read the payload back. For a trajectory log that preallocates its disk files, using fdatasync() eliminates an unneeded disk seek and metadata write per barrier. Even with these system calls, subtle failure modes remain.2 If a drive contains a volatile write cache, it must honor the disk flush command before an acknowledgment truly covers power loss. Alternatively, the write must specify Force Unit Access (a per-write flag that bypasses the drive cache entirely). Even a verified local barrier, however, cannot survive the catastrophic loss of the physical drive or volume. Surviving permanent volume loss requires a replicated storage engine that returns a success acknowledgment only after a quorum of replicas, distributed across distinct failure domains, have committed the record.3 The worksheet requires two durable copies outside the worker volume before dispatch. This chosen placement policy is stronger than the single-volume-loss requirement alone; table 2 lists acknowledgments that satisfy the stated contracts.
2 Crash Consistency in Practice: A study of eleven widely used applications, including databases, key-value stores, and version-control systems, found 60 crash vulnerabilities, because each application’s update protocol depended on subtle file-system persistence behavior that its authors had assumed rather than tested (Pillai et al. 2014). A trajectory log inherits the same exposure, so its durability claim should be checked by injecting crashes between every write and barrier, not inferred from the calls it makes. 
Pillai, Thanumalayan Sankaranarayana, Vijay Chidambaram, Ramnatthan Alagappan, Samer Al-Kiswany, Andrea C. Arpaci-Dusseau, and Remzi H. Arpaci-Dusseau. 2014. “All File Systems Are Not Created Equal: On the Complexity of Crafting Crash-Consistent Applications.” 11th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI), 433–48.
3 Quorum Acknowledgment: Consensus protocols such as Paxos (Lamport 1998) and Raft (Ongaro and Ousterhout 2014) commit a log entry once a majority of replicas store it; because any two majorities share a replica, an acknowledged entry survives the loss of any minority. The guarantee covers only failures the replicas do not share, so a quorum placed on one host or one power domain gives the latency of replication without the durability the worksheet’s contract requires. 
Lamport, Leslie. 1998. “The Part-Time Parliament.” ACM Transactions on Computer Systems 16 (2): 133–69. https://doi.org/10.1145/279227.279229.

Ongaro, Diego, and John Ousterhout. 2014. “In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm.” Proceedings of the 2014 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (USENIX ATC 14), 305–19.



Table 2: Durable Acknowledgment by Failure Domain: The first two rows name the local barriers for their failures; the final row uses the worksheet’s chosen two-off-volume-copy policy. Moving down the table adds a wait, first for the storage device and then for network round trips to the slowest required replica, so the declared failure domain and placement policy set the latency floor of every dispatch.










Failure the contract tolerates
Acknowledgment that survives it
Acknowledgment that does not




Process crash; host and volume intact
Returned write(), which places the bytes in the kernel page cache that outlives the process
An event queued only in the runtime’s own memory


Power loss or host crash; volume intact
Returned fdatasync() or fsync(), with the device write cache flushed or bypassed
Returned write() alone, whose dirty pages were volatile


Permanent loss of the worker’s volume
Acknowledgment from a replicated store after two replicas outside that volume’s failure domain made it durable, under the worksheet’s additional placement policy
Local barrier plus an asynchronous copy that may not have arrived






The implementation must define precisely which failure modes its persistence layer covers, how storage errors surface to the application, and how a replacement worker discovers the complete authoritative history. Underlying storage engines provide the mechanical primitives, but the systems architect must establish the durability contract. When an acknowledgment fails or times out with an ambiguous status, the runtime must hold dispatch and resolve the append according to the storage contract. Resolution means re-reading the authoritative log. If the intent is present, the attempt is admitted but still unsent, so a pause or a failed recheck can still withhold it. If a complete authoritative prefix lacks it, the worker appends it again under the same event identity, which storage deduplicates if the first append did land. Holding back a dispatch during a storage outage may temporarily stall progress, but dispatching before confirmation permanently destroys the evidence required to govern in-flight work after a crash.


↪ Why a durability claim must name both its acknowledgment and the failures it survives, and how durability differs from atomicity and isolation, is developed in Guarantee Boundaries.



If a worker validates a proposal and reserves budget in memory (Transition guards and the admission check) but dispatches the network call before the storage acknowledgment returns, a crash in that gap leaves an untracked phantom effect. Durable execution closes that window by inserting an acknowledged intent write between admission and network release. For an attempt that proceeds to dispatch and later produces an observation, the ordering is
\[
\ValidatedProposalEvent \prec \AdmissionDecisionEvent \prec \IntentAcknowledgmentEvent \prec \ExternalDispatchAction \prec \EvidenceRecordEvent.
\tag{1}\]
In equation 1, \(\ValidatedProposalEvent\) is the validated complete proposal, \(\AdmissionDecisionEvent\) is the admitted authorization and reservation decision, and \(\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\) acknowledges its recoverable ToolIntent and required preceding records under the declared failure domain. The action \(\ExternalDispatchAction\) is dispatch, not endpoint completion. The event \(\EvidenceRecordEvent\) is the later durable recording of received evidence, whose status may still be pending, partial, or unknown. The ordering constrains the events that occur, though an attempt can stop before dispatch or never produce evidence. Its payoff is that the position of a crash in this sequence determines what recovery may conclude (figure 2). A crash before the worker receives \(\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\) means the attempt was never dispatched, though an intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost in transit. Recovery must inspect the complete authoritative prefix to determine whether that intent survived. Once \(\IntentAcknowledgmentEvent\) is durable, a crash at any point before adequate outcome evidence \(\EvidenceRecordEvent\) becomes durable leaves an in-doubt action, an admitted operation whose outcome the surviving evidence cannot settle. Because releasing the network request \(\ExternalDispatchAction\) does not write a separate log record, the surviving log looks identical whether the worker crashed just before sending the packet, while the request was in flight, or after recording a pending or timeout observation. That window is the tool layer’s uncertain outcome (definition \(\ref{dfn-uncertain-outcome}\)) seen from the recovery side, and it is what the fold of section 11.2.1 marked unresolved. Only recorded, correlated evidence establishes an outcome.






Figure 2: Intent Before Dispatch: The runtime validates a proposal, admits it with a reservation, and waits for the intent’s acknowledgment under the declared failure domain before dispatch carries the request past the durability barrier. Where a crash falls determines the recovery state of table 3. Before the worker receives the acknowledgment, dispatch is withheld, but the intent may already be durable if its acknowledgment was lost. An absent intent establishes non-dispatch only when the authoritative prefix is complete. Between the acknowledgment and adequate recorded evidence, including a crash before dispatch, the operation is in doubt; a pending or timeout observation leaves it there. After correlated outcome evidence is recorded, the outcome is established within the endpoint’s contract.



In the crash worksheet, the intent names operation_id=test_r18, attempt_id=attempt1, the immutable ws_r18 input, the selected check, and the endpoint’s repeat contract. It references the applicable Authorized and BudgetReserved decisions, together with the requester and task bindings, control_epoch, and owner_epoch under which they were made. The recoverable prefix must reconstruct the admitted reservation itself, rather than merely a remaining balance.
Admission and control stay coordinated while the barrier is pending. An operator pause or an administrative change in authority can still intercept and withhold an admitted but unsent request, because logging a durable intent records permission to dispatch rather than an irrevocable obligation to execute. The harness’s dispatch-time recheck, the last gate before the request leaves, re-evaluates the admitted attempt against current control state without reserving a second batch of budget. If the release mechanism already dispatched the request across the network, subsequent control actions must treat the request as sent. Conversely, a withheld request keeps its entry in the operation table and its reserved budget until verified evidence confirms that no remote side effects or financial liabilities remain.


↩︎ Dispatch-time rechecks, which re-run budget, authority, and approval checks at the moment of release, are established in Dispatch-time rechecks.
Foundation model invocations require identical rigor regarding identity and liability. Token generation streams over network sockets, and an interrupted invocation can incur charges on the provider’s bill even if a worker crash prevents the client from ever logging the output. The same ordering therefore covers model calls. The ContextBuilt record and the invocation’s BudgetReserved decision become durable before the request leaves, so a crash mid-stream leaves a logged invocation with no ModelReplied. Recovery treats that invocation as in doubt only for its charge, which it settles from the provider’s usage evidence. The lost reply cannot be reconstructed by replaying the prompt, because stochastic sampling produces a different completion, so recovery discards any partial stream and never replays the call. Any retry is a separately admitted invocation, requiring a fresh invocation identity, validated request and context, current admission checks, and a durable budget reservation before dispatch.



The first of the three recovery states in figure 2 (not dispatched) carries a hidden precondition. Following a crash, a recovering worker can treat the absence of a logged intent as proof that dispatch never occurred only if it holds the complete authoritative history promised by the failure domain. This requirement is the completeness rule. An asynchronously updated read replica cannot satisfy this rule, because the replica cannot distinguish between an operation that was never dispatched and an intent whose log record has not yet arrived across the network. Table 3 outlines the recovery states governed by this rule.



Table 3: Recovery States of a Logged Action: These classifications require a complete surviving authoritative prefix. An incomplete replica cannot establish that an absent intent was never dispatched.










Surviving evidence
What it establishes
Consequence for continuation




No durable intent in a complete authoritative prefix, under enforced write-ahead dispatch
This attempt was not dispatched through the mediated path
Reconsider the recorded proposal under current admission checks; do not dispatch automatically


Durable intent plus adequate, correlated outcome evidence
The recorded outcome is established to the extent supported by the endpoint contract
Reuse that evidence within its candidate and check scope; settle charges separately where necessary


Durable intent without adequate outcome evidence, including a timeout or pending ToolResult
The operation is in doubt
Retain its identity, liability, and settlement owner; withhold dependent work until its guards permit continuation






In the crash worksheet scenario, the dispatched test may have failed to reach the service, may still be executing on a remote runner, or may have finished just before the worker crashed. If the executor’s reply accepting the job was never logged, its job handle, job_tests_18, is lost with the worker as well. To resolve this ambiguity, the runtime performs a targeted lookup using the logged operation identity, authenticating and correlating any newly discovered evidence before updating the operation table. A verified test result establishes the check for ws_r18; whether to accept the overall repair remains a distinct policy decision.
The in-doubt status reflects runtime uncertainty rather than external failure, and resolving it is a question about the endpoint. Operation identity and endpoint contracts details the endpoint requirements needed to execute a safe repeat: strict identity scoping, immutable payload binding, retention of prior execution results, handling of concurrent in-flight requests, and coordination between state mutations and returned values. A client-provided idempotency key protects only those endpoints that implement these semantics. Probing an endpoint by resource name provides much weaker guarantees, as a matching name might belong to an unrelated operation, while an absent resource could indicate that a delayed initial request is still in transit. For an in-doubt action, durable execution therefore applies settlement before retry (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-exactly-once-settlement}\)) unchanged. The log supplies the operation identity and its evidence, and only the endpoint’s contract or positive outcome evidence licenses another attempt.


↪ The idempotence and deduplication contracts behind a safe repeat are developed in Repetition and Result Recovery.
