What was checked, on which artifact, for which admission decision?


Transformation
Parent-record identity, transformation implementation/configuration, changed fields, derived identity, and revalidation results
How does the emitted view differ from the source?


Use and partition
Permission decision and scope, retention restrictions, split/group assignment, and corpus membership
Where may this version go, and which evaluation boundary follows it?






The envelope must record only what the runtime interfaces actually reveal. When an agent executes against locally controlled model weights, the envelope binds the loaded base model and adapter checkpoint digests. Hosted inference endpoints, however, typically expose only a reported version string and request configuration; in those cases, the envelope documents those exact parameters rather than fabricating an unverifiable weight hash. Similarly, a prompt-template identifier fails to capture dynamic context injected at runtime, and a container base-image digest omits mutable mounted volumes or external network state. Systems engineers must document omissions explicitly rather than relying on identifiers of ambiguous scope.
Evaluation assessments bind directly to the exact byte representation tested. If a trajectory earns a passing score on a targeted capability test, that verdict applies only to that evaluated representation; any pending criterion remains pending when the record enters cold storage. The downstream evaluation cascade alone determines whether the available evidence authorizes a specific learning use, and cryptographic integrity checks then verify that the assessed byte representation is the exact one a downstream trainer reads.



A trainer decides what to train on by reading the corpus manifest, so it must be able to confirm two things before the first gradient. The first is that the manifest is the one curation issued. The second is that no record was altered or swapped after admission, whether by a broken pipeline script or by anyone with write access to the store. Integrity mechanisms answer those two questions. They establish unmodified bytes, not correct content or permitted use. A cryptographic digest identifies a specified byte representation under standard collision-resistance assumptions. For that digest to remain meaningful across system components, the lineage envelope must fix both the canonical serialization scheme and the schema version over which the hash was calculated. Comparing an artifact against an expected digest detects bit corruption and unauthorized edits. Storing an unauthenticated digest directly beside mutable content in an object store, however, provides no protection, because an adversary or a broken pipeline script can overwrite the data and the digest together.
To guarantee authenticity, an authenticated manifest cryptographically binds expected artifact digests and associated metadata to a trusted issuing authority. Systems commonly use a message authentication code (MAC), such as HMAC as specified in RFC 2104 (Krawczyk et al. 1997), computed with a secret key held outside the dataset in a key management service. Because any party holding a shared symmetric key can forge a valid MAC, production architectures often prefer asymmetric digital signatures (such as Ed25519) when datasets are distributed across multiple worker nodes. The manifest must record the cryptographic algorithm, key version, and authorized issuing scope, and key rotation policies must match the operational lifetime of the corpus. Verification confirms only that the authenticated byte representation has not changed since issuance; it covers nothing outside that boundary.

Krawczyk, Hugo, Mihir Bellare, and Ran Canetti. 1997. HMAC: Keyed-Hashing for Message Authentication. RFC 2104. Internet Engineering Task Force. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC2104.
13 Merkle Tree: A tree in which each internal node holds the hash of its children, introduced to build digital signatures from a conventional one-way function (Merkle 1988). Its useful property is that proving one leaf belongs under a trusted root needs only the sibling hashes along one path, logarithmic in the number of leaves. A corpus manifest can therefore commit to millions of record digests under one root and still verify a single member cheaply, but the root commits only to the leaves that were hashed. 
Merkle, Ralph C. 1988. “A Digital Signature Based on a Conventional Encryption Function.” Advances in Cryptology — CRYPTO ’87, Lecture notes in computer science, vol. 293: 369–78. https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48184-2_32.
Cryptographic integrity must not be confused with semantic correctness. A faithfully authenticated trajectory trace can still hold hallucinated model outputs, an erroneous grader verdict, or private data that downstream consumers are prohibited from seeing. Similarly, computing a Merkle root13 over captured execution events proves that a given event belongs to the recorded tree, but it proves nothing about execution events that the logging harness dropped or failed to observe. Claims about trajectory reproducibility must therefore stay within the reconstruction and re-execution boundaries established in Recorded Trajectory Replay.



Because an authenticated source record is immutable, scrubbing a private file path or API token from a recorded trace in place would break its digest and erase the only copy of what actually ran, often severing the causal link that justified the agent’s next command. At the same time, the data minimization and disclosure boundaries established in Disclosure minimization must be enforced before trajectory content enters an ingestion queue, a model-assisted curation worker, or a training store. To resolve that tension, a derived record is always created as a new version rather than an in-place modification. The derived record binds a reference to its parent trace, the versioned redaction policy and implementation, the explicit set of altered or excised fields, and any intentionally withheld content. Lineage references do not grant read authorization to restricted raw data, and systems must store original raw bytes only where retention policies explicitly permit them. When source records reach their retention expiration limit and are purged, the lineage envelope documents that boundary directly; retaining a cryptographic hash is not the same as retaining the source data. The source also keeps a reverse reference to each derived version, so that a later correction or withdrawal at the source reaches every artifact derived from it (figure 5).






Figure 5: A Derived Record and Its Lineage: Redaction produces a new record version instead of editing the source. The derived record carries its parent reference, the fields its transformation changed or omitted, and the source’s split group, but its assessment is pending until revalidation decides what the new view still supports. The source keeps a reverse reference, so a later correction or withdrawal can reach every derived version.



Heuristic pattern matching and named-entity recognition models act as screening mechanisms rather than complete sanitization guarantees. Engineers must validate these detectors across the full output pipeline using realistic end-to-end test cases, including deeply nested payloads and generated metadata. Synthetic canaries provide an empirical measure of detector recall. The curation audit log must record how many canaries were injected, how many escaped detection, which semantic classes and text transformations were tested, and where the inspection boundary was applied. Observing zero canary escapes bounds the leak probability only for the evaluated canary distribution. False positives carry their own cost, because over-aggressive scrubbing strips necessary context and distorts the training signal.


↩︎ Canary values, planted synthetic secrets whose escape reveals a leaking path, are established in Detectors and canary values.
When scrubbing identifiers across multi-step interactions, curators use consistent pseudonyms to preserve relational dependencies across turns while preventing identity linkage beyond the access scope that the trace’s disclosure boundary permits. Tokenization effects require careful handling: replacing an identifier with a fixed-width placeholder often alters the sequence’s token count and attention boundaries because a placeholder string rarely splits into the same number of subword tokens as the original identifier, shifting every subsequent token index and misaligning any token-level loss masks that were indexed against the unredacted transcript. Similarly, reserializing a structured payload can preserve outer JSON or YAML formatting while silently breaking nested shell escaping, regular expression matches, or tool invocation syntax. Consequently, checking that an artifact parses successfully is distinct from verifying that it still supports the intended learning target.


↪ Re-verifying selected response spans against token offsets after templating or redaction shifts token boundaries is developed in Rendering with versioned templates.
Revalidation must systematically test every property that the transformation could have influenced. This includes validating record structure, ensuring action-observation consistency, verifying that the sanitized context still justifies the target action, and re-evaluating any criteria whose supporting evidence was altered. If a transformation modifies executable code or environment-dependent identifiers, the pipeline must execute the code against an isolated, authorized test fixture to obtain fresh runtime evidence, while archiving prior execution logs as historical artifacts.

Example 15.1: A transformed record needs a new decisionScenario: During a collection run, an agent’s observation records a private system path that a subsequent diagnostic command references, and the source trace captures the successful output of that command. The curation pipeline replaces the path with a sanitized placeholder throughout trace_r19_01_redacted_v1.
Diagnosis: The recorded execution output remains valid evidence only for the original run bound to trace_r19_01; the agent never executed the sanitized placeholder path. The curator must determine whether the sanitized observation and the subsequent command still constitute a coherent learning example. A consistent placeholder can teach an agent how to parse and inspect arbitrary paths without exposing production directory structures. However, replaying the trajectory against an active execution harness requires an authorized, compatible mock fixture; otherwise, the substituted path fails to resolve. If the substitution obscures the causal distinction that prompted the agent’s action, the pipeline must reject the target for supervised training or withhold the record. The derived record inherits the source’s task grouping and train/test split assignment, while all pending evaluation verdicts remain pending until formal revalidation completes.
Systems lesson: Cryptographic integrity establishes which source artifact was transformed, whereas revalidation establishes what the transformed trajectory teaches. Neither operation can alter what physically occurred during the original execution run.





Permission to execute an agent against a task fixture or inspect an internal repository does not convey permission to retain its artifacts, fine-tune models on its data, or publish the resulting corpus. The lineage envelope must record the explicit licensing constraints, the evidentiary basis for data retention, and the designated policy authority or human reviewer who approved data usage. This accounting must cover both the primary task assets and all third-party software dependencies pulled into the environment during execution. Automated license detectors and embedding-based similarity screens help identify suspect components, but they serve as screening tools rather than autonomous legal adjudicators.
When provenance evidence is ambiguous or incomplete, the curation pipeline must withhold the record from downstream consumers while logging the specific withholding rationale. This quarantine is use-specific: an asset held from public pretraining might remain eligible for internal safety evaluations. Furthermore, use-permission holds operate independently of task failure labels, confidentiality tiers, and fault-containment quarantine. Resolving a safety fault or task defect does not automatically grant data-usage clearance.


⇄ Contrast: Incident containment, which holds the work a suspect trajectory might touch rather than withholding a record from one use, is established in Incident Containment.
Approved data permissions operate under strict temporal and organizational scopes. To enforce policy changes, reverse references must connect each source record to its derived views, tokenized dataset partitions, and published corpus manifests. When an upstream data provider revokes permission, or when an organization updates its privacy policies, the system must propagate the restriction or withdrawal to every downstream artifact. The ingestion pipeline immediately halts new admissions under the revoked policy, while the catalog traces all distributed artifacts. Deleting a record from an active storage bucket leaves distributed offline copies and completed model parameter updates intact; managing those downstream exposures requires explicit operational ownership, retraining schedules, and audited unlearning procedures.

Checkpoint 15.2: Defend a derived record's use
Each bullet asks for a decision a curator makes before a derived record ships.

Integrity vs. truth: A manifest’s MAC verifies. Decide which of these it establishes: the bytes are unmodified, the grader verdict is correct, the record is permitted for training.
Transformation: A replacement preserves JSON parsing but changes a path used by a later action. Which historical evidence remains valid, and which learning-use checks must be repeated before admission?
Screening: A detector test inserts canaries of three classes and observes zero escapes. What claim can the report make, and which record classes remain untested?
Lineage: A redacted record’s source task is in the final-test group. Decide whether the redacted version may enter training, and name what must happen when an admitted source is later withdrawn.



A well-architected trajectory record has a verifiable origin, an explicit transformation history, a legally scoped permission envelope, and preserved evaluation boundaries. Connecting an execution trace through this provenance graph into a corpus manifest gives membership a precise meaning: verified fitness for a declared learning consumer. Carrying one record through every stage shows how these decisions fit together.




The recovery run collection_run_r19_01, whose targets section 15.6.2 selected, exercises each stage of that admission and provenance chain. Its refused edit, schema inspection, and corrected edit produced ws_r20, which satisfied repair_accept_v1. The raw trace trace_r19_01 records that sequence without altering any earlier record, neither the pending trial verdict on ws_r19 nor the unresolved earlier test operation test_r18. The curation question is which parts of this record may enter a learning artifact, for which consumer, and on what evidence.
The training objective is recovery from harness refusals, the residual behavior that the campaign’s probes left with the model. The target policy recovery_targets_v1 already fixed which tokens contribute direct supervised loss: the schema query e3, the corrected edit e4, and the final summary e6. The refused proposal e2, the test summary e5, the task prompt, and the intermediate tool responses stay as conditioning context. Target selection is only the first stage of admission. The record that actually enters a corpus is a transformed view of trace_r19_01, so the remaining stages must verify that view, bind its provenance, and publish it to a manifest.


Replacing sensitive fixture paths in trace_r19_01 with synthetic placeholders produces trace_r19_01_redacted_v1, but if that redaction strips the file names the agent needed to deduce the schema, training on the redacted trace teaches the model to guess rather than inspect. While the underlying execution stems directly from the original run, admission filtering must verify whether this sanitized view preserves the causal chain of the recovery lesson rather than assuming the raw run’s pass carries over. The admission pipeline does not demand byte-for-byte fidelity with historical environment state; it requires that the transformed trace still support supervised imitation of the selected targets. Because each predicate evaluates to true, the pipeline admits the transformed example as a verified decision demonstration. Had path substitution stripped the file names essential for the agent to deduce the correct schema, target suitability (\(\text{chk}_{\text{target,demo}}\)) would have failed. Furthermore, while this redacted trace is valid for token-level imitation learning, it cannot serve a downstream consumer that requires executable replay, because executing the synthetic paths would require spinning up a fresh environment with matching mock fixtures. Neither a valid cryptographic digest nor an overall task pass provides blanket approval across different training regimens.



Admitting trace_r19_01_redacted_v1 into a storage bucket without binding its target mask, split group, and grader versions leaves a downstream trainer free to supervise the refused edit e2 by mistake or leak the task into evaluation. Publishing the curated trajectory to the corpus release repair_demonstrations_v1 prevents that drift by recording every link in the artifact’s provenance chain inside the corpus manifest. For this member, the manifest binds the record to its originating run (collection_run_r19_01), task identifier, fixture snapshot, candidate code patch, and evaluation grader versions. It references both the transformed trace (trace_r19_01_redacted_v1) and the target selection policy (recovery_targets_v1), while logging the specific data governance approvals, task group assignments, and split partition versions. Any missing metadata or inactive model dependencies are explicitly tagged as unavailable rather than omitted.
At the corpus level, the manifest catalogs the source data pools, sampling weights, token accounting budgets, domain coverage metrics, and the formal evaluation protocol. Maintaining clear distinctions among raw interaction counts, stored trace tokens, and selected supervised target tokens prevents deceptive accounting. During training, serialization formats and loss masks enforce these target boundaries, ensuring that future trajectory steps never leak into earlier conditioning windows.
This curated trajectory yields a single demonstration artifact. It cannot be repurposed as a preference pair, because the rejected proposal e2 and the later edit e4 follow different prefixes (e4 comes after the refusal and the schema lookup), so they are not alternative continuations of one context. A preference artifact would need competing completions sampled from one saved branch point. Similarly, publishing an environment for reinforcement learning rollouts requires exporting the task fixture, harness configurations, and dynamic graders, rather than static token sequences.
Publishing an immutable corpus manifest establishes a versioned training baseline, which remains separate from deployment governance for any resulting model. Tracking lineage guarantees that if an upstream fixture defect or data privacy request emerges later, pipeline operators can cleanly trace and purge all derived artifacts across downstream model versions. At the infrastructure layer, ephemeral execution sandboxes are destroyed and billed compute charges are settled independently of whether a trace reaches the corpus manifest.



Because every initiated run incurs compute and verification charges whether or not it reaches the manifest, raw trial volume is a deceptive metric for collection economics. A pipeline may execute thousands of autonomous interactions yet emit only a small handful of usable training samples, as trajectories fail safety filters, duplicate existing task solutions, crash during tool dispatch, or remain stalled in asynchronous evaluation queues. Consequently, systems engineers must evaluate collection economics using the cost per emitted artifact, amortizing all spent compute and infrastructure overhead across the accepted dataset.
For a given collection cohort and accounting cutoff, let \(\CollectionCohortCost\) represent the total monetary expenditure incurred across environment provisioning, inference generation, tool sandbox execution, automated verification, human review, redaction transformations, and storage. Let \(\EmittedArtifactCount\) denote the number of valid artifacts emitted for a designated consumer by that cutoff. The cost per emitted artifact is defined as
\[\CostPerEmittedArtifact=\frac{\CollectionCohortCost}{\EmittedArtifactCount},\qquad \EmittedArtifactCount>0. \tag{5}\]
The numerator \(\CollectionCohortCost\) captures all unproductive runs, rejected proposals, and pipeline failures; if a cohort yields zero usable artifacts (\(\EmittedArtifactCount = 0\)), the pipeline registers the incurred financial loss without dividing by zero. Structurally, equation 5 mirrors the cost per accepted task formulation (equation 1.2): the unit cost equals the average cost per attempt divided by the end-to-end emission yield. This metric isolates data acquisition efficiency, distinguishing curation costs from both runtime inference serving and subsequent model fine-tuning.

Math: The selected-and-emitted row of table 15 yields an emission rate of 15 / 500 = 3 percent. The average cost per attempt is $300 / 500 = $0.60. Applying equation 5 yields $0.60 / 3 percent = $20 per emitted artifact. Systems insight: Because unit cost equals attempt cost divided by emission yield, curation yield serves as the primary economic lever. For example, raising yield to 6 percent cuts the unit price in half to $10. With 97 percent of attempts failing to emit a usable artifact, engineering effort should focus on diagnosing nonselection causes before purchasing additional generation compute. High redundancy indicates that the system should launch fewer attempts per task; ineligibility points to split or permission defects caught too late; and backlogged pending evaluations point to verification bottlenecks.


A published manifest documents what was emitted, verifies eligibility across all admission gates, isolates supervision targets, and tallies total acquisition cost. Operational efficiency and curation hygiene, however, are prerequisites rather than guarantees of model improvement. The test of a curated corpus is offline evaluation against held-out task groups under controlled benchmark protocols, where neither a low cost per artifact nor a high emission yield can substitute for task performance.




A data collection pipeline can preserve every execution record faithfully and still assemble a counterproductive training set. The mistakes below stem from confusing raw trace telemetry with the deliberate pedagogical choices required to train an agent, and each carries tangible computational or behavioral costs.

Fallacy: A successful task makes every action in its trace a suitable demonstration.
Task acceptance evaluates end-to-end task completion, whereas target selection decides which specific token sequences should receive gradient supervision. Consider an agent that successfully debugs a codebase after several stumbling attempts. Its transcript might include an initial malformed JSON tool call, a parser rejection from the runtime environment, and a subsequent correction. While that malformed call must remain in the transcript as conditioning context so the agent understands the environment’s feedback, it must never be included in the training loss as a target. In the recovery worksheet, a typical recovery trajectory contains 18,500 stored tokens, but only 2,000 of those tokens are designated as supervised targets (section 15.6). Supervising the entire accepted trace forces the model to memorize and reproduce its own intermediate errors. In a sound curation pipeline, record validity (whether the telemetry accurately reflects what happened), task acceptance (whether the agent fulfilled its objective), and target eligibility (whether an action should be reinforced) are three distinct filtering decisions.


Pitfall: Fine-tuning on every failure before probing its cause.
When an agent fails, the easiest operational reaction is often to bundle the failed trajectories into a fine-tuning dataset. In the intervention ladder worksheet, systematic counterfactual probes demonstrate that 90 percent of observed failures originate in the supporting infrastructure below the model weights, such as malformed tool schemas, missing environment variables, or overly aggressive sandbox timeouts (section 15.2.2). Retraining the model across the entire failure corpus requires only $58 of accelerator time, and that modest price creates a dangerous illusion of progress. Fine-tuning merely encourages the model to memorize ad hoc compensations for broken tooling. As soon as an external API changes or the brittle workaround misfires, the failure resurfaces. Systems engineers should run counterfactual probes first, fix defects in tools and runtime environments directly, and restrict fine-tuning to the remaining 300 genuine behavioral failures.


Fallacy: A random split of collected traces holds out unseen tasks.
Applying uniform random sampling across collected trajectories partitions individual attempts rather than underlying problem instances. When an evaluation harness collects 8 attempts per task and allocates a 80 percent fraction to training, 83.2 percent of the tasks end up present in both the training and test sets (section 15.4). Under this configuration, test metrics reflect the agent’s ability to recall previously seen problem setups rather than its capability to generalize to novel tasks. Data splitting must occur at the granularity of task groups, with environment-seed variants inheriting their group’s assignment. Furthermore, any downstream derivatives (redacted transcripts, paraphrased prompts, or deduplicated variants) must inherit the assignment of their source task so that syntactic transformations do not accidentally leak problem state across the evaluation boundary.


Pitfall: Cheapening the verifier cascade by dropping or loosening a predicate.
When verification overhead begins to strain cluster budgets, engineers often attempt to reduce costs by removing expensive check predicates or loosening test assertions. This strategy alters the semantic definition of success rather than optimizing the system. In the cascade worksheet, reordering evaluation stages based on their computational cost per rejected candidate saved 16.9 percent of total verification work while maintaining the exact same candidate yield of 20.52 percent (section 15.5.3). Dropping a verification check or silently discarding unresolved edge cases shifts the distribution of accepted trajectories, degrading the downstream training corpus. Performance optimizations should focus on scheduling predicates efficiently under fixed acceptance criteria. In addition, execution pipelines must isolate and report inconclusive runs separately rather than collapsing them into either rejections or unqualified admissions.


Fallacy: Setting a recovery percentage by record count fixes the training mixture.
Trajectory counts provide an unreliable unit of measure when balancing mixed training datasets. A curation system operates across three distinct metrics: raw trajectory records, total stored context tokens, and actively supervised target tokens. In the token budget worksheet, recovery trajectories make up 25 percent of total records, but they represent 44.97 percent of stored tokens and 39.06 percent of selected training targets (section 15.6). Because recovery sequences involve multi-step error correction and verbose environment feedback, their token footprint differs substantially from standard trajectories. Specifying mixture proportions solely by record count miscalculates both the gradient signal allocated to recovery behaviors and the computational budget required for training. Engineers must define training mixtures in terms of supervised target tokens, and validate the resulting policy resilience against held-out task benchmarks under a declared compute budget.


Pitfall: Sizing collection staging from average verifier utilization.
Dimensioning staging storage against average verification throughput invites buffer exhaustion during outages. A verifier pool running at an average utilization of 0.75 appears to have substantial headroom during normal operation. However, automated verification runtimes suffer from bimodal service times. When a faulty test fixture, infrastructure timeout, or broken container environment forces every evaluation to run until its hard execution deadline, service throughput collapses while incoming agent trajectories continue to arrive. In the burst exhaustion worksheet, this prolonged tail latency exhausts the staging store in approximately 3.6 min (section 15.8). Buffer capacity must be bounded by worst-case service latency rather than nominal arrival rates. Robust ingestion architectures use credit-based flow control to restrict outstanding verifier reservations, sizing storage watermarks to absorb both in-flight execution bursts and downstream controller response delays.





A trajectory record and a training example answer different questions. The record says what happened under stated conditions. The example asserts that some part of what happened is worth reproducing, for a named learner, and will be judged against evidence that learner never saw. Every mechanism in the chapter keeps those two apart. Probes keep system defects out of the weights. Task-group splits keep evaluation evidence out of selection. Target selection keeps a faithfully recorded mistake in context and out of the loss. Lineage keeps a transformed record from inheriting a decision made about its source.
Collection credits, lineage envelopes, and the corpus manifest make those decisions operational. The price of the result follows the book’s cost-per-accepted-task form twice over. Checking work per admitted record is cascade cost divided by yield, and cost per emitted artifact is attempt cost divided by emission yield, so yield is the lever in both. Self-improvement changes the source distribution with every round, which is why the manifest keeps demonstrations, comparisons, and rollout fixtures distinct and why external assessment stays outside the loop. Key Takeaways: Give every learning artifact a declared use

Weights are the last remedy, not the first: Counterfactual probes place many failures in context, schemas, or the runtime, where a reversible repair removes them for every model version. Training earns only the residual that survives, and demonstrations, preference comparisons, and rollout fixtures each carry their own admission conditions.
A split protects a claim, not a file: With several attempts per task, a random split over traces puts most tasks on both sides, so the test score rewards recall of solved siblings. Assign whole task groups, carry the assignment into every derived record, and fix it before collection begins.
Cheaper checking must admit the same corpus: Ordering independent, fixed-cost predicates within permissible orders by cost per rejection, \(\CheckSlotTime_i/(1-\CheckPassProbability_i)\), cuts verification work at an unchanged accepted set. Dropping or loosening a predicate buys a different corpus, so its lower unit price is not a saving.
A recorded mistake is context, not a target: Recovery records keep the error and its refusal as conditioning history and select only the assessed correction as supervision. Mixtures are specified in selected targets and budgeted in stored tokens, because context per target differs by class.
Self-selected data narrows what it rewards: When the policy supplies its own records, rising acceptance can hide the recoveries the selector rarely keeps. Distinct action sequences per fixture, pass@1 against pass@\(\IndependentAttemptCount\), and an external anchor show whether the loop is still learning or only repeating itself.
Staging is sized for the burst, not the average: A verifier timeout burst, not average utilization, exhausts reserved staging, so each run holds a credit at the record ceiling until durable disposition. The cheapest stage can bind the illustrated planning rate while generation divided by yield sets its active-resource price.
The manifest is the contract the trainer reads: Records and derived artifacts bind to source versions, checks, transformations, permissions, split membership, and intended consumers. Integrity proves unmodified bytes, not truth or permission, so every derived record earns its own admission decision.



Verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)) now has a concrete decision boundary: evidence supports a specified learning use, and the corpus manifest carries that decision through selection and transformation so the trainer can tell context from targets. The trained policy still faces evaluation and still runs under the runtime’s authority and resource controls.



The principles governing trajectory curation adapt lessons from data mining, information retrieval, and relational databases. Data mining first identified data leakage as a systemic failure mode where information about an evaluation target inadvertently reaches the learner through correlated records (Kaufman et al. 2012). In software modeling, duplicated source files were shown to inflate benchmark accuracy artificially until evaluation splits underwent thorough deduplication (Allamanis 2019). Modern screening pipelines borrow directly from web search, where minwise hashing estimated document resemblance from compact signatures (Broder 1997) and locality-sensitive hashing reduced high-dimensional similarity search to sublinear time (Indyk and Motwani 1998). Database query processing supplied the twin mechanisms of admission control and data provenance. Optimizers established how to order expensive filter predicates by their cost-to-selectivity rank to minimize wasted computation (Hellerstein and Stonebraker 1993), while provenance frameworks formalized which source records produced a derived value and why (Buneman et al. 2001).

Kaufman, Shachar, Saharon Rosset, Claudia Perlich, and Ori Stitelman. 2012. “Leakage in Data Mining: Formulation, Detection, and Avoidance.” ACM Transactions on Knowledge Discovery from Data (TKDD) 6 (4): 1–21.

Zelikman, Eric, Yuhuai Wu, Jesse Mu, and Noah D. Goodman. 2022. “STaR: Bootstrapping Reasoning with Reasoning.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 35: 15476–88.

Uesato, Jonathan, Nate Kushman, Ramana Kumar, Francis Song, Noah Siegel, Lisa Wang, Antonia Creswell, Geoffrey Irving, and Irina Higgins. 2022. “Solving Math Word Problems with Process- and Outcome-Based Feedback.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2211.14275, ahead of print. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2211.14275.

Lightman, Hunter, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, Harri Edwards, Bowen Baker, Teddy Lee, Jan Leike, John Schulman, Ilya Sutskever, and Karl Cobbe. 2024. “Let’s Verify Step by Step.” The Twelfth International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR).
Learning from self-generated execution traces shares an equally deep lineage in reinforcement learning and symbolic reasoning. Classical imitation learning demonstrated that a policy trained exclusively on expert demonstrations compounds its errors when deployed, because small mistakes push the agent into unfamiliar states where it cannot recover (Ross et al. 2011). Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell showed that querying an expert on the learner’s own visited states restores linear error bounds; recovery demonstrations are the systems realization of that theoretical remedy. Expert iteration formalized this dynamic into an alternating loop of generation, search-based selection, and retraining, using tree search to discover improved decisions for a neural network to imitate (Anthony et al. 2017). Bootstrapped reasoning extended this loop to language models by sampling reasoning paths and filtering for traces that reached correct answers (Zelikman et al. 2022). Process supervision then tightened verification from coarse terminal outcomes down to individual reasoning steps (Uesato et al. 2022; Lightman et al. 2024).
Every self-training method eventually meets the same problem, because the filter that selects training data is itself an imperfect part of the system it is meant to improve. Production machine learning pipelines first exposed the systemic risks of hidden feedback loops, where an operational model’s outputs silently shape its own subsequent training distribution (Sculley et al. 2015). Reward modeling demonstrated Goodhart’s law directly: excessive optimization against a learned proxy drives reward scores up while true task quality deteriorates (Gao et al. 2023). Training repeatedly on a model’s own unchecked outputs speeds model collapse, in which diversity shrinks with each round and the rare cases in the tail disappear first (Shumailov et al. 2024). Agentic execution sharpens each of these failure modes because trajectories do not exist in isolation. They execute stateful tool calls, operate under specific environment permissions, and can inadvertently manipulate or game their own evaluation harnesses. The safeguards of this chapter, from verifier cascades and disjoint task-group splits to lineage envelopes and dataset manifests (Gebru et al. 2021), apply classical systems isolation and provenance guarantees directly to the trajectory as the atomic unit of machine learning data.

Shumailov, Ilia, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson, and Yarin Gal. 2024. “AI Models Collapse When Trained on Recursively Generated Data.” Nature 631 (8022): 755–59. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07566-y.
For further reading, start with these:

End-to-end arguments (Saltzer et al. 1984): The classic statement of why a function belongs where it can be implemented completely and correctly. In trajectory curation, this principle argues for repairing tool interfaces and runtime environments directly rather than training model weights to work around platform flaws.
Predicate migration (Hellerstein and Stonebraker 1993): The foundational database paper on ordering expensive filter checks by cost per rejection, formalizing the exchange argument used to structure multi-stage verifier cascades.
Imitation learning as no-regret online learning (Ross et al. 2011): The analysis demonstrating why training exclusively on clean expert prefixes leaves an agent unprepared for its own mistakes, establishing the theoretical rationale for recovery demonstrations.
Hidden technical debt in machine learning systems (Sculley et al. 2015): A comprehensive systems catalog of data dependencies and feedback loops that any self-improving corpus pipeline inherits.
Datasheets for datasets (Gebru et al. 2021): The documentation discipline that a corpus manifest adapts into versioned, machine-auditable metadata fields.
Reward-model overoptimization (Gao et al. 2023): A controlled empirical study showing how aggressive optimization against a learned proxy reward drives proxy scores up while true task quality degrades.

Every given below is a hypothetical problem input chosen for round arithmetic, not a measurement of any system. Each problem asks for a calculation and the curation or collection decision it supports.

Sizing a protected split (Basic). A collection job makes \(\IndependentAttemptCount=5\) attempts on each of 2,000 repair tasks. A colleague proposes assigning individual traces to training with probability \(\TrainingSplitFraction=0.9\) and to the final test otherwise.

Compute the fraction and number of tasks whose attempts straddle the partition, and the smallest \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) at which a majority of tasks straddle.
Compute the probability that a given test attempt has at least one sibling attempt of the same task in training, and state what the resulting test score measures.
The team switches to a group split (section 15.4). Treating tasks as independent trials with an acceptance rate near one half, compute how many task groups the final test must hold for the standard error of its task-level acceptance rate to be at most 0.025, and what fraction of the 2,000 tasks that reserves.

Ordering an admission route (Basic). A demonstration route has three independent predicates beyond record adequacy: a permitted-use lookup \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\) that takes 0.05 s and passes 70 percent of records, a sandboxed test run \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\) that takes 30 s and passes 50 percent, and a model-judged target review \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\) that takes 4 s and passes 80 percent. Target review does not need the test result, and the current order is \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{out}}\to \text{chk}_{\text{target}}\).

Rank the predicates by cost per rejection (equation 2) and choose the order.
Compute \(\ExpectedCheckingTime\) per attempted record and per admitted record for the current and chosen orders (equation 1), and the fraction of verifier-slot work the change saves.
A colleague proposes dropping \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\) instead, because it lowers checking time per admitted record further. Compute that figure and the new yield, and explain why the comparison with part (b) is not a cost comparison at all.

Three denominators for one mixture (Basic). A retained demonstration pool holds 20,000 direct-success records averaging 6,000 stored tokens and 1,000 selected target tokens, and 5,000 recovery records averaging 30,000 stored tokens and 2,500 selected target tokens.

Compute the recovery class’s share of records, stored tokens, and selected targets, and the context per target token for each class.
The team wants recovery to supply half of the selected targets. Holding total selected targets at the current value, compute the presentations each class needs, how many recovery records must repeat, and the change in processed tokens.
Holding processed tokens at the current value instead, compute the total selected targets at the same half-and-half mixture. State which budget this team should fix when training time is the scarce resource, and what the arithmetic cannot decide.

Spending a sampling budget on contrast (Intermediate). A collector has 8,000 attempts for 1,000 repair fixtures in three difficulty bands: 400 fixtures with per-attempt pass rate \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.1\), 400 with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.5\), and 200 with \(\AttemptPassProbability=0.9\). Attempts are independent, and each fixture receives \(\IndependentAttemptCount=8\).

For each band and in total, compute the expected number of fixtures that yield at least one success and the expected number of mixed groups (equation 3). Compute the attempts spent per mixed group.
A colleague proposes dropping the easy band and spending its 1,600 attempts on the hard band at \(\IndependentAttemptCount=12\). Compute the new expected number of mixed groups and state what the imitation corpus loses.
Decide whether to adopt the proposal for a group-relative objective and for an imitation artifact, and explain why the easy band’s all-success groups are not wasted attempts.

Reviewing after selection (Intermediate). A cohort makes \(\IndependentAttemptCount=10\) independent attempts on each of 200 tasks. Each attempt succeeds with probability 0.2 and costs $0.50 for generation, verification, and storage. Every successful attempt goes to human target review at $6, which passes 75 percent of the successes it sees, independently. The selector emits at most one artifact per task, the first passing success in attempt order.

Compute the expected number of emitted artifacts, the cohort cost, and \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\) (equation 5).
The team instead reviews a task’s successes in attempt order and stops at its first pass. Show that the set of emitting tasks is unchanged, and compute the expected reviews per task, the new cohort cost, and \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\).
A second proposal halves \(\IndependentAttemptCount\) to 5 with the stopping review in place. Compute \(\CostPerEmittedArtifact\) and the emitted count, and decide between the two proposals, naming what the cheaper unit price costs the corpus.

The research agent’s collector (Intermediate). The research agent reads untrusted sources, so each collection record keeps the retrieved pages that its claims cite, and the permitted-use review of that retained content is expensive. A collector runs 32 accelerators at 40 accelerator-seconds per attempt, checks attempts on 16 verifier slots, and writes records of at most 1 GB to a store that sustains 500 MB/s (decimal units). The independent predicates take and pass as follows: record adequacy \(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\), 0.02 s and 98 percent; permitted use \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\), 6 s and 60 percent; citation grounding \(\text{chk}_{\text{out}}\), 3 s and 70 percent; target review \(\text{chk}_{\text{target}}\), 2 s and 90 percent. No predicate depends on another’s result. Use the saturated planning model with sufficient end-to-end credits, no additional shared service bottleneck, and each write charged at its record ceiling; the calculated rate is not a measurement of actual collector throughput.

Order the predicates by equation 2 and compute \(\ExpectedCheckingTime\) and the yield \(\AdmissionRouteYield\).
Evaluate equation 4, name the binding stage in this model, and compute its planned admitted records per hour. Compute the write bandwidth that would let generation bind, and the admitted rate then.
The binding stage differs from the repair collector of notebook 15.6. Explain why, and evaluate a proposal to cut the record ceiling to 100 MB by truncating retrieved pages. Propose a design that lowers stored bytes without weakening \(\text{chk}_{\text{record}}\) or \(\text{chk}_{\text{use}}\).

Staging production feedback for the support agent (Advanced). The support agent serves customers who are waiting, so its collector captures production sessions it cannot delay or pause. Sessions finish at \(\ArrivalRate=50\) per second and last 120 s, with capture running throughout. A policy-grounding judge assesses each captured record on \(\WorkerCount=40\) slots in a mean of 0.6 s. Records have a ceiling of 250 KB, and staging holds \(\StagingStoreCapacity=4\) GB and at most 10,000 outstanding records (decimal units). During an incident the judge’s endpoint degrades and every assessment runs to its 10 s timeout. The controller needs 20 s to act, and staging starts nearly empty.

Compute the nominal utilization, the degraded capacity, and the staging growth rate. Compute the time until the byte limit and until the record-count limit is reached, and state which binds.
Size the high watermark on the binding limit, counting records from sessions already capturing and growth during the controller’s delay.
Backpressure on the source is unavailable here, unlike in the repair collector. Compute the capture fraction that holds staging steady during the incident, and critique a proposal to keep capturing only the shortest sessions. State what the corpus manifest must record about the uncaptured sessions.

Designing a leakage screen within a review budget (Advanced). A corpus of 100,000 records is screened with 128-component MinHash signatures before split assignment (section 15.4.3). Assume that 2,000 record pairs are true relatives with Jaccard similarity 0.8 and that every other pair has similarity 0.1. Reviewers can inspect 20,000 candidate pairs per screening pass.

For banding designs of 32 bands of 4 rows, 16 of 8, and 8 of 16, compute the expected false candidates among unrelated pairs and the recall of true relatives. Decide which designs fit the review budget.
Redesign the screen so that it keeps the recall of the 32-by-4 design and fits the budget, using the full signature. Justify the chosen threshold with the estimator’s standard error, and estimate the machine work it adds.
Name a relationship that no choice of bands will catch, and the mechanism that must catch it instead.



What’s Next: From corpus membership to learning targetsTranslating an admitted recovery record into a gradient update requires reinforcing the correction rather than the refused proposal it conditions on. Trajectory Fine-Tuning opens with the record this chapter published to repair_demonstrations_v1, whose targets recovery_targets_v1 already fixed. It first asks which parts of the repair behavior belong in weights at all, then turns the curation contract into training examples. Serialization must reconstruct each prefix exactly as the agent received it, loss masking must assign direct supervised loss terms to the selected targets alone, and batching must keep independent examples from reading one another. Preference learning applies a different objective to justified comparisons. Curation decides which material is eligible and why, and the next chapter decides how that material shapes an update and whether the changed policy earns a release under the same runtime controls.

title: 15 Trajectory Curation
text:
Agent stack focus for this chapter.
Why is an accepted agent trajectory not automatically a good training example?
Every agent run leaves a durable record of what it saw, proposed, and achieved, and a team preparing the next policy is tempted to train on that record directly. A record, however, answers a different question than a training example does. An accepted trial can contain a malformed call that the runtime refused, a failure can stem from a broken tool schema that no weight update repairs, and two attempts at the same task split across training and evaluation turn a test score into a measure of recall. Imitating such records teaches the model its own mistakes and workarounds, and filtering them by outcome alone narrows behavior toward whatever the filter happens to reward. Curation therefore decides, before any gradient is computed, whether a failure belongs in the weights at all, which records may serve which learner, which tokens are targets and which are context, and what evidence and permissions travel with every record derived from the original run.

Learning Objectives

Justify a learning use for a residual failure and distinguish imitation material, preference comparisons, and rollout fixtures
Design versioned collection fixtures and protected splits for a stated generalization claim
Construct admission predicates and compare verification costs without changing their criteria
Assign recovery and negative records to appropriate roles while distinguishing trajectory counts, stored tokens, and loss-bearing tokens
Assess how selection rules and sampling budgets change the diversity and yield of a self-improvement loop
Size bounded collection flow against downstream capacity, and price an emitted artifact by attempt cost and emission yield
Defend a versioned corpus manifest with transformation lineage, permitted uses, and intended consumers

title: 15 Trajectory Curation
text:
The evaluation harness of Agent Evaluation and the operational record of Operating Agents produced more than a release decision. While they judged the repair agent (Four lighthouse workloads) over repeated attempts on the connection-pool repair task, they also accumulated a durable trajectory log. The log captures every trial in granular detail: the environment observations delivered to the model, the code edits it proposed, the invalid tool calls rejected by the runtime, the subsequent recovery steps, and the final verdict scored against the task acceptance criteria. Some runs passed cleanly, others failed outright, and several remain stalled in pending states because regression suites or accounting checks timed out. To an engineering team preparing the next iteration of the policy, these accumulated interaction logs look like the natural, abundant raw material for fine-tuning.



Curation changes what the policy learns from its records and leaves every exposure where the runtime closes it.
The machinery built so far, however, does not specify how to translate raw logs into training data. The acceptance contract defined in The Task Acceptance Contract evaluates the final outcome of an entire trial rather than assigning credit to individual tokens or tool calls within it. Consequently, an accepted verdict alone cannot distinguish between an optimal tool call and an accidental stumble that the agent managed to survive. Imitating raw logs reproduces whatever they contain. If an agent wastes ten calls exploring invalid syntax before hitting the correct command, blind imitation trains the next model to repeat that exploratory churn. Furthermore, rigorous evaluation requires held-out task distributions that the training process never touches. If an engineer partitions data naively at the trace level, different attempts on the same underlying task fixture land on both sides of the train-test split, silently destroying evaluation integrity. Finally, because the agent generated these records under its own behavioral distribution, any filtering rule directly shapes what the subsequent policy will produce, inducing feedback dynamics across training generations.
Bridging the gap between raw execution logs and active model training requires a dedicated systems stage. Trajectory curation selects, labels, and transforms recorded interactions for a declared learning use while preserving the evidence and constraints that justify that use. Where evaluation establishes whether a trial satisfied its specification under fixed conditions, curation resolves a different operational question: which behaviors and tasks the learning process should absorb, which steps must be masked or rewritten, and how to preserve statistical isolation across splits. The end product of this pipeline is a versioned, reproducible corpus tailored to specific training consumers, accompanied by strict provenance records rather than an ad hoc collection of success flags. Transforming these admitted records into tokenized inputs and loss objectives becomes the downstream responsibility of Trajectory Fine-Tuning.
This chapter follows the repair agent from diagnosis to a published corpus. A failure caused by a truncated observation is the case whose remedy lies outside the weights, and a recovery from a refused edit becomes the record carried all the way into a corpus. The stages run in the order the risks arise. Before anything is collected, the failure must be shown to belong in the weights (section 15.2), and the evidence that will later judge the trained model must be fixed and protected (section 15.3, section 15.4). Collected records then pass admission checks specific to the learner that will consume them (section 15.5), recovery records are divided into context and targets (section 15.6), and the feedback created when a policy generates its own data is bounded (section 15.7). The remaining sections keep the collector within its capacity (section 15.8), bind every record to its lineage (section 15.9), and carry one record through the whole chain (section 15.10). The first decision is triage, because a failure that does not belong to the model should never reach a corpus.

title: 15 Trajectory Curation
text:
In Agent Evaluation, the repair agent’s trial on pool_repair_01 submitted workspace ws_r19 with its targeted reproducer passing, while regression and resource-accounting checks remained pending. The run was therefore neither an accepted repair nor a valid demonstration. A separate trial of the same task failed outright after the observation interface silently truncated a search result. The postmortem’s controlled ablation traced most of that failure to the interface: once pagination was added, every continuation from the saved prefix reached an accepted repair, even though the ablation did not prove the model blameless. A team that had collected those truncated-observation runs for training would have taught the model to work around an interface defect that a single adapter change removed. An execution failure belongs in the trajectory curation pipeline only after diagnosis confirms that model weights are the right target for repair. Modifying weights is justified only when confronting a genuine capability gap: an operational failure that persists even when the model receives complete context, interacts through a well-formed interface, and runs in a healthy runtime with adequate resources. Every other failure stems from an external system defect that calls for a cheaper, far more reversible engineering fix.


↩︎ The controlled ablation that traced the truncated-observation failure to the interface is established in Controlled diagnostic experiments.


Separating a capability gap from an external system defect starts with decomposing the failing trace, because the final failure verdict on pool_repair_01 alone revealed nothing about which subsystem broke. The postmortem analysis in Incident Postmortems separated three distinct events within that truncated-observation incident: an interface defect (the search excerpt arrived without truncation metadata), a forbidden action proposal (the next response proposed replacing a file outside the repair scope), and a successful runtime refusal (the admission gate rejected that proposal before dispatch). Such findings often coexist within a single execution trace. Adding missing truncation metadata repairs the interface contract. Retaining the admission guard enforces system boundaries against out-of-scope dispatches. Training the policy to seek additional evidence addresses model behavior. Each diagnostic finding demands its own engineering remedy.
Table 1 connects diagnostic findings to candidate system interventions and their corresponding learning objectives. Because multiple failure modes frequently overlap in production traces, engineers must evaluate each candidate intervention under realistic operating conditions. The sequence in which teams investigate and apply these remedies follows directly from their computational cost and operational reversibility.


↩︎ Failure attribution, and the limit of what each finding shows, is established in Fault attribution.



Table 1: Diagnostic Findings and Learning Uses: A direct system repair and a behavioral learning objective can both be justified by the same incident. Each proposal needs its own evidence and scope.










Diagnostic finding
Direct system intervention to investigate
Possible learning use and its limit




A required fact was absent from the delivered context
Repair retrieval or assembly and preserve source and omission status
Teach the model to recognize insufficient evidence and request it; weights cannot supply a reliable current fact that was never observed


A tool description or response violated its interface contract
Correct the schema, documentation, or observation adapter
Teach interpretation of valid status and recovery information; learned habits do not repair the interface itself


An operation encountered an execution failure or unresolved outcome
Investigate endpoint behavior, resource bounds, and recovery ownership
Teach bounded recovery or escalation under represented uncertainty; a retry proposal cannot establish that the earlier effect failed


The model repeatedly chose an unsupported or ineffective continuation
Compare prompts, examples, and targeted policy updates on declared tasks
Collect justified alternative actions or recovery targets; repeated failure alone does not identify a unique cause or prove that training will help









Fine-tuning a model to compensate for an omitted context fact or an ambiguous tool schema is premature fine-tuning, an expensive waste of compute and curation effort on a defect that a prompt or schema fix cures in minutes. To prevent that misallocation, the intervention ladder orders failure remedies by ascending engineering cost and descending reversibility. Its rungs are context retrieval and assembly, tool definitions and schemas, runtime execution controls, supervised fine-tuning (updating weights to imitate selected demonstrations), and reinforcement learning (updating weights to raise a verified reward on fresh rollouts). Engineers test the inexpensive, reversible rungs first by default, advancing to a weight update only when diagnostic evidence establishes a genuine capability gap and confirms that training improves the behavior rather than masking an interface or runtime defect.
This ordering reflects how cost, reversibility, and enforcement guarantees change across the stack. Engineering and compute costs rise sharply at each rung. Editing a prompt assembly pipeline, schema definition, or runtime timeout modifies version-controlled configuration that an engineer can test against integration fixtures in minutes. Retraining weights, by contrast, requires curating a trajectory corpus, running accelerator jobs, and re-evaluating every capability the model serves rather than only the failing task.
Those cost differences are compounded by reversibility and blast radius. A defect repaired at a lower rung reverts cleanly as a configuration change whose impact is limited to the callers of the changed tool or prompt. Updating model weights, by contrast, alters behavior across the entire input space, and rolling back a checkpoint discards every concurrent improvement alongside the targeted fix. Reinforcement learning sits at the top of the ladder for the same reason: beyond the dataset and validation demands of supervised fine-tuning, it requires distributed rollout fleets, isolated reward verification harnesses, and optimization controls that keep the policy from exploiting loopholes in the reward check.
Even when a weight update succeeds, statistical weights cannot replace runtime enforcement. A fine-tuned policy may propose out-of-scope tool calls far less often, but lower observed failure rates do not guarantee compliance on every permitted input. Invariant closure (principle \(\ref{pri-invariant-closure}\)) requires that execution runtimes never assume policy compliance; resource budgets, authorization checks, and process sandboxes remain hard boundaries regardless of how thoroughly the model has been trained.
The end-to-end argument (Saltzer et al. 1984) yields the same conclusion for tool interfaces: a function belongs where it can be implemented completely and correctly. A typed action contract (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-strict-action-abi}\)) provides enforceable guarantees across any model version placed behind it. By contrast, fine-tuning a model to guess fields omitted by an API schema teaches brittle habits that break as soon as the interface changes. An integration test on an observation adapter can verify directly that truncated outputs return explicit pagination markers, resolving the ambiguity at the interface layer without asking downstream models to guess what was cut.
Empirical evidence, rather than administrative habit, decides when a failure climbs the ladder. Engineers test each lower rung with a counterfactual probe, a controlled re-execution of the recorded failure trace with that rung’s suspected defect removed. A context probe begins by injecting the missing fact directly into the prompt. An interface probe resumes matched saved prefixes with corrected tool descriptions or schemas and samples fresh continuations under the controlled conditions of Statistical Evaluation Rigor (since replaying a fixed proposal would test only the validation or adapter boundary, not whether the model chooses a different action). If both checks leave the failure intact, a runtime probe runs the identical tool payload inside an isolated sandbox with relaxed resource limits. Whenever a failure disappears under one of these probes, the result supports a repair at that rung under the probed conditions without ruling out other contributing causes. Probing in ladder order routes each resolved defect to an immediate, reversible repair, so only the failures that survive all three probes reach the weights (figure 1). Even then, checkpoints trained on this residual must pass the evaluation protocol of Statistical Evaluation Rigor rather than ship merely because model weights were the last hypothesis left.






Figure 1: Probes Before Weights: Under the default diagnostic route, counterfactual probes evaluate a measured failure in ascending ladder order. A failure that disappears under a probe routes to an immediate systems repair, modifying versioned artifacts that revert cleanly as configuration. Only failures that survive every lower-rung probe reach the weight modification stages, where supervised fine-tuning precedes reinforcement learning. Engineering cost rises and operational reversibility falls from top to bottom.



The intervention ladder is a diagnostic discipline rather than a rigid queue. When counterfactual probes immediately expose a capability gap in an agent that fails despite complete context, a clear schema, and a healthy runtime, engineers can skip lower-rung changes and proceed directly to targeted training, provided the empirical evidence of the gap is recorded first. Moreover, production environments routinely return partial outputs, transient network timeouts, and service-unavailable errors; training an agent to handle those degraded conditions is a valid behavioral objective, not an excuse to leave broken interfaces unfixed. Notebook 15.1 prices the compute and reliability trade-offs across this hierarchy for a representative failure workload.

Napkin Math 15.1: Pricing the ladder for one failure mixProblem: A hypothetical maintenance agent executes 50,000 trajectories per month, with 6 percent failing (3,000 total failures). Counterfactual probes attribute 70 percent of the failures to a tool schema that omits a required field and 20 percent to sandbox startup timeouts; only the remaining failures survive every probe. One engineering team repairs the tool schema and scales the sandbox pool before considering training. A second team bypasses system repairs and fine-tunes the base model on all failing trajectories using corrected demonstration targets, training on 4,096-token sequences across 3 epochs. What failure modes does each path eliminate, and what is the direct compute cost of the training run?
Variables: The underlying model contains 70.6 billion parameters. Standard transformer training requires approximately 6 floating-point operations (FLOPs) per parameter per token (\(6\Parameters \DatasetSize\)). A dedicated cluster node of 8 accelerators provides a dense 16-bit compute peak of 989 TFLOP/s per device while sustaining 30 percent model FLOPs utilization (MFU). Accelerator rental costs $4 per hour. Both paths assume that diagnostic attribution is correct and exclude data curation, annotation, and software engineering labor.
Math: System-level repairs eliminate the 2,700 failures attributed to interface and runtime defects (90 percent of all failures), deploying and reverting cleanly as versioned configuration updates. In contrast, fine-tuning indiscriminately across all 3,000 failures trains on 3,000 \(\times\) 4,096 \(\times\) 3 = 36,864,000 tokens. Evaluating \(6 \times \text{parameters} \times \text{tokens}\) yields 1.56 × 10¹⁹ FLOPs of total training compute. At sustained cluster throughput, this workload requires 1.8 h of wall-clock time (14.6 accelerator-hours), resulting in an accelerator invoice of $58. Fine-tuning exclusively on the 300 residual failures that survived diagnostic probing costs only $6.
Result: The direct accelerator invoice of $58 is modest, so raw compute expenditure does not govern intervention ordering. The decisive factor is the architectural debt and reliability profile left in production. Under premature fine-tuning, the tool schema still omits the required field and the sandbox pool still times out under load; consequently, those operational failures return whenever the model guesses incorrectly or cluster load spikes. Furthermore, teaching the model to work around missing fields creates fragile behavioral compensations that collapse as soon as the interface changes. Its training corpus also squanders curation and review effort on incidents whose proper remedy was never behavioral. Under the systems repair path, engineers resolve 90 percent of all failures permanently for every model checkpoint, leaving a residual of 300 failures whose curated corpus is focused entirely on genuine policy gaps.
Systems insight: The primary risk of premature fine-tuning is rarely compute expenditure; it is architectural misattribution. While an invoice of $58 appears manageable, training cannot fix the 90 percent of failures rooted below the weights. Only a systems repair resolves those defects permanently across all current and future model generations. The governing engineering principle is to attribute failures with counterfactual probes first, remediate what lies below the weights in software, and train exclusively on the residual capability gap that survives.


Once diagnostic probing isolates a genuine residual failure, engineers must specify the exact behavior to train before gathering examples. For the repair agent, the paginated interface now supplies completeness metadata, but a policy can still ignore it. Runs on the repaired interface that receive that metadata and still draw a conclusion from a partial result form the residual that a learning objective can target. An effective objective does not aim vaguely to “fix failed trajectories.” Instead, it trains the policy to inspect the completeness metadata of a search result, issue a permitted follow-up query when pagination indicates more records exist, and state remaining data boundaries when limits are reached. Evaluating the fine-tuned model requires checking both the final task outcome and the efficiency of the path, including redundant reads, context token use, and unsupported intermediate claims. A policy can easily learn a circuitous investigation habit that raises task acceptance at the cost of high latency and token spend, or an overly aggressive shortcut that skips required checks; neither flaw shows up in cross-entropy training loss alone.



Targeting that residual behavior does not mean keeping only clean, end-to-end successes, because a pipeline that discards every flawed run throws away most of its training signal. A trace that stumbled on a malformed tool call before recovering still demonstrates how to repair the mistake, and a run that failed outright on a subtle race condition still captures a valuable test environment. Depending on what evidence a trace preserves, a single recorded interaction can feed three distinct learning artifacts, each governed by its own admission criteria.
Imitation material consists of complete demonstrations or extracted trajectory segments whose decision steps represent exemplary behavior under the supplied context. When curating an error-recovery sequence, the ingestion pipeline can retain an initial malformed tool proposal and its runtime rejection within the conversational history, while selecting only the subsequent corrected action as the supervised target. Faithfully preserving an error in conversational context provides realism, but supervising a model to imitate an unnecessary retry loop degrades runtime efficiency. Curation explicitly designates the target tokens to be reinforced.
A preference comparison pairs alternative trajectories generated from a shared initial context, attaching an explicit, justified preference ordering. Two runs of a task form a valid comparison pair only when their initial state, environment configuration, and accessible action spaces are identical. Furthermore, a failing or degraded run belongs in the rejected slot only when an evaluator records explicit diagnostic criteria explaining why its trajectory was inferior. These supporting assessments, tie-breaking criteria, and conditioning contexts allow offline preference optimization methods to construct statistically sound loss objectives.


↪ The trajectory preference loss, which scores the preferred and dispreferred records against a frozen reference policy, is developed in The trajectory preference loss.
A rollout fixture bundles a reproducible task environment, versioned configuration fixtures, and an automated grading specification to support online exploration during reward-based reinforcement learning. An unsuccessful execution attempt often reveals a valuable environmental corner case even when none of its recorded actions warrant imitation. In this setting, the trace does not provide demonstration data; rather, it seeds a versioned simulation fixture that recreates the problematic state so the policy can explore alternative trajectories and optimize against the reward specification.


↪ Optimizing a policy against verifiable checks on the rollouts it executes in such an environment is developed in Foundations of Verifiable Rewards.
These three downstream roles explain why a curation pipeline preserves execution failures rather than discarding them. A single flawed trajectory can support diagnostic root-cause analysis, provide multi-turn context for an error-recovery demonstration, serve as a negative example within a preference comparison, or seed a simulation fixture for online reinforcement learning. The intended downstream artifact dictates the admission evidence required to validate the record. Symmetrically, successful trajectories that produce no state mutations (an agent correctly refusing an out-of-scope request or answering a read-only query) constitute valid imitation demonstrations whenever the task specification requires restraint. Producing a nonempty workspace modification is never an inherent admission requirement.
Every proposed trajectory collection campaign must formally document four elements: the specific behavioral capability to be trained, the target artifact format, the empirical evidence required for admission, and the held-out evaluation claim that will assess the trained model. When trajectory evaluations rely on automated model judges or human annotators, those evaluations must operate under explicit rubrics with evaluator coverage and scoring variance fully exposed.
Curation produces defensible artifacts for declared uses, while held-out evaluation decides whether the resulting model update actually improves the system. That separation is the decision boundary of verified trajectory post-training (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-trajectory-post-training}\)), which holds that a recorded outcome does not by itself determine how a trajectory may be used for learning. Two obligations follow before any record is collected. Fixtures must translate the desired behavior into collectible tasks, and the evaluation split must be reserved first, so that data selection never consumes the evidence later used to judge it.

title: 15 Trajectory Curation
text:
When an agent collection worker attempts a complex task such as connection-pool repair repeatedly, it can generate a distinct candidate solution on every run. If an attempt inherits residual state from an earlier repair attempt, however, it no longer demonstrates solving the problem from the declared initial state. Conversely, if a collection pipeline records only the final passing patch, it discards the sequence of tool invocations, intermediate terminal outputs, and error-recovery decisions that explain how that patch was derived. A collection fixture prevents both failures by preserving reproducible task conditions while recording the comprehensive execution evidence demanded by downstream learning algorithms.
The task fixture of Task fixtures already fixes the execution baseline (initial state, dependencies, permitted interfaces, variation policy, evidence boundary, and reset). Trajectory curation layers a collection contract on top of that fixture. The collection contract specifies why the task belongs in the corpus, which interaction records the ingestion pipeline may retain, and what intermediate evidence downstream admission filters will require.


If a new collection run on pool_repair_01 reuses the trial identity of ws_r19, overwrites the unresolved record of test_r18, or lets engineers adjust admission rules after inspecting the sampled outputs, the pipeline corrupts its own audit trail. Separating the versioned identities of the task specification (pool_repair_01), execution fixture (pool_fixture_v1), and evaluation criteria (repair_accept_v1) prevents that collision. Each new collection attempt receives its own run identity and produces an independent candidate artifact, while the historical evaluation candidate ws_r19 stays permanently bound to its original trial, and a newly passing test run never alters an earlier unresolved record such as test_r18.
The collection manifest references the underlying evaluation fixture and records the operational decisions summarized in table 2. Defining these fields before sampling begins ensures that data engineers fix the intended training role and capture requirements in advance, rather than biasing the sample or fitting admission rules retroactively to observed outputs.



Table 2: Collection Decisions Attached to a Fixture: The collection manifest extends the experimental contract with intended use, relationships, and evidence requirements. Actual admission follows inspection of the resulting record.










Collection field
Decision recorded
Consequence for the repair




Learning use
Proposed behavior to improve and intended artifact consumer
Collect evidence for interpreting failed checks and choosing a justified next action, not merely final patches


Source and permitted use
Task origin, access conditions, retention scope, and applicable restrictions on derived data
Permission to inspect a repository does not by itself authorize exporting its contents into a corpus


Task relationships
Stable task identity, source lineage, and links to variants or shared solutions
Repeated attempts and derived variants remain identifiable when splits are assigned


Collection configuration
Sampling system, prompt and tool versions, allowed variation, and attempt-selection policy
Distinguish a policy change from a changed task or collector


Required capture
Delivered context, proposals, matched observations, candidate identity, and criterion-level evidence needed for the proposed use
Preserve what supported each decision, including incomplete observations and rejected proposals


Admission policy
Versioned conditions for accepting a record into each proposed artifact, with unresolved cases handled explicitly
A targeted pass does not become whole-task acceptance or automatic demonstration eligibility






What the manifest must capture depends on the consumer that will train on the artifact. A demonstration selected for supervised error recovery must preserve the diagnostic context, error messages, and intermediate inspection steps that explain why a corrective action was taken.
