title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
This appendix supplies the serving arithmetic behind model-call latency, attention-state storage, and resource occupancy. It provides reusable estimates for comparing prompt processing with generation, sizing retained state, and separating average demand from capacity guarantees. Each estimate states its assumptions so that a reader can substitute another model, serving configuration, or workload without treating the reference values as universal performance claims.


Start from the agent-level question in table 1 and jump to the section that derives its answer. Each entry states the simplifying assumptions behind its floor or pool estimate so that a reader can calibrate it against measured serving telemetry.



Table 1: Question-to-Derivation Lookup: Agent-level questions and the sections that derive their answers.










If you need to know…
Jump to…
What you get




When output generation and prompt processing have different per-token costs
section 1.1
Conditional compute and bandwidth floors, not measured service latency


When attention work matters in long-context prefill
section 1.1
The attention term and the length at which it matches the weight term


How batching changes amortized serving time and per-stream latency
section 1.1
Weight reuse across streams and the limits of a weight-only estimate


How sampling placement, grammar masks, and speculative verification add work
section 1.2
Transfer and storage formulas, plus the conditions for exact speculative sampling


How much memory a trajectory’s context occupies, and how attention design changes it
section 1.3
Bytes per token from model geometry, multi-head versus grouped versus multi-query attention


How tool waits change live state and how load changes waiting
section 1.4
Little’s law with matched boundaries and a scoped single-server waiting approximation


Which model, accelerator, and node values the book assumes
section 1.5
The reference inputs, ready to substitute









Prompt processing can reuse a model’s weights across many token positions, whereas unbatched generation uses those weights for one new position at a time. That difference can make prefill arithmetic-bound and decode bandwidth-bound. Neither regime follows from the phase name alone. Prompt length, batching, attention traffic, and the serving implementation determine which resource limits an actual call. A weight-only estimate isolates the reuse effect before adding those complications.
A model call processes the uncached prompt during prefill and generates new tokens during decode. Both phases use the same weights, but the reference calculation yields a ratio of about 295 between the unbatched weight-transfer floor per output token and the arithmetic floor per prompt token. We compare these conditional floors to explain the bandwidth constraint (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)), not to predict the ratio of measured call latencies or token prices.


Adding more floating-point units to an accelerator does not speed up single-stream token generation when the chip spends most of each step waiting for weight bytes to arrive from high-bandwidth memory. An accelerator has two limits, the rate \(\PeakRate\) at which it performs arithmetic (operations per second) and the rate \(\Bandwidth\) at which its memory delivers data (bytes per second). A computation’s arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) is the number of operations it performs per byte it moves. The roofline model (Williams et al. 2009) gives a performance ceiling \(\AttainableComputeRate\) from whichever limit binds first:

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[\AttainableComputeRate = \min\left( \PeakRate, \; \ArithmeticIntensity \cdot \Bandwidth \right)\]
The two ceilings meet at the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate / \Bandwidth\). Below the ridge, bandwidth supplies the lower ceiling; above it, arithmetic supplies the lower ceiling. Actual performance can fall below either ceiling because of implementation and scheduling overhead. For the reference accelerator at 8-bit precision, \(\PeakRate\) = 1,979 trillion operations per second and \(\Bandwidth\) = 3.35 TB/s, so \(\RooflineRidgePoint \approx\) 591 operations per byte.



A dense transformer with \(\Parameters\) active parameters performs about \(2\Parameters\) weight-related operations per token, one multiply and one add per weight. Its weight payload is \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes, where \(\WeightElementStorageSize\) is bytes per parameter. The approximation counts this payload once per pass; prefill and decode differ in how many tokens share that read. Sparse activation and weight reuse from another cache level require a different traffic count.
In the weight-only model, prefill shares each weight read across \(\SequenceLength\) prompt positions, giving intensity \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength / (\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize) = 2\SequenceLength/\WeightElementStorageSize\). When that intensity exceeds the ridge and arithmetic approaches the stated peak, the per-token time approaches the following floor. Small prompts, kernel tiling, attention, and additional memory traffic can invalidate those assumptions.
\[\PerTokenPrefillTime \approx \frac{2\Parameters}{\PeakRate} \tag{1}\]
Ordinary decode for one stream generates one token per pass, with each token depending on the preceding prefix. If the weights must be read from the modeled memory on every pass, the weight-only intensity is \(2/\WeightElementStorageSize\), or 2 operations per byte at 8-bit precision, about 0.34 percent of the ridge. Streaming those weights imposes a time floor even before attention-state traffic and overhead:
\[\PerTokenDecodeTime \ge \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth} \tag{2}\]
For the reference model, with \(\Parameters\) = 70.6 billion parameters at 8-bit precision, equation 2 gives a decode floor of 21.1 ms per output token, and equation 1 gives about 71 µs per prompt token. In the following comparison only, the time symbols denote these weight-only estimates rather than observed times:
\[\frac{\PerTokenDecodeTime}{\PerTokenPrefillTime} = \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize / \Bandwidth}{2\Parameters / \PeakRate} = \frac{\PeakRate \, \WeightElementStorageSize}{2 \Bandwidth} = \frac{\WeightElementStorageSize}{2} \, \RooflineRidgePoint \tag{3}\]
which is 295 for the reference configuration. Model size cancels in this approximation because both estimates count the same dense-model weights. The result assumes weight-dominated unbatched decode, peak-rate prefill, and negligible attention and serving overhead; it is not a measured ratio shared by every model on the accelerator. Within that model, the same number gives the number of tokens per pass at which arithmetic time meets weight-transfer time, a threshold used in the batching and speculative-decoding estimates below.
The estimate separates two quantities an agent engineer can influence. Shorter output reduces generation work, and avoiding repeated processing of an unchanged input prefix reduces prefill work. Which change matters more depends on the request lengths, serving configuration, and measurement boundary; token counts alone do not determine a service bill. The Cost of a Model Call prices a bounded example under explicit assumptions. A localized edit illustrates the output-side choice by omitting unchanged file contents, without implying that every compact serialization improves task success.



Attention adds prefill work that grows with the context itself, which the weight-only floor in equation 1 omits. The token at position \(\CausalTokenPosition\) compares its query with \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier keys and combines \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier values, about \(4 \LayerCount d \CausalTokenPosition\) operations for a model with \(\LayerCount\) layers and width \(\HiddenDimension\). Summed over a causal prefill of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens, attention adds about \(2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2\) operations to the \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength\) of the weights, so
\[\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) \approx \frac{2\Parameters \SequenceLength + 2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2}{\PeakRate} \tag{4}\]
The quadratic term equals the linear one at \(\SequenceLength^* = \Parameters / (\LayerCount \HiddenDimension)\), about 108,000 tokens for the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80 and \(\HiddenDimension\) = 8,192. At 32,768 tokens, attention adds about 30 percent to the prefill arithmetic, and beyond \(\SequenceLength^*\) it dominates. Under this fixed-throughput approximation, prefill time grows faster than linearly with length. Observed time to first token also depends on queueing, reuse, and the serving schedule. The logical selection problem in Usable Working Context determines which information the request needs; the estimate here prices the processing work without establishing an optimal context length or task-quality threshold.



A server can batch decode steps from several trajectories. If one weight read serves \(\BatchSize\) streams, the step produces one token for each stream. Ignoring the attention state each stream also reads, the time of one step is
\[\BatchedDecodeStepTime(\BatchSize) \approx \max\left( \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth}, \; \frac{2 \Parameters \BatchSize}{\PeakRate} \right) \tag{5}\]
and the step stays at the memory-bound floor until \(\BatchSize\) reaches \(\PeakRate\,\WeightElementStorageSize / 2\Bandwidth\), the ratio of equation 3. Within this weight-only approximation, adding streams up to that threshold leaves step time unchanged, while step time divided by the number of generated tokens falls as \(1/\BatchSize\) toward \(2\Parameters/\PeakRate\). This is amortized serving time, not the latency of one stream or the price charged by a service. Repeated input adds prefill work when the prefix cannot be reused, but the bill also depends on utilization and the service’s accounting rules.
A trajectory cannot batch a future call whose input depends on an observation it has not received. Its current call can nevertheless share a physical serving batch with calls from other trajectories. That batching can change queueing and per-step latency; a dependent client stream is not evidence that the server runs at batch size one. The weight-only estimate also omits attention-state traffic. Each stream reads its own keys and values, approximately \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\) bytes for a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens (section 1.3). Long contexts can therefore bind bandwidth or capacity before the arithmetic threshold in equation 5 is reached. Section 1.4 relates resident state to the number of live trajectories.



A large admitted prefill can delay decode work sharing its execution resources. Chunked prefill divides that work into bounded token slices that the scheduler can interleave or co-schedule with decodes (Agrawal et al. 2024). The token budget limits admitted token positions, not elapsed iteration time; realized gaps and prompt-completion time depend on context lengths, batching, resource contention, and implementation overhead. The weight-only estimate in equation 5 explains one opportunity for amortization, not a latency guarantee. Chunked Prefill Scheduling develops the policy trade-off.

Agrawal, Amey, Nitin Kedia, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, Alexey Tumanov, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2024. “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), 117–34.




Token selection, optional grammar constraints, and speculative verification add work beyond the model’s forward pass. Their placement determines which data crosses a device boundary and which dependencies remain on the generation path. The formulas below separate payload sizes from synchronization and computation costs; a small payload alone does not establish a low latency.


Copying a 128,000-entry floating-point logit vector across a host bus on every decode step of a multi-stream batch moves tens of megabytes per second before a single token is chosen. At each step the model produces one logit per vocabulary entry. Let \(|\TokenVocabulary|\) be the vocabulary size and \(\LogitStorageSize\) the bytes stored per logit. One vector occupies \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes. If \(\BatchSize\) streams each emit \(\PerStreamTokenRate\) tokens per second and transfer one full vector per token to a host sampler, the logit payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes per second. Batching transfers can reduce the number of transfer operations, but not that payload under these assumptions.
Sampling on the accelerator permits an interface that transfers only the selected token identifier. If each identifier occupies \(\TokenIdentifierSize\) bytes, its payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate \TokenIdentifierSize\), giving a payload ratio of \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize/\TokenIdentifierSize\). Neither expression counts protocol framing, requested log probabilities, or synchronization. Those costs must be measured on the actual path before choosing a placement. The calculation concerns an internal serving interface, not the application response format. A service may decode and buffer tokens into response chunks whose boundaries need not match tokens; The Invocation Contract specifies how the runtime handles that response.



A grammar-constrained decoder needs the legal tokens for its current parser state at every step (Grammar-Guided Decoding). With one bit per vocabulary entry, a dense mask occupies \(\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes. If the constraint has a finite-state representation with state set \(\AutomatonStateSet\), a byte-aligned dense table needs \(|\AutomatonStateSet|\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes, excluding transitions and metadata. This formula lets us compare a proposed vocabulary and state count with the memory budget without assuming that every grammar has a small finite-state representation.
Whether the table fits and remains resident in on-chip cache depends on the accelerator and competing working sets. Precomputation permits lookup and filtering during sampling, but table size alone establishes neither the lookup latency nor a required device placement.
A host-mediated implementation may instead transfer the selected token to a host process, advance its grammar state, and return the next mask before sampling continues. The cost depends on the implementation and on how much work overlaps model evaluation. Recursive grammars require additional parser state, while compressed structures and precomputation can reduce masking work. The legal-token mask must be available when selection uses it. When Constrained Decoding Pays for Itself considers when constraining is worth its cost. Finite-state constrained decoding gives the masking argument, whose complete-output guarantee requires reaching an accepting state under the specified grammar and decoder assumptions. An interrupted legal prefix need not parse as a complete object.



Because single-stream decoding reads every target-model weight to emit one token, a smaller draft model can propose \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) candidate tokens in serial so the target model verifies all \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) in a single weight read. Exact speculative sampling preserves the specified target distribution while checking those draft positions in one target-model pass (Leviathan et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2023). A draft distribution \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) proposes \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) tokens \(\DraftCandidateToken_1, \dots, \DraftCandidateToken_k\) autoregressively. The target computes the distributions needed to verify them and to sample after the full draft. Both \(\TargetSamplingDistribution\) and \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) below are normalized distributions at the same prefix after their sampling transformations, including any grammar masks. Scanning left to right, candidate \(\DraftCandidateToken_j\) is accepted with probability

Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning 202: 19274–86.

Chen, C., S. Borgeaud, G. Irving, J.-B. Lespiau, L. Sifre, and J. Jumper. 2023. “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.01318.
\[\DraftPositionAcceptanceProbability = \min\left(1, \frac{\TargetSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}{\DraftSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}\right) \tag{6}\]
At the first rejection, the remaining drafts are discarded and one replacement token is drawn from the normalized residual distribution
\[\ResidualSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) = \frac{\max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken)\right)}{\sum_{\NormalizerTokenIndex \in \TokenVocabulary} \max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex)\right)} \tag{7}\]
If every draft is accepted, the sampler draws one bonus token from the target distribution after the full draft. Otherwise, equation 7 applies at the first rejected position; its denominator is positive when rejection has positive probability. Together with equation 6, this rule preserves the target sequence distribution under exact sampling and consistent prefix state. It does not promise the same sample for the same random seed. Termination or an output limit may shorten an iteration that otherwise emits between one and \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount+1\) tokens.
Weight reuse in equation 5 explains why verification can cost less than separate target passes. Actual benefit depends on draft cost, acceptance, attention traffic, batch composition, and verification overhead. Those terms can erase the saving; the weight-only threshold is not a speedup guarantee. When speculative decoding pays off compares the resulting work and latency at the trajectory boundary.




For the full-attention decoder considered here, generation uses keys and values associated with earlier token positions. The serving system caches those derived vectors rather than recomputing them at each step. Autoregressive Generation introduces this reuse within a call; the storage estimate here follows from the model’s geometry and retained sequence length.


Every token appended to an agent’s working context adds a fixed slice of key and value vectors to accelerator memory across every transformer layer. For a decoder with \(\LayerCount\) layers, \(\KvHeadCount\) key-value heads per layer, head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), and \(\KvElementStorageSize\) bytes per stored element, each token stores one key vector and one value vector per layer and key-value head:
\[\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount \cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \KvElementStorageSize \tag{8}\]
and a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens occupies
\[\KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
For the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80, \(\KvHeadCount\) = 8, \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) = 128, and 16-bit storage, \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) = 327,680 bytes, so a 32,768-token context occupies about 10.7 GB. The Footprint of Retained Attention State turns this into the number of trajectories one node can hold.



The number of key-value heads is a design choice that changes \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) directly. Multi-head attention gives every query head its own keys and values. Multi-query attention shares one key-value head across all query heads (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention sits between them by sharing each key-value head across a group of query heads (Ainslie et al. 2023). Holding the reference model’s layer count and head dimension fixed shows how sharing key-value heads scales both the per-token payload and a long trajectory’s footprint (table 2).

Shazeer, Noam. 2019. “Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head Is All You Need.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1911.02150.

Ainslie, Joshua, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebr’on, and Sumit Sanghai. 2023. “GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).

Storing each key and value element at 8 rather than 16 bits halves the element payload, to 163,840 bytes per token for the grouped design, before scale, metadata, or layout overhead. Lower precision and selective removal of entries require task-quality and implementation validation. The remaining cache alone does not recover a discarded entry, although retained inputs and compatible configuration may permit recomputation. These storage approximations are distinct from changing the model architecture (The Footprint of Retained Attention State).



Memory occupancy depends on how much is held and for how long. A trajectory whose attention state stays resident through a tool wait of length \(\ExternalWait\) occupies
\[\MemoryHoldDuringWait = \KvCacheMemory \cdot \ExternalWait\]
byte-seconds while generating nothing. When a tool wait exceeds the active generation interval and holds the same footprint, idle occupancy exceeds active occupancy. The relevant inputs are the actual retained bytes and their holding interval. The retain, evict, recompute, or offload decision of Paused-State Policies is therefore a per-wait decision rather than a fixed property of agents.



Reserving a contiguous region for each trajectory’s maximum context leaves unused capacity when its retained length is below that cap. Paged storage divides a pool into interchangeable fixed blocks of \(\KvBlockSize\) tokens and maps each trajectory’s positions to blocks through a table (Kwon et al. 2023). Allocation on demand removes variable-extent external fragmentation within that pool; it does not eliminate metadata, temporary allocations, or unused final-block slots. If sequence lengths have uniformly distributed remainders modulo \(\KvBlockSize\), the mean unused tail payload is

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{waste}] \approx \frac{\KvBlockSize - 1}{2} \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
per sequence. Without that distributional assumption, the unconditional bound is at most \(\KvBlockSize - 1\) unused token slots in a final block. Compatible blocks can also be shared, allowing branches and requests with a common prefix to use one physical copy under the serving system’s ownership rules (Paged KV Allocation).




An agent can remain live while it consumes no accelerator execution time. A retained cache, sandbox lease, and harness record can each span a different interval of that trajectory. Capacity estimates therefore begin by choosing the resource and its acquisition-to-release boundary. Little’s law relates average occupancy to that boundary; a separate queueing model estimates waiting under stated arrival and service assumptions.


A server batches decode steps from many trajectories (equation 5). In a fixed-membership batch, finished requests cannot be replaced until the batch drains, although their results need not be withheld. Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries (Yu et al. 2022). A returning trajectory can enter a later iteration when memory, token budgets, and scheduling policy permit; a released slot does not promise admission on the immediately following step.

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.
Batch slots are not independent servers. Their occupants share weight reads, arithmetic, memory bandwidth, and iteration time, so one request can change another’s service rate. Little’s law still applies to a stable measured boundary, but the number of slots cannot be substituted for the number of independent servers in a queueing formula. Predicting delay requires a model or measurements that capture the batching policy and workload mix.



Suppose an agent trajectory spends 20 s waiting on a sandbox or database tool for every 4 s of model execution. Then six times as many trajectories sit alive in the system as are actively running on accelerators. For a stable system with well-defined finite long-run averages, the mean number of items inside a boundary equals their entry rate times their mean time inside that same boundary (Little 1961):

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.
\[\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \tag{9}\]
A trajectory of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns spends each turn in a model call and then in a tool, so its trajectory duration is
\[\TrajectoryDuration = \sum_{t=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1} \left( \ModelTime^{(t)} + \ToolTime^{(t)} \right)\]
under the simplifying assumption that model calls and tool operations run sequentially, with no additional approval, queueing, or runtime delay. As a worked case, let trajectories start at 2 per second, each running 15 turns of 4 s of model time and 20 s of tool time. Each lives 360 s, about 6 minutes, so equation 9, in its trajectory form \(\ConcurrentTrajectories = \TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\), gives 720 live trajectories. Only 17 percent of each trajectory’s time is spent in a model call, so on average 120 of them are calling the model at any moment.
The gap between those two numbers measures the effect of holding state through tool waits in this workload. If every live trajectory keeps a 32,768-token context resident, the attention state totals about 7.7 TB, about 15 nodes’ worth of the reference pool of section 1.5. Holding the same footprint only during the stipulated model-call intervals gives about 2.4 nodes’ worth. This worked case assumes an unchanged context footprint and no extra waiting, so its averages compare two retention policies rather than determining peak provisioning or proving that the serving system can sustain the offered rate. Reloading or recomputing on resumption adds time and work omitted from this comparison, and recomputing those intervals may change the averages; Paused-State Policies develops that policy choice.
Harness records and sandbox leases require their own acquisition rates and holding times, not the whole trajectory lifetime by default. If footprints vary, average memory occupancy follows the byte-time held by each arrival, rather than an unqualified product of mean footprint and mean lifetime. Headroom and admission additionally require variability, reclamation behavior, and resource-specific limits (Capacity for Trajectories, Sandbox Pools and Reset).



A single-server queue isolates how variability and load contribute to waiting. Consider first-come, first-served service with independent, identically distributed interarrival times, independent, identically distributed service times, independence between the two sequences, finite variances, and utilization \(\ServingUtilization < 1\). Let \(\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\) be mean service time and \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) and \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) the squared coefficients of variation of interarrival and service times. Kingman’s heavy-traffic result motivates the following finite-load approximation to mean waiting time; it is not an identity or a tail bound.
\[\QueueWaitTime \approx \frac{\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2 + \QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2}{2} \cdot \frac{\ServingUtilization}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\]
With interarrival variability \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) = 2 and service variability \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) = 1, the variability factor is 1.5. Substitution gives approximate waits of 1.5, 3.5, and 13.5 service times at 50, 70, and 90 percent utilization. These are selected comparison points, not a universal utilization knee or an operating recommendation.
Batching, correlated fan-out, retries, and state-dependent service rates can violate the model. Infinite service-time variance also invalidates the finite-variance calculation. The derivation and its limits follow the single-server heavy-traffic analysis of Boon et al. (2023); multiple-server pools need a separately justified model. Measured deadline compliance, workload mix, and admission policy determine usable capacity. Heavy-tailed queueing theory distinguishes mean waiting from tail behavior.

Boon, Marko A. A., Augustus J. E. M. Janssen, and Johan S. H. van Leeuwaarden. 2023. “Heavy-Traffic Single-Server Queues and the Transform Method.” Indagationes Mathematicae 34 (5): 1014–37. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indag.2023.02.004.



Even when a multi-GPU node has enough compute to batch dozens of decode streams, high-bandwidth memory fills up as soon as the resident trajectories’ contexts exceed the KV pool. For a server with memory \(\NodeHbmCapacity\), weights of \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes (16-bit here, whereas the time floors assume 8-bit weights), and a runtime reserve \(\RuntimeReserveMemory\), the memory left for attention state is
\[\KvPoolMemory = \NodeHbmCapacity - \Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize - \RuntimeReserveMemory \tag{10}\]
and a mean-footprint estimate for contexts of average length \(\MeanContextLength\) is
\[\MaxResidentContextCount = \left\lfloor \frac{\KvPoolMemory}{\MeanContextLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken} \right\rfloor \tag{11}\]
An average footprint does not guarantee that a particular set of requests fits. For the reference node and equal-length unshared contexts, equation 10 leaves 526.0 GB and equation 11 gives 48 resident contexts at 32,768 tokens, before allocator overhead and additional headroom. This is the payload bound derived in The Footprint of Retained Attention State, not an admission or throughput guarantee. When a new allocation cannot fit, the service may queue or reject work, reclaim dormant state, or move or drop eligible state.
A restricted comparison estimates reconstruction of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens by the linear weight-work term \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength/\PeakRate\) and reload by \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken / \HostLinkBandwidth\). Both estimates assume the stated sustained compute and transfer rates. The comparison omits the attention term of equation 4, queueing, allocation, and other overhead. Within that model alone, reconstruction has the smaller estimated duration when
\[\frac{2 \Parameters}{\PeakRate} < \frac{\KvCacheBytesPerToken}{\HostLinkBandwidth}\]
The cancellation of context length follows from those two linear estimates, not from a general property of serving latency. The pause policy in Paused-State Policies additionally considers uniquely reclaimable state, competing demand, resumption likelihood, host and link resources, and the permitted resume delay.




The worked estimates use the MLSysIM entries Models.Language.Llama3_70B, Hardware.Cloud.H100, and Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100. These identify a reference configuration, not a current-product recommendation. Auditing or substituting those estimates requires separating the registry-backed model and hardware inputs from the local precision and reserve assumptions (table 3). The ratio of equation 3 isolates weight reuse; equation 8 sizes the attention payload.
The two calculations use different placement boundaries. Per-token floors use one accelerator’s compute rate and bandwidth with 8-bit weights. The memory pool, by contrast, aggregates 8 accelerators, totaling 687.2 GB, and subtracts one 16-bit model copy and a node-wide reserve. Because that pool estimate assumes a feasible sharding arrangement without counting communication time or per-device imbalance, multiplying memory capacity does not establish an equivalent latency speedup. Memory quantities below use decimal GB consistently with the pool arithmetic, rather than the accelerator’s branded capacity label.

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
Prompt processing can reuse a model’s weights across many token positions, whereas unbatched generation uses those weights for one new position at a time. That difference can make prefill arithmetic-bound and decode bandwidth-bound. Neither regime follows from the phase name alone. Prompt length, batching, attention traffic, and the serving implementation determine which resource limits an actual call. A weight-only estimate isolates the reuse effect before adding those complications.
A model call processes the uncached prompt during prefill and generates new tokens during decode. Both phases use the same weights, but the reference calculation yields a ratio of about 295 between the unbatched weight-transfer floor per output token and the arithmetic floor per prompt token. We compare these conditional floors to explain the bandwidth constraint (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-memory-bandwidth-decoding}\)), not to predict the ratio of measured call latencies or token prices.


Adding more floating-point units to an accelerator does not speed up single-stream token generation when the chip spends most of each step waiting for weight bytes to arrive from high-bandwidth memory. An accelerator has two limits, the rate \(\PeakRate\) at which it performs arithmetic (operations per second) and the rate \(\Bandwidth\) at which its memory delivers data (bytes per second). A computation’s arithmetic intensity \(\ArithmeticIntensity\) is the number of operations it performs per byte it moves. The roofline model (Williams et al. 2009) gives a performance ceiling \(\AttainableComputeRate\) from whichever limit binds first:

Williams, Samuel, Andrew Waterman, and David Patterson. 2009. “Roofline: An Insightful Visual Performance Model for Multicore Architectures.” Communications of the ACM 52 (4): 65–76. https://doi.org/10.1145/1498765.1498785.
\[\AttainableComputeRate = \min\left( \PeakRate, \; \ArithmeticIntensity \cdot \Bandwidth \right)\]
The two ceilings meet at the ridge point \(\RooflineRidgePoint = \PeakRate / \Bandwidth\). Below the ridge, bandwidth supplies the lower ceiling; above it, arithmetic supplies the lower ceiling. Actual performance can fall below either ceiling because of implementation and scheduling overhead. For the reference accelerator at 8-bit precision, \(\PeakRate\) = 1,979 trillion operations per second and \(\Bandwidth\) = 3.35 TB/s, so \(\RooflineRidgePoint \approx\) 591 operations per byte.



A dense transformer with \(\Parameters\) active parameters performs about \(2\Parameters\) weight-related operations per token, one multiply and one add per weight. Its weight payload is \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes, where \(\WeightElementStorageSize\) is bytes per parameter. The approximation counts this payload once per pass; prefill and decode differ in how many tokens share that read. Sparse activation and weight reuse from another cache level require a different traffic count.
In the weight-only model, prefill shares each weight read across \(\SequenceLength\) prompt positions, giving intensity \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength / (\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize) = 2\SequenceLength/\WeightElementStorageSize\). When that intensity exceeds the ridge and arithmetic approaches the stated peak, the per-token time approaches the following floor. Small prompts, kernel tiling, attention, and additional memory traffic can invalidate those assumptions.
\[\PerTokenPrefillTime \approx \frac{2\Parameters}{\PeakRate} \tag{1}\]
Ordinary decode for one stream generates one token per pass, with each token depending on the preceding prefix. If the weights must be read from the modeled memory on every pass, the weight-only intensity is \(2/\WeightElementStorageSize\), or 2 operations per byte at 8-bit precision, about 0.34 percent of the ridge. Streaming those weights imposes a time floor even before attention-state traffic and overhead:
\[\PerTokenDecodeTime \ge \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth} \tag{2}\]
For the reference model, with \(\Parameters\) = 70.6 billion parameters at 8-bit precision, equation 2 gives a decode floor of 21.1 ms per output token, and equation 1 gives about 71 µs per prompt token. In the following comparison only, the time symbols denote these weight-only estimates rather than observed times:
\[\frac{\PerTokenDecodeTime}{\PerTokenPrefillTime} = \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize / \Bandwidth}{2\Parameters / \PeakRate} = \frac{\PeakRate \, \WeightElementStorageSize}{2 \Bandwidth} = \frac{\WeightElementStorageSize}{2} \, \RooflineRidgePoint \tag{3}\]
which is 295 for the reference configuration. Model size cancels in this approximation because both estimates count the same dense-model weights. The result assumes weight-dominated unbatched decode, peak-rate prefill, and negligible attention and serving overhead; it is not a measured ratio shared by every model on the accelerator. Within that model, the same number gives the number of tokens per pass at which arithmetic time meets weight-transfer time, a threshold used in the batching and speculative-decoding estimates below.
The estimate separates two quantities an agent engineer can influence. Shorter output reduces generation work, and avoiding repeated processing of an unchanged input prefix reduces prefill work. Which change matters more depends on the request lengths, serving configuration, and measurement boundary; token counts alone do not determine a service bill. The Cost of a Model Call prices a bounded example under explicit assumptions. A localized edit illustrates the output-side choice by omitting unchanged file contents, without implying that every compact serialization improves task success.



Attention adds prefill work that grows with the context itself, which the weight-only floor in equation 1 omits. The token at position \(\CausalTokenPosition\) compares its query with \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier keys and combines \(\CausalTokenPosition\) earlier values, about \(4 \LayerCount d \CausalTokenPosition\) operations for a model with \(\LayerCount\) layers and width \(\HiddenDimension\). Summed over a causal prefill of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens, attention adds about \(2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2\) operations to the \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength\) of the weights, so
\[\PrefillTime(\SequenceLength) \approx \frac{2\Parameters \SequenceLength + 2 \LayerCount d \SequenceLength^2}{\PeakRate} \tag{4}\]
The quadratic term equals the linear one at \(\SequenceLength^* = \Parameters / (\LayerCount \HiddenDimension)\), about 108,000 tokens for the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80 and \(\HiddenDimension\) = 8,192. At 32,768 tokens, attention adds about 30 percent to the prefill arithmetic, and beyond \(\SequenceLength^*\) it dominates. Under this fixed-throughput approximation, prefill time grows faster than linearly with length. Observed time to first token also depends on queueing, reuse, and the serving schedule. The logical selection problem in Usable Working Context determines which information the request needs; the estimate here prices the processing work without establishing an optimal context length or task-quality threshold.



A server can batch decode steps from several trajectories. If one weight read serves \(\BatchSize\) streams, the step produces one token for each stream. Ignoring the attention state each stream also reads, the time of one step is
\[\BatchedDecodeStepTime(\BatchSize) \approx \max\left( \frac{\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize}{\Bandwidth}, \; \frac{2 \Parameters \BatchSize}{\PeakRate} \right) \tag{5}\]
and the step stays at the memory-bound floor until \(\BatchSize\) reaches \(\PeakRate\,\WeightElementStorageSize / 2\Bandwidth\), the ratio of equation 3. Within this weight-only approximation, adding streams up to that threshold leaves step time unchanged, while step time divided by the number of generated tokens falls as \(1/\BatchSize\) toward \(2\Parameters/\PeakRate\). This is amortized serving time, not the latency of one stream or the price charged by a service. Repeated input adds prefill work when the prefix cannot be reused, but the bill also depends on utilization and the service’s accounting rules.
A trajectory cannot batch a future call whose input depends on an observation it has not received. Its current call can nevertheless share a physical serving batch with calls from other trajectories. That batching can change queueing and per-step latency; a dependent client stream is not evidence that the server runs at batch size one. The weight-only estimate also omits attention-state traffic. Each stream reads its own keys and values, approximately \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\) bytes for a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens (section 1.3). Long contexts can therefore bind bandwidth or capacity before the arithmetic threshold in equation 5 is reached. Section 1.4 relates resident state to the number of live trajectories.



A large admitted prefill can delay decode work sharing its execution resources. Chunked prefill divides that work into bounded token slices that the scheduler can interleave or co-schedule with decodes (Agrawal et al. 2024). The token budget limits admitted token positions, not elapsed iteration time; realized gaps and prompt-completion time depend on context lengths, batching, resource contention, and implementation overhead. The weight-only estimate in equation 5 explains one opportunity for amortization, not a latency guarantee. Chunked Prefill Scheduling develops the policy trade-off.

Agrawal, Amey, Nitin Kedia, Ashish Panwar, Jayashree Mohan, Nipun Kwatra, Bhargav S. Gulavani, Alexey Tumanov, and Ramachandran Ramjee. 2024. “Taming Throughput-Latency Tradeoff in LLM Inference with Sarathi-Serve.” 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 24), 117–34.

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
Token selection, optional grammar constraints, and speculative verification add work beyond the model’s forward pass. Their placement determines which data crosses a device boundary and which dependencies remain on the generation path. The formulas below separate payload sizes from synchronization and computation costs; a small payload alone does not establish a low latency.


Copying a 128,000-entry floating-point logit vector across a host bus on every decode step of a multi-stream batch moves tens of megabytes per second before a single token is chosen. At each step the model produces one logit per vocabulary entry. Let \(|\TokenVocabulary|\) be the vocabulary size and \(\LogitStorageSize\) the bytes stored per logit. One vector occupies \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes. If \(\BatchSize\) streams each emit \(\PerStreamTokenRate\) tokens per second and transfer one full vector per token to a host sampler, the logit payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize\) bytes per second. Batching transfers can reduce the number of transfer operations, but not that payload under these assumptions.
Sampling on the accelerator permits an interface that transfers only the selected token identifier. If each identifier occupies \(\TokenIdentifierSize\) bytes, its payload rate is \(\BatchSize \PerStreamTokenRate \TokenIdentifierSize\), giving a payload ratio of \(|\TokenVocabulary|\LogitStorageSize/\TokenIdentifierSize\). Neither expression counts protocol framing, requested log probabilities, or synchronization. Those costs must be measured on the actual path before choosing a placement. The calculation concerns an internal serving interface, not the application response format. A service may decode and buffer tokens into response chunks whose boundaries need not match tokens; The Invocation Contract specifies how the runtime handles that response.



A grammar-constrained decoder needs the legal tokens for its current parser state at every step (Grammar-Guided Decoding). With one bit per vocabulary entry, a dense mask occupies \(\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes. If the constraint has a finite-state representation with state set \(\AutomatonStateSet\), a byte-aligned dense table needs \(|\AutomatonStateSet|\lceil |\TokenVocabulary|/8 \rceil\) bytes, excluding transitions and metadata. This formula lets us compare a proposed vocabulary and state count with the memory budget without assuming that every grammar has a small finite-state representation.
Whether the table fits and remains resident in on-chip cache depends on the accelerator and competing working sets. Precomputation permits lookup and filtering during sampling, but table size alone establishes neither the lookup latency nor a required device placement.
A host-mediated implementation may instead transfer the selected token to a host process, advance its grammar state, and return the next mask before sampling continues. The cost depends on the implementation and on how much work overlaps model evaluation. Recursive grammars require additional parser state, while compressed structures and precomputation can reduce masking work. The legal-token mask must be available when selection uses it. When Constrained Decoding Pays for Itself considers when constraining is worth its cost. Finite-state constrained decoding gives the masking argument, whose complete-output guarantee requires reaching an accepting state under the specified grammar and decoder assumptions. An interrupted legal prefix need not parse as a complete object.



Because single-stream decoding reads every target-model weight to emit one token, a smaller draft model can propose \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) candidate tokens in serial so the target model verifies all \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) in a single weight read. Exact speculative sampling preserves the specified target distribution while checking those draft positions in one target-model pass (Leviathan et al. 2023; Chen et al. 2023). A draft distribution \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) proposes \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount\) tokens \(\DraftCandidateToken_1, \dots, \DraftCandidateToken_k\) autoregressively. The target computes the distributions needed to verify them and to sample after the full draft. Both \(\TargetSamplingDistribution\) and \(\DraftSamplingDistribution\) below are normalized distributions at the same prefix after their sampling transformations, including any grammar masks. Scanning left to right, candidate \(\DraftCandidateToken_j\) is accepted with probability

Leviathan, Yaniv, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. 2023. “Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding.” Proceedings of the 40th International Conference on Machine Learning 202: 19274–86.

Chen, C., S. Borgeaud, G. Irving, J.-B. Lespiau, L. Sifre, and J. Jumper. 2023. “Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:2302.01318.
\[\DraftPositionAcceptanceProbability = \min\left(1, \frac{\TargetSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}{\DraftSamplingDistribution(\DraftCandidateToken_j \mid \cdot)}\right) \tag{6}\]
At the first rejection, the remaining drafts are discarded and one replacement token is drawn from the normalized residual distribution
\[\ResidualSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) = \frac{\max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\VocabularyToken)\right)}{\sum_{\NormalizerTokenIndex \in \TokenVocabulary} \max\left(0,\; \TargetSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex) - \DraftSamplingDistribution(\NormalizerTokenIndex)\right)} \tag{7}\]
If every draft is accepted, the sampler draws one bonus token from the target distribution after the full draft. Otherwise, equation 7 applies at the first rejected position; its denominator is positive when rejection has positive probability. Together with equation 6, this rule preserves the target sequence distribution under exact sampling and consistent prefix state. It does not promise the same sample for the same random seed. Termination or an output limit may shorten an iteration that otherwise emits between one and \(\SpeculativeDraftTokenCount+1\) tokens.
Weight reuse in equation 5 explains why verification can cost less than separate target passes. Actual benefit depends on draft cost, acceptance, attention traffic, batch composition, and verification overhead. Those terms can erase the saving; the weight-only threshold is not a speedup guarantee. When speculative decoding pays off compares the resulting work and latency at the trajectory boundary.

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
For the full-attention decoder considered here, generation uses keys and values associated with earlier token positions. The serving system caches those derived vectors rather than recomputing them at each step. Autoregressive Generation introduces this reuse within a call; the storage estimate here follows from the model’s geometry and retained sequence length.


Every token appended to an agent’s working context adds a fixed slice of key and value vectors to accelerator memory across every transformer layer. For a decoder with \(\LayerCount\) layers, \(\KvHeadCount\) key-value heads per layer, head dimension \(\AttentionHeadDimension\), and \(\KvElementStorageSize\) bytes per stored element, each token stores one key vector and one value vector per layer and key-value head:
\[\KvCacheBytesPerToken = 2 \cdot \LayerCount \cdot \KvHeadCount \cdot \AttentionHeadDimension \cdot \KvElementStorageSize \tag{8}\]
and a context of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens occupies
\[\KvCacheMemory = \SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
For the reference model, with \(\LayerCount\) = 80, \(\KvHeadCount\) = 8, \(\AttentionHeadDimension\) = 128, and 16-bit storage, \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) = 327,680 bytes, so a 32,768-token context occupies about 10.7 GB. The Footprint of Retained Attention State turns this into the number of trajectories one node can hold.



The number of key-value heads is a design choice that changes \(\KvCacheBytesPerToken\) directly. Multi-head attention gives every query head its own keys and values. Multi-query attention shares one key-value head across all query heads (Shazeer 2019). Grouped-query attention sits between them by sharing each key-value head across a group of query heads (Ainslie et al. 2023). Holding the reference model’s layer count and head dimension fixed shows how sharing key-value heads scales both the per-token payload and a long trajectory’s footprint (table 2).

Shazeer, Noam. 2019. “Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head Is All You Need.” arXiv Preprint arXiv:1911.02150.

Ainslie, Joshua, James Lee-Thorp, Michiel de Jong, Yury Zemlyanskiy, Federico Lebr’on, and Sumit Sanghai. 2023. “GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints.” Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP).

Storing each key and value element at 8 rather than 16 bits halves the element payload, to 163,840 bytes per token for the grouped design, before scale, metadata, or layout overhead. Lower precision and selective removal of entries require task-quality and implementation validation. The remaining cache alone does not recover a discarded entry, although retained inputs and compatible configuration may permit recomputation. These storage approximations are distinct from changing the model architecture (The Footprint of Retained Attention State).



Memory occupancy depends on how much is held and for how long. A trajectory whose attention state stays resident through a tool wait of length \(\ExternalWait\) occupies
\[\MemoryHoldDuringWait = \KvCacheMemory \cdot \ExternalWait\]
byte-seconds while generating nothing. When a tool wait exceeds the active generation interval and holds the same footprint, idle occupancy exceeds active occupancy. The relevant inputs are the actual retained bytes and their holding interval. The retain, evict, recompute, or offload decision of Paused-State Policies is therefore a per-wait decision rather than a fixed property of agents.



Reserving a contiguous region for each trajectory’s maximum context leaves unused capacity when its retained length is below that cap. Paged storage divides a pool into interchangeable fixed blocks of \(\KvBlockSize\) tokens and maps each trajectory’s positions to blocks through a table (Kwon et al. 2023). Allocation on demand removes variable-extent external fragmentation within that pool; it does not eliminate metadata, temporary allocations, or unused final-block slots. If sequence lengths have uniformly distributed remainders modulo \(\KvBlockSize\), the mean unused tail payload is

Kwon, Woosuk, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, and Ion Stoica. 2023. “Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention.” Proceedings of the 29th Symposium on Operating Systems Principles, 611–26. https://doi.org/10.1145/3600006.3613165.
\[\mathbb{E}[\text{waste}] \approx \frac{\KvBlockSize - 1}{2} \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken\]
per sequence. Without that distributional assumption, the unconditional bound is at most \(\KvBlockSize - 1\) unused token slots in a final block. Compatible blocks can also be shared, allowing branches and requests with a common prefix to use one physical copy under the serving system’s ownership rules (Paged KV Allocation).

title: Inference Cost Foundations
text:
An agent can remain live while it consumes no accelerator execution time. A retained cache, sandbox lease, and harness record can each span a different interval of that trajectory. Capacity estimates therefore begin by choosing the resource and its acquisition-to-release boundary. Little’s law relates average occupancy to that boundary; a separate queueing model estimates waiting under stated arrival and service assumptions.


A server batches decode steps from many trajectories (equation 5). In a fixed-membership batch, finished requests cannot be replaced until the batch drains, although their results need not be withheld. Continuous batching admits and retires requests at iteration boundaries (Yu et al. 2022). A returning trajectory can enter a later iteration when memory, token budgets, and scheduling policy permit; a released slot does not promise admission on the immediately following step.

Yu, Gyeong-In, Joo Seong Jeong, Geon-Woo Kim, Soojeong Kim, and Byung-Gon Chun. 2022. “Orca: A Distributed Serving System for Transformer-Based Generative Models.” 16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI 22), 521–38.
Batch slots are not independent servers. Their occupants share weight reads, arithmetic, memory bandwidth, and iteration time, so one request can change another’s service rate. Little’s law still applies to a stable measured boundary, but the number of slots cannot be substituted for the number of independent servers in a queueing formula. Predicting delay requires a model or measurements that capture the batching policy and workload mix.



Suppose an agent trajectory spends 20 s waiting on a sandbox or database tool for every 4 s of model execution. Then six times as many trajectories sit alive in the system as are actively running on accelerators. For a stable system with well-defined finite long-run averages, the mean number of items inside a boundary equals their entry rate times their mean time inside that same boundary (Little 1961):

Little, John D. C. 1961. “A Proof for the Queuing Formula: \(L = \lambda W\).” Operations Research 9 (3): 383–87. https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383.
\[\RequestConcurrency = \ArrivalRate \cdot \RequestTimeInSystem \tag{9}\]
A trajectory of \(\TurnHorizon\) turns spends each turn in a model call and then in a tool, so its trajectory duration is
\[\TrajectoryDuration = \sum_{t=0}^{\TurnHorizon-1} \left( \ModelTime^{(t)} + \ToolTime^{(t)} \right)\]
under the simplifying assumption that model calls and tool operations run sequentially, with no additional approval, queueing, or runtime delay. As a worked case, let trajectories start at 2 per second, each running 15 turns of 4 s of model time and 20 s of tool time. Each lives 360 s, about 6 minutes, so equation 9, in its trajectory form \(\ConcurrentTrajectories = \TrajectoryAdmissionRate\,\mathbb{E}[\TrajectoryDuration]\), gives 720 live trajectories. Only 17 percent of each trajectory’s time is spent in a model call, so on average 120 of them are calling the model at any moment.
The gap between those two numbers measures the effect of holding state through tool waits in this workload. If every live trajectory keeps a 32,768-token context resident, the attention state totals about 7.7 TB, about 15 nodes’ worth of the reference pool of section 1.5. Holding the same footprint only during the stipulated model-call intervals gives about 2.4 nodes’ worth. This worked case assumes an unchanged context footprint and no extra waiting, so its averages compare two retention policies rather than determining peak provisioning or proving that the serving system can sustain the offered rate. Reloading or recomputing on resumption adds time and work omitted from this comparison, and recomputing those intervals may change the averages; Paused-State Policies develops that policy choice.
Harness records and sandbox leases require their own acquisition rates and holding times, not the whole trajectory lifetime by default. If footprints vary, average memory occupancy follows the byte-time held by each arrival, rather than an unqualified product of mean footprint and mean lifetime. Headroom and admission additionally require variability, reclamation behavior, and resource-specific limits (Capacity for Trajectories, Sandbox Pools and Reset).



A single-server queue isolates how variability and load contribute to waiting. Consider first-come, first-served service with independent, identically distributed interarrival times, independent, identically distributed service times, independence between the two sequences, finite variances, and utilization \(\ServingUtilization < 1\). Let \(\mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\) be mean service time and \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) and \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) the squared coefficients of variation of interarrival and service times. Kingman’s heavy-traffic result motivates the following finite-load approximation to mean waiting time; it is not an identity or a tail bound.
\[\QueueWaitTime \approx \frac{\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2 + \QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2}{2} \cdot \frac{\ServingUtilization}{1 - \ServingUtilization} \cdot \mathbb{E}[\RequestServiceTime]\]
With interarrival variability \(\InterarrivalVariationCoefficient^2\) = 2 and service variability \(\QueueServiceVariationCoefficient^2\) = 1, the variability factor is 1.5. Substitution gives approximate waits of 1.5, 3.5, and 13.5 service times at 50, 70, and 90 percent utilization. These are selected comparison points, not a universal utilization knee or an operating recommendation.
Batching, correlated fan-out, retries, and state-dependent service rates can violate the model. Infinite service-time variance also invalidates the finite-variance calculation. The derivation and its limits follow the single-server heavy-traffic analysis of Boon et al. (2023); multiple-server pools need a separately justified model. Measured deadline compliance, workload mix, and admission policy determine usable capacity. Heavy-tailed queueing theory distinguishes mean waiting from tail behavior.

Boon, Marko A. A., Augustus J. E. M. Janssen, and Johan S. H. van Leeuwaarden. 2023. “Heavy-Traffic Single-Server Queues and the Transform Method.” Indagationes Mathematicae 34 (5): 1014–37. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.indag.2023.02.004.



Even when a multi-GPU node has enough compute to batch dozens of decode streams, high-bandwidth memory fills up as soon as the resident trajectories’ contexts exceed the KV pool. For a server with memory \(\NodeHbmCapacity\), weights of \(\Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize\) bytes (16-bit here, whereas the time floors assume 8-bit weights), and a runtime reserve \(\RuntimeReserveMemory\), the memory left for attention state is
\[\KvPoolMemory = \NodeHbmCapacity - \Parameters\,\WeightElementStorageSize - \RuntimeReserveMemory \tag{10}\]
and a mean-footprint estimate for contexts of average length \(\MeanContextLength\) is
\[\MaxResidentContextCount = \left\lfloor \frac{\KvPoolMemory}{\MeanContextLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken} \right\rfloor \tag{11}\]
An average footprint does not guarantee that a particular set of requests fits. For the reference node and equal-length unshared contexts, equation 10 leaves 526.0 GB and equation 11 gives 48 resident contexts at 32,768 tokens, before allocator overhead and additional headroom. This is the payload bound derived in The Footprint of Retained Attention State, not an admission or throughput guarantee. When a new allocation cannot fit, the service may queue or reject work, reclaim dormant state, or move or drop eligible state.
A restricted comparison estimates reconstruction of \(\SequenceLength\) tokens by the linear weight-work term \(2\Parameters \SequenceLength/\PeakRate\) and reload by \(\SequenceLength \cdot \KvCacheBytesPerToken / \HostLinkBandwidth\). Both estimates assume the stated sustained compute and transfer rates. The comparison omits the attention term of equation 4, queueing, allocation, and other overhead. Within that model alone, reconstruction has the smaller estimated duration when
\[\frac{2 \Parameters}{\PeakRate} < \frac{\KvCacheBytesPerToken}{\HostLinkBandwidth}\]
The cancellation of context length follows from those two linear estimates, not from a general property of serving latency. The pause policy in Paused-State Policies additionally considers uniquely reclaimable state, competing demand, resumption likelihood, host and link resources, and the permitted resume delay.

text:
The worked estimates use the MLSysIM entries Models.Language.Llama3_70B, Hardware.Cloud.H100, and Systems.Nodes.DGX_H100. These identify a reference configuration, not a current-product recommendation. Auditing or substituting those estimates requires separating the registry-backed model and hardware inputs from the local precision and reserve assumptions (table 3). The ratio of equation 3 isolates weight reuse; equation 8 sizes the attention payload.
The two calculations use different placement boundaries. Per-token floors use one accelerator’s compute rate and bandwidth with 8-bit weights. The memory pool, by contrast, aggregates 8 accelerators, totaling 687.2 GB, and subtracts one 16-bit model copy and a node-wide reserve. Because that pool estimate assumes a feasible sharding arrangement without counting communication time or per-device imbalance, multiplying memory capacity does not establish an equivalent latency speedup. Memory quantities below use decimal GB consistently with the pool arithmetic, rather than the accelerator’s branded capacity label.

title: 1 Reference Architecture
text:
This appendix is a reference for assigning responsibilities across an agentic machine learning system. Its maps connect task requirements to state owners, interfaces, and evidence obligations, so a design review can identify missing ownership without prescribing a particular implementation stack. The chapters teach the mechanisms; this reference helps a reader locate their boundaries and check the assumptions connecting them.


Consult the entry matching the design decision or missing record. Each section names the component or artifact it governs and points back to the chapter where the trade-off is derived:

When a responsibility has no clear owner, section 1.1 maps it to a logical component.
When deciding which mechanisms a task requires, section 1.2 links contract conditions to design obligations.
When an operation crosses component boundaries, section 1.3 traces the records needed at each handoff.
When choosing an execution boundary, section 1.6 collects the compatibility and isolation questions.
When deciding where information lives and who may change it, section 1.5 distinguishes state ownership and reconstruction contracts.
When placing components or investigating a deployment symptom, section 1.12 identifies assumptions and measurements to check.

The maps describe logical responsibilities. One process may implement several rows; distributing a row across services does not remove its ownership requirement.

Apply the rows to operations and retained records, not merely to a task’s largest exposure label. A local patch needs a workspace boundary; publishing it adds source-side authorization and concurrency requirements. Publication does not imply that reversal is safe, available, or equivalent to undoing its consequences. If the task does not permit publication, withholding that capability removes the need to manage that particular effect without removing obligations for local execution and evidence.



A tool-using turn in a crash-recoverable task provides a bounded interface check. Assume that the harness owns admission, the endpoint exposes an operation contract, and the runtime retains the inputs required for its promised recovery. The sequence below follows one admitted model call and one proposed external operation; answer-only turns, parallel calls, and approval waits take different paths.

Admit the turn. The harness considers a READY trajectory, checks current grants and control state, and reserves the proposed bounded liability against actual consumption and existing reservations while preserving finalization resources. Admitted work moves to CALLING_MODEL (Trajectory States).
Assemble the context. The assembler selects applicable source material and observations within the input budget. Record the delivered input or retained artifact references needed by the recovery contract; a hash identifies content but cannot reconstruct missing bytes.
Call the model. The model service receives the call with an output ceiling and a deadline, reuses the cached prefix where it can (Prefix Caching Across Turns), and returns a proposal with a stop reason and token usage (The Invocation Contract). The log records the reply.
Validate and grant. The tool gateway validates the proposal and applies runtime policy to the session, target, operation, and current preconditions. A discovered descriptor does not confer permission (Interoperable Tool Discovery). Calls requiring approval go to the approval gate before dispatch (Approval Gates).
Write intent, then dispatch. The trajectory log makes the intent durable under the declared storage failure domain before dispatch (Durable Intent Before Dispatch). Where the workflow supplies a compensating operation, its recovery plan is recorded as well (The Trajectory Saga Pattern). The gateway dispatches under the task’s enforced grant and execution limits, preserving a logical operation identity where the endpoint supports that retry contract (Capabilities and Credentials, Retrying Uncertain Actions).
Wait without holding more than needed. The harness moves the trajectory to WAITING_TOOL. The serving memory decides whether the trajectory’s attention state stays resident, is evicted and recomputed, or is offloaded for the length of the wait (Paused-State Policies).
Record the outcome and shape the observation. The gateway correlates returning evidence with its call, preserving known results, partial effects, or unresolved status. Late outcomes can matter for reconciliation even when they should not resume the model. The log records this disposition and the bounded observation (Observation Stream Truncation).
Check progress and continue. Recovery compares task-scoped observations with recent history to assess possible nonprogress (Semantic Watchdogs). The harness applies its guarded continuation or finalization decision. Evaluation assesses acceptance under the declared criteria, including any required residual-duty evidence; its final verdict need not be available when finalization begins (The Task Acceptance Contract).

At each handoff, the receiving owner needs an identity, applicable version, and disposition, not merely a text description of the preceding step. Diagnostic spans can correlate observed calls and outcomes, but only the records and artifacts covered by the durability contract support promised recovery. A final acceptance decision can occur after this turn and can require evidence from outside its trace.



An interrupted response needs a different disposition from a complete proposal. The invocation contract therefore identifies the model and call configuration, input format, output limit, status, and available usage evidence (The Invocation Contract). Deadlines and cancellation specify what the client can stop admitting or consuming and what termination the provider confirms. A local timeout does not prove that generation stopped or that its charge is settled. Token usage is one accounting input; task budgets can also constrain money, elapsed time, tool work, and other resources.
Prefix caching is an optional performance facility rather than a correctness requirement. If it is available, record compatibility, sharing, residency, and routing assumptions before relying on its savings. Session affinity can improve reuse but can also concentrate load; a changed prefix can reduce hits without changing the task’s validity. Prefix Caching Across Turns supplies the reuse conditions, while The Size of the Attention State supplies the memory-sizing model. Behavioral suitability still requires task-level evaluation independently of this interface contract.



When a cached summary or workspace edit is mistaken for an authoritative record, later turns act on unverified state because an agent’s information lives across stores with different writers, lifetimes, and validity rules. The architecture must assign a single component owner to each state class (table 3) and distinguish every derived copy from its source (principle \(\ref{pri-vol3-source-authority}\)). The persistent-record roles in Roles of persistent records further distinguish the claims and evidence retained in durable stores.

Three architectural rules follow from the table. First, a trajectory log records the events captured under its durability and retention contract; it does not establish every claim made in a logged response. Second, reconstruction requires retained inputs and a compatible reconstruction procedure. An index can be rebuilt from available sources, but a preference or observation cannot be recovered merely because an agent originally wrote it. Losing its only retained evidence can change later behavior. Third, the model proposes writes through mediated tools; workspace containment and memory admission enforce different boundaries on those operations. The context assembler selects from these records, and the retrieval contract (The Retrieval Contract) governs how durable information re-enters a call, preserving its applicability, provenance, and retrieval limitations.



Validating a tool call’s JSON arguments at the gateway does not stop the executed binary from reading host credentials or opening an unauthorized socket once it starts running. To cover both boundaries, the tool gateway mediates requests and returning evidence while the isolation envelope constrains execution reach. At the request boundary, the gateway validates arguments, applies session policy and action-time checks, dispatches permitted calls, and returns bounded observations; its retry behavior depends on operation semantics and the endpoint’s supported identity, effect, and result contract, since a timeout may remain unresolved and a key alone does not make repetition safe (Tool Calling). Inside the execution boundary, the envelope enforces the implementation’s permitted resource access, credentials, workspace effects, network reach, and resource use (Agent Sandboxes), because neither a grant nor a descriptor enforces those limits merely by naming them.
Envelope choice depends on required interfaces, the threat model, and the configured enforcement boundary. Rather than assigning universal timings or ranking isolation strength by product name, the comparison in table 4 pairs each envelope class with the compatibility and resource questions developed in Envelope selection.
